units.la: QVÆ vero de nonnullis in ea Articulis controversis, hac Transactione communi partium placito statuta sunt, pro perpetua dictæ Pacis declaratione, tam in Iudiciis, quam alibi observanda habebuntur, donec per Dei gratiam de Religione ipsa convenerit, non attenta cuiusvis seu Ecclesiastici seu Politici, intra vel extra Imperium, quocunque tempore interposita contradictione vel protestatione, quæ omnes inanes & nihili, vigore horum declarantur.
units.tr: But as to the several controverted articles, which by this agreement of the parties have been settled, these shall be held to be observed, both in the courts and elsewhere, for the perpetual declaration of the said peace, until by the grace of God agreement is reached concerning religion itself. No account is to be taken of any contradiction or protest entered at any time, by anyone whether ecclesiastical or civil, within or outside the Empire; all of these are declared by virtue of this instrument to be void and of no effect.

units.la: Iterum, §. 17. Utriusque Religionis Magistratus severè & rigorosè prohibeat, ne quisquam publice privatimve concionando, docendo, disputando, scribendo, consulendo, Transactionem Passaviensem, Pacem Religiosam, vel hanc imprimis sive declarationem sive Transactionem uspiam impugnet, dubiam faciat, aut assertiones contrarias inde deducere conetur. Quicquid etiam contrarii hactenus vel editum, vel promulgatum, publicatumve fuerit, irritum esto.
units.tr: Again, §. 17. The magistrate of each religion shall severely and rigorously prohibit anyone, whether publicly or privately, by preaching, teaching, disputing, writing or advising, from attacking the Treaty of Passau, the Religious Peace, or above all this declaration or treaty anywhere, from casting doubt upon it, or from trying to draw contrary assertions from it. Whatever contrary matter has hitherto been published, promulgated or made public shall be null and void.

units.la: Un gratum vobis Nobilissimi Viri, acceptumque futurum sit Pacis & Germaniæ, quod in Academia vestra, vobis inspectantibus, suscepi patrocinium, adversus antiquas Romani Pontificis machinationes, paci & Germanię æque semper infesti, dubitare me non sinit cum acceptabile pacis nomen & argumentum, tum vestrum pro eâ inter omnes conservandâ studium, & perennandâ etiam hac, quæ ut in se quidem optima singulari Dei munere nobis obtigit, ita felix ut sit & sancta, vos cumprimis animitimini. Revera quantum pridem terrori Belgæ fuimus bello, tantum pace nunc cum illis facta, qui suam nobis debent, omnibus prodigio existimus, & miraculum interpretantur ipsi, qui à nobis per convitium miracula identidem effiagitant, hoc se bellorum nostrorum videre auctoramentum. Crevisse Rempublicam nostram fere antequam nata, scripsit sagacis ingenii vir Bentivoglius, quum Papalis nuncius assisteret Archiduci Alberto, & factis hinc inde induciis: sed armis crevit, vel bello potius tius, cui etiam dum maximè florebat vix arma aliquando suppeterent; jam eluctata ex malis suis, & seipsâ superior, periodum attigit, quam, quo optimo post bella munere,coronavit Deus,magnâ pace. Quando populus Romanus, qui prima adversus exteros arma pro libertate corripuit; mox pro finibus; deinde pro sociis, ut hæc elegantissimi rerum Romanarum scriptoris Annæi Flori verba nostra faciam,superato Philippo Macedonum rege,cum ad Isthmicum spectaculum tota Græcia convenisset, per Præconem recitari hæc verba jussisset: S.P. Q.R. omnes urbes quæ sub ditione Philippi regis fuerunt liberas atque immunes esse jubet, & verba primum minus intellecta populo vel credita, perculsis vehementer,quod in talibus fieri consuevit, maximo & inopinato gaudio omnium animis, iterasset Consulis jussu Præco, tantis inde populus cœlum clamoribus complevit, ut aves quæ supervolabant, attonitas paventesque decidisse, ut revera compertum, Plutarchus scribat, qui in ejus etiam inquirit causas; & pro certo constare, Valerius Maximus; facile ut appareret, verba hæc Livii sunt, „nihil omnino, bonorum multitudini gratius,quam libertatem esse. Noverint hoc illo evo Romani, ista in terris sola gens, quæ sua impensa, ac periculo bella gessit pro libertate aliorum; & experta prædicarit in libertatis suæ auctoribus Romanis olim Græcia; hodie nulli sunt, qui edocti primum suo periculo,tum victoriis,jam pace, sciant ista melius Belgis, quibus ita propria libertatis possessio, ut ab illis se suamque naturam ipsa melius nosse, alii ex illorum exemplo eam demum æstimare videantur. Sed nobis quidem illa eo carior, quo duplex, id est, tota obtigit. Nam quum vel animam nostram,
units.tr: Most noble Sirs, you will be pleased and gratified that, under your watchful eye, I have taken up in your Academy the defence of peace and of Germany against the old machinations of the Roman Pontiff, who has always been hostile to peace and to Germany alike. I cannot doubt this, since you are especially devoted both to the peace, which is acceptable to everyone, and to its preservation among all, and to keeping this peace lasting, which, though it is in itself the best of gifts, we have received as a singular gift of God, and which we pray may be happy and holy as well. Indeed, we who were once a terror to the Belgians in war, and who now, with peace made with them, have become a marvel to all, are the very ones who owe their peace to them. Those who constantly demand miracles from us with their insults now interpret it as a miracle that they see this to be the outcome of our wars. The wise-minded Bentivoglio wrote that our Republic had grown almost before it was born, when the Papal nuncio was attending the Archduke Albert and truces were being made back and forth. But it grew by arms, or rather by war, for which, even while it was flourishing most, weapons were scarcely ever available; now, having struggled out of its troubles and risen above itself, it has reached a period which God has crowned, as the best gift after wars, with great peace. When the Roman people, as these are the words of the most elegant writer of Roman history, Annaeus Florus, which I shall use, first took up arms against foreigners for liberty; soon for their borders; then for their allies, after they had defeated Philip, king of the Macedonians, and when all Greece had gathered for the Isthmian games, had ordered these words to be read out by a herald: The Senate and People of Rome order that all the cities which were under the dominion of King Philip be free and exempt; and when, at the consul's command, the herald repeated the words, which the people at first had hardly understood or believed, all were struck with vehement and unexpected joy, and the people filled the sky with such shouts that the birds flying overhead, stunned and terrified, fell to the ground. Plutarch writes that this was actually found to be true, and he also inquires into its causes; and Valerius Maximus states as certain that this is so. And so it may easily appear, the words of Livy are these: "Nothing at all is more pleasing to the multitude of good people than liberty." Let the Romans of that age know this: that the only nation on earth which waged wars at its own expense and risk for the liberty of others was Greece, which once proclaimed the Romans as the authors of its liberty; today there are none who have been taught, first by their own danger, then by their victories, and now by peace, to know these things better than the Belgians, for whom the possession of liberty is so their own that others seem to value it only by their example. But for us, this liberty is all the dearer because it has come to us twofold, that is, wholly. For while men ambitiously strive to reduce either our soul or our body, or even both, to slavery, both have long pressed upon us: the one the Pope, the other the Spaniard urged, and this one [...]

Nullum terris odiosum magis & intolerandum nomen, quam Papæ: cum quo nulla societas, nulla communio institui potest, quæ non vergat in contrahentis certam perniciem. Belgas quidem nostros, à longinquo tempore adversus Papalem Iurisdictionem & auctoritatem animatos, omnia banna & evocationes Paparum suis ditionibus arcuisse, constat, vel ex Diplomate Arnoldi Ducis, a. cIↄ cccc xxxi i. Wij be-looben alle bannen ende ladinge upt onse lande te keeren/ gelijck onse Voorvaderen dat oock gedaen ende uptgekeert hebben. Scimus, P. Gregorium xiiii.a.cIↄ lↄ lxxvii. Bullam adversus Nostros primum cdidisse, & Cruciatam, uti solet dici, promulgasse, cum plena peccatorum indulgentia omnibus, sub Johanne Austriaco, adversus Belgas, militaturis, tum, & in articulo mortis concedenda: quo pacto non solum æternam beatitudinem præmium istius militiæ temere constituit, sed & metum Purgatorii suis omnem ademisse videtur. Et nemo dubitat, quin ut incæpti belli causa apud Hispanum prima, ita continuati tam diu cum mamagno hujus detrimento & ignominiâ, multa semper steterit apud Papam, utpote qui satis sciret, nihil sibi nisi per Hispanica arma hic superfuturum, & seu victoriis, seu pace cessantibus armis, excidere se haud exiguâ regni sui portione. Unde mirati mecum subinde fuerunt nonnulli, quod qui pacem Germaniæ Papa abrogat, non simul quoque nostram Belgicam Bullâ suâ aliquâ proscribit, futili licet eâ & ridicula; sed quum is Paparum mos, & Romanæ Curiæ consuetudo sit, eamque sequatur contra Germanos, Imperatorem, Galliæ Regem, Suecos, quid causæ obsecro, quod non idem tentet adversus Nos, & Regem Hispaniæ? nisi forte, vel turpem Bullarum suarum apud Belgas vereatur successum, vel nescientibus nobis, hoc jam actum sit, & Regi saltem Hispaniæ constet, eiq; mentē super hac re suam Papa jam diu, vel absque Bullâ publicâ, significaverit. Quippe quam causam se habere dixit Innocentius, irritam pronunciandi pacem Germ., eandem, & forte plures reperturus sit, pari modo, apud nos, in Pace Belgica: quod se inconsulto inita illa sit, per non habentes (quomodo in Bullâ loquitur, de pace Germ.) potestatem, in præjudicium bonorum, jurium, quę prætendit; in favorem hæresis & hæreticorum, id est, doctrinæ Christi, & veræ Reformationis; omnia illa copiosius ipsi in Pace nostrâ occurrent, quam Germanicâ: unde ergo, quod non illam æque exagitat, & Bullâ suâ, quamvis ludicrâ, dignatur, ac hanc? Putatisne aut Papam ignorare articulos pacis nostræ, aut negligere sua quæ putat, aut nobis æquiorem contigisse Innocentium? nequaquam sane. Qui, quod scio haud ita pridem in Papali Consist. ventilatum fuisse, quando agebatur de concordando Galliæ Regę cum Hispano, Nostris adeo invidebant, quod arbitri intercederent Summorum Regum, ut omni opera agendum duxerint, ut illa Nostris tum hic,tum alibi gloria præripiatur,æquabili animo laturos credatis, ita nobiscum egisse Philippum Regem, ut grato animo Reip. nostræ libertatem, & ἀυτονομίαν agnoverit, & jus nostrum supremum in Ecclesiasticis, in Politicis, pręcisâ Papæ per Pacis nostræ fœdus in æternum omni de rebus Belgii cogitatione? bene quidem hæc omnia; sed quod in Imperatore, quod in Germaniâ tam impotenter exagitavit Papa, an idem in Philippo, in Belgio probaturum eum arbitrabimur? nisi forte quid sinistri, aut doli mali hic subsit, quodq; olim datû Hispano consilium, ne sic palam se objiceret Belgis, sed sensim per quietem, & pacis potius insidias illos eversum iret, hoc vel in alterius gratiam, vel in suum quoq; commodû nunc sequatur Papa. Scripsit Thomas Campanella, ex ordine Dominicanorum Monachus, lib. de Monarch. Hispania, c.xxviii. postquam dixisset, bellum Belgicum plus humani sanguinis absorpsisse, quam aquarum hic sit, & plus auri consumsisse, quam sint lapides: Hispan. plus detrimenti percipere ipsam, & contra Hollandis plus boni impertire, quod armis cum illis decertat, quamsi illos quietos relinqueret. Et paulo post addit: Ita ut vanum & absurdum mihi videatur, Belgas, qui in exordio belli oppressi non sunt, diutius domi suæ oppugnare, cum hoc illorum potentiam etiam augeat. Quare duo remedia adhuc supersunt ad hanc rem, quorum prius est divisionis semina inter illos spargere; posterius, illos de finibus suis elicere. Quod deserendâ inter Belg. populum discordiâ, post Lipsium, dicit, uti eo quidem semper collimavit hostium industria, ita ut nunquam permittat Deus, istudq; hostibus gaudium faciat, quo averruncato res nostrę parvę immensum adeo creverunt, ut porro avertat à nobis Deus, continuę preces nostrę sunt, & curæ. Eòdemque, quod anno cIↄ Iↄ cI solenne per omnes Provincias nostras, & Ecclesias, à Proceribus primum, inde à civibus subditisque, unanimiter ac publicè repetitum fœdus, arctiorqueUnio, pro defendendâ unâ & regione, & religione, juxta antiquum nostrum symbolum erecti super Euangeliorum codicem trophęi ferentis pileum, facit; ad exemplum populi Israëlitici, qui exigente id temporum conditione, aliquoties ejusmodi cum Deo, atque inter se fœdus celebrarunt, sub Josuâ, cap. xxiv. sub Rege Asa. Et in hoc omni facimus nos certum fœdus, quodque conscribimus, cum obsignatione Principum nostrorum, Levitarum nostrorum, Sacerdotum nostrorum. II. Chronic, xv. 12. Iniverunt que fœdus de requirendo Iehova Deo Majorum suorum, ex toto corde suo, & ex toto animo suo. v. 15. Latabantur enim omnes Iudei de isto juramento: nam ex toto animo suo juraverant, & toto suo studio eum quasiverant, & reperiebatur ab eis, dabatque ipsis Iehova quietem circumquaque. Ejusmodi sacrum & nationale fœdus, à seculo Reformationis, celebre Scoticum, quod in isto Regno præstit primum a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxx Rex cum tota sua familiâ, addità manuum subscriptione Confessioni fidei, inde ab omnibus Regni Ordinibus, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxi. Iterum a. cIↄ Iↄc. & nuper a. cIↄ Iↄc xxxviii. ab omni populo acceptum & confirmatum. Sed & ante hæc, Respublica Genevensis, auctore præcipue Calvino, cum Collegis Farello, & Coraldo, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxvii. d.xx Julii, palam præeunte publico Scriba, ba, Senatus populusque in Christianam religionem, & disciplinam aliquot capitibus comprehensam, repudiato prius Papatu, juravit. Quae omnia sedulo & sancte ubi sequuti fuerimus, spem haud vanam faciunt, obtenturos nos à Deo omne genus benedictionum, Patriae, & Ecclesiae, Nobis, Posterisque. Hoc ut Deum calidissimis semper votis precamur, ita in vestra quidem Nobiliss. Viri Republica, si quâ aliâ, tum Senatorum dignitate, tum curâ erga Ecclesiam, & politiam, & quod vestrae Civitati proprium, suis sumtibus sustentare Academiam, quae Urbis celebritatem universo orbi communicat, erga hanc sedulitate conspicua, nobis pollicemur, in quibus dum partem me facere aliquam singulari vestra benevolentiâ voluistis, hoc quod nunc oblatum vobis eo, officiorum quoque nostrorum erga istam vestram Remp. capite, si placet, perpetuum hostimentum, Dabam Ultrajecti xx Februarii a. units.tr: Whether men ambitiously seek to reduce our soul, or our body, or indeed both, into slavery, two burdens lay on us long ago: the Pope pressed upon the one, the Spaniard upon the other, and each held the other so tightly that both had to be either accepted together or rejected together. Today we are free of both and immune to both, and after God we owe this to our nobles. Taking up arms to assert and recover our liberty, they declared war on both, a glorious and successful war. There was only this difference between the two adversaries: with the Pope they could never come to terms, but with the King it was open to them to admit him again into favour and make peace whenever it seemed right. No name on earth is more hateful and intolerable than that of the Pope. No partnership or fellowship can be formed with him that does not tend to the certain ruin of the one who enters it. It is established that our Netherlanders, long ago stirred against papal jurisdiction and authority, kept every ban and summons of the popes out of their territories. This is clear from the charter of Duke Arnold in the year 1431: "We have banned all bans and summonses from our lands, as our forefathers also did and expelled them." We know that Pope Gregory XIII, in the year 1577, first issued a bull against our people and proclaimed what is customarily called a crusade, with full indulgence of sins, to all who would serve under John of Austria against the Belgians, and also to be granted at the point of death. In doing so he not only rashly fixed eternal blessedness as the reward of that soldiering, but also seems to have removed from his own people all fear of Purgatory. And no one doubts that, as the cause of the war began with the Spaniard, so the Pope has always kept a great deal of interest in its continuation, at such cost and shame to the Spaniard, since he knew well that nothing would remain for him here except through Spanish arms, and that if the arms ceased, whether through victories or peace, he would lose no small part of his kingdom. Hence some have from time to time wondered with me why the Pope, who annuls the peace of Germany, does not at the same time proscribe our Belgian peace with some bull of his, however futile and ridiculous it might be. But since this is the custom of the popes and the practice of the Roman Curia, and he follows it against the Germans, the Emperor, the King of France, and the Swedes, what reason, I beg you, is there that he should not attempt the same against us and the King of Spain? Unless perhaps he dreads the shameful outcome of his bulls among the Belgians, or unless, without our knowledge, this has already been arranged, and at least the King of Spain knows it, and the Pope has long since made known his view on this matter, even without a public bull. Indeed, the reason Innocent gave for declaring the peace of Germany void, namely that it was made without his consent by men who lacked the power (as he phrases it in the bull, speaking of the German peace), to the prejudice of the goods and rights he claims, and in favour of heresy and heretics, that is, the doctrine of Christ and true Reformation, all these things will occur to him more fully in our peace than in the German one. Why then does he not assail it equally, and deign to honour it with his bull, however ludicrous, as he does that one? Do we suppose that the Pope is ignorant of the articles of our peace, or neglects those things he thinks his own, or that Innocent has been kinder to us? By no means. I know that not long ago it was discussed in the papal Consistory, when the reconciliation of the King of France with the Spaniard was under negotiation, that the Pope's men were so envious of our people because the mediation of the supreme kings was interposed that they judged every effort should be made to snatch that glory from our people, both here and elsewhere. Do you believe they will bear with equanimity the fact that King Philip dealt with us in such a way that he gratefully acknowledged the liberty and autonomy [αὐτονομίαν] of our commonwealth, and our supreme right in ecclesiastical and political matters, with the Pope cut off from all thought about Belgian affairs by the covenant of our peace, for ever? All this is well; but as the Pope has so intemperately assailed the Emperor and Germany, shall we think he will approve the same in Philip and in the Netherlands? Unless perhaps some sinister purpose or evil trick lies hidden here, and the Pope now pursues that counsel once given to the Spaniard, not to expose himself openly to the Belgians, but to overthrow them gradually by quiet and by insidious pretence of peace, whether for another's favour or for his own advantage. Thomas Campanella, a Dominican monk, wrote in his book On the Monarchy of Spain, chapter 28, after saying that the Belgian war had swallowed up more human blood than there is water here, and consumed more gold than there are stones: Spain perceives more harm from it, and on the other hand gives more good to the Dutch, in that it struggles with them in arms, as if it left them in peace. And a little later he adds: So that it seems to me vain and absurd that the Belgians, who were not oppressed at the beginning of the war, should be assailed for longer in their own homes, since this also increases their power. Therefore two remedies still remain for this matter: the first is to sow the seeds of division among them; the second, to draw them out from their own boundaries. That he says the discord among the Belgian people is to be sown, after Lipsius, shows that the industry of our enemies has always aimed at this, so that God never allows it and does not give the enemies that joy. With that averted, our affairs, which were small, have grown immensely; and our continual prayers and cares are that God may further turn them away from us. And the same covenant, solemnly and unanimously renewed in the year 1581 through all our provinces and churches, first by the nobles, then by the citizens and subjects, and the closer union for the defence of both our country and our religion, is made in accordance with our ancient emblem of the trophy bearing the cap, raised upon the codex of the Gospels. It follows the example of the people of Israel, who, as the circumstances of the times required, several times made such a covenant with God and among themselves: under Joshua, chapter 24; under King Asa, 2 Chron. 15; under Joash, 2 Kings 11; under Josiah, 2 Kings 23; and under the leader Nehemiah, chapters 9 and 10. And in all this we make a sure covenant, and write it down, with the seal of our princes, our Levites and our priests. 2 Chron. 15:12. And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul. v. 15. For all Judah rejoiced at the oath, for they had sworn with all their soul, and had sought him with all their desire, and he was found of them; and the LORD gave them rest round about. A sacred and national covenant of this kind, famous since the age of the Reformation, is the Scottish one. The King of that realm first subscribed it, with his whole household, adding the signature of his hand to the Confession of Faith, in the year 1580; then by all the orders of the realm in 1581; again in 1590; and most recently, in 1638, it was received and confirmed by the whole people. But even before these, the Republic of Geneva, chiefly under the authority of Calvin, together with his colleagues Farel and Coraud, in the year 1537, on 20 July, with the public scribe going before, the Senate and people swore to the Christian religion and discipline, comprised in several chapters, having first renounced the Papacy. If we follow all these things diligently and faithfully, they give us no vain hope that we shall obtain from God every kind of blessing, for our country, for the Church, for ourselves and for our posterity. As we always pray this to God with the warmest prayers, so we promise, in your most noble men republic, if in any other, both the dignity of the senators and your care for the Church and the polity, and what is peculiar to your city, to maintain at its own expense an Academy which shares the renown of the City with the whole world, and in this a conspicuous diligence towards it. Since you have been willing to make us a part of it, in your particular goodwill, let this which is now offered to you be, if you approve, a perpetual memorial, at the head of our duties also, toward this your Commonwealth. Given at Utrecht, 20 February 1651.

Iunocentii, quâ irritam velit pacem Germaniæ: quocirca Diatribam Scholasticam aggressus, meditabar duntaxat, quod in principio etiam dico, marginalia quasi quædam ad Bullam Papæ adjicienda. Et hoc ne quis secus interpretetur, ejusmodi in Scholis aliquando ad ventilandum à nobis proponi, sciat, in eo nos habere exempla, quæ si non cum laude, absque vitio saltem imitemur; ne plura dicam, noverit celeberrimum Gerhardum Iohan. Vossium primo Disputationibus in Collegio proposuisse, quæ post plenius elaboravit, Historiam Pelagianismi; & quod non diu ante obitum adornavit scriptum, de Baptismo veterum. Atque ita etiam dum præsens Bulla Pontificia examen Scholasticis Disputationibus instituissem, tribus aut quatuor, respondente Reverendi Viri Pastoris Medioburgensis Filio Doctissimo Danielé de Svvaaf, nunc Ecclesiæ apud VValachros, etiam magna spei Ministro, mox expertus sum quam longe aliud se nobis hic offerret negotium, quam quod Scholasticâ dissertatione absolvi posset. Ita quippe, extra quam putaram, opus sub manibus crevit, & se alia post aliam materia obtrusit, ut de perficiendo libro cogitandum fuerit, id est amphoram instituerem, & currente rota exivit urcem. Hinc ἀδιάφορος scriptum, & nec cura nec tempore ita subactum, ut quidem ipse velim. Pergendum autem fuit, quando semel incæptum, ut non æque facile est cursum sistere, ac intra carcerem se cohibere; vel quomodo expansis velis navis, soluta statione, retineri non ita potest, quin seipsam etiam impellat. Iam argumenti suscepti dignitas, & copia volentem quoq; propellebant, eo fortius, quo pro pace, & Germaniâ, & adversus Papam, & ventosus ejus Bullas dicere, uti haud adeo molestam mihi operam, ita nec frustra collocandam pollicebatur. Neque puto quempiam miraturum, quod Papam adorimur; ubi id magis mirandum foret, si à nemine mine castigaretur. Meretur quippe ejus ambitio, ut ubi se adeo supra Reges & Imperatores non modo efferat, sed illorum quoque regimen turbat, & quantum in se est evertit, pacem & foedera damnat, subditos adversus Dominos incitat, aliter quam illis visum omnia decernit, & agitat, denique tyrannum se ostendit & usurpatorem, tanta unius hominis & Papae vsurpatio comprimatur. Quid Principes, quorum hic proprie causa agitur, facturi sint, cum pro se, tum populo, atque etiam pro pace sua, quam inierunt mutuo, illis relinquo; nostrum fuit, Papae petulantiam reprehendere; illorum, quin omnium, istam coercere, opprimere. Nos allatis Veterum ac recentiorum exemplis ostendimus, quid adversus Papas fieri oporteat, & docemus, quam juste, quamque facile Principes unum hominem compescendo, se & suam dignitatem vindicare, publicam rem stabilire, foedera servare, populum ab aliena tyrannide liberare, (ut verbo dicam) orbem orbi reddere cum maximâ nominis sui gloria & celebritate possint, absque quo neque alius unquam, neque ipsis bene erit, neque vel tutum aliquid habere poterit, sanctumque. Exemplum cape ex praesenti Bullâ P. Innocentii X. Ferierant post infelicem & diuturnum Germaniae bellum, ac tantum non excidium, Principes pacem, qui non alio remedio succurrii tanto malo posse, quam sola pace, arbitrabantur. Pax conclusa, sed post multa & magna tandem molimina, & suprema necessitate atque ac studio suo adactis Principes, in eam venerunt. Solus Papa, quod omnes magna cum gratulatione accipiunt, improbat & damnat, & solvi, non obstante omni juramento & firmitate, jubet, & quod magis est, factam a non habentibus potestatem, ex Vaticano suo inclamat; quo nescio quid magis intolerandum Imperatori, Regibus, & Principibus duci & jactari possit. Illorum nomina, & potestatem, & foedera subjacere arbitrio alieno, & Papae chem, quo abeunt Principum res, si ex nutu illius aut interpretanda sint, aut suspendenda? cujusve, qui sibi nullos supra se agnoscit Principes, (quâ pœnâ & ignominiâ propter gravissimam hic suam castigari Principes aequum est) ita nec ulla Numinis supremi tenetur reverentiâ, quando juramento omnes sic solvit, ut neque Principibus, neque Deo, modo juxta suum placitum, fidem teneantur amplius servare, aut foedus. Notario publico testibusque consignatam: tum Rescriptum adversus execrabilem Antichristi Bullam, in quo hoc suceste dictum transire non possum, ubi ait: Vulgo dicitur, Asinum ideo male cantare, quia altius orditur. Et illa quoque Bulla felicius cecinisset, si non blasphemum ossuum in cœlum posuisset, impudenti plusquam diabolicâ impietate, veritatem etiam contemtam & probatam damnatura. In fine vero concludit: Et sicut ipsi me excommunicant pro sacrilega hæresi suâ: ita ego rursus eos excommunico, pro sancta veritate Dei. Christus Judex fuerit, utra excommunicatio apud cum valeat. Amen.
units.tr: At the outset I resolved not to examine the Bull of Pope Innocent, by which he wishes the peace of Germany annulled, in a lengthy inquiry [ζητήσει]. So, having taken up a scholastic disputation, I intended only what I say at the beginning: to add some marginal notes, as it were, to the Pope's Bull. Lest anyone misread this, let him know that such exercises are sometimes put forward by us in the schools for debate, and that in this we have examples which we may imitate, if not with praise, at least without fault. To say no more, let him know that the most celebrated Gerhard John Vossius first put forward in disputations in the College what he afterwards worked out more fully, the History of Pelagianism, and that shortly before his death he prepared a treatise on the Baptism of the ancients. So too, when I had undertaken an examination of this present Papal Bull in scholastic disputations, three or four in number, with the most learned Daniel de Swaaf answering, son of the Reverend Pastor of Middelburg, now a minister of great promise among the Walloons, I soon found out how far otherwise this business presented itself to us than could be settled by a scholastic dissertation. The work, beyond what I had thought, grew under my hands, and one subject after another forced itself upon me, so that I had to think about finishing the book. That is, I set up an amphora, and when the wheel was turning it came out as a pitcher. Hence the work is indifferent [ἀδιάφορος] and has not been shaped by care or time as I myself would wish. But once begun it had to be carried on, since it is not as easy to stop a course as to confine oneself within a prison; or as a ship with its sails spread, once it has cast off its moorings, cannot be held back without driving itself on. Moreover, the dignity and abundance of the subject, which I had taken up, pushed me on even though I was willing, all the more strongly because it promised that to speak on behalf of peace, and for Germany, and against the Pope and his windy Bulls, was a task not too troublesome for me, nor one to be spent in vain. Nor do I think anyone will be surprised that we attack the Pope, when it would be more surprising if no one at all rebuked him. For his ambition deserves it: he raises himself so far above kings and emperors, and not only that, but also disturbs their government, and as far as he can overturns it; he condemns peace and treaties, incites subjects against their lords, decrees and acts in ways other than seems fit to them, and in short shows himself a tyrant and usurper. Such great usurpation by one man and Pope must be checked. What princes, whose cause is properly at issue here, will do, both for themselves and for their people, and also for the peace which they have made with each other, I leave to them. It was our task to rebuke the Pope's insolence; theirs, indeed everyone's, to restrain and suppress it. By citing examples from the ancients and from more recent times, we show what ought to be done against Popes, and we teach how justly and how easily princes, by curbing one man, can vindicate themselves and their dignity, establish the public good, keep treaties, free their people from foreign tyranny, and (to say it in a word) restore the world to the world, with the greatest glory and renown of their name; without which no one else will ever prosper, nor will they themselves, nor will anything be safe or holy for them. Take an example from the present Bull of Pope Innocent X. After the unhappy and long war of Germany, which came close to destruction, the princes had struck a peace, since they judged that so great an evil could be relieved by no remedy other than peace alone. The peace was concluded; but after many great efforts, and the princes being driven by supreme necessity and their own zeal, they came to it. The Pope alone, which all receive with great rejoicing, disapproves and condemns it, and orders that, notwithstanding every oath and firm undertaking, it be dissolved; and what is more, from his Vatican he proclaims that it was made by men who had no power. What could be more intolerable to be claimed and asserted against the Emperor, kings and princes? Their names, power and treaties are to lie subject to another's will, and the affairs of princes are to be interpreted or suspended at his nod. And he who acknowledges no princes above himself (with what punishment and shame it is right that princes be chastised for so grave a matter) is likewise bound by no reverence for the supreme Deity, since he releases all from their oaths so that they are no longer bound to keep faith or covenant either with princes or with God, provided they act according to his pleasure. (The treaty was sealed by a public notary and witnesses.) Then there is the Rescript against the execrable Bull of Antichrist, in which I cannot pass over this well-turned saying, where it says: It is commonly said that an ass sings badly because he begins too high. That Bull too would have sung more happily if it had not set a blasphemous mouth against heaven, with a shameless impiety more than diabolical, which would condemn even the truth, which has been tried and proved. At the end, however, it concludes: And just as they excommunicate me for their sacrilegious heresy, so I in turn excommunicate them for the holy truth of God. May Christ the Judge see which excommunication has force before him. Amen.

units.la: Ita Bullam Papæ excipere oportuit, & retundere ejus Auctoré. Denique Assertionem scripsit, omnium articulorum per Bullam Leonis X. novissimam damnatorum, ubi articulos doctrinæ suæ in Papæ Bullâ condemnatos defendit, & Scripturâ ac rationibus iterum confirmat. Præter ipsum, Ulrichus Hutteno, Eques, eandem Bullam, additis variis annotationibus, ceu obeliscis, egregiè perstrinxerat. Quæ omnia extant operum Lutheri Tom. II. Latin. Idem in Luthero ardor fecit, ut Pontificum libros decretales, & Ius Canonicum, ubi resciverat libros suos à Pontificis combustos esse, publicè Vvittemberga anno cIↄ Iↄ xx, d. x. Decemb. flammis traderet, hac addità exécratione: quia su contorbasti sanctum Domini, ideoque te conturbet ignis æternus. Ne jam dicam, quæ Idem aliis variorum Episcoporum adversus se Diplomatibus, & Bullulis, ut sic loquar, opposuit, Episcopi Misnensis, anno xx. d. xxiv. Januar. Mauritii, VV armiensis, anno xxiv. d. xx. Januar. tum Brevi P. Adriani VI. anno cIↄ Iↄ xxiii. Deinque Bullâ P. Pauli III. indictionis Concilii Tridentini, anno cIↄ Iↄ xlv. Neque omittendus mihi hoc loco Huldricus Zuinglius, qui quo tempore Norimbergæ, in Comitiis, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxii. P. Adrianus VI. per Legatum suum Franciscum Cheregatum curasset proponi ad deliberationem capita aliquot, quorum summa huc redibat, ut Lutheri nomen, sive Papatus reformatio per Germaniam extingueretur, scripsit hac occasione Suggestionem ad Principes Germaniæ, quæ extat Operum ejus Tom. I. cui in fronte hoc præmisit: Me legat, quisquis defensam velit & Christianam religionem & Germaniæ vindicatam. Quo praeconio ne quis offendatur, sciat absque nomine Auctoris scriptum illud primo prodisse. Adeo sui quoque officii existimavit esse, videre ne quid per neglectum suum res & religionis, & Germaniae detrimenti caperet. Neque possum quin exinde hoc saltem hic exhibeam legendum de Pontificibus quod dicit, & valde ad rem quoque praesentem nostram notandum est: Inveni eos nihil minus proximis fere triginta annis quam Principum concordiam terre potuisse, iis enim sese mutuo conterentibus Roma tacite, sed ampliter suis delictis fruitur. Legati Leonis X. anno clɔ Iɔ xix. coram Imp. Maximiliano orationem dixere, pro colligendis decimis: huic, contra ne Principes in Decimas illas consentirent, alia oratione responsum ab Vdalrico Hutteno, Viro nobili, & Reformatorum suo tempore omnium & singulari patrono: cujus multa cum, & pro Luthero, vide Oper. Lutheri Tom. II. Illa utraque oratio extat in Fasciculo rerum expetendarum. Bilibaldus Pirckheimerus anno clɔ Iɔ xxii. ad P. Adrianum litteras ipse dedit, conquerentes de artibus & facinoribus Dominicanorum, irritatus uti videtur, eorundem machinationibus contra bonum Virum Ioh. Capnionem, quibus causam & occasionem attribuit Lutheranismi: epistolae ejus pars aliqua legitur apud Goldastum, Politic. Imperial. part. xxiv. Quando anno clɔ Iɔ lxxxv. P. Sixtus V. adversus Henricum Regem Navarrae, & Henricum Borbonium, Principem Condaeum, Declarationem edidisset, quā primum illos tanquam haereticos notorios ex communione Christianorum ejiciebat; tum dignitatibus & imperiis omnibus, ac praesertim spe successionis regni Galliae abdicabat: porro ut eorum clientes ac vasalli fidelitatis juramento, quo illis obstricti erant, solverentur; postremo ut a Rege Galliae vi, ferro, armis oppugnarentur, edicebat, Franciscus Hotomannus I. C. Principum nomine, oppositit protestationem & declarationem multiplicis nullitatis, scripto ad eam rem doctissimo & acri libro, Brutum fulmen P. Sixti V. atque alter qui se vocat un Catholique, Apostolique Romain, Gallice ejusdem argumenti scriptum, pro Principibus dedit: Moyens d'abus, entreprises & nullitez du referit & Bulle du Pape Sixte V. Deinde quum anno clɔ Iɔ xcı. Gregorius XIV. Bullas monitoriales in Galliam misisset,
units.tr: It was fitting to receive the Pope's Bull in this way, and to beat back its author. Finally he wrote the Assertion of all the articles condemned by the last Bull of Leo X, in which he defends the articles of his teaching condemned in the Pope's Bull, and confirms them again by Scripture and arguments. Besides him, Ulrich Hutten, a knight, had sharply attacked the same Bull, adding various annotations, as if they were obelisks. All these things are found in the works of Luther, vol. II, Latin edition. The same zeal in Luther made him, when he learned that his books had been burnt by the Pope, publicly commit the decretal books of the Popes and the Canon Law to the flames at Wittenberg on 10 December 1520, adding this curse: Because you have troubled the holy of the Lord, therefore may the eternal fire trouble you. Not to mention what he set against himself in the decrees and, as I may say, little bulls of various bishops: the Bishop of Meissen, in the year 1520, on 24 January; Maurice, Bishop of Wurzburg [Vvirceburgensis? i.e. the Bishop of Merseburg?], in 1524, on 20 January; then the Brief of Pope Adrian VI in 1523. Then the Bull of Pope Paul III announcing the Council of Trent, in 1545. Nor must I omit here Huldrych Zwingli, who, when at Nuremberg, at the Diet, in 1522, Pope Adrian VI through his legate Francesco Chieregato had caused several chapters to be put to deliberation, the sum of which came to this, that the name of Luther, or the reform of the Papacy, should be extinguished throughout Germany, wrote on this occasion a Suggestion to the princes of Germany, which is found in vol. I of his works, and at the head of which he placed this: Let whoever wishes to defend both Christian religion and Germany read me. Lest anyone take offence at this praise, let him know that this writing first appeared without the author's name. So much did he think it his duty too to see that nothing through his neglect should bring loss to the state, to religion, and to Germany. Nor can I refrain from setting out here at least this which he says concerning the Pontiffs to be read, and which must especially be noted for our present matter: I have found that for nearly thirty years they have been able to achieve nothing less than harmony among the princes of the earth; for while these wear each other down, Rome enjoys its own offences quietly but abundantly. The legates of Leo X spoke an oration before the Emperor Maximilian in the year 1519, for collecting the tithes; against this, lest the princes consent to those tithes, a reply was made in another oration by Ulrich Hutten, a noble man and the patron, in his time, of all the Reformers and a unique one: much of which, both for and about Luther, see in the works of Luther, vol. II. Both of those orations are found in the Fasciculus of things to be desired. Bilibald Pirckheimer in the year 1522 himself sent a letter to Pope Adrian, complaining about the arts and crimes of the Dominicans, provoked, as it seems, by their machinations against the good man John Reuchlin, to which he assigned the cause and occasion of Lutheranism; a part of his letter is read in Goldast, Politica Imperialia, part xxiv. When in the year 1585 Pope Sixtus V published a Declaration against Henry, King of Navarre, and Henry of Bourbon, Prince of Condé, by which first he cast them out of the communion of Christians as notorious heretics; then he renounced all dignities and empires, and especially the hope of succession to the kingdom of France; further, that their clients and vassals should be released from the oath of fidelity by which they were bound to them; and lastly, that they should be attacked by the King of France with force, iron and arms, Francis Hotman, Doctor of Law, on behalf of the princes, set against it a protestation and declaration of manifold nullity, in a most learned and sharp book written for that purpose, the Brutum fulmen of Pope Sixtus V; and another, who calls himself "un Catholique, Apostolique Romain," wrote in French on the same subject for the princes: Moyens d'abus, entreprises & nullitez du referit & Bulle du Pape Sixte V. Then when in the year 1591 Pope Gregory XIV had sent monitory Bulls into France,

units.la: sisset, adversus Regem Henricum IV., cum gravibus interdicti in Regem & Regnum minis, iis oppositi Vir quidam doctus, Pium Consilium super Papæ Monitorialibus, quod Gallice primo conscriptum Tussanus Berchetus Lingonensis mox Latinitate donavit. Pridem in causâ Bavaricâ, & transferendi in eam domum Electoratus, ubi Michael Lonigus, præfectus Palatii Vaticani, Consilium dabat Gregorio XV. & ex hoc Aphorismos pro Ecclesiâ Romanâ statu restaurando in Germaniâ, præsertim per translationem & confirmationem Papalem Electoralis dignitatis, collegerant Cardinales, Pontifici itidem tradendos; ad utrumque Notas & Censuram scripsit a. clɔ Iɔ c xxxiii. Gerardus Ioh. Vossius. Ad Bullam Iubilaei ab Urbano VIII. a. clɔ Iɔ cxli. promulgati, distribuem edidit venerandus Collega noster D. Voetius. Qua ante nos exempla, multum confirmarunt animi nostri propositum in oppugnando libere Papa, ejusque Bulla, quum videremus illud huiusmodi Bullarum fatum esse, ut scripto adversario excuti & confutari soleant, si confutari id dicendum sit, quod solum detegere satis est. Historias hic præcipue incubui, ut ex illis hodierna, facta factis redarguerem. Lutherum observo, nusquam plus historiarum in suis disputationibus attulisse, quam quando occasione tum Brevium P. Pauli III. tum Bullæ indictionis Concilii Tridentini, a. clɔ Iɔ xl v scripsit, adversus Papatum Romæ à Sathana fundatum: qui liber valde doctus habetur Operum ejus Latin. Tom. vii. Parum quippe superest quod ex jure cum Papis disputemus, vel quod apud ipsos quid valeat, sita extra juris omnem orbitam se ponentibus, sed & extra factorum etiam, pari proterviâ, regulam. Neque sane tam illorum causa est quod verbum facimus, adversus omnia diu obfirmatorum, quam aliorum, & nostri ipsius, ne defuisse hac in parte officio videremur. Neminem ergo offendent crebra hic adducta allegationes & historiæ, uti nec quod passim proprio sermone, ubi nempe facilis est & hodie obvius, non latine loquentes facio, quod & propter jam datam causam, & propter operis (in tantâ otii tac mihi est penuria) facilitatem, procul ostentatione, vel si quod aliud siniistrum mihi per injuriam hic quis impingat, factum testor: omitto quod & terram aliquando momentum, & proprii sermonis quo quodque scribitur gratia idem facile excusent. Iam si quis futurus sit, ut hoc postremo moneam, qui nostris offensus, Papam forte defendendum putaverit, age procedat, at videat si possit ut in scribendo imitetur modestiam illius, quem fere solum a Nostris hoc nomine laudatum scio, dum immani alioquin rabie solent in nos irruere Scriptores Pontificii, Valentinum Comparem, Vraniensem, cui cum Zuinglio disputatio fuit, & hoc ab eo in ipsa disputatione datur elogium: tibi ingenue tribuo, quod nullum ad huc alium mihi videre licuerit, cujus scripta tantis curis & tanta cum diligentia sine omni cavillandi & convitiandi libidine ad veritatis investigationem penetrent, quanta tu uti soles, Hoc quanto rarius in Pontificiis, eo magis commendari & proponi aliis in exemplum debet: non quod aliorum contumeliis moveamur, aut ladamur, vel eas multum metuamus, sed quod omni ratione Adversarium emendare satagimus, si non in opinione veritatis, ad virtutem saltem hanc, quaquo a Scriptis Theologicis, magno cum nominis nostri opprobrio, eristicis puta, exulat longius, eo majori cum conatu reducere laboramus, & sacra sua sedi postliminio quasi vindicare. Quem in finem valde arrisit illud Valentini Comparis, a Zuinglio ejus adversario, in perpetuam ejus gloriam, scriptis proditum, & hoc mihi loco dicendum; quam longe supra illud, quod in Stephano Gardinero, Vintoniensi olim in Anglia Episcopo, observavit Martinus Bucerus! illum inter disputandum ita excandescere solitum, ut vena quaedam manus inter pollicem & digitum sic intumesceret, & celeri ac perspicuo motu palpitaret, ut illum conspicientes, ad pugnam quam disputationem dicerent parationem. Et hujus scimus plura ubique exempla consimilia, non item illius: quantum vero alter altero praestet, sitque commendabilior, Christianus nemo ignorare poterit, nec etiam Pontificius quamvis aliquis debet.
units.tr: had sent papal monitorial bulls into France against King Henry IV, with grave threats of interdict against the King and the Kingdom, a learned man opposed them with his Pious Counsel on the Papal Monitorials, which Tussanus Berchetus of Langres first wrote in French and soon afterwards gave a Latin dress. Earlier, in the Bavarian affair and the transfer of the Electorate into that house, when Michael Lonigus, prefect of the Vatican Palace, was advising Gregory XV, the Cardinals had drawn up aphorisms for restoring the Roman Church's position in Germany, chiefly through the transfer and papal confirmation of the electoral dignity, and these too were to be handed to the Pope. Gerardus Johannes Vossius wrote notes and a censure on both in 1633. Our venerable colleague D. Voetius published a distinct work on the Jubilee bull promulgated by Urban VIII in 1641. These precedents before us strengthened greatly our resolve to attack the Pope and his bull openly, since we saw that it is the fate of such bulls to be shaken and refuted by written opposition, if one may speak of refuting what it is enough merely to expose. I have devoted myself chiefly to history here, so that I might refute the present by the past, deeds by deeds. I observe that Luther nowhere brought more history into his disputations than when, on the occasion of both the briefs of Pope Paul III and the bull announcing the Council of Trent, he wrote in 1545 against the Papacy founded at Rome by Satan; this book is held to be very learned and is found in the Latin works, vol. VII. Indeed, little remains for us to dispute with the Papists from the law, or about what holds force among them, since they put themselves outside every track of law, and with equal insolence outside the rule of facts too. Nor is it so much for their sake that I speak, against men long hardened in everything, as for the sake of others and of ourselves, lest we seem to have been wanting in our duty in this respect. Therefore the frequent allegations and histories adduced here will offend no one, nor will the fact that I write in my own language, where it is easy and readily at hand today, rather than in Latin; I call to witness that I have done so for the reason already given, and for the ease of the work (for I am short of leisure in so busy a life), far from any display, and if anyone here wrongly charges me with some other ill intent, I leave that charge to him. I pass over the fact that the matter itself sometimes carries weight, and that the language in which each thing is written readily excuses the same. Now if anyone, offended by our words, should think that the Pope must be defended, let him come forward, but let him see whether he can imitate the moderation of that man whom, as far as I know, our people alone have praised in this respect, while otherwise the Papist writers usually rush upon us in monstrous rage: Valentinus Compar of Vraniensis, who held a disputation with Zwingli, and the praise given him by that man in the very disputation. I freely grant you what I have seen in no other to this day: whose writings reach the investigation of truth with such care and such diligence, without any itch for mocking and reviling, as you are wont to use. The rarer this is among Papists, the more it ought to be commended and held up to others as an example: not because we are moved or hurt by the insults of others, or greatly fear them, but because by every means we labour to correct the adversary, if not in his opinion of the truth, at least in this virtue, which in theological writings, to the great discredit of our name, is banished far away, namely, the wrangling spirit; and we labour with all the greater effort to bring it back and, as it were, restore it by right of return to its sacred seat. To this end that saying of Valentinus Compar, recorded by Zwingli his adversary to his everlasting glory, pleases me greatly, and it must be mentioned here: how far it surpasses what Martin Bucer observed in Stephen Gardiner, once Bishop of Winchester in England, namely that he was wont to grow so heated in disputation that a certain vein of his hand between thumb and finger would swell and throb with a quick and visible motion, so that those who saw him took it for preparation for a fight rather than a disputation. We know many similar examples of the latter everywhere, but not of the former; and how much one surpasses the other, and is the more commendable, no Christian can fail to know, nor should even a Papist, however he may be.

units.la: ZELO Domus Dei animum nostrum assiduae commovente, in eam praecipue curam sedulo incumbimus, ut Orthodoxae Fidei integritas, ac Ecclesiae Catholicae dignitas & auctoritas ubique sarta tecta conservetur, neve eorum, qui quaerunt sua potius, quam quae Dei sunt, facta jura Ecclesiastica, quorum Assertos à Domino constituti sumus, aliquod detrimentum accipiant, Nos, qui supremo Judici rationem villicationis nostrae reddituri, negligentiae in credita Nobis Administratione arguamur, sane cum intimo doloris sensu accepimus, quod per plures annos Osnabrugis die 6. Non obstantibus præmissis, ac quibusvis Constitutionibus, & Ordinationibus Apostolicis tam generalibus quam specialibus etiam in Comitiis universalibus editis, & quatenus opus sit, nostra, & Cancellariæ Apost. regula de non tollendo jure quæsito, & Constitutione sel. record. Pii Papæ Quarti Prædecessoris nostri de gratiis qualecunque interesse Cameræ Apost. concernentibus infra certum tunc expressum tempus in eadem Camera præsentandis, & registrandis, ita ut præsentes nullo unquam tempore in eadem Camera præsentari seu registrari necesse sit; legibus quoque Imperialibus & municipalibus, nec non quibusvis etiam juramento, confirmatione Apostolica, vel quavis firmitate alia roboratis Statutis, usibus, & consuetudinibus etiam immemorabilibus, Privilegiis quoq;, indultis, Concessionibus, & litteris Apostolicis quibuscunque locis, & personis, etiam Imperiali, Regali, & alia quavis sive Ecclesiastica, sive mundana dignitate fulgentibus, & alias quomodolibet qualificatis, ac specialem expressionem requirentibus, etiam motu, scientia, deliberatione, & potestatis plenitudine similibus, etiam Cōsistoriali-ter sub quibuscunque tenoribus & formis, ac cum quibusvis etiam derogatoriarum derogatoriis, aliisque efficacioribus, & insolitis clausulis, & decretis etiá irritantibus, & alias quomodolibet in contrarium præmissorum concessis, editis, factis, ac pluries & iteratis vicibus confirmatis, approbatis, & innovatis. Quibus omnibus & singulis etiamsi pro sufficienti illorum derogatione de illis, eorumque totis tenoribus specialis, specifica, individua, ac de verbo ad verbum, non autem per clausulas generales idem importantes mentio, seu quævis alia expressio facienda, aut alia exquisita forma ad hoc servanda foret, tenores hujusmodi, ac si de verbo ad verbum inserti essent præsentibus hoc plene & sufficienter expressis, & insertis, formamque in illis traditam pro servata habentes, ad præmissorum effectum specialiter & expresse derogamus, ac derogatum esse volumus, cæterisque contrariis quibuscunque. Volumus autem, ut earundem dem præsentium transsumptis, etiam impressis, manu Notarii publici subscriptis, & Sigillo personæ in dignitate Ecclesiastica constitutæ munitis, eadem prorsus fides ubique locorum & gentium in Iudiciis, & extra illud adhiberetur, quæ ipsis præsentibus adhiberetur, si forent exhibitæ, vel ostensæ. Datum Romæ apud Sanctam Mariam majorem sub annulo Piscatoris die 26.Novembr. & solenniter ibidem publicatum 3.Ianuar. Anno M. DC. LI. Pontificatus Nostri octavo.
units.tr: Our hearts are constantly stirred by zeal for the house of God, and we devote our careful attention above all to ensuring that the integrity of the Orthodox Faith and the dignity and authority of the Catholic Church are kept whole and intact everywhere. We are also determined that the ecclesiastical rights, of which we have been appointed the guardians by the Lord, shall suffer no harm from those who seek their own interests rather than the things of God. We must render an account of our stewardship to the supreme Judge, and we would be charged with negligence in the administration entrusted to us if we were silent. We have therefore received with a deep sense of grief that, for many years, the articles of the treaties concluded at Osnabrück on 6 August 1648 between our most beloved son in Christ, Ferdinand, King of the Romans and Elected Emperor, with his allies and adherents on the one side, and the Swedes with their likewise allies and adherents on the other, and the articles of the other peace concluded at Münster in Westphalia on 24 October of the same year 1648 between the same Ferdinand, King of the Romans and Elected Emperor, with his allies and adherents on the one side, and our most beloved son in Christ, Louis, the Most Christian King of the French, with his allies on the other, have been drawn up to the very grave prejudice of the Catholic Religion, of divine worship, of the Apostolic and Roman See and the lower Churches, of the ecclesiastical order, and of their jurisdictions, authorities, immunities, liberties, exemptions, privileges, pacts, treaties and rights. Indeed, by the agreements of one or the other of these peaces, among other ecclesiastical goods and other things occupied by heretics, those goods are assigned in perpetuity to the heretics and their successors. In most places the free exercise of their heresy is permitted to the heretics of the so-called Augsburg Confession, and places are assigned for building temples for this purpose. They are also admitted with Catholics to public offices and duties, and to certain archbishoprics, bishoprics and other dignities and ecclesiastical benefices, and they are allowed to share in the chief prayers granted to the said Ferdinand, elected Emperor, by the aforesaid Apostolic See. Annates, the rights of the pallium, of confirmation, papal months and similar rights, and reservations in ecclesiastical goods of the said Augsburg Confession, are excluded. The confirmation of elections or nominations of the alleged archbishops, bishops or prelates of the same confession is handed over to secular power. Many archbishoprics, bishoprics, monasteries, provostships, bailiwicks, commendams, canonries and other benefices and ecclesiastical goods are granted in perpetual fief to heretical princes and their heirs under the title of secular dignity, even with the ecclesiastical designation removed. It is laid down that against such a peace, or any article of it, no canon or civil laws in common use, no special decrees of councils, no rules of religious orders, no oaths or concordats with the Roman Pontiffs, and no other statutes, whether political or ecclesiastical, decrees, dispensations, absolutions or other exceptions, are to be alleged, heard or admitted. The number of the seven electors of the Empire, formerly fixed by apostolic authority, is increased without our consent and that of the said See, and an eighth electorate is set up in favour of Charles Louis, the heretical Count Palatine of the Rhine. Many other things, which it is shameful to recount, are decreed, all of them greatly prejudicial and harmful to the orthodox Religion, to the said See, to the Roman and lower Churches, and to the other matters mentioned above. And although our Venerable Brother, the Bishop of Nerito, our extraordinary Nuncio to the Rhine district and the lower parts of Germany of the said See, carrying out our commands, has openly protested in our name and that of the same Apostolic See that these articles are void, null, unjust, rashly agreed upon by those who had no power, and to be regarded as such by all; and although it is a well-known principle of law that any transfer or agreement concerning ecclesiastical matters made without the authority of the said See is null and of no force or validity; nevertheless, so that the indemnity of the foregoing may be more effectively secured, and wishing to provide, as the duty of the pastoral office entrusted to us from on high requires, and holding the exact texts and dates of both instruments of peace, and of everything contained in them and of the other matters which must be expressed and inserted here, as if they were inserted word for word and were fully and sufficiently expressed and inserted in these presents; we, of our own accord, from certain knowledge and mature deliberation, and from the fullness of apostolic power, declare and decree that the said articles of the one or the other peace, and the other matters contained in the said instruments, which in any way harm or are asserted to cause even the slightest prejudice to the Catholic Religion, to divine worship, to the salvation of souls, to the same Apostolic and Roman See and the lower Churches, to the order and state of the clergy, to their persons, members, property, goods, jurisdictions, authorities, immunities, liberties, privileges, prerogatives and rights of any kind, or which could be said, understood, claimed or pleaded to have harmed or to harm or to have done damage in any way, together with all the consequences that have followed or may in any way follow, were, are, and for ever shall be by law null, void, invalid, unjust, unrighteous, condemned, reprobated, empty, and altogether vain in their force and effect. We also declare and decree that no one is bound to observe them or any of them, even if they have been confirmed by oath; that no right, action, colourable title or ground of prescription is acquired or may in future be acquired or belong to anyone under them, even if a possession or quasi-possession of very long and immemorial time follows, even without any challenge or interruption; that they do not create any status, nor have they done so; and that, just as if they had never been issued, they must be held for all time as non-existent and not made. Nevertheless, for the greater security, and so far as necessary, we decree that whatever has been attempted contrary to this by anyone, with any authority, knowingly or ignorantly, shall always and everywhere be judged and defined as void and empty. Notwithstanding the foregoing, and any apostolic constitutions and ordinances, general or special, even those issued in universal assemblies, and, so far as necessary, our rule and that of the Apostolic Chancery, forbidding the removal of an acquired right, and the constitution of Pius IV of happy memory, our predecessor, concerning graces affecting the Apostolic Chamber in any way, which were to be presented and registered in that Chamber within a certain time then specified, so that these presents need never at any time be presented or registered in that Chamber; likewise imperial and municipal laws, and any statutes, usages and customs confirmed by oath, apostolic confirmation or any other firmness, even immemorial; likewise privileges, indults, concessions and apostolic letters of any kind granted to any places and persons, even those shining with imperial, royal or any other ecclesiastical or secular dignity, and otherwise qualified in any way, and requiring special mention; even if granted by motu proprio, knowledge, deliberation and the fullness of power of the same kind, even granted consistorially, under any tenor and form, and with any derogatory clauses, even derogatory of derogations, and other more effective and unusual clauses and decrees, even annulling ones; and otherwise granted, issued, done, and repeatedly confirmed, approved and renewed, contrary to the foregoing. To all of these and each of them, even if, for their sufficient derogation, a special, specific and individual mention of them and of their whole tenor word for word were required, rather than a general clause having the same meaning, or any other expression, or some other prescribed form were to be observed for this purpose, we derogate, and wish to be derogated, specially and expressly for the effect of the foregoing, their tenors being held as if inserted word for word in these presents, and fully and sufficiently expressed and inserted, and the form laid down in them being held as observed; and to all other things to the contrary whatsoever. We will moreover that to copies of these presents, even printed, subscribed by the hand of a public notary and fortified with the seal of a person constituted in ecclesiastical dignity, the same complete faith shall be given everywhere, among all places and peoples, both in judgement and outside it, as would be given to these presents if they were exhibited or shown. Given at Rome, at St Mary Major, under the Fisherman's ring, on 26 November, and solemnly published there on 3 January in the year 1651, the eighth of our pontificate.

units.la: DISPVTATIO THEOLOGICA, AD BULLAM P. INNOCENTII. X. Abrogantis pacem Germaniæ.
units.tr: THEOLOGICAL DISPUTATION, ON THE BULL OF POPE Innocent X, abrogating the peace of Germany.

units.la: I. VUM non absque singulari divinæ providentiæ virgulâ factum existimem, quod Papæ Innocentii X. Bulla, qua pacem Germaniæ, ante annos aliquot Monasterii, & Osnabrugis, post diuturna molimina & difficultates gravissimas, non cum Germaniæ solius, sed universi orbis Europæi applausu; ideam tandem, & à partibus, quorum intererat, utrimque magno animorum consensu confirmatam, ille solus improbat, facit irritam, damnat, (uti Romæ illa prodiit ex Typographiâ Cameræ, sicut vocant, Apostolicæ, hoc anno clo Io cIↄ) ipsumque Exemplar Romæ impressum, ad me missum sit, ad quod porro, qua Latinè, qua Belgicè recusa hic exemplaria fuerunt: ego non committendum duxi, quo minus adderem ei annotationes, & quasi marginalia; vel ideo, quia pro stylo & consuetudine istius, unde hæc prodiit, Curiæ, cum Glossis eorum Decreta legi solent. Simul videbunt Germani, orbisque adeo universus, Quis, & quod hominum genus Paci semper inimicum haberi debeat, & quam antea profligarunt, incitatis ad opprimendum, persequendum, belligerandumque Principum ac Christianorum animis, eandem nunc invisam Romano Marti, ut ruptam iterum & explosam cupiant.
units.tr: I. I think it has not happened without a singular rod of divine providence that the Bull of Pope Innocent X, by which he attempts to annul the peace of Germany, has been issued. That peace was concluded some years ago at Münster and Osnabrück, after long labours and very grave difficulties, with the applause not of Germany alone but of the whole European world. At last its terms were confirmed by the parties concerned, with great unanimity of minds on both sides. This one man alone disapproves of it, makes it void and condemns it. The Bull came out at Rome from the press of the so-called Apostolic Chamber in this year 1650. A printed copy from Rome was sent to me, and from it copies have been reprinted here, both in Latin and in Dutch. I did not think I should refrain from adding notes to it, as marginal glosses. This is partly because, in keeping with the style and custom of the Curia from which it comes, decrees are usually read together with their glosses. At the same time the Germans, and indeed the whole world, will see who and what kind of men ought always to be regarded as enemies of peace. They will also see that the princes and Christians, whose minds have been roused to oppress, persecute and wage war, long to have the peace broken and cast out again, since it, which they once crushed, is now hateful to the Roman Mars.

units.la: II. Neque hoc mirum videri cuipiam debet, vel piaculum Roma habere, quod ejus Edicta alius oppugnat, & Papæ obloqui, ex Ecclesiæ Ministris, quamvis nulla Episcopali majoritate insignis, aliquis audeat: quum quando melior Roma Episcopos Martyres potius, quam Papas habebat, bene tulit ut Cornelium, ut Stephanum suos, fratres Collegasq; Cyprianus appellaret, neque superiores illos se multum agnoscceret. quo magis jam absque ulla venię prefatione alloquendus Romanus episcopus, suæ, & plurimarum Ecclesiarum unica pernicies, & prędo maximus, nec frater, neque Pater ultra dicendus, ubi extra districtum suum, rebus se immiscet aliis, & politicis, quasi supra ecclesiam, & politiam omnem constitutus, atque dum pro innocentia Christi, aut Petri piscatoris humilitate, non deberet ἀπoτειπ(ειν non μάχῃ pacem, quam alii multo sanguine redemerunt, in filiis sc. suis solus diris omnibus divexat & execratur. Quæ quia minime ferenda est in Ecclesiastico, in Episcopo, ut se putat, in Innocentio, in Petri sc. successore, aut Christi Vicario arrogantia atque improbitas, ob omnium oculos ponenda, & castiganda pro merito videtur.
units.tr: II. Nor should this seem strange to anyone, nor should Rome consider it a sacrilege, that someone attacks its edicts and speaks against the Pope. Some minister of the Church, though marked by no episcopal majority, dares to do so. Once, when Rome was better, it had bishops who were martyrs rather than popes. Cyprian bore well that they called Cornelius and Stephen their brothers and colleagues, and he did not acknowledge those men as his superiors. All the more, then, the Roman bishop, the sole ruin of his own and of very many churches and the greatest robber, must be addressed without any preliminary apology. He is no longer to be called brother or father, when he meddles outside his own district in other matters, and political ones, as if set above the Church and every polity. While, for the innocence of Christ or the humility of Peter the fisherman, he ought to refuse peace, not with war, but with a refusal, the peace which others bought with much blood, he alone harasses and execrates it with every curse upon his own sons. Since such arrogance and wickedness is not to be tolerated in an ecclesiastical man, in a bishop, as he thinks himself, in Innocent, successor of Peter or Vicar of Christ, it seems right that it be set before everyone's eyes and punished as it deserves.

units.la: III. Sanctissimi Domini N. D. Innocentii, Divina Providentia Papa X.)
units.tr: III. Of our most holy Lord N., Innocent, by Divine Providence Pope X.)

units.la: Si vocis Papa aut etymologiam, aut usum antiquum consideres, Patrem significat; & cum vel proprium, naturalem, ex vocis origine; vel usu Ecclesiastico, per metaphoram, episcopum, quasi patrem spiritualem, communis olim denominatio hæc fuit, non episcopo Romano, uti hodie, appropriata. Nonnulla in hanc rem dixi alias, de Theologia Patrum, in initio. Papa πάππας, aut πάππα, unde παππάζειν: à Syriaco, NIN abba, Hebraicè ON ab Pater, unde avus: b. & v. litteræ unius organi inter se commutantur. Apud Callimachum, Diana: Δ'ῷ μοι παρθενίην αἰῶνιον, Ἄππα, φυλάσσειν.
units.tr: If you consider either the etymology or the ancient usage of the word Papa, it means Father. Both by its natural sense, from the origin of the word, and by ecclesiastical usage, by metaphor, it was once a common designation for a bishop, as a spiritual father. It was not yet appropriated to the Roman bishop, as it is today. I have said some things on this matter elsewhere, in "On the Theology of the Fathers", at the beginning. Papa [πάππας] or [πάππα], whence [παππάζειν]: from the Syriac NIN, abba; in Hebrew ON, ab, father, whence the Latin avus. The letters b and v are interchanged, being of one organ. In Callimachus, Diana says: [Δός μοι παρθενίην αἰῶνιον, Ἄππα, φυλάσσειν].

units.la: Da mihi virginitatem perpetuam, Pater, custodire.
units.tr: Give me, Father, to keep perpetual virginity.

units.la: Πάππα, πάππα, & ἄππα apud Suidam. Illud πρὸς πατίας σπῶπκη φωνή: vox venerationis ad Patrem. Hinc παππαππός. Homeri Interpres in Odyss. ζ. πάππα φίλ &c. πάτα, προσφώνησις φιλοφρονητικὴ πατέρα πρὸς πατέρα. Idem Ραψ. ι. παππάζοι. παππα φωνεῖ, παππα κακῶς. Pappos, aviasque trementes, apud Ausonium. Ineptum est, Papam, vi vocis, quasi scil. ἀπαλλάσσω Ρα Ρα, putare quod significet Patrem Patrum: quod Glossa, in proœmio. CleClement. & Remigius Antisiodorensis, de Celebrat. Miss�, & Hosius, in confess. fidei, aliique tenent. Etiam mamma dixerunt Veteres. Mammas atq; Tatas habet Afra, Martialis, lib.
units.tr: [Πάππα, πάππα, and ἄππα] in Suidas. The former is [πρὸς πατέρα σπουδαία φωνή], a respectful voice addressed to a father. Hence [παππαππός]. The scholiast on Homer's Odyssey 6 has [πάππα φίλ] and so on: a kindly address, father to father. On book 18 he has [παππάζοι], [παππα φωνεῖ, παππα κακῶς], that is, "he says pappa, pappa, badly." Pappos, and trembling grandmothers, in Ausonius. It is foolish to think that Papam, by the force of the word, as if from [ἀπαλλάσσω] or the like, means "Father of Fathers." The Gloss says so in its preface, and Clement, Remigius of Auxerre, in On the Celebration of the Mass, Hosius in his Confession of Faith, and others hold it. The ancients also said mamma. Mammas atq; Tatas habet Afra, says Martial in a book.

units.la: 1 Alii nomen Papae à Veteri scriptione derivât quasi P.P. vel Pa. Pa. imperitia hinc unam voculam fecerit. Videsis Corasium Miscell. Iuris lib. v. c. xv. Christoph. Landinus, ad Dantis Aligeri Comœdiam, de Inferno, cant. vii. ubi Pluto exclamat:

units.la: Papè est interjectio admirantis, cioè è voce che dimostra maraviglia, onde il sommo Pontefice, come cosa maravigliosissima tra Christiani è chiamato Papa. Exi-stimat, Papam propter admirationem ita dici, ut rem maxime admirandam, quemadmodum papae interjectio est admirantis. Si non ad etymologiam, ad rem saltem vere satis. Scio quidem Episcopis aliquando datum olim elogium, quo supra alios agnoscebantur, Patris Patrum ; sed non Hormisdae hoc solum, quem Baronius isto adducit, in Martyrologio, ad diem Ianuarii x. verum etiam Alexandrinus ita appellatus fuit, παπὰ παπίμων. Commune primis seculis nomen fuisse Episcoporum, ex epistolis Cypriani, Gregorii Thaumaturgi, Hieronymi, Augustini, Prosperi, Sidonii, aliorumque, notius est, quam ut dici debeat. Cypriano Papæ, presbyteri & Diaconi Roma consistentes scribunt: quæ epistola apud Cyprianum est lib. vii. Sed hic certò scio neminem à splendido risu temperaturum, qui, ubi epistola illa citatur in jure Pontificio I Dist. L.c. absit. Glossam viderit torquentem, ut Cyprianum aliquem in Catalogo Romanorum Pontificum reperiat, quasi nemo aliter Papa dicatur, ubi tamen & hic, & c. De eo, eadem distin&. videt Papam dici Cypriani, & hanc tandem crisin suam interponit: sed forte hæc & ibi mendosa est littera. Lepidum caput, & gnaviter in scriptis veterum, vel Cypriani versatum sc. Gregorio vii. a. clb lxxiii: in Concilio Romano adscribunt Papales, quod adversus schismaticos statuerit, Papæ nomen non ultra commune esse aliis, sed solius Romani proprium. Digna lane res, quæ non ab alio instituereatur, quam ab homine, quem ipsi Romanenses
units.tr: Papè is an interjection of one admiring, that is, a word showing wonder, whence the supreme Pontiff, as a most wonderful thing among Christians, is called Pope. He thinks the Pope is so called from admiration, as a thing greatly to be admired, just as pape is an interjection of admiring. If this is not right for the etymology, it is at least true enough for the thing itself. I know indeed that a title was once given to bishops by which they were recognised above others, Father of Fathers. Not only Hormisdas, whom Baronius cites from the Martyrology at 10 January, was so called, but also the Alexandrian was called [παπὰ παπίμων]. That the name was common to bishops in the first centuries is better known than it needs to be said, from the letters of Cyprian, Gregory Thaumaturgus, Jerome, Augustine, Prosper, Sidonius and others. The Popes Cyprian, presbyters and deacons residing at Rome write: this letter is in Cyprian, book 7. But here I know for certain that no one will refrain from a loud laugh, who, when this letter is cited in Pontifical law, Dist. 50, c. Absit, has seen the Gloss twisting to find some Cyprian in the catalogue of Roman Pontiffs, as if no one else were ever called Pope. Yet here too, and in c. De eo, of the same distinction, it sees Pope said of Cyprian, and at last it interposes this judgement of its own: but perhaps this letter is faulty here. A charming point, and cleverly handled by someone well versed in the writings of the ancients or of Cyprian: the Papalists ascribe to Gregory VII, in the year 1073, that at a Roman council, against the schismatics, he decreed that the name Pope was no longer common to others but belonged only to the Roman. This is a fine matter, not to be settled by anyone other than the man whom the Romans themselves

units.la: pro monstro & Dæmone verius, quam Episcopo habent, cui dixerint, uti apud Ottonem Frisingensem est, in initio librorum ejus de gestis Frederici I. Ænobarbi: sicut hactenus solebas dicere, quod nullus vestrum esset episcopus, ita scias quod nulli nostrum deinceps eris apostolicus. Neque in isto homine præcipitantiam admiramur, qui nó alia arte ad sedem pervenerat, quin eâ horâ, qua prædecessor ejus Alexander defunctus erat, seipsum, sine assensu cleri & populi, ut author est Benno, Cardinalium archipresbyter, in cujus vita, inthronizavit; & perquam facete Abbati Cassinensi advenienti inquiens: frater nimium tardasti: hoc responsum ab illo audiit: Et tu Hildebrande nimium festinasti. Ab isto, & in Romano aliquo Concilabulo, constitutum teneant reliqui Romani Episcopi, ut Papæ, (scilicet ad denotandum, in cujus nomine veniant, appelletur. Plane quemadmodum nomen tyranni, primum in bonam partem sumtum, in communi Regem denotavit, ὡς τύραννος ἴση; postea vero injustis atque improbis Regibus ita proprium mansit, ut eo Regem denominare aliquem pessime nunc audiat. Sunt qui à Gregorio III. qui Syrus erat, & a. DCCXXIX scidit, quippe Syri Abba Patrè dicunt, sed temerè, derivant. Neque quod putant, hoc tamen pacto Romani obtinuerunt: nam & Græci Patriarchæ hodie etiam sic Papas scribut. Patriarcha Alexandr. Ioachim, in litteris a. MDXXX sexto anno... Alberto Comiti à Lewenstein datis apud Chytræum, de statu ecclesiarum, in Gracia; Ὁ μέγας ... Testor ego Ioachim, Papa & Patriarcha magnæ urbis Alexandriæ, & Iudex orbis &c. & in subscriptione, ... Iudex orbis, ab ipso Romano etiam audit, ob litem, ejus delatam arbitrio feliciter aliquando compositam. Quæ nostri ad Bellarminum lib. II. de Romano Pontif. cap. xxxi. super illa Papæ appellatione, disputarunt, prætereo.
units.tr: regard as a monster and a demon rather than a bishop. They said to him, as is recorded in Otto of Freising at the beginning of his books on the deeds of Frederick I Barbarossa: As you have hitherto been accustomed to say that none of you was a bishop, so know that none of us shall henceforth be apostolic. Nor do we wonder at the rashness of this man, who reached the seat by no other art. At the very hour his predecessor Alexander died, he enthroned himself without the assent of clergy and people, as Benno, archpriest of the Cardinals and author of his life, reports. Very wittily, when the Abbot of Monte Cassino arrived, he said: "Brother, you have been too slow." He heard this reply from him: "And you, Hildebrand, have been too quick." From him, and from some Roman conventicle, the remaining Roman bishops hold it established that the one who comes in the name of the Pope should be so called, namely to denote in whose name they come. Just as the name tyrant, first taken in a good sense, came to denote a king in general, [ὡς τύραννος ἴση], so afterwards it remained so proper to unjust and wicked kings that it now sounds very bad to call any king by that name. There are those who derive the name from Gregory III, who was a Syrian and died in 739, since the Syrians say Abba for father; but they derive it rashly. Nor did the Romans obtain the name in the way they imagine. For the Greek patriarchs even today also write Pope in this way. The Patriarch of Alexandria, Joachim, in a letter of 1530, sixth year, given to Count Albert of Löwenstein, is quoted in Chytraeus, On the State of the Churches in Greece: "I, Joachim, Pope and Patriarch of the great city of Alexandria, and Judge of the world, testify," and so on. In the subscription he is styled Judge of the world. Even the Roman himself hears this name, on account of a suit referred to his arbitration and happily settled at some time. What our writers argued against Bellarmine on this name Pope, in book 2, On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 31, I pass over.

units.la: IV. Sanctissimi Domini N.) Hoc, si quippiam, est contra præceptum Domini istud, Matth. xxiii. 8. Vos autem ne appellemini Rabbi: nempe ejusmodi ne quis insignatur titulis vult, qui fastum, qui ambitionem spirant & supra alios arrogantiam; Christi discipulis tantopere prohibitam, quique quod nulli hominum adscribendum, comprehendunt. Christus Patrem allocuturus, ait: Sancte Pater, Ioann. xvii. 11. cujus Vicarius scilicet non nisi sanctissimus dici, & salutari amat.
units.tr: IV. Most holy Lord N.) This, if anything, runs against the Lord's precept in Matth. xxiii. 8: But you must not be called Rabbi. Such a man wants to be marked with titles, breathes pride and ambition and arrogance above others, which Christ forbade so strictly to his disciples, and claims for himself what belongs to no human being. When Christ is about to address the Father, he says: Holy Father, John xvii. 11. Yet his Vicar, it seems, loves to be called and greeted only as most holy.

units.la: V. Innocentii X.) Hic antea dictus Pamphilius. quem mutandi nominis usum à Sergio II. derivant plurimi, qui cum prius Os porci appellaretur, ob deformitatem nominis mutare vocabulum coactus, le Sergium appellari fecit, a. DCCCXLIX. Unde mutandorum nominum consuetudo sumta est, inquit Stella: refert & Platina, qui addit, ab omnibus id non fuisse observatum. Onuphrius autem, primum qui nomen suum, cum adepto Pontificatu mutarit, censet fuisse, non forte Sergium istum, sed Ioannem XII. illo, seculo integro posteriorem. Nostras Adrianus P. nomen suum retinuit, non mutavit cum accepto Papatu. Pamphiliorum familiam ad dignitates ecclesiasticas primus evexit Innocentius VIII. Genuensis, ex familia Cibonum, τῶν κύων; Graecae siquidem prosapiae erant, atque à cubis in insigni positis, graeco nomine originis suae monumentum servare voluerunt. Hinc & hodie Cardinalis Cibo intimae admissionis apud Papam est. Innocentius X. Romanus natione, Neapoli Nuncius, atque episcopus antea fuit, ubi cum totâ suâ familiâ, & fratre, ejusque uxore, aliquamdiu degit: ante Papatum, quem accepit a.
