MDCXLIV. appellatus Iohannes Baptista Pamphilius. Quid vero eum ad Pontificatum evexerit, incertum, nisi forte aliorum dissensiones, & Gallorum, Hispanorumque obversae sibi invicem factiones dum in alium convenire nequeunt, hujus illud faverit fortunae. Et vos quid tandem meritorum in me comperistis, quem Christianae Reip. principem constitueretis? respondebat Cardinalibus, frementibus quod indigno homini, Simiae appellato, quia in familia simiae curam gessisset, galerum suum tradidisset Pontifex factus Iulius III. refert Thuanus, lib. vi. Quum in locum Clementis surrogaretur Paulus V. valde pro Bellarmino in conclavi clamitabat Baronius: faciamus Bellarminum Papam, is sanctus est. Sanctimoniâ commendatum Innocentium fuisse, ut elieligeretur, non dicet ejus Olimpia, neque Cardinalis Palotta. Scilicet, ut sui nominis Innocentium VIII. haud male referat, de quo istud Epigramma.
units.tr: V. Of Innocent X.) He was formerly called Pamphilius. Most people derive the custom of changing one's name from Sergius II, who, because he was first called Pig's Snout and was forced by the ugliness of that name to change it, had himself called Sergius, in the year 849. From this the custom of changing names was taken up, says Stella. Platina also reports it, adding that not everyone observed it. Onuphrius, however, thinks the first to change his name on obtaining the papacy was not perhaps that Sergius but John XII, a full century later. Our Pope Adrian kept his own name and did not change it on receiving the papacy. The first to raise the Pamphili family to ecclesiastical dignities was Innocent VIII of Genoa, of the Cibo family, of the dogs [τῶν κύων]. For they were of Greek descent, and from the whelps set in their coat of arms they wished to keep a memorial of their origin in a Greek name. Hence even today Cardinal Cibo enjoys the Pope's close confidence. Innocent X, a Roman by birth, was formerly Nuncio at Naples and also a bishop, and lived there for some time with his whole family, his brother and his brother's wife. Before the papacy, which he received in 1644, he was called John Baptist Pamphilius. What raised him to the papacy is uncertain, unless perhaps the dissensions of others, and the rival factions of the French and the Spanish, which could not agree on anyone else, favoured this man by chance. "What merits of mine have you finally found, that you should make me prince of the Christian commonwealth?" he answered the Cardinals, who raged that the Pope, once made, had handed his galero to an unworthy man, called Monkey because he had looked after a monkey in his household. So Julius III, as de Thou reports, book vi. When Paul V was put in place of Clement, Baronius cried out loudly in the conclave in favour of Bellarmine: Let us make Bellarmine Pope; he is holy. That Innocent was recommended for his holiness, so that he was chosen, his Olimpia will not say, nor Cardinal Palotta. Clearly, so that one may aptly call to mind Innocent VIII of his name, about whom this epigram was written.

units.la: Quid quaris testes, sit mas, an fæmina Cibo
units.tr: Why ask for witnesses whether Cibo is male or female?

units.la: Respice natorum progenia certa gregem.
units.tr: Look at the sure progeny of his offspring, a flock.

units.la: Tanti quippe est, ne in oblivionem abeant famosa ista Prędecessorum exempla, Pauli III. iuxtaque Laurę ; Ioannis XXIII. Benedicti XII. Clementis V. Ioannis XI. & iuxta Theodorę : Sergii III. cum suâ Marozią : ne Sixtum IV. aut Alexandrum VI. aliosque istius commatis memorem. De qualibus Bellarminus ipse ingenuè, in Præfat. ad libros, de Romano Pontifice, ait, permisisse Deum, Ut etiam quidam parum probi Pontifices aliquando hanc sedem tenerent & regerent. Quales sane fuerunt Stephanus VI. quales Leo V. Christophorus I. Sergius III. Iohannes XII. Alexander VI. aliique non pauci &c. Quis Romæ nunc filiam Pamphilii ignorat, quam vis non pro illâ dignitate, quam nunc parens Innocentius obtinet, opulenter vel liberaliter habitam? unde, mutato nomine, illi merito antiquum illud epigramma, in Paulum II. olim compositum, adscribas: Pontificis Pauli testes ne Roma requiras, Filia quem similis sua docet esse marem. Sanctum non possum, patrem te dicere possum, Cum video natam Paulé sedere tuam.
units.tr: Such is the scale of the matter that these notorious examples of his predecessors must not be forgotten: Paul III and his Laura, John XXIII, Benedict XII, Clement V, John XI, and Theodora; Sergius III with his Marozia. I need not mention Sixtus IV or Alexander VI or others of that kind. Of such men Bellarmine himself frankly says, in the Preface to his books on the Roman Pontiff, that God permitted that some Popes of little probity sometimes held and governed this see. Such indeed were Stephen VI, Leo V, Christopher I, Sergius III, John XII, Alexander VI, and not a few others, etc. Who in Rome does not now know the daughter of Pamphili, who, though not held in that dignity which her father Innocent now holds, is treated lavishly and generously? So, with the name changed, you may fitly ascribe to him that old epigram written long ago against Paul II: "Do not seek witnesses in Rome to Pope Paul, whom his daughter, like him, shows to be a man. I cannot call you holy, but I can call you father, when I see your daughter sitting in Paul's place."

units.la: Marcellum II. scribit Onuphrius, in ejus vitâ, & Thuanus, lib. xv. revocatis ei in memoriam Hadriani IV. verbis, quibus miseram Pontificum Rom. conditionem deplorabat, mensâ manu percussâ subjeciisse; non videre se, quomodo qui fastigium hoc altissimum tenerent, saluti suæ consulere possent. Quis nobis dicet, quid animi sit hodie Innocentius? Pius V. quod dixerit statim ut Papa factus erat: ego, quamdiu fui Religiosus, bene speravi de mea salute, factus Cardinalis cœpi timere, jam creatus Pontifex pæne de ea despero, referunt Papistæ ipsi, & allegat Cornelius à Lapide, in Ecclesiastic. xxxii. 1. & Apoc. iii. 1. Eò ipsè tare exiftimo, quod Erasmus, quantumvis etiam dilectus Leoni P. filius, de eo scripsit in Commentario, ad Psalm. ii. Sic Leonem dedecimum, quum omnia Romæ perstreperent triumphis & gratulationibus, subito mors exemerit rebus humanis, quo transfulerit, incertum. Et Henricus Albi, inter Elogia Cardinalium, de Bellarmino adducit, quod posteaquam præteritus in electione fuisset, deinceps Litaniis suis hoc sigillatim addiderit, quod Deus ipsum à Papatu liberaslet. Nequáquam ego dubito, quin haud paulo aliter animatus sit noster Innocentius. Et tamen in coronatione Papæ Prior Episcoporum Cardinalium solet dicere, cum violenter ad istum locum protrahi: in oratione, eique universæ Christianitatis molem super humeros impositisti, respice quæsumus propitius hunc famulum tuum N. quem de humili Cathedra violenter sublimatum in thronum ejusdem Apostolorum principis sublimamus. Atque ita Innocentius, vel Ioh. Bapt. Pamphilius, Romanus natione, Papa factus est, scilicet, non nisi de Paradyso Italiæ is sumendus, uti adversus Alexandrum II. ab illis qui Cadulum Parmensem episcopum petebant, olim dicebatur. Innocentius Papa Decimus, ad perpetuam rei memoriam) Memoriam, lege, infamiam, & verior erit sensus. Miror autem quod hic nusquam occurrat titulus ille solennis, servus servorum; nisi pro simplicitate sua fastidiat Innocentius stolidam istam hypocrisin, ut servus servorum dicatur, ubi ad ferendas Imperatoribus, Regibus, totique adeo Christiano orbi leges se accingebat. Imo jamdudum omnibus sanæ mentis risum debuit ille titulus, non minus ac alterum illud quod inter solemnia coronati Pontificis usurpatur, ut, quando à sibi assistente Camerario nummorum quantum pugnus capit, lumens inter spargendum dicit: argentum & aurum non est mihi. Videlicet:
units.tr: Onuphrius writes in the life of Marcellus II, and de Thou in book xv., that when the words of Adrian IV were recalled to him, in which he lamented the wretched condition of the Roman Pontiffs, he struck the table with his hand and said: I do not see how those who hold this highest pinnacle can look to their own salvation. Who will tell us what Innocent is thinking today? Pius V, as soon as he became Pope, said: While I was a religious I hoped well for my salvation; when I became a Cardinal I began to fear; now that I am created Pope, I almost despair of it. The Papists themselves report this, and Cornelius à Lapide cites it on Ecclesiasticus xxxii. 1 and Rev. iii. 1. I think the more of this because Erasmus, although a son much loved by Pope Leo, wrote of him in his Commentary on Psalm ii.: So when all Rome rang with triumphs and congratulations, Leo X was suddenly taken from human affairs by death; where he went is uncertain. And Henry Albi, among the Elogia of the Cardinals, cites of Bellarmine that after he had been passed over in the election, he thereafter added to his litanies, singly, that God had freed him from the papacy. I have no doubt that our Innocent is no less disturbed in spirit. Yet at the coronation of a Pope the Prior of the Cardinal Bishops is accustomed to say, as he is dragged violently to that place, in the prayer: You have placed the mass of the whole Christian world upon his shoulders; look mercifully, we pray, upon this your servant N., whom we raise, violently lifted from the humble chair, to the throne of the same prince of the Apostles. And so Innocent, or John Baptist Pamphilius, a Roman by birth, became Pope. Clearly one must take him only from the Paradise of Italy, as was once said against Alexander II by those who sought Cadulus, bishop of Parma. Innocent, Pope the Tenth, to the perpetual memory of the matter) Read infamy for memory, and the sense will be truer. I wonder, however, that the customary title servant of servants does not occur here anywhere. Perhaps Innocent, in his simplicity, disdains that foolish hypocrisy of being called servant of servants, when he is girding himself to lay down laws for Emperors and Kings and indeed the whole Christian world. In fact that title should long ago have been a laughing matter for all sane people, no less than that other one which is used among the solemnities of a crowned Pontiff: when the chamberlain standing by gives him as much money as his fist can hold, he says as he scatters it: Silver and gold are not mine. Clearly:

units.la: Servientant tibi Roma prius Domini Dominorum:
units.tr: Let Rome first serve you as Lord of Lords:

units.la: Servorum servi nunc tibi sunt Domini.
units.tr: Now the servants of servants are your lords.

units.la: VI. Zelo Domus Dei animum nostrum commovente.) Quid Dei? nostra dicere debueras. Neque quæ alia horum ausuum turbarumque, & ea satis nota, obviaque causa: pro innata aula R. præposttera ambitione, ut his Thuani verbis utar, quæ is habet, histor. lib. xx. in fine. Hæc Papæ animum cura angit mordetque unica, imperare omnibus, & jubere ut ad suum nutum tum, & commodum quecunque fiant,& vel stent, vel cadant. Nihil æque sudat, quam ut fedis suæ fastigium semper altius evehat, & bella atque ignes in omnia terrarum loca, in regna, imperia, & Dei domū immittat,pro coronâ suâ,& ventre,quibus non melius consulitur, quam Principibus inter se cómiffis & belligerantibus. Centies mori fe malle, & subjectis mundo per quatuor ejus plagas facibus, incendium rerū omnium ruinâ restinguere,quam loci sui dignitatem minus curare, sæpius auditus fuit dicere,P.Paulus IV. Vtcumque videantur aliquando magis pacifici, & quietis amatores, at ubi rei aliquid agitur, quod quacunque ratione ad se putant trahi posse, vel in quo videtur læsa ipsorum ambitio & majestas, anti-Apostolica illa atque anti-Christiana, hic tumultuare,damnare, ad arma & viros conclamare, & nec superis parcere, neque inferis. Innocentium VIII. scribit Stella, Sacerdos Venetus, in lib. de Vitis & Gestis Pontificum, ad pacem colendam præ reliquis fuisse propensum: nec tamen bellum dissuadebat,cum pro tutela Ecclesiastica ditionis suscipiendum foret. Haud scio quo pacto fit, inquit Erasmus, ut Pontificum autoritas longe plus valeat ad excitandum inter principes bellum, quam ad componendum? in præf. lib. de Conscribendis epist. Sequitur in Bulla Innocentii, agere se hæc, ut VII. Ecclesia Catholica dignitas & auctoritas ubique sarta tecta conservetur) Ecclesiæ Romana dicendum fuerat: nam ne Nostros dicam, qui nominis hujus usurpationem injustam multis doctissimisque scriptis offenderunt, inter Græcos Barlam. lib. de Papæ Principatu, cap. xv. Romana Ecclesia, non unam rem aliquam apud sanctos Patres; sed diversas ac discrepantes sonat. Nam cum Catholicam Ecclesiam dicunt; Christianorum intelligunt cœtum, qui usquam terrarum, de fide recte sentiunt, pietatisque dogmata immota & inconcussa observant. Romanam autem Ecclesiam cum dicunt, ut illam à cæteris in orbe Ecclesiis particularibus distinguant, sic loquuntur. Prout Concilii Carthaginiensis centesimus quartus canon habet, his verbis: De dissensione inter Romanam & Alexandrinam Ecclesiam orta,ad sanctissimum Papam Innocentium scribi placuit; ut utraque Ecclesia inter se pacem & concordiam colat,quam Domi-miminus praecipit. Iam vero pro Catholica Ecclesia, Romanam nemo unquam dixit. Catholicam itidem fidem cum dicunt; eam utique intelligunt, quam omnes recte sentientes Christianam ubicunque locorum profitentur. Christianam autem fidem, Romanam nemo sana mentis dixit. Quinimo non in Romanam aut fidem aut Ecclesiam; sed in Catholicam, seu universalem, atque communem fidem & Ecclesiam credere nobis praeceperunt.
units.tr: VI. Moved by zeal for the house of God.) Of God? You should have said "ours." Nor is there any other cause of these undertakings and disturbances, and a well-known and obvious one: the innate and preposterous ambition of the Roman court, to use de Thou's words, which he gives in Histories, book xx. at the end. This one care vexes and gnaws at the Pope's mind: to command everyone, and to order that whatever is done, whether it stands or falls, be done at his nod and for his convenience. He sweats at nothing so much as raising the summit of his see ever higher, and sending wars and fires into every part of the earth, into kingdoms, empires and the house of God, for the sake of his crown and his belly, for which nothing is better served than by Princes set against one another and at war. Paul IV was often heard to say that he would rather die a hundred times, and, with the world subjected to torches on all four of its quarters, quench the conflagration of all things in general ruin, than care less for the dignity of his place. However much they may sometimes seem more peaceful and lovers of quiet, yet when something is afoot which they think can be drawn to themselves by any means, or in which their own ambition and majesty seem injured, that anti-Apostolic and anti-Christian spirit storms, condemns, cries out to arms and men, and spares neither the heavenly nor the infernal. Stella, a Venetian priest, writes in his book on the Lives and Deeds of the Popes that Innocent VIII was more inclined than the rest to cultivate peace: yet he did not dissuade from war when it had to be undertaken for the defence of ecclesiastical dominion. I do not know how it happens, says Erasmus, that the authority of the Popes is far more effective in stirring up war among princes than in composing it? In the preface to his book On Writing Letters. There follows in Innocent's Bull that he does these things so that VII. the dignity and authority of the Catholic Church be preserved intact everywhere.) It should have said "of the Roman Church." For, not to mention our own writers, who have offended against this unjust usurpation of the name with many learned writings, among the Greeks Barlaam, book On the Papal Principate, ch. xv., says: The Roman Church does not signify one particular thing among the holy Fathers, but different and discordant things. For when they say Catholic Church, they mean the assembly of Christians who anywhere on earth think rightly about the faith and keep the doctrines of piety fixed and unshaken. But when they say Roman Church, to distinguish it from the other particular churches in the world, they speak thus, as the hundred and fourth canon of the Council of Carthage has it, in these words: Concerning the dissension that arose between the Roman and the Alexandrian Church, it has been resolved to write to the most holy Pope Innocent, so that each church may cultivate peace and concord among themselves, as the Lord commands. Now indeed no one has ever called the Roman Church the Catholic Church. Likewise, when they say Catholic faith, they certainly mean that which all who think rightly profess as Christian wherever they are. Nobody of sound mind has called the Christian faith Roman. Indeed, they have taught us to believe not in a Roman faith or Church, but in the Catholic, or universal, and common faith and Church.

units.la: VIII. Eorum, qui quaerunt sua potius, quam quae Dei sunt.) Nescio qui illud hic in fronte occurrat, quod plurimos scio dicere solitos Papis & curiae Papali, ubi eis suam exprobrant ambitionem, id est, vere describunt.
units.tr: VIII. Of those who seek their own things rather than the things that are of God.) I do not know what this heading is that meets me here. I know that very many have been accustomed to say it of the Popes and the Papal court, when they reproach them for their ambition; that is, they describe them truly.

units.la: E multis, ita loquitur Fridericus I. Imp. epist. ad Episcopos Transmontanos, qua eos vocat ad Concilium Papiense, ob negotium vel schisma duorum Paparum, Victoris IV. & Alexandri III. Defuncto itaque Adriano Papa in Calend. Septembris, Cardinales, qui columnae immobiles esse videbantur, quibus sancta & universalis firmissime inniteretur Ecclesia, non quae Dei sunt, sed sua quarentes &c.
units.tr: Among many examples, Frederick I, Emperor, speaks thus in his letter to the bishops beyond the Alps, by which he summons them to the Council of Pavia, on account of the business or schism of the two Popes, Victor IV and Alexander III: Therefore, Pope Hadrian having died on the first of September, the cardinals, who seemed to be the immovable pillars on which the holy and universal Church firmly leaned, seeking not the things that are God's but their own, etc.

units.la: IX. Ecclesiastica, quorum Assertores a Domino constituti sumus.) Tene Deus? imo, quomodo Deus quos ἱέρω εἰς ἐρῆν, Pharaonem, luisque similes, in id te suscitavi, ut in te ostendam potentiam meam, & nomen meum annuncietur per omnem terram.Rom ix. 17. Tu in Ecclesia? imo, sed uti Apostolus loquitur. II Thess. II.4. in domo Dei ut Deum sedentem, gerentem se ut Deum. Cujus explicatio non ab aliis, quam ipsis Papis petenda. Extravag. Ioannis xxii. tit. xiv. de verb. signific. cap. iv. Gloss. in verb. declaramus. ex editione Lugdunensi A. 1616. Credere Dominum Deum nostrum Papam conditorem dicta decretalis & ipsius, sic non potuisse statuere, haereticum censeretur. Sixto IV. & merito in terris crederis esse Deus. Gregorio XIII. Iaponenses, ex instigatione Iesuitarum, ita litteras suas inscribunt, apud Thuanum, lib. lxxxi. Adorando, & coeli Regis locum in terris obtinenti magno & sanctissimo PP. Reddatur epistola magno illi & Sancto Domino, quem adoro Dei vices gerentem. In alia: Sublatis manibus adorans offero haec Sanctiss. D. P.P. magno Dei vices gerenti. Stapletonus, in dedicatione lib. Princip. fid. doct. supremum plane, supremum in terris numen. Ne alia a Nostris infinities
units.tr: IX. Ecclesiastical, of whom we are appointed by the Lord as defenders.) Do you hold God? No indeed, but how does God treat those whom [ἐξήγειρά σε], Pharaoh and others like him? For this very purpose have I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth. Rom. 9:17. Do you hold the Church? No indeed, but as the Apostle speaks: in the house of God, as God sitting, showing himself as God. II Thess. 2:4. Its explanation must be sought not from others but from the Popes themselves. Extravagants of John XXII, title 14, On the meaning of words, chapter 4, gloss on the word we declare, from the Lyon edition of 1616: To believe that our Lord God the Pope, the founder of the said decretal and of himself, could not have so decided, would be counted heretical. To Sixtus IV: and rightly you are believed to be God on earth. To Gregory XIII: the Japanese, at the instigation of the Jesuits, so address their letters, according to Thuanus, book 81: To the great and most holy Lord, who holds on earth the place of the King of heaven, let this letter be delivered; to that great and holy Lord, whom I adore as the vicar of God. In another: With hands raised, adoring, I offer these things to his most holy Lordship the Pope, the great vicar of God. Stapleton, in the dedication of his book Principiorum fidei doctrinalium: the supreme plainly, the supreme deity on earth. Lest I repeat here on the same point the many other things our side has countless times brought forward.

units.la: hic adducta eandem in rem hic repetas. Miratus fui, quod non legerem hic, ad majorem sibi conciliandam authoritatem, Innocentium dicere se, consueto Papis titulo, Dei vicarium: sed titulo, ne Nos dicam, ipsis Iudaeis jam pridem notato, damnatoque. Sic quippe Menasse ben Israel, Iudaeus, & hodiernorum Iudaeorum facile doctissimus, explicans illud Zachariae Prophetae: & super virum socium meum, inquit: Id est, super eum, qui se putat Deo proximum & aequalem esse. Paulo post: Vel potius de Papa Romano capiendum est, qui se pastorem, & proximum a Deo appellat & Dei vicarium interris audire vult. Contra illum, similesque illi, qui potestate sunt inferiores, Deus bellum suscitabit. Pauli V. haec sunt: Paulo V. Vice Deo, Christiana Resp. Monarcha invictissimo, & Pontificia omnipotentia conservatori acerrimo. Hoc est, non Assertorem Ecclesiae esse, sed sui fastus ac arrogantiae.
units.tr: I was surprised that he did not here, to win for himself greater authority, call himself, by the customary title of the Popes, not the vicar of God, but by a title, not to say a name, already long since noted and condemned even by the Jews. For thus Menasseh ben Israel, a Jew and the most learned of today's Jews, explaining that passage of the prophet Zechariah, against the man who is my companion, says: That is, against him who thinks himself near to God and equal to him. A little after: Or rather it should be understood of the Roman Pope, who calls himself shepherd and one near to God, and wishes to be heard as the vicar of God on earth. Against him and those like him, who are inferior in power, God will stir up war. These are the words of Paul V: To Paul V, Vice-God, most unconquered monarch of the Christian commonwealth, and most fierce preserver of papal omnipotence. That is to say, he is not the defender of the Church but of his own pride and arrogance.

units.la: X. Sane cum intimo doloris sensu accepimus, quod per plures annos Osnabrugis die 6. Augusti A. 1648. inter charissimum in Christo filium nostrum Ferdinandum Romanorum Regem & Imperatorem electum cum suis foederatis, & Adherentibus ex una, ac Suecos cum eorum itidem foederatis & Adherentibus ex altera, nec non alterius Pacis Monasterii Westphal. die 24. Octobris ejusdem A. 48. inter eundem Ferdinandum Romanorum Regem & Imperatorem electum cum suis pariter foederatis & adherentibus ex una, atque charissimum etiam in Christo filium nostrum Ludovicum Francorum Regem Christianissimum cum suis similiter foederatis ex altera partibus respective instarum.) Conqueritur pacem factam bonus sc. Innocentius, cum intimo doloris sensu, etiam quae non nisi per plures annos obtineri potuit; videlicet hoc est, pacis filium, atque innocentem esse. Quid ad ipsum, quod Principes, ex bono Reip. consulunt, decernunt, agunt? Non est sine culpa, qui rei, quae ad eum non pertinet, se immiscet, legit ipse inter Regulas Iuris, sui Bonifacii VIII. Dolet pacem idam inter Imperatorem, & Suecum; tum inter Imperatorem, & Gallum. Non ergo sola est haeresis alterius partis, quae eum commoveat, Tros Rutilusve suat, quem sola sua exagitat ambitio, & inquies dominandi turbandique animus vel genius. Cumque illa Capita in partes traxerint reliquos Europæi orbis Principes, ac Status, gauderet Innocentius commissos illos iterum cernere; & hoc agere eum ut assequatur, palam hic profitetur, & per varias ab eo partes tentari, jam omnes experiuntur. In aqua turbulentiori novit sibi semper feliciorem obtingere piscationem, & ex ruinis aliorum, ut Romæ olim, ita sedis suæ pendere incrementum. Gregorius de Heimburg, qui scripsit sub Friderico III. Admonitionem de Papar. Romanorum usurpationibus, part. II, ubi de Henrico IV. loquitur de Cardinalibus & Papa: timentes, inquit, se optatum dominium in Imperium consequi non posse, nisi procuratus dissensionibus in Germanica natio, tunc potentissima. De Alexandro VI. non ignorat Innocentius, quid olim scriptum sit: Libidinosa sanguinis captus siti, Tot civitates inclytas, Tot regna vertit, tot duces letho dedit: Natos ut impleat suos.
units.tr: X. Indeed, with a deep sense of grief we have learned that for many years, at Osnabrück on 6 August 1648, between our most beloved son in Christ Ferdinand, King of the Romans and elected Emperor, with his confederates and adherents on the one side, and the Swedes with their confederates and adherents on the other; and likewise at the Peace of Münster in Westphalia on 24 October of the same year 1648, between the same Ferdinand, King of the Romans and elected Emperor, with his confederates and adherents on the one side, and our most beloved son in Christ Louis, the most Christian King of the French, with his confederates on the other, respective parties. The good Innocent complains that the peace was made with a deep sense of grief, even though it could be obtained only after many years; that is, he is a son of peace and is innocent. What is it to him that princes consult, decree and act for the good of the commonwealth? He is not without fault who meddles in a matter that does not concern him: he reads this himself among the Rules of Law, in the Sext of his Boniface VIII. He grieves that peace was made between the Emperor and the Swede, and then between the Emperor and the Frenchman. So it is not only the heresy of the other party that stirs him: whether Trojan or Rutulian, it is all one to him, and it is his own ambition alone that vexes him, and the restless spirit or genius of dominating and disturbing. Since those heads have drawn the remaining princes and states of the European world into parties, Innocent would rejoice to see them bound together again; and that he is working to bring this about he openly professes here, and all now experience how he is tried by various parts of him. In troubled water he knows his fishing is always more favourable, and, as once at Rome, so the growth of his see depends on the ruins of others. Gregory of Heimburg, who wrote under Frederick III, Admonition on the Usurpations of the Roman Popes, part II, where he speaks of Henry IV, about the cardinals and the Pope: fearing, he says, that they cannot attain the desired dominion over the Empire, unless the German nation, then most powerful, has been stirred up into dissensions. Concerning Alexander VI, Innocent is not unaware of what was once written: Captive of a lustful thirst for blood, he overturned so many famous cities, so many kingdoms, gave so many dukes to death, that he might enrich his sons.

units.la: & in Iulium II. Concitat iratum bellator Iulius orbem, Efferapacificos induit arma duces, Tela dat Italia, tibi dat Germania bellum: Hoc turbante, domo prodit Ibera quies.
units.tr: And of Julius II: The warrior Julius stirs the angry world; he dresses peaceful leaders in arms. Italy gives you weapons, Germany gives you war; with him stirring, Iberian peace has gone forth from home.

units.la: Ferdinandum Imp. ut & Francorum Regem appellat filios suos: nempe ipse Pater, fratres quidem habet, sed Cardinales; Imperatores vero & Reges, filios suos. Ita Papæ, cujus nempe est Status, & dignitatum ordines diribere, Cardinalis Imperatore, ac Rege superior est. Quin & Episcopum Neritonensem, nuncium suum, hic fratrem dicit. Exinde titulus Cardinalium, ab Vrbano VIII. datus, Eminentissimorum. Nempe hi sunt Principes sub Domino nostro Iesu Christo, & ejus in terris Vicario constituti, non super hac vel illa civitate vel Provincia, sed super Gentes & Regna, ac super omnem terram, loquitur de iis noster Rovenius, lib. 1. Reip. Christiana, cap. xv. Atque ideo Cardinales dicti, quod ceu cardines sunt, super quos totus vertatur orbis, juxta id: Domini enim sunt cardines terræ, & posuit super eos orbem. 1. Sam. 11. Et Papa, quum eos creat, sic alloquitur: ad Collegium Apostolicum vocati Consiliarii nostri, & conjudices orbis terrarum eritis: ita Pius II. quando primos suos creavit Cardinales.In antiquo Rhythmo: Ita dicunt Cardinales, ita solent Dii carnales.Alter Cardinales, carpinales, dixit: Conradus, episcopus Moguntinus, in Chronico. Nec aliter Frideric. I. inRescripto, ad P. Vrbanum, eos describit,dicēs:non videmus eos praedicatores; sed praedatores; nō pacis corroboratores, sed pecuniae raptores:atq;ita pafsim alii.Maxima Cardinalium in Ecclesia Romana est potestas,ac dignitas:hinc ad eam Regū fratres & filios assumūt,& promovent potentissimos quosq; ut sc. eā arte sibi habeant devinctos magis obstrictosque Imperatores, Reges, Principes; vel nepotes ac consanguineos suos ad hoc fastigium provehunt, ut supremum quod suis impartiri queunt; vel aliquando etiam ob raras ingenii dotes, eruditionem, folertiam, quosdam in hunc numerum cooptant; haud raro quoque ut numinos, ex vacantibus & venditis beneficiis, lucrentur: unde tales saepe promoveri contingit, qui omnibus pudori sunt & ludibrio. Non dicam Francisцum Rapacciolum, lintearii alicujus filium; vel Iohannem Iacobum Panzirolum, Sartoris; Martium Ginetti, Instītoris; Iulium Mazarinum, cujus parens foro turpiter cesserat; Lelius Falconerius litterarum adeo rudis est, ut vix nomen suum proprium legere vel scribere queat. Franciscus Barberinus adolescens Cardinalis factus est ab Vrbano VIII. cui pedagogum addere opus habuit Ascanium Filomarinum, postea quoque Cardinalem. Atque illi nunc Cardinales rerum potiuntur, atque cum Papa suo omnibus dominantur. Praeter illos quos creant Cardinales, in more habent, ut alios in pectore servent, suo tempore nominandos. Vti Paulus III. quando in tertia Cardinalium creatione, duodecim in ordinem istum cooptassēt,tres alios sibi in pectore reservavit,nominandos per Imperatorem, Regem Francorum, & Remp. Venetam, inquit Onuphrius. Ita quoque Innocentius, in primā quidem creatione Cardinalem Cecchinum cogitabat, sed quem demum in secunda elegit: & alios in gratiam Regis Galliae, puto Mazarinum; vel Hispaniae, ut Montaltum; & Reip. Venetae, BreBregadinum;quos hodie Curia Cardinales habet.Haud abs re erat,quod Sixtus V.datâ hanc in rem Bulla omnibus suæ familiæ declararet Galerum vel non rogatis concedendum esse, propter eximia sc. sua de sede Romana bene merita.Quo major visa Erasmi Rotterodami,sc.Hollandica stoliditas, hâc tantam dignitatem,sponte oblatam renuentis : unde Italus quidã de eo dicere:Erasmum esse sapientê bestiam, qui eo ultrò oblato uti nesciret, quod alii pretio ac precibus adeo ambirent, neq; tamen vel sic impetrarent sæpe. Sed quidquid aliis visum, nunquam desunt qui locum istum percupiant. Quid de nostrate Adriano dices? Episcopus Dertusensis, & Regis Caroli præceptor erat,quando ad purpuram Cardinalitiam à Leone X.proveheretur:& Pontifex à Rege,id quod qui egenas filias in matrimonium elocant ita ut alter eas decenter vestiat,petiit, ut paupertatem illius sublevaret, & præberet unde jam honorificenter pro illo statu & vitæ genere se habere posset:
units.tr: He calls the Emperor Ferdinand, as well as the King of the French, his sons. For the Father himself indeed has brothers, but they are cardinals; the Emperors and Kings are his sons. Thus the Pope, whose it is to arrange the orders of rank and dignity, is superior to the cardinal, the Emperor and the King alike. Indeed he even calls the bishop of Nerito, his nuncio, a brother here. Hence the title of cardinals given by Urban VIII, Most Eminent. Indeed, these are princes under our Lord Jesus Christ, and appointed his vicars on earth, not over this or that city or province, but over the nations and kingdoms and over all the earth, says our Rovenius of them, book 1 of the Christian Commonwealth, chapter 15. And they are therefore called cardinals because they are like the hinges on which the whole world turns, according to that: For the hinges of the earth are the Lord's, and he has set the world upon them. 1 Sam. 11. And the Pope, when he creates them, addresses them thus: Called to the Apostolic college, you will be our counsellors and co-judges of the lands of the world; so Pius II when he created his first cardinals. In an old rhyme: So the cardinals say, so the carnal gods are wont. Another wrote cardinals, carpenters: Conrad, bishop of Mainz, in his Chronicle. Nor did Frederick I describe them otherwise in his rescript to Pope Urban, saying: We see them not as preachers but as plunderers; not as strengtheners of peace but as robbers of money; and so variously others. The greatest power and dignity in the Roman Church belongs to the cardinals. Hence the brothers and sons of kings are taken into it, and they promote the most powerful men, so that by this art they may hold emperors, kings and princes more closely bound to themselves; or they advance their nephews and kinsmen to this height, as the highest thing they can bestow on their own; or sometimes, too, on account of rare gifts of mind, learning and shrewdness, they co-opt some into this number; not seldom, too, they do so for profit from vacant and sold benefices. Whence it happens that such men are often promoted who are a shame and a laughingstock to all. I will not mention Francesco Rapaccioli, son of some linen-weaver; or Giovanni Giacomo Panzirolo, of a tailor; Martio Ginetti, of a schoolmaster; Giulio Mazarini, whose father had shamefully withdrawn from the courts; Lelio Falconieri is so unlettered that he can scarcely read or write his own name. Francesco Barberini, as a youth, was made a cardinal by Urban VIII, and he had to add a tutor for him, Ascanio Filomarino, later also a cardinal. And those cardinals now hold power over affairs, and with their Pope they lord it over everyone. Besides those whom they create cardinals, they have the custom of keeping others in their breast, to be named at a suitable time. Thus Paul III, when in his third creation of cardinals he had co-opted twelve into that order, reserved three others for himself in his breast, to be named by the Emperor, the King of the French and the Venetian Republic, says Onuphrius. So too Innocent, in the first creation, was thinking of Cecchini as cardinal, but in the second he chose him; and others for the favour of the King of France, I think Mazarini, or of Spain, like Montalto, and of the Venetian Republic, Bregadino: whom the Curia today has as cardinals. It was not without reason that Sixtus V, by a bull issued for this purpose, declared to all his household that Galerus was to be granted the dignity even if he had not asked for it, on account of his outstanding services to the Roman see. The Dutch stupidity of Erasmus of Rotterdam seemed all the greater, since he refused this great dignity offered to him of his own accord; whence some Italian said of him: Erasmus is a wise beast, who did not know how to use what was offered him unasked, which others so ambition with money and entreaties, and often do not obtain even so. But whatever others thought, there are never lacking those who long for that place. What will you say of our own Adrian? He was bishop of Tortosa and tutor of King Charles when he was raised to the cardinal's purple by Leo X; and the Pope was asked by the King, as those who marry off their poor daughters ask that another should dress them decently, to relieve his poverty and to provide him with means by which he might then keep himself honourably in that station and manner of life.

units.la: tuum erit deinceps dare operam, ut homo optime de te meritus, magnus nunc vir, & in Magistratu eminenti positus, fortunarum suarum temuitati, vel potius, ut jam id quod est, dicatur, paupertati, qua tot annos ejus vitæ socia nec bella nec placabilis fuit, possit nuncium remittere : atque aliquando tandem, perinde ut illa dignitas postulat, quam tueri debet, laxè ac liberaliter vivere : Scribit ad Carolum Regem Pontifex: estq; inter epistolas Petri Bembi, Pontificis nomine scriptas,lib. xvi. Hunc, si quempiam,cum Martino illo Cardinale compara, quem Bernardus,lib. iv. de Consideratione,ad Eugenium P. ob frugalitatem, paupertatemque tantopere commendat, & Eugenio ob oculos ponit. Sed nostris hominibus,quippe supra modum agrestibus,magnificentius loci istius & pilei dignitatem tuentur atq; æstimant quorumcunque regnorum alii,præsertim Itali. In Concilio Basil. statutum quidê Sess. xxiii. ne plures quam viginti quatuor essent Cardinales; idemq;in Galliis confirmatum sanctione Pragmatica,a.cl ccce xxxviii. à Rege Carolo : sed illius nulla habita ratione. Sixtus IV. & Alexander VI. numerum illum excesserunt: nullus autem impudentior Leone X. qui unâ creatione a. cl
units.tr: It will be your task from now on to see to it that this man, who has deserved very well of you, now a great man and placed in an eminent magistracy, can send away the narrowness of his means, or rather, to say what it really is, his poverty, which has been the companion of his life for so many years, neither warlike nor peaceable, and at last, as that dignity which he must maintain demands, live loosely and generously: So the Pope writes to King Charles, and it is among the letters of Pietro Bembo, written in the Pope's name, book 16. If one must compare anyone with him, compare him with that Cardinal Martin, whom Bernard, book 4 of On Consideration, to Pope Eugenius, commends so highly for his frugality and poverty, and sets before Eugenius' eyes. But our people, being excessively rustic, value and uphold the dignity of this office and of the hat more magnificently than the men of any other kingdoms, especially the Italians. At the Council of Basel it was decreed, session 23, that there should be no more than twenty-four cardinals; the same was confirmed in France by the Pragmatic Sanction of a. cl ccce xxxviii, under King Charles; but no account was taken of it. Sixtus IV and Alexander VI exceeded that number; but none was more shameless than Leo X, who in a single creation, a. cl

units.la: B 3 lxvii alc xvii. fecit Cardinales triginta & unum : inter quos quoque erat noster Adrianus de Trajecto , episcopus Dertusensis in Hispania: adeo ut Leo viderit lxv. Cardinales: quem sequutus Paulus III. habuit Cardinales lxiii. Paulus IV. supremum, qui unquam fuit, attigit numerum Cardinalium lxx. hodie sunt sexaginta & duo. Non excedebant olim numerum liii. Quando crearetur Nicolaus III. non erant nisi septem. Sixtus V. numerum septuagesimum definivit. Clemens VII. epist. ad Franciscum I. ad cujus petitionem creavit Cardinalem Grammontium, antea episcopum Tarbensem, adfert rationem nonnihil istud impedientem, quod paulo ante egregiam Cardinalium turbam fecerat unuaste belle troupe: inter epistolas Principum est, collectas ab Hieronymo Ruscelli, atque ex Italico versas in Gallicum, per Belleforest. Quanti autem gratiam illam æstimet Papa, quid gratiam dico? quando Galeros Cardinalitios, ad Regis, vel Imperatoris petitionem aliquibus confert, satis notū, & pœnitere suum quod tot illos emiserit, quāvis non nisi unum postulasset, Carolus V. testatus fuit in Rescripto, ad Clementis VII. Criminationes, prolixo illo, at vere Imperatorio, dato a.clɔ lɔ xxvi. De pileis autem, diximus unum dunta vas a vestra felicis promotionis exordio a nobis petitum, quem ubi patabamus tam diu differendum, cum esset prima gratia a V. S. manu etiam nostra conscriptis literis petita ac instanter flagitata. Alter vero pileus petitus non fuerat, sed ultro a V. S. oblatus nostroque consensu acceptatus. Sicque alienum censebamus eos nunc pileos tali conditione perstrinxi, quos tamen V. Sanctitatis arbitrio tunc relinquendos putavimus, pollicentes nos de catero pro his nec pro aliis quibuscunque pileis ullam sacturos instantiam. Multa sunt & magna Cardinalium privilegia, quæ ne recenseam, videri quippe possunt, apud Azorium, Institut. Moral. part. II. lib. IV. cap. III. (plures etenim de Cardinalibus, & eorum dignitate scripserunt, Andreas Barbatius, Martinus Landensis, Io. Hieronymus Albanus, Onuphrius Panvinus, præter alios, qui materiam eandem attingunt, ut Bellarminus, de Clericis lib. 1. cap. xvi. Azorius, Rovenius & plurium Card. vitas scripserunt, præter Onuphrium... phrium Panvinum, qui primus illorum historiam, juxta cum Pontificum, recensuit; Aubery, Gallus, à Leone IX. a. clo xlix. post Onuphrium exorsus, unde seriem istorum hominum ordinisque Cardinalitii derivant, finitque in Bonifacio IX. a. clo cccc ii ; Henricus Alby, quoque Gallice, sed posteriorum vitas complexus: praesentium descriptionem dedit Auctor anonymus, Statera giusta di Porporati, quod in Belgicum jam conversum: hoc unum, quod ad rem praesentem facit, attulisse nunc suffecerit, ex Regulis Cancellariis Gregorii XIII. quod Cardinales non comprehendantur sub regulis faciendis: 67. Item cum S. R. Ecclesiae Cardinales ipsi Sanctissimo Domino nostro assistant, ac propterea debeant specialibus prærogativis, & privilegiis gaudere, Idem Dominus Noster Statuit, ordinavit, decrevit, & declaravit, quod in quibuscunque constitutionibus, & regulis per sanctitatem suam in posterum post hanc primam editionem, & suarum constitutionum, & regularum publicationem faciendis, non includantur ipsi Cardinales, nisi illa eorundem Cardinalium favorem concernant, vel ipsae constitutiones edendae de eorundem Cardinalium, vel majoris partis eorum consilio edita fuerint. Ita ubique primas ac potiores tenent Cardinales, atque ipsis etiam Regibus in omnibus praeferuntur: ut non sine gravi causa olim dixisse Clemanges, lib. de corrupto Ecclesiae statu, videri debeat: si artifex quispiam vellet superbia simulachrum effingere, nulla congruentius ratione id facere posset, quam Cardinalis effigiem oculis intuentium objectando. Convivio solemni Papae, quod die coronationis ejus instituitur, Rex aliquis si adsit, sedet in mensa post primum episcopum Cardinalem; nobilior laicus, Imperator aut Rex, aquam ad lavandas Pontificis manus adfert. Quod si plures adsint Reges, mixtim se habent cum primis Cardinalibus, & primum locum tenet Cardinalis, deinde sequitur Rex: si erunt mixtim principes, aut filii vel fratres Regum (si non serviant Papae) debent sedere inter Diaconos Cardinales, vel post eos, pro eorum dignitate & conditione. Primogenitus autem regis, quia Rex futurus putatur, post primum presbyterum Cardinalem. sed nullo modo inter episcopos. Et hoc tam in conviviis quam in aliis publi cis actibus. Primum ferculum portat nobilior Princeps, sive Imperator, sive Rex sit: secundum alium dignior post eum, atq; ita deinceps. Hæc ita descripta in libro Sacrarum Ceremoniarum, à Christophoro Marcello, episcopo Corcyrensi. Quo vero loco Papa habeat Imperatorem & Reges, quorum potestatibus ὑπηρέται Paulus Apostolus omnem animam subjicit, apparet.
units.tr: In 1517, in one creation, he made thirty-one cardinals, among them our Adrian of Utrecht, bishop of Tortosa in Spain, so that Leo is thought to have had sixty-five cardinals. His successor Paul III had sixty-three. Paul IV reached the highest number ever, seventy cardinals. Today there are sixty-two. Formerly they did not exceed fifty-three. When Nicholas III was created, there were only seven. Sixtus V fixed the number at seventy. Clement VII, in his letter to Francis I, at whose request he created Cardinal Grammont, formerly bishop of Tarbes, gives as a reason for hesitation that shortly before he had made a fine troop. This is in the letters of princes, collected by Girolamo Ruscelli and translated from Italian into French by Belleforest. How highly the Pope values that favour (what do I mean by favour?) when he confers cardinals' hats on some men at the request of a king or emperor is well known. Charles V testified, in his long but truly imperial rescript of 1526 answering Clement VII's accusations, that he regretted having asked for so many, although he had requested only one. Concerning the hats, we said that one was asked of you by us from the beginning of your happy promotion, and that, since it was the first favour sought by your hand and by our written letters, and urgently demanded, we thought it should be deferred for so long. The second hat was not requested, but offered of your own accord by Your Holiness and accepted with our consent. So we thought it unfitting to press for these hats, given on such a condition, which we nevertheless judged should be left to the discretion of Your Holiness, promising that from now on we will make no demand for these or any other hats. There are many great privileges of cardinals. Not to list them all, they can be seen in Azorius, Institutiones Morales, part II, book IV, chapter III. Many have written about cardinals and their dignity: Andreas Barbatius, Martinus Landensis, Io. Hieronymus Albanus, Onuphrius Panvinus, besides others who touch on the same matter, such as Bellarminus, De Clericis, book 1, chapter 16, Azorius, Rovenius, and others who wrote the lives of several cardinals. Apart from Onuphrius Panvinus, who first recounted their history alongside that of the popes, Aubery, a Frenchman, began after Onuphrius with Leo IX in 1049, from whom they derive the series of these men and the cardinalitial order, and ended with Boniface IX in 1402. Henricus Alby also wrote in French, but covered the lives of later cardinals. The present description was given by an anonymous author, Statera giusta di Porporati, now also translated into Flemish. It will be enough to cite one thing that bears on the present matter, from the Chancery Rules of Gregory XIII: that cardinals are not included under the rules to be made. Rule 67: Likewise, since the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church assist our most holy Lord, and therefore ought to enjoy special prerogatives and privileges, the same Lord our Lord has established, ordained, decreed and declared that in whatever constitutions and rules his Holiness shall make hereafter, after this first edition and publication of his constitutions and rules, the cardinals themselves are not included, unless those constitutions concern the favour of those same cardinals, or the constitutions to be issued have been issued with the counsel of those cardinals or of the greater part of them. Thus everywhere cardinals hold the first and chief places, and are preferred even to kings in all things. So Clemanges, in his book De corrupto Ecclesiae statu, was not without serious cause when he said that if some craftsman wished to fashion an image of pride, he could do so in no more fitting way than by setting before the eyes of onlookers the likeness of a cardinal. At the solemn banquet held for the Pope on the day of his coronation, if a king is present, he sits at table after the first cardinal bishop; a nobler layman, the Emperor or a King, brings water for washing the Pontiff's hands. If several kings are present, they sit mixed in with the first cardinals, and the first place is held by a cardinal, then the king follows. If princes, or sons or brothers of kings, are present as well (if they are not serving the Pope), they should sit among the cardinal deacons or after them, according to their dignity and rank. The firstborn of a king, because he is thought to be the future king, sits after the first cardinal presbyter, but in no way among the bishops. This holds both at banquets and at other public occasions. The first course is carried by the nobler prince, whether he is emperor or king; the second by another, the more worthy after him, and so on. These arrangements are so described in the book Sacrarum Ceremoniarum by Christophorus Marcellus, bishop of Corfu. In what place the Pope puts the Emperor and the kings, to whose powers the Apostle Paul subjects every soul as ministers [ὑπηρέται], is thereby clear.

units.la: Ex eodem fonte est, quod in sua hac Bulla Innocentius Ferdinandum non simpliciter Imperatorem, sed Imperatorem electum nominat: nempe quia nondum coronationem suam accepit à Papa, & tamdiu ac illud fecerit, electum Imperatorem per μόνον, non simpliciter Imperatorem appellat. Quamvis non hic jam, sed & ante eum plures alii, istam Papæ coronationem jam ab aliquo tempore omisere: Rudolph. I. quia vestigia, ajebat, Romam euntium ipsū terrebant: Maximilian. I. negavit necessarium esse; quia Imperium à Statibus Imperii acceperat. Neque id vel Ferdinandus I. vel Maximilianus II. vel Rudolphus II. vel Mathia, sive Ferdinandus II. aut III. faciendum sibi censuerunt; nec eo minus Imperiū administrarunt tamen, & pro Imperatoribus habiti in Imperio fuerunt. Egoq; existimo, si vel aliquis electus Imperator id jam conaretur, Romam irepro confirmandā suā electione, non id ab Electoribus & Statibus Imperii concedendum fore. Volunt, ut Imperii diadema humiliter de manu Pontificis postulet Romanorum Rex, atque suscipiat. Ut electio Pontifici quam primum offeratur examinanda, tam super forma electionis, quam idoneitate (ut loquuntur) & habilitate persone electi. Non nego quidem Imperatorum nonnullos ab Episcopo Romano coronationem olim accepisse, sed ex solâ id egerunt primum reverentia, & erga Ecclesiam atq; Ecclesiasticos devotione, ut ab Episcopo, coq; magnæ authoritatis, in suo statu consecrarentur. Hoc Papæ mox accipere, quasi debitum ipsis, ac si debuissent ab ipsis coronari Imperatores, si confirmari in sua dignitate vellent: ex facto, & humanitate, sed præpostera, primo erga Episcopum, tum sedem, debitum officium illi, & jus, legem, necessitatem fecerunt.
units.tr: From the same source comes the fact that in this Bull Innocent calls Ferdinand not simply Emperor but Emperor-elect: namely because he has not yet received his coronation from the Pope, and for as long as that has not happened, the Pope calls him Emperor-elect only, not simply Emperor. Yet it is not only he who now does this; several others before him have long since given up this papal coronation. Rudolph I did so because, as he said, the footprints of those going to Rome terrified him. Maximilian I denied that it was necessary, since he had received the Empire from the Estates of the Empire. Neither Ferdinand I, nor Maximilian II, nor Rudolph II, nor Matthias, or Ferdinand II or III, thought this should be done by them; nevertheless they administered the Empire all the same, and were regarded as Emperors in the Empire. And I think that if any elected Emperor were now to attempt it, that is, to go to Rome to have his election confirmed, this would not be granted by the Electors and Estates of the Empire. They want the Roman King to humbly ask for the diadem of the Empire from the hand of the Pontiff and receive it. The election is to be offered to the Pontiff as soon as possible for examination, both as to the form of the election and as to the fitness (as they say) and suitability of the person elected. I do not deny that some Emperors long ago received coronation from the Roman Bishop, but they did so out of reverence alone, and out of devotion towards the Church and the churchmen, so that they might be consecrated in their office by a bishop of great authority. To receive this from the Pope as if it were owed to him, as though the Emperors ought to be crowned by him if they wished to be confirmed in their dignity, was a deed of courtesy, but a misplaced one: first towards the bishop, then towards the see, they made a due courtesy into an obligation, a right, a law and a necessity.

units.la: Indeque ulterius pergentes, ut semper ad altiora serpit ambitio nusquam consistens vel quiescens, in ipsum quoque Imperium potestatem sibi arrogarunt, atque à se omnia dependere arbitrati sunt. Hinc, uti sui juris putabant, Imperatorem facere, & vel approbare electum vel repellere, ita Imperatorem quoque deponere aliquando, in sua potestate situm credi volucrunt; exhibito ejus in nonnullis, quos deponere annisi sunt, exemplo haud uno, istam ob causam quod non accepta primum à Pontifice coronatione, ut minus necessaria, imperium tractare fuissent agressi: uti in Ludovico Bavaro, à P. Iohanne xxii. & Wenceslao, à Bonifacio ix ejectis ab Imperio, apparuit. Postquam Carolus M. coronam à Papa accepit, Carolus Crassus a. 1 cccxc. Constitutionem edidit, de Expeditione Romana, id est, quo comitatu, pompa, modo Imperator Romam, pro coronatione suâ, proficisceretur. Hac occasione solerter Papae uti sciverunt, ut gratitudinis loco, praesertim festivo adeo tempore, à coronatis Imperatoribus plurima impetrarent, praedia, terras, regiones, & potestatis incrementa omnifaria, & nunquâ non confirmationem donationum, sibi suaeq; Ecclesiae, ab aliis seu vere seu falso factarum, vel abolitionem quarundam rerum aut legum adversus Romanenses alibi, vel à Praedecessoribus conditorum. Quale edictum Fridericus II Imp. à. clɔ ccxx. eo die, quo ab Honorio Papa coronaretur, fecit, pro tollendis omnibus statutis & consuetudinibus, quae civitates, vel loca, Potestates, Consules, vel quaecunque alia personae contra libertatem Ecclesiae, vel personas Ecclesiasticas edere, vel servare tentaverint. Atque illam occasionem coronandorum Imperatorum ego constituo inter praecipuas provecti & exaltati Papatus, quodq; in Imperium & Imperatores sibi semper tatum authoritatis adscripserunt, causas. Gregorio V. sub annum clxi. (quod tamen ab aliis Gregorio X.) adscribitur, quod ut gratiam rependeret Otthoni III. qui ad Pontificatum eum promoverat, atque servarat adversus vim tum Crescentii Consulis Romani, tum antiPapae Iohannis, utque etiam Imperium eo melius apud GerGermanos permaneret diuturnum: Solis Germanis licere principem deligere, qui Cæsar & Romanorum Rex appellatus, tum demum Imperator & Augustus haberetur, si eum Romanus Pontifex coronasset. Hinc sibi arrogavit Papa, Imperii coronam conferre, auferre quibus vilum: Tibi Papa coronam, uti post obitum Conradi, Petro Regi Hungariæ quum offerret Imperium; vel Petrus diadema Rudolfo, quando ejecto Henrico, in ejus locum Rudolfum Suecię ducem constituit a. cl⁰. lxxvii. nempe P. Hildebrandus, vel Gregorius vii. qui primus, secus ac solebat, citra consensum Imperatoris Papam se fecerat, primus quoque fuit, qui ex coronatione, quasi debita, tantam potestatem sibi arrogavit, ut Imperatorem minus ei obedientem, extra communionem Ecclesiæ ejicere, & ab Imperio deponere ausus fuerit. Lego & relego Romanorum Regum & Imperatorum gesta, & nusquam invenio quenquam eorum ante hunc à Romano Pontifice excommunicatum, vel regno privatum, inquit Otto Frisingensis Episc. Chronic. lib. vi. cap. xxxv. Atq; inde illud in Comitiis Wormatiensibus a. cl⁰. lxxvi i. Treverensis Episcopus appellavit, obstupendam abusionem novitatis, & inauditum decretum; quibus in Comitiis propterea de deponendo Papa actum, quem sic describunt, Hildebrandum scilicet, Monachum quidem dictum Apostolicum, non pastoris cura, sed invasoris violentia; Apostolicæ Sedi præsidentem, & de Sede pacis Catholicæ, pacis unica vinculum dissipantem: deponuntque postmodum in Comitiis Brixiæ Noricorum a. cl⁰. lxxx. vii. Cal. Iulii. Caulam inter alia, addit Rex in epistolâ ad Hildebrandum, ex ipsis Comitiis scriptâ: in ipsam Regiam potestatem nobis à Deo concessam exurgere non timuisti, quam à nobis auferre ausus es minari, quasi nos à te regnum acceperimus, quasi in tua & non in Dei manu sit Regnum vel Imperium. Unde jam, Henrico ab Hildebrando, & Hildebrando vicissim ab Henrico excommunicato, ejecto, gravissimis dissensionibus bellisque omnia exarserunt; quæ non cum demortuo Hildebrando deservierunt, sed à succedentibus Victore, Urbano, & Paschali fota, tandem & eo usq; perducta fuerunt; ut Henricum V. filium in Parentem incitarint, & bellū ei mo-vevere persuaserint. Verum & ip priori Rudolpho, & in hoc Henrico, utroque à Papâ in Imperatorem Henricum IV instigato, exhibuit Deus justæ sultionis documenta. In illo quidem, propriâ cum urgente conscientiâ quando moribundus abscissam in prælio manum astantibus ostentans, diceret: Iussio Apostolica, & petitio Principum, me fecit juramenti transgressorem, videte igitur manum abscissam, quam juravi Domino meo Henrico non vitæ nec gloriæ ejus insidiari. In hoc ab Historicis notatur, in pœnam rebellionis atque ingratitudinis in Parentem, quod prole ideo caruerit. Auctor Chronici Coloniensis: Disse Kerser ring synen Vader/ ind liesson in der Dechtenisse sterven. Darumb meynemen dat he aenlysse sterve sturve. Neque etiam ab Henrico s. tamen obtinuit, quod volebat, & ob quam causam adeo infectatus Patrem fuerat, Papa: sed relinquere ei Episcopatuum & Abbatiarum in Imperio, pro antiqua à Carol. M. confuetudine, investituram coactus fuit. Quanta proh ista fuit in Imperatore Lothario II. vesania, ut accipendæ à Papa Innocentio coronationis gratia, non tantum forti manu eum Romam reducere, ac reddere urbi, sed se ad Papæ pedes dejicere, & confirmatis ei primum suis honoribus, coronam à manu ejus a. cIↄc xxxiii. ita recipere sustinuerit: unde postea in summum Imperatoris ludibrium, in Laterano historiam coronationis depingi curarunt, Innocentio Pontificali insidente cathedræ, & ad genua sua curvatum habente Imperatorem, subjunctis huic istis versiculis atrocissimè ignominiosis: Rex venit ante fores, jurans prius urbis honores, Post homo fit Papæ, sumit quo dante coronam.
units.tr: Going further from there, since ambition always creeps toward higher things and never stands still or rests, they claimed for themselves power over the Empire itself and judged that everything depended on them. From this they came to believe, as though it were their own right, that making an emperor, approving an elected candidate or rejecting him, lay in their power, and that deposing an emperor at times did too. There was more than one example of this among those whom they tried to depose, for this reason: they had begun to wield imperial rule without first receiving coronation from the Pope, which they regarded as less necessary. This appeared in Ludwig of Bavaria, expelled from the Empire by Pope John XXII, and in Wenceslaus, expelled by Boniface IX. After Charles the Great received the crown from the Pope, Charles the Fat issued in 1390 an ordinance on the Roman expedition, that is, with what retinue, pomp, and manner the emperor was to travel to Rome for his coronation. The Popes knew how to use this occasion shrewdly, so that, in return for their gratitude, especially at so festive a time, they obtained from the crowned emperors very many things: estates, lands, regions, and every kind of increase of power; and always the confirmation of donations made to them and to their Church by others, whether truly or falsely, or the abolition of certain things or of laws enacted against the Romans elsewhere, or of those enacted by their predecessors. Frederick II issued such an edict in 1220, on the day he was crowned by Pope Honorius, to abolish all statutes and customs that cities, places, magistrates, consuls, or any other persons had attempted to enact or maintain against the liberty of the Church or against ecclesiastical persons. I count this occasion of crowning emperors among the principal causes of the advancement and exaltation of the Papacy, and of its always claiming for itself so much authority over the Empire and the emperors. Gregory V, around the year clxi (though by others it is ascribed to Gregory X), to repay the favour of Otto III, who had promoted him to the Papacy and defended him against the violence both of Crescentius, consul of Rome, and of the anti-pope John, and so that the Empire might remain more securely among the Germans for a long time, is said to have decreed: Only the Germans may choose a prince, who is called Caesar and King of the Romans, and who is then held to be Emperor and Augustus, if the Roman Pontiff has crowned him. From this the Pope arrogated to himself the power to confer the crown of the Empire and to take it from whomever he wished: The crown to you, as when, after the death of Conrad, he offered the Empire to Peter, King of Hungary; or Peter gives the diadem to Rudolf, when, Henry having been deposed, he set up in his place Rudolf, Duke of Swabia, in 1077. This was Pope Hildebrand, or Gregory VII, who was the first, contrary to custom, to make himself Pope without the Emperor's consent, and who was also the first to arrogate to himself, from coronation as though it were owed, such power that he dared to expel from the communion of the Church an emperor less obedient to him, and to depose him from the Empire. I have read and re-read the deeds of the Roman kings and emperors, and nowhere do I find any of them excommunicated or deprived of his kingdom by the Roman Pontiff before this man, says Otto of Freising, Chronicle, book 6, chapter 35. Hence the Bishop of Trier, at the Diet of Worms in 1076, called it an astonishing abuse of novelty and an unheard-of decree. At these Diets, therefore, there was action about deposing the Pope, whom they describe thus: Hildebrand, namely, a monk called Apostolic, not by the care of a shepherd but by the violence of an usurper, presiding over the Apostolic See, and from the seat of Catholic peace scattering the one bond of peace; and afterwards, at the Diet of Brixen (Brixia of the Noricans) on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, 1080, they deposed him. Among other things, the King adds in a letter to Hildebrand, written from the Diet itself: You did not fear to rise against the royal power itself, given to us by God, which you have dared to threaten to take from us, as if we had received the kingdom from you, as if the kingdom or empire were in your hand and not in God's. Hence, with Henry excommunicated and deposed by Hildebrand, and Hildebrand in turn excommunicated and deposed by Henry, everything blazed up in the gravest dissensions and wars. These did not end with the death of Hildebrand but were fostered by his successors Victor, Urban, and Paschal, and were at last carried so far that they incited Henry V, the son, against his father and persuaded him to make war on him. But God also showed examples of just retribution, both in the former Rudolf and in this Henry, both of whom had been stirred up by the Pope against the Emperor Henry IV. In the former, indeed, when his own conscience pressed upon him, he showed the hand cut off in battle to those standing by as he lay dying, and said: The Apostolic command and the request of the princes made me a breaker of my oath. See, therefore, the severed hand, with which I swore to my lord Henry that I would not plot against his life or his glory. In the latter, historians note, as punishment for rebellion and ingratitude toward his father, that he was for this reason without offspring. The author of the Cologne Chronicle says: "This emperor let his father die in prison. Therefore, I think, he died without heirs." Nor did the Pope obtain from Henry what he wanted, for which he had so pursued the father; instead, Henry was compelled to leave to the Emperor the investiture of bishoprics and abbacies in the Empire, following the ancient custom from Charlemagne. What madness, alas, was in the Emperor Lothair II, that, to receive coronation from Pope Innocent, he not only led him back to Rome with a strong hand and restored him to the city, but threw himself at the Pope's feet and, after his own honours had first been confirmed to him, consented to receive the crown from his hand in 1133. Whence afterwards, to the Emperor's great mockery, they had the history of the coronation painted in the Lateran, with Innocent seated on the pontifical chair and the Emperor bent at his knees, and added these most shamefully insulting verses: "The king comes before the doors, swearing first the honours of the city; afterwards he becomes the Pope's man, and takes the crown from the hand that gives it."

units.la: Significans Imperatorem Papæ vasallum esse, atque Imperium ab eo habere in feudum. Effigiem istâ conspicatus Romæ Fridericus I. quum ibi coronationis suæ causa degeret, vehementer cum Adriano P. ob eam expostulavit, delerique voluit: quod quamvis promitteret Papa, parum tamen post Imperatoris abitum curavit. Apertius adhuc magisque pudendum exemplum Papalis in coronatione Imp. fastus & usurpationis cape in coronatione Henrici v.a. cl ɔ. cxci. à Cæle-sstino : cujus historiam , ex Rogerii Annalibus , sic refert Baronius: Dominus verò Papa ante ostium ecclesiæ B. Petri supra gradus recepit sacramentum à prædicto Alemanorum Rege , quod ipse Ecclesiam Dei , & jura ecclesiastica fideliter servaret illibata, & quod Tusculanum ei redderet. Deinde introduxit eos Dominus Papa in ecclesiam & unxit eum in Imperatorem,& uxorem suam in Imperatricem. Sedebat autem Dominus Papa in cathedra Pontificali tenens coronam auream Imperialem inter pedes suos,& Imperator inclinato capite, recepit coronam, & Imperatrix similiter de pedibus Domini Papæ. Dominus autem Papa statim percussit cum pede suo coronam Imperatoris, & dejecit eam in terram, significans, quod ipse potestatem ejiciendi eum ab imperio habet , si ille demeruerit. sed Cardinales statim arripientes coronam, imposuerunt eam capiti Imperatoris. Baronius, nempe explicationis ergo ad tantum mysterium, &commentarii, addit: Ut autem id fixum menti ejus hæreret, nempè, dare, custodire, conservare & auferre, si causa exigeret, Imperium esse in voluntate Romani pontificis : ejusmodi voluit commonuisse ipsum exemplo. Imo digna Cardinale observatio , æque ac factum Papæ. Quin palam atque in os patri ejus Friderico I. Adrianus P. exprobrare ausus fuit primò per literas, Imperium teneri abipso, ex donatione sua, inter beneficia à Papâ ei collata; tum per Legatos,in consessu Principum,præsente Imperatore,dictum: à quo ergo habet si à Domino Papa non habet imperium? quo dicto parum abfuit quin confossus gladio fuisset Legatus ille, à prosiliente in impudentissimi hominis cervicem Ottone Palatino, nisi ab intervolante Friderico ictus fuisset inhibitus. Statim autem exire imperio, neque alloqui quempiam in via præcepit. Vnde quid animi in Imperio Principes fuerint super illa Papæ arrogantiâ, & prætensa, ex coronatione, potestate, liquet: sed Adrianus tamen haud aliter sensit, quàm Imperatorem,per se constitui in Imperio,illudque suo habere & tenere beneficio. Quare scripsit ad Germaniæ episcopos , quæ epistola legitur apud Aventinum, lib.vi. Romanum Imperium à Græcis translatum est ad Alamannos, ut Rex Teutonicorum non ante , quam ab apostolico conaretur, Imperator vocaretur. Ante consecrationem Rex, post Imperator. Unde igitur habet Imperium, nisi a nobis? Ex electione Principum suorum habet nomen Regis; ex consecratione nostra habet nomen Imperatoris & Augusti & Caesaris. Ergo pernos imperat. Atque in illum sensum hoc capiunt Papistae curiales: ut haud obscure iis patefiat, eum, qui coronam e manu Pontificis non obtinet revera non esse imperatorem; itaque quemadmodum ad allegatum Hadriani istud factum loquuntur Cardinales, in Aphorismis de Statu ecclesiae restaurando, Gregorio xv. exhibitis haud ita diu in causa ducis Bavariae, per Michaelem Lonigum. Negotium illud coronandi a Papa Imperatoris, vel de ejus tum necessitate, tum vi disputatio in nervum erupit per Imp. Ludovicum Bavarum, cum Iohanne P. xxii. Scindebatur Imperium, vel Electorum studia ut aliquot ties factum, in electione novi Imperatoris: pars Ludovicum, Bavariae; alii Fredericum, Austriae ducem volebant: uterque coronationem per legatos poscebat a Papa, qui, quoniam melius sibi vacuo imperio existimat, neutri annuebat, in Ludovico hoc captans, quod non exspectata coronatione res & gubernacula Imperii, prout Imperatori convenit, tractare aggressus esset. Ludovicus Romam tendit, atque, absente Papa coronam a Cardinalibus accipit, a. MCCCXXVII. quod indigne ferens Papa, qui Avinione herebat, Imperatorem excommunicat, proclamat haereticum, deponit. Vbi videre fuit, quomodo supremam sibi in Imperium potestatem arrogent, & quo fine coronationem illam necessariam aestiment Papae. Bulla Papae MCCCXXIII. anno dignitatis, ut hic quidem scribit, eo quod alii, Pontificatus (nempe insolito verbo in re non minus insolita) octavo, sic incipiebat: Postquam a decessoribus nostris res Romana a Graecis ad Germanos translata, Carolo Magno in fidem atque tutelam commissa est, summus ille honor beneficium Pontificis maximi esse solet. Decretum siquidem est, ut cum Germani Principes Regem iussissent, demum ratum esse, si Romanus Pontifex, universi orbis Christiani Pater atque Princeps, author fieret: nec ante cuiquam Comitiis Caesareis, suffragiis Principum designato Regi, neque administrandi, neque Regii tituli usurpandi ius est, quam primarius Sacerdos, Dei OPT. MAX. legatus suo nomine faveat & aspiret. Praeterea summa potestas maximum Imperium, ubi orbium capite fuerit, penes Maximum Pontificem, cuius beneficium illud est, exstitit. Vides, ut beneficium Paparum faciunt Imperium, ipsos vero directos supremos Dominos. Iam quomodo deponat Imperatorem, & quam obicaulam, similiter audi; Proinde Ludovicus maximo malo suo, non minore Ecclesia Romana detrimento, nec dum a nobis dignus qui imperet judicatus, sua sponte Regium nomen, rerum habenas temere usurpavit, atque in Italia atque Germania occupat. Nos igitur juxta manus caelestis nobis datum, Ludovico praecipimus: ut intra menses sex se abdicet ab Regio nomine, gubernatione, functionibus publicis, rebus gerendis penitus abstineat, a se hactenus acta rescindat, nec posit hac nisi jussu & mandato nostro dignitatem resumat. Quod si obtemperare obtrectaverit, Patriarchis, Episcopis cunctis, Sacerdotibus, Principibus, Civitatibus imperamus, ut eundem deserant, ac nobis parere cogant. Candide, uti passim, hac de re judicat Auctor Chronici Coloniensis, mirum sibi videri, quod Papa Imperatorem invitaret in alienum territorium: Dtt was ouch vremde/ as mich dunkt / dat de Paus den Konynck woulde laden in eyn vremde berlin/ und dat he niet gen Rome selffs quam/ eff nemant dait sende van synt wegen/ so dach dat vur und nat geschiet is. Eyn yglich Dundt is toen ep syner myste. Ex adverso Imperator, in Comitiis Francofurtensibus a. MCCCXXXVIII. constitutione de Imperii Iuribus, & excellentia, & potestate Electi Romanorum Regis, edixit quod Imperator: ex sola electione eorum ad quos pertinet, verus efficitur Imperator, nec alicujus alterius egeat confirmatione seu approbatione: Contra quod aliis & in assertiones detestabiles prorumpunt, contra potestatem & auctoritatem imperialem, & jura Imperatorum, Electorum, & aliorum Principum & Imperii fidelium committentes, fallaciter asserentes, quod Imperialis dignitas & potestas est a Papa, & quod Electus in Imperatorem non est verus Imperator nec Rex nisi prius per Papam sive Sedem Apostolicam confirmetur, approbetur, & coronetur: & per hujusmodi pravas assertiones, & pestifera dogmata hostilis antiquus movet lites, jurgia suscitat, contentiones parit, & seditiones procurat. Ideo ) ad tantum malum evitandum, de consilio & consensu Electorum aliorum Principum Imperii, declaramus, quod Imperialis dignitas & potestas est immediate à solo Deo: & quod de jure & Imperii consuetudine antiquitus approbata, postquam aliquis eligitur in Imperatorem sive Regem ab Electoribus Imperii concorditer, vel majori parte eorundem, statim ex sola electione est Rex verus & Imperator Romanorum censendus, & nominandus, & eidem ab omnibus Imperio subjectis obediri, & administrandi jura Imperii & cetera faciendi, quae ad Imperatorem verum pertinent, plenariam habet potestatem, nec Papae sive Sedis Apostolicae aut alicujus alterius approbatione, confirmatione, auctoritate indiget vel consensu. Et ea propter hac in perpetuum valitura lege decernimus, ut Electus in Imperatorem concorditer, vel à majori parte Electorum, ex sola electione censeatur & habeatur ab omnibus pro vero & legitimo Imperatore, & eidem ab omnibus subjectis Imperio debeat obediri, & administrationem Imperialem, & Imperialis potestatis plenitudinem habeat, & ita habere ac obtinere ab omnibus censeatur & firmiter afferatur. adversantes vel inobedientes pronunciavit crimen laesae majestatis committisse, omnibusque, quae ab Imperio accipiunt, feudis, excidisse. Atque in eundem sensum scribunt Principes, ex Comitiis Renensibus, eodem anno, ad P. Iohannis Successorem Benedictum IX. tum conquerentes, quod P. Iohannes sententias excommunicationis & interdicti (sic dici merentur) ac alias diversas sententias & processus de facto contra Deum, & justitiam, & juris ordinem fulminavit contra praedictum Dominum nostrum, Dominum Ludovicum Romanorum Imperatorem, ac fautores & adhaerentes sibi; tum declarantes, & sententialiter, uti dicunt, definientes, quod vacante Romano Imperio is, qui eligitur concorditer, vel à majore parte Principum electorum, pro Rege Romanorum ab omnibus est habendus; & quod nec nominatione, approbatione, confirmatione, consensu, vel auctoritate Sedis Apostolicae, super administratione bonorum & jurium Imperii indiget, sive titulo Regio assumendo: quodque jura & bona Imperii administrare & gubernare poterit, & de jure & consuetudine, nulla Sedis Apostolicae super hoc licentia habita vel obtenta.
