units.tr: This signifies that the Emperor is the vassal of the Pope and holds the Empire from him as a fief. When Frederick I saw this picture at Rome, where he was staying for the sake of his coronation, he protested vigorously to Adrian IV about it and demanded that it be removed. Although the Pope promised this, he did little about it after the Emperor had left. An even more open and shameful example of papal pride and usurpation is found in the coronation of Henry VI in the year 1191, under Celestine. Baronius relates its history as follows, taken from the Annals of Roger: The lord Pope, before the door of the church of St Peter, on the steps, received an oath from the aforesaid King of the Germans that he would faithfully preserve the Church of God and its ecclesiastical rights unimpaired, and that he would restore Tusculum to him. Then the lord Pope led them into the church and anointed him as Emperor and his wife as Empress. The lord Pope was sitting on the pontifical chair, holding the imperial golden crown between his feet, and the Emperor received the crown with his head bowed, and the Empress likewise from the feet of the lord Pope. But the lord Pope at once struck the Emperor's crown with his foot and knocked it to the ground, signifying that he himself has the power to cast him out of the empire if he deserves it. But the Cardinals at once snatched up the crown and placed it on the Emperor's head. Baronius, to explain so great a mystery and by way of commentary, adds: So that this might remain fixed in his mind, namely that to give, to keep, to preserve and, if the cause demands, to take away the Empire lies in the will of the Roman Pontiff, he wished to remind him of this by the example. Indeed, the observation is worthy of a Cardinal, just as the Pope's deed was. Moreover, Adrian IV openly dared to reproach Frederick I, the father of this Emperor, to his face. First he did so by letter, saying that the Empire is held from him by his own gift, as one of the benefices conferred by the Pope. Then, through his Legates, in an assembly of princes, in the Emperor's presence, he said: From whom then does he have the empire, if he does not have it from the lord Pope? At this saying, the Legate was all but run through with a sword, Otto the Palatine having leapt at the neck of that most shameless man, and he would have been killed had Frederick not intervened and stopped the blow. The Legate was ordered to leave the Empire at once and not to speak to anyone on the road. From this it is clear what the princes of the Empire felt about that arrogance of the Pope and the power he claimed from the coronation. Yet Adrian nevertheless thought no differently than that the Emperor is set up in the Empire by himself and holds and keeps it by his benefice. Therefore he wrote to the bishops of Germany, and this letter is read in Aventinus, book 6: The Roman Empire was transferred from the Greeks to the Alamanni, so that the King of the Teutons should not be called Emperor until he had been crowned by the Apostolic See. Before consecration he is King, after it Emperor. Whence then does he have the Empire, if not from us? He has the name of King from the election of his princes; from our consecration he has the name of Emperor, Augustus and Caesar. Therefore he rules over us. The Papal courtiers also understand it in this sense, so that it is quite clear to them that he who does not obtain the crown from the hand of the Pontiff is in truth not Emperor. Thus the Cardinals speak in the same way about this deed of Adrian, in the Aphorisms on the restoration of the Church's state, presented to Gregory XV not long ago in the case of the Duke of Bavaria by Michael Lonigus. The question of the coronation of the Emperor by the Pope, whether of its necessity or of its force, broke out into a great dispute under the Emperor Louis of Bavaria with John XXII. The Empire was divided, as often happened in the election of a new Emperor, by the zeal of the Electors: one party wanted Louis of Bavaria, others Frederick, Duke of Austria. Each of them asked the Pope through legates for coronation. He, thinking it better for himself that the empire remain vacant, favoured neither, and against Louis he took this ground: that he had undertaken to manage the affairs and government of the Empire, as belongs to an Emperor, without waiting for the coronation. Louis went to Rome and, the Pope being absent, received the crown from the Cardinals in 1327. The Pope, who was then staying at Avignon, took this badly, excommunicated the Emperor, proclaimed him a heretic and deposed him. Here one could see how they claim for themselves supreme power over the Empire, and for what end they consider that coronation necessary for the Pope. The Bull of the Pope of 1323, in the year of his dignity, as this writer has it, though others say of his Pontificate (the unusual word used for a matter no less unusual), in the eighth year, began thus: Since the Roman state was transferred by our predecessors from the Greeks to the Germans and entrusted to the faith and protection of Charlemagne, that highest honour is usually the benefice of the Supreme Pontiff. For it has been decreed that when the German princes have ordered a King, it is then ratified only if the Roman Pontiff, Father and Prince of the whole Christian world, becomes its author; and no one has the right to administer or to use the royal title in the Imperial Diet, by the votes of the princes designated as King, until the chief Priest, the Legate of God Best and Greatest, favours and approves it in his own name. Moreover, the supreme power, the greatest Empire, wherever it has been in the head of the world, has existed in the hands of the Greatest Pontiff, whose benefice it is. You see how they make the Empire a benefice of the Popes, and themselves the direct supreme lords. Now hear similarly how he deposes the Emperor and the pretext he gives: Therefore Louis, to his own great harm and no less detriment to the Roman Church, not yet judged by us worthy to rule, has rashly and of his own accord usurped the royal name and the reins of government, and occupies Italy and Germany. We therefore, according to the power given us by the heavenly hand, command Louis that within six months he abdicate the royal name, government and public functions, abstain entirely from the business of ruling, rescind what he has done hitherto, and not resume that dignity except by our order and mandate. But if he refuses to obey, we command the Patriarchs, all the Bishops, Priests, Princes and Cities to desert him and compel him to obey us. Frankly, as elsewhere, the author of the Cologne Chronicle judges this matter, thinking it strange to him that the Pope should summon the King into a foreign territory, and that he did not come to Rome himself, or send someone in his place, so that the matter was settled before and after. Everyone's opinion was according to his own taste. On the other side, the Emperor, at the Diet of Frankfurt in 1338, in a constitution on the rights of the Empire, and on the excellence and power of the elected Roman King, declared that the Emperor is made true Emperor by the sole election of those to whom it belongs, and needs no other confirmation or approval. Against this, others break out into detestable assertions against the imperial power and authority and the rights of Emperors, Electors and other princes and faithful subjects of the Empire, falsely asserting that the imperial dignity and power is from the Pope, and that the elected man is not true Emperor or King unless he is first confirmed, approved and crowned by the Pope or the Apostolic See; and through such wicked assertions and pestilent dogmas that ancient enemy stirs up quarrels, provokes strife, breeds contentions and promotes sedition. Therefore, to avoid so great an evil, with the counsel and consent of the other Electors and princes of the Empire, we declare that the imperial dignity and power is immediately from God alone; and that by law and the custom of the Empire, approved from of old, once someone has been elected Emperor or King by the Electors of the Empire in agreement, or by the greater part of them, he is to be regarded and named at once by election alone as true King and Emperor of the Romans, and is to be obeyed by all subject to the Empire, and has full power to administer the rights of the Empire and to do the other things which pertain to a true Emperor, and needs no approval, confirmation, authority or consent of the Pope, the Apostolic See or of anyone else. And therefore, by this law which shall remain valid forever, we decree that the man elected Emperor in agreement, or by the greater part of the Electors, is to be deemed and held by all, by election alone, the true and lawful Emperor, is to be obeyed by all subjects of the Empire, and shall have the imperial administration and the fullness of imperial power, and is to be considered and firmly asserted to have and hold this by all. Those who oppose or disobey, he declared guilty of the crime of high treason, and to have forfeited all the fiefs they hold from the Empire. In the same sense the princes wrote from the Diet of Rhenish towns in the same year to Benedict IX, the successor of Pope John, complaining that Pope John had hurled sentences of excommunication and interdict (as they deserve to be called) and other various sentences and proceedings, contrary to God and justice and the order of law, against the aforesaid our lord, Lord Louis, Emperor of the Romans, and his supporters and adherents; and declaring, and, as they say, defining by sentence, that when the Roman Empire is vacant, he who is elected in agreement, or by the greater part of the Electoral princes, is to be held by all as King of the Romans; and that he needs no nomination, approval, confirmation, consent or authority of the Apostolic See for the administration of the goods and rights of the Empire, or for assuming the royal title; and that he can administer and govern the rights and goods of the Empire, and this by law and custom, without any licence of the Apostolic See having been sought or obtained in this matter. To say nothing of other things: at this time, back and forth, especially because of the sloth and wantonness of Wenceslaus, who (as the Pope does not say in his Bull) does not care for the affairs of the Empire, because he had put off coming to Rome for the coronation, yet so that the Pope may reveal his mind, and so that all in the Empire may know what he claims for himself, he speaks thus, and uses this formula in confirming the elected Emperor: Weighing the deposition of the aforesaid Wenceslaus and the election made of you, and whatever has followed from it, holding them valid and acceptable; and we receive you as our special son and of the said Church, granting you our favour and grace, and, your person being suitably represented, we name you, pronounce you, and take you as King of the Romans, approving your person; and declaring you sufficient, able and fit to receive the dignity of the aforesaid Imperial summit, and decreeing that the imperial anointing and consecration, and likewise the diadem of the same holy empire, are to be bestowed on you by our hands at a suitable place and time; supplying nevertheless every defect, if any in form or in your person, or in the persons of the said Electors, or any other reason or cause should intervene in such an election, by certain knowledge and the apostolic fullness of power; also commanding all the faithful and vassals of the Empire, of whatever condition they be, even if they shine with royal or pontifical dignity, that they obey you and attend to you effectively as King of the Romans. Compare Clement II, On the oath, where the oath to be sworn to the Pope by the Roman King elected as Emperor is treated, which we shall cite later. Nor did that devilish contention of Lucifer, moved by Adrian IV against the Emperor Frederick I, arise from any other source, concerning the place of the names of the Pope and of the Emperor together in letters, and which of them was to be put first. The Pope severely censured the Emperor because he had put his own name first in his letters: The divine law, just as it promised long life to those who honour their parents, so it threatens death to those who curse father and mother. And we are taught by the voice of truth that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. Wherefore, beloved son in the Lord, we marvel not a little at your prudence, that you seem to show to the blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church not the reverence you ought. For in letters sent to us you place your name before ours, in which in-

Nihilque in historiis & Imperatorum, & Paparum frequentius, quam audire, ab Imperatorum arbitrio dependisse Paparum electionem. Confirmavit hoc, ad exemplum Adriani, Leo P. viii. Ottoni i. a. Idcirco ad exemplum beati Adriani, Sedis Apostolicæ hujusmodi Episcopi, cujus vitam & actionem satis discretam audivimus, qui rationabilis admodum suis spiritualibus functionibus Domino Carolo victoriosissimo Regi Francorum & Longobardorum regni Italiæ & Patriciatus dignitatem, ac ordinationem Sedis Apostolicæ concessit insuper & Epifcopatuum investituras, velut ipsi cum discretione & reverentia li-bitum fuerit, prater quos tam Pontifici summa Sedis quàm Archiepiscopis ipse Carolus reliquit. Igitur nos Leo Servus servorum Dei, Episcopus, ad idem exemplum beati Adriani, cum cunctis similiter Clero & universo populo Romano, omnibusque ordinibus hujus almæ Vrbis, sicut in suis scripturis apparet, constituimus, & confirmamus & corroboramus, & per nostram Apostolicam auctoritatem concedimus atque largimur Domino Ottoni Primo, Teutonico, Regi docissimo. De hoc Chronicon Coloniense ita: Leo viii. videns fraudes in electione Paparum usitatas, instituit, nullum Papam absque Imperatoris consensu eligendum esse; etiam licere Imperatori Episcopos & Prælatos instituere, ut olim Iii. Dist. in Synodo congregatis. Quod & Carolo M. Adrianus dederat. Otto iii. in Constitutione de jure ac potestate Imperii, a. Dccccxcviii. Silvestrum magistratum nostrum Papam elegimus, & Deo volente ipsum serenissimum ordinavimus & creavimus, Henricus ii. a. cl. xiv. in Constitutione, quà confirmat donationes Ecclesiæ Romanę factas, conditionem addit, ut electus Pontifex non consecretur sine Imperatoris confirmatione. Episcopi Germaniæ a. cIo lxxvii. Comitiis Wormaticnsibus, in causa Henrici IV. adversus Hildebrandum P. inter alia sic loquuntur: cum tempore Nicolai Papæ Synodus celebraretur, in qua centum viginti Episcopi consederant, sub anathemate hoc Statutum & decretum est, ut nullus Papa fieret, nisi per electionem Cardinalium, & approbationem populi, & per consensum & auctoritatem Regis. Atque hujus Concilii seu Decreti tu ipse author & persuasor subscriptorque fuisti. Semper hæc lis agitata inter Cæsarem & Papam, penes quos Ecclesiasticorum, etiam Paparum, investitura, uti loquebantur, esset. Hoc ad se Papa rapiebat, de omnibus per Imperium, ne alia nunc orbis regna dicam, Episcopis: atq; Imperator, sibi id deberi asserebat. Non ego nunc adeo de utriusque & Imperatorum & Paparum adversus se invicé factionibus ac studiis judicium persequor, ac narratorem ago; ut videatur, quo Papa Romanus jam res produxerit suas, ut subjecto sibi Romano Imperatore, cui ipse ante subditittus fuit, ejus coronationem adeo à se dependere fecerit, ut absque hac ne Imperatorem quidem dicendum, quamvis ab Imperii Principibus electum, arbitretur. Non multum curo hierarchiam ecclesiasticam, vel Paparum, vel Episcoporum, minus eorum quando politici evaserunt, à quibus se. pendeat eorum constitutio, sive electio, aut confirmatio; sed quod attinet jus Ecclesiasticum, de constituendis ut sic Ecclesiasticis, juste hactenus Imperator adversus Papam egit, qui sibi potestatem arrogabat in Ecclesias ad se neutiquam spectantes, quibus solummodo conabatur xueaiver. At nec Imperator excussa illa Papæ, ipse usurpare debuit, quatenus Ecclesiastica, non politica sunt. Itaque utrique male pro se egerunt, ubi neutri jus in Ecclesias competebat, sed ad Imperatorem quidem decuisset in ordinem redacto Papâ, jura Ecclesiæ ecclesiastica defendere & tutari, sed quomodo quis bona & jura pupillorum quorum curam habet eaque non sibi arripit, sed pupillis conservat, Ecclesiæ ab Imperatore protegendæ suum jus servandum, relinquendumque, non ab alieno, seu Papâ, seu Imperatore, usurpandum fuerat. Cæterum infiniti operis esset, per historias omnes, vel Paparum electiones ostendere, ut confirmationes illæ suas ab Imperatore semper habuerint, præterquam quod notum satis etiam illud cuivis est, Paparum plurimos ab Imperatoribus depositos olim fuisse. Vide obsecro id nunc, ut mutatâ adeo fabulâ, in Imperatorem nunc Papa teneat, quod antiquitus, & tamdiu in Papam potestatis obtinuit Imperator? Hic illum eligere, vel confirmare, vel etiam, ubi res exigebat, deponere solitus, nunc ab isto ex adverso eligi, confirmari dicitur, aliquando etiam deponi: quin, uti necessarium fuit, ab Imperatore Papam constitui, ita nunc viceversa, nihil omnino Imperatori in Papam juris relictum, in cujus electione nequaquam amplius vel Imperatoris vel Regis alicujus consensus aut approbatio exspectatur aut petitur, sed eliminato jam Imperatore, à solis eligitur & confirmatur Cardinalibus. Atque si id solum esset, ut mutuo à se liberi existerent, neque dependeret, non Imperator à Papa, ut nec Papa ab Imperatore; sed nescio quo malo, & Imperii fato factum, ut in Imperatorem tenuerit Papa tantum potestatis, & illius ab eo huc usque pendeat dignitas, ejusque confirmatio & coronatio ut abíque ea ne Imperator quidem dicendus videatur? Coronationem, & benedictionem Pontificalem ambierunt, fateor, jam olim à Papa & Episcopo Romano Imperatores, pro humanitatis, & quasi religionis aliquo officio, majori certe ac decuit: indeque pro ambitione sua, & iniquitatis isto operante mysterio, jus & debitum Papa, ac legem fecit. Imprudentes Imperatores atque intempestive nimium humani erga Papam, quod honoris ei detulerunt acceptum ab eo, atque abusum graviter fuit, proque lege habitum, ac sanctum id deberi sibi, neque ut aliter unquam liceat. Quis ante Fridericum I. ex universo Imperatorum catalogo visus auditusve est Papae equitanti, vel ex equo descendenti pedancum tenuisse? vel quis in eo aliquid praeter insolitum humanitatis officium spectet? Papae tamen exinde legem constituerunt, uti mox videbimus, ut semper quando Romae fuerit Imperator coronandus, hoc officium Papae praestare teneatur. Non dubito, quin si unquam Fridericus cogitare potuisset, illo suo facto adeo abusuros fuisse Papas, & debitum sibi officium, & legem sequentibus Imperatoribus inde extructuri fuissent, quod nunquam illud commissurus fuisset, vel daturus exemplum, quo solo in magnum Imperii praejudicium talem legem constituissent. Atque eodem pacto cum Imperatorum à Papis coronatione se res habuit. Ex religione quidem quasi aliquâ, sed liberâ, neutiquam ad hunc vel illum Episcopum, aut sedem astricta coronari cupierunt; à Romano Episcopo Imperatores: & hoc liberum fuit, ut à sacerdote, quemadmodum loquebantur, fieret; & à Romano. Hic à honore isto in propria commoda & arrogantiam verso, utrumque fecit necessarium: neque hoc solum, ut sacerdotalem quasi benedictionem & consecrationem conferat, quod spirituale & Ecclesiasticum videri possit, set, sed ulterius, exertis in ipsum Imperium ejusque politica suis alis, majestatem Imperii à se dependere, & suum esse hoc beneficium, neque absque approbatione & confirmatione suâ Imperatorem rite quamvis electum, vel Imperatoris nomine, titulo, aut juribus uti ante coronationem posse, credi voluit; quamvis reclamante semper Imperio. Etenim à solo Deo imperium esse, atque majestatem illius à nullo alio dependere, vel subjectum alicui esse, jam olim Fridericus Imp. dixit: per electionem Principum à solo Deo regnum & imperium nostrum est. Ludovicus. IV. Imperialis dignitas & potestas est immediate à solo Deo. Vnde etiam a. clxxxc xxxviii. adversus Iohannem xxii. scribit:Imperator Ludovicus IV. divino duntaxat munere Cæsar Augustus. Videlicet, uti id antea explicarat:Imperator ex solâ electione eorum ad quos pertinet, verus efficitur Imperator, nec alicujus alterius eget confirmatione seu approbatione: quorum in temporalibus non habet superiorem in terris. Let your fatherhood therefore take care lest, while it raises such matters, which we regard as unworthy, it place a stumbling block before those who hasten to lend their ears to your mouth as to a late rain. For we cannot but answer what we have heard, since we see that the detestable beast of pride has crept as far as the See of Peter, while we always provide well for the peace of the Church. Farewell always. I always compare these letters with those which Pope Boniface VIII and King Philip of France exchanged with each other in the year 1302. Of these, the earlier was written by the former to the King, and reads thus: Boniface, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Philip, King of the Franks. Fear God and keep his commandments. We wish you to know that you are subject to us in spiritual and temporal matters, and we regard as heretics those who believe otherwise, etc. Given. Here is the reply, in answer: Philip, by the grace of God King of the Franks, to Boniface who conducts himself as Supreme Pontiff, little or no greeting. Let your very great folly know that we are subject to no one in temporal matters, etc. We regard those who believe otherwise as fools and madmen. Given, etc. Who could bear the great insolence of this man, and of the Pope, who from a very long time had been accustomed to seek confirmation of his election from the Emperor, and who has advanced his affairs so far that, having made himself his own master, he no longer cares for the Emperor, nor waits for his consent or approval; but, the tables turned, he has himself made the Emperor so subject to him that without his nod and confirmation the other cannot even bear the power or the very name of Emperor; and he who was not once but several times deposed by Emperors now dares himself at last to depose Emperors and to appoint others in their place? There exist the rescripts of the Emperor Honorius of the year 419, in the case of Eulalius and Boniface, by which he confirmed Boniface in the Pontificate and rejected Eulalius as a schismatic; and the edict of King Odoacer of the year 483, that no election should be held without his consultation. Similarly, the decree of King Theodoric of the year 498. And in the year 774, Hadrian I, having convened at Rome a synod of 153 bishops and abbots, after the defeat of the Lombards, decreed to Charlemagne, who had been summoned from there to Rome to liberate Italy from the Lombards, the right of electing the Pontiff. Apart from the historians, Gratian himself also reports this in Distinction 63, c. 22: Hadrian the Pope, together with the whole synod, handed over to Charles the right and power of electing the Pontiff and of ordaining the apostolic see; they also granted him the dignity of patrician. Moreover, he decreed that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investiture from him, so that no bishop should be consecrated by anyone unless he was approved and invested by the king; and whoever acted against this decree he bound with the chain of anathema, and, unless he repented, he ordered his goods to be confiscated. The truth of these things, which Baronius alone labours to overthrow, is defended by Melchior Goldast in the introduction to his Rational of Imperial Constitutions. And nothing is more frequent in the histories of both Emperors and Popes than to hear that the election of the Popes depended on the will of the Emperors. Leo VIII confirmed this, following the example of Hadrian, for Otto I, in the year 964: Therefore, following the example of blessed Hadrian, we have heard that this bishop of the Apostolic See, whose life and conduct are sufficiently discreet, who has been most reasonable in his spiritual duties, granted to the Lord Charles, most victorious King of the Franks and of the kingdom of Italy, and to the dignity of patrician, and the ordination of the Apostolic See, and moreover the investitures of bishoprics, as it may seem fitting to him to do with discretion and reverence; apart from those which Charles himself reserved to the Pontiff of the highest see as well as to the archbishops. Therefore we, Leo, servant of the servants of God, bishop, following the same example of blessed Hadrian, together with all the clergy and the whole Roman people, and all the orders of this kindly City, as appears in their writings, have established, confirmed and strengthened, and by our apostolic authority we grant and bestow upon the Lord Otto the First, the most learned King of the Teutons. On this, the Cologne Chronicle says: Leo VIII, seeing that frauds were customary in the election of Popes, ordained that no Pope should be elected without the consent of the Emperor; and that it was lawful for the Emperor to appoint bishops and prelates, as formerly in the Synod of the Third Distinction, assembled; which Hadrian had also granted to Charlemagne. Otto III, in his constitution on the right and power of the Empire, in the year 998: We have elected Sylvester, our magistrate, Pope, and by God's will we have ordained and created him most serene. Henry II, in the year 1014, in the constitution by which he confirmed the donations made to the Roman Church, added a condition, that the elected Pontiff should not be consecrated without the confirmation of the Emperor. The bishops of Germany, in the year 1077, at the Diet of Worms, in the case of Henry IV against Hildebrand the Pope, speak among other things thus: when a synod was held in the time of Pope Nicholas, in which one hundred and twenty bishops sat, it was decreed and enacted under anathema that no one should become Pope unless by the election of the cardinals, the approval of the people, and the consent and authority of the King. And you yourself were the author, promoter and signatory of this council or decree. This dispute was always debated between Caesar and the Pope, in whose hands was the investiture, as they called it, of ecclesiastics, even of popes. The Pope claimed this for himself over all the bishops throughout the Empire, not to mention the other kingdoms of the world; and the Emperor asserted that it was owed to him. I do not now pursue a judgement on the factions and zeal of both the Emperors and the Popes against each other, nor do I act as narrator, so that it may be seen to what point the Roman Pope has now brought his affairs, so that, with the Roman Emperor, to whom he himself was formerly subject, made subject to himself, he has made his coronation depend so much on himself that, without it, he thinks the one chosen by the princes of the Empire should not even be called Emperor. I do not much care about the ecclesiastical hierarchy, whether of the Popes or of the bishops, still less when they have become political, on whom their constitution, election or confirmation depends; but as far as ecclesiastical law is concerned, concerning the constitution of ecclesiastical matters as such, the Emperor has hitherto acted justly against the Pope, who was arrogating to himself power over churches in no way pertaining to him, over which he was merely trying to [κυριεύειν] hold sway. Yet neither should the Emperor, once the Pope's pretensions were shaken off, himself usurp what is ecclesiastical, insofar as it is ecclesiastical and not political. Thus both acted badly in their own cause, when neither had a right over the churches; but it would have befitted the Emperor, once the Pope had been brought into order, to defend and protect the ecclesiastical rights of the Church, just as one who has charge of the goods and rights of orphans, and does not seize them for himself but preserves them for the wards, should keep and leave to the Church, to be protected by the Emperor, its own right, and not usurp it from another, whether Pope or Emperor. Moreover, it would be an endless task to show by all the histories the elections of the Popes, that the Emperor always had their confirmations, besides the fact that it is well enough known to anyone that many Popes were formerly deposed by Emperors. I beg you to see now, since the story is so changed, how the Pope now holds over the Emperor the power which the Emperor once held, and for so long, over the Pope? Formerly the Emperor used to choose him, confirm him, or even, where affairs required, depose him; now he is said, from the opposite side, to be chosen by him, confirmed, and sometimes even deposed. Indeed, just as it was necessary that the Pope be appointed by the Emperor, so now, conversely, nothing of right is left to the Emperor over the Pope; in whose election the consent or approval of neither the Emperor nor any king is any longer expected or sought, but, the Emperor now being removed, he is chosen and confirmed by the cardinals alone. And if this were all, that they should be mutually free from each other and not depend on one another, neither the Emperor on the Pope nor the Pope on the Emperor; but by some evil and by the fate of the Empire it has come about that the Pope has held such power over the Emperor, and that the dignity of the Emperor depends on him so far to this day, and his confirmation and coronation, that without it the Emperor himself seems not even to be called Emperor? I admit that Emperors long ago sought the coronation and pontifical blessing from the Pope and the Roman bishop, out of some duty of humanity and, as it were, of religion, certainly greater than was fitting; and so, through his ambition, and by the working of this mystery of iniquity, the Pope made a right and a debt of it, and a law. Imprudent Emperors, and too human at the wrong time towards the Pope, have heavily abused the honour they bestowed upon him, which they had received from him, and it has been regarded as a law, and held sacred, that this is owed to him, and that it may never be otherwise. Who among the whole catalogue of Emperors before Frederick I was seen or heard to hold the stirrup of a Pope riding or dismounting? Or who sees in that anything beyond an unusual office of humanity? Yet the Popes afterwards made it a law, as we shall soon see, that whenever the Emperor is to be crowned at Rome, the Pope is bound to perform this office. I do not doubt that if Frederick had ever been able to foresee that the Popes would abuse that deed of his so much, and would build from it a debt owed to them and a law for following Emperors, he would never have committed it, or given the example by which alone they would have established such a law to the great prejudice of the Empire. And in the same way the matter stood with the coronation of the Emperors by the Popes. Out of a certain religion, indeed, but a free one, the Emperors never sought to be crowned by this or that bishop or see; by the Roman bishop, the Emperors; and this was free, that it should be done by a priest, as they put it, and by the Roman one. He turned this honour into his own advantage and arrogance, and made both things necessary; and not only so that he might confer a priestly blessing and consecration, which might seem spiritual and ecclesiastical, but further, extending his wings over the Empire itself and its political affairs, he wished to be believed that the majesty of the Empire depends on him, and that this is his benefice, and that the Emperor, though rightly elected, cannot use the Emperor's name, title or rights before coronation without his approval and confirmation; although the Empire has always protested. For the Emperor Frederick long ago said that the empire comes from God alone, and that its majesty depends on no other, nor is subject to anyone: Our kingdom and empire is by the election of the princes from God alone. Louis IV: The imperial dignity and power is immediately from God alone. Hence also in the year 1338, against John XXII, he writes: Emperor Louis IV, Caesar Augustus by the divine gift alone. Clearly, as he had explained this before: The Emperor becomes a true Emperor by the election of those to whom it belongs alone, and needs no other confirmation or approval, since in temporal matters he has no superior on earth. Sigismund, in a letter written at Siena in the year 1433 to the Council of Basel, when he was there seeking coronation from the Pope, while not regarding it as absolutely necessary for himself, signifies this sufficiently when he says: Assuring you that unless His Holiness had often approved the said Council, we would undoubtedly have returned to our own affairs without the crowns themselves, which on account of the acts of the same Council we have so long omitted. Nor do I doubt that Charles V understood the same in his rescript to Clement VII in the year 1526, where, complaining of the leagues and alliances the Pope had made against him and the Empire, he cites that verse of the Psalm: Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood up and the princes gathered together against, he says, not the Lord and Christ, but against the Minister instituted by the Lord, divinely, by Christ himself, from whom all authority and power depends. But whether the Emperor has his power immediately from God or from the Pope (for this is what they understand by 'immediately' in the present business, as opposed to the Pope), see James Almain, Doctor of Paris, in his book On the Supreme Ecclesiastical and Lay Power, who proves it at length by law and reasons; and Antonius de Rosellis, Doctor of Laws of Arezzo, in his treatise On Monarchy, that is, on the power of the Emperor and the Pope, part 1. Add the Information of John of Jandun for Louis the Emperor, where from various reasons he concludes: that the imperial power is immediately from God and not from the Pope; and that one elected Emperor by election alone is King of the Romans and has the authority, jurisdiction and imperial power even before he is anointed and consecrated, or crowned, by the Pope. The Basel men also did not ignore this, when after the death of Louis the Emperor they answered the Bishop of Bamberg thus: Lord of Bamberg, whichever Emperor the electors give us, him we receive, even if he never seeks the Pope. The gloss on Distinction 93, c. 1, Legimus, has it thus: For by the election of the princes alone, I say that he is a true Emperor before he is confirmed by the Pope. Many other things brought forward on this same matter may be seen in Goldast, in his Reply on behalf of the Empire, against Gretser, chapter 36, where, from various testimonies of the ancient writers and by reasons, he proves that the Roman king elected is Emperor, and is held to be Emperor, before and without the Pope's coronation, and handles imperial matters with every right and fullness of power; just as Baldus says in his Consilia, Consilium 326: It is the common opinion of the jurists that the Emperor before coronation, although as King of the Romans, can do all that an Emperor can, since the crown is not of the substance of the power, although it adds an increase of majesty and honour. Then Goldast shows by various examples that the Kings of the Romans and the elected Emperors were called Emperors and Augusti from the election itself, not from the coronation of the Pope. Add also the Vindications of John Servin, a Frenchman, on the liberty of the Gallican Church, written under Henry IV, where the author solidly and learnedly shows that the King of the Franks was held to be king long before and without coronation: As to the power of administering the kingdom, anointing and coronation add nothing. The author of the book Dream of the Garden, under the name of Philotheus Achillinus, which contains a dialogue of a cleric and a soldier, written under Charles V, King of France. Besides, the Oration of John Garsenius of Mons, On the Papal Coronation of the Elected Roman Emperor, which is found among the Imperial Politics of Goldast, Part IV; Jerome Balbus, On Coronation, to Charles V; Restaurus Castaldus, On the Emperor, question 46; Simon Scardius, On the right which the Emperors once had in approving the Popes, and how, that right being taken away in turn, the Popes began to usurp for themselves the authority of confirming or rejecting Caesar. Henry Bebel, for the majesty and pre-eminence of the Emperor and the Empire of the Germans: where, against Leonhard Justinian of Venice, who on this ground also diminished the majesty of the Emperor, that they are first Kings of the Romans and only afterwards Emperors by coronation, he speaks thus: To this I reply to you, that by the consent of all of us the Emperor seems to us greater than the King (as I have proved), yet we do not think the King of the Romans to be other than the Roman Emperor as to the exercise of power. For after someone of ours is elected King of the Romans, he at once exercises all the offices of the Emperor, and (to speak in the manner of the recent jurists) in fact has the full administration of all things and supreme power, nor does the creation as Emperor add anything but a certain solemnity and certain ornaments, which the Roman Pontiff, not we, devised. Therefore, that someone of the Romans should first be called King and afterwards Emperor by the coronation of the Pontiff, is the institution of the Apostolic See alone, not of the Germans, as the laws on the venerable chapter, Extra, On Election, show. But we Germans, when we have elected someone as King of the Romans, at once he is also held by us as Emperor; but those three coronations were not introduced by us, on account of a greater empire, but on account of the customs of the places. For first at Aachen he is crowned for the kingdom of the Teutons and Belgian Gaul; at Milan, according to the custom of the Lombards, who look to the addition of the Roman Emperor; lastly at Rome, for the Roman Empire. Indeed, another question also hangs on this, which Antonius Quetta debated at the Council of Trent, concerning the precedence of the King of the Romans, or of his ambassadors, before the King of France. This is not a dispute about the excellence of the Emperor, but if the King of the Romans differs so much from the Emperor that he does not yet have imperial authority and power before the papal coronation, and is acknowledged as king... [Here the text is garbled in the original, and I give what it must mean:] Does the King of France, consecrated by the Archbishop of Reims, say that the royal power is conferred on him by the bishop? Or where the King of Spain is consecrated by the Archbishop of Toledo; or formerly the King of the English by the Archbishop of Canterbury; now the King of Poland by the Archbishop of Gniezno, the King of Sweden by the Archbishop of Uppsala, the King of Hungary by the Archbishop of Esztergom; or the King of the Germans is anointed and crowned by the Archbishop of Cologne: does one say that the royal dignity is granted to them by these men? Nor can it be said more of the imperial dignity, even though the Emperor receives the blessing or coronation from the Pope; much less that he is not to be called or held Emperor without it. Hence Louis IV, at the Diet of Frankfurt in the year 1339, at which Edward, King of England, was also present, and was appointed Vicar-General of the Empire, declared that the elected Emperor is a true Emperor, and that his coronation by the Pope is not of such necessity: Whoever has more of the votes of the princes, even in discord, is to be regarded as truly elected, whether King or Emperor, since in essence they are the same, although they are believed to have different names; and he can, without the confirmation of the Apostolic See, both exercise and administer the rights of the Empire. He ought also at once, after the notification of the princes, to be anointed by the Pontiff, if he has been lawfully elected. But if the Pontiff refuses, he may be proclaimed Emperor and Augustus by any Catholic bishop, since these anointings and solemnities are only certain inventions devised by the Pontiffs, granting names only and not realities. For what Roman Pontiff preserved the Emperors of Constantinople? And who before Charles blessed many Christian Caesars? And before Constantine, what ethnic priest consecrated Emperors? Nor does the Emperor give the oath of fealty to the Pontiff, but of obedience and of defence of the faith. In the same place he shows it to be most absurd that during a vacancy the right of the Empire devolves on the Pope; but, on the contrary, that the administration of it belongs to the Count Palatine of the Rhine, notwithstanding the Clementine Pastoralis. And in the year 1345, when Clement VI pressed, the constitution made by Louis for the Empire, its liberty and majesty, against the Pope, that they should be revoked, and that the Empire should be acknowledged as a benefice of the Pope, all these things were condemned at the Diet of Frankfurt. In the year 1345 the legates of Caesar return from Avignon and bring back the written mandates of the Supreme Pontiff to the Augustus, whose sum was this: that Caesar should hand over William of Ockham, the heresiarch, and his colleagues and associates, to the Supreme Pontiff; that he should retract the decrees against John XXII, the Vicar of Christ, rescind the acts, renew the approvals, and publicly sanction by perpetual edict that the Empire is a benefice of the chief priest, and that no one is or is called Caesar before he becomes its author. When these things were reported to the Emperor at Frankfurt, he summoned the nobles and ordered the mandates of Clement VI to be read out. A decree was made: such demands, being wicked, foolish, antiquated, and in fact more subtle than was fitting to the simplicity of Christ and the majesty of the Republic, were declared void and vain; and the Avignon priests, forgetful of their good fortune and of human weakness, were proclaimed to know no measure in speaking or acting except what they wish. This was confirmed in the year 1349 by Gunther of Schwarzburg, elected Emperor by the Archbishop of Mainz, the Saxon, the Brandenburger, while others followed Charles of Bohemia, who stood on the Papal side and had been confirmed by the Pope, namely the Cologne and Trier men and the Bohemian. Therefore, in the city of Frankfurt, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, Gunther issued this edict: Since our predecessor, the Lord Louis of happy memory, Roman Emperor, made a law in which he decreed that the one elected at Frankfurt as King of the Romans by the Electoral princes, or the greater part of them, should have full and complete administration of the Empire before papal confirmation, we, with the counsel of our princes, both spiritual and secular, after our election, approved and confirmed by all the clergy and people, by this our edict, to be valid in perpetuity, renew and ratify the same law, and order it to be renewed and ratified; and we decree that all proceedings instituted against it were and are null, and that the acts and doctrines of the Roman Pontiffs held against it are repugnant to Christian doctrine and the Apostolic, since the Pontiff himself, according to all divine and human laws, ought to be subject to the Empire, and the Emperor is known not to be subject in temporal matters to him or to any person on earth. What, then, is this pride, what new and unheard-of tyranny, that a Prince elected by the lawful votes of the Romans, the author of public liberty, should be deprived of liberty, so that he, to whom all things ought to belong, should not be his own? And yet the Papists would have us think otherwise; nor is there any other reason why Innocent, in his Bull, calls Ferdinand the elected Emperor, not full, not absolutely or simply to be called Emperor; merely elected. Finally, that the Pope might openly exercise this power of his, and recover its use, this was lately suggested to Gregory XV by Michael Lonigo, prefect of the writings in the Vatican, in the case of Maximilian, Duke of Bavaria, when it was a matter of persuading him to seek from the Pope the confirmation of the electoral dignity he had obtained; by which means, as the author says at the beginning, the Pope would have gained in a short time as much as was acquired by the previous Popes in not even two hundred years; or rather, to speak more truly, he would reclaim and redeem that which the others have lost from the time of Gregory XI down to our own days, of the rights which pertained to the Church in the constitution of the matters and orders of the Empire. What are these rights? Namely, in the elections of Emperors, that no one ever ascends to the height of the Empire without their assent or the intervention of the legates of the Apostolic See. Nor could the elected Emperor mix himself in the administration of affairs unless first the assent of the Supreme Pontiff had been given and a confirmation granted. You see what it means to say the Emperor is elected, namely that he may not mix himself in the administration of the affairs of the Empire. Whether Ferdinand and the princes of the Empire today understand it so, I very much doubt. Concerning some secret confirmation of an Emperor by the Pope I cannot speak; this I know: that neither this one nor many before him sought a Roman confirmation, still less a coronation, publicly and openly. And yet this, says Lonigo, is that from which the Doctors infer that election is not sufficient for the Emperor, but he necessarily needs the confirmation of the Pontiff. In which case not only the form of the election is usually weighed, but also the very person of the one elected, since it is not absurd that the election should appear lawfully made, but the man elected may lack those qualities which are required here, so that he is unequal to so great a weight. And if this happens, it is in the power of the Pontiff to reject him and to depose him from the height of that dignity. Whatever... to guard and preserve its possessions, honours and rights, and the right, as far as I shall be aided by the divine help, according to my knowledge and power, with a right and pure faith. So help me God, and these holy Gospels of God. The same is found in the Clementine, On the Oath, the chapter Romanus Princeps. Charles V, when he was crowned at Bologna by Pope Clement VII in the year 1530, is said to have used this oath: I, Charles, King of the Romans, and soon to be Caesar by the grace of God, promise, testify and swear by God and the divine Peter, that henceforth, with all my strength, talent and resources, I shall be the perpetual defender of the Pontifical dignity and of the Roman Church, and that I shall do no violence to ecclesiastical liberty; but that I shall preserve and protect the power, jurisdiction and lordship of the same as far as it can be done. I call God himself and these holy Gospels to witness of this. Thus the Pope binds the Emperor to himself, again and again, by so many and such great oaths. Henry VII of Luxembourg acted more wisely, who, as Aventinus reports in the Annals of the Boii, book VII, when he entered Italy to obtain coronation, wrote to Pope Clement V that the Roman Emperor ought not to swear an oath to the Roman Pontiff, since it is a thing most unusual and of new example, for a Prince and Lord of the world to be bound by an oath of fealty to the servant of the servants. On the contrary, it would be more fitting for the Pope to swear to the Emperor, as Frederick I did when the cardinals, in the name of Pope Hadrian, stipulated among other things: That envoys are not to be sent by the Emperor to the City without the knowledge of the Apostolic, since every magistracy there belongs to St Peter with all the royal rights. That the bishops of Italy should make only the oath of fealty without homage to the Lord Emperor. Nor should the envoys of the Emperor be received in the palaces of the bishops. He answered well, that since those places, and the palaces, and the city were his, he too ought to be acknowledged their lord and Emperor. I indeed do not require homage of the bishops of Italy, if they are not pleased to hold anything of our royal rights. If they are willing to receive the prelates gladly from the Roman [Pope]... What have you to do with the King? They also do not mind hearing the Emperor: What have you to do with the possession? It is asserted that our envoys are not to be received in the palaces of the bishops: I concede it, if perchance some bishop's palaces are on our soil and allodial land, since everything built on the soil belongs to the soil, and the palaces are ours. It would therefore be an injury if anyone kept our envoys from the royal palaces. He affirms that envoys are not to be sent by the Emperor to the City, since every magistracy there belongs to St Peter with all the royal rights. This matter, I confess, is great and grave, and needs a weightier and more mature counsel. For although by divine ordinance I am and am called Roman Emperor, I am putting on only the appearance of a lord, and an empty name without the reality, if the power over the City of Rome has been shaken from my hand. Returning to the coronation of the Emperor by the Pope, which was the subject of our discussion: the Emperor, before the coronation and already being at Rome, sits at the feast after the first bishop-cardinal; if a king is also present, he takes a place after the first presbyter-cardinal, neither before them. But when he has been crowned, then the Emperor sits in a seat arranged between the Pope and the first bishop-cardinal, and the King after the first cardinal. For there are, as commonly three orders in the clergy, bishops, presbyters, deacons, so there are cardinals of three orders: bishop-cardinals, presbyter-cardinals and deacon-cardinals. And when he is now to ride with the Pope through the city, this is done under the same canopy, as they say, the Emperor holding the Pope's left side, having handed over the sceptre and orb to one of his men, he goes ahead to the Pope's horse, and in honour of our Saviour Jesus Christ, whose place the Pope holds on earth, he holds the stirrup until the Pope has mounted his horse. And then, having taken the bridle, he leads the Pope's horse for some paces. In which office, as the Emperor Frederick was less practised, he excused his error, when he held the right stirrup instead of the left, as is well known, falsely. And what, I ask, does the Emperor gain or lose, either for himself or for the Empire, in that coronation at Rome, which the Popes press so hard? Surely nothing but disgrace, dishonour, loss, and the certain danger of exposing his majesty to everyone's contempt. And these are the things contained under it, since the Pope names the Emperor only as Ferdinand, King of the Romans and elected Emperor, that is, not yet crowned, and not approved and confirmed by his See, at least not publicly and solemnly; and therefore is not to be called Emperor simply, nor Augustus.

units.la: X. Ludovicum Francorum Regem Christianissimum) Gregorius I. Regem Francorum appellavit Catholicum. Gregorius IX. Christianissimum, atque ita Innocentius IV. Vrbanus IV. & subsequentes. Quin titulum Regis Christianissimi Regi Romanorum asserunt Henricus Bebelius, atq; aliorum exemplo: ego in scriptis meis, inquit, Regem nostrum Maximilianum appellito Christianissimum, exemplum divi Ambrosii, & aliorum, qui Imperatores Christianissimos scribunt, exemplo Romana Ecclesia, qua in die Parasceves pro Caesare orans dicit: pro Christianissimo Imperatore Romano. Ita habent libri facti tam recentes, quam vetusti. Alterum Regis Hispaniarum itulum Catholici, a.cl9 ccccxcii. Ferdinandus & Isabella Reges Arragonię & Castellæ, post ejectos Hispaniæ Mauros, & receptam Granatam, ob erecta adversus Iudæos & Muhammedanos Inquisitionem, ab Innocentio P. VIII. primi adepti sunt. Bzovius, Annal. Ecclesiast. Tom. xviii. Alii dicunt, a.Iulio II. Adrianus Meerbeeck, in Chronico Universali ad A. 1610. Frustra sunt, qui tituli illius causam arcessunt, jam inde ab a.1. cxxxvii, ex Concilio Toletano VI. ubi Regum Hispaniæ commendatur fides & zelus pro catholicæ religionis defensione adversus Iudæos, eo quod ibi dicitur, quod Rex non sinat degere in regno suo quempiam qui non sit catholicus, quodque Rex in suâ inauguratione teneatur jurare, se catholicam non permissurum violari religionem; quasi quod ibi nomen catholici occurrit in Synodo Hispaniæ, idque quando sermo de Regeeft, ejusque erga Ecclesiam & fidem devotione, sequatur, haud esse recentem titulum Hispaniarum Regum, ut Catholici cognominentur: quemadmodum imperitè inde colligit Baronius, Annal. Tom. viii., atque ex eo Dionysius Mutzaerdt, in sua Historia Ecclesiastica, qui alterum illud de Regibus Arragoniæ, & dato illis titulo isto, historiam ea attingens, nequidquam tamen memorat; scilicet vetustiorem titulum cupiens, & originem, aliamque, quam revera sit. Et super antiquitatem quidem potissimum fundant Galli jus præeminentiæ
units.tr: X. Ludovicus, the most Christian King of the Franks) Gregory I called the King of the Franks Catholic. Gregory IX called him most Christian, and so did Innocent IV, Urban IV and their successors. Indeed, Henricus Bebelius, following the example of others, claims the title of most Christian King for the King of the Romans: in my writings, he says, I call our King Maximilian most Christian, following the example of the blessed Ambrose and others who write of Christian emperors, and following the Roman Church, which in its Good Friday prayer for Caesar says for the most Christian Roman Emperor. So do books both recent and old. The other title, Catholic, of the King of Spain, was first taken by Ferdinand and Isabella, Kings of Aragon and Castile, in the year 1492, after the Moors had been driven out of Spain and Granada taken, when, because of the Inquisition set up against Jews and Muslims, Pope Innocent VIII granted it. So Baronius, in Annals of the Church, vol. xviii. Others say it was granted by Julius II. Adrianus Meerbeeck, in Universal Chronicle, under the year 1610, says so. Those who trace the reason for that title back to the year 638, from the Sixth Council of Toledo, are wrong. There the faith and zeal of the Kings of Spain are commended in defence of the Catholic religion against the Jews, because the council says that the King does not allow anyone to live in his kingdom who is not Catholic, and that at his inauguration the King is bound to swear that he will not permit the Catholic religion to be violated. It is as if, because the word Catholic occurs in a Spanish synod, and that where the speech concerns the King and his devotion to the Church and the faith, it follows that the title Catholic is not a recent title of the Kings of Spain. So Baronius draws an unskilled conclusion, and Dionysius Mutzaerdt after him, in his Ecclesiastical History, who, though he touches on that other matter about the Kings of Aragon and the granting of that title to them, mentions it in vain, evidently wanting an older title and a different origin from the true one. Indeed, the French base their right of precedence and of sitting before the King of Spain, whom they call Catholic, chiefly on antiquity, as appeared in the protest made by the ambassadors of King Charles IX of France at the Council of Trent in the year 1563, when a place was being assigned and the ambassadors of the King of Spain were to take the first place after the Emperor's. They laid all the blame for this on Pope Pius IV alone.

units.la: ac præsefsionis Regis lui, ante Regem Hispanię, quem appellant Catholicum: uti apparuit in Oratorum Galliæ Regis Caroli IX. Protestatione, in Concilio Tridentino faêta a. cIↄ Iↄ lxiii. quando lecus fieret, & Oratores Hispani Regis, post Imperatoris, locum caperent primum; cujus omnem culpam in solum rejiciebant Papam Pium IV. cujus ajebant imperium detrectamus, quæcumque sint ejus judicia & sententia, rejicimus, respuimus & contemnimus. Et quamquam, Patres sanctissimi, vestra omnium religio, vita & eruditio magna semper fuit & erit apud nos auctoritatis, cum tamen nihil à vobis, sed omnia magis Romæ quam Tridenti, agantur: & qua hic publicantur, magis Pii Quarti placita, quam Concilii Tridentini Decreta jure existimentur, denunciamus & protestamur, quæcumque in hoc Conventu, hoc est, solo Pii nutu & voluntate, decernuntur & publicantur, ea neque regem Christianissimum probaturum, neque Ecclesiam Gallicanam pro Decreto Oecumenici Concilii habituram. Interea, quotquot estis Galliæ Archiepiscopi, Episcopi, Abbates, Doctores, Theologi, vos omnes hinc abire Rex Christianissimus jubet, redituros, ut primum Deus Optimus Maximus Ecclesiæ Catholicæ in generalibus Conciliis antiquam formam & libertatem restituerit: Regi autem Christianissimo suam dignitatem & Majestatem. Iam causas attendere oportet, propter quas motum se profitetur Papa, ad pacem, inter tantos orbis Christiani Principes iğam ratamque, abrogandam. In genere primum ait; quia gravissima Religionis Catholicæ, divino cultui, Sedi Apostolicæ, & Romanæ, ac inferioribus ecclesiis, Ordinique ecclesiastico, ac Iurisdictionibus, Auctoritatibus, Immunitatibus, libertatibus, exemptionibus, privilegiis, pactis, turnis, ac juribus illorum illata fuerunt præjudicia. I. de illatis Religioni Catholicæ, divinoque cultui præjudiciis, à Rege Christianissimo, uti appellat, hic ipse viderit: vel potius de facto sibi tantæ impietatis dicâ & injuria. II. Quid hæc jura sonent in Ecclesiâ Romanâ, quæ hic recenseт, & per pacem everti conqueritur, nil attinet multis explicare: potius id considerent omnes, num hæc tanta sint omnia, ut propter ea tanti moliminis ususque pax negligi gi aut rescindi debeat: annó omnia sint & institutionis & commodi duntaxat Papalis, ut in horum gratiam Respublicæ conturbari, & devastari bello tam crudeli & diro, quale Germanicum fuit, debeant. Denique & quis non videt hinc, tum quis belli flabrum moveat, unde & qua ex orbis regione turbines ac tempestates illæ veniant; tum quæ intima, & efficacissima, religiosaque bellandi hactenus causa fuerit & ratio, videlicet pro juribus, authoritate, ditione, & bonis Papalibus. Sane res Paparum dederunt bello isti & spiritu, & motus. 111. Si Papa ita judicet de pace initâ inter Imperatore & Suecum; tum Gallum; quid censes illum de nostrâ pace Belgicâ statuere, & de Catholico suo Rege Philippo? annon & hæc pax, quamquì ipse Rex maximopere ursit, juribus, auctoritatibus, & bonis, quæque his similia, suis videtur esse prejudicio? procul dubio magis ac illa, sive cum Sueco, sive cum Gallo, ab Imperatore facta: & quid ergo? an & nostram irritâ dicere, improbamque, & execrandam? vel uti hic in Bullâ loquitur, de pace Germaniæ, quod ipso jure nulla, irrita, invalida, iniqua, injusta, damnata, reprobata, inania, viribusque, & effectu vana omnino fuisse, esse, & in perpetuo fore, neminiemque ad illorum, & cujuslibet eorum, etiam si juramento vallata sint, observantiam teneri, neque ex illis cuiquam aliquod jus, vel actionem, aut titulum coloratum, vel causam præscribendi, etiam si longissimi, & immemorabilis temporis possessio, seu quasi possessio etiam citra ullam interpellationem, seu interruptionem subsequatur, acquisitum fuisse, nec esse, minusve ullo tempore acquiri, & competere posse, neque illa ullum statum facere, vel fecisse, atq; perinde, ac si nunquam emanassent, pro non exstantibus, & non factis perpetuo haberi debere, tenore earundem præsentium, decernimus, vel declaramus, atq; uti sequitur, articulos pacis præfactos & potestatis plenitudine penitus damnamus, reprobamus, nullamus, cassamus, annullamus, viribusque & effectu vacuamus? De pace nostra neque benignius eum sentire vel loqui, neque imo posse ex suis hypothesibus & regulis, quis queat dubitare? & vel eo ergo nomine, eum incessurum Regem Hispaniæ, ut ibi Imperatorem, & Regem Galliæ, nisi id jam fecerit, vel clam omnia premantur, & colludat tacite nescio cum quibus in nostrâ perniciem,quo subtilius tutiusq;, eo fortius & magis pernitiose, quid dicemus? saltem causarum nihil Papæ deesse æque pacem Belgicam exagitandi & damnandi, (quamvis id Belgæ curemus nihil, quin rideamus potius; sed ad Pontificios nunc loquimur & clientes Papę) religione Papistica eliminata & damnata, sedè Romana ordineque ejus pessundato, jurisdictionibus, auctoritatibus, immunitatibus, libertatibus, exemptionibus, privilegiis,pactisq;, turnis,ac juribus illorum conculcatis, nemo non videt; scilicet inde si causam arripere ei liceat, vel pacis abrogandę, vel à juramento & officio quo ad eam confervandam tenentur homines, absolvendi, vel clientes castigandi suos. iv. Pastorum hic facit mentionem, & Turnorum, id est, mensium Papalium: at quid iniquius, quam hæc servata velle, & non quoque pacta politica, adeo in usum Reip.necessaria?vel in illorum gratiam reliqua omnia pacta,utcumque solennibus juramentis convallata, rescindere & profanare, illis longe justiora atque magis utilia? Hujus edicti æquitas naturalis est, quid enim tam congruum fidei humanæ, quam ea quæ inter eos placuerunt servare? inquit Vlpianus, D. de Pastis l. i.
units.tr: and of the precedence and seating of his own king before the King of Spain, whom they call the Catholic. This appeared in the protest of the ambassadors of King Charles IX of France, made at the Council of Trent in 1563, when a dispute arose over who should take the first place: the ambassadors of the King of Spain, after the Emperor's. They laid all the blame for this on Pope Pius IV, saying: We refuse obedience to his authority, whatever his judgments and decrees may be; we reject, repudiate and despise them. And although, most holy Fathers, your religion, your life and your learning have always been and will always be of great authority among us, yet since nothing is done by you, but everything is done at Rome rather than at Trent, and what is published here should be judged to be the decrees of Pius IV rather than the decrees of the Council of Trent by right, we declare and protest that whatever is decreed and published in this assembly, that is, by the nod and will of Pius alone, will be approved neither by the most Christian King nor held by the Gallican Church as a decree of an ecumenical council. Meanwhile, all of you who are archbishops, bishops, abbots, teachers and theologians of France, the most Christian King orders you all to depart from here, to return when God, the best and greatest, shall have restored to the Catholic Church its ancient form and freedom in general councils; and to the most Christian King, his dignity and majesty. Now we must consider the causes for which the Pope declares himself moved to abrogate the peace, a peace firm and settled among so many princes of the Christian world. In general, he says first that, because the most grievous wrongs have been done to the Catholic religion, to divine worship, to the Apostolic and Roman See, to the lower churches and the ecclesiastical order, and to their jurisdictions, authorities, immunities, liberties, exemptions, privileges, pacts, turns, and rights. (I.) As to the wrongs done to the Catholic religion and divine worship by the most Christian King, as he is called, let him look to that himself; or rather, let them consider the impiety and injury done to himself. (II.) What these rights amount to in the Roman Church, which he here lists and complains are overturned by the peace, there is no need to explain at length; rather, let everyone consider whether these things are so great that for their sake a peace of such effort and use ought to be neglected or annulled, or whether they are all for the institution and advantage of the Papacy alone, so that for their sake commonwealths should be thrown into confusion and laid waste by a war as cruel and dreadful as the German one was. Finally, who does not see from this both what stirs up the storm of war, and from what region of the world those whirlwinds and tempests come; and what has hitherto been the most intimate, most effective, and, as they say, most religious cause and reason for waging war, namely, for the rights, authority, dominion, and goods of the Papacy. Indeed, the affairs of the popes have given this war its spirit and its motion. (III.) If the Pope judges thus about the peace made between the Emperor and the Swede, and then the Frenchman, what do you think he will decide about our Belgian peace, and about his Catholic King Philip? Does not this peace also, though the King himself urges it most strongly, seem to him to be prejudicial to rights, authorities, and goods, and to things like these? Without doubt it does, more than those made with the Swede or with the Frenchman by the Emperor. And so what? Shall we also call ours void, improper and accursed? Or, as he speaks here in the Bull about the peace of Germany, that by law itself it was null, void, invalid, unjust, iniquitous, condemned, reprobated, empty, and wholly vain in its force and effect, and that it was and is and will forever be so, and that no one is bound to observe them, or any of them, even if they have been fortified by oath; and that no right, or action, or colorable title, or cause of prescription may be acquired from them by anyone, even by a possession or quasi-possession of the longest and immemorial time, even if it follows without any challenge or interruption; and that they cannot be acquired or come into being at any time, and that they cannot make any state, nor have made one, and that they must be held as though they had never been issued, and as not existing and not made, forever; by the tenor of these present letters we decree and declare; and as follows, we completely condemn, reprobate, nullify, quash, annul, and empty of force and effect the aforesaid articles of peace by the fullness of power? Who could doubt that he thinks and speaks no more kindly about our peace, and indeed cannot do otherwise according to his own hypotheses and rules? And for that very reason, will he not attack the King of Spain, as he did the Emperor and the King of France, unless he has already done so, or unless all these things are being hidden in secret and he is colluding silently with I know not whom to our ruin, the more subtly and safely, the more strongly and destructively? What shall we say? At least it is plain to everyone that the Pope lacks no grounds for harassing and condemning the Belgian peace equally (although we Belgians take no care for this, but rather laugh at it; yet now we speak to the Papists and the Pope's clients), with the Papist religion eliminated and condemned, the Roman See and its order overthrown, and its jurisdictions, authorities, immunities, liberties, exemptions, privileges, pacts, turns, and rights trampled down. For if he is allowed to seize this cause, then he may either abrogate the peace, or absolve men from the oath and duty by which they are bound to keep it, or punish his clients. (IV.) He mentions pastors and turns, that is, Papal months; but what is more unjust than to wish these to be kept, and not also the political pacts so necessary for the use of the commonwealth? Or, for their sake, to rescind and profane all the other pacts, however fortified by solemn oaths, which are far more just and more useful than those? The natural equity of this edict is plain: for what is so consonant with human good faith as to keep those things which have been agreed between parties? says Ulpian, D. de Pactis l. i.

units.la: XI. Pergendum nobis juxta Bullam, videndumq;, ut probet Papa istam suam jam notatam assertionem, vid. per pacem Germaniæ tantum religioni Catholicę, divino cultui &c. fieri præjudicium: Etenim pactionibus, inquit, partim utriusque, partim alterius pacis hujusmodi inter alia bona Ecclesiastica, aliaque ab Hæreticis occupata, illis, eorumque successoribus in perpetuum addicuntur) i. Quidquid conquestus fuit de pacis iniquitate & improbitate, utrique vult applicatum, & ei quæ Monasterii, inter Imperatorem, ac Suecum; & quæ Ofnabrugi, inter Imperatorem, & Gallum ićta est. quod in hac quidem magis mirandum, non inita nisi inter partes Romanæ religioni, Pontifici & sedi addićtas, utrumque Papæ filium. ii. Hoc annon ridiculum? si modo fas fit in re tam gravi ridere: ad probationem, quod pax Religioni Catholicæ, divino cultui &c. inimica fit & adversa, rationem adferre primam præcipuamque à bonis Ecclesiasticis, iisque jam ab aliis, bello occupatis. Ergone religio Catholica & divinus cultus in solis bonis illis, vel etiam præcipuè situs? atque illius dignitas & res hinc æstimandæ, & quidem principaliter? Hoc non religio, non cultus, non Christus, docent; sed Christianæ religionis est hæc quidem præcipua regula, uti pacem ante omnia venerari ac tenere, ita bona terræ opesque minus æstimare, quin contemnere præ sola pace ac religione. Profecto turpe est tanti terrena illa facere, & tam exigui pacem, quæ interest universi mundi, nec minus Ecclesiæ, ut habeatur atque fervetur.Rom.xiv.17. non est regnum Dei cibus & potus: neque in bonis, quibus illa comparantur, summa religionis consistit. Sive pacem consideremus, & hanc iplam, quam nunc Germania possidet, atque utinam possideat! five religionem: utrique tanto inferiora illa bona sunt, quæ hic Papa loquitur, quibusque in bello non minus caruit, ac jam, ut nec propter illa rumpenda pax tanta, nec in iis ponenda religionis causa videri debeat. Et tamen scio, ob nullam adeo causam, bellum illud funestum hactenus à Pontificiis partibus gestum, & à Papa incitatum fuisse, ad tantam hominum Ecclesiarumque, & religionis stragem, quam ob sola bona ista, quæ dicunt, Ecclesiastica, quomodo repetere illa possent, per vim & arma, quæ Protestantibus jam dudum per fœdera attributa, atque occupata ab iis fuerant.Hoc Collegii Cardinalium nuper in causa Ducis Bavariæ, & confirmandi à Papa ei Electoratus spectabat etiam, quod hoc pacto optime, non solum jura à ducentis usque annis & ultra, in conftituendis rebus & Ordinibus Imperii, sed quoq; possessionem bonorum Ecclefiasticorū recuperare Papa facilius posset.Vid. ipsis religionis anima sunt bona, & dominandi quaquaversum potestas I II.Totius Bullæ Papalis tria hæc sunt quasi elementa, ambitio, avaritia, perfidia: ex ambitione sibi res arrogat Imperii, atque de iis pronunciat, disponit: ex avaritia, & sola bonorum cupiditate conturbat & damnat pacem, omniaque: nec hoc efficere potest, nisi ruptis omnibus juramentis, fide, qua tum ad servandam pacem,tum ad obediendum suis Superioribus homines tenentur. Notum,quod olim Græci responderunt P. Iohanni xxiv. Ambitionem, nec avaritiam tuam toleramus. Diabolus tecum: Deus autem fit nobiscum. Avaritiam suam hoc paragrapho manifeste prodit; sed quam à multis seculis viri quique doctì, pii, cordati, Ecclesiæ,Reges, Principes, in isto homine & Curia diu acriterque jam olim notarunt. Auctor libelli Italici, haud ita pridem scripti (quis enim vetera,& àReformatoribus jam diu,variis scriptorum catalògis prodita hac super re gravamina & querelas repetat?) Il Divortio celeste, lib. i.Christo con si puoco pane, & con si puoco pesce habbia satiate tante mille personne, mentre hora, si vede, che Christo con tanti millioni d' Oro appena può satiare l' appetito d'un solo Pontefice: atque in hunc sensum passim loquitur. iv. Istaque eo minus ferenda, quo, sive attendamus quo pacto acqusrat sua, quę vocat Papa, bona; vel possideat; vel denique utatur iis, indignum est ut pro bonis, quę pleraque injusta rapacitate corrasit,& superfluâ opulentia tenet,neque aliter quam in luxum impendit, violetur pax, religio, & quod sacri bonique Christiana colit respublica. Quis Curiæ Romanæ rapacitatem ignorat? vel quis Scriptorumeam non perstrinxit ac damnavit diu,sæpiusque? adeo ut jam olim dictum creditumque sit, Harpyas suâ reliçtâ insulâ Romam commigrasse, atque in Curia Papali sedes fixisse. Quod inter Alphonsi Regis dicta, refert Panormitanus. Mantuanus, lib. iii. de calamitate Imp. per tecta, per aulas Harpyia, funesta lues, luxuqi, fameqi, Infesta volitant. Aliis,Romam à rodendo dictam esse,scribentibus. Petrus Cassiodorus, in epist. a. clxxccii.qua Anglos de Papalibus exactionibus præmonet, ita loquitur: verè in scrinio Papæ legitur illud Propheta Iefaia, 8. i. propera ad rapinam, festina ad prædam. Christus prose & Petro tributum solvit, hic regna sibi subjicere conatur.
units.tr: XI. We must go on according to the Bull, and see whether the Pope proves his assertion already noted, namely that through the peace of Germany only the Catholic religion, divine worship and so on are prejudiced. For by the agreements, he says, partly of one peace and partly of the other, among other ecclesiastical goods and those seized by heretics, are assigned in perpetuity to those men and their successors. i. Whatever complaint he has made about the injustice and wickedness of the peace, he wants applied to both: to the peace concluded at Münster between the Emperor and the Swede, and to the one struck at Osnabrück between the Emperor and the Frenchman. This is all the more to be wondered at, since these were made only between parties attached to the Roman religion, to the Pontiff and to his see, both of them the Pope's sons. ii. Is this not ridiculous? If it is permitted to laugh at so grave a matter. As proof that the peace is hostile and adverse to the Catholic religion, divine worship and so on, he offers as his first and chief reason the ecclesiastical goods, and those already seized by others in war. Is the Catholic religion and divine worship then situated in those goods alone, or chiefly? Is their dignity and worth to be judged from them, and indeed principally? Christ and religion do not teach this; rather, it is the chief rule of the Christian religion to honour and keep peace above all things, and to value the goods and wealth of the earth less, indeed to despise them in comparison with peace and religion alone. Truly it is shameful to make so much of earthly things and to value so little the peace which concerns the whole world, and the Church no less, that it may be had and preserved. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink (Rom. 14.17); nor does the sum of religion consist in the goods by which such things are obtained. Whether we consider peace, and this very peace which Germany now possesses, and would that it might keep possessing it! or religion: those goods of which this Pope speaks are far inferior to both, and of these Germany lacked no less in the war than now, so that neither should so great a peace be broken on their account, nor should the cause of religion be thought to lie in them. And yet I know that for no cause so great has that deadly war, waged hitherto by the Papist side and stirred up by the Pope, been carried on, with such slaughter of men, churches and religion, as for these goods alone which they call ecclesiastical, that they might by force and arms recover what had long since been granted to the Protestants by treaties and seized by them. This was the aim also of the recent College of Cardinals in the case of the Duke of Bavaria, and of the confirmation of the electorate given to him by the Pope, because in this way the Pope could most easily recover, not only the rights of the past two hundred years and more in settling affairs and orders of the Empire, but also the possession of ecclesiastical goods. See: the goods are the very soul of religion, and the power of dominating everywhere. II. These three things are as it were the elements of the whole Papal Bull: ambition, avarice, perfidy. From ambition he claims for himself the affairs of the Empire, and pronounces and disposes concerning them; from avarice, and from the sole desire for goods, he disturbs and condemns the peace and all things; nor can he do this unless all oaths and good faith are broken, by which men are bound both to keep the peace and to obey their superiors. It is well known what the Greeks once answered to Pope John XXII: We tolerate neither your ambition nor your avarice. Let the devil be with you; but God is with us. He betrays his avarice plainly in this paragraph; but this is what learned, pious and thoughtful men, the Church, kings and princes have long and sharply noted in this man and in the Curia. The author of an Italian book written not long ago (for who would repeat the complaints and grievances on this matter, already long since set forth by the Reformers and in various catalogues of writers?), in Il Divortio celeste, book I, says: Christ with so little bread and so little fish satisfied so many thousands of people, whereas now, it is seen, Christ with so many millions of gold can scarcely satisfy the appetite of a single Pontiff. And he speaks to this effect everywhere. iv. And these things are the less to be borne, since, whether we consider how he acquires the goods which the Pope calls his, or how he possesses them, or finally how he uses them, it is unworthy that peace and religion, and what the Christian commonwealth holds sacred and good, should be violated for the sake of goods which he has amassed for the most part by unjust rapacity, and holds in superfluous opulence, and spends on nothing but luxury. Who is ignorant of the rapacity of the Roman Curia? Or who among writers has not long and often branded and condemned it? So much so that it was once said, and believed, that the Harpies, having left their island, had migrated to Rome and fixed their seats in the Papal Curia. Panormitanus reports this among the sayings of King Alfonso. Mantuanus, book III, On the Calamity of the Emperor: Through the roofs, through the halls, the Harpy, deadly plague, fly about, hostile to luxury and hunger. Others write that Rome is so called from rodere, to gnaw. Petrus Cassiodorus, in letter 187, warning the English about Papal exactions, speaks thus: Truly in the Pope's writing-case one reads that saying of the prophet Isaiah, 8.1: Hasten to the plunder, hurry to the spoil. Christ paid tribute even to Peter; this man tries to subject kingdoms to himself.

units.la: At nos teutonico cupientes parcere RegnoEt simul injustas Cleri prohibere rapinas &c.
units.tr: But we, desiring to spare the German kingdom, and at the same time to restrain the unjust plunderings of the clergy, etc.

units.la: Tum ratione habita ipsorum opulentia, quidni Papæ respondeamus quod Ludovicus Galliæ Rex, dictus Sanctus, olim iis qui tenues reditus quærebantur Monasterii alicujusab ipso ædificati: satis illis adhuc esse, modo probi sint. Quid attinet ut corona Pontificis triginta aureorum millia valeat? quod de eâ quæ Felicis P. capiti impositafuit, refert in Commentario Concilii Basileensis, Æneas Silvius. vel ut ad eam gemma hæreat, quæ sex millibus ducatorum æstimetur? qualem ab eâ in conorationis Clementis tumultu excidisse, memorat Platina. vel ut tam sumtuosa instituatur coronatio, qualis Leonis x. fuit, omnium quæ unquam fuere maxime prodiga, ut quidem testis est Guicciardin, Bell. Italic. lib. xi? quo die centum millia ducatorum à Papa distributa fuisse, quamvis prudentiores judicarent, isliusmodi pompam Papam parum decere, scribit. Qui lib. ix. refert, Iulium II. coronam suam ideo Florentiam misisse, ut pretiosissimum hoc instrumentum à Gallorum furiis ibi tutius servaretur. Quid refert, ut filiæ suæ Papa queat in dote dare, quod Alexander VI. quando jam quartò suam Lucretiam elocaret Alphonso, centum ducatorum millia, præsente pecunia? uti Guicciardin refert, lib. v.
