Quis neget, supra modum ingentes reditus Papam possidere, qui cum sciat quotidie in reditibus habere 26000 coronatorum? qui, quos ei varię orbis regiones, Ecclesiæ, aut Italia; & suum, quod appellat, patrimonium Petri; vel artes suæ Papales, annatæ, reservationes, beneficia, atque istud genus religiosa commenta; aut deniq; sui emissarii nuntii, legati corradunt ubicunq; thesauros, expenderit? Quando Clemens IV. superato Manfredo, Carolum Provinciæ comitem Regem Siciliæ ac Ierusalemi diceret, conditionem adjecit, ut propterea Rex singulis annis quadraginta aureorum millia in Papæ ærarium conferret: sic Platina, Stella: longe plura exacturus, si ditionem pacificâ dedisset, addit Molineus, Comm. de Monarch. Francorum. Ex patrimonio suo, quod ita appellat Papa, ex Ducatu Beneventano, in regno Neapolit. Comitatu Avenionensi, in Gallia; Latio, Umbria, Romandiola, Ducatu Spoletano, Marca Anconitana, Bononia,additis vafallorū tributis,à Rege Hispanię, pro rege Neapolitano, à Duce Parmę & Placentię,à Duce Vrbini,ex ditione Radicofanensi, quotannis percipit decies & octies centena scutatorum millia : ita Auctor Commentarii, de Principibus Italiæ, qui & addit, è ditionibus suis Papam facile posse conscribere exercitum, quinquaginta millium peditum, equitum quatuor,omissis adhuc feudatoriorum subsidiis. Quocum convenit Auctor Relationis,de Statu urbis Romæ & Pontificis, tempore Sixti V. a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxv. scriptę, qui ait : ex agro Piceno & Flaminia creditur viginti quinque millia hominum bello idoneorum & ex Patrimonio, ac Latio fortasse totidem educi posse: adeo illud confirmat hic calculus, & adauget. Scriptus est a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxii. Comentariolus, de Reditibus & exsensis pontificis Romani, quem inseruit suæ de Rep. Romana Descriptioni Scriverius, ubi redituum Papalium accuratam init Auctor rationem: primum, quod ex vectigalibus Romæ inferuntur Camerę coronat. 17000. Ex salinis quotanis 8660. Ex frumenti molitione 16000. Tum quantū Marchia,Romana,Vmbria, Campania, Spoletum, Ancona, & reliqua loca conferant in Thesaurum Papalem,diligenter enumerat: etiam reditum magis incertorum summam construit:quod Collectaria Hispaniæ anuatim censeatur coronat. 40000.Lusitaniæ, 20000. Proventus frumenti in Patrimonio Marchiæ, & Romaniæ, 30000.Duo primi anni P.Sixti dederunt 130000. Reliqua ibi videas.Quin si Papam aut Ππαγματευτης audiamus,Romanæ sedi omnia vectigalia:ex quibus proinde,in subjectionis argumentum, hæc vel illa sibi deberi persuadeant hominibus velint. Sic Angliam olim vectigalem Romano Episcopo Innocentio III. (qui sedit a.cIↄ cxcv.) factam à Rege Iohanne, atque istam ob causam mille marcas sterlingorum ei annuatim pendendas,asserunt. Quod vero de denario Petri ajunt, à Regeinâ primum instituto a. Iↄ ccxl.(ad quem & sequentes annos Iↄ cclxxv. & Iↄ ccccxlvii. videsis Baronii Annales: uti eundem, ad a. Iↄ ccclv. dedonatione Regis Etheluphi.& ad a.Iↄ ccclx ix.regis Salomonis.& a. Iↄcccclxxiv.Beorredi,Merciorum,Regis) non tantanquam tributum Romano Pontifici, sed subsidii loco Anglis Romæ degentibus concessum fuit, uti proinde exserte in epistolâ Regis Eduardi a. ɔ cccc ix. eleemosyna Regis appellatur. Ipseque Baronius, ad a. ɔ cccclxxxviii. Regem Aelfredum memorat, Romam Episcopum Vintoniensem misisse, ad perferendas eo eleemosynas. Eundemque Regem in annum sequentem collectam universalem tam clero quam Laicis imposuisse, Romam & Ierosolymam pro egenis ibi locorum sustentandis, mittendam. Denarius ille erat nummus argenteus, singulis domibus annuatim ab iis persolvendus, impositus: de quo Polydorus Virgilius, Histor. Anglic. lib. iv. & v. Qui idem lib. xv. dejactata illa Regis Iohannis donatione, non aliter, quam ex famâ, & neutiquam servandâ à sequentibus, si vel aliqua intervenisset, donatione loquitur: Ex quo fama est Iohannem cupientem perpetuare memoriam muneris accepti, ea lege fecisse se Innocentii beneficiarium, ut Reges deinceps, à Pontifice duntaxat Rom. juris regni consequerentur. Caeterum has reconciliationis leges, qui secuti sunt reges, minime servarunt, neque annales Anglici de ejusmodi deditione loquuntur. Quare illa omnia onera Iohanni tantummodo, qui deliquisset imposita, non item successoribus sustinenda fuisse, satis constat. & porro: Apud quosdam varie scriptum reperio, de his quae inter Iohannem & Pandulphum, super reconciliatione ejusmodi gesta sunt, quae ut scriptorum arbitrio conficta, nequaquam commemoranda duximus. Primus autem in Anglia denarium istum, vel tributum Inæ, quod vocabant, sustulit Rex Henricus VIII. a. ɔ ɔ xxxiv. Scotiam sibi asseruit P. Bonifacius, quando Eduardo Regi, ne Scotos bello vexaret, edixit: quod id regnum antea in Romani Pontificis fidem & potestatem à Scotis ipsis permissum fuisset, ideoque asseverabat, sibi soli integrum esse, cuicumque liberet, dare auferreve. Polydorus, lib. xvi. Galliam etiam, si quis Baronio credat, Romanæ sedi vectigalem fecit Carolus M. atque ad exemplum Angliæ, illi quoque imponere ejusmodi denarium cogitavit. Vide Annalium scriptorem, ad a. ɔ cclxxxii. ubi idem de Saxonia dicit; atque ad a. ɔ ccciv, de Hungaria: ad a. ɔ ɔ. narrat regnum hoc à Rege Stephano Romanæ Ecclesiæ donatum fuisse. Et Hispaniam, eidem vectigalem factâ, refert ad a. 1o1.& 1o ccccliv. De Regno Siciliæ notissima est historia. Tum in Oriente quas sibi arroget Papa terras & regiones, apud eundem Annalistam videre licet, ad a. 1o ccclx. Laurentius Banck I. C. Professor Franekerensis, in Diascepsi, de Tyrannide Papæ, nuper edita, cap. xiii.xiv. & deinceps ostendit Papales usurpationes non in urbem Romam & agrum Romanum solum, vel patrimonium, quod ita appellant, Petri, sed insuper in Imperium Germaniæ, in Regna Bohemiæ, Dalmatiæ, Croatiæ, Daciæ, Galliæ, Hispaniæ, Aragoniæ, Lusitaniæ, Angliæ, Scotiæ, Hiberniæ, Russiæ, Hungariæ, Poloniæ, Sueciæ, Daniæ, atque Norwegiæ, in quæ dominium sibi arrogant Papæ, & jus quasi illorum hic defensum it Augustinus Steuchus, Pontificis Bibliothecarius, in Laurentii Vallæ Declamationem de Donat. Constantini, lib. ii. Id est, compendio ut dicamus, unus Papa dominus est omnium, κληρονόμος πάντων, atque ei omnia subjecta, vectigalia omnia. Quantum putas ex beneficiis ei accedit lucrosissimis illis, quæ per varias orbis regiones conferт, nempe quousque ei conceditur, & non accisæ ejus sunt alæ, & retusum dominium, per varia Regum & Imperatorum edicta, Pragmaticas, & Concordata; aliter ac Auctor Commentarioli, de Auctoritate Rom. Pontif. qui adducitur in Rep. Romana Scriverii, cujus hæc sententia: Papa est supremus Christianorum Pontifex, omnes Ecclesiasticas & seculares dignitates indifferenter distribuere potest. Incredibile dictu est, quantum ex beneficiorum, tum casuum, aut litium reservatione, Papali erario semper accesserit thesaurorum. Unde Continuator Chronici Abbatis Vrspergensis, sub Imp. Philippo, in hæc verba erumpere coactus fuit: Vix enim remansit aliquis episcopatus, sive dignitas Ecclesiastica, vel etiam parochialis Ecclesia, quæ non fieret litigiosa, & Romam deduceretur ipsa causa, sed non manu vacua. Gaude mater nostra Roma: quoniam aperiuntur cataractæ thesaurorum in terra, ut ad te confluant rivi & aggeres nummorum, in magna copia. Lætare super iniquitate filiorum hominum, quoniam in recompenpenfationem tantorum malorum datur tibi pretium. Iocundare super adjutrice tua discordia, quia erupit de puteo infernalis abyssi, ut accumulentur tibi multa pecuniarum praemia. Habes quod semper sitiisti. Decanta canticum, quia per malitiam hominum, non per tuam religionem orbem vicisti. Ad te trahit homines, non ipsorum devotio aut pura conscientia, sed scelerum multiplicium perpetratio, & litium decisio, pretio comparata. Magnam lucrandi occasionem neglexit noster P. Adrianus, quo mortuo quingenta beneficia, quorum penes ipsum erat dispositio, vacasse, scribit in sua, quae inter Principum Epistolas est, ad Antonium Micheli epistola, Henricus Niger, a. cI⁠ↄ lc xxii. Aliter Praedecessor, promotorque ejus Leo, quē quo die horrendam illam Cardinalium creverat turbam, quingenta ducatorum millia, ex ista secunda omni ratione promotione, lucratum scribunt. Solum Archiepiscopi pallium, si quis illud accipiat, vænit triginta coronatorum millibus: & qui redimere illud tanto pretio nequit aut non vult, cur ab officio removeatur, jam commisit: id ipsum etenim inter cautas depositia Papa Pio Diethcri, quod summam pecuniæ, pro confirmatione & pallio suo debitam, non solvisset, refert Trithemius, in Chronica A.cIↄ ccccclxii. Hoc nimirum est, quod in Novella constitutione clxi. Imperator dicit: officia redimunt potius, quam suscipiunt. atque quod Ambrosius appellavit, Serm. 1. quaestum degeneris mercatura. Quod Papae Romani artificium falle ridebat celebris Iurisconsultus Ioh. Andreas, dicens, haud frustra pro modico plumbi Papam maximam auri molem capere. Adversus Papam Reservationes, quod iis immensam opum vim undiquaque colligerent, integrae nationes, & regna se oppositurae. Inter Germanicae nationis gravamina, quae Legatis P. Adriani, in Comitiis Norimbergensibus exposuerunt Imperii Principes, quintum adversus casus reservatos fuit: quorum sine pecunia nulla poterat haberi absolutio. En exemplum ejus aliquod in epistolis Leonis x. apud P. Bembum, lib. ii. epist. xxvii i. ubi fratribus Bentivolis Papa remittit quidè offensam, verum addit, ita quidem, si mihi praededeiritis sestertium duum millium. Quid Taxam sacrę Poenitentiarię Camerae Apostolicae, Diabolicae verius, dicam? ex qua excerpta nonnulla habes in Protestantium Recusatione Cōcilii Tridentini, & in Musculi Locis Communibus: ubi infanda peccata & flagitia singula suis pretiis æstimantur, quae dicere pudet, nedū agere, minus redimere: bestialitas Turon, 90. ducat. 12. Karl. 6. Simonia, Turon. 36. ducat 9. sacrilegium, furtum, rapina, perjurium, turon 36. duc. 9. & infinita ejusmodi: verum quod ad pauperes, addunt: hæ gratiæ non conceduntur pauperibus, quia non sunt, ideo nō possunt consolari. Vah Ipurcitiē! atqz illa sunt religiosa, poenitentiaria, apostolica! quorum certe infamiam nemo unquam pro merito latis expresserit. Quam rapinam variis immensisque suis exactionibus per omnes orbis regiones regnaque exercuerit Romanus Papa, testari possunt gravamina, arresta, & pragmaticæ adversus illas sanctiones; quin totius orientalis Ecclesiæ hac super re querelæ: etenim hanc causam, inter alia afferunt sui ab Ecclesia Romana divortii. Quod testatur, ex Graecorum monumentis, Petrus Steuartius, Professor Ingolstadiensis, in observat. ad Manuelem Calecam, contra Græcos, ubi refert: Tertia occasio fuit, quam ipsi aliquando nobis in familiari colloquio assignaverunt, superba nimis exactio legatorum Papæ. Dicebant namque referentes, quod quando legati summi Pontificis ab ipsa sede Apostolica annuatim Constantinopolim Chrisma deferebant, nisi octoginta libras auri à Cleró, & urbis populo, praeter alia dona, & munuscula iisdem impenderentur, non recedebant. Taceo ego, ajebant, de pompa & superbia, quam ipsi ostendebant. Hæc ex MS. libro Biblioth. Bavar. A. M. CCLII. Constantinopoli à Prædicatoribus adversus Græcos, conscripto: extatque jam in Biblioth. patrum, Tom. xv. Ne dicam aut Germanorum, aut Gallorum, & præsertim horum, adversus immodicas illas & continuas Romanæ Curiæ exactiones, sanctiones: anni clɔ ccxxxvıı. à Ludovico ıx. & a. clɔ cclxviıı. à Philippo Pulchro, lege Philippinâ, a. clɔ ccciıı. tum à Philippo Valesio. V. cognomento sapiens. & Carolo VI. & VII. à Ludovico XI. præter alia diversaque Curiarum Gallicarum, super eadem re, Arresta. Inter exactiones illas veveniunt etiam Annata, quæ sunt fructus primi anni ex beneficio Prælatorum vacante, ab eo cui id concessum; quod sive ter aut pluries in anno vacet, pro qualibet tituli mutatione à novis dominis semper suæ ad Papam beneficiorum istorum collatorem redundant annatæ. Atque primum institutæ illæ pro subsidio in bellum Turcicum, & sub illa specie à Papis exactæ, iisque concessæ fuere; sed quamvis in illum finem nequidquam impensæ à Papis, tamen semper exigi non desiere. Qua arte, & medio quum immensa opum vis undiquaque Romam semper afflueret, ideo à variis semper restitum, & repugnatum illis constanter fuit. Clemanges, in libro de Annatis non solvendis, numerat ex Ecclesiis Gallicanis hinc emungi ad sexcenta non aginta septem millia septingentaquinquaginta Francorum. Unde quanta per alias etiam Orbis regiones summa sequatur, facile colligi potest. Et quid aliud sunt Papales indulgentiæ? & qui quo rariores illis, ita lucrosiores, jubilæi, quam corrodendorum nummorum artificiosa commenta? vel uti illas Lutherus, in prima sua disputatione anno MDXVII appellavit, Retia quibus virorum divitias pilcarentur. Tales quippe illæ primæ indulgentiæ, ex universi orbis judicio fuerunt, non solum quæ vivis, sed & demortuis prodessent: de quibus Guiccardinus, magni nominis historicus, lib. XIII. quamvis ibidem doctrinam Lutheri pestilens venenum, uti eum alibi lib. xx. auctorem pestis appellet, testatur, manifestum satis fuisse, illas duntaxat nummorum conquirendorum causa præbitas fuisse, quos satis impudenter Commissarii exigebant, in Germania præsertim, ubi vidimus, inquit, Ministros in tabernis per ludum vendidisse potestatem animas educendi ex purgatorio: quodq; indignitatem rei adauxit, Papa sorori suæ Magdalenæ Germanicarum indulgentiarum proventus donarat, quæ proinde episcopum Aremboldum, hominem tali provinciâ dignum, corrogandis istis pecuniis præposuerat. Non aliter ac Campegius Cardinalis, qui in Oratione ad Ordines Imperii, palam profitebatur, se omnem suam fortunam Germanis acceptam ferre. Argumento est palatium Campegiense Bononiæ, quod ideo per jocum peccata Germanorum appellarunt. Samson Mediolanensis, qui Tiguri & in Helvetia indulgentias tum temporis habebat venales, ex illis supra 120000 ducat. lucratus fuisse dicitur. Et quid alia referam ? quum nemo ignoret non alium in finem excogitatas vel commendatas illas fuisse indulgentias, quam ad ditanda Paparum marsupia. Illis succenturiant jubilæos. Polydorus Virgilius de jubileo a.MD.lib.xxvi. non fuit gratuita liberalitas, inquit, Alexander enim saluti hominum prospiciendo, suis quoque commodis serviendum statuerat, quare pretium sua gratia constituit. Krantius, Saxon. lib. iv. cap. xxvi. Bonifacius viii. anno trecentesimo post millesimum primus jubileum instituit. Vtinam solius pietatis gratia! De isto Jubilæo peculiarem tractatum conscripsit Iacobus S. Georgii Cardinalis, ubi c.ix. exponit, quantum ex usualis monetæ minutiis ea occasione corraserint Papani : extat in Bibliotheca Patrum, Tom.xiii. Atque illa causa est, quod à centum annis ad quinquaginta jubilæum contraxit Clemens vi. & post eum à quinquaginta, ad viginti quinque annos, Sixtus iv. Extravag. Comm. de Poenitent. & Remissionibus. hic Bullæ singulorum, Bonifacii VIII primùm, tum Clementis VI. quorumlibet pro suis jubileis, quin etiam ad quintum hodie annum eos deducunt. Nempe hoc medio duminnumeros Romam alliciunt peregrinantes, tanquam ad officinam sacrarum mercium egregiè quæstuosam, quantum inde relinquatur Cameræ. sc Apostolicæ, ex coëmtis indulgentiis oblationibus, donariis &c. quilibet facile colligat. Si quid Roma dabit, nugas dabit, accipit aurum : Mantuanus. Ne jam dicam, quantum Papæ Emissarii, & quotuplices hi, quamque omnes in idem negotium Papæ sui evehendi intentissimi ! regno Papali conferant & attrahant hinc inde nümorum, & potestatis affatim. accipitres pecunia, diceret Ambrosius. discutrentes ad ditanda marsupia, sic Leodiensis ad P.Paschalem ii. posteriummia, & palliata mendicabula, Corn. Agrippa appellat. Quibus forte dictum credas: Ite in orbem universum, predicate dicentes, qui crediderit & decimas solverit, salvus erit, inquit Auctor Exhortationis ad Principes Germaniae, de non solvendis Papae decimis, in Fasciculo Rerum expetendarum, iuxta versiculos P. Iohannis xxii. à Concilio Constantiensi depositi, quos, dum a Comite Palatino teneretur captivus, composuit: Omnibus è terris aurum mihi sponte ferebant, Sed nec gaza juvat, nec quis amicus adest. Sic varias fortuna vices adversa secundis Subdit, & ambiguo nomine ludit atrox. Papa fecit.
units.tr: Then, taking account of their wealth, why should we not answer the Pope as Louis, King of France, called the Saint, once answered those who sought small revenues from a monastery he had built: that they were enough for them, provided they were honest? What does it matter that the Pope's crown is worth thirty thousand gold pieces? Aeneas Silvius reports this of the crown placed on the head of Felix V, in his commentary on the Council of Basel. Or that a jewel valued at six thousand ducats should be set in it, which Platina says fell from it in the tumult at the coronation of Clement? Or that a coronation should be held as lavish as that of Leo X, the most extravagant of all that have ever been, as Guicciardini attests (Bell. Italic. lib. xi), writing that on that day the Pope distributed a hundred thousand ducats, although wiser men judged that such pomp hardly befitted a pope. In book ix he relates that Julius II sent his crown to Florence so that this most precious treasure might be kept there more safely from the fury of the French. What of the dowry the Pope could give his daughter, when Alexander VI, marrying off his Lucretia for the fourth time to Alphonso, gave a hundred thousand ducats in ready money, as Guicciardini reports (lib. v)? Who would deny that the Pope possesses immensely great revenues, since he knows that he has 26,000 crowns coming in every day? These he gathers from the various regions of the world, from the Churches, from Italy, and from what he calls his patrimony of Peter; from his papal devices of annates, reservations, benefices, and that kind of religious inventions; and finally wherever his emissaries, nuncios and legates spend their treasures. When Clement IV, having defeated Manfred, declared Charles, Count of Provence, King of Sicily and Jerusalem, he attached a condition that the King should pay forty thousand gold pieces each year into the Papal treasury; so Platina and Stella report, and Molinaeus adds (de Monarch. Francorum) that the Pope would have demanded far more if the king had surrendered his dominion peacefully. From his patrimony, as the Pope calls it, from the Duchy of Benevento, the Comtat of Avignon in France, Lazio, Umbria, Romagna, the Duchy of Spoleto, the March of Ancona, Bologna, with the tributes of vassals added, from the King of Spain (for the King of Naples), from the Duke of Parma and Piacenza, from the Duke of Urbino, and from the territory of Radicofani, he receives every year eighteen hundred thousand scudi; so the author of the commentary (de Principibus Italiae) reports, who also adds that the Pope could easily raise an army from his dominions of fifty thousand foot soldiers and four thousand horse, not counting the aid of his feudatories. The author of the account de Statu urbis Romae & Pontificis, written in the time of Sixtus V, in the year 1585, agrees with this, saying: from the Picene countryside and Flaminia it is believed that twenty-five thousand men fit for war can be raised, and perhaps as many from the Patrimony and Latium. This calculation so confirms and enlarges that. In the year 1582 was written the little commentary de Reditibus & exsensis pontificis Romani, which Scriverius inserted into his description of the Roman Republic, where its author gives an exact account of the papal revenues. First, from the duties collected in Rome go into the Chamber 17,000 crowns; from the salt-works, 8,660 each year; from the milling of grain, 16,000. Then he carefully enumerates how much the March, the Roman territory, Umbria, Campania, Spoleto, Ancona and the other places contribute to the papal treasury; and he also reckons the sum of the more uncertain income: the collections in Spain are estimated at 40,000 crowns a year, those in Portugal at 20,000, the yield of grain from the Patrimony of the March and of Romagna at 30,000. The first two years of Pope Sixtus gave 130,000. You may see the rest there. Indeed, if we listen to the Pope or to a trader [πραγματευτής], all taxes belong to the Roman See; and so they persuade people to think that this or that is owed to them, as a proof of subjection. Thus they assert that England was once made tributary to the Roman bishop Innocent III (who held the see in 1195) by King John, and that for this reason a thousand marks sterling were to be paid to him each year. As for what they say about Peter's penny, first instituted by the King in 1240 (for the following years, 1275 and 1247, see Baronius's Annals; and for the gift of King Ethelwulf in 855, for King Solomon in 869, and for Beorred, King of the Mercians, in 874, see the same), it was granted not as a tribute to the Roman Pontiff, but as a relief for the English living at Rome; hence in King Edward's letter of 909 it is expressly called the King's alms. Baronius himself, under the year 888, mentions that King Alfred sent the Bishop of Winchester to Rome to carry alms there; and that the same King, in the following year, imposed a general collection, on clergy and laity alike, to be sent to Rome and Jerusalem for the support of the poor there. That penny was a silver coin imposed to be paid each year by each household; of it Polydore Virgil speaks in his Histor. Anglic. lib. iv & v. In lib. xv the same writer, speaking of the alleged gift of King John, says that it rests on nothing but rumour, and was in no way to be observed by his successors, even if some such gift had taken place: From this it is said that John, wishing to perpetuate the memory of the gift he had received, made himself Innocent's vassal on the condition that later kings should receive their kingdom from the Pontiff alone. But the kings who followed did not keep these terms of reconciliation at all, nor do the English annals speak of any such surrender. Therefore it is quite certain that all those burdens were laid only on John, who had offended, and were not to be borne by his successors. And again: I find variously written among certain authors about what was done between John and Pandulf concerning such a reconciliation; since these are fabricated at the will of writers, we have thought them not worth recording. The first in England to abolish this penny, or the tribute called Ine's, was King Henry VIII, in 1534. Pope Boniface asserted his claim to Scotland when he ordered King Edward not to harass the Scots with war: because that kingdom had formerly been entrusted by the Scots themselves to the faith and power of the Roman Pontiff; and therefore he maintained that it was his alone to give or take away to whomever he pleased. Polydore, lib. xvi. France too, if we believe Baronius, Charlemagne made tributary to the Roman See, and following the example of England he thought of imposing such a penny on it as well. See the annalist under the year 782, where he says the same of Saxony; and under the year 904 on Hungary, where he relates that this kingdom was given to the Roman Church by King Stephen, in the year 1000. He also reports that Spain was made tributary to the same see, referring to the years 1010 and 1454. The history of the Kingdom of Sicily is very well known. As for the lands and regions in the East which the Pope claims for himself, one may see them in the same annalist under the year 1060. Laurentius Banck, professor of law at Franeker, in his recently published Diascepsis de Tyrannide Papae, chapters 13 and 14 and following, shows that papal usurpations extend not only to the city of Rome and the Roman territory, or to what they call the patrimony of Peter, but also to the Empire of Germany, the kingdoms of Bohemia, Dalmatia, Croatia, Dacia, France, Spain, Aragon, Portugal, England, Scotland, Ireland, Russia, Hungary, Poland, Sweden, Denmark and Norway, over which they claim lordship for the Popes; and Augustinus Steuchus, the Pope's librarian, defended this right to them in his reply to Laurentius Valla's Declamation on the Donation of Constantine, book ii. In short, one Pope is lord of all, heir of all things [κληρονόμος πάντων], and all things are subject to him, and all taxes too. How much do you think accrues to him from those most profitable benefices which he confers in the various regions of the world, namely as far as he is granted them, and his wings are not clipped and his dominion blunted, by the various edicts, pragmatic sanctions and concordats of kings and emperors? Otherwise the author of the little commentary de Auctoritate Rom. Pontif., cited in Scriverius's Roman Republic, whose view is this: The Pope is the supreme Pontiff of Christians, and can distribute all ecclesiastical and secular dignities indifferently. It is incredible to say how much money has always flowed into the papal treasury from the reservation of benefices, as well as of cases and lawsuits. Hence the continuator of the Chronicle of the Abbot of Ursperg, under the Emperor Philip, was forced to burst out in these words: For scarcely any bishopric or ecclesiastical dignity, or even parish church, remained which did not become a matter of dispute, and the case itself was carried off to Rome, but not empty-handed. Rejoice, our mother Rome, for the floodgates of treasures are opened on earth, so that streams and mounds of money may flow together to you in great abundance. Exult over the iniquity of the sons of men, since a price is given to you in recompense for so many evils. Be glad over your helper, discord, which has burst out of the pit of the infernal abyss so that many rewards of money may be heaped upon you. You have what you have always thirsted for. Sing your song, for you have conquered the world through the wickedness of men, not through your religion. Men are drawn to you not by their devotion or pure conscience, but by the commission of manifold crimes, and by the settlement of lawsuits bought for a price. Our Pope Adrian neglected a great opportunity for gain: Henry Niger, in his letter to Antonio Micheli, which is among the Epistles of Princes, writes in 1522 that when he died five hundred benefices, of which he had the disposal, fell vacant. His predecessor and promoter Leo was otherwise: on the day he created that dreadful crowd of cardinals, they write that he gained five hundred thousand ducats from that second promotion, by every means. The pallium of an archbishop alone, if anyone receives it, is sold for thirty thousand gold crowns; and whoever cannot or will not redeem it at so high a price is already removed from office. Trithemius, in his Chronicle under the year 1462, reports that Pope Pius of Dieth had removed a man from office on this very ground, because he had not paid the sum of money owed for his confirmation and pallium. This is surely what the Emperor says in Novel 161: they buy offices rather than undertake them. And this Ambrose called the profit of a degenerate trade (Sermon 1). The famous jurist John Andreas laughed at this artifice of the Roman Pope, saying that it was no wonder the Pope took a huge mass of gold for a small piece of lead. The Reservations were opposed by entire nations and kingdoms, because by them the Papacy gathered an immense store of wealth from every side. Among the grievances of the German nation, which the princes of the Empire set out to the legates of Pope Adrian at the Diet of Nuremberg, the fifth concerned the reserved cases: for which no absolution could be had without money. Here is one example of this in the letters of Leo X, in Bembus, book ii, letter 27, where the Pope indeed remits the offence to the Bentivoglio brothers, but adds: provided, indeed, that you first pay me two thousand sesterces. And what shall I say of the Tax of the Sacred Penitentiary of the Apostolic Chamber, more devilish than apostolic? From it you have some extracts in the Protestants' Refutation of the Council of Trent and in Musculus's Common Places, where unspeakable sins and crimes, which one is ashamed to speak of, let alone commit, much less redeem, are each priced: bestiality at Tours, 90 ducats, 12 carolus; simony, at Tours 36 ducats, 9; sacrilege, theft, robbery, perjury, at Tours 36 ducats, 9; and countless such things. But as for the poor, they add: these graces are not granted to the poor, because they have nothing, and so cannot be comforted. Oh filthiness! And these things are called religious, penitential, apostolic! Surely no one has ever expressed their infamy as it deserves. The rapine which the Roman Pope has practised through his various and immense exactions in every region and kingdom of the world can be attested by the grievances, the decrees and the pragmatic sanctions against them; indeed by the complaints of the whole Eastern Church on this matter; for among other things they allege this as a cause of their separation from the Roman Church. Peter Steuart, professor at Ingolstadt, attests this from Greek records in his observations on Manuel Calecas, against the Greeks, where he reports: The third occasion was one which they themselves once gave us in familiar conversation: the excessively proud exaction of the Pope's legates. For they said, relating it, that when the legates of the highest Pontiff brought the chrism each year from the Apostolic See itself to Constantinople, they would not depart unless eighty pounds of gold were spent on them by the clergy and the people of the city, besides other gifts and little presents. I say nothing, they said, of the pomp and pride which they displayed. These things are taken from a manuscript book in the Bavarian Library, written at Constantinople by Preachers against the Greeks in 1252; and it now exists in the Library of the Fathers, vol. xv. I will not mention the German or French objections, and especially the French, against those immoderate and continual exactions of the Roman Curia: the decrees of 1237 by Louis IX, of 1268 by Philip the Fair (the Philippine law), of 1303 by Philip of Valois, the Wise, and by Charles VI and VII, and by Louis XI, besides the other and various decrees of the French Courts on the same matter. Among those exactions also come the annates, which are the first year's fruits of a benefice held by prelates which falls vacant, from the one to whom it was granted; and whether it falls vacant three or more times in a year, with each change of title the annates always flow back from the new holders to the Pope, the conferrer of these benefices. These were first instituted as a subsidy for war against the Turks, and were levied by the Popes under that pretext, and granted to them; but although they were never spent for that purpose by the Popes, they never ceased to be collected. By this art and means an immense store of wealth always flowed to Rome from every side, and therefore it was always constantly resisted and opposed by various peoples. Clemanges, in his book de Annatis non solvendis, reckons that some 667,750 francs were squeezed from the Gallican churches. From this one can easily infer how great a sum follows from the other regions of the world as well. And what else are the papal indulgences? And what are the jubilees, the rarer they are the more profitable, but ingenious devices for draining money? Or, as Luther called them in his first disputation in 1517, nets with which men's riches are caught. Such, indeed, were those first indulgences, by the judgment of the whole world, which benefited not only the living but also the dead. Guicciardini, the historian of great name, in book xiii, though there he attests that Luther's doctrine was a pestilent poison, and elsewhere (book xx) calls him the author of the plague, shows clearly enough that those indulgences were offered merely for the sake of collecting money, which the commissioners exacted quite shamelessly, especially in Germany, where, he says, we saw the ministers selling in taverns, as a game, the power of releasing souls from purgatory; and to add to the disgrace of the affair, the Pope had granted the revenues of the German indulgences to his sister Magdalena, who therefore put Bishop Arnoldo, a man worthy of such a province, in charge of collecting this money. Just so did Cardinal Campeggio, who openly declared in his speech to the Orders of the Empire that he owed his whole fortune to the Germans. The Campeggio palace at Bologna is evidence of this, which for a joke they called the sins of the Germans. Samson of Milan, who at that time was selling indulgences at Zurich and in Helvetia, is said to have made more than 120,000 ducats from them. And why should I relate other things, since no one is unaware that those indulgences were devised or commended for no other end than to enrich the purses of the Popes? Jubilees come as a supplement to them. Polydore Virgil, on the jubilee of 1500, book xxvi: It was not a free liberality, he says, for Alexander, while providing for men's salvation, had also decided to serve his own advantage, and so he set a price on his favour. Krantz, Saxonia, book iv, chapter 26: Boniface VIII first instituted a jubilee in the three hundredth year after the thousandth. Would that it were by the grace of piety alone! James of St George, Cardinal, wrote a separate treatise on this jubilee, in which, at chapter 9, he sets out how much the Popes amassed from the small coins of common currency on that occasion; it is in the Library of the Fathers, vol. xiii. And this is the reason why Clement VI reduced the jubilee from one hundred years to fifty, and afterwards Sixtus IV from fifty to twenty-five years (Extravag. Comm. de Poenitent. & Remissionibus). Here the bulls of the individual jubilees, first of Boniface VIII and then of Clement VI, and of whichever Popes, are drawn down even to a five-year jubilee today. Clearly by this means they lure countless pilgrims to Rome, as to a workshop of sacred wares especially profitable, and anyone can easily infer how much flows from the purchased indulgences, the offerings, the gifts, and so on, into the Apostolic Chamber. If Rome gives anything, it gives trifles; it accepts gold: Mantuan. Not to mention how much the papal emissaries, and how many kinds of them there are, and how all of them are most eager for the same business of advancing their Pope, bring into the papal kingdom and draw from every side of money and power in abundance. Hawks for money, Ambrose called them; shakers for enriching the purses, so the man of Liège, addressing Pope Paschal II; wretched and cloaked beggars, Cornelius Agrippa calls them. You might think that was said of them: Go into the whole world, preaching and saying: whoever believes and pays the tithes will be saved, says the author of the Exhortation to the Princes of Germany, on not paying the tithes to the Pope, in the Fasciculus Rerum Expetendarum, after the verses of Pope John XXII, deposed by the Council of Constance, which he composed while he was held captive by the Count Palatine: Gold was brought to me of its own accord from all lands, but neither wealth helps nor any friend is at hand. So fortune, adverse, subjoins varied changes to the prosperous, and cruelly mocks with an ambiguous name. The Pope made them.

units.la: Atque in illis omnibus unicus hamus quo nummos & opes capiunt ab hominibus tantas, est nefanda simonia, quae per omnia illa dominatur: unde non mirandum, thesauros illos in Romanam curiam confluxisse, huc si oculos nostros reflectamus, cum Mantuano, lib. iii. de calamit. Tempor. Quid miramur opes, recidivaque surgere tecta? Thuris odorati globulos, & cynnama vendit Mollis Arabs, &c. venalia nobis Templa, sacerdotes, altaria, sacra, coronas, Ignes, thura, preces, caelum est venale, Deusque.
units.tr: And in all those practices the single hook by which they catch so much money and wealth from people is accursed simony, which rules over all of them. So it is no wonder that those treasures have flowed into the Roman curia, if we turn our eyes there, as Mantuan says in book 3 of On the Calamities of the Times: "Why do we wonder at wealth, and at houses rising again after they have fallen? The soft Arab sells little balls of fragrant incense and cinnamon, etc. Churches, priests, altars, sacred things, crowns, fires, incense, prayers are for sale to us; heaven is for sale, and God too."

units.la: Perinde uti Iuvenalis, satyra i. Criminibus debent hortos &c. Denique quis recenseat vel explicet millenas Pontificum, licet nefandas omnes, ad exigendos captandosque nummos, artes, quibus quae aliorum sunt, ad se rapiunt sine fine, sine mensura? Unde dictum a Lyno I.C. quod curia Papae summopere vellet, quod totus mundus in eam influeret: tanta quippe est in ea auri & argenti sacra fames. Quae eo faciunt omnia, ut insatiabilem hominis istius ἀνάμω ostendant avaritiam ac rapacitatem. Hinc, quod inumeri jam saepius conquesti sunt, potissimam orbis Christiani & pleramque partem vel tenent, vel saltem occupare allaborant. Rex Angliae Iacobus, in Apologia ad Reges &c. ita illos alloquitur: quod si ferio, qui auditis potentissimi, consideretis, videbitis tertiam populi, terraeque vestrae partem Ecclesiae esse, & nihilne vos tantum vel hominum vel dignitatis riotionum detrimentum tangeret? ubique locorum Papæ, & provincia & colonia atquirunter. Antea Clerici prater decimas nihil petebant, & contenti erant. Hodie Papa, Clericorum caput, non nisi cum tertia subditorum, bonorumque vestrorum parte acquiescit. Idem Principes Germaniæ olim in suis Gravaminibus: & Serenissima Venetorum Respublica, in contentionibus suis hoc seculo anno. clɔ lxcvi. cum Paulo V. & ejus nomine Theologus ejus meritissimus Fr. Paulus Servita, peculiari tractatu, ostendit, nempe quod Clerici centesima duntaxat subditorum pars, tamen plus quam tertiam in dominio Patavienfi possiderent, in Bergomasco ultra dimidiam, in cæteris ultra partem quartam. Vnde Nicolaus Crassus I.C. in Antiparænefi, pro Rep. Venetâ, adversus Baronium, non fine causa dixit: Centuplo vos majores facultates & opes, quam pro numero possidetis: & tamen pluribus comparandis adhuc smallis. Atque quod hodie Iesuitæ Reipublicæ offerunt quatuor millliones auri, in subsidium belli Turcici, sed pro ipsorum reductione & restitutione, quam illustre tenuitatis ipsorum argumentum fit, quæso perpendite: quo tamen non obstante, Illustrissimus Senatus, quamvis in grave hoc adversus Turcas bellum nummorum quantum egeat, jubet tamen illos cum istis suis nummis perpetuum exesse. Auctor Vulgaris Historiæ Gallicæ Mercure Francois, ad a.1611. ubi de Iesuitarum reditu in Gallias agit, refert, unum aliquod ipsorum collegium habere in reditibus librarum 20000. Idemque ad a. 1608. in canonizatione Francisci, ait, supra centum millia coronatorum expensa, ab ejus sodalibus, pro hac re fuisse. Et quanti constiterit canonizatio Brigittæ, ab Vrbano v. facta; Andreæ Corsini Carmelitani, Episcopi Fesulani, ab Vrbano. viii. ad instantiam Ludovici xiii. Gall. Regis, in Sanctorum catalogum relati, ego non dicam, satis est de eo dixisse & conquestos fuisse alios. Haud ita diu prodiit calculus reditum quos habent Clerici Gallicani, iplorum 14 Archiepiscopatus, & Episcopatus 95. Parochiæ 140000. Abbatiæ 1356. Prioriæ 12440. Commendæ dæ 2061. Capellaniæ 152000. Abbatiæ Religiosorum 567. Conventus Cordigerorum 700. Conventus Religiosorum 14077.nepe quod illi possident 9000. loca,castella,ac domus jurisdictionem habentes summam, mediam, infimam. Vineas & hortos ultra 17000. adeo ut deprehendatur, singulis annis illos habere in reditibus nummorū 8200000,octoginta duos milliones scutatorum:& singulis diebus 286301. scut.& 20. solidos.Philippus Honorius, lib. de Regno Gallia, hanc init ratio-nem, ut dicat; ex terræ fructibus colligi circiter quindecim millia aureorum; quorum sex sunt Ecclesiasticorum, sesquialter patrimonii Regii, reliquum pro Principibus, Baronibus,aliisque: adeo ut Clerus bene duas quintas Regni partes teneat. Conquestus de eo jam a. clo lo xv. fuit Claudius Sesellius, vir ætate suâ inter primos, Ludovici XII. ad Leonem X. aliquot annos legatus, episcopus postea Massilien-sis, vel ut alii, Taurinensis, lib. 1. de Rep. Galliæ, quando ait: deinde maxima vis pecuniæ, quam nostri ordinis homines, Ecclesiarum præfecti, ambitione quadam & inexplebili cupiditate majora consequendi, profundunt, non excederet provinciarum fines, qua nunc a Romana Curia sectatoribus & alumnis præter omnem modum expilantur ac diripiuntur. Scripsit Aubertus Miræus Notitiam Episcopatuum orbis Christiani, & de Statu Religionis Christiane, ubi quam numerosi ubique locorum sint Romani Clerici, & quæ, quamque immensa loca teneant, ostenditur. Conradus Low, in historia Muhammedica, Germanicè, pag. 83. calculum refert Simonis Wolderi, Imp. Ferdinando exhibitum in Comitiis Augustanis, ut ostenderet, unde subsidia pro bello adversus Turcas facillimè peti possent, atque, monasteria Minoritarum ascendere ad quadraginta millia, atque ordinum trium reliquorum, vid. Augustinianorum, Dominicanorum,& Carmelitarum æstimat non multum pauciora: atque quum in universum sint Ordines septuaginta & duo, præter Canonicorum, & Virginum Collegia, & ecclesias parochiales, censet illorum omnium numerum accedere ad vigesies centum millia: quæ judicabat ille levi tributo ad belli Turcici sustinenda onera in multorum, si non orbis, ruinam secum ferat: potissimum quando respicimus, in quos fines vel usus tanta sua bona impendunt Papæ, videlicet in solos fere luxus, & mundanum typhum, aliaque non multum meliora. Et hoc, uti omnes norunt, magno constat, & qui se illis addicunt nihil unquam adeo curare solent, quam quibuscunque modis, quantumvis illicitis pessimisqi, & insuper habitis rebus omnibus aliis, unum ventrem, & quæ ejus ac carnis sunt, pro Deo habere ac colere. Concinne dixit Ferus, in Matthæum, cap. xvii. Petrus piscaturus pecuniam, hamo tantum utitur, & contentus est; piscaturus homines retia laxare jubetur. Nunc omnia contrario modo fiunt, ad piscandas divitias lata illa retia extendimus, ad piscandos homines vix hamo utimur. O tempora nostra, o Petri successores. Atque in quem obsecro finem adeo clamant & tumultuantur pro suis bonis & opibus, ut omnia prius conturbent & disrumpant, quam ut illis priventur? in eundem nempe, in quem illa impendunt. Loquatur pro me Rex Angliæ Eadgarus, in Oratione ad Clerum Anglicanum, quæ extat in Bibliotheca Patrum: Dicam, dicam, quod boni lugent, mali rident, dicam dolens (si tamen dici potest) quomodo diffluant in comessationibus, & ebrietatibus, in cubilibus, & impudicitiis, ut jam domus Clericorum putentur prostibula meretricum, conciliabulum histrionum. Ibi alea, ibi saltus, ibi cantus, ibi usque ad medium noctis spatium protractæ in clamore & horrore vigilia. Sic sic patrimonia Regum, elecmosyna pauperum, imo quod magis est, illius pretiosi sanguinis pretium profligatur? Ad hoc ergo exhauserunt Patres nostri thesauros suos? ad hoc fiscus regius, detractis reditibus multis detenuit? Ad hoc Ecclesiis Christi agros & possessiones regalis munificentia contulit, ut delicias Clericorum meretrices ornentur? luxuriosa convivia præparentur? canes & aves, & talia ludicra comparentur? ubi gladius Levi, & zelus Simonis? &c. Ego Constantinus, vos Petri gladium habetis in manibus. Iungamus dexteras, gladium gladio copulemus, ut ejiciantur extra castra leprosi, ut purgetur Sanctuarium Domini, & ministrent in templo filii Levi, qui dixit Patri & Matri, nescio vos, & fratribus ignoro illos. Atque hoc est, quod Theodoretus, orat. x. de providentia, ait: de alienis bonis helluantur, & pauperum lachrymis saginantur. Ac Bernardus, serm. lxxvii. in Cantic. Unde vero hanc illis exuberare existimas rerum affluentiam, vestium splendorem, mensarum luxuriem, congeriem vasorum argenteorum & aureorum, nisi de bonis sponsæ. Serm.xxxiij. Omnes amici,& omnes inimici: omnes necessarii, & omnes adversarii, omnes domestici, & nulli pacifici: omnes proximi, & omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt. Ministri Christi sunt, & serviunt antichristo. Honorati incedunt de bonis domini; qui domino honorem non deferunt. Inde is quem quotidie vides metricus nitor, histrionicus habitus, regius apparatus, inde aurum in frænis, in sellis & calcaribus, & plus calcaria quam altaria fulgent. Inde splendida mensa & cibis & cyphis, deinde comessationes & ebrietates, inde cithara & lyra & tibia, inde redundantia torculapия, & promtuaria plena eructantia ex hoc in illud. Inde dolia pigmentaria, inde referta marsupia. pro hujusmodi volunt esse, & sunt ecclesiarum præpositi, decani, archidiaconi, episcopi, archiepiscopi. Atque hæc plurimis ille locis latis graviter atque ad vivum perstringit: lib.iv. ad Eugenium; epist.xlii.ad Archiepiscopum Senonensem, & alibi. Similiter Bernhardus Westerrodus Corbejensis, in suo plan&tu: de Christi patrimonio, sub pompis & præconio viventes intumescunt: Intenti voluptatibus, Et mundi vanitatibus, De cappis erubescunt. Non solum noto monachos, sed etiam canonicos, Et fictas moniales &c. Illos autem, qui adeo bonis abutuntur, minus pro illis loqui oporteret, verum potius adimi illis ea,& ablata impendi in usus longe meliores. Quæ erat sententia Iohannis Wiclephi, articulo xvii. inter art. xlv. ob quos condemnatus à Papanis fuit: Domini temporales possunt ad arbitrium suum auferre bona temporalia ab Ecclesiasticis habitualiter delinquentibus: non in eum tamen sensum, quasi aut non agnosceret bona illa Ecclesiastica esse, vel usum Ecclesiasticum habere debere, aut in quoscunque alios usus à Dominis temporalibus impendi posse, quod forte quis ita capiat. M. Iohannes Hus Academiæ Pragensis Rector, a. cIↄ ccccx. Determinationem supradicti articuli edidit, atque ita præfatur: protestor tamen, quod non est intentionis meæ, sicut nec universerniverfitatis, suadere quod Principes vel faculares Domini auferant bona à Clero, quando volunt, & qualiter volunt, & convertant, quò volunt. Et in ipla determinatione §. xii. ait : Pari evidentia Clericis habitualiter delinquentibus bona temporalia facta sunt aliorum Ecclesia ad profectum. Concedens quidem, ut bona quibus aliqui in grave damnum Ecclesiæ abutuntur, illis auferantur, ab habitualiter delinquentibus, id est, ex habitu, non solum ex actu, uti id quoque alias licet; sed non minus tamen data Ecclesiæ agnoscit, eique, si non apud hos, apud alios impendenda. Poggius Florentinus, in epist. ad Leonard. Aretinum, de Huffo & Hieronymo Pragensi, refert, Hieronymum sic in Concilio Huffum suum defendisse : illum nihil adversus Ecclesia Dei statum sensisse, sed adversus abusus Clericorum, adversus superbiam, fastum ac pompam Prælatorum. Nam cum Ecclesiarum patrimonia primo deberentur pauperibus, tum hospitibus, deinde Ecclesiarum fabricis: indignum illud bono viro videbatur, dispendi illa meretricibus, convivis, equoris ac canum jugine, cultura vestimentorum, & aliis rebus indignis religione Christiana. Hæc de Huffo Poggius. Atque ita sententiam Huffi capit & tuetur Andreas Willetus, Synopsi Papismi Controv. general. v. qu. vi. Istamque honorum Ecclesiasticorum dilapidationem, & abusum Reformati semper præcipuè notarunt. Calvinus, Institut. lib. iv. §. 10. Non attingo hic extranea vitia, sed duntaxat intestinum malum, quod in ipsorum institutione radicitus haret. Addam vocem, qua male sonabit in eorum auribus; sed quia vera est, dicere oportet, eodem loco habendos esse Canonicos, Decanos, Capellanos, Præpositos, quicunque otiosis sacerdotiis aluntur. Quale enim Ecclesia ministerium præstare queunt? Qui in Canonicos degenerarunt, Presbyteri esse debuerant, ut fuerunt olim, qui Ecclesiam cum Episcopo in commune regerent, & veluti collega ejus essent in munere pastorali. Dignitates illæ capitulares quas vocant, nihil prorsus spectant ad veram Ecclesiæ gubernationem: multo minus Capellanie, & reliqua sax talium nominum. Quo igitur loco eos omnes habebimus? Certè & verbum Christi, & veteris Ecclesia observatio, eos à Presbyteris honore excludit. Presbyteros tamen se esse contendunt: sed detrahenda est larvula: sic reperiemus mus, totam eorum professionem alienissimam esse ac remotissimam ab illo munere Presbyterorum, quod & Apostoli nobis describunt & in prima Ecclesia requisitum fuit. Omnes ergo ejusmodi ordines qui-buscunque titulis insigniantur, novitii quum sint, certè nec Dei institutione, nec antiqua Ecclesiæ observatione suffulti, locum nullum habere debent in descriptione regiminis spiritualis, quod ore Domini ipsius consecratum Ecclesiæ recepit. Aut (si rudius ac crassius me loqui malunt) quando Capellani, Canonici, Decani, Prapositi, & ejus farina otiosi ventres ne minimo quidem digito particulam ullam attingunt ejus officii, quod in Presbyteris necessario requiritur, non est ferendum ut falso sibi honorem usurpando, sanctam Christi institutionem violent. Et §. 15. Ipsam vero bonorum dispensationem alio transtulerunt: & ita composuerunt, ut nihil fingi queat magis inordinatum. Quemadmodum enim latrones, jugulatis hominibus, prædam inter se dividunt: ita illi post excinctum verbi Dei lumen, quasi jugulata Ecclesia, putarunt expositum esse prædæ ac direptioni quicquid in sanctos ujus decatum erat. Itaque facta divisione, rapuit ad se quisque quantum potuit. Chemnitius, in Exam. Conc. Trident. part. 1. de S cript. Canonica: Non igitur eo modo Scriptura vocatur canonica, sicut vocantur horæ canonicæ; aut sicut nunc ἐκγία, γαρίγες ἀργυρὶ abligurientes bona Ecclesiastica, vocantur Canonici. Grotius, in Annotatis ad Cassandrum, cap. de Canonicis: & utinam ne nunc quidem multi sint tales, intelligit Canonicos irregulares. Sed quid facias cum Collegia talia multis in locis impleant Principes iner uduti, & otiosi nobiles, exclusis qui in vita sanctimonia principatum, & ex eruditione nobilitatem habent? & Reges & episcopos cura spectat hæc ut corrigantur: sed id ita demum sperabimus, si quis alios corrigere debent, prius semetipsi corrigant. Rivetus ad hæc, vocem illam Grotii veram & liberam esse, prædicat. Grotius iterum, in Animadversionibus, non utilia tantum sed & plane, si Ecclesiam sanare, & resarcire volumus, necessaria. Ad quæ Rivetus, calculum addens suum, siat ergo, ait, quod petitur, & corrigantur, quæ non tantum utilia putat D. Grotius, sed plane necessaria ad Ecclesiam sanandam. Non repugnamus. Ex illis ita explicatis patet nunc, quam immerito pro suis sc. bonis ita exæstuet Papa, ut in illorum gratiam jubeat aboleri pacem, fœdera, juramenta omnia, & bellum iterum ac faces Germanię inferat, quum illa sua bona, Papalia videlicet (distinguo enim bona Ecclesiastica, à Papalibus sic dicti s) tam male acquisita, nec teneat neque utatur illis bene, sed omnia quantum potest pessimè. In Papatu, qui non aliter spectari potest quam rhapsodus aliquis, & variis ex rebus mixtum corpus, bona consideranda sunt diversorū generum, Papalia, Hierarchica, Principum vel Imperii, idololatrica plane aut superstitiosa, deniq; simpliciter ecclesiastica, eaq; aut pure talia, aut potissimum, data videlicet in usum Ecclesiæ Christi; quæ aliquando contra distinguuntur ad bona pauperum, aliquando pro iisdem habentur, ut Ecclesiastici sub pauperibus, pauperes sub Ecclesiasticis comprehendantur & intelliguntur. Neque enim putandum, quotiescunque Veteres hoc in negotio, vel in piis testamentis pauperes nominant, nòn sæpe etiam clericos vel Ecclesiasticos includi, quasi quum pauperum bona dicuntur, non quoque intelliguntur clerici, vel iis legata bona fuisse. Pauperes enim aliquando hic distinƥti à clericis intelliguntur, ut quoties quadripartitam bonorum sacrorum partitionem loquuntur, xii. qu. ii.c. Quatuor autem tam de reditu quam de oblatione fidelium pro ut cuiuslibet ecclesiæ facultas admittit (sicut dudum rationabiliter est decretum) convenit fieri portiones: quarum una sit pontificis, altera clericorum, tertia pauperum, quarta est fabricis applicanda. &c. can. seq. De reditibus ecclesiæ vel oblatione fidelium sola episcopis ex his una portio remittatur. dua ecclesiasticis fabricis & erogationi pauperum profutura à presbytero sub periculo sui ordinis ministrentur: ultima clericis pro singulorum meritis dividatur. c. 30. Mos est Apostolica sedis ordinato episcopo præcepta tradere, ut de omni stipendio quod accedit, quatuor debeant fieri portiones: una videlicet episcopo & familiæ ejus, propter hospitalitatem atque susceptionem: alia clero, tertia vero pauperibus, quarta ecclesiis reparandis. atque ibidem Palea quæ inscribitur, ex Concilio Toletano: insuper confirmamus, ut si aliqua ab ipsis accipiant dona, statim in quatuor dividant partes: ita ut prima pars secundum Apostolorum præcepta tituam. An frustra scriptum est: Labores injustorum pii edent? Quapropter magis mirari debetis quod adhuc tenetis aliquid quia quod aliquid amisistis. Item si qua jam praecisi possidere coepistis, quia vobis ablata, nobis Dominus deus dedit: non ideo concupiscimus aliena: quia illius imperio cujus sunt omnia facta sunt nostra: & juste nostra sunt. vos enim utcbamini ad praecisionem, nos ad unitatem. Alioquin & primo populo Dei possent illi objicere aliena rei concupiscentiam, qui divina potestate ab eorum facie, quia ea terra male utebantur, expulsi sunt: & ipsi Iudai a quibus ablatum est regnum secundum verbum domini,& datum est genti facienti justitiam,possunt objicere aliena rei concupiscentiam: quia Christi ecclesia possidet ubi persecutores Christi prius regnabant. Eadem ratione, & authoritate Augustini, respondit Melanthon a. clɔ lɔ xl. ad qu. utrum reditus donati Ecclesiis, ad Euangelii ministros alendos, & ad studia consei vanda eripiendi sint otiosis, impiis & oppugnantibus Euangelium? quod ita.
units.tr: Likewise Juvenal, Satire 1: They owe their gardens to crimes, &c. In short, who could list or explain the thousand arts by which the Pontiffs, however wicked they all are, seize and snatch up without end or measure whatever belongs to others, in order to extract and grab money? Hence the jurist Lynus said that the Papal court would very much like the whole world to flow into it, since there is such a sacred hunger for gold and silver in it. All these things serve to show the insatiable [ἀνάμω] greed and rapacity of that man. Hence, as countless people have often complained, they either hold, or at least labour to seize, the chief and greater part of the Christian world. King James of England, in his Apology to the Kings, addresses them thus: "But if you, who hear the most powerful, would consider, you will see that a third part of your people and land belongs to the Church. Would not this loss of men and dignity touch you at all? Everywhere the Pope acquires provinces and colonies, and is never satisfied. Formerly the clergy asked for nothing but tithes and were content. Today the Pope, the head of the clergy, is not satisfied unless he has a third part of your subjects and goods." The German princes once said the same in their Grievances; and the most serene Venetian Republic, in its disputes with Paul V in the year 1606, and his most deserving theologian Fra Paolo Servita, showed in a special treatise that the clergy, though only the hundredth part of the subjects, possessed in the Paduan territory more than a third, in the Bergamask more than half, and in the rest more than a quarter. Hence the jurist Nicolaus Crassus, in his Antiparaenesis for the Venetian Republic against Baronius, said not without reason: "You have a hundred times greater wealth and resources than your numbers warrant, and yet you still want more." And as to the fact that today the Jesuits offer the Republic four million gold pieces for the Turkish war, if only it will restore and reinstate them, please weigh carefully what a striking proof of their poverty this is. Nevertheless, the most illustrious Senate, although it lacks so much money for this grave war against the Turks, nonetheless orders them to leave the Republic with their money for ever. The author of the vernacular History of France, Mercure François, for the year 1611, where he treats of the return of the Jesuits to France, reports that one of their colleges has an income of 20,000 pounds. And for the year 1608, in the canonization of Francis, he says that more than a hundred thousand crowns were spent on the matter by his fellows. As for what the canonization of Bridget, made by Urban V, cost, or that of Andrea Corsini, the Carmelite, Bishop of Fiesole, enrolled among the saints by Urban VIII at the request of Louis XIII, King of France, I will not say; it is enough to have said this, and that others have complained. Not long ago there appeared a reckoning of the revenues that the French clergy have: 14 archbishoprics, 95 bishoprics, 140,000 parishes, 1,356 abbeys, 12,440 priories, 2,061 benefices held in commendam, 152,000 chaplaincies, 567 monasteries of religious, 700 convents of Franciscans, and 14,077 convents of other religious; so that they possess 9,000 places, castles and houses with jurisdiction of the high, middle and lower kind, and vineyards and gardens of more than 17,000, so that it is found that each year they have 8,200,000 in income, eighty-two million crowns, and every day 286,301 crowns and 20 shillings. Philippus Honorius, in his book On the Kingdom of France, makes this calculation, saying that from the fruits of the land about fifteen million gold pieces are collected, of which six are the Church's, one and a half the royal patrimony, and the rest for princes, barons and others; so that the clergy hold well over two-fifths of the kingdom. Claudius Sesellius complained of this already in the year 1515. He was among the foremost men of his age, served for some years as envoy from Louis XII to Leo X, and was later Bishop of Marseilles, or, as others say, of Turin. In his first book On the Republic of France he says: "Next, the vast sum of money that the men of our order, the heads of the Churches, spend with a certain ambition and insatiable desire to obtain greater things, would not exceed the boundaries of the provinces, which are now plundered and ransacked beyond all measure by the followers and pupils of the Roman Curia." Aubertus Miraeus wrote the Notice of the Bishoprics of the Christian World, and on the State of the Christian Religion, where it is shown how numerous Roman clerics are everywhere, and what, and how immense, the places they hold. Conradus Low, in his German History of Muhammad, page 83, reports the calculation of Simon Wolder, presented to the Emperor Ferdinand at the Diet of Augsburg, to show where subsidies for the war against the Turks could very easily be sought. He reckons that the houses of the Minorites amount to forty thousand, and of the three remaining orders, namely the Augustinians, Dominicans and Carmelites, not much fewer; and since in all there are seventy-two orders, apart from colleges of canons and virgins and parish churches, he thinks the number of all of them comes to two thousand million. He judged that a light tax on these would bring, if not the ruin of the whole world, at least the ruin of many, to sustain the burdens of the Turkish war; especially when we consider for what ends or uses they spend such great goods on the Pope, namely almost solely on luxury and worldly pride, and other things not much better. And this, as everyone knows, is clearly so; and those who devote themselves to them are accustomed to care for nothing so much as to have, by whatever means, however illicit and wicked, and setting aside all other things, one belly, and the things that belong to it and to the flesh, as their God and to worship. Ferus neatly said on Matthew, chapter 17: "Peter, when he was fishing for money, used only a hook and was content; when he was to fish for men, he was told to let down nets. Now everything is done the other way round: to fish for riches we spread wide nets, and to fish for men we hardly use a hook. O our times, O successors of Peter!" And to what end, I beg you, do they cry out and make such an uproar for their goods and wealth, that they would rather throw everything into confusion and tear it apart than be deprived of them? To the same end, namely that to which they spend them. Let King Edgar of England speak for me, in his Oration to the English Clergy, which is in the Library of the Fathers: "I will say, I will say, what the good lament and the wicked laugh at; I will say, grieving (if indeed it can be said), how they run to waste in drinking-bouts and drunkenness, in beds and immodesty, so that the houses of the clergy are thought to be brothels of harlots and a meeting-place of actors. There are dice, there are dances, there is singing, there are vigils protracted until midnight amid shouting and uproar. Thus, thus the patrimonies of kings, the alms of the poor, nay, what is worse, the price of that precious blood, are squandered? Did our fathers therefore exhaust their treasures for this? Did the royal treasury withhold so many revenues for this? Did royal munificence give fields and possessions to the Churches of Christ for this, that the delights of the clergy might be adorned with harlots, luxurious banquets prepared, dogs and birds and such playthings bought? Where is the sword of Levi, and the zeal of Simon? &c. I, Constantine, you have the sword of Peter in your hands. Let us join right hands, let us join sword to sword, so that the lepers may be cast out of the camp, that the sanctuary of the Lord may be cleansed, and the sons of Levi, who said to their father and mother, I do not know you, and ignored their brothers, may minister in the temple." And this is what Theodoret says in his tenth oration On Providence: they gorge themselves on other people's goods and fatten themselves on the tears of the poor. And Bernard, sermon 77 on the Song of Songs: "Whence, do you think, come this abundance of wealth, this splendour of clothing, this luxury of tables, this heap of silver and golden vessels, if not from the goods of the bride?" Sermon 33: "All are friends, and all are enemies; all are kinsmen, and none are peaceable; all are neighbours, and all seek what is their own. They are ministers of Christ, and serve antichrist. The honoured walk about on the goods of the Lord, and do not render honour to the Lord. Hence that theatrical sheen which you see every day, that actor's dress, that royal display; hence gold on the bridles, on the saddles and spurs, and the spurs shine more than the altars. Hence splendid tables with dishes and cups, then drinking-bouts and drunkenness; hence the lyre and harp and pipe; hence overflowing wine-presses and storerooms full belching from this to that. Hence jars of spices, hence purses stuffed full. For such things they want to be, and are, the provosts, deans, archdeacons, bishops and archbishops of the churches." He pricks these things in very many places, sharply and to the quick, in book 4 to Eugenius, letter 42 to the Archbishop of Sens, and elsewhere. Similarly Bernhard Westerrode of Corvey, in his lament: "On the patrimony of Christ: living under display and proclamation they swell up. Intent on pleasures and the vanities of the world, they blush at their capes. I name not only monks, but also canons, and feigned nuns, &c." But those who abuse goods in this way ought not to be spoken for; rather, these goods should be taken from them and spent on much better uses. This was the opinion of John Wycliffe, in article 17, among the articles 45 for which he was condemned by the Papists: "Temporal lords may at their pleasure take temporal goods away from ecclesiastics who habitually offend." Not, however, in that sense, as if he did not acknowledge those goods to be ecclesiastical, or did not hold that they ought to have an ecclesiastical use, or could be spent by temporal lords on whatever other uses, as someone perhaps might take it. Master John Hus, Rector of the University of Prague, in the year 1410, published a determination of the above article and prefaces it thus: "I protest, however, that it is not my intention, nor that of the university, to persuade that princes or secular lords should take goods away from the clergy when and how they wish, and convert them where they wish." And in the determination itself, §12, he says: "With equal clarity, goods have been made the goods of others for the advancement of the Church, when clerics habitually offend." He concedes indeed that goods which some abuse to the grave damage of the Church should be taken from them, from those who habitually offend, that is, from the habit, not only from the act, as is also permitted elsewhere; yet he nonetheless acknowledges that the gifts are the Church's, and that they must be spent, if not by these men, then by others. Poggius of Florence, in a letter to Leonardo Aretino, on Huss and Jerome of Prague, reports that Jerome defended his Huss in the Council in this way: "He thought nothing against the state of God's Church, but against the abuses of the clergy, against the pride, arrogance and pomp of the prelates. For since the patrimonies of the Churches ought first to belong to the poor, then to guests, and then to the building of churches, it seemed unworthy to a good man that they should be spent on harlots, banquets, the upkeep of horses and dogs, the cultivation of clothing, and other things unworthy of the Christian religion." So far Poggius on Huss. And Andreas Willet takes and defends Huss's opinion in this way, in his Synopsis of Papism, general controversy 5, question 6. The Reformed have always especially noted this squandering and abuse of ecclesiastical goods. Calvin, Institutes book 4, §10: "I do not touch here on foreign vices, but only on the internal evil, which is rooted in their very institution. I will add a word that will sound bad in their ears; but because it is true, it must be said: canons, deans, chaplains, provosts, and whoever are fed by idle benefices, must be counted in the same place. For what ministry of the Church can they perform? Those who have degenerated into canons ought to have been presbyters, as they once were, who governed the Church in common with the bishop and were, as it were, his colleagues in the pastoral office. Those capitular dignities, as they are called, have nothing whatever to do with the true government of the Church; much less chaplaincies, and the rest of that sort of names. Where, then, shall we place them all? Surely both the word of Christ and the observance of the ancient Church exclude them from the honour of presbyters. Yet they contend that they are presbyters; but the little mask must be torn off, and so we shall find that their whole profession is most alien and most remote from that office of presbyters which the Apostles describe to us and which was required in the early Church. Therefore all such orders, by whatever titles they are adorned, being recent, and supported neither by the institution of God nor by the ancient observance of the Church, ought to have no place in the description of the spiritual government which the Church received from the mouth of the Lord himself consecrated. Or (if they prefer that I speak more rudely and crudely), when chaplains, canons, deans, provosts, and idle bellies of that sort do not touch even the smallest particle of that office which is necessarily required in presbyters, it is not to be tolerated that they, by falsely usurping the honour, violate the holy institution of Christ." And §15: "They have transferred the very dispensation of the goods to another use, and have arranged it so that nothing more disorderly can be imagined. For as robbers, when they have slain men, divide the spoils among themselves, so they, after the light of God's word was extinguished, as if the Church were slain, thought that whatever was in its sacred use was exposed as booty and plunder. And so, the division made, each seized as much as he could." Chemnitz, in his Examination of the Council of Trent, part 1, on Canonical Scripture: "Scripture is not therefore called canonical in the way that the canonical hours are called so, or as those now who fatten themselves on ecclesiastical goods are called canons." Grotius, in his Annotations to Cassander, chapter on canons: "And would that even now there were not many such, he understands irregular canons. But what can you do, when such colleges in many places are filled by princes in name, and idle nobles, while those who have the principal place in holiness of life and the nobility of learning are excluded? And kings and bishops have the care to correct these things; but we shall hope for this only if those who ought to correct others first correct themselves." Rivet, on these words, declares that Grotius's statement is true and free. Grotius again, in his Animadversions: "not only useful but also plainly necessary, if we wish to heal and repair the Church." To which Rivet, adding his own vote, says: "Let then what is sought be done, and let those things be corrected which Dr Grotius thinks not only useful but plainly necessary for healing the Church. We do not object." From these things thus explained it is now clear how undeservedly the Pope rages so much for his own goods, that for their sake he orders peace, treaties and all oaths to be abolished, and brings war and firebrands back into Germany again, since he neither holds nor uses those goods of his, that is, Papal goods (for I distinguish ecclesiastical goods from Papal ones so named), so badly acquired, well, but uses them all as wickedly as he can. In Papacy, which can be regarded as nothing other than a rhapsodist and a body mixed from various things, goods of different kinds must be considered: Papal, Hierarchical, of Princes or of the Empire, idolatrous plainly or superstitious, and finally simply ecclesiastical, and these either purely such, or chiefly so, namely given to the use of Christ's Church. Which are sometimes distinguished from the goods of the poor, and sometimes are held to be the same, so that ecclesiastics are included under the poor, and the poor under the ecclesiastics. For it is not to be thought that whenever the Ancients in this matter, or in pious wills, name the poor, the clergy or ecclesiastics are often not included as well; as if when the goods of the poor are spoken of, the clergy are not also understood, or goods had not been bequeathed to them. For the poor are sometimes understood here as distinct from the clergy, as often as they speak of the fourfold division of sacred goods, 12 qu. 2, c. "But the four portions of the revenue and of the faithful's offerings, according as the means of each church allow (as has been reasonably decreed long ago), are to be made: one of which is for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and the fourth is to be applied to the fabric." &c., the next canon: "Of the revenues of the church or the offerings of the faithful, one portion alone is to be remitted to the bishops; two are to be administered by the presbyter, under peril of his order, for the ecclesiastical fabric and for the relief of the poor; the last is to be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each." Canon 30: "It is the custom of the Apostolic See, when a bishop is ordained, to give instructions that from every stipend that comes in four portions shall be made: one, namely, for the bishop and his household, on account of hospitality and reception; another for the clergy; a third truly for the poor; a fourth for the repair of the churches." And there, the Palea that is inscribed from the Council of Toledo: "Moreover we confirm that if they receive any gifts, they shall at once divide them into four parts, so that the first part, according to the precepts of the Apostles, ... " Is it in vain that it is written: the labours of the unjust the pious shall eat? Wherefore you ought rather to wonder that you still hold anything, since you have lost something. Likewise, if you have begun to possess anything that was taken from you, the Lord God has given it to us: we do not therefore covet what belongs to others; by the command of him whose all things are, our things have been made, and they are rightly ours. For you tended towards separation, we towards unity. Otherwise they could object to the first people of God the covetousness of what belongs to others, who were driven out from their face by divine power, because they misused that land; and the Jews themselves, from whom the kingdom was taken away according to the word of the Lord and given to a nation doing justice, could object the covetousness of what belongs to others, because the Church of Christ possesses where the persecutors of Christ once reigned. By the same reasoning and the authority of Augustine, Melanchthon answered in the year 1540 the question whether the revenues given to the Churches for maintaining the ministers of the Gospel and for supporting studies should be taken away from the idle, the impious and those who oppose the Gospel: that they should."

units.la: Nam etsi ad ministros Ecclesiae Euangelicae non pertinet gubernatio imperii mundani, tamen Magistratus politicus efficere debet, ut quisque suum teneat. Iam hi reditus sunt non impiorum Canonicorum, sed sunt vera Ecclesiae. Quare & Magistratus reddere eas Ecclesiis veris debet, & poenam sumere ab impiis tanquam praedonibus. Magna profecto necessitas est, acerrime hanc causam agi. Nisi enim facultates restituantur Ecclesiae, boni pastores & pauperes scholastici fame peribunt, studia extinguentur, decrunt Ecclesiae & Reipublicae literati. Ideo opitulari & juvare studia honestorum adolescentum debent Magistratus. Nam praeterquam, quod Deus eos facere hoc jubet, etiam Canones ipsi hoc flagitant, videlicet eis opem ferre ex Ecclesiarum opibus.In quaest. Wittemberg. (occurrit in Consiliis Melanthonis, part. i. pag. 427. & apud Pezelium, part. vii. ) Quarto, Iam ergo, in Ecclesia Papali non applicari bona ista in pios & sacros usus, videlicet in quos data sunt, sed aut otiosis intervire ventribus, aut quod supra jam diximus, in omne luxum & profanitate ablumi,res notior est, quam ut dici debeat. Dominicus Gravina, lib. Congeminata vox turturis, cap. xvi. p. 280. cx Paulo Laymanno adducit: quis nesciat haereticos sub initio harum haeresen plausibilius oppugnasse Ecclesiam Dei & sacrilegam invadendorum Monasteriorum, ac bonorum Ecclesiæ cupiditatem palliasse, quam clamando: Monachos esse inutilia terræ pondera, ventres pigros, stupidas pecudes, &c. non esse bona illa à majoribus suis pro hominibus inutilibus, otiosis, ignavis fundata. Inverti à Monachis intentiones tectatorum, bona illa ad publicam utilitatem impendenda, fundandas ex eis scholas, constituenda ex illis stipendia Concionatorum, pauperum, studiosorum, & eorum qui curam animarum, & sacramentorum administrant, & similia. Quæ licet ea quidem parte, qua vota, & instituta Monastica condemnantur, hæretica: & ea, quæ illa bona ad hæreticos prædicantes, ac studiosos volebant converti Ecclesiæ Catholicæ pernitiosa fuerint &c. ex ea tamen parte, qua contendebant melius esse bona illa applicari iis, qui publicam Ecclesiæ utilitatem melius, & efficacius procurant, vera fuerunt ac laude digna, & à Catholicis merito perpendi, ac reipsa perfici debent.
units.tr: For although the government of the worldly realm does not belong to the ministers of the evangelical Church, the civil magistrate must still see to it that each man keeps what is his own. Now these revenues belong not to impious canons but truly to the Church. Therefore the magistrate ought both to restore them to the true churches and to exact punishment from the impious as from robbers. There is indeed great necessity that this cause be pursued most vigorously. For unless the resources are restored to the Church, good ministers and poor scholars will perish of hunger, studies will be extinguished, and both the Church and the commonwealth will lack learned men. Therefore magistrates ought to aid and support the studies of respectable young men. For apart from God commanding them to do this, the canons themselves also demand it, namely that help be brought to them from the resources of the churches. (This occurs in Melanchthon's Consilia, part i, p. 427, and in Pezelius, part vii.) Fourthly, that in the Papal Church these goods are not applied to the pious and sacred uses for which they were given, but are either spent on the bellies of idlers or, as we have said above, squandered on every kind of luxury and profanity, is too well known to need saying. Dominicus Gravina, in his book Congeminata vox turturis, chapter 16, p. 280, cites from Paulus Laymann: who does not know that at the beginning of this heresy the heretics attacked the Church of God more plausibly, and cloaked their sacrilegious desire to seize monasteries and the goods of the Church, than by crying out that monks are useless burdens on the earth, lazy bellies, stupid cattle, and so on, and that those goods were not founded by their ancestors for useless, idle and lazy men? The intentions of the testators, they said, were perverted by the monks: those goods were to be spent on public utility, schools were to be founded from them, and from them were to be established stipends for preachers, the poor, students, those who administer the cure of souls and the sacraments, and the like. Although these views, in the part where monastic vows and institutions are condemned, are heretical, and although those schemes which wished those goods to be turned over to heretical preachers and students were pernicious to the Catholic Church, and so on, nevertheless in that part where they contended that those goods were better applied to those who promote the public utility of the Church better and more effectively, they were true and worthy of praise, and should rightly be weighed by Catholics and actually carried out.

units.la: Quod autem frustra exspectes à Papalibus, quodque iuste ibi conquereris hærere vitii, neq; corrigi pro merito, illud à nostris hominibus emendari, & reformatum apud nos esse, quis est qui ultra vitio vertat? Atque ita nostri interpretantur illud Apoc. IX. 21. & qui non resipuerunt à furtis suis ... de alienatione bonorum cultui divino dicatorum ad pigros ventres, & à pluribus ad pompam mundanam: quemadmodū in istum locum loquuntur Commentatores nostri Belgici. Confer Iohannē Gerhardi Confess. Catholic. lib. 1. p. 915. In Canonicos quidē ita invehitur Rovenius noster, lib. 1. Resp. Christiana, cap. XXVI 1. quod ipsos pudeat divinas laudes pro se decantare, sacris initiari, aut sacris operari, non nisi de temporalibus in Capitulis tractent, venationi aut aucupio vacent, potitationibus, conviviis & comessationibus (ut non dicam turpioribus rebus) patrimonium Christi prodigant &c. beneficia ac prabendas pueris & indoneis conferant, imo prabendas simoniace vendant. &c. legem Domini nec sciant, nec discant, assidui in plateis, in Ecclesia tardi, velociores ad congregandos canes, quam ad alendos pauperes &c. Quinto, accusant quidem nos passim Papani, bona Ecclesiastica à nostris in prophanos usus converti: sed dicimus, doctrinæ Reformatæ haud alium esse sensum, quam data Ecclesiis Christi bona, pro intentione ac voluntate donatorum testatorumq;Ecclesiis relinquenda,atque in usus sacros ecclesiasticos religiose impendenda esse. Ludovicus Lavaterus, Theologus Tigurinus, homil. v. inEsdram, hanc in rem ita loquitur : Nostra aetate non desunt, qui quod alii largiti sunt ad conservationem cultus Dei, in privatos usus convertant, & temere profundant. Accusant Papistae, non solum in concionibus suis, sed publicis scriptis, Evangelicos principes & Magistratus, quod opes Ecclesiae, & ornamenta sacrilego ausu in prophanos usus convertant. Accusant concionatores Evangelicos, quod suum Magistratum ad sacrilegia perpellant. Felicianus episcopus Scalensis hoc anno 1583. librum precationum Caroli Calvi Imp. edidit, in cujus praefatione Tigurinos bonorum Ecclesiasticorum direptione accusat. &c.
