Respondeo ad illam episcopi narrationem, de voluntate, & consensu Abbatisse, monasterium hoc, ut alia quoque in meliorem usum mutatum esse. Conversum enim est ab Amplifs. Senatu Tigurino in scholam, & collegium, in quo aliquot bonarum litterarum Studiosi adolescentes, cum paedagogo alantur. Quis et eiusdem Ecclesiae usus sit, non est obscurum, conservandi ex illis sunt ministri, alendi Studiosi bonarum litterarum, pauperes, artificia necessaria ex his extruenda, pars ad futuras calamitates reponenda est. Et post, si qui sunt vel principes, vel oeconomi, qui opes illas non recte administrant, sed ea sibi retinent, quae non debeant, illos nequaquam defendo. Atque idem homil. xxix. Quod am sit officium, vel quomodo se gerere debeant procuratores thesaurorum Ecclesiae, vigilare, custodire opes sacras, & in usus legitimos distribuere debent, semperque cogitare, quod thesauri illi Dei sint, quodque magnum sit scelus, rem Deo consecratam in usum prophanum convertere. Non solum hominibus accepti & expensi erit danda ratio, sed etiam Deo, quem nemo potest fallere. Si officium suum diligenter exequuti fuerint, praemium ferent, sin minus, poenas dabunt, & graves quidem. Exempla habes in Rege Balthasare, apud Danielem: In Achane, in libro Iosue, in Ananias, & Sapphira. Etiam in sacrilegis apud Ethnicos. Similiter loquitur homil. liiii. in Nehemiam. Iohannes Gerhardi, celebris Theologus Ienensis, Confessionis Catholicae lib. i. pag. 914. ad eandem Papistarum, de bonis Ecclesiasticis per nostros direptis, atque in alios usus conversis, objectionem, respondet: Accusant nostros, quod rapinam bonorum Ecclesiasticorum approbent. Aiphonsus a Castro lib. 6. adv. haereses verbo Ecclesia haresi 4. Impius Lutherus suadere audet Principibus, ut Ecclesias diripiant atque spolient. Resp. 1. imo vero nostri majorum pietatem in conferendis bonis ad necessarios Ecclesiae usus commendant, de abusu eorum hodierno conqueruntur, & ad veros ac legitimos usus illa applicanda esse, docent. Lutherus von den Concilis vnd Kirchen tom. 7. Jen. Germ p. 261. Man sihet wol / wie mit grossem Ernst die alten Keyser die Pfarren vnd Schulen gemeynet/ daß sie so reichlich die Stifter begabet haben. Denn das es erstlich Schulen gewesen sind / zeugen diese Namen / Probst / Dechant / Scholasticus / Cantor / Canonici / Vicarii Custos / etc. Aber was ist draus werden? Nach GOTT/ daß sie doch noch etwas thun wolten / blieben was sie sind / behielten was sie hetten / weren Fursten vnd Herren / richteten aber wiederumb lectionen an / vnnd zwungen die Thumhern / vicarien / Chor Schuler / daß sie des Tages eine lection in der heiligen Schrift hörten / damit es wider doch etliche massen einer Schulen gestalt hette / auff daß man Pfarrer vnd Bischof haben kondte / vnd bulffen al so die Kirchen regieren / etc. GOTT / wie unmeßlich groß gut konnten sie thun bey den Kirchen / vnd Gott würde ihnen jren Richthum oder gewalt wol gönnen vnd lassen p. 275. Darumb haben die vorigen Keyser Konig vnd Fursten recht wol gethan / daß sie mit solchem Fleiß so viel Schulen / hoch vnd klein / Kloster vnd Stifft gebawet / daß sie der Kirchen haben reichen großen Vorrath von Personen schaffen wollen / aber durch die Nachkommen schändlich zum Mißbrauch verkehret sind. Alse solle jetzund Fursten vnd Herren auch thun / der Kloster Guter zum schulen wenden / vnd viel Personen stifften zum Studio, werdens unsere Nach emen mißbrauchen / so haben wir zu unsere Zeit das unsere gethan. Idem in Genesim cap. 54. pag. 616. Exemplum Pharaonis profecto dignissimum est, quod omnes Reges, Principes, Magistratus, Nobiles in conspectu habeant ac summo studio imitentur, in sovendis & sustentandis piis, Pastoribus, Ministris Ecclesiae & Scholasticis. Sed contrarium hodie fit, non solum à Pontificiis, sed etiam ab iis, qui emendationem Ecclesiarum instituunt, sed eo pretextu Ecclesias spoliant iis bonis, quae ad conservationem Ministerii & Scholarum conferenda erant. Tom. 2. Iilebiensi p. 33. Wozu soll man nun solche Guter brauchen. Hier an man nicht besser antworten denn daß man acht habe auff der Stiffter Willen vnd meynung / welches sie nicht anders gewesen ist / denn daß sie zu Gottes Dienst vnd Ehre solche Guter haben wollen geben. Ob sie nun nicht recht angetroffen haben / ist doch ihren Willen vnnd meynung nach hierinne zu richten / daß man sie noch zum Gote {s} tcs tesdiensi rnd Ehrebrauche/ als da sind Pfarrer/ Predigerj / Schulen vnd was mehr zum Gottesword / Sacrament vnnd Seelsorgen gehöret. Vnd wiewol Gottes Dienst in allen Stenden vnnd Aempteen oder Wercken geschicht/die man auch fördern soll/so sind doch obgenandte Stende /nemlich die Seelsorge vnd das Predigampt/ Schulen/ etc. die höchsten / nöthigsten vnd fürnemsten / welche die alten Fürsten mit ihren Stifften vnd Klöstern sonderlich gemeynet/ vnd ans-länglich also gehalten ist. Iom. 5. Germ. Jen. p. 131. Wen sie ihre Stiffter vnd Klöster hielten dafür / and auch also brauchten/ daß man die chrisliche Jugend darinnen erziehe /vnd den Glauben vnd Zucht lehreten damit man seine Personen heiße/ zu Christlichen Emptern/vnd weren also nicht anders denn Christliche Schulen/ wie sie von Anfang gestiffter sind/ vnnd die Namen der Prae-laten / als Probst/ Dechant / Scholasticus/ Cantor vnd dergleichen/ noch wol anzeigen/ so werens seine Stiffter. In articulis Schmalcaldicis, art. 3. partis 2. Collegia Canonicorum & Cœnobia olim optima intentione majorum fundata ad educandos viros doctos & castas ac modestas fœminas, debebant rursum converti in talem usum, ut Pastores, Concionatores & alii Ecclesiarum Ministri haberi possent, Item alii idonei ad Politicam administrationem sive ad Rempub. in civitatibus & regionibus, ac pie educatæ virgines ad Oeconomiam & liberorum educationem.
units.tr: That you look in vain for correction from the Papists, and that you rightly complain that their faults persist and are not properly amended, who could blame our people for amending and reforming those faults among us? Thus our writers interpret the passage in Apoc. 9:21, and they did not repent of their thefts ... of the alienation of goods dedicated to divine worship, some to lazy bellies, and most to worldly pomp, as our Belgian commentators read that place. Compare Johann Gerhard, Confessio Catholica, book 1, p. 915. Our Rovenius inveighs against the canons in this way, book 1 of the Christian Response, chapter 26: they should be ashamed to sing divine praises on their own behalf, to be initiated into sacred things, or to perform sacred duties; they discuss only temporal matters in their chapters, devote themselves to hunting and fowling, and squander the patrimony of Christ on drinking, banquets and revelries (not to mention more shameful things); they confer benefices and prebends on boys and the unfit, and even sell prebends by simony; they neither know nor learn the law of the Lord, are constantly in the squares, slow in the church, and quicker to gather dogs than to feed the poor. Fifth, the Papists everywhere accuse us of turning the goods of the Church to profane uses. But we say that the doctrine of the Reformed has no other sense than that the goods given to the churches of Christ must be kept for the churches, according to the intention and will of the donors and testators, and must be devoted religiously to holy ecclesiastical uses. Ludwig Lavater, Zurich theologian, homily 5 on Ezra, speaks to this effect: In our own age there are not lacking those who turn to private uses, and squander rashly, what others have given for the maintenance of the worship of God. The Papists accuse not only in their sermons but in published writings the Evangelical princes and magistrates, that they turn the resources and ornaments of the Church to profane uses with sacrilegious daring. They accuse the Evangelical preachers of driving their magistrates into sacrilege. In the year 1583 Bishop Feliciano of Scala published a book of prayers of the Emperor Charles the Bald, and in its preface he accuses the Zurichers of plundering the goods of the Church, etc. I reply to the bishop's account that this monastery, like others too, was changed to a better use with the will and consent of the abbess. For it was converted by the most illustrious Zurich Senate into a school and college, in which some young students of good letters are maintained together with a tutor. What the use of the same Church is, is not obscure: from these resources ministers are to be supported, students of good letters are to be maintained, the poor are to be relieved, necessary crafts are to be established, and a part is to be set aside against future calamities. And afterwards: if there are any princes or stewards who do not administer those resources rightly, but keep for themselves what they ought not, I by no means defend them. And the same in homily 29: What the duty is, or how the stewards of the Church's treasuries ought to conduct themselves, is that they must watch over and guard the sacred resources and distribute them for lawful uses, always bearing in mind that those treasuries belong to God, and that it is a great crime to turn to profane use a thing consecrated to God. Account will be required not only of men, who receive and spend, but also of God, whom no one can deceive. If they have carried out their office diligently, they will receive a reward; if not, they will pay penalties, and heavy ones indeed. You have examples in King Belshazzar in Daniel, in Achan in the book of Joshua, in Ananias and Sapphira, and also among the heathen in the case of sacrilegious persons. He speaks similarly in homily 54 on Nehemiah. Johann Gerhard, the renowned theologian of Jena, Confessio Catholica, book 1, p. 914, answers the Papists' objection concerning the goods of the Church seized by our people and turned to other uses in this way: They accuse our people of approving the plunder of the goods of the Church. Alfonso de Castro, book 6 against heresies, under the word Church, heresy 4: the impious Luther dares to advise princes to tear apart and despoil the churches. Reply, first: on the contrary, our people commend the piety of our forefathers in giving goods for the necessary uses of the Church, they complain of the present abuse of them, and they teach that those goods must be applied to true and lawful uses. Luther, On the Councils and Churches, vol. 7 Jena German edition, p. 261: One sees well how the old emperors, with great earnestness, intended the parishes and schools, and so richly endowed the foundations. For that they were at first schools, these names bear witness: provost, dean, scholastic, cantor, canons, vicars, custodian, etc. But what has become of them? Whatever God may have wanted them still to do, they remained what they are, kept what they had, were princes and lords; but they again established lectures, and compelled the cathedral canons, vicars and choristers to hear one lecture a day in Holy Scripture, so that in some measure it had again the form of a school, so that one might have pastors and bishops, and thus they helped to govern the churches, etc. God, how immeasurably great good they could have done for the churches, and God would have allowed them their wealth and power well enough. p. 275. Therefore the former emperors, kings and princes did very well in building with such diligence so many schools, high and low, monasteries and foundations, because they wanted to furnish the Church with a rich and great store of persons; but through their descendants these have been shamefully turned to abuse. So now princes and lords should also do the same: turn the monastery goods to schools, and establish many persons for study. If our descendants abuse these, we at least will have done our part in our time. The same, on Genesis, chapter 54, p. 616. The example of Pharaoh is truly most worthy that all kings, princes, magistrates and nobles should keep it before their eyes and imitate it with the greatest zeal in cherishing and sustaining pious pastors, ministers of the Church and scholars. But today the opposite happens, not only among the Papists but also among those who undertake the reform of the churches, and who, under that pretext, strip the churches of those goods which ought to be bestowed for the support of the ministry and the schools. Vol. 2, Iilebiensis, p. 33: What then should such goods be used for? Here one can answer no better than by attending to the will and intention of the founders, which was nothing other than to give such goods for the service and honour of God. If they have not hit upon the right thing, nevertheless their will and intention should be the guide, so that they are still put to the service of God and to honourable use, such as pastors, preachers, schools, and whatever else belongs to the Word, the sacraments and the care of souls. And although the service of God takes place in all estates and offices or works, which also should be furthered, yet the aforementioned estates, namely the care of souls and the preaching office, schools, etc., are the highest, most necessary and chief, which the ancient princes especially intended with their foundations and monasteries, and it is sufficiently established thus. Vol. 5, Jena German edition, p. 131: If they held their foundations and monasteries to be for this, and also used them so that Christian youth might be educated in them and taught the faith and discipline, so that persons might be trained for Christian offices, and they were thus nothing other than Christian schools, as they were founded from the beginning, and the names of the prelates, such as provost, dean, scholastic, cantor and the like, still indicate, then they would be truly foundations for that purpose. In the Schmalkald Articles, part 2, art. 3: The colleges of canons and the monasteries, once founded with the best intention of our forefathers to educate learned men and chaste and modest women, ought in turn to be converted to such use that pastors, preachers and other ministers of the churches may be had, likewise others fit for political administration, or for the state in cities and regions, and virgins piously brought up for household management and the education of children.

units.la: Hęc Gerhardus. Familiaris Pontificis adversus nos est querela, bona ecclesiastica à nostris privatos profanosq; usus teneri atq; consumi. unde Rovenius tractatu de Missionibus, part. 1v. Invenies plerosque, ait, bona aliqua præsertim Ecclesiastica aut officia vel beneficia injuste possidentes. Negamus hoc nostros plerosque facere, & si quispiam, in eo certe agit contra doctrinæ nostræ manifestam atque unanimem regulam. Scimus enim supremas Testatorum voluntates & donationes secundum placitum donantium servandas esse, neq; usquam magis vel religiosius quam in causis piis & Ecclesiasticis. Hoc jus natura, & religio pariter docent ac confirmant. Lex est xii. Tab. Vt quisq; legassit suæ rei, ita jus esto. In jure canonico xiii. qu. 11 cap. 4. Ultima voluntas defuncti modis omnibus servari debet, præcipue in testamentis piis, quando aliquid Ecclesiæ vel pauperibus legatur. 11. qu. 11. per totum. & xvi qu. c. similiter c. quia juxta c. possessiones. addc Tiraquellu, lib. de privilegiis pia causa. Quę ratio est, quod Deus tam severe prohibuerit punieritque bonorum suo cultui vel ecclesiæ consecratorum direptionem ac profanationé. Vide Ios. vii. Prov. xx. xv. Dã. v. 2. 3. Ioel. iii. 5. 12. emolumenta, crimen est. Sin vero pauperibus erogat captivum redimit, misericordia est. Isidorus Pelusiota, lib. 1. epist.269. At tu contra omnino faciens, Ecclesia & pauperum bona domi tua impie & nefarie collegis. Huic igitur impietatis finem impone. Idem lib.iii. epist. Inter opera Hieronymi, tomo quarto, pag.322. epistola occurrit ad Damasum Papam, de panibus oblationum in nullos usus privatos aut laicos vindicandis: Testes idonei quos ad hanc rem corroborandam concitavi, hi sunt. Gregorius Nazianzenus, mirabilis doctor Cyrillus, Athanasius, Theophilus, Anatolius, Chrysostomus, Eustachius, Eusebius Chronographus, & noster Hilarius, qui omnes uno ore, eodemque consensu, velut vera Sp. S. organa, anathematis mucrone sentiunt esse feriendos, qui in usus laicorum, panes oblationum contulerint, quia omnino sacerdotibus solis debentur. Non solum autem de Panibus in Ecclesia, hoc sanxerunt Patres nostri, sed de omnibus, quae altari offeruntur: docentes, atque docentes, magnum nefas esse, & per omnia diabolica temeritate hoc fieri, ubicumque acciderit, & valde esse intolerabile Sancta Ecclesia, ut sine vindicta sacrorum canonum remaneat. Gregorius Thaumaturgus, epist. canonica, c.iii.epist. iii. Non ecce Achaz Zare filius in eo quod Deo dedicatum erat, peccavit, & in omnem Israel synagogam ira pervenit? Atqui hic unus solus peccavit, sed non solus in suo peccato est mortuus. Nobis autem quicquid non nostrum, sed alienum est, ab hoc tempore lucrum Deo dedicatum esse existimandum est. Nam & ille quidem Achaz ex praeda accepit, & ipsi nunc ex praeda accipiunt. ac ille quidem, ea quae erant hostium, qui vero nunc sunt, ea quae sunt fratrum, perniciosò lucro lucrifacientes. Ad quem locum Theodorus Balsamo, in Scholiis: Nota praesentem canonem propter eos qui res ecclesiarum & monasteriorum rapiunt, & , ut semel dicam propter eos qui quae sunt Deo dedicata, tanquam propria vendicant. Plurima in hanc rem sunt in Capitularibus Caroli M. & Filiorum. Lib. i. c. xlviii. ex concilio Gangrensi, ut nulli liceat oblata, quae ad pauperes pertinent rapere vel fraudare. c.lxxxiii. Statuimus, ut neque nostris, neque filiorum, & Deo dispensante successorum nostrorum temporibus, qui nostram vel progenitorum nostrorum voluntatem vel exemplum imitari voluerint, ullam penitus divi-sio sionem aut jacturam patiatur. Lib. 11.cap. xxxii. Lib. v. cap. clxxxvii. lib. vi. c. lxxxix. Præcipimus, ut nullus laicorum vel clericorum ex prædiis vel rebus, quæ ad sedes pertinent Episcoporum, sive de illis Ecclesiarum rebus, quæ in eorum parochiis sita esse noscuntur, sine illorum jussione aut consensu Episcoporum, ad quorum pertinent curam, qui cunque ambiant, concupiscant atque accipiant: ne cupidos sanctarum rerum ignis, qui in eis est, illos favillosius exurat. Ejusdem libri c. cix. c. cxiii. c. cxvi. c. ccxcvi. c. cccı. c. ccciiı.c.cccv. quaecunque de his rebus quae ad laudem Dei sunt vel supplementum sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ ejusque sacerdotibus, atque ornatum præstare possunt Domino Ecclesiæque, sive a quibuscunque ultro offeruntur, Domino indubitanter consecrantur, & ad jus pertinent sacerdotum. Et quia Christum & Ecclesiam unam personam esse veraciter agnoscimus, quaecunque Ecclesiæ sunt, Christi sunt. Et quæ Ecclesiæ vel in supradictis vel in quibuscunque speciebus, sive pollicitationibus, sive pignoribus, sive scriptis sive corporalibus rebus offeruntur, Christo offeruntur, & quæ ab Ecclesia ejus quocunque commento alienantur vel tolluntur, sive alienando, sive vastando, sive invadendo, sive minorando, sive dirípiendo, Christo tolluntur. c. cccxx. quia sicut a sanctis patribus instructi sumus, gravissimum peccatum hoc esse dignoscitur, testante sacra scriptura, quæ ait: quis abstulerit aliquid patri vel matri, & dicit hoc non esse peccatum, homicidii particeps est. Pater noster sine dubio Deus est qui nos creavit, mater nostra Ecclesia, quæ nos in baptismo spiritualiter regeneravit. Ergo qui Christi pecunias & Ecclesiæ fraudat vel rapit sive vastat vel alienat, homicida ante conspectum justi judicis esse deputabitur. De quo quidam sapientum dicit, qui rapit pecuniam proximi sui iniquitatem facit, qui autem pecuniam Ecclesiæ abstulerit sacrilegium facit. c.cccxxii.c.cccxxiii. Sciendum est omnibus, quod sacrilegium sit res Ecclesiæ quocunque modo injuste ab Ecclesiis quibus jure debentur auferri, & in aliud transferri. Lib.vii.c.cv. Nam multa regiones quæ rerum Ecclesiarum invasiones, vastationes, alienationes, vexationesque, & sacerdotum, reliquorumque servorum Dei oppressiones vel quascunque injurias, quæ jam dicta illicita, & adulteria vel sodomiticam luxuriam, vel commixtionem meretricum seIlata Stata fuerunt, nec in bello seculari fortes nec in fide stabiles perstiterunt, & qualiter Dominus talium criminum patratoribus ultrices poenas, per Saracenos & alios populos venire & servire promisit, cunctis earum gesta legentibus liquet, & nisi nos ab his caveamus, similia nobis supervenire no dubitamus, quia vindex est Deus de his omnibus. item c. cxlvi i.c.cli i. c.clxxxviii. c. cxcix. c. ccxc. Haec eo etiam diligentius ex Capitulis illis prosequuti sumus, quod ex illis potissimum concinnavit suum de sacrilegio laico commentarium, Ichannes Filesacus Theologus Parisinus, seu Veteris Ecclesiae Gallicanae querelam, de beneficiis bonisque Ecclesiasticis, & eorum reditibus a laicos male occupatis usurpatisque, jam a temporibus Clodovei, & deinceps sub Carolo Martello, sub Pipino, & Carolo Magno, Ludovico Pio, de quo id postea ex antiquo isti us aevi Scriptore refert, quod mandavit filio Pipino, per Armoldum Abbatem, res Ecclesiasticas, quae in regno ejus erant, quas vel ipse suis attribuerat, vel ipsi sibi praeripuerant, absque cunctatione Ecclesiis restitui. Tum sub Carolo Calvo Rege, Ludovico Balbo, ejusque filiis, & aliis, quam male saepe Ecclesiasticorum bona a laicis (uti vocant) usurpata fuerint, & notatum id ab historicis sit, vir in antiquitate Ecclesiastica bene versatus, profert. Quae neutiquam infringit, quod non leguntur Galliae Reges vel Imperatores eo nomine anathemate fuisse percussos a Romano Pontifice, quo modo is quidem postea sua fulmina violentius detorsit in Henricum IV. Nam non illo adhuc tempore audebat id in Reges vel Imperatores Papa, quod postea in Henricum IV. nec ab intermisso Pontificis anathemate bene quis probet, jure egisse hac in re Principes, ob quam tum a Theologis, tum a variis Galliae conciliis reprehensos eos fuisse, satis constat. Deinde apud Filesacum observo, quod jam antea quoque notavi, in negotio bonorum Ecclesiasticorum a Veteribus, sub pauperum nomine, saepe comprehendi etiam Clericos. Ita quidem ille, pag. mihi 838. units.tr: Thus Gerhard. The Papists' complaint against us is a familiar one: that ecclesiastical goods are held and consumed by our people for private and profane uses. So Rovenius, in his treatise on the Missions, part 4: "You will find that many of them, as he says, unjustly possess certain goods, especially ecclesiastical ones, or offices or benefices." We deny that most of our people do this, and if anyone does, he certainly acts against the plain and unanimous rule of our doctrine. For we know that the last wills of testators and the gifts of donors must be kept according to the wishes of those who give, and nowhere more religiously than in pious and ecclesiastical causes. Natural law and religion alike teach and confirm this. The law of the Twelve Tables says: "As a man has bequeathed his property, so let the law stand." In the canon law, 13 qu. 11 cap. 4: "The last will of a deceased person must be kept in every way, especially in pious testaments, when something is bequeathed to the Church or to the poor." 11 qu. 11 throughout; and 16 qu. c.; similarly c. quia; and c. possessiones. Add Tiraquellus, the book on privileges in pious causes. The reason is that God forbade so severely, and punished so harshly, the plundering and profaning of goods consecrated to his worship or to the Church. See Josh. 7; Prov. 20:15; Dan. 5:2-3; Joel 3:5, 12. If a man takes the revenues, it is a crime; but if he gives them to the poor or ransoms captives, it is mercy. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, letter 269: "But you, acting entirely to the contrary, impiously and wickedly gather the goods of the Church and of the poor into your house. Put an end, therefore, to this impiety." The same, book 3 of his letters. In the works of Jerome, volume 4, page 322, there occurs a letter to Pope Damasus, on not claiming the bread of the oblations for any private or lay uses: The competent witnesses whom I have called to confirm this matter are these: Gregory Nazianzen, the admirable teacher Cyril, Athanasius, Theophilus, Anatolius, Chrysostom, Eustathius, Eusebius the chronographer, and our Hilary. All of them, with one voice and by one consensus, as true instruments of the Holy Spirit, judge that those who have applied the bread of the oblations to lay uses are to be struck with the sword of anathema, because it is due solely to the priests. Our Fathers decreed this not only about the bread in the Church but about everything that is offered on the altar, teaching again and again that it is a great wickedness, and done with diabolical rashness wherever it happens, and that it is wholly intolerable for the holy Church that it should remain unpunished by the penalty of the sacred canons. Gregory Thaumaturgus, canonical letter, chapter 3, letter 3: Did not Achan, the son of Zerah, sin in what was dedicated to God, and did not wrath come upon the whole synagogue of Israel? Yet he alone sinned, but he did not die alone in his sin. For us, indeed, whatever is not ours but another's must be regarded from this time on as gain dedicated to God. For that Achan took from the spoil, and now these men also take from the spoil: he took what belonged to the enemies, but those who now exist take what belongs to the brothers, making a gain that brings ruin. On this passage Theodore Balsamon, in his Scholia: Note that this canon is aimed at those who seize the property of churches and monasteries and, to speak once for all, who claim as their own what is dedicated to God. There are many things on this matter in the Capitularies of Charlemagne and his sons. Book 1, chapter 48, from the Council of Gangra: that it be permitted to no one to seize or defraud the offerings which pertain to the poor. Chapter 83: We decree that in the times of ourselves, of our sons, and of our successors, whom God shall grant, who wish to imitate our will or the example of our forebears, no division or loss of it shall suffer at all. Book 2, chapter 32. Book 5, chapter 187. Book 6, chapter 89. We command that no one, whether layman or cleric, shall seek, covet, or receive from the estates or goods that belong to the sees of bishops, or from those church goods which are known to lie in their parishes, without the order or consent of the bishops to whose care they belong, whoever they may be: lest the fire of the holy things that is in them burn the greedy more fiercely in ashes. Of the same book, chapters 109, 113, 116, 296, 301, 303, 305. Whatever of these things can furnish praise to God, or support the holy Church of God and its priests, or ornament for the Lord and the Church, whether they are offered freely by anyone, are without doubt consecrated to the Lord and belong to the right of the priests. And since we truly acknowledge that Christ and the Church are one person, whatever belongs to the Church belongs to Christ. And whatever is offered to the Church, in the aforesaid kinds or in any kinds, whether by pledges, by promises, by writings, or by bodily things, is offered to Christ; and whatever is alienated or taken from his Church by any device, whether by alienating, laying waste, invading, diminishing, or plundering, is taken from Christ. Chapter 320: since we have been instructed by the holy Fathers that this is recognised as a most grave sin, as the holy Scripture attests, which says: "Whoever has taken anything from his father or mother, and says it is no sin, is a partner in murder." Our Father without doubt is God, who created us; our mother is the Church, which has spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore whoever defrauds, seizes, lays waste, or alienates the money of Christ and of the Church will be judged a murderer before the sight of the righteous judge. Of this one of the wise men says: whoever takes the money of his neighbour commits iniquity, but whoever takes the money of the Church commits sacrilege. Chapters 322 and 323. It must be known by all that sacrilege is the seizing, in any way unjustly, of the property of the Church from those churches to which it is rightfully due, and its transfer to another use. Book 7, chapter 105. For many regions... Stata fuerunt, that is, the invasions, devastations, alienations, and vexations of the property of the Churches, and the oppressions of priests and of the other servants of God, or whatever injuries, which have been declared unlawful, and adulteries, or sodomitical lust, or intermingling with prostitutes, were established; and in secular war they did not stand firm, nor did they remain steadfast in faith; and how the Lord promised that avenging punishments would come upon the perpetrators of such crimes, through the Saracens and other peoples, and that they would serve them, is clear to all who read their deeds. Unless we guard ourselves against these things, we doubt not that similar things will come upon us, for God is the avenger of all these things. Likewise chapters 146, 151, 188, 199, 290. We have pursued these matters the more diligently from those chapters because from them chiefly John Filesac, a Parisian theologian, put together his commentary on lay sacrilege, or the complaint of the old Gallican Church about ecclesiastical benefices and goods, and their revenues, badly occupied and usurped by laymen, already from the times of Clovis, and thereafter under Charles Martel, under Pepin, and under Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. Of him, a writer of that ancient age reports that he ordered his son Pepin, through Abbot Arnold, that the ecclesiastical goods which were in his kingdom, whether he himself had assigned them to his own people or they had seized them for themselves, be restored to the Churches without delay. Then under King Charles the Bald, Louis the Stammerer, his sons, and others, the historians note how often the goods of the clergy were badly usurped by laymen (as they are called). A man well versed in ecclesiastical antiquity brings this forward. This by no means weakens the point that we do not read of the Kings or Emperors of Gaul being struck with anathema by the Roman Pontiff on that account, in the way that he later hurled his thunderbolts more violently against Henry IV. For at that time the Pope did not yet dare to do against kings or emperors what he later did against Henry IV, nor can anyone well prove, from the anathema of a pontiff that was not lasting, that the princes acted rightly in this matter; it is well established that they were rebuked for it both by theologians and by various councils of Gaul. Next, in Filesac I observe what I have already noted before, that in the matter of ecclesiastical goods the Ancients, under the name of the poor, often included even the clergy. Thus he writes, on page 838 of my edition: Not without reason did these bishops, when they had called the goods of the Church the patrimony of the poor, assign them partly to the clergy, partly to the other needy, by which they signified that there are two kinds of poor in the Church. Of the first kind are the clergy themselves, who are devoted to the divine ministry, and for whom care must first be taken. So the Roman Synod under Pope Symmachus judges.

units.la: K tim caeteris egentibus assignarunt, quo pauperes duplicis generis esse in Ecclesia significarunt. Prioris generis sunt ipsi Clerici, qui divino ministerio sunt mancipati, quorum in primis cura habenda fit. Ita censet Synodus Romana, sub Symmacho Papa. De donis autem sanctorum, id est, Catholicorum virorum, vel matronarum, qua osseruntur Ecclesiis Dei, pascantur pauperes spiritu, id est, servi Dei, & cuncti Ecclesiastici ordinis, degentes caste & pie sub regula Christi. Idem, ut hoc obiter quoque addam, adversus illos, qui dum audiunt vel legunt, bona Ecclesiae pauperum vocari, & pauperibus quidem potissimum bona olim dici data fuisse, inde putant, Clericos a bonorum istorum usu protinus abigendos esse, quod praeterquam parum esset, ut ex manifesta distinctione pauperum bona pauperibus, & Clericorum his vendicaremus, scire tamen oportet, antiquitus sub pauperibus, etiam Clericos comprehensos fuisse, qui hic eodem fere cum pauperibus censu veniebant: uti hoc quoque habet Martinus ab Azpilcueta, Doctor Navarrus, Apolog. de Redit. Eccles. pag. 331. Moneo, dixisse me in praefato libello, num. 10. per pauperes in hoc proposito de dando superflua redituum ecclesiae pauperibus, non solum intelligi personas inopes, sed etiam ecclesias & monasteria tam saecularia, quam regularia, & alia omnia loca & opera pia. Caeterum Concilii Meldensis Patres, apud Baronium, Tom. xi. ad A. cI.5 ccxlv. sic loquuntur peccata enim populi comedunt, qui contra auctoritatem divinam, & nec intercessionis ope, nec praedicationis consilio, vel quocunque divino auxilio pro peccatis eorum qui ea dederant, laborant, nec pio operi ad quod fideles fidelium eas tradiderat, servire permittunt. De quo periculoso facto, vos Principes Christianissimi venerabiliter admonemus, & devotissime obsecramus, ut memores salutis vestrae praesentis scilicet & aeternae; memores etiam largitatis progenitorum vestrorum erga sanctas Ecclesias, propter quam feliciter regnaverunt, & sibi contrarios superaverunt. Etiam Leges civiles injustam pronunciant bonorum ecclesiasticorum alienationem, vel in prosanos usus applicationem. Est autem alienatio, dicunt: omnis actus, per quem dominium transferti. C.de fund. donat.l. 1. & D.de verb. signif. lxvii. alienatum non proprie dicitur, quod adhuc in dominio venditoris manet. Unde in Sexto Decret. post titulum, de non alien. reb. Eccles. (subjungitur tit. de rerum permut. Atque in Extravag. Comm. titulus de emptione & vendit. In Capitularibus Caroli M. vel potius Ludovici F. lib. II. c. xxix. Alienationis autem verbum continet venditionem, donationem, permutationem, & Emphyteuseos perpetuum contractum: sed omnes omnino sacerdotes hujusmodi alienatione abstineant. Videri possunt praeterquam Iuris Institut. lib. II. tit. I. §. 8. quae etiam per nostram constitutionem alienari & obligari prohibemus: excepta causa redemtionis captivorum: loquitur de rebus sacris, ut appellant, quamvis temere ita, a Pontificali nempe consecratione, dictis, verum hoc nisi sermo est, de aedibus, & donariis, quae ad ministerium Dei dedicata sunt. Adde Novell. vii. de non alienandis aut permutandis rebus Ecclesiasticis. Novell. iii. c. 3. Novell. xlvi. De Ecclesiasticarum rerum immobilium alienatione & solutione. Novell. cxx. de alienatione & emphyteusi rerum Ecclesiae: quibus alienatio rerum Ecclesiae prohibetur. Hac Novell. c. vii. Et quoniam cognovimus ab aliquibus fieri alienationes monasteriorum, ut haec a sacra figura in privatorum conversationem transferantur, & hoc omnibus modis prohibemus. Item C.de Sacro S. Eccles. l. Privilegia l. jubemus. l. privilegia magna Eccles. l. Sancimus nemini. l. Constantinopolitana. C. De sepulchro violato. l. Res religioni destinatas D. de contrah. emtione l. & liberi. de his quae non sunt in commercio. l. xxii, Si quid sacri vel religiosi est, ejus venit nihil. l. si in emptione. l. qui officii causa. l. Pacta conventa. Adde Imp. Manuelis Commeni conflit. cap. ix. & Alexii C omneni. Non haec eo faciunt, quasi putem nunquam licitam esse bonorum Ecclesiasticorum alienationem, quod non ipsi Canones simpliciter volunt, eam in casibus aliquibus concedentes & probantes; sed ut ostendam, nos jure alienissimos esse a bonorum Ecclesiasticorum, eorumque (incontulta & invita Ecclesia) direptione, profanatione, & in usus privatos applicatione: ut immerito Papistae nobis hic objiciant istorum midireptionem aut profanationem, vel ejus à nobis susceptum patrocinium, vel Papa in sua Bullâ justam inde petat causam & occasionem, propter bona Ecclesiastica quasi à nobis non in Ecclesiasticos usus impensa, pacem Germaniæ inquietandi, irritandiq;e. Constans quippe Reformatorum hæc est doctrina, seu Lutheranorum, seu Reformatorum, Theologorum ac Iurisconsultorum, bona in pios usus data, isthuc, & non in privatos profanosq; applicanda esse. Sic Lutherus, de quo jam ex Iohanne Gerhardi audivimus; eftq; apud Ioh. Conradi Damhauwerum Disp.xvi. in Decal.ad viii, preg. Præterea Tom. ii. Ienensi Lutherus, in Consilio wie die geistlichen guter zu handeln sind/A.cl.ɔ.xxiii. Aber die dritter weise ist die beste/ dass man alles andere zum gemeinen gut eines gemeinen Kastens gelangen/ daraus man nach Christlicher liebe/ gebe/ und leibeallen die im lande durfftig sind/ es sey ebel oberbuerget/ damit man auch der Stiffter testament vnd willen erfullen. Den wie wol sie geiret vnd verfuret sind/ dass sie es zu Kloster geben haben/ ist dennoch ja jr meynung gewesen/ Gott zu ehren/ und zu dienst geben/ und das den also fellet. Dan ist kein grosser Gottesdienst/ denn Christlich liebe die den Durfftigen hilft und dienet/ wie Christus am jungsten tage selbs wird bekennen Math. 25. Daher auch vorzeiten der Kirchen guter bona Ecclesiastica, das ist/gemeine guter hiesen/ wie ein gemeinen Kasten/ fur alle die unter den Christen durfftig waren. atque ad illam normam Reformatio Ecclesiarum juxta ac bonorum instituta & præscripta fuit. Hoc Zuinglins apud Tigurinos egit: cujus consilio, Reditus Ecclesiastici quoque vel ministris ordinabantur Ecclesiarum, vel bonarum literarum doctoribus, vel reliquis sacerdotum & monachorum, vel pauperibus. Erant inter illos juvenes ingeniosi non pauci, quibus pietatis magis placebant studia: hi tales retenti, ad usus Ecclesiarum Tigurina ditionis fovebantur, & occasione oblata emittebantur. quemadmodum de eo scribit in vita Zuinglii, Melchior Adamus. Idemque refert in præfat. Historia Sacramentaria, Rodolphus Hospinianus, ubi historiam reformationis Ecclesiæ Tigurinæ breviter ennarrat. neq;; quod hic ait, post expensa in pauperes, & Ministros, & Scholas bona, siquid supereft, id publicis servari necessitatibus & calamitatibus levandis, bona illa extra usus suos debitos, & pios, & contra naturam ipsorum impendi, vel usurpari à laicis, significat.
units.tr: partly to the rest of the needy, and in this way they indicated that there are two kinds of poor in the Church. The first kind are the clergy themselves, who are devoted to the divine ministry and for whom care should above all be taken. So the Roman Synod under Pope Symmachus judges. But from the gifts of the saints, that is, of Catholic men or matrons, which are offered to the Churches of God, let the poor in spirit be fed, that is, the servants of God and all of the ecclesiastical order, who live chastely and piously under the rule of Christ. The same author, to add this in passing, speaks against those who, when they hear or read that the goods of the Church are called goods of the poor, and that goods were formerly given chiefly to the poor, therefore think that the clergy must at once be driven from the use of those goods. Although it would be of little use to claim the goods for the poor and the clergy for themselves on the basis of a clear distinction between the poor, we must know that in ancient times the clergy too were included under the name of the poor, since they came under about the same assessment as the poor. Martin of Azpilcueta, Doctor Navarrus, also holds this in his Apology on Ecclesiastical Revenues, p. 331: I advise that I said in the aforementioned little book, number 10, that by the poor, in this proposal about giving the surplus of church revenues to the poor, are understood not only needy persons but also churches and monasteries, both secular and regular, and all other places and pious works. Moreover, the Fathers of the Council of Meaux, as cited by Baronius, Tom. xi, ad A. 845, ccxlv, speak thus: For they devour the sins of the people, who, contrary to divine authority, and neither by the help of intercession nor by the counsel of preaching, nor by any divine aid whatever, labour for the sins of those who gave them, nor allow them to be devoted to the pious work for which the faithful handed them over to the faithful. Concerning this dangerous deed we, most Christian princes, earnestly admonish you and most devoutly beseech you, to remember your salvation, both present and eternal; to remember also the generosity of your forefathers towards the holy Churches, on account of which they reigned happily and overcame their adversaries. The civil laws also declare the alienation of ecclesiastical goods, or their application to profane uses, to be unjust. Now alienation, they say, is every act by which ownership is transferred. Code, On the foundation of gifts, law 1; and Digest, On the meaning of words, 67: That is not properly said to be alienated which still remains in the seller's ownership. Hence in the Sixth Decretal, after the title On not alienating church property, follows the title On the exchange of things; and in the Extravagantes Communes is the title On buying and selling. In the Capitularies of Charlemagne, or rather of Louis the Son, book 2, chapter 29: The word alienation includes sale, donation, exchange, and the perpetual contract of emphyteusis; but let all priests altogether abstain from such alienation. One may also consult the Institutes, book 2, title 1, §8: which we also forbid to be alienated or encumbered by our constitution, except for the cause of redeeming captives. This speaks of sacred things, as they call them, although rashly so called from their pontifical consecration; but this is true only if the reference is to buildings and gifts dedicated to the ministry of God. Add Novel 7, On not alienating or exchanging ecclesiastical things; Novel 3, chapter 3; Novel 46, On the alienation and payment of immovable ecclesiastical things; Novel 120, On the alienation and emphyteusis of church property, by which the alienation of church property is forbidden. From this Novel, chapter 7: And since we have learned that some make alienations of monasteries, so that these are transferred from their sacred purpose to private use, we forbid this in every way. Likewise in the Code, On the sacred and holy church, the laws Privilegia, Jubemus, Privilegia magna Ecclesiae, Sancimus nemini, Constantinopolitana; in the Code, On the violated sepulchre, the law Res religioni destinatas; in the Digest, On contracting for purchase, and the law Liberi, On those things which are not in commerce, law 22: If anything is sacred or religious, nothing of it is sold; the law Si in emptione, the law Qui officii causa, the law Pacta conventa. Add the Constitution of the Emperor Manuel Comnenus, chapter 9, and of Alexius Comnenus. I do not say these things as though I thought that the alienation of ecclesiastical goods was never lawful, since the Canons themselves do not simply will this, but allow and approve it in certain cases. Rather, I want to show that we are altogether far removed, by law, from the plundering, profanation, and application to private uses of ecclesiastical goods, done without consultation and against the will of the Church. So the Papists wrongly object to us here the plundering or profanation of these goods, or our patronage of them, and the Pope in his Bull seeks from this a just cause and occasion for disturbing and annulling the peace of Germany on account of church goods, as if they had been applied by us not to ecclesiastical uses. For this is the constant doctrine of the Reformed, whether of the Lutherans or of the Reformed, of theologians and jurists alike: that goods given for pious uses must be applied to those uses, and not to private and profane ones. So Luther, of whom we have already heard from John Gerhard; and it is also found in Johann Conrad Dannhauer, Disputation 16, on the Eighth Commandment, page 8. Moreover, in the Jena edition, vol. 2, Luther, in his counsel How ecclesiastical goods are to be handled, 1523: "But the third way is the best: that all the other goods be brought into a common chest of the commonwealth, from which, out of Christian love, one gives and provides for all in the land who are in need, whether they be noble or common, so that the will and testament of the founders may also be fulfilled. For although they were deceived and misled into giving them to the monasteries, their intention was nonetheless to honour God and to give in his service, and that is what happens. For there is no greater service of God than Christian love which helps and serves the needy, as Christ himself will confess on the last day, Matt. 25. Therefore also in former times the goods of the Church, that is, common goods, were called like a common chest for all who among Christians were in need." And according to this norm the reform of the Churches and of their goods was instituted and prescribed. This Zwingli did among the Zurichers, by whose counsel the church revenues were also assigned either to the ministers of the churches, or to the teachers of good letters, or to the rest of the priests and monks, or to the poor. There were among those not a few gifted young men, who were more pleased by the studies of piety; such men, when retained, were supported for the use of the churches of the Zurich district, and when an opportunity offered they were sent out. as Melchior Adam writes of him in the life of Zwingli. Rudolf Hospinian also reports the same in the preface to his Sacramentarian History, where he briefly recounts the history of the reformation of the Zurich Church. Nor does what he says here, that after the goods have been spent on the poor, the ministers, and the schools, whatever remains is to be kept for public needs and to relieve calamities, mean that those goods are spent or seized by laymen outside their proper and pious uses and contrary to their nature.

units.la: Hoc enim si fiat, aperte damnat idem Auctor, de Templis, lib. v. de Origine bonorum Ecclesiasticorum, in fine quando inquit: Hac propterea pluribus commemoro ut intelligant pontifices, quam iniquè Christiani Principes & magistratus, qui bonorum & reddituum Ecclesiasticorum abusus, ad normam verbi Dei, & canonum Conciliorum primitiva Ecclesia, in ordinem redegerint, furti sacrilegiique, hactenus accusati fuerint: quum ipsi interim ter sacrilegi iis per fas & nefas ad omne scelus pro libidine sua abutantur. Licet Euangelicorum nonnullos etiam non omni culpa liberare velim, qui primum bona Ecclesiastica sibi vendicarunt ceu sua, iisque partim latam sibi faciunt ditionem, partim arces atque aedificia struunt, partim thesauros augent, negletis interim aut parcè habitis ministris ecclesiarum & pauperibus. Deinde œconomos iis praficiunt duros simul ac rigidos, qui malint derogare quam erogare. Sed reddent hi infideles dispensatores Domino bonorum istorum gravissimam in die judicii ultimi rationem. Nempe Principes & magistratus bona illa non fisco attribuendo, sed ad normam verbi Dei, & canonum Ecclesiasticorum errogando, laudabiles se praestant, atque à Pontificiorum calumnia immunes. Nonnullos vero alios, qui bona Ecclesiastica sibi vendicant, ceu sua, culpabiles dicit: & non modo in hoc, quod illis in luxum utuntur, ad arces domosque struendas, neglectis Ministris. Quibus neque id adversatur, quod ultimo dicit, de decimis, aliisque bonis Ecclesiasticis, è manibus laicorum, qui illas emerint &c. ad parochias non transferendis, nisi precibus & pecuniis redimantur: sic enim & redimi illas, & atiisficri aliqua solum ratione possessoribus suadet. Philippus Melanthon, in Consil. Theolog. ita semper docuit, bona Ecclesiastica, ad usus Ecclesiasticos applicanda, Papalia reformanda, atque in usum pristinum, bonum eum ac salutarem postliminio reducenda esle: secus si fieret, damnabat. Praeter id, quod antea ex eo adduximus, Consil.part. II. pag. 186, de facto Laurentii, mortem potius oppetendam, quam tradendam Imperatori pecuniam Ecclesiae existimantis, sic judicat: Non injuria igitur Divus Laurentius je ei opposuit. Nam in manifestis injuriis Magistratui non est indulgendum, præsertim si salus Ecclesiæ, & gloria Dei agatur. Quare recte fecisse Divum Laurentium judico, quod in hac re Imperatori est adversatus. Quod cum ita sit, facilè intelligi poterit, quo in scelere sint nostris temporibus avari Pontifices, Canonici, & similes, qui non solum bona Ecclesiarum ad se rapiunt, sed etiam de iis turpissimè helluantur, eaque conferunt non ad profanos usus tantum, sed etiam ad delendum & opprimendum Euangelium. Et crudeliter faciunt centauri, qui manus injiciunt talibus Ecclesiæ bonis, non ad se pertinentibus, unde pauperes scholastici & pii Pastores ad conservationem ministerii ali debebant. Hos cum patiantur esurire, ut ipsi suum luxum expleant, proculdubio Deus olim gravissimas pœnas hujus rapacitatis ab eis exiget. Idem, pag.144. ad quæst: An pater pius, & vere amplexus Euangelium possit petere reditus ex sacerdotio Collegii Canonicorum, pro studiis filii, & an fruens talibus reditibus peccet? ita respondet: Primum, si filius obligatur, ut pro ipso alius celebret usitatas ipsis Missas, aut addatur alia impia obligatio, manifestum est, nequaquam tales obligationes recipiendas esse, & fugiendas collegia & reditus, si requiratur ullam impiam obligationem, juxta regulam, fugite idola. Secundo, si nulla addatur impia obligatio, petere eos reditus, & frui illis reditibus, res licita & concessa est. Imo hæc ipsa bona sunt initio à Regibus ad hunc principalem usum ordinata, ut sint docentium & discentium stipendia, seu alimenta. Hoc certissimum est. Nec ideo reditus ipsi, frumenta, pecuniæ, sunt res male, quia antea tenuerunt impii. Sicut vasa Ægyptiorum non erant res malæ, etiamsi Ægyptii fuerant impii. Ac pie Israelitis licuit ut illis vasis. Ita universa rerum natura condita est ad usus piorum, & propter eos. Quanquam igitur sæpe impii plurimis rebus magis fruuntur, tamen ubi conceditur, licet pius frui eisdem rebus: sicut videmus emtionibus, venditionibus, donationibus, locationibus, & aliis contractibus, resipsas, & earum usum transferri. Parte 1. Consil. Theol. ubi de constituenda Academia Lipsica: Cum autem jam mutentur monasteria, rectissimum est, ut bona rursus transferantur ad juvandas Ecclesias & scholas, ac ad alendos pastores & pauperes scholasticos: Nemo militat suis stipendiis, inquit Paulus, & hæc opes data sunt Ecclesiis, ut sint stipendia docentium & discentium. Idem clamitant veteres Canones. Ideo boni viri, & potentes in Republica annitantur omnibus viribus, ut ex opibus monachorum, quantum obtineri potest, constituantur parochia & scholae. Saepe soleo per jocum recitare veterem versiculum de his, qui accusati in judiciis, praedam dividebant cum judicibus, ut se redimerent. Sententia versiculi haec est: Qui multa furatus est, & pauca dat judici, elabitur. Ὁ πολλὰ κλέψας ἐλλίγα δὲ ςῶ ἀποδῶ ξειτω. Sic de his direptionibus monasteriorum interdum dico: Eos qui tenent illas possessiones, si saltem pauca deciderent ad Ecclesias & scholas juvandas, veniam sperare posse. Ceteris prosecto nullo modo ignoscendum est, qui devoratis his opibus sinunt pastores cum familiis fame perire, scholas deseri, extingui literarum studia.
units.tr: If this were done, the same author would plainly condemn it in his book On Temples, book 5, On the Origin of Ecclesiastical Goods, near the end, where he says: I mention these matters at length so that the pontiffs may understand how unjustly Christian princes and magistrates have hitherto been accused of theft and sacrilege for bringing the abuses of ecclesiastical goods and revenues back into order, according to the norm of God's Word and the canons of the Councils of the primitive Church; while those very men, thrice sacrilegious, meanwhile misuse those goods, rightly or wrongly, for every crime at their pleasure. I would not, however, wish to free from all blame some of the Evangelicals too, who first claimed ecclesiastical goods for themselves as if they were their own, and with them partly made for themselves wider domains, partly build citadels and buildings, partly enlarge their treasuries, while meanwhile the ministers of the churches and the poor are neglected or sparingly provided for. Then they set over these goods stewards who are hard and rigid at once, who would rather withhold than pay out. But these unfaithful stewards will render to the Lord of these goods a most grievous account on the day of the final judgment. Clearly, by directing those goods not to the fisc but to the needs of the Church according to the norm of God's Word and the canons, princes and magistrates show themselves praiseworthy and immune from the calumny of the Papists. He calls culpable, however, some others who claim ecclesiastical goods as their own, and not only for this, that they spend them on luxury, on building citadels and houses while the ministers are neglected. Nor does what he says at the end conflict with this, about tithes and other ecclesiastical goods, which are not to be transferred from the hands of laymen who bought them to the parishes, unless they are redeemed with prayers and money; for he advises that they be redeemed, and that the possessors be satisfied, only in some way. Philip Melanchthon, in his Theological Opinions, always taught this: that ecclesiastical goods are to be applied to ecclesiastical uses, that Papal arrangements are to be reformed, and that those goods are to be restored by right of return to their former, good and wholesome use; and if it were otherwise, he condemned it. Besides what we cited from him above, in Opinions, part 2, p. 186, concerning the deed of Laurence, who thought he should rather meet death than hand over the Church's money to the Emperor, he judges thus: Not without reason, therefore, did St. Laurence oppose him. For one must not be indulgent to magistrates in manifest injuries, especially when the salvation of the Church and the glory of God are at stake. Wherefore I judge that St. Laurence acted rightly in opposing the Emperor in this matter. This being so, it can easily be understood in what crime greedy pontiffs, canons and the like are in our times, who not only seize the goods of the churches for themselves, but also feast most shamefully on them, and apply them not merely to profane uses but also to destroying and crushing the Gospel. And the centaurs act cruelly who lay hands on such goods of the Church, which do not belong to them, from which poor scholars and pious ministers ought to be supported for the maintenance of the ministry. Since they allow these to go hungry so that they may satisfy their own luxury, God will undoubtedly one day exact most grievous punishments from them for this rapacity. The same author, p. 144, in answer to the question whether a pious father who has truly embraced the Gospel may seek revenues from a canonry's priesthood to pay for his son's studies, and whether one who enjoys such revenues sins, answers thus: First, if the son is bound to have another celebrate the customary Masses on his behalf, or some other impious obligation is added, it is clear that such obligations are by no means to be accepted, and that colleges and revenues are to be shunned if any impious obligation is required, according to the rule: flee idols. Second, if no impious obligation is added, to seek those revenues and enjoy them is a lawful and permitted thing. Indeed these very goods were at the start ordained by kings for this principal use, that they might be the stipends or sustenance of teachers and learners. This is most certain. Nor are the revenues themselves, the grain and money, bad things because the impious once held them. Just as the vessels of the Egyptians were not bad things, even though the Egyptians were impious; and it was lawful for the Israelites to use those vessels piously. So the whole nature of things was created for the use of the pious, and on their account. Although, therefore, the impious often enjoy most things more, yet where it is permitted, the pious may enjoy the same things; just as we see that the things themselves, and their use, are transferred by purchases, sales, gifts, leases and other contracts. Part 1 of the Theological Opinions, where he speaks of establishing the Academy at Leipzig: Now that the monasteries are being dissolved, it is most right that the goods be transferred again to help the Churches and schools, and to support ministers and poor scholars: "No one serves as a soldier at his own expense," says Paul, and these resources were given to the Churches so that they may be the stipends of teachers and learners. The old canons cry out the same. Therefore good men and those powerful in the commonwealth should strive with all their strength that parishes and schools be established, as far as can be obtained, from the wealth of the monks. I often recite in jest the old little verse about those accused in court who divided the booty with the judges so as to buy their release. The sense of the verse is this: "He who has stolen much and gives a little to the judge gets away." Ὁ πολλὰ κλέψας, ὀλίγα δὲ τῷ κριτῇ ἀποδοὺς ἐξελθέτω. So I sometimes say of these plunderings of the monasteries: that those who hold those possessions may hope for pardon if at least they gave up a little to help the Churches and schools. But certainly no pardon is to be granted to the rest, who, having devoured these resources, allow the ministers and their families to perish of hunger, the schools to be deserted, and the study of letters to be extinguished.

units.la: Ibidem Theologi Wittembergenses, Iustus Ionas, Philip. Melanthon, Nic. Amsdorffius, & Iohannes Doltz, ad quaestiones aliquot, ex aula Electoris ad ipsos missas, inter quas & haec erat: Quarto, Cum plerumque templa & monasteria, ad missarum celebrationem extructa & fundata sint, fore ut cessante causa, simul & cessaret effectus, hoc est, ut ad illum finem destinata & legata, simul intercideren t, sicque monasteriis & templis debiti reditus, pensionesque adimerentur. ita respondent: De fundationibus, & quando praesentes missae introductae sint, de quibus habent III. & IV. articuli, satis constat, collegia vetera, monasteria & templa initio non fundata, constituta, regiisque opibus locupletata fuisse, ad lectionem missarum, vel horarum canonicarum deblaterationem, absque fructu & utilitate Ecclesiae ac fidei Christianae, quod nunc fere fit, sed potius, ut juventus in sacra scriptura & religionis doctrina erudiretur, Itaque vetera collegia coenobia, & dioeceses fuerunt scholae juvenum Christianorum, usque ad Augustini, imo Bernhardi aetatem. Ad hunc finem omnia bona, facultatesque Ecclesiastica legata & donata fuerunt, ut inde stipendia, & quasi pramia laborum darentur pastoribus, doctoribusque Ecclesiarum, & sustentarentur tenues scholastici, aliique pauperes: Quod veterum historiarum monumenta perspicue indicant. Tum, quamvis sciant, quod recentes fundationes collegiorum aut coenobiorum, ab annis quadringentis aut quingentis fere omnes missarum & cantionum usitatarum causa constitutae, mamagnificeque (quod apparet) auɬɬa sunt. Nec ideo violantur injuriæ afficiuntur jura donationum illarum , quia autores earum ab impiis sacrificulis persuasi ac decepti , putarunt se iis fundationibus, sibi, suaque familia & posteritati rem profuturam ad salutem animarum instituere, qui profecto si revocarentur in vitam, damnarent ipsi facilitatem , credulitatemque hac in re suam , cum viderent solummodo ad explendam sacerdotum avaritiam, & pecuniarum aucupia à sacerdotibus has donationes primum expetitas , aut postea translatas esse. Atque hæc ipsa sunt, ad quæ respicit Sleidanus, Comment.lib.iii. Eandem originem collegiorum Ecclesiasticorum, & Canonicorum assignat Melanthon, Consil.pag.515. Hæc quæstio jam agitari solet , cum Episcopi & Canonici, defensuri suum otium,voluptates,& impios ritus , allegant vetustatis judicium. Vera igitur antiquitas quarenda est. Satis constat, Prophetas olim habuisse cœtus discipulorum, Eliam , Elifæum, & similes, quibus enarrabant legem Dei, & promissiones divinas,& tradebant historias. Ad hæc studia alii alias bonas artes addebant. Hunc morem imitati sunt Iohannes Baptista & Christus. Ita duces Ecclesiæ semper scholasticos cœtus secum traxerunt. Et consentaneum est, vetustiora esse exempla huius rei. Atqsde collegiis Virginum, ubi de abusibus Ecclesiarum emendandis, aitabolerentur hac vota. Et tamè pauperibus puellis præsertim nobilibus, consulatur ex his reditibus, qui per certos quastores ad hos usus quotannis colligantur, & quodam ordine distribuantur. Nam in pagis aut locis desertis, virginum cœtus esse, non videtur utile, sed si placet aliqua monasteria virginum converti in scholas puellarum nobilium & aliarum, id fiat in urbibus, ubi est honesta disciplina. Et præsint, honestæ, piæ & graves matronæ. Tales scholas aliquas puellarum esse sine ullis vinculis votorum optandum esset, in quibus nobilium filiæ & aliæ puellæ discerent literas, & doctrinam Euangelii, & assuefierent ad ipsa exercitia & bonos mores,nuptura cum vellent. Pezelius, ad illa, ex Melanthone adduƈta, part.vii. Argum. & Resp. pag. 325. Qua Ecclesia olim donata sunt liberalitate piorum Principum,eas donationes perpetuo valere dubium non est, dum finis servatur, videlicet, ut donata Ecclesiæ ad pias caussas referan-tur, tur, sicut eo referri debent. De quo notum est dictum vulgare: Quod semel dicatum est Domino, ad profanos usus amplius non est transferendum. Nec ad bona monasteriis & Ecclesiis relicta extendi debet, quod l.5. C. de pagan. Loca & bona, Ethnicorum sacris attributa, fisco vendicantur. Illa enim daemonis dedicata fuerunt, ut Paulus ad Corinth. ostendit, quae fiscus quasi vacantia quoquo modo potest occupare. At haec Deo & Ecclesiae Christianae consecrata sunt. Quae quanquam ante haec tempora magnis tenebris fuit oppressa, hoc tamen non ad ejus depredationem valere debet, sed eo, ut quae ad impios usus Ecclesiae relicta sunt, in pios convertantur. De quo qui volunt consilium Schurffii videre possunt, cent. 1. Conf. 48. Caeterum in aulis, à quibus occupantur bona Ecclesiastica, hac specie, quod ad Ecclesiae & Scholarum usum conferri oporteat; fere idem accidit, quod in Apologo narratur de quodam viatore egente ac esuriente, qui in itinere orabat Mercurium, ut sibi offerret aliquid mercium, quas in via alicubi relictas invenire posset. Pollicebatur etiam se dimidium templo illius dedicaturum esse. Tum pergit viator dicta prece, bona cum spe. Cumque jam stadium unum atque alterum emensus esset, invenit plenos calathos amygdalarum & palmularum. Etsi aviditati viatoris ac spei non respondebat hoc munus, tamen recte sapienter, quod dicitur: ὀτι ᾧ τις, ἰσαίνει, Boni consulit mercem, nullo quaesitam sumptu ac labore. Properat igitur in forum, ut inde aliquid pecuniae lucretur. Sed properanti occurrit Mercurius, ac prius partiri pradam jubet. Hic callide rusticus memorem se promissorum inquit, ac dimidium daturum, videlicet amygdalarum putamina & palmularum nucleos. Hoc modo aula bona Ecclesiastica cum Ecclesiis & Scholis partiuntur. Idem p. 318. Certum est à piis Regibus & Principibus initio donatas esse Ecclesiis has opes, quas nunc tenent, propter hanc causam, ut ad sustentationem docentium ac discentium stipendia conferrentur. Nec fuerunt Collegia Canonicorum, imo & monasteria olim aliud, quam Schola, in quibus juventus erudiebatur, & fiebat doctrinae propagatio. Postea tanti abusus accesserunt, ut à seipsis prorsus degenerarint vetera illa collegia, quae etiamnum iis in locis, ubi Papatus regnat, ἱεροσυλία & officina videntur esse horribilis Idolatriae, foedissimarum libidinum, luxus & multorum scelerum. Vt autem Elias pascebatur à Corvis afferentibus ad eum panes & carnes, Sic ubi reformata sunt collegia, non est per se peccatum ad sumptum studiorum tolerandum, frui stipendiis, quibus alioqui Canonici multi abutuntur: Modo non accedat obligatio impia: Et illi qui ejusmodi sumptibus sustentantur, fungantur suo officio, & cogitent non ad officium, non ad luxum dari stipendia, sed pro labore studiorum, & ut Ecclesia consulatur. Calvinus, lib. de Necessit. Reformandæ Ecclesiæ: Similis impudentia est, quod diripi apud nos Ecclesiæ opes, & in profanos usus converti clamitant. Si nihil hic apud nos peccari dixero, mentiar. Et sane, raro tantæ rerum conversiones fiunt, quin secum trahant aliquid incommodi. Si quid igitur hic peccatum est, non excusso. Caeterum, qua fronte nobis crimen hoc adversarii intendunt? Ecclesiæ facultates in alienos usus convertere, sacrilegium esse dicunt. Assentior. Adjiciunt, fieri hoc à nobis. Excipio, nos minime subterfugere, quin pro nobis respondeamus: modo ipsi quoque ad causam discendam vicissim parati veniant. Mox igitur de nobis: interea videamus quid ipsi faciunt. Tum pag. seq. de Nostris respondens, ita ait: Hi sunt, qui inexpiabilis sacrilegii nostros principes accusant, quod patrimonium Ecclesiæ, Deo consecratum, rapuerint per vim & summam injuriam: & nunc in profanos usus dilapident. Iam quidem testatus sum, nolle me omnia, quæ apud nos fiunt, excusare: quin potius non majorem alicubi rationem haberi, ut in eos tantum usus impendantur Ecclesiæ reditus, quibus sunt dedicati, mihi displicere profiteor. Mecum etiam id gemunt omnes boni. Verum, hoc tantum in praesentia agitur: rapuerintne per sacrilegium Ecclesiæ bona principes nostri, cum ex sacerdotum & monachorum erepta manibus, ea ad se receperunt? Num quia aliorsum ea conferunt, quàm ad saginandos illos ventres, ideo ipsa profanant? Suam enim adversariis, non Christi, nec Ecclesiæ, causam agunt. Fateor certe, grave judicium pronunciari adversus eos, qui Ecclesiam polluaverint, ut sibi raperent quod illius erat. Sed ratio simul additur; quia veros ministros frandent suo victu: quia, pauperes fame necando, rei sint sanguinis. Hoc autem quid ad nostros adversarios? Et in libro de candalis, circa finem: Quoniam sacris opibus ditati sunt nonnulli, alii famem suam utcunque ad tempus fedarunt, nos prædandi magis cupidine, quam pio Dei Zelo ad res novandas adductos esse jactant Euangelii hostes: multi qui prætextum capiant repellendi Euangelii, maledicis illis vocibus us assentiuntur. Ego verò, siqui replendis suis crumenis Ecclesia bona prædati sunt, non excuso. Et libri nostri, quantopere abhorreamus ab ejusmodi sacrilegiis, diserti sunt testes. Verum, ut partis nostræ delictis, si qua sunt, patrocinium meum accommodare animus non est: ita calumnia non est ferenda, quod in prædam cessisse malevoli homines criminantur, quicquid fœdis illis gurgitibus, hoc est sacrificiis Baal & monachis ademptum est. Certe, ex quibus locis profligata est Papatus impietas, illic saltem pars eorum redituum, quos scorta, & lenones cum sacerdotibus vorabant, in pauperes erogatur: aliquanto plus impenditur in scholas, quam fieri solebat: aluntur veri Pastores, qui salutis doctrinam populo ministrant: sumptus quoque ad tuendum Ecclesiæ statum non pauci fiunt. Sacrilegium inquit, Ecclesiæ facultates in alienos usus convertere; atque nobis hoc objectum, omni modo satagit diluere, tantum abest, ut vel concedere velit, vel propugnare. Et in eos tantum usus impendendos Ecclesiæ reditus docet, quibus sunt dedicati: aliter si fiat, sibi id, juxta cum bonis omnibus, displicere attestatur. Domini enim est terra & plenitudo ejus, non hominum. Quicunque enim aliquid donavit Ecclesiæ, is imprimis Domino id obtulit & sanctificavit. Quod si cum Domino non est, neque etiam apud Christianos valere debet, quicquid tandem in bonis, Domini ordinaverit aut destinarit.
