units.tr: Likewise the Wittenberg theologians, Justus Jonas, Philip Melanthon, Nicholas Amsdorf and Johann Doltz, answered several questions sent to them from the Elector's court, among which was this: Fourthly, since churches and monasteries were for the most part built and founded for the celebration of Masses, it will follow that when the cause ceases the effect ceases too; that is, that the bequests and endowments made for that purpose will likewise lapse, and so the monasteries and churches will lose their due revenues and pensions. They answered thus: It is well established, from the foundations, and from the time when the present Masses were introduced, as the third and fourth articles state, that the old colleges, monasteries and churches were not at first founded, established and enriched with royal resources for the reading of Masses or the mumbling of the canonical hours, without fruit or benefit to the Church and the Christian faith, as now almost happens; but rather so that young people might be instructed in Holy Scripture and the doctrine of religion. Thus the old colleges, convents and dioceses were schools of Christian youth, down to the time of Augustine, indeed of Bernard. To this end all the goods and property bequeathed and given to the Church were intended, so that from them stipends, as it were rewards for labours, might be paid to the ministers and teachers of the churches, and poor students and other needy persons might be supported. The monuments of the old histories clearly show this. Then, although they know that the recent foundations of colleges or convents, nearly all made four or five hundred years ago for the sake of customary Masses and chants, have been magnificently (as is evident) endowed. Nor for this reason are the rights of those gifts violated or injured, because their authors, persuaded and deceived by impious priestlings, thought they were establishing something that would profit their own salvation, their families and their posterity; who, if they were called back to life, would certainly condemn their own ease and credulity in this matter, since they would see that these gifts were first sought by priests, or afterwards diverted, merely to satisfy the avarice of the priests and their pursuit of money. These are the very things to which Sleidan refers, Commentaries, book 3. The same origin of ecclesiastical and canonical colleges is assigned by Melanthon, Consilia, p. 515. This question is commonly raised when bishops and canons, defending their idleness, their pleasures and their impious rites, appeal to the judgement of antiquity. The true antiquity must therefore be sought. It is well established that the prophets once had gatherings of disciples, Elijah, Elisha and others like them, to whom they expounded the law of God and the divine promises, and taught histories. To these studies others added other good arts. John the Baptist and Christ imitated this custom. Thus the leaders of the Church have always drawn scholastic gatherings around themselves. And it is consistent that the examples of this are older. And concerning the colleges of virgins, where these vows are spoken of in the context of correcting the abuses of the churches. Yet provision is made, especially for poor girls, particularly noble ones, from these revenues, which are collected each year by certain treasurers for these uses and distributed in a certain order. For in villages or deserted places a gathering of virgins does not seem useful; but if it pleases anyone, some convents of virgins may be converted into schools for noble girls and others, and this should be done in cities where there is honest discipline, and where honest, pious and serious matrons preside. It would be desirable that there be schools of this kind for girls, without any bonds of vows, in which the daughters of nobles and other girls might learn letters and the doctrine of the Gospel, and be accustomed to the practices and good morals of their own sex, to be married when they wished. Pezelius, on these matters, quoting Melanthon, part 7, Argument and Response, p. 325. There is no doubt that the gifts once bestowed on the Church by the generosity of pious princes remain valid forever, provided the purpose is kept, namely that what has been given to the Church be referred to pious causes, as it ought to be referred. Of this there is the common saying: What has once been dedicated to the Lord must not be transferred again to profane uses. Nor should it be extended to the goods left to monasteries and churches, as in Code 5, On pagans: places and goods assigned to the sacred rites of the heathen are claimed by the treasury. For those were dedicated to the demon, as Paul shows to the Corinthians, and the treasury may seize them in whatever way, as if they were ownerless. But these have been consecrated to God and to the Christian Church. Although the Church was oppressed by great darkness before these times, this must not be made to serve for its plunder, but rather so that what was left for impious uses to the Church should be turned to pious ones. Those who wish may consult the counsel of Schurff on this, Century 1, Consultation 48. Moreover, in the courts by which ecclesiastical goods are seized, under the pretext that they ought to be applied to the use of the Church and the schools, almost the same thing happens as is related in the fable of a certain traveller, poor and hungry, who on his journey prayed to Mercury that he would offer him some goods which he might find left somewhere on the road. He even promised that he would dedicate half of them to Mercury's temple. Then the traveller went on, his prayer said, with good hope. And when he had gone one stadium, and then another, he found baskets full of almonds and dates. Although this gift did not answer to the traveller's greed and hope, nevertheless he wisely and rightly acted as the saying goes: Whoever takes what comes is well content [ὅτι ᾧ τις ἰσαίνει], and he made the best of the goods, which had been sought with no expense or labour. He hastened therefore to the market, that he might gain some money from them. But Mercury met him as he hurried, and ordered him first to share the booty. The clever countryman replied that he remembered his promises and would give half, namely the shells of the almonds and the kernels of the dates. In this way the court divides the ecclesiastical goods with the churches and schools. The same, p. 318. It is certain that these riches, which the churches now hold, were given to the churches at first by pious kings and princes for this reason, that they might be contributed as stipends for the support of teachers and learners. Nor were the colleges of canons, and indeed the monasteries too, once anything other than schools in which young people were taught and the propagation of doctrine took place. Afterwards such great abuses arose that those old colleges utterly degenerated from themselves, and still today, in those places where Papacy reigns, they seem to be a [sacrilege, ἱεροσυλία] and a workshop of horrible idolatry, most foul lusts, luxury and many crimes. But just as Elijah was fed by ravens bringing him bread and meat, so when the colleges have been reformed, it is not in itself a sin to accept, for the expenses of study, the stipends of which many canons otherwise abuse; provided only that no impious obligation is attached, and that those who are supported from such expenses perform their office, and bear in mind that stipends are given not for office or luxury but for the labour of study, and so that the Church may be served. Calvin, in the book On the Necessity of Reforming the Church: It is a similar impudence that they cry out that the Church's wealth is being plundered among us and turned to profane uses. If I were to say that nothing wrong is done here among us, I would be lying. And indeed such great transfers of things rarely happen without bringing some inconvenience with them. If anything wrong has been done here, I do not excuse it. But with what face do our adversaries bring this charge against us? They say that to turn the property of the Church to other uses is sacrilege. I agree. They add that this is done by us. I make this exception: that we by no means shrink from answering for ourselves, provided they too come ready in turn to argue the cause. Let us therefore speak of ourselves presently; meanwhile let us see what they themselves do. Then on the following page, answering about our own people, he says: These are the men who accuse our princes of an inexpiable sacrilege, because they have seized by force and great injustice the patrimony of the Church, consecrated to God, and now squander it on profane uses. Indeed I have already testified that I do not wish to excuse everything that is done among us; rather I profess that I am displeased that in some places greater account is not taken, so that the revenues of the Church are spent only on those uses to which they have been dedicated. All good men groan with me about this. But at present this only is under discussion: have our princes seized the goods of the Church by sacrilege, when they have taken them out of the hands of priests and monks and received them into their own? Do they profane them because they apply them to other purposes than to fattening those bellies? For they are pursuing the cause of their adversaries, not of Christ or the Church. I certainly confess that a grave judgement is pronounced against those who have polluted the Church, so as to seize for themselves what belonged to it. But a reason is also added: because they defraud the true ministers of their sustenance, because by starving the poor they are guilty of blood. But what has this to do with our adversaries? And in the book On Scandals, near the end: Since some have been enriched by sacred resources, and others have somehow relieved their hunger for a time, the enemies of the Gospel boast that we were moved to revolution more by the desire for plunder than by a pious zeal for God; and many who seek a pretext for rejecting the Gospel assent to those slanderous words. As for me, if any have plundered the goods of the Church to fill their purses, I do not excuse them. And our books are eloquent witnesses of how greatly we abhor such sacrileges. But I do not intend to lend my defence to the faults of our side, if any exist; nevertheless the calumny must not be borne, that malicious men accuse us of having handed over to plunder whatever has been taken from those foul whirlpools, that is, from the sacrifices of Baal and the monks. Certainly, in those places from which the impiety of the Papacy has been driven out, at least a part of those revenues, which prostitutes and pimps devoured together with the priests, is now spent on the poor; considerably more is spent on schools than was customary; true ministers, who bring the doctrine of salvation to the people, are supported; and not a few outlays are made for maintaining the state of the Church. He says that to turn the property of the Church to other uses is sacrilege, and he is at pains, in every way, to dissolve the charge brought against us as if it had been made against us, so far is he from wishing either to concede it or to defend it. And he teaches that the revenues of the Church must be spent only on those uses to which they have been dedicated; if it is done otherwise, he testifies that this displeases him, together with all good men. Nor does he prove anything here, except that they should be spent either on the schools, or on the poor, the ministers, and the outlays for maintaining the state of the Church. So that it seems to me he has done violence no less to his own conscience than to Calvin, who does not acknowledge that sentence as his, nor the same as ours, which is the common view of the Churches; or he wishes to persuade us that only Calvin rebukes those princes who neglect the ministry, or who undermine it by withdrawing support from the ministers. And in the book On Scandals he castigates not private persons but whoever fill their purses with the goods of the Church, or, as he puts it, have been enriched by sacred resources; and no less those who assent to such men when they act so. Indeed he teaches that those goods which formerly passed to the sacrifices of Baal and the monks, and so to the impious Papacy, must be spent on the poor, the schools, the ministers, and the other expenses of the Church. What do you say, if I may ask, whether he himself says this here, or does not deny it: that after the Church, the schools and the poor have been abundantly provided for by the Christian magistrate, something should be taken from the mass of goods commonly called ecclesiastical to add to the decency of his family? Whatever the case, this has nothing to do with the point; but I do not see how that great man's mind can be passed over and overlooked in this way, and another opinion invented for him, and a game made of it, unless it is done. Where does Calvin say anything about supporting families from ecclesiastical goods? Certainly not here, where he nevertheless speaks of the uses of those goods, not even a word; and he brings forward everything else, according to the intention of the donations, for which those goods are to be spent, but says nothing about families; while you cling only to these words, omitting all the rest. But unless the holy ministry can be provided for in some other way, I beg you, in what words anywhere does Calvin say this? And as if the only ones were honourable and ancient families, and not any promiscuous ones, even the lowest, which, to use Calvin's words, strive to be enriched by sacred resources or to fill their own purses. To whoever imprudently seeks or lends patronage to such men, I command that he apply himself to reading Calvin's writings with a mind more sincere and calm than he has hitherto done, lest he go securely into an opinion alien to Calvin and to the other Reformers, and hostile to the Reformation, to the great scandal and disgrace of all. Calvin's mind is set forth to us by his close associate Theodore Beza, in the preface to his sermons on the Resurrection of Christ, to the Estates of Belgium, where he thinks that the honoured Estates must be warned reverently, chiefly on two points, the second of which concerns the abuse of ecclesiastical goods: The other point, which all good people cannot be persuaded of, is that which is reproached to you by one of your quarters, which I do not know why has come to nestle outside its own country, in order to disturb more at ease the holy and upright form of ecclesiastical order, which is common to you and to the French Churches, openly blaming you as having not only transferred the ecclesiastical goods to other uses, but as squandering them and depriving the faithful pastors of the Churches of their just and due maintenance. If this abuse were truly imputed to you (which I by no means believe, though such disorders may arise in lesser confusions), the fault would truly be inexcusable before God and before men, and one could not remedy it too soon or too well, or shut the mouths of such persons. He places beyond doubt that it is committed by the Estates, not only that the ministers are not well provided for from ecclesiastical goods, but also that those goods (which he recognises as ecclesiastical, and on whose behalf he speaks to the Estates) are applied to some use other than the ecclesiastical; otherwise he confesses it to be a great scandal and a fairly inexcusable sin. Calvin, in his letter to Farel, written in 1549, reports how, chiefly on the advice of Bucer, it was thought fit to proceed with the ecclesiastical goods and their disposition; yet he hoped for something better, for he begins his account thus: I wish I could tell you something better about the ecclesiastical goods. Nor does he by any means approve either that the magistrate should dispose of canonries with a clear conscience, or that the ecclesiastical goods should be secularised, as someone might wish, who, citing this passage of Calvin, has not rightly omitted its last words: If this is obtained, it will be a tolerable condition amid things so dissipated. For Calvin expressly censures here that the princes administer the ecclesiastical goods at their own discretion, and he rebukes those who take it hard that the gain to which they have already grown accustomed should be torn from their hands. And afterwards he says: The remaining resources should be brought into more legitimate use, such as prebends, chapels, priories and the rest. By legitimate use I mean that they should be destined for ministers and schools, for the poor, and for the other burdens of the Church. If this is obtained, it will be a tolerable condition amid things so dissipated. And the advice of Bucer which he approves, he approves in no other way than because Bucer had shown from the ancient custom of the Church that those goods were bequeathed under that condition; and he took refuge in the tablets of the bequest, and from them taught how the matter was to be handled. Those who think that these goods are to be spent on profane and private uses, alien from our doctrine and from Calvin's opinion, will not wish this manner or law to be followed. And in another letter to the same Farel, written in 1545, Calvin, testifying to the fervour with which he engages in this subject, says: Indeed I do not cease to declare openly in sermons, whenever the opportunity allows, that I call God and men to witness that a grave judgement hangs over us. I have done the same several times in the Senate; yet I do not seem to have discharged myself in this way, while I see that I have achieved nothing. But I follow Ambrose, who, keeping for himself the teaching and office of a pastor, and being ready to lay down his life to defend them, allowed the fields to be taken by the tyranny of the Emperor Valentinian. For this is how our magistrates suspect the contest to be one of rivalry, because we bear it with ill grace that what they have taken for themselves has been snatched from our hands; unless perhaps they pretend this, so that they may detract from the credit of our zeal. Nor, however, must we avoid suspicion to such a degree that we connive at sacrileges. It is only worth considering how far it is expedient to press the contest. He had said a little before: this evil can hardly be corrected except by the consent of the churches; and he had commended the example of the princes of Germany, who promise restitution of all they have seized, if ever they come to some pious agreement. Bucer himself, in his Defence of the Christian Reformation of Hermann, Archbishop of Cologne, p. 404: This accusation has been instituted against the Gazophylacium, chiefly on account of the Masses that have been hired. They say that it must be carefully weighed whether ecclesiastical goods, which were destined by men for this purpose, that the memory of the dead might be kept piously and holily, may lawfully be converted to alms. Response: We have the power and the command to dispense and distribute, as best accords with the will of the Lord, all goods that have been offered to the Lord and are from then on the property of no man; even when they have been destined by those who gave them to the Churches, out of error, contrary to the will of God. For the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, not men's. Now indeed the perversion of the Masses is manifest, as we have shown above, namely making Masses by hire and purchase, which abuse has been confirmed over a long time. This we ought to remove from the midst; and nevertheless to retain what has been given to the Lord and to the Church for such an abuse, and to apply and dispense it to the will and pleasure of the Lord and to the usefulness of the Church, that is, to the religion of Christ in the ministries and instruments, to divine and salutary studies, and finally to the care and support of the poor. For whoever has given anything to the Church has first offered it to the Lord and sanctified it. And although something may have been destined by his gift and bequest, out of ignorance, contrary to what pleases the Lord, yet if it is with the Lord, nothing can be more pleasing to him than that his offering should be most fully applied and dispensed according to the will of the Lord. But if it is not with the Lord, then whatever has been ordained or destined by men concerning the goods of the Lord ought not to hold even among Christians. Nor should the Christian commonwealth have less right in such a case than the commonwealth of this world. Now the human commonwealth has this right: that if anything is bequeathed to some city for a spectacle which the city does not wish to be exhibited among itself, what was bequeathed does not pass to the heirs, but remains with the commonwealth and is converted to some other use which pleases the city. Digest, On use and usufruct through a legacy, the law Legatum and those following. Why, then, should not this right rather belong to the city and to the commonwealth of Christ? Why have not our adversaries any just reason to find fault with our plan, by which all those things that have been gathered by the so-called brotherhoods, and which were destined out of ignorance not for the true worship of God, are to be placed in the Gazophylacium and ordered to a truly Christian dispensation. You see how he teaches that goods offered to the Lord, although in Masses etc. they were offered with error, the error must be corrected and the abuse guarded against; but what is permitted under that abuse is kept as given to the Lord and the Church; indeed these goods are understood to belong to none other than the Lord and to no man's property. Nor does it stand in the way that in book 2 of On the Kingdom of Christ, written to King Edward of England, he writes that when otherwise it cannot be done, and the treasury is exhausted by wars, help should be given from ecclesiastical resources; in which case of necessity, as all are bound to relieve the commonwealth, so too the Churches, whose safety also lies in its well-ordered state, in which the Church itself is contained, together with its ministers, schools and poor, as he says in the same place. For it is not fitting that the commonwealth should not be helped in extreme necessity, or that the Church, poor and needy, should abound in wealth. Bullinger, On the Institution and Office of Bishops, book 2: The Church holds these resources, offered from the collections of the faithful, for this purpose, that by them the ministry of the Word may be supported and cherished, and the want of the poor in the Church relieved; whence it follows that they are then rightly dispensed when they go to the ministers and the poor, p. 114. Let pious magistrates learn, from the dreadful example of Ananias, Sapphira and Julian, not to abuse ecclesiastical resources for profane matters, while meanwhile the affairs of God and the Church are neglected and passed over. And afterwards: Before the poor have been relieved, and ecclesiastical matters have been ordered (as is fitting), let no prince or magistrate take a penny from the sacred treasury, unless they wish to incur the most grave anger and vengeance of the most powerful Deity. And against the Anabaptists, book 3, chapter 9: Meanwhile it is also clear that colleges and churches, especially the older ones, were founded by kings, princes and private men for the ministry of the Church in preaching and the sacraments, and not for the sake of any abuse; which, with the truth as witness, you cannot count among the things sacrificed to idols. For although in the course of time they were turned to abuse through public error, they have now been reformed, that is, restored to their ancient use. Moreover St Augustine rightly says, in his letter to Publicola, 153, that when wealth is transferred from heathen idolatry to the worship of God, the same thing happens as happens to men: those who before were impure in unbelief are now holy, spotless and pure in faith, and so on. We have cited Lavater's opinion above. Musculus, in his Common Places, on the eighth commandment: Bishops and the other prelates, together with clerics and monks, commit sacrilege without any infamy, when they transfer the ecclesiastical goods to profane uses. Then those too commit sacrilege who take the ecclesiastical goods from prelates and clerics and convert them to their own private uses; which some princes did long ago, and would that many who nevertheless boast greatly of the Gospel of Christ did not do so today. With these things agree very well what the same author says in his commentary on Galatians 3:15, where he says that the wills of our ancestors made under the Papacy are not to be kept by posterity, namely insofar as (as he says) they dissent from the will and truth of God, and were not to be established at the beginning so that second Masses might be instituted, and other superstitious forms of worship. For he speaks openly, and had raised the question of certain legacies for vigils and for the Masses of the dead to be celebrated yearly; which he is unwilling, and rightly so, that posterity should keep up to now, and so the error of those men be confirmed, rather than that they be changed to other and better uses. Daneus, Isaiah, part 4, book 1, chapter 5. Balduin, Commentary on the Laws of Constantine, p. 28: Far from it, he says, that what was bequeathed to the Church or its college, individuals may seize by their own right and claim privately for themselves. Nor was it to be tolerated that the churches, enriched by the benefaction of Constantine, should spend their resources on any uses other than truly pious ones, or obey the foolish pleasures of testators who left them, as we know many bequests were left to the churches by men either mad or bewitched by superstition. Indeed, it was only when superstition had prevailed that the bequests left to the churches began to be very frequent. But why do we not here again use the civil laws, which declare that if anything is left to a city for the celebration of a spectacle which may not lawfully be held, it must be converted to other and better uses? Digest 17, On use and usufruct, and the income and revenue of bequests; the law Legatam, 5, Digest, On the administration of things pertaining to the city. At Strasbourg it was done thus at the Reformation, in 1524, so that the ecclesiastical resources were distributed either to the poor or to the ministers of the Church. Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, in 1526, transferred the revenues of the monasteries to the University of Marburg and likewise to four hospitals. The Bernese, in 1528, converted monasteries and convents into schools, the revenues of the convent of Interlaken, of the college of Zofingen, of the monastery of Königsfelden, and finally of the college of Irregular Canons being transferred to the grammar schools of Düren, Zofingen, Brugg and Bern. A similar thing the Synod of Edam wished to be done among us, in 1586, article 13; and that of Alkmaar, in 1605, grievance 25. Scultetus, in his Ecclesiastical Annals, at the year 1525, where he has related how in England the revenues of the monasteries were applied to two colleges built by Cardinal Wolsey; a matter which, as some have noticed, was believed to have brought destruction, or at least the greatest calamities, on all who had touched it, like the Toulouse gold. He adds: If divine justice has punished so severely those who, indeed, converted to better uses the goods dedicated to the Church, though not administered with much holiness, but who did not do so with a view to those uses, but were driven by wicked desires, what do we think awaits those who seize and plunder the ecclesiastical goods, however occasion offers, without discrimination, for the sole purpose of enriching themselves? Such care for the ecclesiastical goods was taken in the Reformation of the Duchy of Württemberg, whence in 1587, as reported by Binder, in his Theses on the Ecclesiastical Goods, a decree was issued: The Church's chest, with all its belongings, shall by no means be altered, much less the spiritual goods of our and our principality's prelacies, monasteries, provostships, foundations, canonries, prebends, and the whole income of such a church chest, shall be used in no way for private purposes, or for any other purposes, but by sound and good counsel of the city shall be used solely and alone for the maintenance of the churches and schools, and so for the promotion of the honour of God and of the poor. In the Description of Belgium, where it is spoken of Groningen and the Ommelanden, p. 285, concerning the Academy that was founded, for which a huge sum was assigned to be drawn each year from monastic revenues, p. 298: the agreement between the city and the rural landowners was to this effect: monasteries and monastic goods, and whatever is of that kind in the city and the countryside, and likewise in the old and suburban district, shall by common consent be applied to pious uses. In accordance with this, again in 1600, a rule was written for the College of Deputies: Let them see to it together that no one turns goods of this kind, dedicated to pious or public uses, to his own use. A dispute arising in 1595 between the Emdeners and Count Edzard was settled, among other things, through the intervention of the Lords Estates, in such a way that the goods pertaining to the support of children, preachers, schools and the poor should remain. That no one may deny that this is read in our Meteren, let him look in book 17, folio 351, where among the articles of agreement is this: The goods for the maintenance of children, preachers, schools and the poor shall remain bound to that purpose, as well those of the great church and the hospital at Hinta, as the Estates' lands lying at Hinta, which were taken from the provostship and endowed by the late Count Douwe's mother, of blessed memory, for the great church; these shall again be bound to that purpose and remain so, and the Count shall no longer trouble himself with the administration of the church goods. Surely this is how the Estates judged: that the pious wills and bequests of the dead are to be kept, and not to be infringed or annulled, nor to be taken from the poor, the ministers and the schools at the discretion of the magistrate, nor disposed of at his pleasure or applied to other uses. This very matter had not long before been the cause of the bishops being rejected from Belgium, and from it there also arose the beginnings of war: [illegible, ~10 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters]. Helfricus Ulricus Hunnius, a Papist jurist, son of Aegidius Hunnius, a Lutheran theologian, gathered together Twelve Responses of Protestants against the usurpation of ecclesiastical goods, or their application to any uses other than pious ones, by whomsoever. Here the first place is taken by Hieronymus Schurff, who in Century 1, Consultation 48, says: From these things it is also clear how ill-advised it is for the lord prince, that it belongs to his illustrious lordship to seek this right, etc., because he is emperor in his duchy, and it is written: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; for that text entirely proves against his Serenity, as appears from that passage of St Ambrose, and above in the answer given to the first question. For it is shown from the text of Christ by Ambrose that the emperor himself cannot decree concerning the property of the things of the Church. And in Decretum, Distinction 96, where the text says, among other things: It is unjust and like sacrilege that what each has given, or at least left, to the venerable Church for the salvation and rest of his soul, for the sake of the poor, should be transferred from those whom it was most fitting to preserve it. And therefore whoever seizes the property of the churches commits the horrible crime of sacrilege, even if he himself gave it to the churches. Chapter Sunt opes, where there are also the words of St Ambrose, with the three following, 17, question 4. And from these things it is clearly inferred against the ribalds of our time, who ask the princes for the property of the churches, that they sin against God, against nature and against all right, by appropriating to themselves and their uses what has been given to the Church for the common benefit of the poor. Finally: much less can the Illustrious Prince and Lord Duke C. appropriate to himself by his own authority, but under the penalties of sacrilege and of the other laws inflicted on invaders of ecclesiastical property, he is bound to abstain from such a purpose. The same, Consultation 90: It follows now from what has been briefly adduced above, that the goods of the churches cannot be seized by laymen, even by the emperor himself, or by other kings and princes, since neither possession nor ownership of such things of the Church is vested in them, or alienated to laymen by any title. And consequently, that alienation made by them, of whatever pre-eminence or dignity, is as if made by a non-owner, and is void by law itself, and transfers no right or ownership, nor can it transfer any to those to whom such alienation has in fact been made. And thus those who receive or invade the property of the Church by a title that the law condemns, and from a non-owner, are said to plunder it from prelates and clerics, etc. For every alienation of immovable property of churches, monasteries, hospitals and other pious places, by whatever title, whether by gift, exchange, etc., is generally forbidden by law. For this appears from civil law by the paragraph Nos igitur, the whole Authentic On not alienating and exchanging church property, column 2, the paragraph hoc vero iubemus, Authentic On alienation and emphyteusis, column 9, with the concordance. And the emperor says in the said law iubemus, among other things: For those things which belong to the rights of the most blessed Church, or which may perhaps come to it hereafter, it is fitting that they be guarded inviolably, untouched, as the holy and religious Church itself; so that, as she is the perpetual mother of religion and faith, so her patrimony may be preserved unharmed forever. Matthaeus Wesenbeck, Consultation 4: This must be said above all of ecclesiastical goods, which it is now customary to hold and join with fiefs. For such goods, like the churches themselves, are of divine right, and have the same privileges as the churches. Code, last law, On the Holy Churches; in the Authentic On Churches, title; chapter Grandi, On supplying negligence of prelates; chapter 2, On full restitution, book 6; Andreas Tiraquellus, On the privilege of pious causes, at the beginning. Ernst Cothmann, vol. 2, Consultation 100, where, among other things, he cites the saying of Ambrose, adduced also by us above, On not handing over basilicas and their patrimony, and says: By these words the most serious author made it clear that one who handles things entrusted to God, the churches and the poor, grievously offends against that part of the Decalogue which severely forbids theft. What then would we think Ambrose would say, if he had fallen upon these times? What if that voice of his, crying out, looked upon and contemplated our present morals? As he said to Herod to his face: It is not lawful for you to take your brother's daughter to wife; so he would now cry out too: It is not lawful for you to possess the things dedicated to God, the Church and the poor, and to turn them to your own uses. But Ambrose is dead, and the voice of the crier is silenced, or at least so hoarse that it no longer makes any sound. And this is what is commonly said and deplored today: that there are few Ambroses. And at the end: Hence Hieronymus Schurff is not unreasonably said, as Philip calls him, to be wise, most serious and most seriously judging; he always and perpetually gave a legal answer for sacred things and for the poor against the lords of the earth, and he judged that the ribalds of our time, who ask that the property of the Church be assigned and appropriated to them by the princes, sin against God, nature and all right. But also the most elegant Ulrich Zasius says: Those who have seized ecclesiastical buildings and goods are not safe, neither in a court of contention, and much less in a court of conscience. Finally Master Matthaeus Wesenbeck says: Sacred things cannot become profane, nor ought they. Since they are of no one's goods but of divine right, how, in heaven's name, are they taken from God and the Church by sacrilege. He concludes at last: things consecrated directly and precisely to God, to the Church and to the poor are very badly possessed by lay possessors, and it is to be wished that they be restored. But there is no judge before whom they may be reclaimed. The day of the Lord will therefore judge, and others. For it pleases me to end and close this question as proposed in this way, with St Augustine, Decretum, chapter Quid dicam, 14, question 4. Henricus Andreas Cranius, Treatise on the Peace of Religion, Problem 5: That ecclesiastical goods, such as monasteries, convents, colleges, and other such sacred goods, seized since the time of the Treaty of Passau and converted to pious uses, pertain to the state of the Augsburg Confession, has been said in the preceding connected matters; and on this occasion it is asked here, and not uselessly inquired: but whether goods once dedicated to God (that is, destined from the beginning for the Church, for sacred uses, and for the poor), when their use for which they were first given has lapsed, can be reduced to the form of patrimonial and feudal goods, and be justly possessed by laymen? The negative opinion, received by the common calculation of the holy doctors, is truer than every law, and was lately maintained with pious zeal, and also with most urgent reasons, by the most famous jurist, Master Ernst Cothmann, in Consultation 100, page 358, where he calls this question illustrious and difficult, and most suited to our morals and times. Matthaeus Wesenbeck, Consultation 37; Hieronymus Schurff, Century 1, Consultation 48. This negative opinion rests on the following reasons, etc. The same jurists of Tübingen, in their response of 1529, cited by Helfricus Hunnius, page 42; Johann Schneidewin, on the Institutes, On the division of things, number 10; Petrus Syringius, Dissertation on the Peace of Religion, conclusion 38. What has once been dedicated to God must not be transferred to profane uses, chapter Semel Deo, On the Rules of Law, in Sixth book; law Sancimus, and law Ut inter, Code, On the Holy Churches. This right, which arose from Jehovah himself, and has been sanctioned by nature and by the common law of nations, is most gravely taught by Master Ernst Cothmann, response of law 100, number 18, and throughout; P. Matthaeus Wehner, practical observations, under the word "unjust goods"; Coler, On the process of execution, part 2, chapter 3, number 181, where he says that what has once been dedicated to the Church is the holy of holies, and therefore cannot be taken without incurring sacrilege. If this pious and honourable admonition were properly observed by all those who have laid profane hands on sacred goods, it could easily answer Erasmus Burghard, in his [book] ... chapter 16, indeed the word "M." — where he inveighs, not without reproach to the Protestants, against their profanation. Christophorus Binder, in his Theses on the Goods of the Church, p. 15: Those priests acted unjustly who turned to private uses things dedicated to God, which cannot be in anyone's goods, and in which the uses of all private persons expire. P. 40: The people, the clergy, the kings, all alike, by voice, doctrine, confession and laws, have testified that such gifts, consecrated to God, belong only to God, or to the Church on earth, which as a pious mother ought to foster the worship of God from them, kindly feed learned and faithful ministers, and have a perpetual care of the poor, that none may be in need. P. 117: The magistrate must hold this, that he has been appointed by God as the procurator of the necessity of the poor, and the advocate or nurse of the Church. Therefore, let him not, by a blameworthy usurpation, claim for himself the ownership of the goods of the Church; but, like a superintendent and advocate, let him arrange everything in these matters properly, as one who will one day render account to God. Theodore Reinking, Treatise on Secular and Ecclesiastical Government, book 3, part 1, chapter 3: Apart from the cases and the mode stated above, things dedicated to divine worship are not to be transferred to profane use, even if the purpose for which they were dedicated to God has been removed; for then they are to be converted to another pious use, by what Jerome says. Schurff, Consultation 48, number 11, Century 1. And so monastic goods and others destined for the celebration of Papist ceremonies are rightly transferred, after the Reformation, by the states of the Augsburg Confession, to the ministry of the Evangelicals and the support of the academies, and to other pious causes; on which matter see at length Hortleder, in Reichshandlung, book 4, chapter 7, number 10, page 126. Melchior Goldast, in his Reply on behalf of the Empire, dedicated to the Landgrave of Hesse, reports that he once heard this most just utterance from Frederick IV, Count Palatine (who certainly did not live at the court of the King of Utopia here): I do not want my Fritz to have a hand in the priests' goods; I would not wish to have so much as a finger's breadth of ecclesiastical possessions for my Frederick (who was Elector of that name). Frederick Balduin, Wittenberg theologian, Casus Conscientiae, book 4, chapter 4: Therefore we boldly affirm that those who do nothing else, and will do nothing in future, than that at a certain time they are present in the choir, and either themselves or through others mumble their canonical hours, and yet receive very ample revenues from ecclesiastical goods, do not live a life of the kind that pleases God, because they do not attain the purpose of the founders, but live in idleness, and serve neither God nor their neighbour in any way. As long as they persist in this manner of life, they can have neither a God who is propitious nor a peaceful conscience. The same judgement is to be made of Papal canons, whether they are called regular or irregular. For it could be doubted, not without reason, that they are in such a manner of life as pleases God. For although the ecclesiastical goods were founded by our pious ancestors out of pious devotion and with the best intention, namely that schools might be set up in which useful men of the Church would be educated, that the poor might be supported, that public buildings, whose use is in the public worship of God, might be restored, or that money might be at hand for redeeming captives, of which purpose more will be said in its place: nevertheless they themselves do not attain that purpose and intention of the pious ancestors. For they do not duly serve either God or their neighbour. Johann Gerhard, Common Places, Volume 6, On the Political Magistrate, p. 597: Let the pious magistrate beware lest, by seizing the ecclesiastical goods and turning to private uses what has been dedicated to the sacred, he bind himself to great sacrilege. The vulture that carries stolen flesh and coals from the altar into its nest burns both the nest and the chicks; so the harpies and vultures who seize ecclesiastical goods by force will find that these things bring them not profit but ruin. Those plunderers of ecclesiastical goods are rightly compared to the soldiers who stripped Christ of the garments which the pious generosity of others had given him; so they turn the goods of the Church, collected by pious ancestors, to private uses, and leave Christ naked in his members. But if some magistrate, more like Julian than Constantine's successor, claims the ecclesiastical goods for himself, let the minister of the Church admonish him gravely, and yet not resist stubbornly and obstinately, much less violently and seditiously; but let him think that the tranquillity of the Church and the preservation of true religion may be redeemed, at the cost of these fleeting things, not only lawfully but also laudably. For if Hezekiah did rightly, who sent to the King of the Assyrians, from whom war was to be feared, all the silver found in the house of the Lord and the plates of gold which he himself had fixed there, and so bought political peace by this means (2 Kings 18:15); how much less can it be condemned if a minister of the Church gives up the goods of the Church to a magistrate who seizes them by force and haughtily scorns all admonitions, so as to procure peace and tranquillity for his Church. Therefore it must be carefully considered when it is fitting to imitate the example of Laurence the martyr, who refused the sacred treasure to the tyrant Decius, and when rather the example of Augustine, who restored the deeds of the donors of the fields of the Church to the donor, when they had been placed in his keeping. Posidonius, Life of Augustine, chapter 24. Which same thing, before him, Tilenus, in his Syntagma, Disputation on the origin of the goods of the Church: It is not lawful for the ecclesiastical resources to be converted by the political magistrate to other uses than sacred and pious ones. But neither is it fitting for the ministers of the Church to resist the princes who demand them stubbornly and obstinately. Yet here a no common prudence is needed, so that we may consider when the examples are to be imitated: of Laurence, who refused the treasures to Decius; of Ambrose, who refused to hand over the basilica to Valentinian; and of Augustine, who restored the deeds of the donors of the fields of the Church to the donor when they had been put in his keeping. On this matter there are frequent declamations by theologians in their sermons. Eò hæc Icias facere, ut doceamus, calumniam nobis fieri, quando nobis exprobratur, nos bona Ecclesiastica profanare, & quæ data à piis & Christianis olim fuerunt in usus pios, in Ecclesiæ, pauperum, Scholarumque sustentationem, illa à nobis in alios, in privatos profanosq; usus converti, & non manere Ecclesiastica. Quod pro fundamento Papa in Bulla sua adducit, ut pacem Germaniæ, cum Protestantibus factam, vid. quasi bo-nonorum Ecclesiasticorum violatoribus, faciat irritam. Non hæc eo fine allata à nobis sunt, quasi humanis autoritatibus agere propositum nobis sit, vel nescíamus quantum illis infra Dei verbum debeatur, aut in illis fiduciam anchoram figamus: inepte; sed ut quæ hic sit Reformatorum & Protestantium Doctorum sententia ac doctrina manifesto constaret, illa paulo diligentius explicata fuere: quæ frustra fit, & imperitus atque imprudens nimium, qui in alium sensum adducat vel torqueat, quam qui ex adductis auditisque Auctorum verbis jam perspici poterit, ut se omnes uno ore fateantur, ex bona donatorum intentione, ac communi Ecclesiæ jure, bona Ecclesiæ in usus pios data, iisdem applicanda esse, non privatis, vel profanis. Quod nequaquam infringit, si quandoque, neutiquam ut priorem illam & generalem sententiam tollant, etiam aliquando addunt, summâ in necessitate atque Reip. penuria, ubi cum exitio Reip. imminet simul detrimentum Ecclesiæ, ut & hæc, & illa servetur, poscile illi ex Ecclesiæ opibus inter alia prospici & succurri; uti neque de superfluo bonorum Ecclesiasticorum est quæstio; vel de conservandis aliqua exinde ratione honestis familiis; nam inter alia sunt aliquando hunc in finem donata, fundataque: sed respiciendæ, uti alias, ita & hic, bonorum fundationes, atque ex iis de illorum dominio, usuque pronunciandum. Eccur enim deteriori, vel iniquiori conditione habeatur Ecclesia, quam alia? Unde, ut quis solo Magistratus arbitrio, bona Ecclesiastica aliter vel accipiat vel impendat, quam in fines usuque ecclesiasticos, adversus donationum & donatorum voluntatem, nemo hactenus docuit Reformatorum; uti nec quod bona Ecclesiastica sint juris publici, & quia protéguntur à Magistratu, ideo ad usus suos ab eodem ordinari possint, & sic suo addici. Quod si ita esset, profecto nec ego, nec alii Ecclesiis quippiam facile legaremus, quibus haud liceret securis esse, quod bona in pios usus à nobis data iisdem servirent, quæ tamen sola nostra hic voluntas, & absque quâ evanida esset pie testandi intentio. Neque docent Reformati, donata Ecclesiis. quamvis non omnino pure & sancte, sed cum aliqua etiam superstitiosa aut idololatrica appendicc, prorsus e censu Ecclesiasticorum ideo abolenda esse, & per omnia ad Magistratum, non ad Ecclesiam pertinere; sed reformanda, & uti bonum id servandum, quod expoluere Donatores suarū voluntatū fuisse, ut ad cultum Dei in Ecclesia, in Ministerio, in pauperibus, & Scholis bona illa impenderentur, ita si quid illis pro conditione temporum adhæret erroris vitiiq;, tollendum esse id solū, uti in reformatione doctrinæ, arbitrantur. Adeo quæ bona Ecclesiastica sunt, apud nos naturam suam servant, & Ecclesiis relinquuntur, in usus pios sanctosque. Non docemus, licere aut testatorum ultimas piasque voluntates temerare & rescindere, aut in ea quę Ecclesiis, seu pauperibus debentur, inuolare, & in usus alienos tradere ea aut impendere. Sarta tecta conservanda singulis sua, & quæ Cæsaris Cæsari; Deo autē, atque Ecclesiæ, quæ ejus sunt, relinquenda. Non aliter nos docemus, vel Protestantium Ecclesiæ: & secus si quando cum bonis illis vivitur, quando id fit, dolemus atque reprehendimus. Peccatum dicimus, docemus neutiquam. uti quando adversus doctrinam sæpe alias peccatum committitur, seu apud nos, seu apud Papistas, & quoscunq;. Atque istum in finem fecere tot adducta Protestantium Doctorum, & Iurisconsultorum quorundam, juxta Verbi divini regulam, & Ecclesiæ tum canones, tum leges ciuiles, Patrumque Veterum sententiam, testimonia, doctrinam illam nostram ostendentia, tum confirmantia: ut omnem Papanis, hinc adversus Nos odii bellique causam libenter sumentibus, prætextumsic etiam demeremus.
units.tr: Here he adds many unhappy examples of people who vainly entangled themselves in church property for private and profane uses. To this end he cites some passages from Luther's Pastoral and from Nicolaus Selnecker's commentary on Haggai, and concludes with this: "No one has ever prospered who has boasted of church goods" (Iacus Foeclerus, in Disterminator of the Ecclesiastical and Political Government, p. 29). The Church has certain goods of its own, which in ancient times were distributed by its stewards in such a way that one part went to the clergy, a second to the poor, a third was spent on the repair of buildings and other uses, and a fourth was finally left to the bishop, to be given to exiles rather than to his own household. Henricus Eckardi, in Considerations on whether church goods should be confiscated, published in 1633: church goods are nothing other than collected alms (fol. 41). Church goods are the property of Christ, who redeemed his Church with his blood, and who assigned them to his believers and prescribed to them how and in what manner they should use them: Christ is the proprietor and heir (III). Church goods are to be used only in extraordinary cases, and in cases of need for the rescue of the fatherland; but in time of peace they are to be used for the support of the poor, the sick, travellers, widows and orphans, the infirm and people of that kind (fol. 59). The answer of Duke John Frederick of Saxony and of Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, in the year 1540, on 11 April: church goods are to be applied to maintaining the preaching office, the Christian schools, and the other needs of the Church and the land, as Holy Scripture, the ancient councils and the canons plainly testify. Benedict Carpzov, on the Lex Regia, chapter III, section x: Indeed we concede this, that bishoprics and reformed colleges are to be converted, not by being profaned, but to other pious uses, namely the maintenance of the ministry, of the schools and academies, and the spreading of the pure and sincere word of God. For what has once been dedicated to God ought not to be transferred to profane uses (c. Leme, De Regulis Iuris in 6; l. Sancimus; and l. Ut inter, C. De Sanctissimis Ecclesiis). We cannot deny, indeed (the words are of Henricus Petrejus in his treatise On Monasteries, p. 74), that there are examples of those who have dared to handle and snatch away things dedicated to God, to invade monasteries and turn their revenues to profane uses, and, forgetful of their office and duty, intent only on feasts and purses, and utterly neglectful of learning and the poor, have boldly devoured the bread of Christ; but they have digested it badly, and have truly, though too harshly, experienced that the devout curses of the founders have not lacked serious effect. Whoever takes the goods, may his lungs and liver rot in his body. That is: whoever does this, may you, just avenging God, punish with poverty, sickness, disgrace and shame. Petrejus, in the place cited, reports that he has seen curses of this kind in some monasteries. Carpzov likewise, chapter iv, section iv, throughout: those things once dedicated to God are so dedicated that they cannot be transferred without some further sacrilege (Lev. 27:28; c. Semel Deo, extr. De Regulis Iuris in 6; l. Sancimus; and l. Ut inter, C. De Sanctissimis Ecclesiis). Ernst Cothmann traces this right to Jehovah himself, and holds it sanctioned by nature and by the common law of the nations (Responsa iuris 100, throughout). Matthias Coler, On Executive Process, part 2, chapter 3, n. 181. Everhard von Weisbe, in his treatise On Prerogative of Succession, letter H, 7. Henricus Petrejus, in his treatise On Monasteries, p. 55. Therefore, says Lambert Danaeus, princes who claim for themselves, or transfer to other uses, the ecclesiastical goods of a state, that is, goods already consecrated to God, are guilty of expiation before God, and so is the commonwealth (De Republica Christiana, lib. 3, cap. 2). To such men, according to Luther's judgement, the same thing happens that once befell the eagle, which, as it looked on, saw a sacrifice being prepared on the altar of Jupiter from the flesh of a lamb; swooping down and carrying off a good part of it, a burning coal clung to its wings, with which it afterwards burned both its nests and the chicks for which it had brought the prey (Petrus Fridericus, De controversia causarum, lib. 3, cap. 18, n. 51). See also Carpzov, Jurisprudentia Consistorialis, lib. 11, tit. xix, On Church Goods, Definitions 290 and the following. Micrelius, in his Syntagma historiarum, part 11, p. 305: The Protestants themselves answered at the Diet of Hagenau in the year 1540 that they had not seized the goods of anyone, but that after the restoration of their doctrine to purity they had also restored the goods, which had been destined from the beginning for lawful and honourable uses but had afterwards been diverted by ecclesiastics to other ends. They had learned this from Luther, who orders that the abuse, not the church goods themselves, be abolished, lest it be the avarice, rather than the Christian faith, that is hostile to the monasteries. He likewise inveighs everywhere against those who, under the pretext of reforming the churches, despoil the churches of those goods which were to be devoted to the maintenance of the ministry and the schools. To what end all this? you will ask, and for what purpose such a laborious citation of so many authors on the same matter? I bring these things forward so that we may teach that a calumny is being made against us when it is cast in our teeth that we profane church goods, and that we convert to private and profane uses those goods which were given by pious and Christian people in former times for pious uses, for the support of the Church, of the poor and of the schools, and that they therefore cease to be ecclesiastical. This the Pope adduces as the foundation in his Bull, so that by it he may make void the peace concluded with the Protestants in Germany, as if they were violators of church goods. These things have not been brought forward by us as though we intended to act on human authorities, or as though we did not know how much is owed to them beneath the Word of God, or as though we fixed our hope on them as an anchor; that would be foolish. Rather, they have been explained somewhat more carefully so that the opinion and doctrine of the Reformed and Protestant teachers may clearly stand out; it is vain, and too unskilled and imprudent, for anyone to lead or twist them into another sense than that which will be evident from the words of these authors as cited and heard, so that all of them confess with one voice that, by the good intention of the donors and by the common right of the Church, church goods given to pious uses are to be applied to those same uses, not to private or profane ones. This in no way is overturned if, at times, while by no means abandoning that first and general opinion, they also add that in the greatest necessity and scarcity of the commonwealth, when the ruin of the state is imminent and at the same time loss to the Church, so that both the one and the other may be preserved, it may be permitted that provision be made for and assistance given from the resources of the Church, among other things. Nor is the question about the superfluity of church goods, or about maintaining honourable families from them in some way; for among other things some goods have at times been given and founded for this purpose. But the foundations of the goods are to be regarded here, as elsewhere, and judgement is to be pronounced from them concerning their ownership and use. For why should the Church be held in a worse or more unfair condition than others? Hence no one among the Reformed teachers has hitherto taught that anyone, by the will of the magistrate alone, may receive or spend church goods otherwise than for ecclesiastical ends and uses, against the will of the donations and the donors; nor that, because church goods belong to the public law and are protected by the magistrate, they may therefore be disposed of by him for his own uses and so be assigned to him. If that were so, certainly neither I nor others could easily bequeath anything to the Churches, since they would not be able to be sure that the goods given by us for pious uses would serve those uses; yet this will of ours alone is what would make the intention of piously bequeathing empty. Nor do the Reformed teach that gifts made to the Churches, although not altogether purely and holily, but with some superstitious or idolatrous addition, are therefore to be utterly removed from the property of the Church and to belong entirely to the magistrate rather than to the Church; rather they are to be reformed and kept as a good thing, namely what the donors' wills showed was intended, that those goods should be spent on the worship of God in the Church, on the ministry, on the poor and on the schools. So, if anything of error or fault clings to them because of the conditions of the times, they hold that only this is to be removed, as in the reform of doctrine. Thus, among us, the goods that are ecclesiastical keep their own nature and are left to the Churches for pious and holy uses. We do not teach that it is lawful to violate or rescind the last pious wills of testators, or to steal what is owed to the Churches or to the poor, or to hand over or spend these on alien uses. Let each keep what is his, securely and intact: "render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God, and to the Church, the things that are God's" (Matt. 22:21). We teach nothing otherwise, nor do the Churches of the Protestants; and if at any time it happens that people live otherwise with those goods, when this happens we grieve and rebuke it. We call it sin; we by no means teach it. Just as sin is often committed against doctrine elsewhere, whether among us, among the Papists, or among any others. And for this purpose so many citations from Protestant teachers and certain jurists have been made, showing and confirming that doctrine of ours by the rule of the divine Word, by the canons of the Church, by both civil laws, and by the opinion and testimony of the ancient Fathers; so that we may also thereby deprive the Papists of every pretext, since they willingly take up from this the cause of hatred and war against us.

units.la: Quod autem oggerant, data illa bona Ecclesiastica fuisse, in usus longe alios quam nunc apud Reformatos obtinet, in Missarum sacrificia, aliaque, quæ Reformati abolent abhorrentque omnia, & pro animarum redemtione ex flammis Purgatorii, pro peccatorum satisfactione, ad promerendam cælestem gloriam, ad colendos invocandosque Sanctos, & quæ plura prisca Papatus devotio in votis habuit, testatoresque bonorum fapius expresserunt in ultimis suis voluntatibus, à nobis jam habita pro superstitiosis atque idololatricis: ad ea respondeo, nec omnia, quæ in bonis habet Ecclesiæ, data in usus finelque illos sublestos esse; nec quæ data, cum addita ejusmodi aliqua improbanda conditione, dum pro fine habuerunt donatores pii, Deo atque Ecclesiæ vel pauperibus illa consignare, extra hos bonos fines impendenda esse, bene emendanda ex præscripto Reformationis, & scorias illas abscindendas quo pura Deo redduntur, in cultum purum. Neque enim Reformatio ubi adhibetur, seu doctrinæ, seu moribus, sive disciplinæ, aut rebus bonisque Ecclesiæ aliis, tollit id quod bonum in iis est, sed servat quammaxime, & liberat ab adhærente vitio, non destruit omnino vel abolet. Isa.lx.8. ut quando quis mustum in botro reperit, is dicit ne perdito illum, quia benedictio est in eo. Servat bona, eaque in pios olim usus data, in eoldem impenditur uti loquens Spanhemius in Dedicatione Part. iii. Dub. Euangelic. ad venerandum Vsserium Armachanum, in sacros usus confers, quæ sacris usibus jam olim destinata fuere. Etiam, quamvis sub Papatu, destinata olim usibus sacris bona illa, atque in eoldem nnuc conferri probat Sic Reformati, & Protestantes hac de re vulgo judicant. Melanthon, in Confil. Theol. part. i. pag. 15. Nec ideo violantur injuriave afficiuntur jura donationum illarum, quia autores earum ab impiis sacrificulis persuasi ac decepti, putarunt se iis funtionibus, sibi, suaque familiæ & posteritati rem profuturam ad salutem animarum instituere, qui profecto si revocarentur in vitam, damnarent ipsi factilitatem, credu litatemque hac i. re suam, cum viderent solummodo ad explendam sacerdotum avaritiam, & pecuniarum aucupia à sacerdotibus has donationes primum expetitas, aut postea translatas esse. Bucerus, in Defens. Christianæ Reformat. Hermanni Archiepiscopi Coloniensis, pag. 105. Potestatem habemus & mandatum, omnia bona quæ Domino oblata, & posthac nullis hominibus propria sunt, juxta voluntatem Domini, quam optime impendendi & dispensandi, etiam contra quam ab his, qui ea Ecclesiis donarunt, ex errore contra vovoluntatem Dei fuerunt destinata. Domini enim est terra & plenitudo ejus, non hominum. Iam vero manifesta est Missarum perversio, quemadmodum supra demonstravimus, conductas precioque redemptas missas facere, qui abusus longo tempore confirmatus est. Quae e medio tollere debemus, & tamen nihilominus, quod Domino & Ecclesiae ad talem abusum donatum est, retinere, & ad voluntatem placitumq; Domini, & Ecclesiae utilitatem impendere ac dispensare, hoc est, ad religionem Christi in ministeriis & instrumentis, divina & salutaria studia, procurationem denique & sustentationem pauperum provehendam. Bullingerus, adversus Anabaptistas, lib. III. cap. IX. nam etsi temporis progressu propter publicum errorem ad abusum conversa sint, nunc tamen reformata, hoc est antiquo usui restituta sunt. (loquitur de opibus Ecclesiasticis) qua initio abusus gratia quaesita sunt, nunc autem non amplius in abusum conferuntur. Unde, in Synodo Mediolurgensi. CIↄ Iↄ lxxxI. ad quaestionem: an Canonici, aliique retinentes beneficia, possint admitti ad coenam, atque in ordinem Seniorum aut Diaconorum cooptari? responsum fuit: illos ad abjurationem omnis superstitionis, & ad verum usum bonorum suorum adhortandos esse: quod ubi fecerint a communione S. coenae arceri non posse: non vero, nisi cum magna cautela, ad Seni-oratum vel Diaconatum admittendos, jubet Synodus, abdicata superstitione, servari in usum suum verum bona isthaec ecclesiastica. Hieronymus Schurpffius, Consil. xlvi. Cent. I. Et isto casu, quando scilicet bona sunt destinata in aliquem usum certum pium, ut ibi perpetuo remaneant, non possunt in illum usum impleri, debent converti in alium pium usum, l. Legatum civitati, cum ibi notat. per Bartol. ff. de usufruct. Johan. de Imola, & Panormitan. & alii. in d. cap. Nos quidem. ante sin. quando fuit relictum fuit factum contemplatione persona vel Collegii, nullo habito respectu ad piam causam, argum. l. sunt personae. ff. de religios. & sumpt. fun. Wesembecius, Consil. 4. num. 23. sacra semel facta, amplius privata fieri nequeunt l. inter 83. sacram 3. de verbor. obligat. Schurpffius conf. 48. licet cent. I. Posito etiam, quod abusus essent consecuti. Nam tunc non in fiscum Principis rederedigenda: sed in meliorem magisque verum usum sunt convertenda. l. Legatum 16.ff. de usu & usufr. legat.l.Legatum 5. de admin. rer. ad civit pertinen.l.final. de opere public. Alb. l. si usufruct. in sin.quib.mod.usufr. Iacob. de Roydis num. 30. Idque cum authoritate Consilii vel superioris. Clement. 2. de religios. domib. Hieron. Schurff.d. conf. 48. Licet num. 11. &c. Idem, in Paratitlis l. ad tit Codicis de Paganis, Num. 2. Hieronymus Treutlerus, select. Disput. xiii. Thes. 11. Item quaeritur: An relicta ad pias causas, deficiente causa, ob quam data sunt, fiant cadu ca & ad haeredes revertantur? Quod itidem negandum, magisque dicendum est quod ad alias pias causas converti debeant. argum. l. 16. l. 17. ff. de usu & usufruct. legato. l. 5. de administrat. rer. ad civit. pertinen. l. 13. ff. de pollicitat. l. 83. §. 5. de verbor. obligat. junct. c. qui semel. 19. q. 3. facit doctrina Bart. in d. l. 5. Wesenbec. in para. Cod. de pagan. sacrif. & templ. & confil. 4. num. 23. confil. 37. num. 6. & aliquot sequent. Reusner. 2. consultat. jurid. quaest. 7. Cujacius lib. 2. quaest. Papinian. ad l. ult. ff. de his qui not. infam. ubi notabiliter allegat Melanthonem, quem dicit hoc recte accommodare ad mores sua patria, hoc est, ad hodiernum Imperii Romano-Germanici statum. Schneidewinus ad instit. de Rerum divis. num. 10. Porro circa hunc §. Notabitis quod data, oblata & relicta ad certum usum pium, si in ipsum propter certam aliquam causam converti nequeant, puta quia vel usus ipse desinit, vel quia detegitur esse impius, ut si aliquid sit relictum pro celebratione Sanctorum: Non tamen pertinent ad haeredes ipsius concedentis, nec ad prophanos usus converti debent. Quod enim semel Deo dicatum est, amplius ad prophanos usus transferri non debet. Binderus, in Thesibus, de bonis Ecclef. pag. 108. Indignos esse ventres istos extra controversiam est. Verum hoc non est odisse scelera, & medio commodo, exonerare Ecclesiam otiosis & turpibus ministris. Ecclesia enim pro sua autoritate, ab officio amovet indignos, otiosos, turpes, fanaticos, & substituit meliores, ac interim pie dispensando Ecclesia bona administrat, nec alio transfert. Harent quoque in aliis ordinibus vitia, quae tamen illa sa Repubi. & fisco salvo, honestis mediis corriguntur, & tolluntur. Expendant hic Principes, tanquam nutritii & Advocati Ecclesiæ, quid muneris divinitus illis commissi rationes postulent, quidque sinceriores quoque Canones illis concedant. Si quis Sacerdotem aliquid ex rebus collatis defraudare providerit, aut honesta ratione compescat, aut Episcopo vel judici corrigenda denuntiet. Quod si Episcopus taliaagere tentet, metropolitano ejus hoc insinuare procuret: si autem metropolitanus talia procuret, Regis hoc auribus intimare non differat, cap. 16 quæst. 7. Glossa addit (Regis) ut cum corrigat, cum per Ecclesiasticum corrigi non potest, ut 11. quæst. 1. petimus 17. di. nec licuit. Idem Pag. 118 Verum an non plurima ex superstitione & idololatrico errore Ecclesiæ data sunt? pro remedio animæ, celebrando anniversario, liberatione e purgatorio, redimendis missis, fundandis altaribus, precibus post mortem faciendis, & aliis fovendis erroribus? inde ergo auferenda hæc bona, & hoc fine data, concludere nonnulli volunt. Respondetur: aliqui posterioribus seculis, cum plene dominaretur AntiChristus suis superstitionibus, hoc fecere, non omnes, ut ex literis fundationum patet. Non itaque à singularibus procedit argumentum. Deinde intentio & mens dantium spectanda est, quæ certe non errores & idololatriam fovendam respexit, sed in genere CULTUM: etsi in specie cultus, uti tum erant tempora, erratum fuerit. Genus ergo manet, in specie error est. Præterea litera fundationum, etiam eorum, qui sua qua habuere temporalia, in remedium animæ dederunt, expresse pauperum mentionem faciunt. Relicta itaque ab illis sunt Eleemosyna, & subsidia pauperum. Qui finis in se non tantum licitus, sed & pius est. Et pag. seq. Objicitur & illud, Episcopos, Clericos, & Monachos, plurima hypocrisi, fraudibus & impostu-ris acquisivisse. Respondetur; 1. nominanda essent in specie bona his mediis acquisita. 2. non tam hæ fraudes (quæ equidem infinitæ fuere) quam intentio dantium & fundantium considerandæ est. Ea autem non tam respicit personam hypocritæ, & impostoris: quam sub ejus nomine Ecclesiam, cui tanquam religiosus servit. 3. usa est Ecclesia illis longo tempore, & etiamnum hodie adhibentur, pro sublevanda necessitate pauperum, conservando cultu, & nervo necessitatis. Purgantur itaque usu & fine, ac tuta sunt temporis præscriptione. 4. nihil inde concluditur; quædam hisce artibus illicitis acquisita sunt, non omnia: plerisque tanquam rationabiliter, & sponte datis hactenus Ecclesia usa est. 102
units.tr: As for their objection that those Church goods were given for uses far different from those now current among the Reformed, namely for the sacrifices of the Mass and other things which the Reformed abolish and utterly abhor, for redeeming souls from the flames of Purgatory, for the satisfaction of sins, for earning heavenly glory, for honouring and invoking the saints, and for the many other things which the ancient devotion of Papacy held in its vows, and which the founders of the goods often expressed in their last wills, things we already regard as superstitious and idolatrous: to these I reply that not all the goods the Church holds were given for those uses and ends, nor are the goods given with some such condition added, which the pious donors had in mind when they meant them for God, the Church, or the poor, to be spent outside those good ends. They are to be properly purged according to the rule of the Reformation, and those dregs are to be cut away, so that they are returned pure to God, for pure worship. For the Reformation, wherever it is applied, whether to doctrine, morals, discipline, or the other goods and possessions of the Church, does not remove what is good in them, but preserves it as far as possible and frees it from the vice clinging to it; it does not destroy or abolish it altogether. Isaiah 60:8: as when someone finds must in a cluster, he says, Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it. It preserves the goods, and those once given to pious uses are spent on the same uses, as Spanheim says in the Dedication of the third part of his Dubia Evangelica, addressed to the venerable Ussher of Armagh: you bring to sacred uses what was already long ago destined for sacred uses. Even though under Papacy those goods were destined for sacred uses, it is proved that they are now to be applied to the same uses. Thus the Reformed and Protestants commonly judge in this matter. Melanchthon, in the Consilium Theologicum, part i, p. 15: Nor are the rights of those donations violated or harmed because their founders, persuaded and deceived by impious priests, thought they were establishing something to profit the salvation of souls, for themselves, their families and posterity, by those functions; who, if they were called back to life, would certainly condemn their own facility and credulity in this matter, since they would see that those donations were first sought by priests, or afterwards transferred, only to satisfy priestly greed and their pursuit of money. Bucer, in the Defence of the Christian Reformation of Hermann, Archbishop of Cologne, p. 105: We have the power and the commission to spend and dispense, as best we can according to the will of the Lord, all goods offered to the Lord and thereafter owned by no men, even contrary to the purpose which those who gave them to the Churches, through error and against the will of God, had assigned. For the earth and its fullness is the Lord's, not men's. Now the perversion of the Masses is plain, as we have shown above, namely making Masses by hire and by purchase with money, an abuse confirmed by long custom. These we must remove from the midst; and yet, nonetheless, what was given to the Lord and to the Church for such an abuse we must retain, and spend and dispense according to the will and pleasure of the Lord and the benefit of the Church, that is, to advance the religion of Christ in its ministries and instruments, its divine and saving studies, and finally the care and sustenance of the poor. Bullinger, against the Anabaptists, book III, chapter IX: for even if, through the progress of time and because of a public error, they were turned to abuse, now, however, they are reformed, that is, restored to their ancient use. (He speaks of Church wealth) which at first were sought for the sake of abuse, but now are no longer applied to abuse. Hence, in the Synod of Milan, 1581, to the question whether canons and others holding benefices may be admitted to the Lord's Supper and enrolled among the elders or deacons, the answer was that they are to be urged to renounce all superstition and to make true use of their goods; and when they have done so, they cannot be kept from communion in the Holy Supper; but they are not to be admitted to the eldership or the diaconate except with great caution. The Synod orders that, superstition being renounced, these ecclesiastical goods be kept for their true use. Hieronymus Schurpff, Consilium 46, Centuria I: And in this case, namely when the goods are destined for some certain pious use, so that they remain there perpetually, they cannot be applied to that use; they must be converted to another pious use, see the law Legatum civitati, with the note of Bartolus, Digest, on usufruct; Johannes de Imola, and Panormitanus, and others, on the chapter Nos quidem, near the end; when something has been left out of regard for a person or a college, with no regard had to a pious cause, see the argument from the law sunt personae, Digest, on religious and funeral expenses. Wesembeck, Consilium 4, no. 23: things once made sacred can no longer become private, law inter sacram, 83, on verbal obligations. Schurpff, Consilium 48, in Centuria I: granted even that abuses had followed. For then they are not to be returned to the Prince's treasury, but are to be converted to a better and truer use. Law Legatum 16, Digest, on the use and usufruct of legacies; law Legatum 5, on the administration of things pertaining to the city; the final law, on public works; Albericus, law si usufructus, near the end, on the ways usufruct ends; Jacobus de Roydis, no. 30. And this with the authority of a council or superior: Clementines, on religious houses; Hieronymus Schurpff, in the said Consilium 48, Licet, no. 11 and following. The same, in the Paratitla on the title of the Code concerning pagans, no. 2. Hieronymus Treutler, Select Disputations xiii, Thesis 11: Likewise it is asked: whether things left for pious causes, when the cause for which they were given fails, lapse and revert to the heirs? This too must be denied, and it must rather be said that they ought to be converted to other pious causes. Arguments from law 16, law 17, Digest, on the use and usufruct of legacies; law 5, on the administration of things pertaining to the city; law 13, Digest, on promises; law 83, §5, on verbal obligations, joined with the chapter qui semel, 19 q. 3. The doctrine of Bartolus on the said law 5 supports this, and Wesenbeck on the paratitla of the Code concerning pagan sacrifices and temples, and Consilia 4, no. 23, and Consilium 37, no. 6, and several following. Reusner, 2 Juridical Consultations, question 7. Cujacius, book 2, Questions on Papinian, on the law ultimo, Digest, on those who are noted with infamy, where he notably cites Melanchthon, whom he says applies this correctly to the customs of his own country, that is, to the present state of the Roman-German Empire. Schneidewin on the Institutes, on the division of things, no. 10. Moreover, concerning this §, note that things given, offered, or left for a certain pious use, if for some particular cause they cannot be converted to that very use, for instance because the use itself ceases, or because it is discovered to be impious, as if something were left for the celebration of the saints, do not pass to the heirs of the one who granted them, nor ought they to be converted to profane uses; for what has once been dedicated to God ought not to be transferred again to profane uses. Binder, in the Theses on the goods of the Church, p. 108: That those bellies are unworthy is beyond dispute. But this is not to hate crimes, and by a convenient means to relieve the Church of idle and shameful ministers. For the Church, by its own authority, removes the unworthy, the idle, the shameful, the fanatical from office, and substitutes better men; and meanwhile, dispensing piously, the Church administers its goods and transfers them to no other use. Vices also cling to other orders, which nonetheless are corrected and removed by honest means, the commonwealth and the treasury remaining safe. Let the princes weigh this here, as nurses and advocates of the Church, what the duties committed to them by God require, and what even the purer canons concede to them. If anyone has planned to defraud a priest of something from the goods conferred, let him either restrain him by honest means or report him to the bishop or judge for correction. But if the bishop tries to do such things, let him take care to hint at it to his metropolitan; but if the metropolitan does such things, let him not delay in bringing it to the ear of the King, Chapter 16, question 7. The gloss adds (of the King), so that he may correct, since it cannot be corrected by the Church, as in 11 q. 1, we ask, and 17 d., nec licuit. Binder, same page, p. 118: But is it not true that very many things were given to the Church out of superstition and idolatrous error, for the remedy of the soul, for celebrating anniversaries, for liberation from purgatory, for purchasing Masses, for founding altars, for prayers to be made after death, and for fostering other errors? Some therefore wish to conclude that these goods, given for this end, must be taken away. The answer is that some did this in later centuries, when Antichrist reigned fully with his superstitions, but not all, as appears from the charters of foundation. The argument therefore does not proceed from particular cases.
