Next, the intention and mind of the givers must be considered, which certainly did not look to fostering errors and idolatry, but in general to WORSHIP, although in the particular kind of worship, as the times then were, there was error. The genus therefore remains; the error is in the species. Moreover, the wording of the foundations, even of those who gave their temporal goods for the remedy of the soul, expressly mentions the poor. Things left by them are therefore alms and support for the poor. This end is not only lawful in itself but also pious. And on the following page: There is also the objection that bishops, clergy, and monks acquired very many things by hypocrisy, frauds, and impostures. The answer is: 1. the goods so acquired by these means ought to be named specifically. 2. It is not so much these frauds (which were indeed countless) that must be considered, as the intention of the givers and founders. That intention regards not so much the person of the hypocrite and impostor as the Church under his name, which he served as a religious man. 3. The Church has used those goods for a long time, and they are still used today, for relieving the need of the poor, for preserving worship and the sinews of necessity. They are therefore purged by use and purpose, and are secure by the prescription of time. 4. Nothing follows from this: some things were acquired by these illicit arts, not all; and for the most part the Church has hitherto used what was given reasonably and willingly. 102

units.la: hannes Winustede Quedelburgensis Conc. 11. adversus avaritiam, & usurpationem bonorum Ecclesiasticorum: Den das ist die gantze vnd höchste Andacht vnd meinung gewest / aller vnser Vorfahren / Stiffter vnd Stiffterinne / der grossen Thumbstiffte vnd Klöster / Als Caroli Magni, Henrici Aucupis, Der dreyer Ottonum / vnd wie sie denn mehr geheissen haben / Ob gleich der leydige Sathan / solche jhr gute meinung durch seinen bittern hass / So er zu Gottes Reich trget / vielfeltiger Weise in Abgötterey vnd Missbrauch / durch den leydigen Geitz gezogen vnnd verfelschet hat / So ists doch gleich sehr offenbar / aus ihren eygen gegeben Privilegien / Das jhr Principal Andacht inn dem ja so gut gewest ist / Wie Davidis vnd Salomonis etc. Nemlich / das Gottes Name gelobet vnd gepredigt werde / vnd der einige Christen Glaube erhalten
units.tr: Johannes Winustede, Quedelburgensis, Conc. 11, against the avarice and usurpation of ecclesiastical goods: For this was the whole and highest devotion and intention of all our forefathers, founders and foundresses of the great cathedral foundations and monasteries, such as Charles the Great, Henry the Fowler, the three Otto, and whatever else they were called. Although the wretched Satan, through his bitter hatred toward God's kingdom, has in many ways drawn and corrupted their good intention into idolatry and abuse through wretched greed, it is nonetheless quite evident from their own granted privileges that their principal devotion was indeed good, as with David and Solomon etc. Namely, that God's name be praised and preached, and the one Christian faith be preserved.

units.la: Brosenius, lib. Aurum Tolosanum, cap. 111. Siehe / Christlicher, lieber Leser / also seynd vor diesem die Geistlichen Güter recht vnd wol gebraucht worden. Wann dann nun die Geistliche Intention den Kirchen gegeben vnd zugewand / auch etliche hundert Jahr vber recht vnd wol mit grossem Nutzen der Christenheit seynd gebraucht / vnd noch ferner zu allgemeiner Wolfahrt der Christlichen Kirchen (wann man sich nur eines bessern Bedenken / vnd dermal eins die Handgriff lichen Irrtumbs vnd schendlichen Missbrauch wolte abthun) können nützlich angewand werden / was wollen dann Crispinus, Thrasibulus vnd andere Leute zum Trost ihres verwundeten Gewissens sagen / es wehren Baal Güter / die den Vorelter durch die falsche Lehr vom Fegfewr wehren abgelogen vnd abgestolen / vnd könte vnd möchte man sie derwegen mit guten sicheren Gewissen von den Kirchen wieder wegnehmen? vnd zum Weltlichen Privat. Nutzen gebrauchen: Aber diesem an Geistlichen Gütern verliebten Leuten gebe ich ertlich diese Antwort / daß die Lehre vom Fegfewer new vnd vber vierhundert Jahr nicht alt sey. Dann Gratianus hat 1150. das Corpus juris Canonici zusammen geschrieben / darinnen ist Causa. 33. quaest. 3. de poenitent. distinct. 7. cap. 3. dieser Canon befindlich: Qui egerit veraciter poenitentiam, & solutus fuerit a ligamento, quo erat astrictus, & à Christi corpore separatus, & bene post poenitentiam vixerit, sicut ante poenitentiam vivere debuit, post-reconciliationem quandocunque defunctus fuerit, ad Deum vadit, ad requiem vadit, regno Dei non privabitur, à populo diaboli separabitur. Allhier gehebe: der Pabst selber daß man damals vber 400. Jahren /von keinem Fegfewr gewust haben /sonsten wurde der Canon sagen, Vadit prius in purgatorium & post purgationem ad Deum. Nun ists ja ferner notorium vnd allen verstandigen Leuten bewust / daß die Stiffte / Collegia vnd Klöster dieser Zeit / vnd sonderlich in hac dioecesi Halberstadiensi faste alle vor vier hundert / funff hundert / sechshundert / sieben hundert vnd mehr Jahren zu Gottes Ehren fundiret vnd begutert seyn. Dahero wird solcher nichtiger Pretext vom Fegfewr darnieder geschlagen / dis aber bleibet war / daß weil man damals noch von keinem Fegfewr gewust / vnd damals keine Güter auß Furcht des Fegfewrs den Kirchen haben können geschenckt werden. Darnach wirds / furs andere / gestanden / daß als man vor zwey hundert / drey hundert vnd etliche mehr Jahren viel predigens vom Fegfewr beginnen zu machen / vnd den Leuten vorgeschwaget / wie man durch Seel- vnd Winckelmessen wieder auß dem Fegfewr in kurtzen könte erlöset werden / das dahero damals noch etliche Güter den Stifften vnd Klöstern seynd zugewand worden. Aber darauf folget lange nicht: Ergo mag ein jeder die Kirchen / Stiffte vnd Klöster mit allen Güter promiscue zu sich reissen vnd prophaniren. Sic mendose colligis Dn. Menelae, Ihr irret Herr Juncker Menelae. Solche Argumentatio dienet nicht Gottes Gnade zu erlangen. Du wirst gewißlich weinig chartas oder instrumenta donationis fönnen bey vnd fürbringen / darinnen allein diese Formalia befindlich: Haec bona dedico atque offero Deo pro remissione peccatorum, pro requie animae, & pro missarum solemniis. In allen denen Chartis donationum, so ich gelesen fen wird auch zugleich alius finis vnd En vrsach mit hinbengesetzt/ als/ hæc bona offero in honorem Dei, ad serviendum ex his Deo, item in clericorum ac pauperum alimoniam. Apud Binderum, in Thesibus. pag. 78. occurrit tabula fundationis Monasterii Maulbronnensis, quæ ita habet: Anno 1147. Hat der Ehrsam Ritter / vnd geborne Freyher / Herr Walther von Lamersheim all sein Gut/ Gott in seinen Dienst gegeben vnd richtet ein Conbent an zu Eckenweiler des Dorffs bey Lamersheim gelegen/ so er dar zu gegeben mit allen seinen Zugehörden.
units.tr: Brosenius, lib. Aurum Tolosanum, cap. 111. See, Christian, dear reader: this is how the spiritual goods were rightly and well used in former times. Since the spiritual endowments were given and assigned to the churches, and were used for several hundred years rightly and well, to the great benefit of Christendom, and could still be usefully applied to the general welfare of the Christian churches (if only one would, on better consideration, remove the palpable error and shameful abuse), what then will Crispinus, Thrasibulus and other people say, to comfort their wounded consciences? Were these goods of Baal, which the forefathers were deceived and robbed of by the false doctrine of purgatory, and could and might one therefore with a good and secure conscience take them back from the churches and use them for worldly private benefit? But to these people, who are in love with spiritual goods, I first give this answer: that the doctrine of purgatory is new and not yet four hundred years old. For Gratian compiled the Corpus Juris Canonici in 1150, and in it, in Causa 33, quaest. 3, de poenitent., distinct. 7, cap. 3, this canon is found: "He who has truly done penance, and has been loosed from the bond by which he was bound, and separated from the body of Christ, and has lived well after his penance, as he ought to have lived before his penance, after reconciliation, whenever he dies, goes to God, goes to rest, will not be deprived of the kingdom of God, and will be separated from the people of the devil." Here note: the Pope himself shows that about four hundred years ago no one knew of any purgatory; otherwise the canon would say, "He goes first into purgatory and after purgation to God." Now it is further notorious and known to all sensible people that the foundations, colleges and monasteries of this age, and especially in this diocese of Halberstadt, were almost all founded and endowed for God's honour four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, seven hundred or more years ago. Hence this empty pretext about purgatory is struck down; but this remains true: since people at that time still knew nothing of purgatory, no goods could be given to the churches out of fear of purgatory. Next, it must be admitted that when, two hundred, three hundred or some more years ago, much preaching about purgatory began to be made, and people were told that by masses for souls and private masses one could soon be redeemed from purgatory, then some goods were in fact given to the foundations and monasteries. But it by no means follows from this: therefore everyone may snatch and profane churches, foundations and monasteries together with all their goods. "You reason badly, Lord Squire Menelaus", you are mistaken. Such an argument does not serve to obtain God's grace. You will certainly be able to bring forward few charters or deeds of gift containing only these formal words: "These goods I dedicate and offer to God for the remission of sins, for the rest of the soul, and for the solemnities of the masses." In all the charters of donation that I have read, another purpose and cause is also added, as: "These goods I offer in God's honour, to serve God with them, likewise for the maintenance of clergy and poor." In Binder's Theses, p. 78, there occurs the deed of foundation of the Maulbronn monastery, which reads thus: "In the year 1147 the honourable knight and noble lord, Lord Walther von Lamersheim, gave all his goods into God's service and established a convent at Eckenweiler, a village situated near Lamersheim, which he gave for this purpose with all its appurtenances."

units.la: Atque ex Constitutionibus Ecclesiasticis Ducatus Wurtenbergensis pag. 328. Es soll in den armen Kirchen eingezogen werden/ alles was bis anher auff Vigilien / ewige Liecht/ Wachs vnnd Oel gewendt ist worden. Item was der Heiligen Fabric/ Præsenz/ Salve. Syend/ Brüder vnd Pflegschafften / vnd dergleichen fallen haben. Pag. 415. Dieweil obgemelter Stifftungen Gefäll vnd Einkommen/ zu der Kirch (vnd Verrichtung von Gottes Werck vnd Sachen innmassen man damalen darfür gehalten) ergeben/ solle dasselb nach erlanter Wahrheit/ vnd eröffnet ein Licht des Worts Gottes/ billich der Kirchen vnd derselben Christlichen Ministerien anhangen/ vnd den zugehörigen andern nothwendigen Sachen/ vnd derselben Notfäll zu Steur/ Hülff vnd guten fomen. Wie dann auch vnser endliche Meinung vnd Will/ daß solches alles bey der Kirch/ ohne geminderet oder geschmälert/ dieser vnser Verordnung nach Gewißlich vnd unwiderruflich also bleiben/ vnd davon nichts hingeben oder alienirt: auch da auffer sondern nothwendigen Ursachen nichts verändert oder abgelöset/ also bald das erlöste Geld/ vnnd Haupt Summa der Kirchen zu gutem/ wieder zumb an Zinß/ vnd mit ligenden Güter anbelegt/ vnd unsere Landthoffnung der Kirchen Abt/ bey ihren Pfichten/ damit sie uns zugethan/ ernstlich darob halten/ sich fleißig erinnern vnd bedencken sollen/ dafür diese Güter vnd Einkommen/ mit Nachtheil der Kirchen/ auch Mangel der Ministrorum. Schulen/ Studien/ vnd anderer piarum causarum, der Kirchen anhängig/ anderst dann zu Unterhaltung Rug Rotturfft derselbigen Schulen/ demnach sie einmal Gott dem Herrn ergeben/ angewendet werden wolten/ daß der ernstliche Zorn Gottes darduch erwecket vnd zubesorgen derselb nicht an solchen Kirchen Gut vnd Gefällen/ als einem zeitlichen vnd geringsten allein angehen / sondern zu noch mehrer Straff/ mit Verlierung seines Göttlichen Worts vnd Segens/ sich gewißlichen erstrecken würde. Dann wir hievon zu unserm Privat vnd sondern Nutzen/ das wenigst nicht anzuwenden/ sondern zu Erhaltung obgeherter Kirchen Sachen gänzlich können vnd gebrauchen laßen gedenckten.
units.tr: And from the Church Ordinances of the Duchy of Württemberg, p. 328: "In the poor churches shall be collected everything that until now has been applied to vigils, perpetual lights, wax and oil. Likewise what has fallen to the holy fabric, the presence (the endowed altar-service), the Salve, the brotherhoods and fraternities, and the like." P. 415: "Since the revenues and income of the aforesaid foundations were given to the church (and to the performance of God's work and affairs, as was then thought), these should, according to the truth now known and the light of God's Word, rightly belong to the church and its Christian ministry, and be applied with aid, support and good will to the other necessary matters belonging thereto and to their emergencies. Likewise it is our final opinion and will that all this shall remain with the church, without diminution or reduction, certain and irrevocable according to this our ordinance, and that nothing be given away or alienated from it; nor shall anything be changed or detached from it, except for truly necessary causes; and as soon as the redeemed money and the principal sum of the church are again invested to its benefit at interest and in landed property, our land-government and the abbots of the churches shall seriously hold to this under their oaths by which they are bound to us, and shall diligently remember and consider that these goods and income, to the detriment of the churches and also to the lack of ministers, schools, studies and other pious causes belonging to the churches, should not be applied otherwise than for the maintenance and needs of those schools, since they have once been given to the Lord God; for otherwise the serious wrath of God would be aroused thereby, and it must be feared that it would extend not merely to such church goods and revenues, as a temporal and least matter, but would, to still greater punishment, extend to the loss of His divine Word and blessing. For we do not intend to apply the least of these to our own private and personal use, but to be able and to allow them to be used entirely for the maintenance of the aforesaid church affairs."

units.la: Confer Edward Elton, in decal. ad prec. VIII. pag. 279. Carpzovius, adleg. Regiâ Germ. cap. 111. sect. x. dicimus ergo, ea quæ antea ad usum illicitum collata fuerant, post reformationem ad alios veræ pietati consentaneos usus transferenda esse, ut memoria testatoris alio & licito genere celebretur, l. legatum 6. ff. de usufr. legat, & arg. l. 4. ff. de admin. rer. ad civit. pertin. ubi Bartol. exemplum posuit in testatore, qui pro Missis canendis centum legaverat, quæ, si propter interdictum Ecclesiæ, Missa non posset cantari, in alium pium usum merito converterentur. Modest. Pistor. vol. 2. consil. 54. num. ult. Nicol. Reusner. lib. 4. decis. 7. per tot. Matth. Coler. part. 2. decis. 224. Quod si fiat, nulla ratio altera. exstitit, cur bona Ecclesiastica publici juris permissa e faucibus Pontificiorum erepta, iisdem domino restituì debeant. Et cap. iv. sect, iv. sequ. equaquam metuendum id erit, si dicamus, Reditus & bona à Pontificibus sacris sanctisque usibus destinata ac postea justo bello recuperata, prophanis commoditatibus haut applicanda, sed ad verum & ab omni superstitione purgatum usum sacrum convertenda esse, quod omnino fieri debet, ex Evangelicorum quoque Statuum & Ordinum Imperii sententia. Petr. Syring. de Pace Religion. concl. 58. lit. b. Modest. Pistor. vol. 1. consil. 54. n. ult. Matth. Coler. part. 1. decis. 224. Nicol. Reusner. lib. 4. decil. 7. Hinc cum fundationes Collegiorum & Cænobiorum C. optimâ quondam intentione majorum, ad educandos nempe Viros doctos & castas modestasque fœminas facta) in abusus converterentur, ita ut reformatio fuerit suscepta, non fundatorum haeredibus bona illa reddita fuere, arg. l. legatum. 6. ff. de Usufr. legat. & l. 4. ff. de administr. rer. ad Civit. pertin. ubi Bartol. sed superstitione saltem rejecta, in parilem rursus usum ut à Principibus convertantur, exigit sanctio Pacis Religiosæ de Anno 1555. als auch den. Christoph. Befold. dict. cap. 4. Modest. Pistor. & Reusn. dict. loc. Quo etiam respicit Responsio Electoris Saxon. & Landgravii Hass. data 11. c April. c Anno 1540. apud Frider. Hortleder. de causa belli german. lib. 5. cap. 9. ubi inter alia haec verba habentur.
units.tr: Compare Edward Elton, on the Decalogue, on the prayers, p. 279 (VIII). Carpzovius, on the Regia lex of Germany, ch. 111, sect. x. We say, therefore, that those things which were previously devoted to an unlawful use must, after the Reformation, be transferred to other uses consistent with true piety, so that the memory of the testator may be honoured by a different and lawful kind of service: Digest, law "legatum" 6, on the usufruct of legacies, and by argument from law 4, Digest, on the administration of things pertaining to the state, where Bartolus gave the example of a testator who had bequeathed a hundred for the singing of Masses; if, because of the Church's prohibition, Masses could not be sung, the money would rightly be turned to another pious use. Modestinus Pistor, vol. 2, consultation 54, last number. Nicolaus Reusner, book 4, decision 7, throughout. Matthaeus Coler, part 2, decision 224. And if this is done, there is no other reason why the Church goods, once snatched from the jaws of the Papists and restored to public law, should be returned to the same lords. And in ch. 4, sect. iv and following: "There will by no means be cause for fear if we say that revenues and goods which the Pontiffs had assigned to sacred and holy uses, and which were afterwards recovered by a just war, are not to be applied to profane advantages, but are to be converted to true sacred use, purged of all superstition; which must certainly be done, according to the opinion also of the Evangelical States and Orders of the Empire." Peter Syring, on the Peace of Religion, conclusion 58, letter b. Modestinus Pistor, vol. 1, consultation 54, last number. Matthaeus Coler, part 1, decision 224. Nicolaus Reusner, book 4, decision 7. Hence, when the foundations of colleges and monasteries, made with the excellent original intention of our ancestors (namely, to educate learned men and chaste and modest women), were turned to abuses, so that when the Reformation was undertaken those goods were not restored to the heirs of the founders (argument from law "legatum" 6, Digest, on the usufruct of legacies, and law 4, Digest, on the administration of things pertaining to the state, where Bartolus), but only superstition was rejected, the holy Peace of Religion of the year 1555 requires that they be turned by the princes to a similar use, as also Christoph Besold, the aforesaid chapter 4, Modestinus Pistor and Reusner, in the places cited. To this also refers the answer of the Elector of Saxony and the Landgrave of Hesse, given on 11 April in the year 1540, in Frederick Hortleder, on the causes of the German war, book 5, ch. 9, where, among other things, these words are found.

units.la: Darumb von den Kirchen Gütern / so noch vorhanden seyn / erbieten wir uns So in einem Christlichen Concilio oder Versamlung/ die Handel zu Christlicher Vergleichung gebracht werden / daß wir alsdann die Güter zu der Kirchen/ Schulen und andern gemeinen Landes Notdurfften in unsern Landen und Gebieten/ ohne Beschwerung wollen folgen lassen/ wie solches also dann offt Christlichen ynedo oder Reichs Tag beschlossen wird. Dann die Kirchen-Güter sollen angewendet werden zu erhalten das Predigampt / die Christliche Schulen und anderen Kirchen und Landes Notdurfft/ wie das Glar zeuget die Heilige Schrifft/ die alten Concilia, und die ältesten Canones &c. Idque si ab omnibus, qui prophanas manus bonis ejusmodi admoverunt, strictè observatum fuisset, non habuisset causam exclamandi Autor Autonomiæ non sine opprobrio Protestantium, hilce verbis. Wo seyn ihrer Elteen Stifte und Klöster ? Ist es nicht alles prophaniret, abgethan/ niedergerissen und verwüstet / Seyn nicht aus Bisthumen weltliche Fürstenthumb / aus den Kirchen Zeughäuser / Reßtalle / Tanzhäuser / Pulverkasten / Badehäuser :c. aus den Klöstern gemacht worden / part. 3. cap. 16. Atque ita quam non ii simus, qui bona Ecclesiastica profanamus, ut quæ sub Papatu Ecclesiis data, neque omnino benè, sed cum superstitione multum coinquinata, ex principali tamen donatorum intentione ad sacros usus analogos impendere docemus, apparet. Distinguimus finem hic in Donatorum intentione principalem & summum, à secundario: tum in genere finem proprium, & analogum. Quamvis in donationibus vel legatis Ecclesiæ factis, in fine secundario erratum aliquando ab hominibus fuerit, quod putarent Dei cultum in rebus aliquibus superstitiosis situm, & Ecclesiæ ministerium esse hoc quod Papicolæ suadebant, dum tamen finis principalis erat in cultum Dei, Ecclesiæ ministerium, animarum conversionem &c. sua donare, hoc bonum diumque fuit, in quo sane fraudare donatorum intentiones, easque frustrare nobis quidem religio est: dumque errarunt in hoc, quod putarent illum Dei cultum situm in rebus adeo frivolis abominandisque ac Papani tradebant, reformatio per Dei gratiam id nunc corrigit, quod si scivissent, secuti procul dubio multum fuissent: atque in usus sanctiores legata ipsorum impendimus, in quo & votis ipsorum respondemus, dum sacris usibus illa attribuimus; & ea augemus, dum in meliores revera, ac ipsi opinabantur, usus convertimus. Quemadmodum si adfuissemus illis donatoribus Reformati, nequidquam vel dissuasores esse ne Deo Ecclesiæque legarent, esse potuissemus, vel invertere licuisset pias legationes, sed sanctam illam intentionem fovissemus, docuissemusque juxta doctrinam Reformatam in usus probos sua applicare, ita jam, non hoc Reformatio docet, ut aboleamus pia Majorum legata profanemusque, sed servemus, & si qua in re egeant, corrigamus, & melioremus, ad usum nempe, sicuti omnino voluerunt, duntaxat sacrum, non profanum, privatum, aut alienum, sed si necesse, sanctiorem & puriorem, saltem divinum piumque. In legibus talia occurrunt, in quibus tutò corrigere Testatorum voluntates licet: C. de religios. & sumpt. l. & si quis §.9. Quid ergo, si ex voluntate testatoris impensum est? nec voluntatem sequendam, si res egrediatur sumptus rationem. D. deconfirm. tutore l. x. Utilitatem pupillorum Prætor sequitur: non scripturam testamenti vel codicillorum. Franciscus Sarmentus, lib. de Reditib. Ecclesiast. part. iv. c. iii. licet princeps non possit tollere, vel mutare testantium, vel contrahentium legitimam voluntatem in non pios vsus ordinatam, ut dictum est, tamen cum rerum publicarum & piarum causarum praecipue sit illis commissa cura, poterit semper voluntatem, vel legata ad pias causas facta arbitrio suo ex causa commutare, hoc probatur in l. legatum ff. de administrat. rer. ad civitat. pertinent. & in Clemen. quia contigit de religio. do. elegantissime declarat R. Episcop. Segob. lib. 3. varia. resol. c. 6. nu. 7. & Io. Dried. lib. 2. de libertat. ecclesiast. pag. 206. Paulus Laymannus Iesuita, in Defensione & c. Societatis Iesu, in causa Monasteriorum Germaniae, ei, quamvis Benedictinorum, aliorumve Ordinum antea fuissent, concedendorū, pag. 23. dicit Secundo, quod circa ultimas voluntates, ac pias fundationes, ob supervenientem aliquem casum, aut circumstantiarum mutationem, secundum Epeijkiam, interpretationem facere, & iccirco materialem aliquam mutationem instituere, non ad plenitudinem potestatis suprema, sed ad ordinariam potestatem superioris pertineat. Quā ratione Covarruv. docet in c. tua n. 12. de Testam. auctoritate Episcopi posse pecuniam à testatore in certum usum pium, non ita necessarium, destinatam, expendi in alium item usum pium, magis Christiana Reipub. necessarium, cui necessitati aliunde subvenire nequeat: dummodo id fiat cum consensu heredis aut executorum; prout hoc idem respondit Sa. ver. Testamentum, n. 33. Nam in tali casu non tollitur testatoris, aut fundatoris voluntas, sed in melius commutatur. Cum unius cuiusque Christiani fundatoris intentio ac voluntas habitualis, atque interpretativa sit, si quipiam ab ipso ad Dei gloriam relictum, aut donatum sit pro certa pia causa aut loco atque iudicio Ecclesiasticorum Praelatorum, magis cessurum sit ad Dei cultum, & Ecclesiae utilitatem, ut alio applicetur (maxime si etiam haeres, aut successor ejus ita judicet) quod contentus esse velit, talem mutationem materialem fieri. Quandoquidem in ejusmodi piis dispositionibus defunctorum non propria jura seu commoda, sed solius Dei cultum & Ecclesiae Catholicae augmentum spectantium, hac principalis intentio potissimum consideranda est; ut si ea tenetur, nihil contra mentem defuncti, aut fundatoris actum esse censeri debeat. Notae sunt Clericorum Papalium ab a. cIↄ Iↄcxxix disputationes in Germania, super Monasteriorum bonorumq; Ecclesiasticorum, quae à nostris, quovis pacto, recuperassent, ad alios ordines, quam quorum illa bona antea fuerunt, praesertim ad Iesuitas, translatione: ubi scriptis acriter inter se certarunt Iesuitae, & Ordines caeteri, quorum causa hic agebatur, & praesertim aliis Benedictini. Vbi enim Caesar, a. clɔ lxxxix. d. vi. Martii, edicto Restitutionis, monasteria & bona Ecclesiastica, quae Papales sibi ablata a tempore pacis Passaviensis querebantur, & quorum causa Protestantibus litem coram tribunali Imperii intentarant, vel quae armis repetita, illis assignasset, ut juxta regulam fundationum, personis idoneis, & cuilibet quod ei deberi videretur, redderetur: mit taugleichen den fundationen und stiftungen gemäß /ordentlich beruffenen/ und qualificirten personen besetzen und zulassen/ und also einem jedwederen zu dem jenigen was ihm gebürth etc. atque ea de causa tum ad Oratorem suum Savellum Romae, tum ad diversos Editi sui Executores Commissarios per Germaniam scripsisset, variaque jam suis Ordinibus assignasset, tum etiam Brevi suo, super publicato isto Edicto restitutorio, gratulatus Imperatori fuisset Papa, ejusdem anni supradicti die v. Maij; inde Ordines inter se contendere ac disputare: Iesuitis urgentibus, quod, quia pro extinctis & vacantibus haberi debeant monasteria bonaque a Protestantibus occupata antea, non necesse esset illa suis Ordininibus iterum assignare, quorum ex fundatione vel donatione prius fuissent; sed quod vel alteri Ordini, piaeve causae, aut illis, qui Ecclesiae videbantur plus officii praestare ususque, id est, ipsis Iesuitis, praeteritis aliis Ordinibus, ea possent attribui. Hinc libri scripti, isto titulo: Disceptatio, seu quaestio, utrum bona Ecclesiastica & Monasteria, maxime nuper ex haereticorum manibus erepta, & victricibus Imperatoris armis recuperata, ad alias familias transferri, an potius antiquis Ordinibus, eorum quondam possessoribus, restitui possint, & vero debeant? Tum: pro S. Caesarea Majestate, ejusdemque ad suum Oratorem instructione, super impediendis antiquarum fundationum mutationibus suscepta defensio: contra judicium duorum Theologorum, super translatione restituendorum in imperio Coenobiorum ad Societatem Jesu. Sequutus est Paulus Laymannus Iesuita, Professor Dilinganus, scripsitque magnum volumen: Justa defensio &c. in tanta Menasteriorum extinctorum, & horrorum Ecclesiasticorum vacantium. Hic, cum suis, rem ita accepit, quod Monasteria, ubi omnes eorum professi sunt mortui, pro extinctis, & bona eorundem Ecclesiastica pro vacantibus habenda sint, ideoque ad alia Collegia, vel scholas; & parochias in Germania libere applicanda. Et quia Iesuitæ hic præcipue in sua commoda intenti erant, & vacare docebant illa, ut hæc specie melius adse raperent, tanquam reliquis Ordinibus ipsi fructuosiores, & Romanæ ledi magis utiles, inde odium illud inter Iesuitas cæterosque Ordines domesticum quasi & naturale vehementer recruduit. Gaspar Scioppius pro Ordinibus Monasticis scripsit, Astrologiam Ecclesiasticam, id est, Disputationem de claritate ac multiplici virtute Stellarum in Ecclesiæ firmamento fulgentium, seu ordinum Monasticorum. Cui addidit: Astrum inextinctum, scilicet, pro Veterum Ordinum honore ac patrimoniis adversus famosum volumen Pauli Laimanni Iesuita in Monachos editum. uti frontispicio libri aperte loquitur. Verum non probe egisse mihi videtur Scioppius, quidquid sit de causa, quod librum non suum, vid. Astrum inextinctum, cum sua ad Imperatorem allocutione, ita ut fecit, conjunxerit, & sub suo nomine, quasi proprium fœtum ediderit, quem non ignorabat suum minime esse, sed Romani Hay, Ordinis Benedictini, qui librum istum, quem a.clɔ Ɩɔcxxx i scripsit, & Scioppius in suas manus devolutum a.clɔ Ɩɔcxxxiv. suo sub nomine edidit, ipse a.clɔ Ɩɔcxxxvi, suo cum nomine, atque additis variorum approbationibus demum emisit. Qua de re, in præfatione libri sui Romanus Hay contestatus fuit: Porro cum hoc ipsum nostrum Opusculum, à nobis ex jussu præcipuorum Ordinis nostri per Germaniam D.D. Abbatum, anno 1631 scriptum, ante sesquiannum in aliorum manus deveniens, nobis insciis & invitis, citra nomen Auctoris & debitam approbationem in lucem datum fuerit, Lectorem monere volumus, nos illam editionem ex officina Sangeorgiana 4.1634. (est hic liber Scioppii) pro fœtu nostro non agnoscere; quippe qua & manca, & per librariorum incuriam, tot mendis deformata prodierit, ut rara sit pagella, in qua, non dico littera, sed integra verba, sæpiusque sententiæ sunt prætermissæ. imo læpe integra folia; uti in ipsa illa præfatione, prout eam vel Scioppius, vel Hayus posuit, videre est. Nisi, quod alii in lucem emittere scriptum vel non ausi fuerunt, vel intempestivum arbitrati sunt, tum ob rem inter Ordines controversam, & à Commissariis Cæsareis privatim examinandam, neq; publicis scriptis exagitandam, præsertim absque nomine Auctoris, & Typographi, & approbatione Theologorum, id Scioppius pro antiquo suo & obfirmato erga Iesuitas affectu, sub suo nomine extrudere nequidquam veritus fuerit: sed male interim consuluit Lectoribus, qui legere nos voluit Gasparis Scioppii Astrum inextinctum, quod non ejus, sed Romani Hay est: atq; satis illi quoque exprobrat, qui adversus utrumque scripsit Astri inextincti deliquium Iohannes Crusius, Iesuita, in libri sui præfatione. Rationem tituli illius inde sumunt, quod tum per astrum Monasteria intelligunt, tum inextincta volunt, adversus principalem Iesuitarum hypothesim, qui præsuppononunt, extincta esse. Unde titulum libri sui Hay sic declarat; jus agendi antiquorum Religiosorum Ordinum, pro recipiendis suis Monasteriis (quæ nonnulli perperam extincta fuisse dicunt) & bonis Ecclesiasticis restituendis. Iesuitas hac in parte etiam perstrinxit Iuniperus de Ancona, in Consultatione, subjuncta Ludovici Soteli Relationi, de statu Ecclesiæ Iaponicæ, ad Vibanum
units.tr: Therefore, concerning the church goods that still exist, we offer that, when matters are brought to a Christian settlement in a Christian council or assembly, the goods shall then be left, without burden, to the church, the schools, and the other common needs of the land in our territories and dominions, as is often decided at Christian diets or imperial diets. For church goods are to be applied to maintain the preaching office, the Christian schools, and the other needs of the church and the land, as the Holy Scripture, the ancient councils, and the oldest canons, etc., make plain. And if all who have laid profane hands on goods of this kind had strictly observed this, the author of the Autonomia would not have had cause to cry out, to the discredit of the Protestants, in these words. "Where are your old foundations and monasteries? Is it not all profaned, abolished, torn down and laid waste? Have not bishoprics been made into secular principalities, church buildings into arsenals, stables, dance halls, powder magazines, bathhouses, etc., and monasteries into..." (part 3, chap. 16). And thus it appears that we are not those who profane ecclesiastical goods, since we teach that what was given to the churches under the papacy, though not rightly and indeed greatly polluted with superstition, is to be spent on sacred uses analogous to the donors' principal intention. Here we distinguish the principal and highest end of the donors' intention from the secondary end, and in general the proper end from the analogous end. Although in gifts or bequests made to the Church, men have sometimes erred in the secondary end, supposing that the worship of God lay in certain superstitious things, and that the ministry of the Church consisted in what the Papists taught, yet since the principal end was the worship of God, the ministry of the Church, the conversion of souls, and so on, to give their goods for this was good and pleasing to God; and in this we indeed count it a sin to defraud the donors' intentions and frustrate them. And since they erred in supposing that the worship of God lay in such trivial and abominable things as the Papists taught, the Reformation, by the grace of God, now corrects this; for had they known it, they would doubtless have followed it greatly. And we spend their legacies on holier uses, in which we also satisfy their wishes, while we assign those goods to sacred uses and increase them, by turning them to better uses, as they themselves supposed. Just as, had we been present to those donors as Reformed men, we could not have been mere dissuaders from giving to God and the Church, nor would it have been lawful to overturn pious bequests; but we would have fostered that holy intention and taught them, according to Reformed doctrine, to apply their goods to good uses. So now the Reformation does not teach that we should abolish the pious legacies of our forebears and profane them, but that we should preserve them and, where they lack something, correct and improve them, namely for the use they wholly intended, which was sacred, not profane, private, or foreign, but if necessary holier and purer, at least divine and pious. Such cases occur in the laws, in which it is safe to correct the wills of testators: C. de religios. & sumpt. l. & si quis §.9. "What then, if the expense was made by the will of the testator?" The will is not to be followed if the matter exceeds the reckoning of expense. D. de confirm. tutore l. x. The praetor follows the advantage of the wards, not the wording of the testament or codicils. Franciscus Sarmentus, in his book de Reditibus Ecclesiasticis, part 4, chap. 3: although a prince cannot remove or alter the lawful will of those who bequeath or contract, ordained to uses not pious, as has been said, yet since the care of public affairs and pious causes is especially committed to them, he may always, by his own judgment and for cause, change the will or the legacies made to pious causes. This is proved in l. legatum ff. de administrat. rer. ad civitat. pertinent., and in Clementine "quia contigit" de religios. dom., and it is most elegantly declared by R. Bishop Segob., Varia resolutio book 3, chap. 6, no. 7, and by John Dried, de libertate ecclesiastica book 2, p. 206. Paulus Laymannus, a Jesuit, in his Defensio of the Society of Jesus, in the cause of the monasteries of Germany, p. 23, says, secondly, that concerning last wills and pious foundations, on account of some case supervening or change of circumstances, to make an interpretation according to equity (epieikeia), and therefore to institute some material change, belongs not to the fullness of supreme power but to the ordinary power of a superior. On this ground Covarruvias teaches, on c. tua n. 12, de Testamentis, that by the authority of a bishop money destined by a testator for a certain pious use, not so necessary, may be spent on another pious use more necessary to the Christian commonwealth, to which need cannot be otherwise relieved, provided this is done with the consent of the heir or executors; and the same answer is given by Sa, s.v. Testamentum, n. 33. For in such a case the will of the testator or founder is not taken away but changed for the better. Since the intention and habitual and interpretative will of any Christian founder is that, if something has been left or given by him to the glory of God for a certain pious cause or place, and it is judged by the ecclesiastical prelates that it would be more conducive to the worship of God and the good of the Church that it be applied to another use (especially if his heir or successor also so judges and is content that such a material change be made), then such a change should be made. For in such pious dispositions of the dead, the concern is not their own rights or advantages but solely the worship of God and the increase of the Catholic Church; so this principal intention is above all to be considered, and if this is kept, nothing against the mind of the deceased or founder ought to be judged to have been done. Well known are the disputations of the Papal clerics in Germany from the year 1529 onward, concerning the monasteries and ecclesiastical goods which our people had recovered by whatever means, and which were transferred to other orders than those to which those goods formerly belonged, especially to the Jesuits; in which the Jesuits and the other orders, whose cause was then being argued, and especially the Benedictines, contended bitterly with one another in writing. For when the Emperor, on 6 March 1629, by the Edict of Restitution, had written to his envoy Savelli at Rome and to the various commissioners executing his edict throughout Germany, ordering that monasteries and ecclesiastical goods, which the Papists complained had been taken from them since the Peace of Passau, and whose cause the Protestants had brought to litigation before the tribunal of the Empire, or which had been recovered by arms, were to be assigned to them, so that they be restored according to the rule of foundations, to suitable persons and to each what seemed due to him, with suitable persons, appointed and qualified according to the foundations and endowments, and thus to each what is due to him, etc.; and when the Pope had also congratulated the Emperor on the published Edict of Restitution by his Brief of 5 May of the same year; and when already, in various places, he had assigned goods to his own orders, then the orders began to contend and dispute among themselves: the Jesuits insisting that, since the monasteries and goods seized by the Protestants were to be held as extinct and vacant, it was not necessary to assign them again to those orders to which they had belonged by foundation or gift; but that they might be given to another order, or to a pious cause, or to those who seemed to render more service and use to the Church, that is, to the Jesuits themselves, passing over the other orders. Hence books were written under this title: Disputation, or question, whether ecclesiastical goods and monasteries, especially those recently snatched from the hands of heretics and recovered by the victorious arms of the Emperor, can and indeed ought to be transferred to other families, or rather restored to the ancient orders, their former possessors? And then: A defence undertaken for His Imperial Majesty, and on his instruction to his envoy, concerning the prevention of changes to ancient foundations: against the judgment of two theologians, concerning the transfer to the Society of Jesus of the convents to be restored in the Empire. There followed Paulus Laymannus, a Jesuit, professor at Dillingen, who wrote a great volume: Just defence, etc., in so great a case of extinct monasteries and vacant ecclesiastical offices. He and his associates took the matter thus: that monasteries in which all the professed have died are to be regarded as extinct, and their ecclesiastical goods as vacant, and so are freely to be applied to other colleges or schools and parishes in Germany. And since the Jesuits here were chiefly intent on their own advantage, and taught that these goods were vacant so that they might more easily seize them under this pretext, as more profitable to themselves than to the other orders, and more useful to the Roman see, from this there broke out again vehemently that hatred between the Jesuits and the other orders, as if it were domestic and natural. Gaspar Scioppius wrote for the monastic orders Astrologia Ecclesiastica, that is, a disputation on the brightness and manifold virtue of the stars shining in the firmament of the Church, or the monastic orders. To this he added Astrum inextinctum, that is, in defence of the honour and patrimonies of the ancient orders, against the infamous volume of Paulus Laymannus, a Jesuit, published against the monks, as the title page of the book plainly says. Yet it seems to me that Scioppius did not act honestly, whatever the reason, in joining to his own address to the Emperor a book not his own, namely Astrum inextinctum, and in publishing it under his own name as if it were his own offspring, though he knew it was not his at all but that of Romanus Hay, a Benedictine, who had written that book in 1630, and which Scioppius, having got it into his hands in 1634, published under his own name; and Hay himself in 1636 published it under his own name, with the addition of various approbations. On this matter Romanus Hay, in the preface to his book, declared: Moreover, since this our little work, written by us in 1631 by order of the chief men of our order, the Lord Abbots throughout Germany, has come into other hands a year and a half ago, without our knowledge and against our will, and has been brought to light without the author's name and due approval, we wish to warn the reader that we do not acknowledge that edition from the Sangeorgian press of 1634 (this book is Scioppius's) as our offspring; since it came out both defective and, through the carelessness of the copyists, so disfigured with so many errors that there is scarcely a page in which not only letters but whole words, and often sentences, have not been omitted, indeed often whole leaves; as one can see in that very preface, as either Scioppius or Hay has printed it. Unless that other matter, which others did not dare to bring to light or thought ill-timed, because of the dispute between the orders, to be privately examined by the imperial commissioners and not to be argued in public writings, especially without the name of the author and printer and without the approval of theologians, Scioppius, out of his old and fixed affection towards the Jesuits, was not ashamed to put forth under his own name in vain. But meanwhile he has ill served the readers, who he wished should read Gaspar Scioppius's Astrum inextinctum, which is not his but Romanus Hay's; and John Crusius, a Jesuit, who wrote against both Astri inextincti deliquium in the preface to his book, sufficiently reproaches him too. They take the reason for that title from this: that they understand by the star the monasteries, and wish them to be unextinguished, against the principal hypothesis of the Jesuits, who presuppose that they are extinct. Hence Hay so explains the title of his book: the right of acting of the ancient religious orders, to recover their monasteries (which some wrongly say have been extinguished) and to have their ecclesiastical goods restored. Juniperus de Ancona also attacked the Jesuits on this point, in the Consultatio appended to Ludovicus Sotellus's Relatio de statu Ecclesiae Iaponicae, ad Vibanum

units.la: VIII. Adversus Hayum, inq; ejus Astrum Notas quoq; fecit Eu- genius Lavanda Ninivensis.
units.tr: VIII. Against Hay; Eugenius Lavanda of Nineveh also wrote notes on his Astrum.

units.la: Quin ulterius progressa hæc disputatio est, contentionibus aquarum fluctus imitantibus, qui ubi se mel ruptis aggeribus expatiantur, ad alia mox atq; alia, contra ac quis facile opinetur, facile propelluntur. Adversus Ordines dum de bonis disputabatur, quo ea melius illis auferri possent, illorum vitia in medium produci caperunt, idq; se cum fructu hic agere alii arbitrati sunt, ut scandala illorum propalarent, quasi eorum qui non satis digni essent, quibus ista bona redderentur. Adversus quæ se oppositi Dominicus Gravina, & qui ejus ad hoc argumentum spectantia edidit, Thomas de Saria, primum libro, sub tit. Vox Turturis, seu de florenti usque ad nostra ,,tempora Benedicti, Dominici, Francisci, & aliarum Religiónum num statu: quo quæ in honorem illarum familiarum dici ab illis potuisse videntur, prolata. Adversùs hæc pro Iesuitis a. clɔlɔcxxxı prodiit scriptum Monachii impressum Cavea Turturis, sub nomine Georgii Riedelii: in quo Ordines magnifice perstringuntur. Ex quo, qui alterum ei oppositum scriptum, Congeminata vox Turturis, è manuscriptis Tractatibus Gravinianis, iterum Thomas de Sarria, post præfationem, in singulari Indice, hæc nimirum protulit: 1. In religionibus gravia, multiplicia, orbi nota scandala reperiuntur. habetur in dicto lib. p. 8. 28. 51. 61. 65. Iustissime infamia denotari possunt religiosi, quando ipsi propriam famam prodigunt 126. nam & iustissime peccator hac quoque pœna multatur, ut qui bestiis assimilatur, famæ etiam dignitate privetur. 125. & p. 25 3. subinde etiam recte pronunciari posse, paucos ex regularibus laxis salutem adepturos esse eo quod raro solidè resipiscant. Quando stylum acuimus contra hæreticos, tunc defectus Religiosorum exemplare non possumus, possumus vero cum parænetice loquimur. pag. 35. In religionibus, non Centuriæ, sed nec Decades perfectorum possunt numerari, p. 111. proinde nonnisi, cum ætatis nostræ dedecore antiquorum agmina recensentur, ob mores illis antiquis beatis absimiles, 97. 99. Minime floridus est religiosorum præsens status, 39. 47. 88. 89. Pauci in eo mundo crucifixi. 93. Adeo infecunde vineæ religiosorum, ut vix racemi colligi possint, 47. 241. Religiones ante, & post Concilium Tridentinum deformatæ, 41. 49. Ardere flammis antiquam portionem domus Christi, veterum scilicet religionum, 81. Vix seni aut deni produci possunt ex universis Regularium Chronicis, qui in Theutoniæ Imperio doctrina, vel sanctitate floruerint, 2. 5. Hæretici in opinione confirmantur, quod intra suos fines, in dictis religionibus, nil generosum & excellens, sed meri pepones, allia & nasturtia nascantur, ibid. Pauci reperiuntur in religionibus Mendicantibus apti ad missiones, & conversionem infidelium, pag. 98. Aliorum religiosorum multitudo aliorum velificat, ibidem. Ad perfectionem non properant, qui pauculis secularibus convertendis insistunt. Vbi non est Ordo Iesuitarum, non apparet genuina sacramentorum frequentia, rudium Catechismi, nec ab aliis hæc & alia exercitia supplentur, ubi illa deficit. 219. Paucissimos piè victuros & salvandos regulares; plurimos salutem perdituros, 8. Non habetur florentissimus status religionum ex palmis eorum, qui pro Domino obierunt, & in Chronicis Ordinum leguntur, nam ex morte illata à Barbaris, vel hæreticis, & ex ipso martyrio præcedentis sanctitatis testimonium non colligitur: cum alio fine, quam Christi causa occumbere potuerint, nempe ex occidentium avaritia, timore politicæ eversionis, ipsorum occisorum temeraria provocatione, spontanea oblatione, 94. Inaniter recensentur, ad confusionem hæreticorum miracula, martyria, rigor vitæ, vel pœnitentiæ in Chronicis regularium descripta, cum hæc illi ut superstitiones, & somnia habeant 233. 234. Hodie visionum, ut divinationum insolita apud regulares audacia emergit, prout quisque magis se à publico contrahit, & orationi intentus est, 96.97. Ad saftum, & spumas hujus seculi pertinent tituli Doctorum & Inquisitorum, pag. 178. inde nec commendandæ exemptiones, prærogativæ, privilegia eorum. dem. ibidem. Nec Ordinum splendor habetur ex iis qui ad Ecclesiasticas dignitates assumpti. Vnde non sunt proponendæ oculis Regularium Thiaræ, Purpureæ, sunt enim velut vinum resplendens in vitro quod epotatum mordet ut coluber, pag.101. Proinde ab Episcopis oculos avertendos, ut à fœminis, 102. Novis Rechabitis non præponendi crateres, & vina preciosa, videlicet gemmatæ mitræ, purpureæ cum aurora certantes, 177. Hæretici Iesuitas proscribunt, alios religiosos benigne retentos alunt, non enim mordent lapidem, qui eos non ferit: originem suam agnoscunt, eique cognatam sobolem odisse nequeunt. 146. Multos in habitu Monastico damnari & specie recti nos falli, quid enim lateat in corde tentatio prodit, nam & Eremicolas legimus continuæ orationis & severissimæ vitæ & tamen Severiana labe corruptos, à regno cœlesti extorres, 106. Societatis Iesu ampliora mereatur tur, quam habeat, privilegia. Praterea ex Laymanno adducit ,, idem: à Nullo genere hominum majus damnum est illatum ,, Ecclesiæ, quam à veteribus Ordinibus, à quibus catervatim ,, pestilentesegressi sunt Hæresiarchæ. Monachos esse inutilia ,, terræ pondera, ventres pigros, stupidas pecudes: non esse Cœ- ,, nobia illis tradita à magnatibus tanquam pro hominibus ,, ,, inutilibus, ociosis, ignavis. Neque tamen omnia attulit, vel ex Riedelii Cavea, quæ ad Religiosorum Ordines pertinent, de quibus inter alia & hoc: Religiosorum multitudini il,,lud adaptari quod scriptum est in Esai. multiplicasti gentes, nō magnificasti lætitiam. quod Sarria citat, pag. 21. qui quantumvis congeminet vocem Turturis, multis paralangis strepitu cavcæ est inferior. Atque ita primum de bonis, tum de suo loco & dignitate Ordines cum Iesuitis contenderunt. Ordines pro se sic argumentabantur: Cæsar, ratione supremi ossicii sui, & vi à se editi Edicti, Monasteria recuperata iis restituere debet, qui olim iis spoliati fuerunt: atqui ordo v.g. Benedicti hoc vel illo Monasterio olim privatus fuit: quare iis illud videatur restituendum. Adjungebant: alienatio Monasteriorum & Ecclesiasticorum bonorum vel à Rom. Pontifice absque legitima causa facta, contraria est legi naturali ac divinæ: at Monasteriorum illa translatio ad Scholas, seminaria, aut Collegia Societatis Jesu est alienatio quædam facta sine legitima causa; proinde contraria legi naturali ac divinæ. Non quidem negari potest, sæpe factam Monasteriorum ab Ordine, ad Ordinem translationem, cujus indicem aliquem adfert Laymannus, in Appendice; sed uti hoc non licet absque justa causa, quæ potissimum est, quando Monachi vita & moribus, & disciplinæ contemtu ejusmodi pœna & privatione dignos se faciunt, ita hic ubi bellica armorum tempestate spoliatos se dicebant reliqui Ordines (quorum præcipui erant Benedictini,) Monasteriis bonisque suis, Iesuitis illa concedi, & non propriis Ordinibus, ferre illi haud poterant. Ego quidem existimem, ex Edicto Restitutorio Cæsaris (de quo non disputo nunc quam iniquum fuerit in Protestantes, & intempestivum) neutiquam concludi posse, animum Imperatoris fuisse transferre bona & Monasteria ad Ordines alios, vel ad Iesuitas, sed in genere tantum edixisse, illa, Protestantibus ablata, suis reddenda esse; atque quamvis jura non obstent, quominus Monasteria & bona aliquando transferri in alios possunt, semper vero ad usus Ecclesiasticos, cæteris tamen paribus (loquor nunc ad Pontificios) præferendos esse pristinos dominos vel possessores, & non urgente translationis necessitate, æquius videri, & hoc Edictum Cæsaris probare quoque, ut juxta rationem, fundationem, & usum aut possessionem præcedentium, non Iesuitis, in aliorum præjudicium, sed quorum illa fuerunt Ordinibus (ex sensu Cæsareo loquor, & Pontificio) applicarentur. Pro Veteribus Ordinibus, adversus Iesuitas, judicavit quoque, & scripsit ad S. Congregationem Romæ a.cIↄ Iↄcxxx Cardinalis Richelius. Neque adeo hoc disputarunt Ordines Monasticis: an transferri in alios religiosos monasteria, bonaq;, gravi aliquando de causa, possint; ac an causa talis aliquahodie adesset, ob quā Monasteria jā essent transferenda? quæ secunda apud Hayum, vel Scioppium, quæ tractatur, est quæstio. In controversia, de qua mox obiter quoque, alia Martinus Aspilcueta, Navarrus, Apol. de Reditib. Eccles. pag. 90. dixit: Nam argumenta non tendunt ad probandum, quod Monarchæ non possunt mutare voluntates defunctorum; sed quod nemo antequam id justa de causa fiat, potest rebus in unum usum pium dicatis, uti ad alium; & quod nullius Monarchia, saltem spiritualis, justa de causa, imo neque injusta, statuit, ut beneficiarii possint in usus profanos uti rebus dicatis ad pios. Verum illa omnia de monasteriis Germanicis sopita nunc vel decisa sunt pacis nuperæ articulis, ubi decretum, restituenda omnia esse in statum, quem a. xxiv hujus seculi habuerunt. Quare, quum juxta Pontificios etiam, bona Ecclesiarum transferri possint in alias Ecclesias, vel collegias, dummodo ad usus pios, & meliores applicentur, neque hoc fit aut contra naturam & jus bonorum istorum, vel fundatorum intentionem ac voluntatem, quid adeo obstat, si apud nostras illa permaneant Ecclesias, atque hic ad usus bonos, pios, sanctos, meliores etiam quam sub Papatu, & Ecclesiarum nostrarum sa-cta ēta jam adhibeantur ? nam bona Ecclesiastica quoad Dominium, sunt Ecclesiæ ejus particularis cui donata sunt, inquit Laymannus Iesuita, pag. 5. non verò pertinent ad Romanum Pontificem tanquam ad Dominum, inquit. De quo vehementer disputant Canonistæ, cui bonorum Ecclesiasticorum adscribendum sit dominium. Alii Christo assignant, cujus proinde illa dicantur patrimonium: sed hoc alienum est à præsenti quæstione, quum dominium Dei aut Christi uti supra omnia est, ita non adversatur dominio humano, quod distinctionem rerum ponit apud homines, & de quo hic quæritur, non de illo. Quare Pontifici Romano alii; alii Ecclesiæ; quidam universali; melius particulari, cui illa attributa sunt; alii denique pauperibus adscribunt. Vide Franciscum Sarmientum, lib. de Redditibus Ecclesiasticis, cap. 1. Antonium Marsilium Columnam, lib. de Ecclesiasticorum Redituum origine, & jure, part. III. Verum hæc alio insuper fine ab illis disputantur, &c. ob quæstionem præcipue agitatam post Archidiaconū celebri Canonista, & qui in variis Galliæ, Hispaniæ; Academiis, ut Caturci, Tholosæ, Salmanticæ, & Conimbricæ Canonum Professor fuit, Martino ab Azpilcueta Navarro, primum in Manuali Confessariorum, cap. xxv. num. 126. tum in singulari ejus argumenti libro, de Reditibus beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, primum Hispanice, deinde etiam Latine; denique in libri illius Apologia: an Clerici beneficiarii sint reddituum suorum Ecclesiasticorum domini, ita ut de illis etiam queant disponere. Quod adeo negabat Navarrus, ut non tantum assereret, Clericum ne vestis quidem, qua se quotidie induit, dominum esse, pag. 1 i. sed nec panè etiam quem manducat, ejus esse, pag. 14. verum etiam, quod aliam movit quæstionem, Clericum abstentem reditibus, vel beneficiarium impendentem superflue, vel profane reditus suorum beneficiorum teneri ad restitutionem, pag. 125. atque de reditibus beneficiorum beneficiarium testari non posse pag. 154. Hoc potissimum argumento, quod Christus est bonorum Ecclesiasticorum dominus, non generali solum ratione, qua Domini est terra & plenitudo ejus, sed speciali quoque & humana dispositione, sicut alii omnes; benefi-ciarii autem dispensatores tantum & procuratores. In hanc etiam sententiam videtur loqui Cornelius à Lapide, in 1. Ioann. III. 17. Contrarium vero alii rectius tenuerunt, Clericos non solum de fructibus seu reditibus Ecclesiasticis pofse sibi & his qui sibi seruiunt necessaria affumere, sed quod & reliqua quæ supersunt, non iterum teneantur erogare in pauperes, vel alios vsus Ecclesiæ, sed quod possint de illis, prout fibuerit, disponere, tanquam veri & proprii istorum reddituum domini. Quæ fuit sententia Thomæ, quamvis in aliam, & suam eum trahere allaboret Navarrus. Alias plures super hac re opiniones profert Sarmentus, lib. de Redit. Eccles. part. II. sed illæ sunt præcipuæ atque posterior illa, quæ etiam Sarmenti est, tot tamque validis ab eo part. IV. astruitur rationibus & argumentis, ut quod alii ea dissolvere possint, ego quidem non videam. Primo argumentatur ex tex. in c.2. de cleric.non residentibus, ubi clericis non residentibus in pœnam adjicitur ne dominium distributionum acquirant, sed ad restitutionem teneantur, ergo apparet fi residerent effici dominos earundem. Secundo, probatur per textum in c. pervenit extra de fideiussor. ubi probat textus, quod, fi clerici are alieno gravati reperiantur, debet satisfieri creditoribus de fructibus beneficiorum; quod fieri non deberet, fi non effent domini fructuum, non enim de alieno debito solvi possunt, effet namque debitum delicto commutare. Ne omnia ejus argumenta colligam, aliqua duntaxat, sexto loco ita argumentatur:quod ex prædicta divisione pauperibus, vel pauperi tribuitur, ita fit ipsius pauperis, ut nulla obligatione astrictus sit, etiam si aliquid sibi super sit, restituere. nec aliquis unquam pauperis rem sibi datam pleno jure ejus effici negavit, ergo idem dicendum est de clerico quoad portionem sibi assignatam. Tum, si miles suum facit stipendium, si suam mercedem, quare clericus reddit us in stipendium sibi assignatos suos non efficiet? Consuetudinem etiam adducit: nam in Hispania consuetudo est, cujus origo memoriam excedit, qua clericis non episcopis permissum est, ut in vita, & in morte de fructibus beneficiorum disponant, & habeant successores ab intestato, si intestati decesserint, episcopi vero in vita tantum disponunt, addit Columna,cap.xxxvi. & Galliam.Eandem sententiam sequitur is Antonius Marsilius Columna, lib.de Ecclesiasticorum redituum origine, part.iii. cap. xxi. qui ibidem neque vult argumentum illud, quemadmodum vulgo sumitur, procedere, à non dominio clericorum, ad restitutionis obligationem, ad-eoque non esse commiscendas quæstiones, an Clerici benefi-ciarii sint domini reddituum Ecclesiasticorum, &, an si male illos consumant, ad restitutionem teneantur. Insuper cap. xxvi. alias rationes, pro sententia Thomæ (quam & cap. ult. docet, Clericos non modo bonorum vel reddituum suo-rum Ecclesiasticorum dominos facere, sed etiam ab omni restitutionis onere liberare) adducit, postquam cap. superiori xxv. ad rationes, à Sarmento allatas multum respondisset. Hanc tamen ille sententiæ tuæ adhibet cap. xxxiii. limitationem, ut quamvis Clericus non teneatur ad restitutionem, vel si maximè Ecclesiæ rebus abutatur, tamen hoc non procedat, quando ipse prorsus officium deserit. Sententiæ suæ numerat assertores quinquaginta quinque Doctores; adversariæ quæ Archidiaconi, triginta & quatuor. cap. xxxiv. & xxxv. Compendiose Sarmentus in præfat. ad P. Pium v. oraverat eum, ut apostolica sua authoritate, ad quid ex præcepto homines teneantur, quidve ex consilio hic sequi expediret, constitueret; sed nec hactenus (quod sciam) id fecit Papa, neque in plurimis istiusmodi litigiis, quantumcunque etiam vehementer inter suos agitatis, id conatur quidem: quod mirum profecto, quum & penes se esse judicium Theologicarum quæstionum infallibile, & jura omnia in scrinio pectoris sui asservari, asserat, denique & inter alios, ab ipsius communione alienos, atque de rebus multum gravioribus, judicem se adiri velit, qui non domi suæ fluctus istos componere poterit, aut vult. Sed in viam. Scimus hoc ab ipsis adeo Gentilibus cum religione servatum, ut & testatorum ultimas implerent voluntates, & Deo aliquando consecrata ne quis temeraret, aut in suos converteret usus. Hoc Pythagoram isto lym. symbolo denotasse volunt: ne coacervet ligna cupressina, id est, Deo consecrata bona, siquidem ex cupresso Iovis formabatur sceptrum. Pisistratus, apud Laertium, in vita Solonis, hinc scribit: Denique Atheniensium singuli decimas frugum suarum separant, non in usus nostros consumendas, verum sacrificiis publicis commodisque communibus: & siquando bellum contra nos ingruerit, in sumtus deputandas. Ex legibus XII Tabularum est: Sacrum, Sacrove commendatum qui clepserit, rapseritque pariter caesio esto. Qui nuper scripsit, vel edidit hodiernorum Brachmannum, aut Brachminum historiā, Rogerius, de eorum vita, doctrina, moribusque; ait, neq; Regem nec quempiam audere agrum vel villam Brachminibus donatam ipsis auferre, quia Numinis sui verentur gravem vindictam, si quando pauperibus Brachmannis sua auferre conarentur, lib. I. cap. VI. quale quid accidisse narrant suo Regi Rama Dewelo, ejusque ministro, dum e Pagodum aedibus thesauros quosdam auferre molirentur. lib. II. cap. X. Adde Valerium Maximum lib. I. cap. 1. Quae dum non ignoramus, jubent nos à violandis bonis Ecclesiasticis, id est, iisque Deo in cultum ejus, Ecclesiaeque Ministerium data, donata sunt, abstinere; eoque nos fortius abstolvunt ab illa contumelia, quam nobis frustra impingit Papa, quasi bona Ecclesiis auferamus, & non in usus Ecclesiasticos impendenda doceamus. Quod secus se habere, puto jam abunde ex iis quae attulimus, constare cuivis posse. v. Quin etiam olim in foedere Passaviensi concessa sunt imperiali authoritate Protestantibus bona Ecclesiastica, quaecunque tum, quantumlibet à Papistis derivata & occupata, nostri possiderent, inque usus Ecclesiasticos impenderent. Atque ante foedus Passaviense, in conventu Haganoico a. clo Ixxh ad Pontificiorum objectionem, de bonis Ecclesiasticis à nostris interversis, aliosque in usus direptis applicatisque, responderunt: se nullius bona occupasse, tantum post resi auratam puritatis suae doctrinam, bona quoque ad legitimos honestosque usus, quibus principio fuerant destinata, sed ab Ecclesiasticis postmodum interversa, denuo applicasse, eoque primum capita doctrinae definienda, verum de bonis esse loquendum. Ita in Historia Conc. Trident. lib. i. Apud Sleidanum, lib. xiii. sed neminem ab se spoliatum, & hanc ipsam quaestionem ad colloquium & futuram actionem pertinere, nec sequestrationem fieri posse dicunt, absque magna sua ditionis ecclesiastica politia dissipatione, scholarum etiam atque pauperum incommodo: & quia non longum sit tempus ad colloquii diem, ut eo res omnis differatur, petunt: ibi se demonstraturos, quanto plus laborent atque soliciti sint de gloria Dei, deque ecclesiarum emendatione, quam de possessionibus atque bonis: ac licet docere jam possint, quomodo nonnulli diver(sa partis, id genus facultates ad se fere rapiant, velle tamen eosque differre: cumque tunc ejus rei sermo fiet, liquidum esse futurum, utri possessiones illas in suum emolumentum privatum magis, quam ad honorem Dei convertant, & quid obstet, quo minus in meliores usus applicentur. Quid ergo nunc tandem de novo litem ob bona illa Nostris adjudicata, vindicataque movet Papa? Praecipue quum illa etiam Passavien sis hac nupera Osnabrugensi iterum confirmata pax sit art. v. Decretu in Conventu tum primo Lintzii mox Passaviae habito, d. 11. Augusti a. cIↄ Iↄ Ii. est, quod pax religionis, sive controversia componantur, sive non componantur, erit rata & firma. denique a. cIↄ Iↄ lv. d. xxv Septemb. in Comitiis Augustanis confirmata illa Passavien sis pax, statutumque, ut bona Ecclesiastica, dummodo non essent Status Imperii, aut ad eosdem spectarent, quaeque ante transactionem, Passavien sem occupassent Nostri, & ad pios usus transtulissent, nec in judicio, nec extra judicium, repeti, neque ideo conveniri Nostripossent. Sleidanus, Comment. lib. xxvi. Thuanus, hist. lib. xvi. Quorum non satis callens est quisquis aliter haec capit, quam, quod cum pax illa religionis Augustae a. 1555. ficeret, convenerit inter Imperatorem & Principes Protestantes Imperii, ut bona Ecclesiastica ab istis occupata, in usus pios converterentur. Quod enim dictum, ut manerent in eo statu, in quo tempore illo erant, hoc significat, illa penes Protestantes mansura, quae jam illi tenerent, non vero Pontificiis cedenda esse: at, ut apud Protestantes etiam in usus sacros applicata erant: cui illi sane noluerunt ullo pacto adversari; huic quidem quod dicerent Pontificii, non satis fideliter bona illa à Protestantibus ad usus sacros applicari, ideoque quasi non servatis pacis Passaviensis conditionibus, tuto illa ab ipsis repeti posse. Nam sic ex tabulis foederis argumentabantur Bonorum Ecclesiasticorum detentores, etiam in externo foro censeri, & ad restitutionem compelli debent.
units.tr: The dispute went further still, like the surging of waters: once the dykes are broken and the floods spread out, they are soon driven on to one thing after another, in a way no one would easily have expected. While the debate about the property of the religious orders was under way, with a view to taking those goods away from them more easily, their faults began to be brought into the open. Some thought they would gain something by exposing this, namely to reveal the scandals of the orders, as if they were people unworthy to have those goods restored to them. Against this stood Dominicus Gravina, and Thomas de Sarria, who published what bears on this subject. In the first book, under the title Vox Turturis (The Voice of the Turtledove), Sarria set out, from the flourishing time of Benedict, Dominic, Francis and the other orders down to our own times, the state of the religious orders, and he put forward whatever could seem to have been said in honour of those families. In reply to this, in 1631, a writing was printed at Munich in defence of the Jesuits under the name of Georg Riedel, Cavea Turturis (The Turtledove's Cage), in which the orders are savagely attacked. Thereafter Thomas de Sarria, who had written against the other writing, Congeminata vox Turturis (The Doubled Voice of the Turtledove), drawn from the manuscript treatises of Gravina, again after a preface and in a special index, brought forward the following points, namely: 1. In the religious orders there are serious, numerous scandals, known throughout the world. This is found in the said book, pp. 8, 28, 51, 61, 65. Religious men can most justly be called infamous when they squander their own good name (p. 126), for the sinner too is most justly punished by this penalty, that, since he is compared to the beasts, he is also deprived of the dignity of a good name (p. 125). And on p. 253 he says that it can also rightly be declared, from time to time, that few of the lax regulars will obtain salvation, because they seldom repent in earnest. When we sharpen our pen against heretics, we cannot hold up the faults of the religious as an example; but we can when we speak in the manner of exhortation (p. 35). Among the religious orders, not hundreds, nor even tens, of perfect men can be counted (p. 111). Hence the ancient companies are reckoned up only with shame to our own age, for their morals are unlike those blessed ancients (pp. 97, 99). The present state of the religious is by no means flourishing (pp. 39, 47, 88, 89). Few in this world are crucified (p. 93). The vineyards of the religious are so unfruitful that scarcely a cluster can be gathered (pp. 47, 241). The religious orders were deformed both before and after the Council of Trent (pp. 41, 49). The ancient portion of the house of Christ, that is, the old orders, is burning with flames (p. 81). Scarcely six or ten can be brought forward from all the chronicles of the regulars who flourished in learning or holiness in the Empire of the Germans (pp. 2, 5). Heretics are confirmed in their opinion, because within the borders of those orders nothing noble or excellent grows, but only mere melons, garlic and cress (ibid.). Few are found among the mendicant orders fit for missions and the conversion of unbelievers (p. 98). The multitude of the other religious is a burden that weighs down the rest (ibid.). Those who devote themselves to converting a few laymen do not hasten towards perfection. Where the Order of the Jesuits is not present, the genuine frequent use of the sacraments, the instruction of the ignorant in the catechism, and these and other exercises are not carried on by others to make up for their lack (p. 219). Very few regulars will live piously and be saved; very many will lose their salvation (p. 8). The most flourishing state of the orders is not shown by the palms of those who died for the Lord and are read of in the chronicles of the orders. For the testimony of previous holiness is not gathered from death inflicted by barbarians or heretics, or from martyrdom itself, since they could have fallen for some other purpose than the cause of Christ: namely, through the greed of their killers, fear of political overthrow, the rash provocation of the slain themselves, or voluntary offering (p. 94). Miracles, martyrdoms, and the rigour of life or penance described in the chronicles of the regulars are recounted to no purpose, to the confusion of heretics, since they regard these as superstitions and dreams (pp. 233, 234). Today a strange boldness in visions and divinations emerges among the regulars, in proportion as each withdraws more from public life and is intent on prayer (p. 96, 97). The titles of Doctors and Inquisitors belong to the froth and foam of this age (p. 178). Hence their exemptions, prerogatives and privileges are not to be commended (ibid.). Nor is the splendour of the orders found in those who have been raised to ecclesiastical dignities. Hence the purple mitres of the regulars are not to be set before our eyes, for they are like wine sparkling in a glass which, once drunk, bites like a serpent (p. 101). Accordingly, bishops must turn their eyes away from them, as from women (p. 102). Bowls and precious wines, that is, jewelled mitres vying with the purple of dawn, are not to be set before the new Rechabites (p. 177). Heretics proscribe the Jesuits, while they keep and nourish the other religious kindly; for the stone does not bite one who is not struck by it, and they recognise their own origin and cannot hate the offspring related to them (p. 146). Many are condemned in monastic habit, and we are deceived by the appearance of what is right; for what lies hidden in the heart is revealed by temptation. For we read of hermits who were of continual prayer and most severe life, and yet, corrupted by the stain of Severus, were cast out from the heavenly kingdom (p. 106). The Society of Jesus deserves more ample privileges than it has. Besides, the same author quotes from Laymann: "No class of men has done more harm to the Church than the old orders, from which the heresiarchs went out in droves, pestilent men. The monks are useless burdens on the earth, lazy bellies, stupid cattle; the monasteries were not given to them by the magnates as to men who were useless, idle and sluggish." Nor did he bring forward everything, even from Riedel's Cavea, which pertains to the orders of the religious; among other things, this too: that what is written in Isaiah, "You have multiplied the nations, you have not increased the joy," is to be applied to the multitude of the religious. Sarria cites this at p. 21; but however much he doubles the voice of the turtledove, he is inferior in the noise of his cage to many parrots. And so the orders first contended with the Jesuits about their property, and then about their own place and dignity. The orders argued for themselves as follows: The Emperor, by reason of his supreme office and by the force of the edict he issued, must restore the recovered monasteries to those who were once despoiled of them. But the Order of Benedict, for example, was once deprived of this or that monastery; therefore it seems that it ought to be restored to them. They added: the alienation of monasteries and ecclesiastical goods, made without lawful cause, whether by the Roman Pontiff or by anyone else, is contrary to natural and divine law. But the transfer of those monasteries to the schools, seminaries or colleges of the Society of Jesus is a kind of alienation made without lawful cause; therefore it is contrary to natural and divine law. It cannot indeed be denied that the transfer of monasteries from one order to another has often been made, of which Laymann brings forward some index in his Appendix; but just as this is not permitted without a just cause, which is chiefly when monks make themselves worthy of such punishment and deprivation by their life, their morals and their contempt of discipline, so here, where the remaining orders (chiefly the Benedictines) said they had been despoiled of their monasteries and goods in the storm of war, they could not bear that those things should be granted to the Jesuits and not to their own orders. For my part, I think that from the Emperor's Edict of Restitution (about which I do not now dispute how unjust it was towards the Protestants, and how untimely) it cannot in any way be concluded that the Emperor's intention was to transfer the goods and monasteries to other orders, or to the Jesuits; he only decreed in general that those things taken from the Protestants were to be returned to their own owners. And although no laws stand in the way of monasteries and goods being sometimes transferred to others, yet, other things being equal (I am now speaking to the Papists), the former lords or possessors should always be preferred for ecclesiastical uses, and, unless there is an urgent need for transfer, it seems more equitable; and this Edict of the Emperor also proves that, according to reason, foundation and the use or possession of the earlier holders, those goods should be applied not to the Jesuits to the prejudice of others, but to those orders to which they belonged (I speak in the sense of the Emperor and of the Pontiff). Cardinal Richelieu also judged and wrote in favour of the old orders against the Jesuits, to the Sacred Congregation at Rome, in 1630. Nor did the monastic orders dispute this: whether monasteries and goods may ever, for a grave reason, be transferred to other religious; and whether such a reason exists today, by which monasteries are now to be transferred. This second question is the one treated by Hay or Scioppius. In the controversy I mention in passing, Martín de Azpilcueta, the Navarrese, said in his Apologia de Reditibus Ecclesiasticis (p. 90): "For the arguments do not tend to prove that monarchs cannot change the wishes of the dead; but that no one, before this is done for a just reason, can use things dedicated to one pious purpose for another; and that no monarchy, at least a spiritual one, has decreed, for a just reason, or even an unjust one, that beneficed men may use for profane purposes things dedicated to pious ones." But all those matters concerning the German monasteries have now been laid to rest, or decided, by the articles of the recent peace, where it was decreed that everything is to be restored to the state it was in on 1 January of this century. Wherefore, since according to the Papists too, the goods of churches may be transferred to other churches or colleges, provided they are applied to pious and better uses, and this is not done against the nature and right of those goods, or against the intention and will of their founders, what hinders their remaining in our churches, and being now applied here to good, pious, holy and better uses, even better than under the Papacy, and to the holy needs of our churches? For ecclesiastical goods, as regards ownership, belong to the particular church to which they were given, says the Jesuit Laymann (p. 5); they do not pertain to the Roman Pontiff as to their lord, he says. This is hotly disputed by the canonists, to whom the ownership of ecclesiastical goods is to be ascribed. Some assign it to Christ, whose property they are therefore said to be; but this is foreign to the present question, since the dominion of God or Christ is over all things, and so it does not oppose human ownership, which establishes the distinction of things among men, and it is that which is asked here, not the other. Hence some ascribe it to the Roman Pontiff, others to the Church, some to the universal Church, more properly to the particular church to which the goods were assigned, and finally others to the poor. See Francisco Sarmiento, de Redditibus Ecclesiasticis, bk. 1, ch. 1; Antonio Marsilio Colonna, de Ecclesiasticorum Redituum origine et iure, part 3. But these matters are debated by them for a further purpose as well, namely the question chiefly stirred up after the Archdeacon, Martín de Azpilcueta, the Navarrese, a famous canonist who was professor of canon law in various academies of France and Spain, such as Cahors, Toulouse, Salamanca and Coimbra: first in his Manuale Confessariorum, ch. 25, n. 126, then in his special book on this subject, de Reditibus beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, first in Spanish and then also in Latin, and finally in the Apologia of that book. The question is whether beneficed clerics are the owners of their ecclesiastical revenues, so that they may also dispose of them. Navarrus denied this so strongly that he not only asserted that a cleric is not even the owner of the clothing he puts on every day (p. 11), nor even of the bread he eats (p. 14); but also, raising another question, that a cleric who abstains from his revenues, or who spends the revenues of his benefices superfluously or on profane things, is bound to restitution (p. 125); and that a beneficed man cannot make a will concerning the revenues of his benefice (p. 154). His chief argument for this was that Christ is the lord of ecclesiastical goods, not only by the general reason by which the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord, but also by a special and human disposition, as all others are; while beneficed men are only stewards and procurators. Cornelius à Lapide also seems to speak in this sense, on 1 John 3.17. Others, however, more rightly held the contrary: that clerics may not only take for themselves and for those who serve them what is necessary from the fruits or revenues of the Church, but that they are not bound to pay out again to the poor or to other uses of the Church what remains over, but may dispose of it as they please, as the true and proper owners of those revenues. This was the opinion of Thomas, although Navarrus labours to draw him into another opinion of his own. Sarmiento sets out several other opinions on this matter in his de Redditibus Ecclesiasticis, part 2; but these are the chief ones, and the latter, which is also Sarmiento's own, is supported by him with so many and such strong reasons and arguments in part 4 that I, for my part, do not see how others could dissolve them. First he argues from the text in c. 2 de clericis non residentibus, where, as a penalty for clerics who are not resident, it is added that they do not acquire ownership of the distributions, but are bound to restitution; therefore it appears that if they were resident they would become the owners of them. Second, it is proved by the text in c. pervenit, extra de fideiussoribus, where the text shows that if clerics are found burdened with debt, the creditors must be satisfied from the fruits of the benefices; which would not have to be done if they were not owners of the fruits, for they cannot be paid from another's debt, since that would be to change the punishment into a crime. Not to gather all his arguments, I will set out only a few; in the sixth place he argues thus: what is given to the poor, or to a poor man, by the aforesaid division, becomes so much the property of the poor man himself that he is not bound by any obligation to restore it, even if something is left over to him; nor has anyone ever denied that a thing given to a poor man becomes his by full right; therefore the same must be said of a cleric as regards the portion assigned to him.
