units.tr: In these matters we had to be more careful, because to refute properly the objection that the Pope and the Papists raise against us concerning Church property, we had to remove the charge that our Churches and our doctrine are hostile to it. On this charge the papal abrogation and condemnation of the German peace is built, as though we wished Church property (and the first and all the doctors of the Reformation speak of it fearlessly, as we have now amply seen) to be spent, contrary to its nature, not on the uses of the Church but on the uses of private persons. Those who hold this are the Church property of Christ, given and bequeathed for ecclesiastical uses. Nothing is gained against us by what a learned man recently wrote concerning the canons, whom I otherwise value highly. In that writing he displayed, I admit, a wide reading, but almost only that; his judgement is poor, and his fairness and respect, both towards others and towards his own venerable teacher, are very bad. Because that book has been printed under this one bad disposition, I certainly grieve for it, and the author himself will grieve for it too (I am quite sure) when he has grown more mature. Or else the man whom he now attacks so unworthily will, once dead, be missed, and the book will have lost its weight with readers of sound and composed mind through its own fault. What, I beg you, is it that a matter cannot be handled without insults, not among learned men? And a matter so great, which demands a clear judgement and a settled mind? Is this how a cause is won, when you tear to pieces the names of others, whom in view of their age, rank or office you ought always to respect, and insult them so insolently? You will acknowledge neither what God has bestowed on others so abundantly, nor how to use well what has been given to you. But by the just judgement of God it comes about that, driven by such purposes, you neither do what you ought, nor even do what you seem to be doing. Certainly in the book I mean, one may readily observe that when it is read again, once its author has sometimes calmed his mind, outside those passages in which the surge of feeling was conceived and poured out, he will, I think, come to disapprove of it himself, if not the matter, at least the manner of handling and treating it. For example, I recall Andreas Zebedaeus (on whom I want you to read that whole paragraph which Beza writes in the Life of Calvin under the year 1555, and judge whether those things can be fittingly applied here). After he had long and bitterly opposed Calvin with various calumnies, and when Calvin was dead and he himself was about to die, at Nyon, a town four miles from Geneva, he summoned the leading citizens, freely acknowledged the truth he had attacked, detested all his own writings, and ordered all his papers to be burnt in his sight. Indeed our present author has neither used, nor been able to use, what those whom he seems to favour wish to use. There are four hypotheses on which his whole disputation rests, and once these are dislocated or removed the whole thing (I do not refuse to let him be the judge here) collapses. In all of them I will show with one finger how badly he has gone astray, because I do not now intend to enter upon that subject; I will show and defend only what my disputation requires, namely that the teaching of the Church is no other than I asserted before from our doctors: that Church property must be spent on ecclesiastical uses, not on the uses of private persons. First, he argues as if the matter he treats concerned only the idolatrous property of the Churches, that is, goods granted to the Church but only for idolatrous and superstitious uses, as though the Church had no other property free from superstition, or as though the question did not extend even to those. At least then let him allow that whatever goods are found to have been given to the Churches and the poor, outside idolatrous and superstitious use, remain safe and entire for those very persons to whom they were given, and that they are to be held apart from his disputation and its conclusion. That he fixes his disputation constantly on idolatrous property appears from pages 28, 97, 228, 229, 231, 239, 289, 325, and so on, whence he also everywhere calls them idolatrous and pseudo-ecclesiastical goods. Although indeed much under the Papacy, and chiefly from the ninth century [κτήμα], as you say on p. 28, was given to the Churches out of the opinion of merit and for the redemption of souls, etc., it must by no means be said either that all were imbued with these erroneous opinions, or that all the gifts were built on this false foundation. And so that this may stand, I hope you will not pronounce the same about the time when Papism began to decline and to sink towards its end; nor about the earlier centuries, the middle time, as you say on p. 13, in which, after Constantine, there was great liberality of princes and private persons towards the Church, when many gave whole estates to the Churches consecrated for that purpose, as you show from Basil; nor how far you make the Germans converted to Christ wholly free from the doctrine of Antichrist, p. 83, down to the times of Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, which was in the year 845. He succeeded Willibrord in the bishopric of Utrecht; at that time the German Churches were, as is clear not only from the charters and the confirmations of earlier gifts made under that Boniface by King Pepin, but also from the dispute which arose at that time between our Church of Utrecht and that of Cologne, admirably endowed by the kings of the Franks and others. The archbishop of Cologne asserted that Utrecht belonged to him, by a gift of King Dagobert; Utrecht maintained that it looked directly to the Roman see; but our church could not stand against Cologne, which, as Beka says, abounded in great resources. Therefore the gifts made to the Churches up to this point ought by no means be regarded as antichristian. But let the charters themselves be inspected, for to them the disputation returns, and the matter itself declares that they should be heard as soon as possible; and who would refuse? It will certainly become clear that various bequests were made to the Churches, with every notion and mention of papal superstition omitted, or at least indicated only faintly. You will find, in the customary formulas: for the love of God, for the honour of God, for love of divine worship, for the support of clergy so that they might be constantly free for prayer, to obtain mercy at the last judgement, for the house of God, for performing the service of God, for the work of the Church, we give to God, in honour of our Lord Jesus Christ, for the love of God, for the cause of the fear of God, on account of God. Also: We favour the just and reasonable petitions of the priests out of love of divine worship, and we expect the reward of this from the grace of Christ, as is read in the charter of King Conrad under Bishop Rabbod. For reforming and confirming the worship of religion, in the charter of Dagobert, King of the Franks, in the year 639. Elsewhere: that they might always be free for the service of God. On account of the name of the Lord, or heavenly love. For the love of God. In the charter of Hincmar and other bishops, at the Synod of Verberie, in the year 870: for the uses, they say, of lights, of the matricular, and of other things which are needed in the Churches in the aforesaid monastery of Vedast. In the same place: for a hospital of true poor people, etc., and this and that. In a charter granting to the same monastery by Charles the Bald: providing for the future, if in any way we can provide for the salvation of the faithful and the stability of the Churches of Christ. In another: that there may not fail in them (that is, in the Churches) the praise of God from the mouths of men, and the holy worship of the Christian religion, whence mortals aspire to blessedness. Baldwin of Jerusalem, in the year 1081, in a charter for building a church in the city of Valence: That this place may not be empty of divine worship, we have appointed clergy there to serve God. Elsewhere: for the use of those serving the Lord there, to be of benefit for ever. For the increase of the service of God, of God. For the increase of divine worship. For the conversion of unbelievers, which Nolter, as he does at p. 83, to explain as if they were Christians not yet conformed to the rule of antichristian faction, is surely a wretched and ridiculous interpretation. But the mission of Boniface is recorded in Aventinus as undertaken for the enlightenment of the Gentiles, although Christian churches were already in Germany. Reply. There were Churches of Christ professing the name in Germany even before Boniface, even before Willibrord; nor was Christianity introduced into these regions by them. Heda, at the beginning of his history, says that the Evangelical word had long since been sown in lower Germany; Willibrord and others came here from England. But no one except the most ignorant of historians would deny that very many places were still given over to heathenism in the times of Boniface and Willibrord, for whose conversion to the Christian religion they laboured, and were sent chiefly to undertake this, although, through the error of their age, they set themselves to serve the Roman Pontiff more than was right. And that by "Gentiles", for whose enlightenment they were destined, are meant idolaters, pagans and unbelievers, to be brought under the Roman discipline and not Christians, is most certain. For where have you ever read that Christians who professed the doctrine of Christ were called unbelievers, or Gentiles, or pagans, and that by Christians themselves and the teachers of Christianity? Surely Egbert the Englishman, who sent Willibrord to these shores, just as, before him, Wigbert is said to have sent both from here and from there, sent him so that he might there preach the Evangelical truth to an unbelieving people. Willibrord also sent disciples into the bounds of his diocese, to preach the doctrine of eternal blessedness to an unbelieving people; and Boniface began at Mainz to preach the word of eternal blessedness, and converted the Franks with the Thuringians from the error of unbelief, and went to the unbelieving people of Frisia, by whom he was also slaughtered. Would you call those men Christians? Or when you hear of Gentiles, and think of Adalbert, a disciple of Willibrord, who after the conversion of very many Gentiles died in the Lord, and so Suidbert, do you think of them as Christians brought under the discipline of the other, that is, the Roman Church? Likewise, when you read about Willibrord, or Clement (for so Pope Sergius named him): It also happened that the holy Clement visited the Gentile people of his diocese in Walachria, where an image of Mercury was worshipped with great reverence, whose statue this same holy bishop at once broke and disdainfully cast aside as a profane idol? Or what of the fact that Boniface himself is said to have converted the people from the barbarous idolatry of heathenism, and came into Germany to abolish the profane worship of idolatry and to instruct the rude people with evangelical teachings? Because he was a famous preacher to the conversion of pagans, do you therefore speak of Christians? In the letter which Boniface wrote to Pope Stephen, he relates how Willibrord was sent by Pope Sergius to preach to the pagan nation of the Frisians on the shores of the Western Ocean, whom for the most part he converted to the Christian faith, and whose shrines and temples he destroyed, etc. But since the bishop of Cologne now raises a controversy against him, asserting that the Church of Utrecht belongs to him, on this ground: that a church once built in the castle of Utrecht, afterwards destroyed by pagans, had been given to him by King Dagobert of the Franks, together with the castle; and Willibrord afterwards rebuilt it and consecrated it to St Martin. Boniface pressed that the Cologne church had been granted on this condition, that it should convert the Frisian nation to the faith and be its preacher; and because it had not preached, nor converted the Frisians to the faith of Christ, but the Frisian nation remained pagan until the preaching of Willibrord, Boniface thought it unseemly that the Church of Utrecht should be subject to anyone other than the Roman Pontiff, since it preached to the Frisian nation, because a great part of that nation was still pagan. Who of men could ever understand this otherwise than of Gentiles not yet initiated into Christ? Who, although there were some Christians and Christian churches here and there, nevertheless made up the greatest crowd, and by whom the Christians were incessantly and grievously harassed and oppressed, even in this place of ours; already by the Frisians, then by the Saxons, Danes and Normans. And the reason for Boniface, after the death of Willibrord, leaving Mainz and coming here again was, namely, lest the people, long since converted by his preaching, should fall back into idolatry and sect, as John of Beka writes in his Chronicle. Hence, now, when mention is made in the charters of ancient gifts either of Gentiles or of their conversion, it is clearer than the sun that by these must be understood only ethnic idolaters, who in those times were still many to be converted to the Christian faith, and by no means true Christians, who would have to be brought to the rule of antichristian faction to which they had not yet been conformed, as the author of the book we have in hand rashly maintains, at p. 83. Yet the same author, when he says at p. 386 that Charles the Great founded churches, placing clergy over them, not only so that through these paganism might as it were be driven out and the Christian religion propagated, etc., in these words does he not contradict himself, and understand here the conversion of pagans and ethnics to the Christian religion? So that in that age the Gentiles were not understood as those not conformed to the antichristian rule, he himself will have to see. Let us now hear some charters of those times, by which gifts were made to the Churches for the conversion of Gentiles. After Boniface, under Gregory, the third bishop of the Church of Utrecht, King Charles, in confirming the gifts made by his predecessors, speaks thus: for the very cause of God, through their testaments, that in the lights or stipends of the monks and canons who there convert the Gentiles to Christianity, and by the mercy of the Lord teach the converts they have, so that by that the Christians may preserve their Christianity. What other Gentiles are these, if not those opposed to Christians, and to be converted to Christianity, who were still there after the first bishops? Will he call Christians, and those the very best, Gentiles, and so plainly mark them in the gifts? No Roman Pope will be produced who ever spoke so, no emperor, nor anyone else, speaking of Christians, of those whom they wished to be conformed in some way to the rule of the Roman faction. Nor at that time was there so great a difference between Christianity and Papism; nor would any prudent or sound-minded man in those places have designated them so, calling Christians not Romans therefore Gentiles, or unbelievers, or pagans. Finally, if perhaps such persons had been counted among the Gentiles, they would not simply have been called Gentiles, unless with an added fuller explanation and distinction from the commonly known Gentiles who were still met with in that time and place, especially in testaments and gifts, where this too was always observed, and the matter was explained, beyond all doubt, very plainly and in several words and ways, as is customary. In the charter of the Emperor Louis, under Bishop Rixfrid: Likewise let the agents of the state not presume to take or use for the fisc any of the same tenth part, but let the Prelate of the same Church, with all the clergy and people subject to him, be able to supply sustenance, to keep the lights going in the same see, and to nourish and teach the Gentiles who are converted to Christianity. And at the end: As it was established and confirmed by our lord the Emperor, and our grandfather, and our predecessor kings, through this authority, so let it be kept and guarded inviolably at all times, so that it may please the servants of God who there abide with their bishop, and those whom they have converted from the Gentile rite to the true faith of Christ, to pray continually to God for us, our wife, our offspring, and the whole Christian people. Are those brought under the rule of the Roman Church said to be Christians, converted from the Gentile rite to the true faith of Christ? Or what was there before such a conversion so discordant from the likeness of the Roman Church that they ought therefore to be called Gentiles, or why should such ample gifts be needed to the Churches for such a conversion, and established for that purpose? Or what was that form of the Roman Church so commended, since Papism had not yet reached its peak [ἀκμήν] in that time, so that those brought to it would only then have been regarded as Christians and converts? But I fear I may be judged to spend more labour than is fitting in exploding this rash judgement, by which the author thinks that the Gentiles and their conversion, when they are recorded in the acts of those times, are not to be understood as Gentiles, ethnics, idolaters, but as true Christians who are yet to be arranged to the rule of the antichristian faction. Perhaps someone may stand by this, unless he has since been taught otherwise; but certainly I do not greatly fear that others will go along with him in the same opinion. What, then, is this? Gregory, writing to Boniface, congratulates him that God has opened among those nations a way of salvation and a door of mercy; therefore by nations Christians are understood. Why not pagan nations? So Boniface himself writes to Pope Stephen. Or what is it to argue thus: at the Synod of Metz in 864 the Normans and Danes are called pagans, although some Harald had preached to them forty years before; therefore the Synod did not understand the Normans as pagans but as Christians; or, therefore there were no longer any pagan Normans; or at least not those whom the Synod wishes to be kept away. In a charter of Otto I, in the year 948, given to the monastery of Gembloux, we still read: from false Christians, or pagans, etc., so that even at that time Christians were not free from the assault and oppression of pagans. Pagans are opposed to Christians, and elsewhere for that reason are called unbelievers. In a charter of King Dagobert, in the year 640: and if on account of the devastation of pagans, or unbelievers, or Christians. But I pass over these. We have seen enough how, apart from other sacred uses and ends removed from papal superstition (as our author puts it, not conformed to the rule of the antichristian faction; or, as he says there, whole and thereby free from the doctrine of Antichrist), very many goods were given to the Churches, and that very many were also bequeathed for the conversion of Gentiles and the support of converts. It follows, therefore, that before all else in this business, as I always say, we must begin there, and from what instruction of consciences this matter and its settlement are to be sought: that the foundations and charters of the gifts and ecclesiastical goods themselves should be inspected, from which you may then judge soundly about the use of the goods. This certainly is nothing more equitable; both so that it may be established which goods were given purely to sacred uses, and which perhaps stained with some mark of superstition, on which you base the perpetual foundation of your disputation and objections; and because law and reason dictate that as we judge other goods, in what manner and according to what principles, so, certainly on no less reasonable grounds, we should judge ecclesiastical goods too, and in what way we wish the supreme wills and dispositions of our gifts and bequests preserved, with equal reverence towards the pious institutions of our ancestors in particular. We do not wish our last wills to be frustrated, especially in religious matters; therefore we provide expressly in the testament that this shall not happen, as Philippe de Mornay does in his Testament, p. 12: ne puisse estre divertie. Nor shall we, in a like cause, apply the same religion to the testaments of our ancestors, which demand the same with such curses? Those who perhaps oppose us here in no way uphold the gifts, so that by their terms every dispute might be decided; and yet this would be most equitable and most certain. On the other hand, to wish to suppress or obscure them is not the mark of an ingenuous disputation, and is a grave prejudice. Especially since the greatest of our own doctors, Luther, Melanchthon, Calvin, Bucer, and nearly every other, even in the passages cited by a learned man (but drawn from the manuscripts of the theologians whom he so vehemently attacks), refer to the intention of the gifts. At p. 281 of the same book Calvin, praising Bucer's counsel on disposing of those goods: since those goods were bequeathed on this condition, which the Canons hold today, etc. At p. 200 Melanchthon: and for this reason these resources which the Churches now hold were given by pious kings and princes; which our author, who undeservedly now belabours him, unduly and against reason exaggerates, to define any gifts whatsoever. And the General States themselves ordered by public edict in the year 1580 that in the business of the ecclesiastical goods of the Silvaducensis district the charters of foundation should be carefully inspected; from these it might be clear whether they belonged to lay right, as many said, or rather were to be referred to the Quaestor of ecclesiastical goods. Therefore, even according to the mind of our author, who shapes his whole disputation about pseudo-ecclesiastical and idolatrous goods, so that these may be applied to the uses of private persons, at least goods truly and purely ecclesiastical, given to the use of the Church or of the poor, and in addition of the schools, with no mention of error or papal superstition interposed, will have to be excluded from this reckoning. And I hold that these, by the confession of all, ought to pass to those uses for which they were piously bequeathed. For, as Saravia rightly said in his book on sacrilege, chapter 4: that many gifts were once made, partly superstitious, partly excessive, does not thereby follow that they were not lawful, pious, pleasing to God, consonant with the Word of God, and useful and necessary to the Church. As for the rest, let it be examined, since they have been defiled by the perverse doctrine and opinions of Papism, how great an error has been committed; and whether it is not right, according to the sense of the Reformation, to correct this, and yet to keep those goods for pious and analogous uses, as we have heard above, judged by various doctors of the Reformation. Or let the opinions of any theologians and reformed jurists be sought, the case and the formula or charter of the gifts being set out, so that from them the matter may be handled as shall seem fair. For I gladly admit that concerning papal ecclesiastical goods, as the cases are not everywhere the same, so the opinion is not found the same among all; but just as the errors of Papism are some more grave than others and have been received and expressed more or less by men, so let the reformed here judge what is to be decided about those goods according to the opinion of the Reformers, and how they are everywhere to be kept, as far as can be done, and corrected, and the pious vows and deeds of whomever promoted. Without tumult, litigation, or prejudice to anyone, the judgement of the doctors can easily be consulted here; and thus the conscience of anyone may at last be quieted about the goods he possesses, when it has been established with certainty and truth what kind of nature they have. So, in the author's argumentation or syllogism, we constantly deny both premises: first, that some ecclesiastical goods stained with papal superstition may therefore be spent on private, not ecclesiastical, uses; and second, that all the goods in question are of that kind. He lays down this second hypothesis, from which he proceeds, as though the question were only about the surplus of any ecclesiastical goods whatever, and only that were being treated; whereas the controversy is not about surplus but about the nature and use of ecclesiastical goods in themselves. But if he wishes that, since the goods have been spent on the uses to which they were given, so that an abundance of ecclesiastical wealth may not be a burden either to the Church or to the commonwealth, any surplus may also be placed to other uses than ecclesiastical, provided that first it remains established that ecclesiastical goods by their nature are to be spent on ecclesiastical uses, we again concede that, after hearing the opinions of the doctors on it, it be determined what seems fitting and good for both the Church and the state. But first, as the most agreed-upon law, that goods purely ecclesiastical be spent nowhere else than here; and no deliberation about surplus is to be undertaken before the Church has been well provided for everywhere. For I know that the opinions of the doctors on this point vary. Calvin himself, writing to Farel about the consensus of theologians in this matter, in that letter we cited before, written in the year 1545, on 13 October, and certainly this vice, with which you are now in conflict, will hardly ever be corrected in speaking of the use of ecclesiastical goods, unless by the consensus of the Churches. Meanwhile, as far as he is concerned, he says that in his sermons and in the senate he repeatedly rebuked the rash seizers of those goods. It is worth while to think so much, he says at the end, as far as it is expedient to contend. Conversely, where there is consensus, as in goods truly ecclesiastical and their ecclesiastical use, it is a matter of great rashness to wish to oppose it. Thus, in the case of vicariates, to be spent only on the ministers of the Church, all those whom our author so unworthily harasses agree (the ministers; I do not intend what he snaps at, I doubt whether he has ever seen a manuscript); but the consensus of all is set down in this, that apart from the buying or selling of ecclesiastical benefices, it is to be condemned to apply vicariates to any use other than the holy ministry; which even our author holds in light regard. But whatever principle holds for vicariates must be observed everywhere in other cases too: namely, since those were endowed and founded for the divine ministry, it is rightly taught that in the whole business of these goods the foundations are to be regarded, and that judgement about their use is to be given from them. This is the one thing that in this whole disputation (certainly the only argument of an honest and upright cause; for what is of service to men [Θ γάρ εστιν ἀνθρώπων ἀφελείας]) we press to be done. First, that what is owed to the Churches (I always include under the Churches also the poor and other pious causes), as given and bequeathed to the Churches, be assigned to them; for surplus cannot be understood or held to be otherwise than what remains over and above, once the ecclesiastical goods have been applied to ecclesiastical uses. Therefore this must be held in the first place, and afterwards the surplus considered. And this can only be done with the consent of the Church. Our author, p. 239: For the magistrate acknowledges ecclesiastical goods, and wishes them to be such; the Church can alienate them only with its consent, or at least its participation (as we shall show more fully in the second section, concerning parochial goods). But where, and when, will surplus be judged? Or on whose judgement will it depend? Unless these are first decided, you urge the surplus in vain. You say that you desire, after the example of the Tigurines, who distributed their ecclesiastical goods for the use of the Church's ministers and of the schools, that the same always be done, and that the first care be taken of the ministers and the schools, p. 191. If the magistrate cannot provide for them from anywhere other than ecclesiastical goods; and if he can from elsewhere, does he not still wish the first care of ministers and schools to be taken by the magistrate? Or not from ecclesiastical goods? Or why first from ecclesiastical goods, if they cannot be provided for otherwise? Clearly you see that ecclesiastical goods are first to be spent on ecclesiastical uses, and this before the surplus is disputed. Well, the same author, on p. 353, also writes that the income of a vicariate cannot be denied by the patron to a needy minister; if the minister cannot decently support his family from parochial goods, and with the income of the vicariate taken from him he must be kept alive by hunger; the patron cannot at all be excused if he withdraws such vicariate income from one who does not deserve it, even if he himself does not receive it, and it is established that it goes either to the poor or to students of theology. What is the reason for this, unless because vicariates are founded and established for the maintenance of ministers? We do not wish, he says on p. 198, that anything be ceded by the magistrate's authority, from the mass of goods as it were ecclesiastical, to nobles or to any others, before provision has been made for the Churches, the schools, and, as law and prudence dictate, also for the poor. On surplus (he wishes it to appear that he disputes only that) after provision has been made for the Churches and the other usual charges, pp. 220 and 324. The magistrate, from the mass of ecclesiastical goods, has amply provided for the care of the Church, the schools and the poor, for ordinary and extraordinary cases, as pp. 325 and following. At p. 562: Since in both the first and the second section it has often been presupposed by us that a Christian and orthodox magistrate cannot dispose of the surplus of ecclesiastical goods, as it were, for the advantage of any private person, unless he has first provided sufficiently for the Churches, the schools, and also for the poor in the case of extraordinary needs. Add pp. 151, 155, 212, 216, 309, 388, etc., in which he repeatedly inculcates that he disputes only about the surplus of ecclesiastical goods, once the Churches, the poor and the schools have been abundantly provided for; and he does not allow anyone to take anything from those goods before he has seen that the Churches, schools and poor have been abundantly provided for. Therefore the Churches, the schools and the poor must first be heard, whether perhaps they are in need, and as long as the necessities and wants can be shown here, it is not lawful for anyone to touch their goods. Let this be observed; and so, I think, before we vainly dispute about surplus, all ecclesiastical goods will be distributed so well for the uses of the Churches, the poor and the schools, and not for superfluous ones, that the consciences of men will be better secured, so that they do not too readily burden themselves with the hasty seizing of those goods. Indeed, when we have considered what defect and poverty of ministers there generally is, how great the need of the poor rural ministers, of widows and orphans, and the necessity of building new temples and churches in many places; likewise of schools and what pertains to them; then how great the common calamity of the poor, the needy and the weak, which must be provided for exiles and strangers; what excellent institutions could be set up for the care of the conversion of unbelievers and of converts; or what is required for the support of those who come to the Church from Papacy and elsewhere, which now is much neglected for lack of resources and means; what aid must be supplied to foreign Churches and others that are oppressed, scattered or laid waste; what it would be fitting to pursue for the advancement and promotion of learning or of religion, and similar pious works, for which those goods were given to the Churches, so that we may provide for them not only for the present but also for the absent and for the future. That all these things are already provided for everywhere, or even that there is enough among us, no one who knows will say, who considers even the poverty of almsgiving alone, to be cared for most conveniently, if it were adjudged to it from the mass of sacred goods, which our ancestors piously gave for that end, and for which they expressly wrote in their gifts: for the use of strangers and the poor. Or: for daily alms and hospitality, and other works of mercy. Or: by which the poverty of the poor of Christ may be relieved, etc. Just as we do not greatly disapprove when some of our own people take support for their studies or ministry from ecclesiastical or scholastic goods of another place, for instance the Church of England, so too it is just and fair that from the goods of our Church, where it is richer than others, needy foreigners also be helped; and thus the purpose and use of ecclesiastical goods is maintained, and at the same time it will be well for the Churches everywhere, and better provided that men do not rashly defile themselves with those goods, especially as long as it is not established whether there is any surplus of goods; which, so long as it is not, seems to bring no fruit to themselves or their patrons. And thus it is clear that nothing has been done for those in whose favour our author laboured to write his book. I think it not out of place here, when there are such great outcries about superstitious ecclesiastical goods and surplus, to add what occurs in the French history, Recueil des choses memorables pour le fait de la religion, etc., from Henry II, in the oration to the Queen, on the means of settling the tumults, p. 345.

units.la: ,,Premierement, Madame, il faut entendre que les biens ecclesiastiques ne sont point d'une mesme espece. Car les uns ont esté ordonnez pour le povres: les autres pour l'entretenement des Pasteurs, & des temples: les autres pour l'entretenement des escoles: les autres ont esté donnez pour des services superstitieux & idololatriques: les au-tres ont esté mesme acquis par les Ecclesiastiques. Quant aux biens de povres, ce seroit un sacrilege d'y toucher, il faut que cela demeure: ,,Mais il faudroit qu'on choisist des gens de bien pour les distribuer, & qu'ilz rendissent publiquement conte d'an en an pour le moins: ,,Quand aux revenus, & rentes qui ont esté donnees pour l'entretenement des pasteurs, il faut regarder que pourra suffire, selon le lieu & charge qu'ils auront. Qu'on ait souvenance que les gras benefices ont amené avec l'avarice, & l'ambition, une infinité d'autres maux.
units.tr: First, Madam, it must be understood that ecclesiastical goods are not all of one kind. Some have been ordained for the poor; others for the support of pastors and churches; others for the support of schools; others were given for superstitious and idolatrous services; and others were acquired by the ecclesiastics themselves. As for the goods of the poor, it would be sacrilege to touch them; they must remain as they are: but it would be necessary to choose good people to distribute them, and to have them render public account from year to year at the least: as for the revenues and rents given for the support of pastors, one must consider what will suffice, according to the place and the charge each holds. Let it be remembered that rich benefices have brought, along with avarice and ambition, an infinity of other evils.

units.la: ,, Et d'autre part qu'on considere que l'indigence pourroit beaucoup distruire un Pasteur & le rendre contemptible, quand il seroit contraint de mendier, ou gaigner sa vie avec grande difficulté: & qu'il ne pourroit avoir livres, ne les choses necessaires à son estat.
units.tr: On the other hand, let it be considered that poverty could greatly undo a pastor and make him contemptible, when he would be forced to beg or to earn his living with great difficulty, and could not have books or the things necessary for his station.

units.la: ,, Pourtant il faudroit pourvoir aux pasteurs en telle sorte, qu'ils ne fussent ne trop riches, ny indignes aussi. Que les temples qui seront commodes à prescher & assembler le peuple, soyent entretenus avecques les Maisons des Pasteurs, & que soit sans grande jumptuosité.
units.tr: Yet provision should be made for pastors in such a way that they are neither too rich nor, on the other hand, unworthy. Let the churches that are suitable for preaching and gathering the people be maintained together with the pastors' houses, and that without great extravagance.

units.la: ,,Il faut aussi que les revenus qui sont ordonnez pour entretenir des escoliers, qui servent apres au Ministere, & à la republique, avecques leurs Docteurs, soient restituez; comme les plus anciennes Abbayes, qui n'estoyent anciennement qu'escoles, ainsi que les gens savans le savent. Or quand on aura extrait pour les choses susdites une partie des biens ecclesiastiques, combien pensez-vous, Madame, qu'il en restera encores ? Addere qui ni liceat, ad id quod de superfluo bonorum Ecclesiasticorum, in ulus Ecclesiasticos hactenus diximus, virum doctum, quem ab isto nostro Auctore rhapsodicum indignanter dici, plurimi nti-rentur, neque alio responso dimitti, Carpzovium in Comment. ad Legem Regiam German.cap. iv.lect.iv. pag. „Sunt profecto infinitæ ferè causæ piæ, ad quas Reditus isti „conferri possent: Clamant nudi, clamant famelici, conque„runtur & dicunt: Nostrum est, quod effunditis, nobis „crudeliter subtrahitur quod inaniter expenditis: Nostris „necessitatibus detrahitur, quicquid accedit vanitatibus ve„stris, ut refert ex Bernhard. Christ. Befold. lib. 1. Polit. cap. „4. Utque reditus isti Ecclesiastici in equestribus ordinibus „constituendis impenderentur, quibus non solùm Potentio„rum secundo geniti sese alere & sublimes Imperii dignita„tes in sua integritate conservari possent, sed etiam quod „perpetuas pro Lege & grege excubias agerent, firmum ha„beretur præsidium, suadet Nicol. Betl. de pact. Famil. illustr. „cap. ult. cui consentit Befoldus de Success. Regia disp. 6. & Pe„trus Syring. dist. concl. 38. lit. b. Et nunquam deficiet causa „parilis, quæ reditus & bona Deo semel dicata excipere pos„sit. Si scilicet ejusmodi bona vel ad alium cultum divinum, „vel ad salutem Reipublicæ: vel ad conservandum ministeri„um: vel ad pias scholas constituendas: vel ad juvandos pau„peres, vel ad conditionem Nosocomiorum quoquo modo „meliorem efficiendam, vel ad causam Studiorum conferan„tur, arg. l. sanctimus 21. l. quoniam 26. C. de SS. Eccles. cap. cum „secundum Apostolum. 16. extr. de prabend. Veluti pro Mo„nasteriis Scholas, Nosocomia, Xenodochia, Orphanotrophia „laudatissimos quosdam Germaniæ Principes constituis„se, refert & commendat Everh. à Weihe in aulico Politico, „reg. 216. Hocque juris apud Euangelicos obtinere, probat „Sententia Elect. Saxon. Scabinorum Lipsiensium, in hunc modum. Pronuntiat: Und obwohl das Closter Gerbstedt ein geistliches Gut ist: So ist doch dabey wol zu bedencken, daß solches den Ordens Personen / und nachdem nun mehr das Closter leben abgethan / und dar sieht des heiligen Evangelii an Tag kommen / auch den selbigen Kirchen / die Christliche Religion reformiret ... Kirchen und Schulen zu Nutz verordnet worden / in ansehung daß zu des Vnterhalt- ung solche Güter angewendet werden sollen / wie dasselbe durch Hieron. Schurff. cent. 4. consil. 47. n. 11. usque ad. n. 15. & in cent. cent. consil. 99. mit vielen Rechtsgründen hat dieselbe ausgeführet / auch von Wesemb. Cons. 37 n. 6. & seq. confirmirt / und durch des Heiligen Römischen Reichs de An. 1555. zu Augspurg publicirten Abschied / und Churfurst Mauriz hochlöblicher Gedächtniß publicirten Landes Ordnung für ... von dem Vberlauf der geistlichen Guter ... & ... seq. befestiget wird. &c. in causa Ornamis, Edelen von Plats Mensf. Febr. Anno 1623.
units.tr: It is also necessary that the revenues ordained for maintaining students, who afterwards serve in the ministry and the commonwealth, together with their teachers, be restored; likewise the oldest abbeys, which formerly were nothing but schools, as learned men know. Now when a part of the ecclesiastical goods has been extracted for the aforesaid purposes, how much do you think, Madam, will still remain? Let me add, as far as it is permitted, to what we have said so far about the superfluity of ecclesiastical goods being used for ecclesiastical purposes: a learned man, whom this author of ours indignantly calls rhapsodical, is cited by very many, and should not be dismissed with any other answer. Carpzov, in his commentary on the German Lex Regia, German.cap. iv.lect.iv. pag.: "There are indeed almost endless pious causes to which these revenues could be devoted. The naked cry out, the hungry cry out, and they complain and say: what you pour out is ours; what you waste in vanities is cruelly withheld from us; whatever is added to your vanities is taken from our needs, as Bernhard Christoph Befold reports, lib. 1. Polit. cap. 4. And that these ecclesiastical revenues should be spent on establishing equestrian orders, by which not only the younger sons of the powerful could support themselves and the high dignities of the Empire be preserved intact, but also a firm protection would be had for them to keep perpetual watch for the law and the flock, is urged by Nicolaus Betl, de pact. Famil. illustr. cap. ult., with which Befold agrees, de Success. Regia disp. 6, and Peter Syring, dist. concl. 38 lit. b. And a similar cause will never be lacking which could receive revenues and goods once dedicated to God: namely, if such goods are conferred either on another divine worship, or on the safety of the commonwealth, or on the maintenance of the ministry, or on founding pious schools, or on aiding the poor, or on improving in any way the condition of hospitals, or on the cause of studies, arg. l. sanctimus 21. l. quoniam 26. C. de SS. Eccles. cap. cum secundum Apostolum. 16. extr. de prabend." Thus he reports and commends that certain most praiseworthy princes of Germany, out of monasteries, established schools, hospitals, guesthouses and orphanages; see Everhard von Weihe, in Aulicus Politicus, rule 216. That this law obtains among the Evangelicals is proved by the sentence of the Lipsian scabini of the Elector of Saxony, in this manner. They pronounce: "And although the cloister of Gerbstedt is spiritual property, yet it must well be considered that it was ordained for members of the order; and now that the monastic life has been abolished and the holy Gospel has come to light, it has been appointed for the use of the same churches, which the Christian religion has reformed ... churches and schools, inasmuch as such goods are to be applied to their maintenance; as Hieronymus Schurff has set out with many legal reasons, cent. 4, consil. 47, nn. 11 to 15, and in cent. cent., consil. 99; also Wesembeck, Cons. 37, n. 6 et seq., has confirmed it; and it is established by the recess published at Augsburg in the year 1555 of the Holy Roman Empire, and by the land ordinance published by the Elector Maurice of most laudable memory, concerning the overflow of spiritual goods ... et seq., etc." In the case of Ornamis, noble of Plats, Mensf., February, in the year 1623.

units.la: 1603. Vel, si malit, Bezam audiat ubi egit de Triplici episcopatu, & respondet ad quæstiones aliquot sibi à Glamio propositas, quarum sexta est de opibus Ecclesiasticis: Ad facul„tates ecclesiasticas, inquit, quod attinet, primum omni„um vehementur cavendum arbitramur, nequis se sacrarum „facultatum contactu contaminet. Etenim si ejusmodi sa„crilegia, etiam inter Idololatras, Dominus insignibus poe„nis ultus est, quid in eos censebimus decretum iri, qui Ec„clesias ipsas spoliarint, & vero ejus cultui consecrata prophanaverint? Deinde addit: Sicut autem copia Ecclesiam „obruit: ita verendum est, ne inopia prorsus eam affligat, „quum in vero Ministerio tuendo non minus hodie parci „sordidiq; sint plerique, quam olim prodigi Reges ac Prin„cipes ipsi fuere. Tenendum igitur modum hac in re necessa- „rio arbitramur. Is autem, nostro judicio, optimus erit, „si in omnibus Ecclesiis, tum quis sit sumptus quotidianus „necessario faciendus dispiciatur, tum ad extraordinaria „multa, quorum iniri certa ratio non potest, aliquid refer„vetur: & quidem hoc non parce, non tenuiter, quum Dei „beneficio abundet Ecclesia: sed benigne, ac liberaliter sup„putetur. Erit ergo parœchiarum, & Pastorum incundus is „numerus, qui populis admodum sufficiat, & honestum cui„que stipendium decernendum. Presbyteris quoque, qui „Pastoribus adjunguntur, prospiciendum erit, ut suum mu„nus commode tueri possint. Iniquum etiam fuerit mor„tuorum Pastorum viduas, & liberos ad egestatem redigi. „Ecclesiæ quoque non minimæ sunt partes, scholæ, & Aca„demiæ, illius videlicet seminaria. Ptochotrophiis, Nosoco„miis, Xenodochiis prospiciendum est. Habenda quoque „publicorum sacrorum ædificiorum ratio, ut sarta tecta con„serv's ventur, ac nova, si sit opus, extruantur. Postremo (ut „ante dixi) quum abundent Ecclesiæ, constituendum erit „quod in ærarium sancta quotannis inferatur, unde quod in„gruentibus belli vel famis necessitatibus sufficiat, perii possit. Hæc Beza. Atqui illi potius homines de bonorum Ecclesiasticorum usu vel superfluo loquantur, qui quantum ubique Ecclesia egeat, quid sumtuum requirat, ut digne omnibus & in praesenti, & futuro provida cura prospiciatur, norunt, non alii, non qui ei, ejusve rebus iniquiores, existimant fere, quod Saravia talibus exprobat in epist. Dedic. ad lib. de triplici episcopatu: dotare Ecclesias praediis & proventibus, esse superfitiosum & Papisticum; illas bonis omnibus spoliare, esse religiosum & Evangelicum. Et cum superfluo opum Ecclesiasticarum, quod forte sit, scin' ut Beza velit agi? eodem loco: Quod superesse ,,deprehendetur, non quidem cum aliis publicis redditibus ,,confundendum (alterius enim haec naturae sunt, quam,,quam non optimis semper artibus ab avaris sacerdotibus quaesita) sed seorsim seponendum. Neque sequentia ejus nos fugiunt, aut laedunt: si publica regni necessitas id po,,stulat, in ejus usum consumi fas esse arbitramur: prae,,sertim si populus eo subsidio sublevatur. Ejusdemque cum Beza sententiae est Hadr. Saravia: seperatae manent o,,pes Ecclesiasticae à vulgaribus, in eaque nihil juris sibi ven,,dicet fiscus, earumque dispensatio permittatur Ecclesia,,rum ministris. Hoc enim in negotio, quamvis in alio dissentientes Beza atque Saravia iste, nullatenus dissonabant, ut nihil in Saraviam hic quidem dici posset, quod non simul Bezam impetat. Quippe sic exserte Beza, in praefat. ad Tractationem Saraviae, de gradibus Ministrorum, loquitur: quod ad illam sacrilegam bonorum Ecclesiasticorum usurpationem, & sacri ipsius Ministerii contemtum attinet, in eo tibi communis est nobisque querela. Quae autem illa Saraviae hac in parte querela sit, cum variis in locis, praesertim in tractatuum suorum prologis, tum ex professo libro tertio, de Ministrorum gradibus ostendit, ubi de sacrilegiis, & poenis Sacrilegorum integram instituit tractationem. Et quidem quem ille abusum hoc in negotio carpit, cum in Belgio notat, quo tum respexit quoque Beza, in sua de eodem argumento, seu bonorum Ecclesiasticorum apud nos profanatione & alienatione, contestatione ad Illustres Belgii Ordines, in praetat. lib. de Resurre-
units.tr: 1603. Or, if he prefers, let him hear Beza, where he treats of the Triple Episcopate and answers some questions put to him by Glanius, the sixth of which concerns ecclesiastical wealth. "As for ecclesiastical resources," he says, "we think that above all things it must be most vehemently guarded against that anyone should defile himself by touching sacred property. For if the Lord has punished such sacrileges with notable penalties even among idolaters, what judgment shall we think will be passed on those who have despoiled the churches themselves and profaned what was consecrated to his true worship?" He adds: "Just as abundance overwhelms the church, so it must be feared lest poverty utterly afflicts it, since in maintaining the true ministry nowadays many are no less stingy and sordid than the prodigal kings and princes once were. We therefore think a measure must be kept in this matter. This, in our judgment, will be best if in all the churches both the daily expense that must necessarily be incurred is examined, and something is set aside for the many extraordinary needs for which no certain reckoning can be made; and this not sparingly or meanly, since the church abounds by God's blessing, but generously and liberally estimated. There will therefore be a suitable number of parishes and pastors sufficient for the people, and an honourable stipend decreed for each. Provision must also be made for the elders who are joined to the pastors, so that they can carry out their office decently. It would also be unjust for the widows and children of dead pastors to be reduced to poverty. The church also has no small duties towards schools and academies, which are its seminaries. Provision must be made for almshouses, hospitals and guesthouses. Account must also be taken of public sacred buildings, that they be kept in repair and new ones built if need be. Lastly (as I said before), since the churches abound, something must be established that is brought into the sacred treasury each year, from which what suffices for the pressing needs of war or famine can be drawn." Thus Beza. But rather let those men speak of the use or superfluity of ecclesiastical goods who know how much the church everywhere lacks, what expenses it requires, so that worthy and provident care may be taken for all, both now and in the future; not others, nor those who are rather unfair to it and its affairs, as they mostly are. Saravia reproaches such people for this in the dedicatory epistle to his book on the Triple Episcopate: to endow churches with lands and revenues is superstitious and Papistical; to strip them of all goods is religious and Evangelical. And as for the superfluity of ecclesiastical wealth, which perhaps exists, do you know what Beza wants done with it? In the same place: "What is found to be left over is not indeed to be merged with other public revenues (for these are of another nature, and were not always sought by avaricious priests by the best arts), but to be set apart separately. Nor do we overlook or object to what follows: if the public necessity of the kingdom demands it, we judge it lawful for that to be spent on its use, especially if the people is relieved by that aid." Hadrian Saravia holds the same opinion as Beza: "the ecclesiastical funds remain separate from common revenues, and the treasury claims no right over them, and their distribution is to be left to the ministers of the churches." For in this matter Beza and that Saravia, though disagreeing on another point, did not differ at all, so that nothing could be said here against Saravia which would not also strike Beza. Indeed Beza speaks expressly thus in the preface to Saravia's treatise on the degrees of ministers: as for that sacrilegious usurpation of ecclesiastical goods and the contempt of the sacred ministry itself, in this we share a common complaint with you. What complaint Saravia makes in this part he shows in various places, especially in the prefaces to his treatises, and ex professo in the third book, on the degrees of ministers, where he sets out a complete treatment on sacrileges and the punishments of sacrilegious persons. And indeed the abuse which he censures in this matter, when he notes it in Belgium (which Beza too had in view), in his own work on the same subject, that is, on the profanation and alienation of ecclesiastical goods among us, in his address to the Illustrious Orders of Belgium, in the preface to the book on the Resurre-
