Ordines; tum ex iis quæ scripsit aut in historiâ vitæ Calvini; aut denique adversus Leidensis Academiæ Professorem, Saraviam. Tertio & hoc salsum est, quod supponit, & disputationis suæ facit cardinem Auctor,quod bona Ecclesiastica Magistratus fisco publico adscripserit. Non sane.Novit quippe Magistratus noster Cyprianum illud : patrimonium Deo creditum nec rei publicæ eripit, nec fiscus invadit. Et in Diplomatibus illud exlerte aliquando legi: & procuratores Reip. de eadem decima parte accipere, aut usurpare ad fiscum non præsumant, ut in confirmatione donationum Ecclesiæ nostræ factarum à Ludovico Imp. sub episcopo Rixfrido. ut nullus judex publicus, aut aliquis ex judiciaria potestate in supra scriptis rebus Ecclesiæ Dei, aut rectoribus ejus aliquam calumniam ingerere præsumat, in Henrici 11. Diplomate a. cIↄ III. Alibi, ne aliqua Imperialis vel Regalis, aut Episcopalis persona, vel aliquis publicus exactor hujus donationis nostræ authoritatem præsumat infringere.Si quis, quod absit, hujus nostræ confirmationis edictum infringere tentaverit, mille libras auri purissimi componat, quarum partem dimidiam Fisco nostro, reliqua vero prædicta Ecclesiæ Traj. persolvat. aliaque similia. Istud in Diplomatibus obvium: ne qua canonica sæcularisve persona. Ut nullus successorum nostrorum Regum seu Imperatorum ut nullus Dux vel Comes atque Vicarius, seu quislibet ex judiciaria potestate, nostram, vel antecessorum nostrorum Regum & Imperatorum auctoritatem violare præsumat. Conradus 11. a.cIↄ cxlvi. Nullus unquam dominator adveniat, qui hoc infringere audeat. Lietbertus, Cameracensis episcopus, a, cIↄ lxx. nec ego, nec alius Episcopus, seu clericus, sive Rex, sive Comes, sive sæcularis persona violare audeat ex his quidquam, quod continetur hac scriptura. Ita ubi bona Ecclesiastica supersunt, Magistratus sollicite cavet, ne in fiscum inferantur, in communem cum reliquis Reip. bonis massam; sed segregata ab aliis, servantur, aliqua in beneficia seu stipendia sacra aut scholastica, multa Canonicis relicta, quæ non fiscum communem, quo pertineant, sed distincta & separata ab eo aerario sua habent & quaestuam, atque usum. Huc facit, quod Ordines Generales in negotio bonorum Ecclesiasticorum Silvae Duc. a. cIↄ Iↄcxxx. xı.d Iunii edixerunt, ut acccurata ratio bonorum Ecclesiasticorum ibidem haberetur, atque inspectis donationibus eorundem catalogus deerretur ad bonorum Ecclesiasticorum Quaestorem: non dicunt, ad fiscum.
units.tr: of the Resurrection of Christ, which passage we cited above. How completely this was the mind of the venerable theologian Beza appears both from that preface to the Lords of the States, and from what he wrote in the history of Calvin's life, or finally against Saravia, professor at the Academy of Leiden. Third, the author also takes as the hinge of his whole disputation something false: that the Magistrate has assigned ecclesiastical goods to the public treasury. Certainly not. Our Magistrate knows that saying of Cyprian: "A patrimony entrusted to God neither is snatched from the commonwealth nor does the treasury seize it." And I have read in the charters, stated plainly on one occasion: "and let the stewards of the commonwealth not presume to take or appropriate for the treasury any part of the same tithe," as in the confirmation of the donations made to our Church by Emperor Louis under Bishop Rixfrid; "that no public judge, or anyone from the judicial power, presume to bring any accusation against the aforesaid things of God's Church or against its rectors," in the charter of Henry II, in the year 1003. Elsewhere: "let no imperial or royal or episcopal person, or any public collector, presume to infringe the authority of this our donation. If anyone, which God forbid, shall attempt to break the edict of this our confirmation, let him pay a thousand pounds of purest gold, half of which to our treasury, and the rest to the aforesaid Church of Utrecht." And other similar things. This is common in the charters: "that no ecclesiastical or secular person ... that no successor of ours, of the kings or emperors, that no duke or count or vicar, or anyone from the judicial power, presume to violate our authority or that of our predecessor kings and emperors." Conrad II, in the year 1146: "let no ruler ever come who dares to break this." Liétbert, bishop of Cambrai, in the year 1070: "neither I nor any other bishop, or cleric, or king, or count, or secular person dare to violate anything contained in this writing." Thus, where ecclesiastical goods remain, the Magistrate carefully takes care that they are not carried into the treasury, into the common mass of the commonwealth's goods; but they are kept separate from the others, some for sacred or scholastic benefices or stipends, many left to the canons, who hold and use them not for the common treasury to which they would belong, but as a separate and distinct fund from that chest. To this point is what the General States, in the matter of the ecclesiastical goods of the Duchy of Silva, decreed on the eleventh of June in the year 1530: that an accurate account of the ecclesiastical goods be kept there, and that, after examining the gifts of these, a list be delivered to the Quaestor of ecclesiastical goods; they do not say, to the treasury.

units.la: Quare errat graviter qui dixerit, bona Ecclesiastica fisco seu aerario publico a Magistratu nostro addicta esse, vel ad hoc illa pertinere, quemadmodum fisco rem adscribere, vere ac proprie accipitur, & non uti loquitur implicite vel tacite, vel interpretative, pag. 290.325.338.567. Neque ex cura Magistratus, circa illa bona, vel ex praescripto illis ordine aut regula aliqua, sequitur fisci publici esse, magis quam de reliquis privatorum, aut orphanorum, aut quorumcumque Collegiorum bonis in Rep. sitis, quorum supremum patrocinium & cura quidem penes Magistratum est, sed ad defensionem & protectionem tum hominum, tum quae eorum sunt, bonorum, non autem destructionem. Non quia illa protegit Magistratus, ideo ejus sunt, vel penes ipsum ut ea in alios, quam postulant, usus disponat: quemadmodum Nostep male colligit pag. 95. Bona haec Ecclesiastica vulgo dicta, juris publici sunt. Quae vero talia sunt, ut protegantur a Magistratu, ita ab eodem ordinantur ad suos usus. Bona Ecclesiastica juris publici sunt, sed Ecclesiastici, non politici. Neque quae a Magistratu protegantur, ideo ab eo ordinantur ad suos usus, cum non jam aliquis bonorum nostrorum census, sed omnia Magistratus forent, ad suos usus disponenda. quod non credo ullus velit, vel de se, suisque bonis, vel talem habere Magistratum. E contrario, quemadmodum & supra diximus, quomodo nos velimus servata nostra bona, praesertim pia, & in usus sanctos a nobis destinata, ita equum quoque est ut erga Majorum nostrorum similia bona nos perinde geramus, id est, ne ea diripiamus, aut alienemus. Prout Conradus II
units.tr: Therefore he greatly errs who says that the ecclesiastical goods have been assigned by our Magistrate to the treasury or public chest, or that they belong to it, in the way that to assign a thing to the treasury is properly and strictly understood, and not as he speaks implicitly, tacitly or by interpretation, p. 290, 325, 338, 567. Nor does it follow from the Magistrate's care for those goods, or from any order or rule prescribed for them, that they belong to the public treasury any more than the other goods of private persons, or of orphans, or of any colleges situated in the commonwealth, over which the Magistrate holds the highest patronage and care, but for the defence and protection both of persons and of what belongs to them, not for their destruction. It is not that because the Magistrate protects them, they are therefore his, or that he has them at his disposal to apply to other uses than those they require, as Nostep wrongly infers, p. 95: "These so-called ecclesiastical goods are of public right. But those which are of such a kind that they are protected by the Magistrate, are by the same man ordained to his own uses." Ecclesiastical goods are of public right, but of an ecclesiastical, not a political, kind. Nor do those which are protected by the Magistrate for that reason get ordained by him to his own uses, since then not some part of our goods but all would be the Magistrate's, to be disposed of for his own uses; which I do not think anyone would wish, either concerning himself and his own goods, or to have such a Magistrate. On the contrary, as we said above, just as we wish our own goods to be kept, especially pious ones, destined by us for holy uses, so it is also fair that we conduct ourselves in the same way towards the similar goods of our ancestors, that is, that we do not plunder or alienate them. As the Emperor Conrad II speaks in the charter of the year 1146, by which he confirms the possessions of the Church of Cambrai: "He who wishes his own arrangements to be kept by his successors must preserve the privileges of his predecessors. Fourth."

units.la: Imp. loquitur in Diplomate a.cIↄ cxlvi. quo confirmat possessiones Ecclesiæ Cameracensis, Prædecessorum debet privilegia conservare, qui sua vult adecessoribus instituta servari. Quar- to. Quemadmodum Auctor in tota hac disputatione se semper in angustias proripit, non agit de plano, primum non de bonis Ecclesiasticis, sed pseudo-ecclesiasticis & idololatricis; tum nec de hisce adeo, ac de horum superfluo sententiam suam vult intelligi, ita in erogandis iis ad privatos, cui fiscum comminiscitur intercedere, limitare & restringere illam etiam erogationem passim videtur, ad familias honoratas, quas sc. conservari Reip. interfit, & quibus sustentandis facere illa bona cupiat. Verum, praeterquam quod admodum varius sit in designandis hisce familiis, quas nunc nobiles & honoratas,de Rep. bene meritas, nunc simpli- citer & solum honestas appellat, ut ludos fecisse in re seria videri possit: quæso, quæ solæ illæ nobiles, illustresque familiæ, quibus illa bona contingant? quasi non quivis, haud sæpe honoratus adeo, æque possit ista adipisci, ac alius majoris notæ; & quid ni tam illis, quam istis ea obtingant? vel sit ita, ut solæ nobiles honoratæque [familiæ, sed quæ ne inæreant Reip. interfit, hinc partem capiant, & ex solis bonis EcclesiasticoPapalibus seu idololatricis, horumque superfluo, post abunde curatam Ecclesiam, scholas, pauperes, partem habeant, vide, quam parum ex illorum voto tum egerit, quibus tamen videri voluisti permagna præstitisse, & ut non operæ pretium fuerit tantum sibi odium, aliis optimis viris contumeliam fecisse libro, quem Synodus (ut videas aliam esse Ecclesiæ nostræ sententiam) idcirco valde scandalosum judicavit. Neq; de illustrium familiarum sustentatione nostra hic vertitur quæstio. Ego nihil in specie de Canonicis hic loquor; solummodo sententiam Ecclesiæ, & Theologorum nostrorum tueor de usu & applicatione bonorum Ecclesiasticorum ad Ecclesiastica, non in usus privatorum: & hunc in finem tum doctrina, tum Doctores nostri vindicandi mihi fuerunt, atque enervandum temerarium consilium, quo imprudens SeScriptor nonnunquam Nostros in aliam sententiam pertrahere, & eorum verba pervertere conatus fuit. Quod me, uti necessitate defendendæ doctrinæ, atq; responsionis nostræ adversus Papalem de bonorum Ecclesiasticorum apud nos abusu objectionem, ita sic quoq;, quamvis breviter, fecisse confido, ut nihil omnino in operoso illo Auctoris nostri, hanc ad rem ipsectans, scripto fit, quod ex hac nostra ad primum Papæ, de bonis Ecclesiasticis, in Bulla argumentum responsione, (ostensis, dirutisque quatuor illis generalibus, quæ hactenus notavimus scripti illius fundamentis vel hypothecibus,) solvi ac dilui non possit. Quod in ejusmodi scriptis semper facile est, quæ quam multa sibi agenda sint in respondendo, quam vero pauca pro se habeant in argumentando, longa & prolixa tractatione ostendunt & loquuntur. Non ita, uti ille fecit Sect. 1. cap. xxxii. controversia hic quæ sunt proponenda, sed meo quidem judicio, ad hæc quatuor capita, quæ hic quæstio de bonis Ecclesiasticis in genere, revocanda. Ita ut primo quæratur:
units.tr: Just as the author throughout this whole disputation always hurries himself into straits, not dealing plainly, first not about ecclesiastical goods but about pseudo-ecclesiastical and idolatrous ones; then not even about these, but he wishes his opinion to be understood about the surplus of these; so in the distribution of these to private persons, into which he invents that the treasury intervenes, he everywhere seems to limit and restrict that distribution to honourable families, namely those whom it concerns the commonwealth to preserve, and whose support he desires those goods to provide for. But, apart from the fact that he is very inconsistent in designating these families, calling them now noble and honourable, well deserving of the commonwealth, now simply and only respectable, so that he might seem to have been playing games in a serious matter: I ask, which are those noble and illustrious families alone to whom those goods fall? As if any man, not often very honourable, could not obtain them just as well as another of greater note; and why should they not fall to those as well as to these? Or grant it be so, that only noble and honourable families [are to be served], but such as it concerns the commonwealth not to be lost, and let them take a share from these, and let them have a part only of the papal or idolatrous ecclesiastical goods and their surplus, after the Church, schools and the poor have been amply provided for: see how little he has acted according to the wishes of those whom you nevertheless wanted to seem to have accomplished very great things for, and how it was not worth the trouble to have stirred up so much hatred for yourself and such contumely against other excellent men by a book which the Synod (so that you may see that the opinion of our Church is different) therefore judged to be very scandalous. Nor is the question here about the maintenance of illustrious families. I here speak of the Canons in no particular way; I only defend the opinion of the Church and of our theologians about the use and application of ecclesiastical goods to ecclesiastical purposes, not to the uses of private persons; and to this end I have had to vindicate both the doctrine and our teachers, and to refute the rash design by which this imprudent writer has sometimes tried to draw our people into another opinion and to pervert their words. I trust that I have done this, as the necessity of defending the doctrine and of our reply against the Papal objection concerning the abuse of ecclesiastical goods among us compelled me, so also briefly, in such a way that nothing at all in that laborious writing of our author, bearing on this matter, is left unanswered, which cannot be dissolved and refuted by this our reply to the first argument of the Pope concerning ecclesiastical goods in the Bull, once those four general foundations or pledges of that writing which we have so far noted have been shown and overthrown. This is always easy in such writings, which, as long, prolix treatment shows and declares, have so much to do in answering and so little to offer in arguing for themselves. Not as he did in Sect. 1, chap. xxxii, the matters to be put forward here, but in my judgement they are to be reduced, concerning ecclesiastical goods in general, to these four heads. So that first the question be asked:

units.la: Annon Bona Ecclesiis, vel earundem Ministris, pauperibus, Scholis data, legata, in non aliospuam illorum usus Ecclesiasticos, pios debeant, juxta intentionem & voluntatem donantium, quousque possunt, impendi? Speɛtamus hic bona vere Ecclesiastica, eaq; non nisi in usus Ecclesiasticos dicimus expendenda, juxta voluntatem donantium. Quomodo & olim bona Ecclesiastica administrata, notat bene Salmasius, lib. de Trapezitico fœnore, pag. 419. At olim distinctio siebat bonorum Ecclesiæ & ipsius Episcopi. Propriis se alebat, ac tuebatur: ecclesiastica ita ex ipsius sententia administrabantur, ut in pauperes & infirmos erogarentur, aut captivis liberandis impenderentur, ac similibus piis causis. Omnino piis causis. Atq; in ipso libro quam præ manibus habemus, nonnulla occurrunt, quæ nostræ favent sententiæ quæq; ideo adscribenda, Pag. 204. ad allegata Calvini verba, quibus is dixerat: Iam quidem tc status sum, nolle me omnia, quæ apud nos fiunt excusare: quin potius non majorem alicubi rationem haberi, ut in eos tantum usus impendantur Ecclesiæ reditus, quibus sunt dedicati, mihi id displicere fateor. Mecum id etiam gemunt omnes boni ait: Quod addit se cum multis aliis stomachari, quod Ecclesiæ reditus non destinentur in eos usus, quibus sunt dedicati; nos utroque pariter pollice probamus, si intelligatur de reditibus bona intentione usibus Ecclesiæ destinatis, nec aliter SS. Ministerio prospici queat: Quorsum hæc cauda, si utroque pollice probes verba & sententiam Calvini? Pag.211. Zanchium inquit secum facere: Non officit quoque nobis Zanchius cap.24. Confess. quando num.29. huncin modum loquitur: Cum vero multa bona, liberalitate Principum & aliorum piorum fuerint olim donata, & nunc etiam alicubi donentur Ecclesiis: judicamus, si qua Ecclesia talia habeant bona, diligenter curandum esse ne dilapidentur, neve in profanos usus, multo vero minus in sacrilegos convertantur, conversave dissimulentur: sed in eos duntaxat distribuantur, ad quos etiam donata fuerunt, ad pios nimirum usus. Probamus autem illam veterem bonorum Ecclesiasticorum partitionem, ut una scilicet pars cedat piis Episcopis, id est, Doctoribus, ministrisque verbi, & eorum familiis: alia Clericis; id est, Studiosis ministerio Ecclesiæ deputatis, & omnibus Ecclesiæ inservientibus: tertia pauperibus & peregrinis: quarta Ecclesiis, Scholisque reparandis, ad quam partem pertinent non solum ædes ministrorum, doctorum, studiosorum, bibliotheca cum suis libris, instrumenta denique & alia res omnes, templis & scholis necessaria, verum etiam nosocomia & xenodochia, aliaque similia loca, ubi illi degunt, quorum peculiarem curam suscipere debent Ecclesiæ. Hastenus Zanchius, Iam noster: Quis vero ita cæcutit, qui non videat cum loqui de bonis vere Ecclesiasticis, àquibus admodum distincta sunt illa, quæ per errorem & superstitionem in Papatu sunt oblata. Dein Zanchius præsupponit, ante omnia cultui sacro, & reliquis illius appendicibus prospiciendum esse; de superfluo bonorum quasi Ecclesiasticorum, si consuluisset, non potuisset non idem respondere, quod nos fuse supra & Scriptura & rationi consentaneum esse docuimus. De bonis ecclesiasticicis superstitione Papali nonnihil commaculatis, mox videbimus, impræsentiarum sufficit nobis illa tua consessio de bonis vere Ecclesiasticis. Et de superfluo bonorum ecclesiasticorum quia nec hic agitur, neq; consultus Zanchius aliquid respondit, frustra hic verbum. Nunc cum Zanchio, Polano, & aliis probat veterem illam bonorum Ecclesiasticorum in quatuor partes distributionem: & tamen eam ipsam alibi supra modum exagitat: vide pag.23.176.324. Pag. 215. Zepperum sibi quoque non adversum ait, quin hac illius verba, summam totius discursus continentia, & agentia de bonis vere Ecclesiasticis, id est Ecclesiis debitis ad necessarium subsidium, quae inveniuntur pag. 184. & ex antecedentibus explicationem admittere debent, pro nostris adoptare non debeamus: In tot igitur, inquit, divinarum & aequissimarum sanctionum speculum intuentes Christiani principes & magistratus, Deo dent, quae Dei sunt: Ecclesiis, quae Ecclesiarum: &c. Pag. 353 de Vicariatibus non subtrahendis Pastori inopi, inquit: Verum si ex bonis Parochialibus commode familiam sustentare non queat, ipsique destituto Vicariatus reditibus, luctandum sit cum fame, excusari neutiquam potest patronus, si immerenti subducat tales Vicariatus reditus, etiamsi ipse illos non percipiat, confletque eos aut pauperibus, aut Theologiae studiosis cedere. Quae etenim causa, quod vicariatus debeat cedere Pastori; quam quia in subsidium Pastoris illi fundati sunt? quo pacto quod refert pag. 587. ex historia Gelricae Pontani, ab Arnoldo Egmondano duce tria Canonicorum beneficia hac lege Magistratui jure patronatus addicta esse, ut in neminem conferantur nisi qui juris studio operam navans, certo eoque brevi temporis spatio Doctoratus vel Licentiae laurea coronari mereatur, quae vulgo Doctorales praebendae hodierno die nominantur, non ausit credo afferere, praebendas illas, propter istam fundationem, debere aliter, quam in illum finem mapplicari, ut juris studiosi in suum usum cedant. Et quare non simili jure Ecclesiastica? Quomodo autem cum illis a se dictis iterum conveniat, quod pag. 362. ubi postquam distinxisset bona parochialia in Papalia, (seu ex Papatu ad nos derivata, & Reformata, id est, bona a viris piis, Ministrorum, sacrorumque ab iis administrandorum usibus relicta; tamen dicit, aliud non statuendum de bonis his, ac illis, ego non laboro, qui contradictionibus aliorum explicandis non vaco.
units.tr: Should goods given to churches, or to their ministers, to the poor, or to schools, for no other use than their ecclesiastical and pious uses, not be spent, as far as possible, on those uses according to the intention and will of the donors? We are looking here at goods truly ecclesiastical, and we say they are to be spent only on ecclesiastical uses, according to the will of the donors. Salmasius rightly observes how ecclesiastical goods were administered in the past, in his book on trapezitic interest, p. 419: But in former times there was a distinction between the goods of the Church and those of the bishop himself. He supported himself and maintained his own household from his private property; the ecclesiastical goods were administered, on his own view, so that they were paid out to the poor and the sick, or spent on ransoming captives, and on similar pious causes. Certainly on pious causes. And in the very book we have before us there are some passages that favour our view, and these should be cited. P. 204, on the words of Calvin that were alleged, in which he had said: Now indeed, as things stand, I do not wish to excuse everything that happens among us; rather, I admit that it displeases me that in some places the revenues of the Church are not given proper consideration, so that they are spent only on those uses to which they have been dedicated. He says that all good men groan with him about this; and he adds that he, along with many others, is vexed that the revenues of the Church are not assigned to those uses to which they have been dedicated. We approve this with both thumbs, if it is understood of revenues devoted to the uses of the Church with good intention, and provided the holy ministry cannot otherwise be provided for. Why this tail, if you approve Calvin's words and meaning with both thumbs? P. 211. He says that Zanchius is on his side too: "Zanchius does not hurt us either, in chapter 24 of the Confession, where in section 29 he speaks in this way: Since many goods were formerly given to the churches by the generosity of princes and other pious people, and are still given in some places, we judge that if any church has such goods, care must be taken that they are not squandered, nor turned to profane uses, much less to sacrilegious ones, nor allowed to be so turned; but they should be distributed only to those for whom they were given, namely to pious uses. We approve that old division of ecclesiastical goods, so that one part goes to the pious bishops, that is, the teachers and ministers of the Word, and their families; another to the clerics, that is, the students appointed to the ministry of the Church and all who serve the Church; a third to the poor and to strangers; a fourth to the repair of churches and schools, to which belong not only the houses of the ministers, teachers and students, the library with its books, and finally the instruments and all other things necessary for churches and schools, but also hospitals and guesthouses and other similar places where those people live whose special care the Church ought to take up." So far Zanchius. Now our own view: who is so blind as not to see that when we speak of goods truly ecclesiastical, those are quite distinct from the things that were offered in Popery through error and superstition? Then Zanchius presupposes that, before all else, provision must be made for the sacred worship and its other appendages; if he had been consulted about the surplus of so-called ecclesiastical goods, he could not have answered otherwise than we have shown at length above to be consonant with both Scripture and reason. We shall shortly see about ecclesiastical goods somewhat tainted by Papal superstition; for the moment that confession of yours about goods truly ecclesiastical is enough for us. And since the surplus of ecclesiastical goods is not under discussion here, and Zanchius, when consulted, has said nothing on it, the word is spent in vain here. Now, with Zanchius, Polanus and others, he approves that old division of ecclesiastical goods into four parts, and yet elsewhere he attacks it beyond measure: see pp. 23, 176, 324. P. 215. He says that Zepper is not against him either, provided that those words of his, which contain the sum of the whole discourse and deal with goods truly ecclesiastical, that is, goods owed to the Churches for necessary support, which are found on p. 184 and must admit explanation from what goes before, we do not adopt for our side: Looking, then, at the mirror of so many divine and most equitable sanctions, let Christian princes and magistrates give to God what is God's, and to the Churches what is the Churches', etc. P. 353, on not withdrawing vicarages from a needy pastor, he says: But if the parish minister cannot comfortably support his family from the parish goods, and, the vicarage revenues having been withdrawn, must struggle with hunger, the patron cannot in any way be excused if he takes away such vicarage revenues from one who has done nothing to deserve it, even if he does not receive them himself, and they are granted to the poor or to students of theology. For what reason should a vicarage go to a minister, if it was founded for the support of the minister? How does this agree with what he reports on p. 587, from the history of Gelderland by Pontanus, that by a condition set by Duke Arnold of Egmond three canonries were assigned to the magistrate by right of patronage, on the terms that they be conferred on no one except one who, devoting himself to the study of law, deserves to be crowned with the laurel of doctor or licentiate within a certain and short space of time; these are commonly called doctoral prebends today. I do not think he would dare to assert that those prebends, because of that foundation, must be applied otherwise than to that end, so that they go to the use of law students. Why, then, not by a similar right the ecclesiastical goods? But how does this agree again with what he says on p. 362, where, after distinguishing the parish goods into Papal ones (that is, derived to us from Popery) and Reformed ones (that is, goods left by pious men for the uses of ministers and of the sacred things to be administered by them), he nevertheless says that nothing else should be decided about these goods than about those? I am not taking the trouble to explain the contradictions of others.

units.la: II. Quæstio mihi videtur hæc: Num quando bona quæ– dam Ecclesiis, vel earum Ministris, Pauperibus, Scholis data, legata quidem sunt in non alios usus quam Ecclesiasticos, pios;sed vero addita est aliqua conditio superstitionis, aut idololatriæ Papalis, oporteat tum illa bona servare tamen ad usus illos primos & principales Ecclesiasticos, saltem pios & analogos, reformatis istis erroribus; an autem pro profanis habere & communibus?
units.tr: II. The question seems to me to be this: when certain goods given or bequeathed to churches, to their ministers, to the poor, or to schools were indeed given for no other uses than ecclesiastical and pious ones, but some condition of superstition or of Papal idolatry has been added, ought those goods nevertheless to be preserved for those first and principal ecclesiastical uses, at least pious and analogous ones, once these errors have been reformed; or ought they rather to be regarded as profane and common?

units.la: III. Qu. Num in Magistratus arbitrio fit, & potestate bona Ecclesiis, aut pauperibus legata, sive in Papatu, sive in Ecclesiis Reformatis, sicco suo addicere, eademque in alios, quam sacros, ecclesiasticosve usus, quibus data, applicare?
units.tr: III. Question: Is it within the power and authority of the magistrate to assign to his own purse goods bequeathed to churches or to the poor, whether under the Papacy or in the Reformed Churches, and to apply those goods to other uses than the sacred or ecclesiastical ones for which they were given?

units.la: IV. Num quis nec in Ecclesiastico constitutus ministerio, nec in Scholis, neque ex pauperum censu qui fit, tamen queat bona conscientia in privatos suos usus accipere bona, quæ non in alios fines, quam pro Ecclesia, Scholis, pauperibus, data fuerunt?
units.tr: IV. Is it possible for anyone, who is neither installed in the ecclesiastical ministry, nor in the schools, nor among those who are supported from the poor-fund, to take goods in good conscience for his own private uses, goods which were not given for any end other than the Church, the schools, or the poor?

units.la: Hæc mea sententia in controversia generatim versantur, de usu bonorum Ecclesiasticorum; de bonis vere Ecclesiasticis, ad Ecclesiastica impendendis; de Ecclesiasticis Papalibus reformandis, atque ad usus pios, analogos applicandis; de Magistratus potestate circa illa bona non destructiva, sed conservativa & defensiva; de privatis, ut se a bonorum Ecclesiasticorum occupatione & temeratione abstinere debeant. Certe non leve hic negotium, bene ac solide ut consulas hominum conscientiis, super bonorum istorum usu, ubi plures sane sunt ejusdem, & quis dubitet an probi animi, cum Guiljelmo Cantero, nostrate, viro in Græcis eruditissimo, quod varia ejus monumenta testantur, Theodori Canteri Fratre, de quo Melchior Adamus, inter vitas Germanorum Philosophorum refert, quod Reditus Ecclesiasticos, ut iis illicitos qui altari non serviunt, constantissime semper aversatus est. Ne Petrum Martyrem dicam, qui ubi Papatui valedixisset, Lucensibus vel annulum, quem gestare solitus erat, remisit, quo declararet, se nihil bonorum collegii in privatos usus voluisse convertere, inquit quit Scriptor vitæ ejus. Præcipue quando attendimus graves illas & diras execrationes, quibus olim piarum donationum Auctores devoverunt illos quoscumque, qui in usus profanos aut privatos sua pia vota averterent: Nemo successorum Regumq; valeat hac infringere, vel auferre. Si quis quod tamen non credo futurum, adversus hasce donationum ac beneficiorum litteras, quam injustam interpellationem, jus vel injuriam facere voluerit, in primis iram Dei omnipotentis incurrat, & à liminibus S. Ecclesiæ Dei efficiatur extraneus, & sit authoritate nostra Episcopali anathematizatus, sitque maledictus eadem maledictione, quâ descendit super Dathan & Abiron, quos terra vivos absorpsit; & quod repetit evindicare non valeat. Sit præsens traditio ad instar testamenti à nobis facta, omni tempore firma & stabilis permaneat stipulatione subnixâ, quam propriâ manu subter firmavi, & sigilli mei impressione roboravi. In diplomate Caroli F. Pipini R.Si quis vero, quod futurum esse non credimus, sive nos ipsi, vel aliquis de haeredibus vel prohaeredibus, seu qualibet oppositâ vel extranea persona, qui contra hanc donationem, quam nos pro divino intuitu & animæ nostræ remedio ad instar testamenti fieri & affirmari decrevimus, venire aut agere, vel eam infringere conaverit, in primis iram Dei cœlestis incurrat, à liminibus sanctorum, vel consortio Christianorum efficiatur extraneus, insuper inferat una cum socio Fisco nostro aurei libras quinque, argenti etiam pondera decem coactus exolvat, & quod repetit evindicare non valeat, sed præsens donatio ad instar testamenti à me facta, omni tempore firma & stabilis permaneat, cum stipulatione subnixa. Illaque usitata ad confirmandam donationis stabilitatem in fine Diplomatum occurrit formula. Hanc itaque authoritatem, ut tam nostris quam successorum nostrorum temporibus inviolabilem obtineat firmitatem, manu propria subtus firmavimus, & Sigilli nostri impressione jussimus roborari. Vel: Ac ut hac traditionis nostra concessio firmiorem in Dei nomine obtineat vigorem, verisque per successentium curricula temporum ab omnibus credatur, inviolabiliterque servetur, ac incorrupta jugiter perduret, manus nostræ scripto illud firmavimus, & annuli nostri impressione jussimus corroborari. praecipientes, ut nullus habeat potestatem aliquid horum auX ferendi, sed perpetua firmitate inconvulsa permaneant. Si quis hanc ingenuitatis chartam infringere tentaverit, vel molitus fuerit, irâ Dei omnipotentis, & sanctæ Dei Genetricis Mariæ, & sanctæ Crucis, sanctiq; Martini incurrat, & omnium Sanctorum. Et excommunicatus & anathematizatus sit ex parte Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti. Dedimus autem ea lege, ut eadem Ecclesia sancti Petri perenniter absq; omni contradictione obtineat, & interdicimus, ne alicujus violentia inde auferat vel alio transponat. His omnibus absq; omni contradictione peractis: Episcopus banno interdixit, ne quis sive de bonis Ecclesiæ à Comitissa traditis, sive de his quæ Comitissa concesserat, se intromitteret, ac violenter in suos usus redigeret. Quicunq; vero hoc præsumeret, banno subjaceret, atq; omnipotentis Dei & SS. omnium contra se iram sentiret. Ut autem omnia firma & inviolata permaneant, interfuere testes idonei. Si quis vero irritum facere voluerit, & à fratribus illis hanc ecclesiam alienare voluerit, ira Dei maneat super ipsum, & anathematizatus omnibus Christianis sit, sicut Ethnicus & Publicanus. Et ne quis huic dono vel distinctionibus prædictis obvias manus injiciat, anathema maranata facimus omnibus qui faciunt, aut facientibus consentiunt, aut præsentes loco suo non defendunt. Et ne alicui mortalium huius vel impostierum facultas aut occasio contradicendi valeat suboriri, omnem quæ aliquo modo moveri posset calumniam, edicto Regali submovemus, statuentes ne aliqua unquam persona magna sive parva Impp. donationem, & nostram confirmationem, aliquo ingenio infringere præsumat. Cujusmodi occurunt passim in Diplomatibus, à Wilhelmo Heda, in Historia Vltrajectina productis. Alibi quî auferre hac donaria præsumserit, fulmine divino intereat ipse: in Biblioth. Pp. T. VIII. pag. 268. ut inviolabiter conservetur, ab hodierno videlicet die & deinceps. Qui vero nostrâ auctoritatem parvi penderint, illudq; qualicumq; modo temerare præsumpserint, per nostram Pontificalem auctoritatem reddantur extranei a liminibus sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ, & à cœtu Christianorum, & à regno Dei, & descendant cum Dathan & Abiron in infernum viventes, & cum Juda traditore Domini nostri Iesu Christi, accipiant partem & societatem in die judicii, & cum diabolo damnationem æternam, amen. Perpetualiter tribuo. Iugi ævo possidenda. Ut æternaliter conserventur inviolabiliter. In Diplomate Hilsundis Comitissæ (apud Myræum hæc, in lib. Diplomatum Belgicorum) a. Io.cccccxcii. Ecclesia,sed & nostra irre cuperabiliter damnamus, & ab omni consortio Sanctorū in hoc & in futuro seculo excommunicamus,sicuti contemptores divinæ gloriæ,& ecclesiasticæ reverentiæ invasores. In altero ejusdē Lietberti diplomate: „Quicumq; ergo huic cœnobio de concessis & concedendis „aliquid subripere voluerit,& regiæ firmitati contraire tenta„verit,hic à corpore & sanguine Domini,&cómunione pacis „alienus fiat,& nisi resipuerit, & ad satisfactionē venerit, æ„ternę maledictionicū diabolo &angelis ejus damnādus sine sine subjaceat.Crebro legas,anathemate caveri piorū legatorū alienationem:Perpetuo condemnans anathemate quicumq;, qui in posterum hæc præsumeret minuere, aut infirmare. In Diplomate Balduini Hierosolimitani: tremendo Dei judicio se sciat subjacere, & nisi „poenituerit, non solum pro suis, sed etiam pro alienis reatibus Inferni poenas subire. Iohannes Taruanensis episcopus, in Diplomate a. cIↄ cxix. Si qua sane ecclesiastica saecularis„ve persona hanc nostrae constitutionis paginam sciens, te„mere eam infringere tentaverit, secundo tertiove commo„nita, si non satisfactione condigna emendaverit, potestatis „honorisque sui dignitate careat, reamque se divino judicio „de perpetua iniquitate cognoscat, & a sanctissimo corpore „Dei ac Domini Redemtoris nostri Iesu Christi aliena fiat, „atque in extremo examine districtae ultioni subjaceat. Alibi: „excommunicantes & aeternae maledictionis anathemate „condemnantes eos, qui quovis malignitatis ingenio quidli„bet horum infringere tentaverint. Pro infideli habent, quisquis pia temerare aut infringere testamenta ausus fuerit. Carolus Calvus, in Diplomate a. Ioccclxxv. pro Monasterio Vedastino: A corpore & sanguine Christi alienus fiat. Atque ejusmodi plura. Neque iterum me torqueo quomodo conciliem quod Auctor noster perpetuo disputans pro privatorum jure, ex concessione Magistratus, in illa bona, pag. 220. ex bonis quasi Ecclesiasticis Magistratus in usus privatorum disponit. atque haec passim: idem tamen pag. 239. calumniam sibi fieri clamitat, quando asseritur, per ipsum Magistratui jus concedi bona pseudo Ecclesiastica non tantum in publicos, sed privatos suos ac suorum usus convertendi. Idem etiam alibi sic publicos Reip. usus loquitur, ad quos Magistratus bona illa applicet, ut privatorum suorum causam oblitus videatur, & neglexisse. pag. 222. in salutem reip. pag. 228. publicus usibus. pag. 229. publicos illos, quos notavimus usus: ut omni ex parte appareat verum id esse, quod initio diximus, egisse eum nec quod debuit, neque etiam illud quod agere vilus fuit. Sed ita nunquam defuerunt nobis exercitamenta & disputationes super bonis illis, accidit que, quod Beza in vita Calvini narrat, nec pari popoterant aliunde fideles pastores Ecclesiastica bona Pontificiis erepta, non sic, ut oportuit, plerisque locis administrari. Multi tunc clamores: multa querela, multi denique scribendo ac loquendo labores, sed frustra plerumque suscepti: aperte quidem profitente Calvino, se quidem tot sacrilegiis minime favere, quae divinitus tandem sciret severissimè vindicanda; sed in eo tamen justum Dei judicium agnoscere, quod bona tam male prius à sacrificis acquisita, non sineret Dominus Ecclesiarum ararijs inferri. Quod Calvino negotium Genevæ, idem in prima reformatione Thomæ Crammero fuit, in Anglia, super eodem argumento, cum Rege Henrico viii. cupiente universum cœnobiorum censum inferri in fiscum suum; sed refragante Crammero, aliisque Ecclesiasticis, qui magis ex re atque officio fore Christiano judicabant, si quidquid ex bonis Monasteriorum, quod quidem immensum erat, in necessarios egenorum ac scholarum usus converteretur. Ex qua Regis, & Ecclesiasticorum dissensione, prima Reformationis ibi locorum oborta remora fuit. Adeo vulgare est, ut hac de re contendant cum Politicis Theologi Reformatores; ut nihil causæ habuerit Sanderus, lib. 1. de Schism. Anglie. & ex eo Mart. Becanus, Opusc. Theol. Tom. iv. de Titulis Calvinift. pag. 108. Reformatoribus ex probandi Monasteriorum per Angliam direptionem, cui illi, sub Regis etiam ira odioque, acriter restiterunt. Quod nec Becanus ignoravit, qui nostros de eo assatim conquestos scribit, in hæc verba: id non modo fatentur, sed etiam conqueruntur ipsi Aduersarii, prasertim Lutherus in cap. 49 Genesios. Rivius, in lib. de scientia, Sarcerius in lib. de ratione conservandi veram religionem, Hadrianus Saravia in lib. de diversis gradibus ministrorum Ecclesiæ. addit porro ipsa Lutheri verba. units.tr: This is my opinion on the controversy as a whole: on the use of ecclesiastical goods; on goods that are truly ecclesiastical, which must be devoted to ecclesiastical purposes; on the reform of Papal ecclesiastical goods, and their application to analogous pious uses; on the power of the magistrate over those goods, not to destroy them but to preserve and defend them; and on private persons, who ought to abstain from seizing and misusing ecclesiastical goods. This is certainly no small task, if one is to advise men's consciences well and soundly about the use of these goods, of which there are indeed very many. Who could doubt the upright mind of Wilhelm Canter, our countryman, a man most learned in Greek, as his various writings attest, and of his brother Theodor Canter, of whom Melchior Adam reports among the lives of German philosophers that he always most firmly rejected ecclesiastical revenues for those who do not serve the altar, as unlawful for them? I say nothing of Peter Martyr, who, when he had renounced the Papacy, sent back to the people of Lucca even the ring he was accustomed to wear, to show that he had wished to turn none of the goods of the college to private uses, as the writer of his life tells us. This is especially so when we consider those grave and dreadful curses with which the founders of pious gifts once cursed all those who turned their pious intentions to profane or private uses: Let no successor of kings be able to infringe or take these things away. If anyone, which I do not believe will happen, shall wish to act unjustly, or to do wrong, or to make an unjust challenge against these letters of donation and benefice, let him first incur the wrath of almighty God, and be made a stranger to the thresholds of the holy Church of God, and let him be anathematized by our episcopal authority, and be cursed with the same curse by which the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram alive; and let him not be able to reclaim what he seeks to vindicate. Let the present gift, made by us in the manner of a testament, remain firm and stable at all times, supported by a stipulation, which I have signed below with my own hand and strengthened with the impression of my seal. In the diploma of Charles, son of Pepin the King: But if anyone, which we do not believe will happen, whether we ourselves or any of our heirs or successors, or any opposing or foreign person, shall attempt to come against or act against or infringe this gift, which we have decreed and affirmed for the sake of divine regard and the remedy of our soul, in the manner of a testament, let him first incur the wrath of heavenly God, be made a stranger to the thresholds of the saints and to the fellowship of Christians, and moreover let him pay, together with our fisc as partner, five pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver, and let him not be able to reclaim what he seeks to vindicate; but let the present gift, made by me in the manner of a testament, remain firm and stable at all times, supported by a stipulation. The formula commonly found at the end of diplomas, to confirm the stability of a gift, is also this: We have therefore signed this authority below with our own hand, so that it may hold inviolable firmness both in our times and in those of our successors, and we have ordered it to be strengthened with the impression of our seal. Or: And so that this concession of our gift may have firmer force in the name of God, and may be believed by all and inviolably kept through the course of the succeeding times, and may endure continually uncorrupted, we have confirmed it with the writing of our hand, and ordered it to be corroborated with the impression of our ring; commanding that no one have power to take away any of these things, but that they remain unshaken in perpetual firmness. If anyone shall attempt or contrive to break this charter of freedom, let him incur the wrath of almighty God, and of the holy Mother of God Mary, and of the holy Cross, and of St Martin, and of all the saints. And let him be excommunicated and anathematized on the part of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We have given it on this condition, that the same church of St Peter may hold it forever, without any contradiction, and we forbid that it be taken away from it by anyone's violence or transferred elsewhere. All these things having been done without any contradiction, the bishop by ban forbade anyone to meddle with either the goods of the Church given by the countess or those which the countess had granted, or to bring them by force into their own uses. But whoever should presume to do so shall be subject to the ban, and shall feel the wrath of almighty God and of all the saints against him. And so that all these things may remain firm and inviolate, suitable witnesses were present. If anyone shall wish to make this void, and to alienate this church from those brothers, let the wrath of God remain upon him, and let him be anathematized by all Christians, like a heathen and a tax collector. And that no one lay hands in opposition to this gift or the aforesaid distinctions, we make an anathema maranatha against all who do so, or who consent to those doing so, or who do not defend them when present in their place. And so that no opportunity or possibility of contradicting this or any future thing may arise for any mortal, we remove by royal edict every calumny which could in any way be stirred up, decreeing that no person, great or small, shall presume in any way to break the donation of the emperors and our confirmation. Such formulas occur everywhere in diplomas, produced by Wilhelm Heda in his History of Utrecht. Elsewhere: whoever shall presume to take away these gifts, let him perish by divine lightning: in the Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. VIII, p. 268, that it may be inviolably preserved, from this day onward. But those who make little of our authority, and presume to violate it in any way, let them be made, by our pontifical authority, strangers to the thresholds of the holy Church of God and to the assembly of Christians and to the kingdom of God; and let them go down alive with Dathan and Abiram into hell, and with Judas the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, receive a portion and fellowship on the day of judgment, and with the devil eternal damnation, amen. I grant it in perpetuity. To be possessed for everlasting time. That it may be eternally and inviolably preserved. In the diploma of Hinc, bishop of Mainz, and others, of which we have also spoken above: condemned by the judgment of us all, bound by the chains of anathema from the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from almighty God, whom he did not fear to wrong, since he himself said: he who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me; separated from the assembly of the saints for eternity by the just judgment of God, let him perish in hell, with those whose worm does not die and whose fire is not quenched; unless he repent worthily with public satisfaction, deposed, if he be a layman, from the belt of secular service; if a cleric, from the dignity of ecclesiastical honour. Elsewhere: And if anyone hereafter (which I do not believe will happen), whether I myself, which God forbid, or any of my heirs or successors, or any other person, shall presume to come against or challenge this little charter of donation, and does not withdraw from it, let him be excommunicated and cut off from the thresholds of the Church of God, and moreover on the day of the dreadful judgment let him give an account for this. In the diploma of Countess Hilsund (here cited from Miraeus, in the book of Belgian diplomas), of the year 1091: whoever does otherwise, let him have a portion with Dathan and Abiram, and let his sin not be forgiven him either in this age or in the future. So be it, so be it. Of Warin, bishop of Beauvais, of the year 1123: we announce penalties of hell, threatening with the menace of this our prohibition the one who neglects it, just as, on the contrary, we wish true blessedness to the one who keeps it. Of Liétbert, bishop of Cambrai: we irrevocably condemn this man, by the fearful authority of the divine name, of the whole holy Church, and of ourselves, and we excommunicate him from all fellowship with the saints in this age and the future, as despisers of divine glory and invaders of ecclesiastical reverence. In another diploma of the same Liétbert: Whoever therefore shall wish to take away anything from this monastery, of what has been granted and is to be granted, and shall attempt to oppose royal firmness, let him be estranged from the body and blood of the Lord and from the communion of peace; and unless he repent and come to satisfaction, let him lie condemned to eternal curse with the devil and his angels without end. You may often read that the alienation of pious bequests is guarded by anathema: condemning forever with anathema whoever shall presume in future to diminish or weaken these things. Henry III, of the year 1089: let him suffer the peril of his honour and office, or be struck by the vengeance of excommunication. In the diploma of Baldwin of Jerusalem: let him know that he is subject to the fearful judgment of God, and unless he repent, he shall undergo the pains of hell not only for his own guilt but also for the guilt of others. John, bishop of Thérouanne, in a diploma of the year 1119: If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to infringe it, and when warned a second or third time does not amend it by fitting satisfaction, let him lack the dignity of power and honour, and let him know that he is guilty before the divine judgment of perpetual iniquity, and let him be estranged from the most holy body of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and undergo the severe vengeance at the last examination. Elsewhere: excommunicating and condemning with the anathema of eternal curse those who by any malice of cunning shall attempt to infringe any of these things. Whoever has dared to violate or break pious wills, let him be held as an unbeliever. Charles the Bald, in a diploma of the year 875, for the monastery of St Vaast: let him be estranged from the body and blood of Christ. And many more of this kind. Nor do I again torment myself as to how our author, while arguing throughout for the right of private persons, by the grant of the magistrate, may reconcile this with what he says on p. 220: the magistrate disposes of goods, as it were ecclesiastical, for the uses of private persons, and so on everywhere. Yet on p. 239 he cries out that a calumny is being made against him when it is asserted that, through him, the magistrate is granted the right to turn pseudo-ecclesiastical goods not only to public but also to his private uses and those of his own. He likewise speaks elsewhere of the public uses of the commonwealth to which the magistrate applies those goods, so that he seems to have forgotten the cause of private persons, and to have neglected it: p. 222, for the safety of the commonwealth; p. 228, for public uses; p. 229, those public uses which we have noted. So it appears in every respect true what we said at the start: he has acted neither as he ought, nor even as it was his wish to act. But we have never lacked such exercises and disputes about those goods, and what Beza relates in the life of Calvin has happened: the faithful pastors could not otherwise administer the ecclesiastical goods snatched from the Papists, and not as they ought in most places. Many outcries were raised, much complaint, and finally many labours in writing and speaking were undertaken, but mostly in vain; Calvin openly declared that he by no means favoured so many sacrileges, which he knew would at last be most severely avenged by God; yet he recognised in it the just judgment of God, that the Lord did not allow goods so badly acquired by the priests before to be brought into the purses of the Church's enemies. What happened to Calvin at Geneva happened in the first Reformation in England to Thomas Cranmer, on the same question, when King Henry VIII wished the whole income of the monasteries to be carried into his own treasury; but Cranmer and other churchmen resisted, who judged it more fitting to duty and to the Christian office, if whatever came from the goods of the monasteries, which indeed was immense, were turned to the necessary uses of the poor and the schools. From this disagreement between the King and the churchmen there arose a first hindrance to the Reformation in those places. So common is it that the theologians and the Reformers contend with the politicians about this matter, that Sanders, book 1, on the Schism of England, and from him Martin Becanus, Opuscula Theologica, vol. IV, On the Titles of the Calvinists, p. 108, had no reason to charge the Reformers with approving the plundering of the monasteries throughout England, which they resisted sharply even under the anger and hatred of the King. Becanus, who wrote that our people complained of this at length, did not fail to know it, in these words: not only do the adversaries themselves admit this, but even complain of it, especially Luther on Genesis chapter 49, Rivius in his book on knowledge, Sarcerius in his book on the way of preserving the true religion, Hadrian Saravia in his book on the different grades of ministers of the Church. He further adds Luther's own words. In the year 1565, the ministers of the county of Mansfeld, in their confession against Paul Eber etc., among other things which the teachers of the Gospel should all consider as deforming the Church of God and whose remedies they should all think about, put this: the goods of the Church have vanished. Indeed, in this year 1651, in the Synod of Sweden, article 111, the grievance was repeated: since in various earlier synods it was decreed that the nobles and cities should insist that the sacred goods of pastorates, vicarages, etc., could not and should not be alienated, sold, or applied to other uses than pious ones, it is asked whether this should not be demanded anew on this occasion. It pleased all the classes that it should be done, according to the various decrees on this matter in earlier synods. So uniform in this matter is the opinion of the teachers, synods and churches, that ecclesiastical goods must be claimed for ecclesiastical uses, and it is a matter of conscience for us to depart from this opinion or not to follow and defend it.

units.la: §.xii. Atque hæc fuit prima causa, cur se juste abrogare putet Papa pacem Germaniæ, ob bona videlicet Ecclesiastica, per pacem hanc, Protestantibus in perpetuum adjudicata. Sequitur altera, quæ petitur à libertate religionis, exercitiorumque, pace hac Protestantibus concessa: Hereticis, Augustana, ut vocant, Confessionis liberum sua hæresos Exercitium in plerisque locis permittitur, & locorum pro ædificandis ad hunc effectum templis assignatio permittitur. Resp. 1. Hæc nimirum odii Papalis erga nos causa est, quod videmur ipsis hæretici:sed quod nos inter illas contumelias blasphemiasque reponimus, quas non modo bono animo ferre jubet Petrus, sed in quibus ferendis nos beatos æstimat. si contumeliam patiamini in nomine Christi, beati: nam ille gloria Deique spiritus supra vos quiescit. 1.Pet. iv. 14. & 16. si quis patiatur ut Christianus, ne pudeat, quin glorificet Deum hac in parte. Et jam istis elogiis à multo tempore assueti sumus, ut hæretici dicamur, utque divina veritas & Christus per nostrorum latus ita passim calumnientur. Parum id est, ni etiam Turcæ, & qui Turcis deteriores, quod palam (ne infamem librum Calvinorum dicam) Turfin in Concilio Tridentino dixit Cardinalis Farnesius, Pauli iii nepos, apud illos audiamus. addo & pejores Paganis: quem in finem Guiljelmus Rosseus, qui de justa Reip. Christianæ in Reges impios & hæreticos authoritate librum scripsit, maledicentissimum in Henricum Navarræum Regem, caput quintum inscripsit: Calvinismus Paganismo longe detestabilior; ejusque
units.tr: §.xii. And this was the first reason why the Pope thinks he may justly abrogate the peace of Germany: namely, the ecclesiastical goods, which this peace has adjudicated to the Protestants in perpetuity. The second follows, drawn from the liberty of religion and of worship that this peace grants to the Protestants: To the heretics of the so-called Augsburg Confession, the free exercise of their heresy is permitted in most places, and the assignment of places for building churches for this purpose is permitted. Reply 1. Surely this is the cause of the Papal hatred against us, that we seem to them to be heretics. But we count this among those insults and blasphemies which Peter not only bids us bear with a good mind, but considers us blessed in bearing. If you suffer reproach for the name of Christ, you are blessed, for the glory and the Spirit of God rests upon you. 1 Pet. 4:14 and 16. If anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this respect. And now for a long time we have been accustomed to these titles, that we are called heretics, and that divine truth and Christ are everywhere slandered through our side. It would be a small matter, were we not also to hear it from the Turks, and from those worse than Turks, as the Cardinal Farnese, nephew of Pope Paul III, openly said at the Council of Trent (I will not call it the infamous book of the Calvinists), about Turfin. I add also, worse than the pagans: to this end William Rosseus, who wrote the book On the Just Authority of the Christian Commonwealth over Impious and Heretical Kings, inscribed the fifth chapter of his most abusive book against Henry, King of Navarre: Calvinism is far more detestable than paganism; and he draws this conclusion from it: that the Calvinists are truly possessed by the Devil, and are true monsters and portents in the Christian religion. We are little moved by all these things, as by the devilish darts received in the cause of Christ; and we answer as Bernard once did, in book II of On Consideration, also to Pope Eugenius: If God deigns to use me as a shield, I gladly receive on myself the slanderous tongues of those who tear me down, so that they do not reach him. If it were pleasing here, I could digress into a very lengthy disputation, so as to drive the calumny of heresy away from us and our churches; but both because this has been abundantly accomplished by our churches and our countless teachers, which is quite plain to the whole world, and because we have come rather to examine what concerns the present Bull of the Pope, we pass over those matters securely, as sufficiently known and refuted.

units.la: que conclusionem hanc facit: quod Calvinista sint vere a Diabolo possessi, sintque in religione Christiana vera monstra atque portenta. Quibus omnibus, ut Diabolicis spiculis in Christi causa exceptis, nos parum movemur, regerimusque, quod olim Bernardus lib. II. de consider. ad Eugenium quoque Papam: bonum mihi si me dignetur Deus uti pro clypeo, libens excipio in me destrahentium linguas maledicas, ut non ad ipsum perveniat. Hic si liberet, possem excurrere in prolixam valde disputationem, ut haeresis calumniam a nobis nostrisque Ecclesiis propellerem; sed, tum quia abunde id ab Ecclesiis & Doctoribus nostris infinitis praestitum, quod Orbi satis superque constat, tum quia quae Bullam Papae praesentem spectant, potius examinaturi accessimus, illa ut nota dilutaque satis, secure praeterimus.
units.tr: Whatever the Pope says about the heretics of the Augsburg Confession, the same also touches the Reformed, whom the Roman party places all in one class. And the articles of the Peace of Münster or Osnabrück of 1648 make the Reformed equal to the men of the Augsburg Confession. Art. VII: By the unanimous consent of His Caesarean Majesty and of all the Orders of the Empire, it has pleased that whatever right or benefit, both all other constitutions of the Empire and the Religious Peace and this public transaction, and in it the settlement of grievances, grant to the other Catholic and Augsburg Confession-attached states and subjects, this too should belong to those who are called Reformed among them.

units.la: II. Quod de haereticis Augustanae Confessionis ait Papa, perinde & Reformatos tangit, quos uno ordine omnes habet Romanus. Atque articuli pacis Monasteriensis sive Osnabrugensis a. 1648 pares faciunt cum Augustanae Confessionis hominibus, Reformatos. Art. VII. Vnanimi quoque Caesarea Majestatis, omniumque Ordinum Imperii consensu placuit, ut quicquid juris aut beneficii, cum omnes alia Constitutiones Imperii, tum Pax Religionis & publica haec Transactio, in eaque decisio Gravaminum, caeterisque Catholicis, & Augustanae Confessioni addictis Statibus & subditis tribuunt, id etiam iis, qui inter illos Reformati vocantur, competere debeat.
units.tr: II. As to what the Pope says about the heretics of the Augsburg Confession, it touches the Reformed equally, whom the Roman Church includes in one and the same class. And the articles of the Peace of Münster or Osnabrück of 1648 place the Reformed on a level with the adherents of the Augsburg Confession. Art. VII. By the unanimous consent also of His Caesarean Majesty and of all the Orders of the Empire, it has been agreed that whatever right or benefit, both all the other Constitutions of the Empire and the Peace of Religion and this public Transaction, and in it the settlement of grievances, grant to the other Catholic states and subjects, and to the states adhering to the Augsburg Confession, should likewise belong to those who among them are called Reformed.

units.la: In fine: Sed praeter Religiones supra nominatas nulla alia in sacra Imperio Romano recipiatur vel toleretur. intelliguntur, tres Religiones, Reformata, & Augustanae Confessionis, & Romano-Catholica, quae vocatur. Sic enim exlerte in exemplari Germanico, quod authoritate Caesarea, & Moguntini Electoris concessione impressum Moguntiae a. 1659 juxta originale, quod in Imperiali Directorio Moguntino, ad marginem legitur: uber bemelte drey religion sollen seine im reich gebuldet werden. III. Iam quod ad libertatem exercitii religionis, Protestantibus concessam, quae Papam tantopere urit, ita est, illa rata habetur & firma, hac communi pace Germaniae, eoque magis
units.tr: In the end: But besides the religions named above, no other shall be admitted or tolerated in the Holy Roman Empire. By these are understood three religions: the Reformed, the Augsburg Confession, and the Roman Catholic, as it is called. For so it is clearly stated in the German copy, which was printed at Mainz in 1659 by imperial authority and with the permission of the Elector of Mainz, according to the original, and which is read in the margin of the Imperial Directory at Mainz: the three religions named above shall be tolerated in the Empire. III. Now as to the freedom of exercising religion granted to the Protestants, which so greatly galls the Pope, it is held valid and firm, and by this common peace of Germany, and all the more so

units.la: uber bemelte, drey religion sollen seine im reich gebuldet werden. gis quo ex dissensionibus circa religionem belli causas potissimum ortas nemo ignorabat. Quocirca, si pacem amarent, ut illa semper bello præferenda est, belli terminus & finis, in hoc convenire necesse habuerunt, quod multis etiam ante Imperialibus decretis de pace religionis statutum sæpius foerat, ut ab ambabus utriusque religionis partibus libertas & pax religionis sartastecta custodiretur, ad exactam mutuamque, uti jam loquuntur æqualitatem, & (quod bene addiderunt) non curata cujusquam pacis istius adversarii oppositione vel protestatione, sive Ecclesiastici, sive politici. Hæc ipsa fœderis verba: Cum autem præsenti bello magnam „partem Gravamina, quæ inter utriusque Religionis Ele„stores, Principes & Status Imperii vertebantur, causam & „occasionem dederint, de iis prout sequitur, conventum & „transactum est. 1.
