units.la: Ad Thuanum, similis cū eo de religionis dissidiis sententiæ, inGallia præsertim,plures est reperire; & siVtenbogardo credimus, in historia vitæ suæ cap. xvi. & xvii. Archiepiscopus quoque Rothomagensis; quoíque politicos appellant. Thuanus lib. xliv. ad a. clo lo lxvi i i. denominationis illius ponit originem,eaque dénotatos scribit optimates, pacis studiosos, qui majorum religionem amplectuntur, inquit, sed à turbis & factionibus, & prorsus de à Lotharingorum partibus alieni sunt: quales memorat inter Proceres quidem,Carolum Cardinalem Borbonium, Michaelem Hospitalium Cancellarium, Momorantios. Hæc ille ad Condæi litteras, quas ad Regem Carolum ix.discessus sui ex aula causas explicaturus,isto anno dedit, quarumque summam Thuanus, sed eas integras exhibet Auctor Commentariorum de Statu religionis & reip. in Gallia sub Carolo ix.part.ii. Verba Condæi Principis in epistolâ erant: tum & eos, qui Romanam religionem sequuntur, nec illorum Lotharingorum partibus favent quos politicos vocant, quod pacis tranquillitatisque studiosi, turbarum sint hostes. vide Thuanum quoq; lib. li i. ad a.clo lo lxxii.& lib.lvii.ad a.clo lolxxiv. A. Caslandri partibus plures olim stabant, Wicelus, Metellus, Hoppterus (de quibus nonnulla in epistolis illustrium Belgarum) quod instar prodigii non immerito censet Dan. Heinsius, in sua ad illas epistola praefatoria, Ximenius, Hispanus & Theologus. De Andrea Fricio Modrevio hoc est judicium Vorstii, antequam hic apostataret, in Apol. pro Eccles. adverf. Monasteriensis, pag 240. quod politicus magis quam Ecclesiasticus esset. Marcus Antonius de Dominis utramque Ecclesiam, Romanam & Reformatam conferebat navibus quae in omnibus, praeterquam in sola pyxide, conveniebant: utraque (dicebat) religio in praecipuis essentialibus ac fundamentalibus eadem, utraque Christum habent pro Domino ac Mediatore, utraque idem baptisma &c. Discrimen Romanensium navium ac Reformatarum non est in fundo aut in rudentibus, sed duntaxat in pixide. Romana haec navis, vas satis probum bene aedificatum, non putre, neque in fragmenta & frusta defluens, apprime instructa malis, funibus ac rudentibus, ac anchoris, Luculentam mappam hydrographicam habet, vectores, ac milites omnes pariter sub eodem vexillo sunt, eundemque imperatorem solum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum habent. Atque nullum discrimen inter hanc navem & reformatam. Unicam tamen differentiam praecipuam animadverto: ex qua nascuntur & oriuntur quamplurima & alia dissentanea ac pugnantia, nimirum, gubernatorem navis qui clavum tenet Romanae navis repudiasse ordinariam pixidem & reliquisse praxin & usum mappa hydrographica, & recepta, unde est quod vertigine quadam, e suo cerebro novam chartam procuderit, pixidem sibi duntaxat propriam, falsam, & ineptam effinxerit, quae polum nequaquam intuetur & cujus lingula magnetis infecta non est. Haec in Concione, quam Lond. habuit Ital. a. cIↄIↄ cxvi i. atq; a. prec. cIↄIↄcxvi. inconsilio suae professionis vel discessus ex Rapatu, jam delinearat; sed haud probe ista. Transeo quae adversus Cassandrum, Milletcrium, Grotium, similesque tum Nostri tum alii copiose dixerunt, neque vel de syncretismo aut unione utriusque Ecclesiae, nostrę & Romanae, aut intempestivo illorum qui combinare ista allaborant, studio nunc ago, quivulgo quantum utriusque placere cupiunt, tantum & displicent; uti de Minaeis vel Nazaraeis sui saeculi Hieronymus loquitur, in epist. ad Augustinum, dum volunt & Iudei esse & Christiani, nec Iudei sunt nec Christiani. Nam praeterquam quod articuli & dogmata Papatus in Concilio Tridentino ita formata studio sint, ut quam maxime ab omni convenientia abesse, neque ulla rima concordiae esset reliqua, quam istis temporibus aliquando agitatam vehementer horrebant Patres; unde Auctor historiae Conc. Trid. lib. II. pag. 229. de Vega, & ejus super negotio liberi arbitrii sententia sermonem instituens, inquit: Et quamvis ille disceret omni studio in concordiam incumbendum, ab eo tamen abhorrebat Patrum auris atque animus, quibus grave causa praejudicium quodammodo videbatur, nullam e controversiis posse reconciliari. Quo magis frustra illi sunt, caeteri magni ac doctissimi viri, qui conciliationem quaerunt in doctrina, tam diligenter adversus omnem reconciliationem, & rimam concordiae, ut idem Auctor loquitur. pag. 211. constituta; quamque conciliari posse magnis clamoribus denegant Papistarum praecipui: Bellarminum vide lib. III. de Laicis, cap. XIX. Hosium, (utrumque Cardinalem) epist. ad Sigismundum Poloniae Regem, quae est epistolarum ejus CXXXIV, ne alios dicam. Unde nostris istiusmodi compositiones cum irreconciliabili Roma, (quas dum aliqui moliuntur, non duas combinant Ecclesias, sed aliam tertiam ex suo cerebro, qualis nempe ipsis videatur utramque esse debere, formant, quavis à neutra parte agnitam & comprobatam) haud immerito semper suspectae fuerunt. Melanchthon, ut hunc solum nominem, coque mavis quo ab henoticis illis in suas aliquando partes trahi solet, Testamento suo, quod a. MDXLIX ompofuit, postquam longo rerum usu didicisset quam vanae essent plerumque religionum conciliationes: Erunt etiam fortassis inquit nova dogmatum conciliationes sophisticae post hanc aetatem, ubi restituentur veteres errores nonnihil fucati, & hae conciliationes corrumpent doctrinae puritatem, quae nunc traditur. De his quoque praemonco meos, ne sophisticas conciliationes approbent. Adde Pezelium, part. VII. argum. Melanth. pag. 607. Praeter illas inquam, nisi concordiae omnis ratio, quam commendant pacis nuperæ articuli, à Papa ipso aliquando incipiat, frustra est quod in illa reperienda alii occupentur, & quousque non saltem eo delcendit ille, ut quod Imperatores censent omnino ad pacem inter homines colendam necessarium esse, hoc super negotio pacis religionis, omnino approbet, jubeo omnes ab opere syncretismi in religione tentandi otiosos esse ac feriari: nam & hinc factum ut in fumum abierint quacunque alii de componendis religionis dissidiis multo studio dixerunt, quod Papæ ea non probarentur, vel à Papa non prodiissent, religionis Papalis summo ic. arbitrio. Alterutrum, qui de concordanda utraque religione sunt acturi, vel Papam comprehendunt una vel excludunt. Ni in limine profiteantur se Papam secludere, & donec ab ipso pendent, nisi ipse articulos compositionis cudat & probet, emendationemque à se ipso inchoet, quod hactenus neutrum egit, facturus num sit aliquando, dubitent alii, sagacior mecum quisque, haud credit, nihil quidem perfici fructuosi aut solidi poterit. Abjuratoautem prius Papa, ejusque obedientia, tum, si quando, fieri aliquid hac in re utile atque laudabile, præsertim loco illius constituto unico ad res fidei & religionis gnomone S. Scriptura, poflet. Politici autem hac in parte Papis longe meliores sunt & religiosiores, qui & cogitant nonnunquam de ineunda in religione dissidiorum compositione, quod in regno Poloniæ nuper Conventus Thorunensis a. cIↄ Iↄ cxlxv. præ se tulit; & denique omnium curæ commendavit & studio nupera Germaniæ pax Osnabrugensis: Verum ad pacem quantum confert Imperium, conferunt & politici, tantum adversatur unus Papa. Imperatores pacem religionis saltem politicam sanciunt, dum Ecclesiasticam non possunt, nam duplex potest esse, politica, & Ecclesiastica; Papa nec hanc, neque illam fert, sed utriusque æque est inimicus & adversarius. Iubent pacis articuli, ut studium suum huc quisque conferat, ut post politicam religionis pacem, id est ut tres istæ vel duæ religiones, Protestantium Euangelica, & Romana una habitent in Imperio, & æqualibus fruantur privilegiis, tandem ctiam etiam ratio inveniatur pacis quod ad religionem Ecclesiasticæ, pro majori utriusque in unum coadunatione in religione & Ecclesia; eo magis, quo satis compertum hodie verum esse, quod rerum politicarum experientissimus & illustris vir Ludovicus Camerarius haud ita pridem scripsit,in præfat. Epistolarum Huberti Languneti, à se editarum: cuncta bella quibus hoc infausto sæculo nostro Christianus orbis concussus est, à persecutionibus religionis causa suscepti originem suam traxisse. Facileque prælagiendum, ex eodem fonte & pacis rupturam primo sequuturam; & bella alia. Negotium vero pacis religiosæ deceret Papam quidem primum capessere atque adoriri. Iubet Imperium, ut pacis fœdera ab omnibus custodiantur, utque nullus se audeat ei opponere vel obloqui; & post ratam pacem Cæsar denuo a. præcedente cIↄ lↄ l.d.xxvii. Iunii omnia attentata, disputationes, conciones aliasve contraventiones contra conclusionem & instrumentum pacis sub gravi pœna prohibuit: quæ tantum abest, ut confirmet pro officio (si quod ejus sit officium) Papa, ut maxime quidem ipse transgrediatur. Olim a. cIↄ lↄ lxxxiii. d.ii. Oct. Imp. Maximilianus i i. pacem religionis, adversus Doctoris Georgii Ederi libellum turbulentum ac seditiosum quamvis pro fide Romana adversus Protestantes scriptum, ita tuitus est, ut tali decreto Auctorem istum, eundemq; aulicum suum notarit, unde exemplum nunc sumat Ferdinandus Imp. quid in simili casu agendum sibi sit. decretum ita habet: Sacra Cæsarea Majestas Consiliario suo Aulico Georgio Edero, I.V. Doctori, significari jussit, suam Majestatem in libro, quem sua Majestati nuper offerri voluit, molestissime & indignantissime ferre nimiam ejus vehementiam, acerbitatem & immodestiam, injuriosaque verba in multos Imperii Status ac personas, inprimis autem Augustanæ Confessionis socios, quorum non modo religionem & confessionem, sed statum quoque, honorem & dignitatem gravissime lasserit; injuriaverit ac condemnarit: quum tamen & ipsi & omnibus notum sit atque constet, quanto zelo, labore ac sollicitudine tam Majestatis suæ majoris laudatissimi, quam ipsa etiam sua Majestas, tot jam annos in omnibus Imperii Comitiis ac Congregationibus semper intenti fuerint, ut quod à communibus etiam Imperii Statibus in Pace religionis & alias salubriter accordatum & constitutum est, nemo alterum in honore, dignitate, statu, conscientia, aut alio quocunque modo, taxet, molestet, offendat, ladat, calumnietur aut injuriet: id quod suâ Majestas non modo in Imperio, sed Regnis quoque & Principatibus hereditariis summa ope hactenus nixa fuerit, ut diligenter & exacte observaretur. Quapropter sacra Cæsarea Majestatis liber ille à Doctore Edero editus summopere displicet, & disgratissimus est: nec ea sibi persuadere poterat, tantam imprudentiam, audaciam & immoderationem in eum cadere potuisse, qui tanto tempore suæ Majestatis Consiliarius in Aula extiterit quippe cui pra cæteris cognitum ac perspectum est, ne summos quidè homines, nedum Majestatis suæ Consiliarios decere, contra Majestatis sacræ & sacri Imperii Constitutiones & pacem religionis, atque adeo suæ Majestatis in Imperio factam severam ordinationem, quidquam tale vel in ipsis suis hereditariis terris publicandum curare, & quæ sequuntur. extat integrum apud Goldastum Constitut. Imperial. Tom. III. Quarto, quod Protestantibus Papa invidet libertatem exercitii religionis, locaque pro ædificandis hunc in finem templis, non tantum incurrit in statum Imperii, ubi, quemadmodum offendit Dux Casimirus in Declaration sur le point de Gebhard Archevesque de Cologne, aliisque qui de pace religionis in Germania scripserunt, liberum exercitium religionis unicum est medium stabiliendæ certæ in Imperio pacis, atque unionis; verum nec alibi, in Regno Galliæ auditur: siquidem æquum & necessarium judicant orbis Principes, Reformatis illa neutiquam denegare. In Gallia quidem ab a. cIↄ Iↄ Ixɪ. edicto Caroli ix. d. xvii. Ianuarii, quod inde Ianuarium appellatum fuit, atque iterata jussione ad Parlamentum Parisiense Rex promulgari, servarique inviolabiliter atque sine infractione, (uti in litteris suis loquitur) jussit, pacem religionis Reformatis primum decretam. Iterum edicto Martii quod appellant, a. cIↄ Iↄ Ixii. d. xix. istius mensis. edicto a. cIↄ Iↄ Ixiii. d. xiv. Decembris. Alio, a. cIↄ Iↄ Ixviii. d. xxiii. Martii. quo confirmatum tum edictum pacificationis, uti illud appellatur, anni cIↄ Iↄ IXXII. diei xix. Martii, cujus articulus primus ita habet: A sçavoir Que tous ceux de la Religion pretendue reformee, joussent dudit Edict de pacification purement & simplement, & qu'il soit executé en tous ses poincts & articles selon sa premiere forme & teneur, levant & ostant toutes restrictions, modifications, declarations & interpretations qui ont esté faites depuis le jour & date d'iceluy iusques à la publication de ces presentes. Edicto a. cIↄ Iↄ lxx. d. xi. Augusti, quod edictum perpetuum dicitur, & irrevocabile. Iterum a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxiii. d. xi. Augusti. A Rege Henrico iii. a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxvi. d. xiv. Maij, edicto perpetuo & irrevocabili. Alio, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxvii. mense Septembri, edicto item perpetuo & irrevocabili. A.cIↄ Iↄ lxxxi. d. xxvi Ianuarii, tum praecedentia edicta tum articuli Neracenses, saper eodem negotio conclusi (a.cIↄ, Iↄ lxxix ult. Februar. inter Reginam matrem Catharinam, & Regem Navarræum Henricum, aliosque Religionis Reformatæ deputatos) fuere confirmati, ampliati, & declarati, ut habet Edicti titulus. A Rege Henrico iv. a.cIↄ Iↄ xcii. mense Iulio, edicto Nannetensi. A.cIↄ Iↄ xcix. d. xxv. Februar. edicto perpetuo & irrevocabili, par edict perpetuel & irrevocable. Post eadem Regis, à Regina matre a. cIↄ Iↄ cx. Iterum à Ludovico Rege, in regiminis sui primordiis. Quae omnia tum necessitatem, tum æquitatem ejus confirmant, quod in Imperio, & pace Germaniæ adeo offendit Papam, vid. non aliter pacem haberi posse quam decreta pace religionis, & Protestantibus concessa exercitiorum Sacrorum libertate. 'Nam & Reges Galliæ in illis suis edictis hanc causam adferunt, quod strustra alio modo,& severa persequutione rè agere publicam conati hactenus fuerint. In primo edicto a.cIↄ Iↄ lxi, Carolus Rex: quelques remedes que nos Predecesseurs ayent tenté pour y pourvoir, tant par la rigueur & feverité des punitions. In edicto anni cIↄ Iↄ lxii. voyant neantmoins que tout le mal & inconvenient que sort de ceste guerre, tourne à la diminution & dommage de nostre Royaume: & ayant experimenté, avec nostre grande perte, tel remede n'y estre propre ne convenable. Edicto a. cIↄ Iↄ lxviii. prevoyant la desolation qui pourroit ci apres advenir, si par la grace & misericorde de nostre Seigneur lesdits troubles n'estoyent promptement pacifiez. Henricus iii. edicto a. clo lo lxxvii. nous ayant l'experience en nostre Majorite de vingt-cinq ans fait cognoistre, que de la continuation des armes & de la guerre ne peut provenir le bien que nous avons tant desiderè & procure. Vbi ergo Imperatores & Reges experimento se doctos fatentur ne armis & bellis rem hanc ulterius agant, pacem vero religionis sectandam omnino esse, & ultro citroque observandam, quis ille spiritus, qui Papam agitat adversus Principes, & pacem; adeo e republica, & communi Christianorum omnium bono necessariam? Quare Rex Henricus iv. in instructione Perrono, anno. clo lo xcv. d. ix. Maji data, pro impetranda sui cum Papa Romano reconciliatione, expresse injunxit, ne conditiones ullas admittent sui, quae Regi foedissent turpes & nocivae, qualis si cogeretur Rex bellum indicere Hugonotis, & hunc in finem revocare edicta per Reges Praedecessores suos pro pace regni facta. Noluit Rex, ut hisce & talibus se ullo pacto implicerent Legati, gnarus quam illa Reip. necessaria sint ut nunquam turbentur, & quibus evertendis tamen, cumque iis omni reip. & regno, assidue, incumbat Papa. Vnde & Perronus postea Papae Paulo v. satagenti, pro innata Papis turbandi libidine, Regem adversus subditos suos Religionis Reformatae instigare, oblo culos posuit, quod per bella civilia partes Reformatorum in regno semper fuissent adauctae & magis confirmatae: la ou il avoit toujours falu qu' à la sin de chaque rupture, si leur eust donné plus de places de seureté, qu'ils n'en avoient auparavant: d'autant que par la guerre civile, les Heretiques s'accroissoient de force & de party en France, plusieurs des Catholiques se rangeants avec eux, & les Princes dehors mesme le fomentans: Inter Perroni legat. lib. iii. Deinde arcanum aliud politicum, ex quo in regno isto necessarium sit nostros non plane opprimi vel exscindi, quamvis hoc Papae indesinenter urgeant, promit Cl. vir Hubertus Languetus, epist. ad Camerarium, pag. 20. quae proinde non gravabor hic adjicere: factum est enim hic decretum (reclamante Pontifice & omnibus Ecclesiasticis) quo permittitur Regi, ut ex bonis Ecclesiasticis divendat reditus annuos centum millium coronatorum. Qui ejusmodi fundos emunt (etiamsi nostrae religioni adversentur) nolunt nos in contentione de religione plane succumbere, ne nobis oppressis, Ecclesiastici eos fundos ab ipsis repetant. Ego etiam existimo eos qui jam rerum potiuntur, neutram partem velle plane opprimi, ne pars victrix ipsis praescribat. Prima libertas Nostris concessa in Gallia fuit haec ut extra urbes sacra Nostri sua profequerentur. Edicto Ianuarii, quod primum libertatis fuit, a. cIↄ lᴐ lxi. art. iv. Defendant sur lesdites peines, à tous Juges, Magistrats, & autres personnes, de quelque estat, qualité, ou condition qu'ils soyent, que lors que ceux de ladite Religion nouvelle iront, viendront, & s'assembleront hors desdites villes, pour le faict de leur dite Religion: ils n'ayent à leur empescher, inquieter, molester, ne leur courir sus en quelque sorte ou maniere que ce soit. Tum a. cIↄ lᴐ lxii. Nobilibus concessum fuis in aedibus sacra recipere, & frequentare, pro se & suis, avec leurs familles & sujets. Inde in urbes, & suburbia, speciatim ad id destinata & recensita, in Edicto a.cIↄ lᴐ lxx. art.viii.ix. cumque in finem datae urbes obsides, à Reformatis servandae, Rupella, Montalbanum &c. art. xxxix. Deinceps a.cIↄ lᴐ lxxvi. plena libertas data ubiq; locorum religionis, liberi exercitii, Scholarum, & Synodorum Art. iv. Et pour ne laisser aucune occasion de troubles & differents entre nos subiects, Avons permis & permettons l'exercice libre, public & general de la Religion pretendue reformée: par toutes les villes & lieux de nostre Royaume, & pais de nostre obeyssance & protection, sans restriction de temps & personnes, ne pareillement de lieux & places, pourveu qu'iceux lieux & places leur appartiennent, ou que ce soit du gré & consentement des autres proprietaires, auxquels ils pourroyent appartenir. Esquelles villes & lieux ceux de ladite Religion pourront faire prescher, prier, chanter de Psalmes, administration du Baptesme, & de la Cene, publication & celebration de mariages, escholes & leçons publiques, correction selon ladite Religion, & toutes autres choses appartenans au libre & entier exercice d'icelle. Pourront aussi tenir Consistoires & Synodes, tant provinciaux que generaux. Hæc sub Henrico III. Ejusdem Edicti art. VIII. Pourront lesdits de la Religion faire edifier & construire des lieux pour faire ledit exercice excepté à Paris. Atque hic statutum, quod religio nostra vulgo in Galliis appellatur prætensæ Reformationis, art. XVI. En tous actes & actions publiques où sera parlé de ladite Religion, sera usé de ces mots, Religion pretendue reformee. Quorumcumque locorum datur Nostris libertas, etiam edicto a. cIↄ Iↄ LXXVII. art IV. Conventus Neracensis, art. II. Edictum A. cIↄ Iↄ XCIX. Atque non solum publicae domus egenorum, hospitalia, &c. vel scholæ nostris hominibus promiscue cum aliis oblatæ, edicto a. cIↄ Iↄ LXIII. art. XVIII. Les pauvres & miserables personnes seront receues ès aumosnes publiques & hospitaux, sans respect ni distinction de religion, pour y estre traittés & secourues en leurs maladies & necessitez, selon la charité qui nous est commande de Dieu, & qui se depart esdits hospitaux ordinairement. A. cIↄ Iↄ LXX. art. XV. Ne sera faite difference ni distinction pour raison de religion à recevoir tant és universitez, escoles, hospitaux, maladeries, qu'aumosnes publiques, les escoliers, malades. A. cIↄ Iↄ LXXVII. art. XV. aliisque; sed & ad officia, dignitates, status, nostri æq; cum aliis admittuntur. Edicto a. cIↄ Iↄ LXX. art. XXII. Et pour oster toutes plaintes à l'advenir, avons declare & declarons ceux de ladite Religion capables de tenir & exercer tous estats, dignitez, & charges publiques, Royales, seigneuriales, & des villes de ce Royaume, & estre indifferemment admis & receus en tous conseils, deliberations, assemblées, estats & fonctions qui dependent des choses susdites, sans en estre en sorte quelconque reiettez, n'en empeschez d'en jouir incontinent apres la publication de ce present Edict. tum edicto a. cIↄ Iↄ LXXVII. art. XIX. Quem in finem ipsæ supremæ Parlamentorum curiæ constitutæ fuerunt ex nostræ religionis hominibus partim, partim ex Pontificiis æquali numero. a. cIↄ Iↄ LXXVI. art. XXIII. Avons ordonné & ordonnons, qu'en nostre Cour de Parlement de Paris sera establie une Chambre composee de deux Presidens & seize Conseillers, moitié Catholiques & moitié de ladite Religion. atque similiter per sesequentes articulos, in reliquis Parlamentorum curiis, Tholosano, Grenobilensi, Burdegalensi, Aquensi, Dionensi, Rotomagensi, & Bretannico constitutû. & confirmata edictis a.cIↄ Iↄ lxxv I I. & clɔIↄ xc I x. Quæ omnia non abs re fuisse quod diligentius rimati fuimus, atque hic latius explicimus non ignorabunt, qui quantum in pace colenda tum Ecclesiis, tum quibuscumque situm sit, perpenderint. Multum etiam juvat usuique est, scire quo pacto & quo fundamento pax religionis, præterquam in Imperio, alibi etiam, præsertim apud Gallos, quorum cum Imperio eandem nunc pacis causam tantis diris execratur Papa, constet. Vbi & id quoque observare licet, quod quemadmodum supra cum pace in Imperio sancitum ostendimus, ut ad eam bene servandam inhiberentur aliorum, & Concionatorum adversus pacem oppositiones ac sermones, idem hic à primo tempore factæ pacis statutum suisse edicto, a.cIↄ Iↄ lxi. art.xi. Et ensemblable à tous prescheurs, de n'user en leurs sermons & predications d'injures & invectives contre lesdits Ministres & leurs fectateurs : pour estre chose qui à jusques ici beaucoup plus servi à exciter le peuple à sedition, qu'à le provoquer à devotion. Vnde jam satis apparet, quam longe melius animati sint plerumque politici, Imperatores, Reges ad pacem servandam, præ Pontifice Romano, dum illi omnia eò conserunt, & quæcumque adversari possint impediunt, hic solus, cum suis, obluctatur, & neque pacem suadet aut facit, neque ab aliis factam, servari vult, aut probat. Auctor Vindicar. Gallic. adverf. Alex. Patricium Armachanum, respondens Hispanis succensentibus, quod in Galliæ regno tuto degant Reformati: fides, inquit, suadenda est, non imperanda, oratione quidem, non ferro, & docendo, non jubendo, monendo, non minando: Nemo Rex certè animis imperare potest; natura contumaces sunt, & celeres planeque igneos habent motus, & in contrarium atque arduum eristuntur. Inquisitores autem fides respuit Gallia, eorumque oculos horret & expavet, fictiones quippe ea res induxit, & per hos sacros indagatores Hispani Reges plures purpurâ. Jure quam Dei cultores efficiunt.
units.tr: Similar opinions about the religious dissensions can be found in many others, especially in France, as with Thuanus. According to Utenbogaert, the Archbishop of Rouen is also among them, in the history of his life, chapters 16 and 17. People call them politicians. Thuanus, book 44, under the year 1566, gives the origin of this name and describes by it the nobles who were eager for peace, who embrace the religion of their ancestors, he says, but are alien to the tumults and factions, and altogether to the party of the Lorraine family. Among the great men he mentions Cardinal Charles of Bourbon, Michel de l'Hôpital the Chancellor, and the Montmorencys. He wrote this in the letter of Condé, which he issued that year to explain to King Charles IX the reasons for his withdrawal from the court. Thuanus gives a summary of it, but the author of the Commentaries on the State of Religion and of the Commonwealth in France under Charles IX, part 2, gives it in full. The words of Prince Condé in the letter were: and also those who follow the Roman religion, and do not favour the party of those Lorrainers whom they call politicians, since they are zealous for peace and tranquillity and are enemies of tumults. See also Thuanus, book 51, under the year 1572, and book 57, under the year 1574. In former times many stood on the side of Cassander: Wicelius, Metellus, Hoppterus (on whom some things are written in the letters of illustrious Belgians). Daniel Heinsius, in his prefatory letter to those letters, thinks this is a prodigy and not unreasonably so, as does Ximenius, a Spaniard and theologian. On Andreas Fricius Modrevius there is this judgement of Vorstius, before he himself turned apostate, in his Apology for the Church against the Monasteriensis, page 240: that he was more a politician than an ecclesiastic. Marcus Antonius de Dominis compared the Roman and the Reformed Church to ships which agreed in everything except the compass: Both religions (he said) agree in the chief essentials and fundamentals; both hold Christ as Lord and Mediator; both have the same baptism, etc. The difference between the Roman and the Reformed ships is not in the hull or the rigging but only in the compass. This Roman ship is a fine vessel, well built, not rotten, nor falling apart into fragments, excellently equipped with masts, cables, ropes and anchors; it has a splendid nautical chart; its passengers and soldiers are all under the same banner, and they have the same commander, our Lord Jesus Christ alone. And there is no difference between this ship and the reformed one. I observe one principal difference, however, from which very many other discordant and conflicting things arise: namely, that the helmsman who holds the tiller of the Roman ship has rejected the ordinary compass and abandoned the practice and use of the nautical chart, and, from some giddiness of his brain, has produced a new chart of his own, and has fashioned for himself a compass which is his alone, false and useless, which never looks to the pole, and whose needle is not infected with the magnet. He had said this in a sermon, which he gave in London in the year 1616, and which he had already drafted in the year 1616 on the occasion of his profession, or of his departure from Rome; but these things were not sound. I pass over what many on our side and others have said at length against Cassander, Milletière, Grotius, and similar men. Nor am I now concerned with syncretism or the union of the two Churches, ours and the Roman, nor with the untimely zeal of those who labour to combine these things, who please each side as much as they displease it. Jerome speaks of the Minaeans or Nazarenes of his own age in his letter to Augustine: while they want to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither Jews nor Christians. For apart from the fact that the articles and dogmas of Papacy were so formed in the Council of Trent, with such care, that they are as far as possible from all agreement, and no chink of concord remained, which the Fathers vehemently dreaded being stirred up at any time in those days; so that the author of the History of the Council of Trent, book 2, page 229, when discussing de Vega and his opinion on the question of free will, says: And although he learned that every effort must be bent on concord, yet the ears and minds of the Fathers shrank from it, to whom it seemed in some way a grave prejudice to the cause that any of the controversies could be reconciled. All the more vain, then, are those other great and most learned men who seek reconciliation in doctrine, since the same author says that the Fathers set themselves so diligently against every reconciliation and every chink of concord, as stated on page 211. And the chief Papists cry out loudly that it can be reconciled: see Bellarmine, book 3, On Laymen, chapter 19, and Hosius (both cardinals), in his letter to Sigismund King of Poland, which is letter 134 of his letters, not to mention others. Hence compositions of this kind on our side with an irreconcilable Rome (while some labour at them, they do not combine two Churches but form a third one out of their own brain, of the sort they think both ought to be, which is acknowledged and approved by neither party) have always rightly been suspect. Melanchthon, to name only him, whom the henotics are wont to draw over to their side, in his testament, which he composed in 1549, after learning from long experience of affairs how vain the reconciliations of religions usually are, says: There will perhaps also be, after this age, new sophistical conciliations of doctrines, when old errors, somewhat painted over, will be restored, and these conciliations will corrupt the purity of the doctrine which is now handed down. I warn my people beforehand about these things too, that they should not approve sophistical conciliations. Add Pezel, part 7, Argument of Melanchthon, page 607. Apart from those, I say, unless every plan of concord, which the articles of the recent peace commend, begins at some point with the Pope himself, it is in vain that others are busy in seeking it; and so long as he does not at least go so far as to approve in this matter of the peace of religion what the Emperors think absolutely necessary for cultivating peace among men, I order all who would attempt the work of syncretism in religion to be idle and to rest. For this is also why whatever others have said at great length about settling the dissensions of religion has come to nothing, because the Pope did not approve them or they did not come from the Pope, the supreme judgement of the papal religion being his. Those who are going to treat of reconciling the two religions must either include the Pope or exclude him. Unless they declare at the outset that they exclude the Pope, and that, so long as they depend on him, unless he himself coins and approves the articles of the composition and begins the amendment from himself (which he has so far never done), others may doubt whether he will ever do so, but every man wiser than I am will not believe it; nothing fruitful or solid can be achieved. The Pope must first renounce both himself and his obedience, and then, if ever, something useful and praiseworthy can be done in this matter, especially if a single rule for matters of faith and religion is set up in his place, namely Holy Scripture. The politicians, however, in this respect are far better and more religious than the Papists, for they sometimes think about entering into a settlement of the dissensions in religion, as the recent Convention of Thorn in the kingdom of Poland, in 1645, showed; and finally they have committed to everyone's care and zeal the recent peace of Osnabrück in Germany. But as far as the Empire contributes to peace, the politicians contribute too; only one man, the Pope, opposes it. The Emperors ratify the peace of religion at least in its political aspect, since they cannot do so in its ecclesiastical aspect, for it can be of two kinds, political and ecclesiastical; the Pope bears neither, but is equally the enemy and adversary of both. The articles of peace order that each should bring his zeal to this, so that after the political peace of religion, that is, so that these three or two religions, the Protestant Evangelical and the Roman, may dwell together in the Empire and enjoy equal privileges, a plan may finally be found for peace in ecclesiastical religion too, for the greater union of both in one religion and Church; all the more because it is now sufficiently established that what Ludwig Camerarius, a most experienced and illustrious man in political affairs, lately wrote in the preface to the letters of Hubert Languet, which he edited, is true: all the wars by which the Christian world has been shaken in this unhappy age of ours had their origin in persecutions undertaken for the sake of religion. And from the same source it is easy to foresee that the rupture of the peace will follow first, and other wars after. But the business of religious peace would most fittingly be taken up and attacked first by the Pope. The Empire orders that the treaties of peace be kept by all, and that no one dare oppose or speak against them; and after the peace was ratified, the Emperor again, on 27 June of the preceding year 1650, prohibited under heavy penalty all attempts, disputations, sermons or other infringements against the conclusion and instrument of peace. Far from the Pope confirming this in the performance of his duty (if it is his duty at all), he is most eager to transgress it himself. Formerly, in 1583, on 2 October, the Emperor Maximilian II defended the peace of religion against the turbulent and seditious little book by Doctor Georg Eder, although it was written for the Roman faith against the Protestants, in such a way that by this decree he marked the author as his own courtier, so that Emperor Ferdinand may now take from that an example of what must be done in a similar case. The decree runs thus: His Sacred Imperial Majesty has ordered it to be made known to his court counsellor Georg Eder, Doctor of Both Laws, that His Majesty is most displeased and indignant at the excessive vehemence, bitterness and immodesty of his book, which he wished to offer to His Majesty, and at the injurious words against many states and persons of the Empire, especially the allies of the Augsburg Confession, whose religion and confession, and also their state, honour and dignity, he has most gravely injured, wronged and condemned; although he and everyone know and it is established how, with what zeal, labour and care, His Majesty and his most praiseworthy predecessors have for so many years always been intent at all the Diets and Assemblies of the Empire, so that what has been wholesomely agreed and established by the common states of the Empire in the peace of religion and otherwise, no one may tax, trouble, offend, harm, slander or wrong another in honour, dignity, state, conscience, or in any other way; which His Majesty has hitherto striven with all his might to have diligently and exactly observed, not only in the Empire but also in the kingdoms and hereditary principalities. Wherefore His Sacred Imperial Majesty is greatly displeased by that book published by Doctor Eder, and finds it most unacceptable; nor could he persuade himself that such imprudence, audacity and immoderation could fall upon one who had been His Majesty's counsellor at court for so long, since he knows better than most that not even the highest men, let alone His Majesty's counsellors, should bring about the publication of anything of the kind, even in His Majesty's own hereditary lands, against the Sacred Imperial Majesty and the constitutions of the Holy Empire and the peace of religion, and indeed against the severe ordinance made by His Majesty in the Empire; and what follows. The whole text is extant in Goldast, Imperial Constitutions, volume 3, quarto. As to the Pope grudging the Protestants freedom in the exercise of religion and places for building churches for this purpose, he not only offends against the state of the Empire, where, as Duke Casimir has objected in his Declaration on the position of Gebhard, Archbishop of Cologne, and others who have written on the peace of religion in Germany, the free exercise of religion is the only means of establishing a sure peace and union in the Empire; but it is not heard elsewhere either, in the kingdom of France, for the princes of the world judge it fair and necessary not to deny that to the Reformed in any way. In France, indeed, by the edict of King Charles IX of 17 January 1562, which was called the January edict, and by a repeated command of the king to the Parlement of Paris to promulgate and observe it inviolably and without infraction (as he says in his letters), the peace of religion was first decreed for the Reformed. Again by the so-called March edict of 19 March 1563; by the edict of 14 December 1563; by another of 23 March 1568, by which the edict of pacification, as it is called, of 19 March 1572 was confirmed, the first article of which reads: Namely, that all those of the so-called Reformed religion enjoy the said Edict of Pacification purely and simply, and that it be carried out in all its points and articles according to its first form and tenor, lifting and removing all restrictions, modifications, declarations and interpretations which have been made from the day and date of that edict until the publication of these present letters. By the edict of 11 August 1570, which is called the perpetual edict and irrevocable; again by that of 11 August 1583. By King Henry III, by the edict of 14 May 1576, a perpetual and irrevocable edict; another, of September 1577, likewise a perpetual and irrevocable edict. By the edict of 26 January 1581, both the preceding edicts and the Articles of Nérac, concluded on the same business (on 28 February 1579, between Queen Mother Catherine and King Henry of Navarre and other deputies of the Reformed religion), were confirmed, enlarged and declared, as the title of the edict has it. By King Henry IV in July 1592, the Edict of Nantes. By the edict of 25 February 1599, a perpetual and irrevocable edict, a perpetual and irrevocable edict. After these, the same edicts were issued by the Queen mother in 1610, and again by King Louis at the beginning of his reign. All these confirm both the necessity and the justice of it, which so offends the Pope in the Empire and the peace of Germany; that is, that peace cannot be had otherwise than by the decreed peace of religion and the freedom of sacred exercises granted to the Protestants. For the kings of France also, in those edicts of theirs, put forward this reason, that until then they had tried in vain to settle the public matter in another way, by severe persecution. In the first edict, of 1561, King Charles says: whatever remedies our predecessors have tried to apply, both by the rigour and severity of punishments. In the edict of 1562: seeing nevertheless that all the evil and inconvenience which come from this war turn to the diminution and damage of our kingdom; and having experienced, to our great loss, that such a remedy is neither suitable nor fitting. In the edict of 1568, foreseeing the desolation which might come hereafter, if by the grace and mercy of our Lord the said troubles were not promptly pacified. Henry III, in his edict of 1577: our experience in our majority of twenty-five years has made us know that from the continuation of arms and war there can come no good which we have so much desired and sought. Where then the Emperors and Kings confess that, taught by experience, they should no longer pursue this matter by arms and wars, but that the peace of religion must absolutely be followed and observed on both sides, what is that spirit which drives the Pope against princes and peace, so necessary for the commonwealth and the common good of all Christians? Hence King Henry IV, in his instructions to Perron, given on 9 May 1595, for obtaining his reconciliation with the Roman Pope, expressly enjoined that his envoys should admit no conditions which would be foul and harmful to the King, such as if the King were compelled to declare war on the Huguenots, and to this end to revoke the edicts made by his predecessor Kings for the peace of the realm. The King did not wish his envoys to become entangled in such things or the like in any way, knowing how necessary these things are to the commonwealth that they should never be disturbed, and yet it is precisely to overturn them, together with the whole commonwealth and kingdom, that the Pope constantly applies himself. Hence Perron also later set before Pope Paul V, who was busy, driven by the Papists' innate lust for disturbing things, to incite the King against his subjects of the Reformed religion, the fact that through the civil wars the party of the Reformed in the kingdom had always been increased and more strongly established: whereas it had always been necessary that at the end of each rupture they should be given more places of security than they had before; for through civil war the heretics grew in strength and in party in France, several Catholics joining them, and the princes outside even fomenting it. In Perron's Legations, book 3. Next, Hubert Languet, that distinguished man, in his letter to Camerarius, page 20, sets forth another political secret, from which it is necessary in this kingdom that our people should not be wholly crushed or uprooted, although the Papists insistently urge this: I shall not therefore be burdened by adding here that a decree has been made here (the Pontiff and all the ecclesiastics protesting) by which the King is permitted to sell from the ecclesiastical goods annual revenues of a hundred thousand crowns. Those who buy such estates (even if they are opposed to our religion) do not want us to be completely overcome in the contention about religion, lest, with us crushed, the ecclesiastics should reclaim those estates from them. I also think that those who now hold power do not want either side to be wholly crushed, lest the victorious party prescribe terms to them. The first liberty granted to our people in France was this: that our people could perform their sacred rites outside the towns. By the January edict, which was the first grant of liberty, in 1561, article 4: We forbid, under the said penalties, all judges, magistrates and other persons, of whatever estate, quality or condition they may be, that when those of the said new religion go, come and assemble outside the said towns for the business of their said religion, they shall not hinder, disquiet, molest or pursue them in any way or manner whatsoever. Then, in 1562, it was granted to the nobles to receive and frequent sacred rites in their houses, for themselves and theirs, with their families and subjects. Thereafter, in the edict of 1570, articles 8 and 9, they were allowed the towns and suburbs specially appointed and listed for this purpose; and towns were given as pledges, to be kept by the Reformed for this end, Rochelle, Montauban, etc., article 39. Then in 1576 full liberty was given everywhere of religion, free exercise, schools and synods, article 4: And so as to leave no occasion for disturbances and disputes between our subjects, we have permitted and do permit the free, public and general exercise of the so-called Reformed religion, in all the towns and places of our kingdom, and the lands under our obedience and protection, without restriction of time or persons, and likewise of places and sites, provided those places belong to them, or that it be with the consent of the other owners to whom they might belong. In those towns and places those of the said religion may have preaching, prayer, the singing of psalms, the administration of baptism and of the Supper, the publication and celebration of marriages, schools and public lessons, discipline according to the said religion, and all other things pertaining to the free and entire exercise of it. They may also hold consistories and synods, both provincial and general. These were under Henry III. Article 8 of the same edict: those of the said religion may build and construct places for the said exercise, except at Paris. And here a statute, by which our religion is commonly called in France the so-called Reformed religion, article 16: In all public acts and transactions where the said religion is mentioned, these words shall be used: the so-called Reformed religion. Liberty is granted to our people in whatever places, also by the edict of 1577, article 4; the Convention of Nérac, article 2; the edict of 1599. And not only public poor-houses, hospitals, etc., or schools are offered to our people in common with others, by the edict of 1563, article 18: The poor and wretched persons shall be received into the public alms and hospitals, without respect or distinction of religion, to be treated and succoured in their sicknesses and necessities, according to the charity which God commands us, and which is ordinarily dispensed in those hospitals. By the edict of 1570, article 15: No difference or distinction for reason of religion shall be made in receiving, whether into universities, schools, hospitals, leper-houses, or public alms, the scholars and the sick. By that of 1577, article 15, and others; but our people are also admitted equally with others to offices, dignities and states. By the edict of 1570, article 22: And in order to take away all complaints in future, we have declared and do declare those of the said religion capable of holding and exercising all estates, dignities and public offices, royal, seigneurial and of the towns of this kingdom, and of being indifferently admitted and received into all councils, deliberations, assemblies, estates and functions which depend on the aforesaid matters, without being rejected or hindered in any way from enjoying them immediately after the publication of this present edict. Then by the edict of 1577, article 19. For this purpose the supreme courts of the Parlements were established, partly from men of our religion and partly from Papists in equal number. By the edict of 1576, article 23: We have ordered and do order that in our Court of Parlement of Paris there shall be established a Chamber composed of two presidents and sixteen councillors, half Catholics and half of the said religion. And in like manner, through the following articles, it was set up in the other Parlements, at Toulouse, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Aix, Dijon, Rouen and Brittany, and confirmed by the edicts of 1572 and 1599. Those who have weighed how much both the Churches and whatever else depends on the cultivation of peace have to do with it will not be unaware that it was not without reason that we examined these things more carefully, and explain them here at greater length. It is also very helpful and useful to know by what means and on what foundation the peace of religion is established, not only in the Empire but also elsewhere, especially among the French, against whom the Pope now curses with such dire imprecations the same cause of peace as the Empire. Here it is also permitted to observe that, just as above we showed that for keeping this peace in the Empire it was decreed that the oppositions and sermons of others and of preachers against the peace should be forbidden, so here too from the first time the peace was made, it was a statute by the edict of 1561, article 11: And likewise to all preachers, that in their sermons and predications they use no insults or invectives against the said ministers and their followers, since that has hitherto served much more to stir the people to sedition than to provoke them to devotion. Whence it is now sufficiently clear how much better disposed, for keeping the peace, the politicians, Emperors and Kings usually are, compared with the Roman Pontiff: while they bring everything together for it and hinder whatever could oppose it, he alone, with his own people, struggles against it, and neither urges nor makes peace, nor wishes it kept when made by others, nor approves it. The author of the Vindication of the Gauls against Alexander Patricius, Archbishop of Armagh, replying to the Spaniards who were angry that the Reformed live safely in the kingdom of France, says: faith must be persuaded, not commanded, by speech, not by the sword, by teaching, not by ordering, by admonishing, not by threatening. No king can certainly command minds; they are by nature stubborn, quick and plainly fiery in their motions, and they rise up against what is hard and contrary. But France rejects inquisitors of faith and shudders and dreads their eyes; for that business has brought in fictions, and through these holy investigators the Spanish kings make more purple-clad men than worshippers of God.

units.la: Quinto, tanta quidem rei, quam agimus hujus nostrae est æquitas, ut non in Germania solum Galliaque, de quibus diximus, sed ubique terrarum, & apud nos in Belgio, Religio Reformata quam primum innotuit, patrocinium sui apud quosvis, apud Primores, apud adversarios quamvis Pontificios, impetraverit: stimulante nempe ad id homines propria ipsorum conscientia, religioni tam divinæ omnem concedendam esse, quà hominum conscientiis, qua sacris exercitiis, libertatem. Hoc, sub avertenda à cervicibus animisque subditorum sacra Inquisitione, & libertatis defensione bene intellectum; & quemadmodum in bello nostro distinguere fuit eos, qui in censu belli venebant, & qui id gerebant, apertius ac prius causa illa protegendæ religionis libertatisque ab illis significata & commendata fuit, quam his, & inter causas Belli plures erat ista sane non minima, quæ ex religionis oppressione oriebatur, non apud illos primum, qui à Reformatione Lutheri & Zwinglii, huic in no, stris terris addicti fuerant, sed & antiquiores, Waldenses, quos quantopere vexarit & à multis seculis in his ipsis regionibus oppresserit Papistica factio, & ut inde prima dolorum bellorumque postea secutorum initia repetenda sint, abunde atque erudite docuit celebris vir, Boxhornius Histor. Belgic. lib. 1. Iam uti necesse habebat Ecclesia, quemadmodum in ortu suo sub Gentilibus, ita in Reformatione hac sub Papatu, extra urbes primum convenire, & sacra sua celebrare, ita primus indultæ libertatis hic gradus fuit, quod supra etiam observavimus in Gallia, ut Nostris liceret extra urbes sacra sua sequi & frequentare. Illud a. cIↄ lxvi d. xxviii. Novemb. hic in urbe ita statuit princeps Auriacus. Videlicet eo tempore ac anno, (quo referente Famiano Strada, Iesuita „Bel. units.tr: Fifthly, the justice of the cause we are pursuing is such that the Reformed Religion, as soon as it became known, won protection for itself not only in Germany and France, of which we have spoken, but everywhere on earth, and among us in the Netherlands, from leading men and even from opponents, Papists included. For people were moved to this by their own consciences, which held that a religion so divine should be granted freedom both for men's consciences and for its sacred exercises. This was rightly understood as a plea to keep the sacred Inquisition from the necks and minds of subjects and as a defence of liberty. And just as in our war one had to distinguish between those who were counted in the war's reckoning and those who waged it, so that cause of protecting religion and liberty was put forward and commended to the former more openly and earlier than to the latter. Among the causes of the war this was certainly not the least, arising from the oppression of religion. It was felt not first among those who had embraced the Reformation of Luther and Zwingli in our lands, but also among the more ancient Waldenses, whom the Papist faction vexed so greatly and had oppressed for many centuries in these very regions. That the first beginnings of the sorrows and wars that followed are to be traced back to this, the famous man Boxhorn has taught fully and learnedly in Histor. Belgic. lib. 1. Now, just as the Church in its origin under the Gentiles had to meet first outside the cities, so in this Reformation under the Papacy, and this was the first step of the liberty granted, as we observed above also in France, that our people might be allowed to follow and attend their sacred services outside the cities. That was decided here in the city by the Prince of Orange on 28 November 1566. In that very time and year (as Famianus Strada, the Jesuit, reports in „Bel. Belgici lib. v.“) such a great multitude of villagers, chiefly country folk, and then of townsfolk too, flocked together with incredible eagerness to hear the Gospel, that once in the district of Tournai they easily exceeded eight thousand men, and at a still more crowded sermon near the islands they gathered in great numbers, to a total of

Hoc videlicet anno, in Belgio Reformatæ conciones publice cæptæ, à Flandria Occidentali, inde per Orientalem, Brabantiam, Walloniam, Geldriam, Frisiam, Transisulaniam, Hollandiam, Zeelandiam, Ultrajectum quoque: in campis primum, & agris, atque quia à vi sibi & insidiis Papistarum ubique metuebant, le via lecum gestare arma, quibus se communirent, defenderentque, cogebantur. Antverpiæ mense Iunio, extra urbem primum, mox dei III. Iulii libello supplice locum intra urbem habendis concionibus, multis gravibusque additis rationibus, postularunt, quę instante hieme impetrarunt; postquam cum Nobilibus Gubernatrix d. xxv Augusti convenerat (quę Strada, uti alia quæ Nostris favere videntur, Iesuitæ, non historici fide, omittit) art. VI I. ut quo loco jam frequentatæ essent conciones, permitterentur haberi, solum absque armis & scandalo. Iuxta quod, ubivis locorum, in urbibus etiam, ubi xxv die Augusti, vel antea habitæ palam conciones nostræ, permissæ fuerunt. Quo tempore, & qua occasione respondit Hispaniæ Regi Maximilianus Imp. mitissimi prudentissimiq; animi Princeps optimus, mense Septembri ejusdem hujus anni MDLXVI. (qui primus fuit impetratæ pro religione hic nostra libertatis) non aliter agendum in religionis negotio esse, tum sibi in Germania, tum Regi in Belgio, quam pacifice & molli per omnia via, non vi aut armis, atque juxta illam methodum se operam nomenque offerre suum, mediatorem ut ageret inter Regem & Belgarum populum, ad componendas hic exortas turbas & dissidia. Quæ sequenti anno similia scripsit ad Gubernatricem Margaretam; denique iis ipsis pacificationis consiliis immortuus fuit in Comitiis R henoburgensibus a. MDLXXVI.
