Tum quia causæ illæ, per quas adducti homines in Annatas consenserant, non ultra erant, cessant causæ quæ tunc erant, eo quod non fit passagium ultramarinum, vel aliud virtuosum ex talibus pecuniis, dixit Clemanges; tum quia per Annatas illas committeretur Labes simoniæ, & clarum perjurium, scandalumque, & damnatio animarum, uti idem loquitur. Hinc Clerus Gallicanus illis reclamavit in Responsione illa à Clemange, ipsius nomine exhibita Concilio Constantiensi, adversus Iohannem de Scribanis, Camerae Apostolicae, uti vocant, Fiscalem. In Anglia nihil percipiebat, nisi de paucis Episcopatibus. In Hispaniæ aliquot regnis, etiam nihil. In Italiâ ipsâ parum: scilicet resistentibus undique quam plurimis. Florentini, quia Papa male Abbatiam alicui commiserat, illum privaverunt potestate conferendi in ipsorum dominio, per quinquennium. In aliquibus Germaniæ dioecesibus ac Provinciis nihil omnino etiam Annatarum Papa percipiebat, quinencæ litteræ Apostolicæ, quæmadmodum vocantur, admittebantur, nisi Episcopis placeret, qui illas aliquando repudiabant. Curia Parisiensis, anno cIɔ ,,cccc vi. dictum fuit, quod dictus Benedictus & officiarii sui ,,cessabunt in nostris regno Delphinatu ab exactionibus an,,natarum primarum, fructuum & emolumentorum', prae„laturarum & aliorum beneficiorum quorumcunque vacan„tium, seu quæ vacaverunt, aut vacabunt, tam pro primis „annatis, quam etiam fructuum & emolumentorum, qui „tempore subtractionis alias eidem Benedicto factæ & vaca„tionis prælaturarum, dignitatum, & aliorum beneficiorum „obvenerunt seu obveniunt qualitercunque. Tum, quod Officiarii Benedicti P. forte collegissent, jussu Regis detineba„tur: Et si aliquid ex his, quæ levata seu exacta fuerunt, occa-„sione prædictorum apud collectores seu subcollectores, „aut alios quoscunque existit seu remanet sub manu nostra, „arrestabitur, & id arrestavit & arrestat ipsa curia nostra, i„psisque ne aliquid eidem Benedicto seu hoc, cuiquam alteri „tradant, aut solvant, inhibebitur, & inhibet etiam eadem „Curia nostra. Edictum hoc, præterquam in Fasciculo rerum expetend. sol. cxcvi. etiam legitur apud Carolum Molinæum, Operum Tom. iii. pag. 471. in Commentario ad Edictum Henrici II. contra Parvas Datas, & abusus Curiæ Romanæ. Datæ intelliguntur, Bullæ à Datariis Papæ, qui ita dicuntur, sub singulis diebus datæ, vel suis quoque datis (ut vulgo dicimus) signatæ, quarum institores Banquiers in Edicto appellati, id est trapezita per regnum Galliæ tum multi erant, qui hoc Papalis negotiationis mercimonium tractabant, & variis per Edictum istud co- rcebantur legibus, factum a. cI3 I3 l. Quæ repressa etiam fuerant a. cI3 I3 xlvii. pluribusque inante diverforum Regum Edictis, quibus exactionum Papalium omne genus, reservationum, provisionum, annatarum &c. sapienter & provide inhibuerunt. Ludovicus ix. a. cI3 ccxxviii. & cI3 cclxviii. celebri illa Pragmatica sancivit: Item exactiones & onera gravissima pecuniarum, per curiam Romanam Ecclesiæ regni nostri impositas vel impositas (quibus Regnum nostrum miserabiliter depauperatum existit) sive etiam imponendas vel imponenda, Levari aut colligi nullatenus volumus: nisi duntaxat pro rationabili, via & urgentissima causa, inevitabili necessitate, ac etiam de expresso & spontaneo jussu nostro, & ipsius Ecclesiæ Regni nostri. A Philippo Pulchro, lege Philippina dicta a. cI3 cccIII. à Carolo vi. a. clɔ cccİxxxv. quod Edictum, ad Stylum Curiæ Parisiensis part. iii. tit. xxxvii. exhibet Carolus Molinæus: & in eo adversus Cardinales,hi exprimuntur, aliosque episcopos ipsius summi Pontificis authoritate suffultos, & beneficia Ecclesiastica cumulatim ad se rapientes, atque extra regnum exportantes ablumentesque, decernitur, ut Regii Officiales fructus, reddititus, & proventus temporalitatis beneficiorum ecclesiasticorum in quibus defectus supra tactos aut aliquos eorundem repererint, quæ dicti cardinales, & alii viri ecclesiastici quicunque maximè extra regnum nostrum suam moram trahentes, obtinent, ac etiam annuas pensiones quas dicti cardinales, aut alii super beneficiis regni nostri percipiunt, ad manum nostram realiter ponant, ac ponere tenebuntur. & quæ sequuntur ejus commatis plura, remedium infandis Clericorum Romanensium abusibus adhibentia. Idem Carolus edicto a. clɔ ccclxxxviii. & clɔcccxcv. Item Curia Parisiensis a. clɔ cccexviii. & a. clɔ ccccxxv. Carolus vii. a. clɔ xxxviii. Ludovicus xi. a. clɔ ccccclxiv. & a. lxxviii. Et contra easdem Curiæ Romanæ exactiones usurpationesque, sub Carolo viii appellavit Academia Parisiensis, quæ appellatio in Senatu Parisiensi admissa fuit. Adeo viriliter & constanter se illis Paparum artibus & tyrannidi hac in re opposuerunt semper Galli. Molinæus dicto libro, vel Commentario annotat Taxam vacantiarum de Ecclesiis Francicis descriptam in libris Camerae Papae adscendere ad sexcenta nonaginta septem millia septingenta Francorum, non computatis Prælaturis non taxatis, & aliis beneficiis, quorum exactiones fere tantundem faciunt. Hic quantus vir suerit Carolus Molinæus, neminem qui vel Galliam, vel bonas litteras & jura novit, latere potest; at idem sua eruditione, candore, & zelo pro Regis regnique adversus Papalem tyrannidem libertate id consecutus fuit, ut quia igne expurgari scripta ejus non possent, diro anathemate fuerint condemnata, singulari Bullâ, à P. Clemente viii. a. clɔ lɔ ,,cii. d.xxvi. Augusti: Motu proprio, & ex certa scientia, ac ma,matura deliberatione nostris, hac nostra perpetuo valitura ,constitutione omnia, & quæcunque prædicti Caroli Moli,næi Hæretici scripta, opera, & commentaria, Beatorum ,Apostolorum Petri, & Pauli, ac nostra authoritate de no,vo perpetuo damnamus, reprobamus, interdicimus, & a,nathematizamus, eorumque lectionem, & retentionem ,universis, & singulis Christi fidelibus cujuscumque status, ,gradus, ordinis, conditionis, dignitatis, honoris, & præ,minentiæ, licet de illis specialis, & individua mentio ha,benda foret, existant, etiam sub excommunicatione latæ ,sententiæ, aliisque censuris, & pœnis in indice librorum ,prohibitorum contentis, ac etiam suspicionis ipsius hære,sis, quantumvis scripta, opera, & commentaria ipsa, jam ,quovis modo fuisse expurgata prætendant, districte perpe,tuo interdicimus, & prohibemus. Et propterea omnes, & ,qualcunque licentias quibusvis personis tam ab ordinariis ,locorum, quam etiam ab ipsis Cardinalibus super edicto ,indice deputatis, ac supremis Sanctæ universalis Inquisitio,nis contra hæreticam pravitatem Inquisitionibus, ac à no- ,bis, & Apostolica sede quomodo libet concessis legendi, & ,retinendi libros ejusdem Caroli Molinæi, etiam sub alio ,nomine inscriptos, vel expurgatos, cum non aliter, quam ,igne expurgari possint, evocamus, cassamus, & annulla,mus, inhibentes omnibus, & singulis supradictis,ne de cæ,tero hujusmodi licentias cuiquam concedant, vel impartiantur. & quæ sequuntur. Verum ad propositum. Annatas inhibet Concilio Basileense sess.xxi. Cujus decretum omnino adscribi meretur, tum ut ratio Annatarum & Exactionum, à Papis adhiberi solitarum hinc melius discatur; tum ut crimen Simonię per hasce commissum, & Germanicæ nationis adversus illas perpetua Protestatio, Paparumque hac ob rem à Concilio Superiori reprehensio & condemnatio omnibus constent, denique & Innocentii hodie impudentia coarguatur non exigentis solum eadem, quæ tam districte Synodus inhibuit, sed vel hinc audentis etiam Germanorum luxare statum statum & pacem. Sacrosancta generalis synodus Basileensis, in Spiritu sancto legitime congregata, universalem repraesentans, ad perpetuam rei memoriam. In nomine Spiritus sancti paracleti statuit haec sancta synodus, quod tam in curia Romana, quam alibi, pro seu in confirmatione electionum, admissione postulationum, praesentatione, dispositione, electione, postulatione, praesentatione etiam a laicis facienda institutione, installatione & investitura, de ecclesiis etiam cathedralibus & metropolitanis, monasteriis, dignitatibus, beneficiis, officiisque ecclesiasticis quibuscunque, nec non ordinibus sacris & benedictione ac pallio, de caetero nihil penitus ante vel post exigatur ratione literarum bullae sigilli, annatarum communium & minutorum, servitiorum, primorum fructuum, deportuum, aut sub quocunque alio titulo, colore vel nomine, praetextu cujusvis consuetudinis, privilegii vel statuti, aut alia quavis causa vel occasione, directe vel indirecte, solum scriptoribus, abbreviatoribusque & registratoribus litterarum seu minutarum, pro ipsorum labore competenti salario solvendo. Huic autem sacro canoni, si quis exigendo, dando, vel promittendo contraire praesumpserit, poenam incurrat adversus Simoniacos infligendam, & in ipsis dignitatibus ac beneficiis taliter obtentis, nullum jus ac titulum acquirat. Obligationes quoque, promissiones & censum ac mandata & quicquid in praejudicium decreti hujus salutaris fieri contingeret, nullas obtinere vires, atque irrita censeantur. Et si (quod absit) Romanus Pontifex, qui praeteris universalium conciliorum exequi & custodire canones debet, adversus hanc sanctionem aliquid faciendo ecclesiam scandalizet, generali concilio deferantur. Caeteri vero pro modo culpae juxta canonicas sanctiones per suos superiores digna ultione puniantur. Confer etiam Vdalrici Hutteni, nobilis viri orationem, contra Decimas: ubi & de Pallis &c. adversus Decimarum exactionem, per legatos Leonis x. coram Maximiliano Imp. anno, cIↄ IↄxIx. quae ex-tat tat in Falciculo Rerum expetendarum,sol.xxxvii. In Comitiis Norimbergensibus a.cIↄIↄ xxiii.Imp. Carolus v.epistolâ ad P.Hadrianum vi. exponens Imperii tum egestatem, tum necessitatem ex continuis Turcarum adversus Imperium molitionibus, illius quidem causam aperte rejiciebat in Papales exactiones, atque Hadriano pristinum vel proprium Annatarum usum ob oculos ponens, postulabat eas non ultra Romam exportari, sed in usum Germaniæ, præcipue tum adversus Turcam, impendi: de Proceribus Imperii loquitur, Itaque inter cætera cum meminissent annatas, quas novi antistites Rom. Pontifici solvere consueverunt, ab origine ea maxime ratione concessas esse, ut hujusmodi pecuniis Christi fidei hostes arcerentur: Nunc autem ipsi Turcæ magna parte inferioris Pannoniæ occupatæ, Germaniæ inhient: æquum esse, ut hujusmodi annatæ in Germania retineri, & illic in hunc usum converti debeant. Cumque d. xxv Novemb. Pontificis ad Comitia Legatus Franciscus Chieregatus, nomine Papæ exposuisset, quæ hic à Germanis posceret, Ferdinandus Fratris Caroli Locum tenens cæterique Electores & Principes, inter cætera responderunt, de Annatis quidem: Cum autem Ordines sacri Romani Imperii nihil dubitent, beatitudinem Pontificis pro comperto habere, Principes Germaniæ in solutionem Annatarum ad aliquot annos sedi Apostolicæ solvendarum, ea lege ac conditione consensisse, ut illa in oppugnationem perfidissimi Turcæ, & defensionem fidei Catholicæ convertentur: Ex quo autem numerus annorum, intra quos Annatæ illæ solvi debeant, nunc longe intervallo transactus sit, neque Annatæ illæ à beatitudinis suæ prædecessoribus Pontificibus Romanis in hunc usum, in quem decretæ sunt conversæ: Ob id, si modo necessitate exigente, communia auxilia in oppugnationem Turcæ per Germaniam essent decernenda & colligenda, causatur inde populus Germanicus, quare Annatæ prius jam multis annis in hunc usum reservatæ, ad hoc opus non applicentur, aversaturque alia in se ob hanc causam gravamina recipere. Ex quo Prælati Ec „clesiastici pro Annatis sedi Apostolicæ solvendis, ut plurimum suis subditis super indicta, & collectas imponere, & talia ab eisdem recuperare causaverunt. Quare Illustriss. princeps Dominus Locum tenens, aliique Principes & Imperii Romani Ordines vehementer orant, ut beatitudo Pontificis velit hæc & alia paterno affectu considerare, & illas Annatas, quæ post obitum Episcoporum, aliorumque prælatorum, seu Ecclesiasticorum, ad Curiam Romanam solvendæ fuerint, in futurum non exigere, sed illas fisco sacri Romani Imperii applicandas relinquere; ut eo commodius justitia, pax & tranquillitas nationi Germanicæ conservari, & respub. eo melius per hæc ordinari, possintque per Germanicam nationem aliis Christianis potentibus contra Turcam communem hostem auxilia & præsidia præstari: quod alias & absque eo, minime sperandum erit.
units.tr: §.xiii. Hitherto we have examined those points in the Papal Bull that attack the Peace of Germany: first, the ecclesiastical goods possessed by the Protestants (the Popes have always given first and foremost regard to these, as if they were the very soul of the Papal religion); second, the freedom of religion confirmed in the Empire, and the admission of Protestants, on equal terms with others, to public offices and duties. There follows his complaint about the revenues lost to him and the Churches of Germany that have been taken away by right or by usurpation. He says: "Annates, the rights of the pallium, of confirmation, the Papal months, and similar rights and reservations are excluded from the ecclesiastical goods of the Confession of Augsburg." Reply: What the Pope here censures is contained in art. v. of the Peace of Germany, §. iv., where the rights of electing and nominating, according to each place's customs and ancient statutes, are to remain unimpaired, so far as they agree with the constitutions of the Empire, the Treaty of Passau, the Religious Peace, and above all this declaration and agreement; and in respect of the archbishoprics which remain with the Confession of Augsburg, they contain nothing against that Confession. And §. v.: "If any claim is made, under the name of annates, pallium fees, confirmations, Papal months, and similar rights and reservations, against the immediate ecclesiastical goods of the States of the Confession of Augsburg, by anyone, at any time, or in any manner, such a claim shall lack validity and shall not be enforced by the secular arm." The Pope, in complaining about these provisions, commits two offences here. The first is that he claims these things as rights for himself; the second is that he wishes them preserved to himself even in the goods of the Protestants, and grieves at being excluded from them. Of these, the one is ridiculous and absurd enough, the other is also wicked. For, first, as regards annates, which again do not pertain to the use of the Church but to goods, these are the first-year fruits which are owed to the Pope from a vacant benefice. They were first instituted or devised by him under the pretext of a war against the Turks, as if it were holy; but on that occasion the custom was used only for his own advantage, so that under this pretext he might wring a great quantity of money from men and enjoy a perpetual tribute from it. The beginning of annates is traced to John XXII, to whom they were granted for a time, from other dignities and benefices, excepting abbeys, for a war overseas against the Turks. Others trace it to Boniface IX; Theodoric of Niem, who was his secretary, and Stella, eager to increase ecclesiastical dignity, say that he first imposed the use of annates on all ecclesiastical benefices, on this condition: that whoever obtained a benefice should pay half a year's income to the Apostolic Chamber. Platina says the same, and adds: "Yet there are those who ascribe this invention to John XXII. All admitted this custom except the English, who granted it only for bishoprics, and did not accept it for other benefices." Then other Pontiffs at times instituted similar exactions, for stated certain causes; and the clergy, princes and peoples at times tolerated these, and at times also refused them, as happened in England and elsewhere. But regarding vacant benefices and the first-year fruits of the greater prelacies, abbeys and bishoprics, no other origin is recorded than the voluntary and gratuitous offering of certain men who, having been elected in discord to an abbey or a cathedral church, appealed to the Roman Curia and in that way became superiors and were confirmed. At first, whenever a benefice fell vacant, even more than once in a year, annates were demanded from the new beneficed men: "And whenever they fell vacant (even if they had been vacant three or more times in a year), for every change of title they wished to have and to exact the fruits of the first year of the benefice or prelacy that was vacant, and sometimes far beyond that; and sometimes the Pope had the annates of each vacancy, and the Cardinals nonetheless had a half share; and because of vacancies, prelates were sometimes deprived and transferred against their will, and sometimes other prelates were chosen, who perhaps ought not to have been preferred, because they offered more (under other pretexts), from which slaughter, war and scandals have followed, not yet put to rest." So says the man who, at the time of the Council of Constance, lodged an appeal against that decree on this matter concerning the non-payment of annates, and wrote in the name of the Gallican Church, Nicolas Clemanges. It was first published by Orthuin Gratius in the Fasciculus Rerum Expetendarum, and then by Johann Martin Lydius, with the works of Clemanges, who at the end of that treatise also gives forms of obligation for annates. But in the Concordats of the German Nation of 1447 with Pope Nicholas V, this was so far settled that annates were not to be paid for all benefices, nor for the smaller ones, nor were they to be excessive or burdensome to the state of the Church; they were not to be paid for all churches or places, and only once, even if a benefice happened to fall vacant twice or more within a year; and so the debt of annates did not pass to the successor. Here are the very words of the Concordat: "It likewise pleases us that, in arranging the provision of the said see, the manner of annates should run as follows. From all cathedral churches and monasteries of men only, which are or will be vacant, let there be paid from the first year's fruits, from the day of vacancy, the sum of money assessed in the books of the Apostolic Chamber, which are called common services; and if any have been assessed excessively, which shall be provided for specially, in burdened regions, according to the quality of things, times and regions, so that they are not too heavily burdened, for which we shall give a commission in the parts to those who petition, that they may diligently inquire and relieve them. The said assessments are to be paid, one half within a year from the day of peaceful possession by the whole or the greater part, and the other half within the following year; and if within a year they have been vacant twice or more, they are to be paid only once; nor shall such a debt pass to the successor in the church or monastery. But from all other dignities, personages, offices and secular and regular benefices whatsoever, which are conferred by authority of the said see, or which shall be provided for (except by virtue of expectative graces, or for the cause of exchange), annates or half-fruits are to be paid according to the usual assessment, within a year from the time of possession; and such a debt likewise shall not pass to the successor in the benefice. But from benefices which do not exceed the value of twenty-four gold florins of the Camera, nothing shall be paid; and this observance shall endure henceforth, unless it happens to be changed in like manner in a future Council, with the consent of the same nation." Either he pays the whole first-year fruits, or half of them, to the Pontiff, who has obtained an ecclesiastical benefice, as annates. Azor, Institutiones Morales, part ii., book vii., chapter xii., cites Cosmas, the author of the gloss on the Pragmatic Sanction, title De Annatis; and Duaren, book vi., De Sacris Ecclesiae Ministeriis; and John Andreae, on chapter Inter caetera, De officio Ordinarii, who by various arguments disapprove of the use of annates, because they are "contrary to the whole divine law and the constitutions and laws of the Canon." Martin Meyer, Chancellor of Mainz, in a letter of congratulation to Aeneas Sylvius on his attainment of the Cardinalate in 1457, while lamenting that Sylvius's Cardinalate fell in those times, when "frequent complaints (he said) are brought against the Roman Pontiff", adds among other things about annates: "Annates or half-fruits are demanded without any delay of time, and it is plainly known that more than is owed is extorted." These grievances, against the reply of Aeneas Sylvius, were afterwards confirmed on behalf of that same Martin of Mainz by Jacob Wimpheling of Schlettstadt, in 1510, in his Replica, "On the Grievances of the German Nation and Empire against the See and the Roman Curia." And thus very many have always rightly objected to those annates and resisted them, for many reasons. Partly because the causes for which men had consented to annates were no longer in existence: "the causes which then were have ceased, because no overseas passage or other virtuous undertaking is made from such moneys," said Clemanges; partly because by those annates there would be committed "the stain of simony, and manifest perjury, and scandal, and the damnation of souls," as the same author says. Hence the Gallican clergy protested against them in that reply which Clemanges, in their name, presented to the Council of Constance against John de Scribanis, the so-called Fiscal of the Apostolic Chamber. In England the Pope received nothing except from a few bishoprics. In some kingdoms of Spain, nothing either. In Italy itself, little: of course, because very many resisted everywhere. The Florentines, because the Pope had badly committed an abbey to someone, deprived him of the power of conferring benefices in their dominion for five years. In some dioceses and provinces of Germany the Pope received nothing at all of annates; the so-called apostolic letters were admitted only if the bishops were pleased, and at times they rejected them. The Parisian Curia, in the year 1406, "it was declared that the said Benedict and his officials shall cease in our kingdom of the Dauphiné from exactions of the first annates, fruits and emoluments of prelacies and other benefices whatsoever, vacant, or which have been vacant, or will be vacant, as well for the first annates as also for the fruits and emoluments which, at the time of the withdrawal previously made from the same Benedict, and of the vacancy of prelacies, dignities and other benefices, have accrued or accrue in any way whatever." Also, because the officials of Benedict P. had perhaps gathered them, they were held back by order of the King: "And if anything of these things which were levied or exacted, by reason of the aforesaid, is or remains in the hands of the collectors or subcollectors, or of any others whatsoever, under our hand, it shall be arrested, and our own Court has arrested and does arrest it; and they are forbidden to hand over or pay anything of it to the same Benedict or to anyone else; and our own Court also forbids it." This edict is read, besides in the Fasciculus Rerum Expetendarum, p. 196, also in Charles Dumoulin, Works, vol. iii., p. 471, in the commentary on the Edict of Henry II against the Small Dates and the abuses of the Roman Curia. By Datae are meant bulls dated by the Datarii of the Pope, who are so called, dated under each day, or sealed with their own dates (as we say in common speech), whose agents, called Banquiers in the Edict, that is trapezitae (money-changers), were then many through the kingdom of France, who carried on this merchandise of Papal business, and were restrained by various laws in that Edict, made in 1551. These had also been suppressed in 1547, and before that by many edicts of various kings, by which they wisely and providently forbade every kind of Papal exaction: reservations, provisions, annates, and so on. Louis IX, in 1228 and 1268, sanctioned that famous Pragmatic: "Likewise we are unwilling that exactions and most grievous burdens of money, imposed or to be imposed by the Roman Curia on the Churches of our kingdom (by which our kingdom is miserably impoverished), should be levied or collected in any way, except only for a reasonable, urgent cause, by unavoidable necessity, and also by express and spontaneous order of ourselves and of the Church of our kingdom." By Philip the Fair, the law called the Philippine, in 1303; by Charles VI, in 1385. This edict Charles Dumoulin gives in the Style of the Parisian Court, part iii., title xxxvii.; and in it, against the Cardinals, those are named, and other bishops who are supported by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff himself, and who seize ecclesiastical benefices in heaps, and carry them out of the kingdom, is decreed, that the royal officials shall lay hold, in our hand, of the fruits, revenues and income of the temporalities of the ecclesiastical benefices in which they find the defects mentioned above or any of them, which the said cardinals and other ecclesiastical men, especially those who prolong their stay outside our kingdom, obtain; and likewise the annual pensions which the said cardinals or others receive from the benefices of our kingdom; and many more things of that sort follow, providing a remedy for the unspeakable abuses of the Roman clergy. The same Charles issued an edict in 1388 and in 1395. Also the Parisian Curia in 1418 and in 1425. Charles VII in 1438. Louis XI in 1464 and in 1478. And against these same exactions and usurpations of the Roman Curia, under Charles VIII, the University of Paris appealed, and this appeal was admitted in the Parisian Senate. So manfully and constantly have the Gauls always opposed themselves in this matter to those arts and tyranny of the Popes. Molinaeus, in the said book or commentary, notes that the tax of vacancies from the churches of France, entered in the books of the Papal Chamber, amounts to 697,700 francs, not counting the untaxed prelacies and other benefices, whose exactions amount to nearly as much. How great a man Charles Dumoulin was, no one who knows Gaul, or good letters and law, can be ignorant; but by his learning, candour and zeal for the freedom of the King and kingdom against Papal tyranny, he achieved this, that, since his writings could not be purged by fire, they were condemned by a dreadful anathema, by a single Bull of Pope Clement VIII, on 26 August 1602: "By our own motion, and from certain knowledge and mature deliberation, by this our constitution, which shall be valid forever, we condemn, reprobate, forbid and anathematize anew, with the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and of ourselves, all and whatever writings, works and commentaries of the aforesaid Charles Dumoulin, the heretic, and we forbid and strictly interdict forever their reading and retention to all and each of the faithful of Christ, of whatever state, rank, order, condition, dignity, honour and eminence, even if special and individual mention of them should be made, even under the sentence of excommunication, and other censures and penalties contained in the Index of prohibited books; and also, although they pretend that the same writings, works and commentaries have already been purged in any way, of suspicion of the same heresy. And therefore we recall and annul all and any licences which have been granted to any persons, both by ordinaries of places, and also by the Cardinals themselves deputed over the Index, and by the supreme Inquisitions of the holy universal Inquisition against heretical depravity, and by us and by the Apostolic See in any manner, to read and retain the books of the same Charles Dumoulin, even those inscribed under another name, or purged; since they cannot be purged otherwise than by fire; and we forbid all and each of the aforesaid persons to grant or impart such licences to anyone henceforth." And so on. But to the matter in hand. The Council of Basel forbids annates in session xxi. Its decree deserves to be quoted in full, both so that the reason for annates and the exactions customarily used by the Popes may be better learned from it, and so that the crime of simony committed through these, and the perpetual protest of the German nation against them, and the reproof and condemnation of the Popes on this account by the higher Council, may be known to all; and finally so that the impudence of Innocent today may be exposed, who not only demands the very things which the Synod so strictly forbade, but even from this dares to disturb the state and peace of the Germans. "The holy general Synod of Basel, lawfully assembled in the Holy Spirit, representing the universal Church, for the perpetual memory of the matter. In the name of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, this holy Synod decrees that henceforth nothing whatever be demanded, either before or after, by reason of letters, bulls, seals, common annates and minutes, services, first fruits, deports, or under any other title, colour or name, whether in the Roman Curia or elsewhere, for or in the confirmation of elections, the admission of postulations, presentation, disposition, election, postulation, presentation even made by laymen, institution, installation and investiture, concerning even cathedral and metropolitan churches, monasteries, dignities, benefices and ecclesiastical offices of any kind, nor for sacred orders and the blessing and pallium; directly or indirectly, on the pretext of any custom, privilege or statute, or any other cause or occasion whatever; except only the payment of a competent salary to the writers, abbreviators and registrars of letters or minutes, for their labour." Whoever shall presume to demand, give or promise anything contrary to this sacred canon, let him incur the penalty to be inflicted against simoniacs; and let him acquire no right or title in the dignities and benefices so obtained. Let obligations, promises and bonds, and mandates, and whatever may happen to be done to the prejudice of this salutary decree, be held to have no force and be deemed void and invalid. And if (which God forbid) the Roman Pontiff, who ought to observe and keep the canons of the universal councils, should by doing anything against this sanction give scandal to the Church, let him be referred to a general council. But the rest, according to the measure of their fault, are to be punished with fitting vengeance by their superiors according to the canonical sanctions. Compare also the oration of the noble man Ulrich von Hutten, against the Tithes, where also about Palls etc., against the exaction of tithes, through the legates of Leo X, before the Emperor Maximilian in the year 1519, which is found in the Fasciculus Rerum Expetendarum, p. 37. At the Diet of Nuremberg in 1523, the Emperor Charles V, in a letter to Pope Adrian VI, setting forth both the poverty of the Empire at that time and its need arising from the continual attacks of the Turks against the Empire, openly rejected the cause of this in the Papal exactions; and setting before Adrian the former or proper use of annates, he demanded that they should no longer be carried out to Rome, but be spent for the use of Germany, especially then against the Turk. He speaks of the princes of the Empire: "Therefore, among other things, since they remembered that the annates which the new bishops were accustomed to pay to the Roman Pontiff had been granted from the beginning chiefly for this reason, that by such money the enemies of the Christian faith might be kept off; now, however, the Turks themselves, having occupied a great part of lower Pannonia, are aiming at Germany: it is fair that such annates should be retained in Germany, and be converted to this use there." And when on 25 November the Pontiff's legate to the Diet, Francis Chieregati, in the name of the Pope had set forth what he demanded here from the Germans, Ferdinand, the locum tenens of his brother Charles, and the other Electors and Princes, among other things replied, concerning the annates indeed: "Since, however, the Orders of the Holy Roman Empire do not doubt that the blessedness of the Pontiff is aware of it, that the princes of Germany consented to the payment of annates to the Apostolic See for some years, on this law and condition, that they should be converted to the assault on the most treacherous Turk and the defence of the Catholic faith; but since the number of years within which those annates ought to be paid has now long since passed, and those annates have not been converted by the predecessors of his blessedness, the Roman Pontiffs, to this use for which they were decreed: on this account, if now, with necessity demanding it, common aids are to be decreed and collected throughout Germany for the assault on the Turk, the German people complain that the annates, long since reserved for this use, are not applied to this work, and they are averse to taking up other burdens on this account. Hence ecclesiastical prelates, to pay the annates to the Apostolic See, have for the most part caused their subjects to be taxed and collections to be imposed, and to recover such things from them. Wherefore the most illustrious prince, the Lord Locum tenens, and the other princes and Orders of the Roman Empire earnestly beg that his blessedness will be pleased to consider these and other matters with a fatherly affection, and in future not to exact those annates which, after the death of bishops and other prelates or ecclesiastics, were to be paid to the Roman Curia, but to leave them to be applied to the treasury of the Holy Roman Empire; so that justice, peace and tranquillity may be more conveniently preserved for the German nation, and the commonwealth may be better ordered by these means, and aid and protection may be furnished by the German nation to the other Christian powers against the common enemy the Turk: which otherwise, and without this, will be scarcely to be hoped for."

units.la: Ad quæ cum Pontificius legatus regessisset: Quo ad Annatas non persolvendas Romæ, sed in Germania retinendas, pro sustentatione Imperialis gubernii, habita ea declaratione, quæ facta est verbo difficultate, quæ fieri posset ad eam concedendam, reservatur responsio ipsi Pontifici, quæ dabitur, vel Imperiali regimini, vel suturo Principum conventui, prout magis expedire sue Sanctitati videbitur. jusserunt Principes, Legatum acquiescere in data prima responsione: cui annexuere Centum Germanicæ Nationis Gravamina, quæ quum de multis aliis loquantur rebus, quarum emendatio a Papa postulabatur, ita imprimis illas taxabant Curiæ Rom. exactiones, quibus Germania miserum in modum divexabatur & exhauriebatur. Iterum Carolus a. MDXXVI d. XVII. Septemb. in Rescripto ad P. Clementem VII. vere Imperatorio, abusum Annatarum ei exprobat, & quod illis adjutus bella sæpe movet in ipsos Imperatores: Si eam (inquit) ad rem recte advertat V. Sanctitas, comperiet quod ex Imperio regnisque ac Dominiis nostris Hispaniarum, utriusque Siciliæ, Germaniæ, Galliæ, Belgicæ, ac superioris Burgundiæ, plusquam ex caterorum omnium regnis, ac Dominiis simul junctis, lucri & commodi sedi Apostolicæ ac Rom. curiæ accedit. Non enim patiuntur Reges alii ita passim & laute Ecclesiarum spolia & annatas ex eorum regnis ad Rom. curiam deferri: qualia autem sint ea lucra, ex centum illis Gravaminibus Nationis Germanicæ colligi poterit: quibus tamen ex ea devotione & observantia, quæ semper V. Sanctitati ac Apost. sedi assecti sumus, nusquam aures præstare curavimus, nec his animum adjicere. Quod si justa aliqua ratione vel causa Apostolicæ sedes his lucris careret, non essent claves aurea, quæ bellorum Archivia pro libito aperire, & claudere solent, nec V. Sanctitas ex regnorum nostrorum pecuniis, atque redditibus exercitum in nos concitaret, nec temporalia arma moveret, quibus potius jusstum videretur, ad nostram defensionem uti. Vtinam omnes isto zelo præditi essent, atque adversus Papam, ambitionem & rapacitatem ejus armati Reges, & Principes! certe non istud sui Status detrimentum sentirent à sede Romanâ, non oppressiones illas & tyrannidem, ac jam quidem patiuntur; neque istud animi aut vitium accresceret Papæ, quo nunc in sum- mum Supremarum Potestatum ludibrium, adversus omnes petulanter insurgit, cunctisque terrori est, vel esse saltem velit.
units.tr: When the Papal legate replied to these demands, he said: As to the annates not being paid at Rome but being retained in Germany for the support of the Imperial government, with the declaration that was made verbally on the difficulty that might be encountered in granting it, the response is reserved to the Pope himself, which will be given either to the Imperial government or to the future assembly of the Princes, as His Holiness shall judge more expedient. The Princes ordered the legate to abide by the first reply given. To this they annexed the One Hundred Grievances of the German Nation, which, although they speak of many other matters whose correction was demanded from the Pope, chiefly condemned those exactions of the Roman Curia by which Germany was wretchedly harassed and drained. Again, Charles, in a rescript to Pope Clement VII dated 17 September 1526, truly imperial in tone, reproaches him with the abuse of annates and with his habit of stirring up wars against the emperors themselves with their proceeds: If Your Holiness (he says) should consider this matter rightly, you would find that from our empire, our kingdoms and dominions of Spain, both Sicilies, Germany, France, Belgium and Upper Burgundy, more gain and profit accrues to the Apostolic See and the Roman Curia than from all the kingdoms and dominions of the others put together. For other kings do not allow the spoils of churches and annates to be carried so freely and lavishly from their kingdoms to the Roman Curia. What sort of gains these are may be gathered from those hundred Grievances of the German Nation; yet, out of that devotion and reverence which we have always shown to Your Holiness and the Apostolic See, we have never taken care to lend them an ear or to give them our attention. But if for some just reason or cause the Apostolic See were deprived of these profits, there would be no golden keys, which are wont to open and shut the archives of wars at will, nor would Your Holiness stir up an army against us from the money and revenues of our kingdoms, nor would you take up temporal arms, which would rather seem right to use in our own defence. Would that all kings and princes were endowed with this zeal and armed against the Pope's ambition and rapacity! Certainly they would not feel this loss of their estate from the Roman See, nor would those oppressions and that tyranny, which they now indeed suffer, be inflicted on them, nor would that spirit or vice grow in the Pope, by which he now petulantly rises up against all, making himself the mockery of the supreme powers and a terror to everyone, or at least wishing to be one.

units.la: Similiaque sunt, quæ hic addit in Bullâ suâ Papa, de jure Pallii &c. credo quod & Pallium conferre Protestantibus (est illud vel Patriarchale, vel Archiepiscopale, de corpore beati Petri sumtum, in quo est plenitudo Pontificialis officii, cum Patriarchalis vel Archiepiscopalis nominis appellatione, uti hæc habentur in Romano Pontificali, sol. 36.) cupiat, & juramentum ab illis fidelitatis, quod in Romana Ecclesia ad Pallii acceptionem fieri consuevit, exigere etiam, quo pollicetur Patriarcha vel Archiepiscopus: ab hac horâ in antea fidelis & obediens ero beato Petro, Sanctaque Apostolicæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ, ac Domino nostro Domino N. Papæ N. ejusque successoribus canonice intrantibus &c. Ad retinendum & defendendum Papatum Romanum, & Regalia Sancti Petri adjutor eis ero: salvo meo ordine, contra ominem hominem. &c. quæ exigere, omnino impium est: & dolere quo minus apud Protestantes obtineant, stultum. Annon nunc Germani, & Protestantes Pallium recusent, & Confirmationem Papalem? quum ante seculum hac de re, a. cIↄIↄ xxii inter Gravamina Germanicae nationis caput xxxvii hanc in formam conceptum fuerit: Insuper Pontifices summi multa ac varia in curia Romana excogitarunt officia, quae ipsi immani vendunt precio: quod quidem illi persolvere coguntur, qui (ita iubente Pontifice) opera talium indigent officialium, seu scriptorum. Hinc evenit, ut natio Germanica, praecipue vero Episcopi quoties Pallium redimunt, aut confirmationem a Romano petunt Pontifice, ac multi alii oppido aggraventur, ac longe plus, quam elapsis annis, pecunias suas dilapidare compellantur. Hinc facile conjicere licet, quot Roma, quantique laquei pro emungendis nummis tendantur. Quapropter talia officia merito deleri debent. Et ad Pallii quidem mentionem merito Germania cohorrescat, quod adeo metuebat Archiepiscopus Moguntinus Iacobus, ut jam moriens dixerit, se non adeo dolere de sua morte, quam ob id, quod subditi sui pauperes iterum pro pallio gravem exactionem dare cogerentur. Et in Replica ad Aeneam Sylvium Iacobus Wimphelingius, pro Moguntino scribens, pro pallio ipsis imposita (ait) viginti aureorum millia.
units.tr: Similar things are what the Pope adds in his Bull about the right to the pallium, and so on. I believe he also wishes to confer the pallium on the Protestants (it is either the patriarchal or the archiepiscopal pallium, taken from the body of the blessed Peter, in which lies the fullness of the Pontifical office, under the name of patriarchal or archiepiscopal, as these things are set out in the Roman Pontifical, p. 36), and to exact from them also the oath of fidelity which is customarily sworn in the Roman Church when the pallium is received, by which the patriarch or archbishop promises: From this hour onward I will be faithful and obedient to blessed Peter, and to the holy Apostolic Roman Church, and to our lord N., Pope N., and his canonically entering successors, etc. I will be their helper in retaining and defending the Roman papacy and the regalia of Saint Peter, saving my own order, against every man, etc. To demand these things is altogether impious, and to grieve that they are not obtained among the Protestants is foolish. Do the Germans and the Protestants now not refuse the pallium and the papal confirmation, since a century ago, in the year 1522, the following was drawn up on this matter among the Grievances of the German Nation, chapter 37: Moreover, the supreme Pontiffs have devised many and various offices in the Roman Curia, which they sell at an outrageous price; and those who need the services of such officials or scribes (as the Pontiff commands) are compelled to pay for them. Hence it comes about that the German nation, and especially the bishops, whenever they redeem the pallium or ask the Roman Pontiff for confirmation, and many others, are greatly burdened, and are compelled to squander far more money than in past years. From this one may easily conjecture how many and how great are the snares Rome sets to squeeze out money. For this reason such offices ought rightly to be abolished. And at the very mention of the pallium Germany rightly shudders; so much did Archbishop Jacob of Mainz fear it that, as he lay dying, he said he did not grieve so much at his own death as at the fact that his poor subjects would again be forced to pay a heavy exaction for the pallium. And in his Reply to Aeneas Sylvius, Jacob Wimpheling, writing on behalf of the Mainz archbishop, says that twenty thousand gold pieces were imposed on them for the pallium.

units.la: Pari ratione hic conqueritur Papa exclusos ab Ecclesiasticis Augustanæ Confessionis Mensis Papales, qui ex sententia Concordatorum sunt alterni, Ianuario mense primo Papali, tum Martius, Majus, Iulius, September, & November, quoque servata velle, & apud Augustanæ Confessionis socios, res est perquam ridicula, & insanum in Papa arguit amorem sui.
units.tr: In the same way the Pope here complains that the Papal months, which by the terms of the Concordats alternate, are excluded from the ecclesiastical benefices of the Augsburg Confession: the first Papal month is January, then March, May, July, September and November. He wishes these to be observed also among the companions of the Augsburg Confession. This is a most ridiculous matter, and it reveals in the Pope an insane love of himself.

units.la: Reservationes quas addit, intellige beneficiorum per ipsum solum conferendorum, legere illas est in Regulis Cancellariæ Apostolicæ, ut vocantur, in primis ejusdem Constitutionibus, ubi de Reservationibus agitur generalibus & specialibus, Ecclesiarum Cathedralium, & Monasteriorum virorum, Cardinalium, Collectorum, Curialium, Cubicolariorum, Cursorum &c. quae ibi videri possunt, suntque variorum Pontificum, Gregorii xiii. Clementis viii. cum diversorum super illas Glossis, & commentariis, imprimis Rebuffi, & Gomecii. Sed quid hæc ad Augustanam Confessionem ejusque Socios? quibus jam olim Germania se opposuit, etiam in Concilio Constantiensi a. cIↄ cccccxvi. ubi primo loco Deputati Provinciarum Germanicæ Nationis pro auserendis illis Reservationibus sic apud Synodum primò, tum „apud Sigismundum Imperatorem: Imprimis ad tollenda illa scandala, quæ hactenus ex diminutione divini cultus Simoniacæ extorsionis pecuniarum, ambitione & cupiditate „proventuum Ecclesiasticorum beneficialium, & possessionum eorum desolatione accciderunt in Ecclesia Dei, &c. „Pro illorum scandalorum materia reseccanda videtur, quod „per hoc sacrum generale Concilium tolli, auferri, & revocari debeant reservationes omnium & singulorum beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, tam majorum quam minorum, „quæ saltem in corpore juris non clauduntur, ut sunt videlicet illæ, quæ introductæ sunt in exsistentia ad regimen, aut „per quascumque regulas Cancellariæ, &c. quod hujusmodi reservationes futuris temporibus nullatenus per quemcumque Summum Pontificem fiant sine declaratione, authoritate, consensu, & approbatione Concilii generalis.
units.tr: As for the reservations which he adds: understand them as benefices to be conferred by him alone. One may read them in the so-called Rules of the Apostolic Chancery, in its first constitutions, where general and special reservations are treated, of cathedral churches and monasteries of men, of cardinals, collectors, curials, chamberlains, couriers, and so on, which may be seen there. They are the work of various Popes, Gregory XIII and Clement VIII, together with the various glosses and commentaries upon them, especially those of Rebuffus and Gomez. But what has this to do with the Augsburg Confession and its companions? Germany opposed these reservations long ago, even at the Council of Constance in the year 1416, where, first of all, the deputies of the provinces of the German nation, to have them removed, spoke first before the Synod and then before the Emperor Sigismund: "First of all, to remove those scandals which hitherto have arisen in the Church of God from the diminution of divine worship, from simoniacal extortion of money, from ambition and greed for ecclesiastical benefice revenues, and from the desolation of their possessions, etc. For the cutting out of the matter of those scandals it seems that by this holy general Council all reservations of all and each of the ecclesiastical benefices, greater as well as lesser, which are not at least enclosed in the body of law, should be abolished, removed and revoked, namely those which have been introduced in the manner of the ruling of the Church, or by any rules of the Chancery, etc.; and that in future times such reservations should in no way be made by any Supreme Pontiff without the declaration, authority, consent and approval of a general Council."

units.la: Iterum in Comitiis Moguntinis a. cIↄ cccccxxvii. tempore Concilii Basileensis, pro tollendis Germanicæ Nationis gravaminibus Proceres censuerunt, à Papa postulandum esse, cap. „v. In primis siquidem cassct, annullet, & irritet omnes & „singulas reservationes, tam generales quam speciales sive „particulares Ecclesiarum Metropolitanarum, Cathedralium, Collegiatarum, Monasteriorum, dignitatum & beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum quorumcunque, quibus pro elec„tione provideri consuevit, sive per extravagantes Ad regimen, & Execrabilis, aut per regulas Cancellariæ, seu quascunque alias constitutiones aut ordinationes introductæ „sint, reservationibus in Corpore juris clausis duntaxat exceptis. Vt norit Papa, quam serio hoc tum etiam urserint Imperii Principes, & ut Papam ipsum his legibus constringere nequicquam fuerint veriti, audiat caput istorum Avisamentorum, sic app ellant, penultimum: Vt autem præmissa ,,misla firmiter observentur, polliceatur Papa pro fe & fuc,,cessoribus suis se omnia præmissa & singula inviolabiliter ,,observaturum, & contra ea vel ipsorum aliquod in toto vel ,,in parte nullo umquam tempore innovaturum, decernen,,do initurum, &c. Pro firmiori subsistentia committet Ro,,mano Regi & Principibus Electoribus, & aliis, quos secum ,,duxerint assumendos, super eorum observantia Pragmati,,cam sanctionem conficiendi, at pœnis & censuris vallandi ,,& corroborandi potestatem. Unde & in Concilio Basileensi Expestationes & Reservationes beneficiorum prorsus reprobatas fuisse, scribit in Chronico Citizensi Paulus Langius, Monachus: & Goldastus Constitut. Imperial pag. 202. ponit inter Concilii Basileensis Constitutiones, ad Gravamina Principum Germaniæ, cap. 16. Darneben sind auch die besonderen Reserva-ten vnd vorbehaltungen / wie sie genant werden mogen / der Pfründen / so bis-nach verledigt werden / sie sein durch Romische Bischoff selbs / oder durch des Romischen Stuls Legaten geschehen / furthen als von ihnen selbs ohn weiter Er-klarung auch also vnkrafftig erkant. Atque omnia ista sive Reservationes, Menses Papales, jura Pallii, ac Confirmationis, Annatæ sub idem genus & categoriam Exactionum Papalium referri quum debeant, quæcunque olim (ut hæc quamplurima semper) adversus ista acta scriptaque, tum politice, tum Ecclesiasticæ fuerunt, quorum aliqua a Nobis in præcedentibus significata, etiam hæc quæ jam examinavimus, petere & jugulare censenda sunt.
units.tr: Again, at the Diet of Mainz in the year 1427, at the time of the Council of Basel, the princes judged that for the removal of the grievances of the German nation the Pope should be asked, in chapter 5: "First of all, he should quash, annul and make void all and each of the reservations, whether general or special or particular, of metropolitan, cathedral and collegiate churches, of monasteries, dignities and ecclesiastical benefices of whatever kind, which are usually provided by election, whether they have been introduced through the extravagants Ad regimen and Execrabilis, or through the rules of the Chancery, or any other constitutions or ordinances, the only exception being reservations enclosed in the body of law." That the Pope may know how seriously the princes of the Empire urged this at that time, and how little they feared to bind the Pope himself by these laws, let him hear the penultimate chapter of those proposals, as they call it: "Moreover, that the aforesaid things may be firmly observed, the Pope shall promise for himself and his successors that he will inviolably observe all and each of the aforesaid things, and will never at any time innovate against them, or any part of them, in whole or in part, decreeing and enacting, etc. For their firmer maintenance he shall commit to the Roman King, the Electoral Princes and such others as they may choose to associate, the power of drawing up a pragmatic sanction concerning their observance, and of fortifying and strengthening it with penalties and censures." Hence Paulus Lang, the monk, writes in his Citizen Chronicle that at the Council of Basel expectatives and reservations of benefices were utterly condemned; and Goldast, in the Imperial Constitutions, p. 202, lists among the constitutions of the Council of Basel, in answer to the grievances of the princes of Germany, chapter 16: Besides, the special reservations and provisions of benefices, however they may be named, which in future fall vacant, whether they are made by the Roman bishops themselves or by legates of the Roman See, shall likewise be recognised as null and void, without any further declaration from them. And since all these things, the reservations, the months of the Pope, the rights to the pallium and confirmation, and the annates, ought to be classed under the same genus and category of Papal exactions, whatever has been done in the past against these acts and writings, both politically and ecclesiastically (as very many things always have been), and some of which we have indicated in what precedes, must be regarded as aimed at and striking at the very throat of these matters we have now examined.

units.la: §.xiv. Præterea hoc mirum quam urit Papam, quod in Bulla, magna cum indignatione expectorat: Contra pacem hujusmodi, ullumve ejus articulum nulla jura Canonica, vel Civilia, communia, specialia Conciliorum decreta, Religiosorum Ordinum Regulas, juramenta aut concordata cum Romanis Pontificibus, ullave alia Statuta, sive politica, sive Ecclesiastica; Decreta, Dispensationes, Absolutiones aut alias Exceptiones allegari, audiri vel admitti debere disponitur. Resp. Quod inter Pacis articulos torvo adeo vultu hic intuetur, est quod occurrit art.v.§.1. non ,,attenta cujusvis seu Ecclesiastici seu Politici, intra vel extra ,,Imperium, quocunque tempore interposita contradictio,,ne vel protestatione, quę omnes inanes & nihili, vigore ,,horum declarantur. & passim, uti in tali Pacificatione debuit, excluduntur quæcunq; alias in contrarium adferri possent, præsertim Ecclesiastica, vel Papales dispensationes,aut Ordinum Religiosorum regulæ &c.quę quid ad politiam,vel ut ad illa se flectant & componant Principum de gubernandis aut tranquillandis rebus transactiones,& decreta?si Papa audiri in talibus debet, vel attendi ejus dispensationes,absolutiones,& exceptiones,certum est nullam unquam pacem certa firmari inter Principes haberiq; posse,aut nihil fructus a maximis etiam celeberrimisq; Politicorum conventibus, intercedente hoc Graccho, exspectandum esse. Si quid Ecclesiastici ess(et Papa, vel sui haberent, solo Ecclesiastico contentos esse oporteret,nō rebus politicis se immiscere,& quod Apostolus inquit II.Tim. II.4. ἐμπλέκεσθαι ταῖς τοῦ βίου πραγματείαις, nedum ut rumpant illa quæ pacis sunt, & classicum primi canant, solique. Videant in Iure suo I. Dist. lxxxviii. Episcopi & Ecclesiastici secularia negotia non curent. & Dist. xlv. Episcopi & Ecclesiastici non sint percussores. Dist. xc. Episcopi non sint litigiosi: & qui istis Distinctionibus habentur canones. In sexto Decretalium Bonifacii VIII. lib. III. tit XXIV. Necelerici vel Monachi secularibus negociis se immisceant. Decret. Gregor. lib. III. tit. I. iterum, Ne clerici vel Monachi &c. Sic Imperatores Honorius, & Theodosius sapienter edixerunt, in Codice Iuris, de Episc. & Cler. l. XVII. Placet nostrę clementiæ, ut nihil commune Clerici cum publicis actionibus,vel ad curiam pertinentibus, cujus corpori non sunt annexi, habeant. Certe ubi Supremæ Potestates, quemadmodum in hoc pacis negotio, quid vel deliberant vel agunt, præsertim quod tantopere necessarium,& e re publica habetur,ac pax Germaniæ, ut hic immensum illis inferior,& alterius corporis,atque status Papa se ingerat, & leges vel præscribat, vel inter suos facta constitutiones, aut pro arbitrio erogandas dispensationes omnibus præferat, pro re putidissima apud cunctos benesenlatos merito haberi debet. Præcipue illæ Dispensationes nes, quę ut nummis cmtæ, vel temerario motu, id est, proprio, à Papis impertitę, jam diu orbi Christiano risum debent, atque à plurimis, à Germanis præsertim, reclamatæ, & multis semper gravaminibus causam præbuerunt. Sed Concordata memorat cum Rom. Pontificibus. Hæc a. clo ccccxlvii inita inter Imp. Fridericum iii. & P. Nicolaum v. pro unione inter Imperium Germanicum, & sedem Papalem: quibus primo loco sibi cavit Papa de provisione Ecclesiarum, & beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum, inter quæ recenset etiam ossicium centum & unius scriptorum litterarum Apostolicarum, & viginti quatuor Pœnitentiariæ præfata sedis, & viginti quinque Abbreviatorum. Quare etiam quænam mensēs Papales sint, hisce Concordatis statutum: ut & modus Annatarum, de quibus modo diximus: denique & indultum Eugenii iv pro dicta natione, usque ad tempus futuri generalis concilii, confirmatum. Sed primum, non ab omnibus vel plerisque Germaniæ Principibus, aut ex eorum consensu Concordata illa fuerunt; sed à paucis, à Moguntino præsertim cum Imp. Friderico, reliquis in concilium non uti decuit adhibitis, neque aliquo tempore celebratis Comitiis, ut in iis negotium hoc examinari & decidi potuisset. Tum in præjudicium Concilii Basileensis, in quo de beneficiorum provisionibus, reservationibus, annatis aliter constitutum erat, illaque abrogata & damnata, hæc Concordata in gratiam & pro confirmanda usurpatione Romanæ sedis in Imperium, cui assiduo intenta, excogitata à parte Pontificiâ fuerunt. Denique nec ipsos Romanę sedis Episcopos hisce Concordatis fideliter semper stetisse, verum sæpe illis contraivisse, nec servasse ea, palá non è vulgo aliqui, sed ipsi Imperii Proceres, atque adeo Imperatores testati fuere. Nec dissitebatur in Comitiis Norinbergensibus ipse P. Adrianus vi. cujus Legato, hac super re; ,,respondebant Principes: Ad hęc beatissimus Pontifex paterno amore testatur, sibi etiam dum in minoribus esset, ,,plurimum displicuisse, quoties Concordatis Principum ,,per curiam Rom. derogaretur, suaque Beatitudini hanc cer,,certissimam esse sententiam, etiamsi Principes nunquam ,,requirent, sui Pontificatus tempore penitus abstinere, uni,,cuique, & maxime nationi Germanicæ, jus suum conserva,,re, illique nationi peculiares favores impendere. Adeoque in Coronationibus Imperatorum, in Capitulationibus, ut dici solet, vel Lege Regia, in quam jurant, art. xv. hic est: ,,Cumque præter & contra Concordata Principum, & con,,venta pactata inter Ecclesiam, Pontificiam Sanctitatem Se,,demque Romanam, & Germanicam Nationem, informi,,bus gratiis, tescriptis annatis Ecclesiarum, per multiplica,,tionem & coacervationem Officiorum in Aula Romana, ,,reservationibus item & dispensationibus, aliisque modis, ,,in damnum Ecclesiarum, Cleri, & privilegiorum ab iis ob,,tentorum, quibus ab ejusmodi oneribus liberati sunt, præ,,terea in præjudicium juris patronatus & Dominorum seu,,dalium continuo & absque intermissione manifeste aga,,tur: & exinde non tolerandæ vetitæque societates & con,,tractus sive comparationes, ut nobis relatum est, ineantur: ,,quod nos debemus ac volumus de consilio Electorum, ,,Principum, aliorumque Statuum: cum Sanctissimo Patre ,,nostro Papa Sedeque Romana, enixius agere, ut in poste,,rum caveantur & inhibeantur: adhæc videre, ne prædicta ,,Concordata Principum, & conventa pactata, privilegia ,,item & libertates, amplius violentur & prævaricentur, sed ,,ut in suo vigore ac stabilitate serventur & manuteneantur. ,,Quæ vero jam oborta sunt super iis gravamina, & abusus ,,irreplerunt, facere ut juxta normam tractatus in Comitiis ,,Imperialibus anno 1530. Augustæ habiti & conclusi, stol- ,,lantur; & ne deinceps talia inconsultis Electoribus contingat aut permittantur, præcavere. Hoc Carolus v. Ferdinandus i. Rudolphus ii. Matthias, Ferdinandus ii. ipseque Ferdinandus iii. a. cIↄ Iↄcv i. d. xxiv. Decembris, Rationes, sub coronationem testati & polliciti fuerint, ut nihil causæ nunc habeat Papa, Concordatorum illorum partem observantiam causandi, præsertim quantum spectat partes Protestantium, & apud hos. Quodque in Instrumento Pacis omnia & quæcunque seu politica pacta, seu Ecclesiastica alia excluduntur, quæ isti obviare possint, ex communi & usitata in talibus agendi ratione factum, firma ut habeantur & indissoluta, quæ alias jam per hoc, tum per illud statutum facile dissolverentur; præcipue à parte Papali, àqua consuevit bonarum rerum omnium provenire rescissio & jactura; &huc quin ante omnia respexerint Pacis Conditores haud dubito, quum dicerent, art.v.§.1. non attenta cujusvis seu Ecclesiastici seu Politici, intra vel extra Imperium, quocunque tempore interposita contradictione vel protestatione, quæ omnes inanes & nihili, vigore horum declarantur. Atque simili planè formâ in ratificandâ pace, sacra præsertim quæ Religionis dici solet, Principes alios, & Gallos uti consuevisse, superius à nobis visum est. In Avisamentis (uti dicuntur) vel Consiliis Moguntinis, tempore concilii Basileensis, a. cIↄ Iↄ XXVII in publicis Moguntiæ Comitiis, ab Imperii Statibus factis, super corrigendis Germanicæ nationis gravaminibus, hac conclusione se mutuo devinciunt Principes: Super præmissis avisamentis concordent, Serenissimus Dominus Romanorum Rex, Illustrissimi Domini Principes Electores, invicem velle assistere, & alterutrum se defendere contra omnem hominem, eos vel alterum eorum conjunctim vel divisim, occasione præmissorum molestare, invadere, seu quomodolibet perturbare conantem. Quin ipse hic Papa suam Bullam confirmare sic satagit, adversus omnes in contrarium Constitutiones, sublata cuiuslibet quavis aliter judicandi declarandi, & interpretandi facultate, & authoritate semper & ubique irritum & inane pronuncians, quidquid secus super his a quoquam quavis authoritate scienter vel ignoranter contigerit attentari. Non obstantibus præmissis ac quibusvis Constitutionibus & Ordinationibus Apostolicis tam generalibus quam specialibus etiam in Comitus universalibus editis. Legibus quoque Imperialibus & municipalibus, nec non quibusvis etiam juramento, confirmatione Apo-
units.tr: §.xiv. Moreover, what especially galls the Pope, and what he spits out with great indignation in the Bull, is this: It is ordered that against this peace, or any of its articles, no canon or civil law, common or special, no decrees of councils, no rules of religious orders, no oaths or concordats with the Roman Pontiffs, and no other statutes, whether political or ecclesiastical, nor decrees, dispensations, absolutions or other exceptions shall be alleged, heard or admitted. Answer: as for the article of the peace which he eyes so grimly here, it is what occurs in art. v, §1: "No contradiction or protest entered at any time, whether ecclesiastical or political, inside or outside the Empire, is to be counted, and by virtue of these provisions all such are declared void and of no effect." Throughout, as the peace had to be framed, everything that could be brought forward to the contrary is excluded, especially ecclesiastical or papal dispensations or the rules of religious orders, and so on. What have these to do with politics, or with the agreements and decrees of princes arranged to govern or calm affairs? If the Pope is to be heard in such matters, or his dispensations, absolutions and exceptions are to be regarded, it is certain that no firm and lasting peace could ever be secured among princes, nor could anything be expected to come of even the greatest and most celebrated political assemblies, with this Gracchus interceding. If the Pope or his people had any ecclesiastical business, they ought to be content with ecclesiastical matters alone and not meddle in political affairs. As the Apostle says, 2 Tim. 2:4: "No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life" [ἐμπλέκεσθαι ταῖς τοῦ βίου πραγματείαις], far less should he break up what belongs to peace and sound the trumpet for war all by himself. Let them look in their own law: I Dist. 88, "Bishops and clergy should not concern themselves with secular business"; Dist. 45, "Bishops and clergy should not be strikers"; Dist. 90, "Bishops should not be litigious"; and the canons contained in these distinctions. In the Sixth Book of the Decretals of Boniface VIII, Book III, title 24, "Neither clergy nor monks should meddle in secular business." Likewise in the Decretals of Gregory, Book III, title 1, again, "Neither clergy nor monks" etc. So also the emperors Honorius and Theodosius wisely decreed in the Code of Law, On Bishops and Clergy, Book XVII: "It is our pleasure that the clergy have nothing in common with public business, or with matters pertaining to the court, to whose body they are not attached." Surely, when the supreme powers deliberate on or carry out something in this business of peace, especially something so necessary and so much in the public interest as the peace of Germany, it ought rightly to be considered a most filthy thing among all well-disposed people that the Pope, who is immensely inferior to them and belongs to another body and estate, should thrust himself in, prescribe laws, and set his own dispensations, made as he pleases, above the constitutions agreed among them. Those dispensations especially, which are bought for money or granted by the Popes out of rash impulse, that is, by their own authority, have long been a laughingstock to the Christian world and have been protested against by many, especially by the Germans, and have always been a cause of many grievances. But he mentions "concordats with the Roman Pontiffs." These were concluded in 1447 between Emperor Frederick III and Pope Nicholas V for the union of the German Empire and the papal see. In them the Pope first of all secured for himself the provision of churches and ecclesiastical benefices, among which he also lists the office of the hundred and one writers of apostolic letters, the twenty-four of the penitentiary of the said see, and the twenty-five abbreviators. For this reason too, what the papal "months" are was settled by these concordats, as well as the manner of the annates mentioned just above; and finally the indult of Eugene IV for the said nation, lasting until the time of a future general council, was confirmed. But, first, these concordats were not made by all or most of the princes of Germany, nor with their consent; they were made by a few, chiefly by the Elector of Mainz with Emperor Frederick, the others not being called into the council as was fitting, and no diet being held at any time in which this matter could have been examined and decided. Then, these concordats were devised in prejudice of the Council of Basel, in which provisions of benefices, reservations and annates had been otherwise settled, and those practices abrogated and condemned; and they were contrived, by the papal side, to win favour for and confirm the usurpation of the Roman see over the Empire, at which it was constantly aiming. Finally, that the Roman bishops themselves have not always faithfully kept to these concordats, but have often acted against them, and have not observed them, has been openly attested not only by some of the common people but by the great men of the Empire themselves, and even by the emperors. At the Diet of Nuremberg, Pope Adrian VI himself did not deny it; to his legate on this matter the princes answered: "Moreover, the most blessed Pontiff testifies with paternal love that, even while he was still in a lower office, it greatly displeased him whenever the concordats of the princes were overturned by the Roman court; and this is his most certain opinion, that even if the princes never asked for it, during his pontificate he would wholly refrain from such things, preserve the right of each person, and especially of the German nation, and bestow special favours on that nation." Indeed, in the coronations of emperors, in the capitulations, as they are commonly called, or the Golden Bull, which they swear to, art. xv runs: "Since, besides and against the concordats of the princes and the agreements made between the Church, the Pontifical Holiness, the Apostolic See at Rome and the German nation, by the multiplication and heaping up of offices in the Roman court, by unformed favours, rescripts, annates of churches, reservations and dispensations, and by other means, to the harm of the churches, of the clergy and of the privileges obtained by them, by which they were freed from such burdens, and moreover to the prejudice of the right of patronage and of lords and patrons, is continually and without interruption openly pursued; and since, as has been reported to us, unbearable and forbidden associations, contracts or purchases are entered into: we ought and wish, with the counsel of the electors, princes and other estates, to press as urgently as we can with our most holy father the Pope and the Roman see, that these abuses be guarded against and forbidden for the future; furthermore, to see to it that the said concordats of the princes and agreed agreements, privileges and liberties, are no longer violated or prevaricated against, but are kept and maintained in their force and stability. As for the grievances and abuses which have already arisen and crept in, to see that they are checked according to the norm of the treaty concluded at the imperial diet held at Augsburg in 1530; and to take care that in future such things do not happen or be permitted without the consent of the electors." Charles V, Ferdinand I, Rudolf II, Matthias, Ferdinand II, and Ferdinand III himself, in the year 1615, on 24 December, have attested and promised these terms at their coronations, so that the Pope now has no ground for alleging the observance of those concordats in part, especially as far as the Protestant parties and their members are concerned. And that in the instrument of peace all and any political or ecclesiastical agreements which might stand in its way are excluded, is in accordance with the common and usual way of acting in such matters, so that they may be held firm and undissolved; otherwise they would easily be dissolved by this or that statute, especially on the papal side, from which the cancelling and loss of all good things commonly results. I have no doubt that the framers of the peace had this above all in view when they said, in art. v, §1: "No contradiction or protest entered at any time, whether ecclesiastical or political, inside or outside the Empire, is to be counted, and by virtue of these provisions all such are declared void and of no effect." And we have shown above that the other princes, and the French, were accustomed to proceed in exactly the same way in ratifying a peace, especially in sacred matters, as they are called, of religion. In the so-called Mainz Advice or Counsels, at the time of the Council of Basel, in the year 1427, at the public diet held at Mainz by the estates of the Empire, concerning the correction of the grievances of the German nation, the princes bound themselves to one another by this resolution: "Concerning the aforesaid advice, the most serene lord King of the Romans and the most illustrious lords the Electors agree to assist one another and to defend each other against every man who, either the one or the other of them, jointly or severally, on account of the aforesaid matters, attempts to molest, invade or in any way disturb." Indeed this Pope himself is so eager to confirm his Bull against all contrary constitutions, declaring void and of no effect, always and everywhere, whatever anyone has knowingly or unknowingly attempted in these matters, with the faculty and authority of judging, declaring and interpreting otherwise being set aside. Notwithstanding the foregoing and any apostolic constitutions and ordinances, general or special, even those issued in universal councils; likewise imperial and municipal laws, and any statutes, customs and usages, even immemorial, confirmed by oath, by apostolic confirmation or by any other firmness, privileges too, indults, concessions and apostolic letters of whatever kind, in whatever places and to whatever persons, even those shining with imperial, royal, or any other ecclesiastical or secular dignity, and otherwise in any way…

units.la: F f Sholica, vel quavis firmitate alia roboratis Statutis, usibus, & consuetudinibus etiam immemorabilibus, privilegiis quoque, indultis, Concessionibus, & litteris Apostolicis quibuscunque locis, & personis, etiam Imperiali, Regali, & alia quavis sive Ecclesiastica, sive mundana dignitate fulgentibus, & alias quomodolibet qualificatis, ac specialem expressionem requirentibus, etiam motu, scientia, deliberatione, & potestatis plenitudine similibus, etiam Consistorialiter sub quibusunque tenoribus & formis, ac cum quibusvis etiam derogatoriis, aliisque efficacioribus, & insolitis clausulis, & decretis etiam irritantibus, & alias quomodolibet in contrarium praemissorum concessis, editis, factis, ac pluries & iteratis vicibus confirmatis, approbatis, & innovatis. quibus omnibus per hanc suam Bullam Papa specialiter & expresse derogat, & derogatum esse vult, caeterisque contrariis quibuscumque. Hoc demum est excludere quaecumque in contrarium constitutiones, gravius certe diriusque quam Politici pro suis decretis loquuntur, & hi pro pace feriendâ observandaque, Papa pro eâ abrogandâ & tollendâ; illi leges figunt pro authoritate ipsis concessa rebus politicis & Ecclesiasticis proficuas, quas Hic nulla fultus potestate, ex mera usurpatione & tyrannide, diffringere satagit & proculcare. Utri quaeso melius? Hic flocci facit Apostolicas (ut vocat) Ordinationes: qualis ipse obsecro Apostolus? vel an Apostolica jam sibi secure contrariantur? & Apostolica tua authoritas, tum confirmatio aliâ convelli tuto potest ac explodi? Quis hinc ultra credat istis Apostolicis? vel spiritum Apostolicum dominari Papis? Videlicet in istud opprobrium debuit per istos adduci nomen Apostolicum, & coram omnibus prostitui quando jam apud Papas adeo nihil ultra Apostolici superest, ut Guiccardinus etiâ, celebris Historicus, lib. xvi. Bell. Italic. §.12. ubi de Leone x. verba faciens, cum dixisset bonum, hac interpretatione utendum sibi duxerit: non loquor de bonitate Apostolica, quoniam corrupto hoc saeculo Paparum probata est bonitas, quando aliorum hominum non superat malignitatem. Et hoc quam rarum sit, omnes sciunt, atque ipse non ignorabat. Vnde jam minoris faciendum, quod & universalia Comitia, & quamvis authoritatem, leges quoque Imperiales & municipales, vel juramento etiam, confirmatione Apostolica, & quavis firmitate roborata Statuta, usus, consuetudines immemoriales, privilegia, personas etiam Imperiali, Regali, & alia quavis dignitate fulgentes, omnia deniq; tam levi halitu hic difflat & præle contemnit. Scilicet id est bullas facere. Quam verò hoc jam ridiculum, exprobrare Imperatori, Regibus, Principibusque, quod pro confirmando Pacis decreto adversus id nulla alia Statuta sive politica, sive Ecclesiastica, decreta, dispensationes, absolutiones aut alias exceptiones, ei derogantes, allegari, audiri vel admitti velint, & quod interim ipse Papa pro sua adversus Pacis illud decretum improbissimâ Bulla adeo nec Ecclesiastici, nec Apostolici, neque Imperialis Regalisve aliquid audiri vel adduci in contrarium sinit?
units.tr: ...Apostolic confirmation, or by any other firmness strengthened, statutes, customs and usages, even those beyond memory, and likewise privileges, indults, concessions and letters Apostolic of whatever kind, for any places and persons, even those shining with imperial, royal, or any other dignity, whether ecclesiastical or secular, and otherwise qualified in whatever way, and requiring special mention, even those granted, issued, or made by similar motu proprio, knowledge, deliberation and fullness of power, even consistorially, under whatever wording and forms, and with whatever derogatory and other more effective and unusual clauses and decrees, even those declaring nullity, and otherwise granted, issued, or made in contrary to the foregoing, and confirmed, approved, and renewed many times and repeatedly. By this his Bull the Pope specifically and expressly derogates from all of these, and wishes them to be derogated, and from all other contrary things whatsoever. This, finally, is to exclude every contrary constitution, certainly more gravely and harshly than the politicians speak in their decrees; and they do so for striking and observing the peace, the Pope for abrogating and removing it. The former fix laws, by the authority granted to them, that are beneficial to political and ecclesiastical affairs; the Pope, supported by no power, by mere usurpation and tyranny, strives to break and trample these underfoot here. Which of the two, I ask, is better? He thinks little of what he calls Apostolic ordinances: what sort of apostle is he, I ask? Or are Apostolic things now safely opposed to one another, and can your Apostolic authority, and confirmation too, be safely overturned and hissed down by others? Who after this would believe these Apostolic documents? Or that the Apostolic spirit rules the Popes? Clearly the name "Apostolic" had to be dragged by these men into this disgrace and exposed before everyone, when among the Popes so little of the Apostolic is left that Guicciardini too, the famous historian, in book 16 of the Italian Wars, §12, where he speaks of Leo X, after saying "good," thought fit to use this qualification: I do not speak of Apostolic goodness, since in this corrupt age of the Popes goodness is proved only when it does not surpass the malice of other men. How rare this is, everyone knows, and he himself was not unaware of it. Hence what is now to be valued less: the universal diets and whatever authority, the imperial and municipal laws too, and even those bound by oath, by Apostolic confirmation, or by any other firmness strengthened statutes, usages, immemorial customs, privileges, and persons shining with imperial, royal, or any other dignity; in short, all of them he here blows away with such a light breath and treats with contempt. Clearly this is what it means to issue bulls. How truly ridiculous it is to reproach the Emperor, kings and princes that, to confirm the decree of peace, they want no other statutes, whether political or ecclesiastical, decrees, dispensations, absolutions, or other exceptions derogating from it to be alleged, heard, or admitted, while the Pope himself, in his most shameless Bull against that decree of peace, allows nothing to be heard or adduced to the contrary, whether ecclesiastical, apostolic, imperial, or royal?

units.la: §.xv. Ultima, quam contra Pacis articulos Papa adfert, ratio nunc superest examinanda, quæ concernit Electorem Palatinum: Numerus, inquit Papa, Septem Electorum Imperii olim Apostolicâ authoritate præfinitus, sine nostro & sedis præfatæ beneplacito augetur, & octavus Electoratus in favorem Caroli Ludovici Comitis Palatini Rhenii hæretici institutur. Quod Illustrissimum Electorem Palatinum tangit in Pacis instrumento, continetur ejus art iv. In Papæ illis verbis hoc primo est ridiculum, quod hic Apostolicam clamat authoritatem, quam alias in hac Bulla modo ipse non extenuat solum, sed rejicit. Unde quid de illa authoritate habendum sit, nos satis docuit. Præterquam quod intolerandus Christianis ille Apostolici nominis sit abusus, nominationem Apostolicam tam profane commiscere & convertere cum Papali. Tum falsissimum hoc, numerum septem Electorum Papali authoritate olim præfinitum fuisse. Scilicet duo sunt quæ sibi temere attribuit Papa, per quæ non multam, sed supremam omnemque potestatem sibi competere in Imperium arguit. Primo, quod à Papa facta sit imperii translatio, à Græcis ad Francos, a Leone iii. ad Carolum M. a. dcccc i. Quod multis modis salfalsum esse evincunt utriusque Imperii historiæ, & rationes variæ. Nam præterquam quod jure disputari posset, an proprii & stricti nominis translatio hic intercesserit. Nicolaus Cusanus de Concord. Cathol. lib. III. Admittendo ea quæ de patriciatu Caroli dicta sunt non sequitur, quod ea propter fuit de Græcis imperium translatum. Et paulo post: Ego enim Coloniæ in majori Ecclesia, volumen ingens omnium missivarum Adriani primi ad Carolum, & ipsius Caroli responsiones, & insuper copias omnium Bullarum vidi & fateor me nunquam translationem illam legisse, tamen Imperii nomen multum lego commune antiquitus fuisse.
