Confer & Hug. Grotium, lib. de jure belli & Pacis II. cap. IX. Quæcunque facta hic in persona Imperantis mutatio, non ea per Papæ unius authoritatem suprema, quasi supra populum aut Imperium, facta vel fuit, vel fieri (etiam si facta fuisset) jure potuit. videlicet Papa considerato ut episcopo, non ut cive primario, vel populi nomine quid agente aut dicente. Quum, ceu verræ & propriæ suæ causæ, Caroli in Regem Romanum electio nulli debeatur quam S. P. Q. R. quemadmodum antiquitus idem fieri consuevit, ad quam jure belli & victoriis de Longobardis viam sibi pararat quidem Carolus & jus, sed quam placito & voluntati Romani populi, quam testati multis modis fuere, & per Episcopum, qui Regem etiam unxit & coronavit, acceptam habuit, accedente Orientalium, tum Imperatricis Irene, tum sequentium Nicephori, & Michaelis approbatione, ac consensu. Aventinus, Annal. Bojor. lib. IV. Pontifex, Senatus Populusque Romanus Imperium transferre jure suo in Germanos, Carolumque tacito senatus consulto, plebiscitoque decernit. Sigebertus, in Chronico, ad a. 801. Romani, qui ab „Imperatore Constantinopolitano jamdiu animo defecerant, nunc accepta occasionis oportunitate, quia mulier excæcato Imperatore Constantino, filio suo, eis imperabat, „uno omnium consensu, Karoli Regi Imperatorias laudes „acclamant, eumque per manum Leonis Papæ coronant, „Cæsarem & Augustum appellant. Radulphus de Columna, vel ut alii scribunt Pandulphus, lib. de translatione Imperii quem secutus suo scripto de verbo ad verbum inscruit Marsilius Patavinus, de eodem argumento, quia sicuti dicit cap. 1. istius Landulphi (sic scribit) sententia in quibuldam à sua dissonabat. Quare etiā à Scardio in Sylloge Historico Politico Ecclesiastica, ubi utriusque exhibet scriptum, non Marsilius Columnæ, sed hic illi præponendus fuerat) Vterque eodem fere modo refert, Carolum à Leone coronatum, atque à populo acclamatum fuisse: Carolo Augusto à Deo coronato, Imperatori &c. Sic Landulphus Columna. Marsilius: Carolo Augusto à Deo ordinato &c. Similiter Lupoldus de Babenberg, sola Dei patientiā Decretorum D. vocatus (sic ipse de se, in libri frontispicio) lib. de juribus regni & Imperii Romani, cap. 1. & cap. iii. acclamante inquit, & petente populo Romano. Leonardus Aretinus, Histor. Florent. lib. 1. pag. 17. Constat, nullius magis quam populi Romani id munus esse, Imperatorem creare. Nam Pontificatus per illa tempora, loquitur de temporibus Caroli M. magis ab Imperatoria authoritate pendebat, nec quisquam præsidebat nisi quem post senatus, Cleri, & Papæ Romani electionem, Imperatoria comprobasset authoritas. Michael Coccinius, Tubingensis, de Imperii à Græcis ad Germanos translatione, Romanis, aliisque Italiæ populis eam attribuit: Romani itaque & reliqui Italiæ populi Græcorum perspicientes avaritiam simul & ignaviam, ac e regione Germanorum fortitudinem, industriam, & justitiam, imperium de Græcis transtulerunt ad Germanos, in Caroli M. personam. Et talem Imperii translationem Romanorum caeterorumque, Italiæ populorum consensu & authoritate factitatam: suamque vim & efficaciam habuisse haud dubitandum est. Nec obstat quod scribit Innocentius tertius, ad Berchtoldum Zaringiæ ducem, sedem Apostolicam Romanam imperium in personam Magnifici Caroli de Græcis translatum esse in Germanos. Nam sedem Apostolicam non in alio sensu Imperium translatum esse concedimus, quam imperium transferentibus consensisse, ut transferendum declarasse: sed talis translatio vim & efficaciam suam habuit à consensu populi. Onuphrius Panvinus, de Rom. Princip. lib. iii. (qui etiam exstat in Chronico Chronicorum Politico Tom. iii. collecto à Ioh. GuGualterio Belga) in initio, de Carolo M. Imperator appellatus Roma in Basilica S. Petri in Vaticano, cleri, senatus, populusque Romani consensu consecratus & coronatus ibidem a Leone Papa III. anno Domini DCCCI. ineunte, VIII. Cal. Ianuarii, videlicet die Natalis Domini. Idemque Onuphrius, lib. de Comitiis Imperatoriis, cap. I v. de eadem re hunc in modum loquitur: Quare cum Rom. Imperii majestas omnia sibi Barbaris vendicantibus abolevisset, neque in ea foemina quamvis alta indolis, multum prasidii inesse videretur, ejus rei occasione Romani adducti, & praecipue Leo Papa III. qui tum vivebat, ejusdem populi scito, Clerique rogatu, Carolum M. Francorum Regem & Patricium Romanorum, qui per eos dies in urbem venerat, ob egregia in Christianum nomen & Romanam sedem merita, Romanorum Occidentis Imperator primus appellavit, inunctumque ac diademate aureo redimitum, Augustum appellavit. Similiter plures alii, quos adducere proclive, si haec a nobis prosequenda esset controversia, quam ex professo Illyricus tractavit, quem sibi oppugnandum propositi Bellarminus lib. de Translat. Imp. Romani, sed cum ab aliis, tum a Franc. Iunio in Notis egregie exenteratus. Nicolaus Cusanus, tum temporis Decanus Sancti Florini Confluentiae, Theol. Decretorumque Doctor, (ut non habuerit Bellarminus, lib. II I. de Translat. cap. IV. quare ad eludendum ejus testimonium, juventutem ei adeo saltuose exprobraret) de Concord. Cathol. lib. III cap. III. in initio: Verum adhuc volunt quidam, & est opinio vulgatissima, imperium translatum in Germanos per Adrianum, in personam Caroli Magni, juxta ea quae Innocent. 3. dicit in c. venerabilem, de electione, sed fateor me nunquam in antiquis ac probatis libris hoc legisse. Denique summus Theologus, Collega noster Gilbertus Voetius, in Dissertatione HistoricoTheolog. de Translatione Imperii a Graecis ad Francos, quae copiosissime & accurate totum hoc negotium explicat, & confirmat argumentis, quorum lubens susceptus sim defensionem. Verum summum, & quod Papa in Bulla proponit, usurpationis in Imperium suae argumentum est, quod sibi arrogat Electorum in Imperio institutionem, videlicet a Papali auauthoritate eos defluxisse initio, atque adhuc dependere, unde inquit: Numerus septem Electorum Imperii, olim Apostolica authoritate praefinitus, sine nostro & sedis praefata beneplacito augetur. Illud (dico) salsissimum esse, quod Papali (blasphemum est dicere Apostolica) authoritate olim numerus septem Electorum in Imperio praefinitus sit. Vult dicere, à Papa Gregorio v. sub Ottone iii. circa a. locccxcvi aliis a. clxiv. Marsilius Patavinus, de translat. Imp. cap. xi.) ordinem & numerum Electorum in Imperio constitutum fuisse, quo & Bellarmini facit disputatio de transl. Imper. lib. iii. & Azorii, Instit. Moral. part. ii. lib. iv. cap. xix. Sed, praeterquam quod nullo id istius temporis probato historico, nec ex prolato tanti negotii diplomate, vel Bulla (quas caeteroquin & prolixas de istiusmodi rebus facere solent Papae, atque oporteat, certe & asservare, imo quas ne quidem comminiscuntur, uti alias consuetum hoc quidem ipsis est artificium, ut multa ejus circa res Imperii,& donationem Constantini &c. extant documenta) ostendere aut probare possunt, quare de eo mihi dicere liceat, quod Nic. Culano, de Constantini illa: sed in veritate supra modum admiror, si res ita est, eo quod in authenticis libris, & in historiis approbatis non invenitur. & Lupoldus de Babenberg. lib. de Zelo Veter. Princip. Germ. cap. vii. jus & potestatem eligendi Regem Romanorum ab Ecclesia Romana ad certos Principes Germania provenisse, nec in Historiis seu Chronicis nostris gesta Regum seu Imperatorum continentibus reperitur expressum reclamant. Historici, Scriptores Papales, & Rerum Germanicarum,& Electores ipsi, atque Imperatores. Aurea Bulla Caroli iv. data a. clo ccclvi cap. i. ponit Principes Electores juxta antiquam laudabilem consuetudinem, & sic saepius, nulla Papae, vel Papalis authoritatis, unde illa dimanet, facta mentione. Vt & Papa Innocentius iii in c. Venerabilem, de electi potestate. Decretal. lib. i. tit. vi. ad querelam & objectionem Germaniæ Principum, de Legato Romano Episcopo Prenestino, quod se temerè immiscuisset negotio electionis, nempe in messem alienam misisset falcem suam, & electioni ctioni se ingerens, principum derogasset dignitati, uti apud Papam loquebantur Principum Legati, inter quos erat quoque Saltzburgensis Archiepiscopus, & Abbas de Salomona: respondit Papa: sicut justitiam nostram nolumus ab aliis usurpari, sic jus Principum nobis nolumus vendicare. Verum illis Principibus jus & Potestatem eligendi Regem & Imperatorem post modum in recognoscendo (ut debemus) ad quos de jure & antiqua consuetudine noscitur pertinere. Principes Electores, in litteris scriptis ad Benedictum xii. ex Comitiis Renensibus a. clɔ cccxxxvii. in causa electi ab ipsis Imp. Ludovici iv. adversus Paparum interdicta, pro suo in Electione Imperatorum „jure sic loquuntur: quod jura, honores, bona, libertates, „& consuetudines dicti Imperii, & nostra, nobis in electio„ ne Imperii competentia ex consuetudine vel de jure, ma„ nuteneamus, defendamus, & illibata conservemus toto „posse & viribus nostris, contra omnes homines cujuscum„ que praeminentiae, dignitatis, seu status existant; & quod „hoc non obmittamus propter aliqua particula rerum & „personarum, aut praecepta, mandata, processus, per quem„ cumque aut in quemcumque modum & formam prolati „sint, vel inantea proferantur, contra Imperium & nos vel, Coelectores nostros; per quae dicto Imperio ac nobis & „Coelectoribus nostris in praedictis juribus, bonis, homini„ bus, libertatibus, & consuetudinibus praejudicatum sit, vel „in futurum posset praejudicium generari. Michael Coccinius, de Imperii a Graecis ad Germanos translat. Sed Imperator imperium tenet a Deo, ministerio electionis Imperii Electorum, quod jus eligendi ad certos Germaniae principes pervenit ab Othone III. de consensu Principum & populi Imperio subjectorum. Nicolaus Cusanus, de Concordantia Catholica lib. iii. cap. iv. de Otthone iii. loquitur: & hic Imperator consensu procerum Primatum, & utriusque status cleri & populi, perpetuos Electores, qui vice omnium elegerunt, ordinavit tempore Gregorii 5. Alemanni, consanguinei quondam Othonis. Non est igitur eo modo concedendum, Electores a Romano Pontifice potestatem eligendi habere, sic quod nisi ipse consentiret, non haberent, aut si vellet, ab ipsis tollere posset. Quis rogo dedit populo Romano potestatem eligendi Imperatorem: nisi ipsum jus divinum & naturale? Et deinde: Unde electores qui communi consensu omnium Alemannorum, & aliorum qui Imperio subjecti erant, tempore secundi Henrici constituti sunt, radicalem vim habere ab ipso communi omnium consensu, qui sibi naturali jure Imperatorem constituere poterant: non ab ipso Romano Pontifice, in cujus potestate non est, dare cuique Provincia per mundum Regem, vel Imperatorem, ipsa non consentiente. Nec quippiam Bellarmini causam juvat, in quo tamen is exceptionem suam fundat, quod consensum Pontificis intervenisse dicat Culanus; nam & auctoritatem praecipuam ejus institutionis ad consensum omnium eorum refert, qui ad imperium pertinent, quod nec diffitetur de ipso, neque probat Bellarminus, & dicit Cusanus, consensum Pontificis hic spectari ut in Comitiis, ubi vigor defixionis non ab ipso primo omnium Pontifice, sed ex communi omnium & ipsius & aliorum consensu dependet. Illaque valde communis est sententia, quae ordinis Electoralis in Imperio institutionem attribuit, non Gregorio v. sed Ottoni III Saxoni, dicto propter eximias ejus virtutes, mirabilia mundi. Pro qua plurimi certe stant Auctores, quos nominant Joachimus Cluten, in Sylloge rerum quotidianarum §. 24. Iustus Sinolt, de Vicariis Imperii. §. 19. Antonius Kolerus, de Iure Imperii Germanici thes. 45. Simon Scardius, de Electi. Imper. cap. 11. Auctor Anonymus, de translat. Imperii, cap. VII. apud Goldastum Politic. Imperial. Part. IX. adde Michaelem Schiferer, de origine & potestate Modernorum Electorum. Henricum Bruningium, de variis Universitatum speciebus, §. 9. Eliam Schedium, de Dis Germanis pag. 23. Alii vero diu post Othonem Electorum Imperii collegium & officium institutum volunt: inter quos post Aventinum, qui lib. v. Annal. de Electoribus loquens, ait; Ego illos demum post fata Frederici II. institutos, & a Gregorio x. constitutos esse competentum habeo: princeps est Onuphrius Panvinus, Veronensis, Eremita Augustinianus, lib. de Comitiis Imperatorum, qui olim editus Basileae a.lvIII. inde cum notis Friderici Hortlederi, quomodo eum suis Politicis Imperialibus inseruit Goldastus, in initio. Ille Onuphrius, cap. vi. postquam falsum & absurdum dixisset, Electores sub Othone III. à Gregorio v. Pont. Max. Saxone, in gentis suæ gratiam, institutos fuisse. addit: quod salsissimum esse, eoque trecentesimo anno post in ordinem hunc redactos fuisse post Friderici II. Imperatoris obitum, nunc demonstrabo. id est, inter annum clɔ ccl. quo Fridericus II. decessit, & clɔ cclxxx. quo Rudolphus Habspurgensis, post diutinum xxiii annorum interregnum, Electorum suffragiis, ut cæteri ipsum sequuti, Rex Romanorum creatus fuit: tamen (inquit) quo potissimum anno, vel quibus de causis, aut à quo Pontifice, vel in quo Germanorum Principum conventu, aut generali vel provinciali concilio id factum fuerit, mihi adhuc incompertum est. Sed tamen per hæc tempora, tam numerus Electorum, quam etiam particularium eorundem actionum, apud horum, vel posteriorum temporum Scriptores, speciatim mentio haberi capit: singulorumque nomina, cum dignitatis appellatione, recensentur. sic ille: adversus quem hac de re alium librum scripsit Simon Schardius, originem Electorum antiquiorem volens, & pro communi sententia eam vendicans Othoni III. Qui liber, præterquam apud Goldastum, inter Politica Imperialia, etiam legitur ultimus in Syllog e Historico-Ecclesiastica variorum Auctorum edita ab ipso Schardio. Sed me quidem hujus argumenta solum Innocentii ac Hostiensis auctoritate, ut ipse loquitur cap iv. ... antis, movere non possunt, ut credam, ab Othone III Electorum ordinem institutum fuisse. Neque ideo tamen Onuphrio accedo, ut institutos dicam circa tempus Rudolphi Habspurgensis, vel ob argumentum quod ipse valide urget adversus institutionem illorum Ottonianam, ex Auctorum hac de re silentio: etenim ut non ad Othonis, ita nec ad Habspurgensis tempora tam illustris & momentosi instituti origo ab Historicis refertur, utrimque silentibus: verum, ut post Othonem, maxime vero post Fridericum II. rebus Imperii per internecinas dissensiones sic exigentibus, concedam Imperatoris electionem non per omnes, uti olim, Imperii Status & Primores, sed quosdam tantum Principes, eosque nec certo forte primùm numero, nec eosdem, factam fuisse, paulatim tamen per pauciores, & principaliores, eosdemque, adde eos quibus dein dignitas electoralis solis adjudicata; non tamen asseram lege eos certa, utcumque quidem consuetudine, etiam antiquâ, Electores fuisse & septem, illos partim Ecclesiasticos, partim seculares, qui hodie, usque ad Carolum IV. & promulgatam ab eo in Comitiis Norinbergensibus a. clɔ cccIvı. d. IV Idus Ianuarii, Bullam auream, quâ primo loco dignitas & ordo Electorum Imperii lege perpetuâ confirmatur & stabilitur. Non nego, ante hoc tempus nomen & rationem Principum Electorum satis cognitam in Imperio fuisse, sed ex certa & Imperialis institutionis lege perpetua ac universaliam diu septem illos habitos fuisse solos Electores, ut nunc, hoc non video. Plures|paucioresque electioni Imperatoris olim interfuisse constat, primum multos, inde pauciores. Et postquam diuturnâ consuetudine praecipui aliqui Imperii Principes huic negotio admoti, non tamen (uti videtur) ex lege quadam lata, factave institutione, sed sic tamen usu, quem necessitas & pacis publicæ commodum suadebant, nato procul dubio ex particularibus negotiis & recessibus, quæ indagari hic oporteat multum lucis allatura, lex aureæ Bullæ super illa re facta, & septem Electorum istorum ordo constitutus, vel confirmatus fuit. Res ipsa exigere potius visa est ut primum ex consuetudine ageretur, tum lege. Et in Aureâ Bullâ, ubi Electorum ponuntur regulæ, ad consuetudinem fit recursus. Cap. I. & Principes Electores ad electionem hujusmodi juxta antiquam laudabilem consuetudinem habuerint profecisci. Cap. IV. §. 2. Caeterum, quoties & quando deinceps sacrum vacare contiget imperium, extunc Moguntinensis Archiepiscopus potestatem habebit, sicut potestatem habuisse dignoscitur ab antiquo, caeteros Principes antedictos, suos in dicta electione consortes, litteratorie convocandi. §. 3. Primo quidem interrogabit Trevirensi Archiepiscopo, cui primam vocem competere declaramus, sicut invenimus haereditarius computisse. Vides, ut secundum antiquam consuetudinem & observantiam formet leges. Cap V. §. 3. Et quamvis Imperator sive Rex Romanorum super causis propter quibus impeditus fuerit, habeat, sicut & consuetudine introductum dicitur coram Comite Palatino Rheni, sacri Imperii Archidapifero, Electore principe respondere. Sic illos Principes ante quoque fuisse Electores liquet, multaque observasse quae hic lanciun tur ex consuetudine, quae deinceps ex lege, & communi Comitiorum senatus consulto servanda decernuntur. Marquardus Frcherus, Origin. Palat. part. 1. cap. xv. ubi dixisset Imperium, postquam in stirpe Carolina aliquandiu haereditarium fuit, ea deficiente rursum ad electionem rediisse: eligebant autem Principes, inquit, quos Germania multos variosque habebat, & in his etiam Antistites, & sine discrimine, quotquot Comitiis adesse volebant. Prima tamen partes esse solebant potentiorum & qui officia in aula gesserint. Propendet autem in sententiam de Institutione Electorum Ottoniana, non vel in Onuphrii illam, vel quae Carolum IV illorum institutorem facit. Quamvis citra ullum praejudicium bene dici queat, Principes multos, interque eos Palatinum electoria potestate a primis temporibus givilum fuisse, utut nondum ex constituta certa aliqua lege. Quemadmodum cap. xvi. quod in Bulla aurea dicitur cap. v. de consuetudine, id explicat, usu antiquo. Ioh. Ioachimus a Rusdorf, in Vindiciis Palatinis cap. III. Effo sane, fuerit Electoratus ab antiquo, & ante Carolum IV. Imperatorem, connexus Bavaria Ducatui, & non Palatinatui Rheni, fuerit etiam aliquando alternatio inter Palatinos & Bavaros pacta & usitata, quid tum? Nonne utrumque fuit rudi illa aetate, quando Septemvirorum officia, dignitates & functiones, quando eorum successiones, gradus, praerogativae, ordo, regalia, assignat & in feudum concessi Principatus, nondum legibus & certis praescriptionibus erant distincti, & constabilitis? Postea per aure; am Bullam Imperatores & Ordines illius aevi, experti quantum Resp. noceret tum divisio & dissensio inter eos &c. communi consensu, certum orainem in successione & possessione praescripserunt, cuilibet Electoris suum gragradum, jus & munus assignando, & lege perpetuo valitura declarando, & faciendo, quibus Electoralem dignitatem terris annexam esse oporteat, & usu receptum sit. Ita omnino volo, ea quę circa electionem Imperatoris quidem obtinuerunt, sed ex usu, per Aureæ Bullæ legem demum confirmata fuisse & constabilita. Onuphrius, à cujus sententia & calculo haud adeo multum recedimus, nisi quod legem, quam ille octoginta annis ante auream Bullam concipit, nonreperit, nos nullam facimus, & ejus loco consuetudinem ponimus, ex qua lex sponte sequuta fuerit, cap. ix. hac de re sic loquitur:
units.tr: §.xv. The last reason the Pope brings against the articles of the Peace remains to be examined. It concerns the Elector Palatine: The number of the seven Electors of the Empire, once fixed by Apostolic authority, is increased without our consent and the consent of the aforesaid See, and an eighth Electorate is instituted in favour of Charles Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine, a heretic. This touches the most illustrious Elector Palatine in the instrument of Peace, and is contained in its article iv. In the Pope's words the first absurdity is that he here claims an Apostolic authority, which elsewhere in this Bull he not only diminishes but rejects. What is to be thought of that authority we have already sufficiently shown. Besides, it is an abuse of the Apostolic name, intolerable to Christians, to mix up and convert the Apostolic title so profanely with the Papal one. Then comes this utterly false claim, that the number of seven Electors was once fixed by Papal authority. Indeed there are two things by which the Pope rashly attributes to himself, and argues that he holds, not some measure of power over the Empire, but supreme and total power. First, that a transfer of the Empire was made by the Pope, from the Greeks to the Franks, from Leo iii to Charles the Great, in the year 801. The histories of both Empires, and various arguments, prove that this is false in many ways. For, apart from the question whether a transfer in the proper and strict sense took place here at all, Nicholas of Cusa, in De concordantia catholica book iii, says: Granting what is said about Charles's patriciate, it does not follow that the Empire was on that account transferred from the Greeks. And a little later: For I have seen at Cologne, in the greater church, a huge volume of all the letters of Hadrian i to Charles, and Charles's own replies, and moreover copies of all the Bulls; and I confess that I have never read that transfer, though I read much to the effect that the name of Empire was held in common in ancient times. Compare also Hugo Grotius, On the Law of War and Peace book II, chapter IX. Whatever change of ruler was made here, it was not, and could not lawfully have been made, by the sole supreme authority of the Pope, as if above the people or the Empire; for the Pope acted or spoke as a bishop, not as a leading citizen, or in the name of the people. Since the election of Charles as King of the Romans is owed to no one as its own true and proper cause except the Senate and People of Rome (S.P.Q.R.), just as this was customarily done in ancient times, Charles had indeed won for himself, by the right of war and by his victories over the Lombards, a way and a right to it; but he received it by the pleasure and will of the Roman people, which they attested in many ways, and through the Bishop, who also anointed and crowned the King, with the approval and consent added of the Eastern rulers, both of the Empress Irene and of the successors Nicephorus and Michael. Aventinus, Annals of Bavaria book IV: The Pontiff, the Senate and the Roman people by their own right transfer the Empire to the Germans, and decree Charles by a tacit senatorial decree and plebiscite. Sigebert, in his Chronicle, under the year 801: The Romans, who had long since revolted in mind from the Emperor of Constantinople, now, seizing the opportunity, since a woman was ruling over them in the name of her son, the Emperor Constantine having been blinded, with one consent of all acclaim King Charles with imperial praises, and crown him by the hand of Pope Leo, and call him Caesar and Augustus. Radulphus de Columna, or, as others write, Pandulphus, On the Transfer of the Empire, whom Marsilius of Padua followed in the same subject and copied word for word into his own writing, though, as he says in chapter 1 of this Landulph (so he writes), his opinion differed from his in some points. Hence also by Scardius in his Historical, Political and Ecclesiastical Miscellany, where he presents both writings, it should have been Marsilius placed before Columna, not the other way round. Both report in almost the same way that Charles was crowned by Leo and acclaimed by the people: To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, Emperor, etc. So Landulph Columna. Marsilius: To Charles Augustus, ordained by God, etc. Similarly Lupold of Bamberg, called by the sole patience of God a Doctor of Decrees (so he calls himself on the title page of his book), On the rights of the Kingdom and of the Roman Empire, chapter 1 and chapter iii: at the acclamation and request, he says, of the Roman people. Leonardo Aretino, History of Florence book 1, page 17: It is established that the office of creating an Emperor belongs to no one more than to the Roman people. For at that time the Papacy (he is speaking of the times of Charles the Great) depended more on the imperial authority, and no one presided unless the imperial authority had approved him after the election by the Senate, the clergy and the Roman Pope. Michael Coccinius of Tübingen, on the transfer of the Empire from the Greeks to the Germans, attributes it to the Romans and the other peoples of Italy: The Romans and the other peoples of Italy, therefore, perceiving the greed and at the same time the sloth of the Greeks, and on the other hand the courage, industry and justice of the Germans, transferred the Empire from the Greeks to the Germans, in the person of Charles the Great. And that such a transfer was carried out with the consent and authority of the Romans and the other peoples of Italy, and had its own force and efficacy, there is no doubt. Nor does it stand in the way that Innocent iii writes to Berthold, Duke of Zähringen, that the Apostolic See transferred the Empire from the Greeks to the Germans in the person of the Magnificent Charles. For we concede that the Apostolic See transferred the Empire in no other sense than that it agreed with those transferring the Empire, and declared that it was to be transferred; but such a transfer had its force and efficacy from the consent of the people. Onuphrius Panvinus, On the Roman Princes book iii (which is also found in the Chronicon Chronicorum Politicum, volume iii, collected by Johann Gualther of Belgium), at the beginning, on Charles the Great: He was called Emperor at Rome, in the Basilica of St Peter in the Vatican, consecrated and crowned there by Pope Leo iii with the consent of the clergy, the Senate and the Roman people, in the year of the Lord 801, at the beginning of the eighth day before the Kalends of January, that is, on the day of the Lord's Nativity. The same Onuphrius, in On the Imperial Diets chapter iv, speaks thus on the same matter: Therefore, when the majesty of the Roman Empire had been abolished by the Barbarians laying claim to everything, and since no great support seemed to lie in a woman, however high her spirit, the Romans were led by this occasion, and especially Pope Leo iii, who was then living, by the decree of the same people and at the request of the clergy, to name Charles the Great, King of the Franks and Patrician of the Romans, who had come to the city in those days, on account of his outstanding merits toward the Christian name and the Roman See, the first Emperor of the Romans of the West, and, anointed and crowned with a golden diadem, called him Augustus. Similarly many others, whom it would be easy to cite, if this controversy were to be pursued by us, which Illyricus has treated professedly, and whom Bellarmine proposed to attack in his On the Translation of the Roman Empire, but who has been thoroughly gutted both by others and by Franciscus Junius in his Notes. Nicholas of Cusa, at that time Dean of St Florin's at Koblenz, Doctor of Theology and of Decrees (so that Bellarmine did not have him, in On the Translation book iii, chapter IV, which is why he reproached his youth so abruptly, to evade his testimony), in De concordantia catholica book III chapter III, at the beginning: But some still maintain, and it is a very common opinion, that the Empire was transferred to the Germans through Hadrian, in the person of Charles the Great, according to what Innocent 3 says in chapter Venerabilem, on election; but I confess that I have never read this in ancient and approved books. Finally, our colleague, the most eminent theologian Gisbert Voetius, in his historical and theological dissertation On the Translation of the Empire from the Greeks to the Franks, which explains and confirms this whole business most fully and accurately with arguments, whose defence I gladly undertake. But the greatest argument, and the one the Pope puts forward in the Bull, of his usurpation over the Empire is that he claims for himself the institution of the Electors in the Empire, namely that they flowed from Papal authority at the beginning and still depend on it; whence he says: The number of the seven Electors of the Empire, once fixed by Apostolic authority, is increased without our consent and the consent of the aforesaid See. That (I say) is most false, that the number of seven Electors in the Empire was once fixed by Papal (it is blasphemous to say Apostolic) authority. He means that under Otto iii, by Pope Gregory v, in about the year 996 (Marsilius of Padua, On the Translation of the Empire chapter xi, says 1164), the order and number of the Electors in the Empire was established; to which the argument of Bellarmine On the Translation of the Empire book iii and of Azor, Institutes of Moral Theology part ii book iv chapter xix, also tends. But, apart from the fact that they can show or prove this by no approved historian of that time, nor by any diploma or Bull of such a great affair produced (though the Popes are accustomed to make many such documents about such matters, and indeed ought to keep them, and even to invent them, since this is a device habitually used by them, as many documents of theirs concerning the affairs of the Empire and the Donation of Constantine etc. survive), I may say about it what Nicholas of Cusa said about that Donation of Constantine: but in truth I wonder beyond measure, if the matter is so, that it is not found in authentic books and approved histories. And Lupold of Bamberg, in his book On the Zeal of the Old Princes of Germany chapter vii, protests: that the right and power of electing a King of the Romans passed from the Roman Church to certain Princes of Germany is not found expressed in our Histories or Chronicles containing the deeds of Kings or Emperors. Historians, Papal writers, writers on German affairs, and the Electors themselves, and the Emperors, protest. The Golden Bull of Charles iv, given in the year 1356, chapter i, names the Electoral Princes according to the ancient laudable custom, and so often, with no mention of any Papal authority or Papal power from which it flows. As also Pope Innocent iii in chapter Venerabilem, On the power of election, Decretals book i, title vi, in reply to the complaint and objection of the German Princes concerning the Roman legate, the Bishop of Palestrina, that he had rashly meddled in the business of election, that is, had put his sickle into another's harvest, and by interfering in the election had derogated from the dignity of the Princes (as the Princes' legates, among whom was also the Archbishop of Salzburg, and the Abbot of Salomon, said before the Pope): the Pope replied: Just as we do not wish our justice to be usurped by others, so we do not wish to claim for ourselves the right of the Princes. But the right and power of electing a King and Emperor belongs, by right and ancient custom, to those Princes, whom we acknowledge afterwards in recognising (as we ought) the one elected. The Electoral Princes, in their letters written to Benedict xii from the Diet of Rhens in the year 1337, in the case of the elected Emperor Louis iv, against the interdicts of the Popes, speak thus, by their right in the election of Emperors: that we shall maintain, defend and preserve unimpaired with all our power and strength, against all men of whatever eminence, dignity or status they may be, the rights, honours, goods, liberties and customs of the said Empire, and ours, which belong to us in the election of the Empire, by custom or by right; and that we shall not neglect this on account of any particular matter or persons, or any precept, mandate or process, by whomsoever and in whatever manner or form they have been or shall hereafter be issued, against the Empire and us or our fellow Electors; by which prejudice might be done, or might in future be caused, to the said Empire and to us and our fellow Electors in the aforesaid rights, goods, men, liberties and customs. Michael Coccinius, on the translation of the Empire from the Greeks to the Germans: But the Emperor holds the Empire from God, by the ministry of the election of the Electors of the Empire; the right of electing has come to certain German princes from Otto iii, with the consent of the Princes and of the people subject to the Empire. Nicholas of Cusa, On the Catholic Concordance book iii chapter iv, speaks of Otto iii: And this Emperor, with the consent of the chief Princes and of both the estate of the clergy and of the people, established perpetual Electors, who elected on behalf of all, in the time of Gregory v, the Germans, once kinsmen of Otto. It is not therefore to be conceded in that way, that the Electors have the power of electing from the Roman Pontiff, so that they would not have it unless he consented, or that he could take it from them if he wished. Who, I ask, gave the Roman people the power of electing an Emperor, except divine and natural law itself? And then: Whence the Electors, who were established in the time of the second Henry by the common consent of all the Germans and of the others who were subject to the Empire, have their radical force from the common consent of all, who could by natural law set up an Emperor for themselves; not from the Roman Pontiff himself, in whose power it is not to give to any province a King or Emperor through the world, the province not consenting. Nor does anything help Bellarmine's cause, on which however he founds his exception, that Cusanus says the consent of the Pontiff intervened; for Cusanus also refers the principal authority of this institution to the consent of all those who belong to the Empire, which Bellarmine neither denies of him nor proves; and Cusanus says that the consent of the Pontiff is here regarded as in the Diets, where the force of the decree depends not on the first of all Pontiffs himself, but on the common consent of all, both his and of others. And that opinion is very common which attributes the institution of the Electoral order in the Empire, not to Gregory v, but to Otto iii of Saxony, called, on account of his outstanding virtues, the wonder of the world. For this view there certainly stand very many authors, whom Joachim Cluten names: in his Miscellany of Everyday Matters §.24; Justus Sinolt, On the Vicars of the Empire, §.19; Antonius Kolerus, On the Law of the German Empire, thesis 45; Simon Schard, On the Election of the Emperor, chapter 11; the anonymous author, On the translation of the Empire, chapter VII, in Goldast's Politica Imperialia part IX. Add Michael Schiferer, On the origin and power of the modern Electors; Henry Bruningius, On the various kinds of universities, §.9; Elias Schedius, On the German Gods, page 23. But others think the college and office of Electors of the Empire was instituted long after Otto: among them, after Aventinus, who, speaking of the Electors in book v of his Annals, says: I hold that they were finally instituted after the death of Frederick II, and established by Gregory x; the chief is Onuphrius Panvinus of Verona, an Augustinian hermit, in his book On the Imperial Diets, which was first published at Basel in 1558, then with notes by Friedrich Hortleder, and which Goldast included in his Politica Imperialia at the beginning. That Onuphrius, chapter vi, after having said that it was false and absurd that the Electors were instituted under Otto iii by Gregory v, the Supreme Pontiff, a Saxon, for the favour of his nation, adds: that this is most false, and that they were brought into this order three hundred years later, after the death of the Emperor Frederick II, I will now demonstrate. That is, between the year 1250, when Frederick II died, and 1280, when Rudolf of Habsburg, after a long interregnum of twenty-three years, was created King of the Romans by the votes of the Electors, the others following him: yet (he says) in which year especially, or for what reasons, or by which Pontiff, or in which assembly of the German Princes, or in a general or provincial council, this was done, is still unknown to me. But nevertheless through these times, both the number of the Electors and also the particular acts of the same, are specifically mentioned by the writers of these or later times; and the names of each, together with the title of their dignity, are recounted. Thus he. Against him Simon Schard wrote another book on this matter, wishing the origin of the Electors to be older, and claiming for Otto iii the common opinion. This book, besides being in Goldast among the Politica Imperialia, is also read last in the Historical-Ecclesiastical Miscellany of various authors published by Schard himself. But indeed the arguments of this man, on the authority of Innocent and Hostiensis alone, as he himself puts it in chapter iv (...), cannot move me to believe that the order of Electors was instituted by Otto iii. Yet I do not therefore agree with Onuphrius that they were instituted about the time of Rudolf of Habsburg, nor on account of the argument which he presses hard against their Ottonian institution, from the silence of authors on this matter: for just as the origin of so illustrious and momentous an institution is not traced by the historians to the time of Otto, so nor to the time of Habsburg, both being silent; rather, I shall concede that after Otto, and especially after Frederick II, when the affairs of the Empire, under the pressure of internecine dissensions, required it, the election of the Emperor was no longer made by all the Estates and leading men of the Empire, as formerly, but by certain Princes only, and these perhaps not at first in a fixed number, nor always the same; yet gradually by fewer and more principal ones, the same ones, and to these add those to whom the electoral dignity was afterwards adjudged alone. Yet I shall not assert that by fixed law those were Electors, and seven, though by some custom, even an ancient one, they were; partly ecclesiastical, partly secular, who today, down to Charles iv, and to the Golden Bull promulgated by him at the Diet of Nuremberg in the year 1356, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, by which first of all the dignity and order of the Electors of the Empire is confirmed and established by perpetual law. I do not deny that before this time the name and the rank of the Electoral Princes was sufficiently known in the Empire, but that by a certain and perpetual and universal law of the Imperial institution those seven were long held to be the only Electors, as now, this I do not see. More or fewer, it is established, were present at the election of the Emperor in former times, at first many, then fewer. And after some principal Princes of the Empire had been brought to this business by long custom, not however (as it seems) by some law passed or made as an institution, but thus by practice, which necessity and the advantage of public peace suggested, arising without doubt from particular affairs and recesses, which ought to be investigated here, as they will bring much light, the law of the Golden Bull was made on that matter, and the order of these seven Electors was established or confirmed. The thing itself seemed rather to require that it should first be settled by custom, then by law. And in the Golden Bull, where the rules of the Electors are laid down, recourse is had to custom. Chapter I: and the Electoral Princes have been accustomed to set out for such an election according to the ancient laudable custom. Chapter IV, §.2: Moreover, as often as and whenever the holy Empire shall happen to be vacant, the Archbishop of Mainz shall have the power, as he is known from of old to have had the power, of summoning by letter the other aforesaid Princes, his partners in the said election. §.3: First of all he shall ask the Archbishop of Trier, to whom we declare the first vote belongs, as we have found he has hereditarily possessed. You see how he frames laws according to ancient custom and observance. Chapter V, §.3: And although the Emperor or King of the Romans, on account of causes by which he may have been hindered, is said by custom introduced to be bound to answer before the Count Palatine of the Rhine, Archdapifer of the holy Empire, the Elector Prince. Thus it is clear that those Princes were Electors even before, and observed many things that are here laid down from custom, which afterwards are decreed to be observed by law and by the common senatorial decree of the Diets. Marquard Freher, Origins of the Palatinate part 1 chapter xv, after saying that the Empire, after having been for some time hereditary in the Carolingian line, when that line failed returned again to election: The Princes, however, elected, says he, those whom Germany had in many and various kinds, and among these also the Prelates, and without distinction, as many as wished to be present at the Diets. Yet the first place was usually held by the more powerful and those who had served in offices at court. He inclines, however, to the opinion on the Ottonian institution of the Electors, neither to that of Onuphrius nor to that which makes Charles iv their founder. Although it may well be said, without any prejudice, that many Princes, and among them the Palatine, possessed electoral power from the earliest times, though not yet by any fixed law. As chapter xvi explains what is said in chapter v of the Golden Bull about custom, namely ancient usage. Johann Joachim von Rusdorf, in Vindiciae Palatinae chapter III: Grant indeed that the Electorate was from of old, and before Charles iv the Emperor, attached to the Duchy of Bavaria and not to the Palatinate of the Rhine; grant also that there was at one time an alternation between the Palatines and the Bavarians, agreed upon and practised; what then? Was not each of these in that rude age, when the offices, dignities and functions of the Seven, when their successions, grades, prerogatives, order, regalia, and the principalities assigned and granted in fief, were not yet distinguished and established by laws and fixed prescriptions? Afterwards, through the Golden Bull, the Emperors and Estates of that age, having learned how much division and dissension among them harmed the commonwealth, by common consent prescribed a certain order in succession and possession, assigning to each Elector his own rank, right and office, and declaring and making by a law destined to remain in force forever which lands ought to be annexed to the Electoral dignity, as has been received in practice. So altogether I am willing that those things which indeed obtained in the election of the Emperor, but from practice, were at last confirmed and established by the law of the Golden Bull. Onuphrius, from whose opinion and reckoning we do not very far depart, except that the law which he conceives eighty years before the Golden Bull he does not find, while we make none, and in its place we put a custom from which a law spontaneously followed, chapter ix, speaks thus on this matter:

units.la: Quare facile fuit, ut eo potissimum tempore, quo res Imperii civilibus discordiis affiictissima erant, jus eligendi Imperatorem à cateris Principibus, ad VII hos Electores tantum transferretur, hæcque institutio exorta sit. Quam postea, quum adhuc nova & mutans esset, Carolus IV. Imp. reformavit, stabilivit, atque in aureTam bullam redegit. Iustus Gebhardus in Discursu, de S. Rom. nationis Germ. Imperio, (editus una cum aliis à Nicolao Hampelio, in Nucleo Discursuum, seu Disputationum in jus Publicum, Giessæ a. clɔ lxxxi) th. 49. inquit: Electoralis Collegii Auctorem si quaeras, & de moderna septemviratus constitutione investigationem si instituas, vix alium cum Beutero monstraverim, quam aureæ Bullæ conditorem Carolum IV. qui solus numerum septenarium primusque sic absolvit, ut essent tres Ecclesiastici, & quatuor politici. Nobilcu facit Ant. Colerus, de jure Imp. Germanici §. 47. 48. nec enim absurdum mihi videor, si Electores sensim cepisse: consuetudine vero jus certum familiis acquisitum, per Carolum IV. confirmatum dicam plenissime. Sic & Dresserus, quem eo loco adducit. Bernhardus Bertramus, de Comitiis Imperii Romano-Germanici, §. XXIX. Mihi hæc, quam & alibi defendi, stat sententia; occultis initiis, & non injuria publici boni imitatu annuentibus cateris Principibus aliquot annorum inter jectu, intra sanctius & strictius consilium Electores jus suum revocasse, præeuntibus Dresslero, Heigio, Paurmeistero & aliis. Rationes, quibus, persuadeor, habeo praegnantes. Sed hic omissas alio loco latius exponam. Iohannes Nordermannus, de jure Principatus §.19.84. Probabilius est ab Ottone III. jus eligendi Imperatorem ad Principes omnes esse translatum, qui postmodum ad septenarium numerum redacti. Iohannes Limnæus, de jure publico Imp. Rom. lib. III. cap. 1. cujus est quod in Republ. sive Statu Imperii Romano-Germanici Tom. II. pag. 127. legitur, de Electorum Imperii Institutione, nonnullis rationibus de nonstratum it: Collegium] Electorale, non tam speciali & expressa alicujus constitutione, quam consuetudine sensim Ordinum consensu approbata introductum, postque aliquot mutationes intervenientes, tandem à Carolo IV. & reliquis Imperii Proceribus, Aurea Bulla formatum fuisse. Benedictus Carpzovius, ad L. Regiam German. cap. x. sect. v. Hos nostræ circa originem Electorum in Imperio sententiæ deprehendi, ut non audiri ultra debeant Papani vel Papæ, quando sibi illorum institutionem temere arrogant. Quemadmodum nec in nupera sancienda pace hoc ullatenus curarunt Imperii Principes, dum de numero Electorum, non consulto Papa, disposuerunt, prout ipsis visum, eoque licet indignante & vehementer etiam fremente, cujus vanam opinionem & arrogantiam sic optime exploserunt, & quomodo nos redarguere & confundere eam debeamus, hoc argumento peremtorio docuerunt.
units.tr: Therefore it was easy that, at that very time when the affairs of the Empire were most afflicted by civil discord, the right of electing the Emperor was transferred from the other princes to these seven electors alone, and this institution arose. Afterwards, while it was still new and changing, Emperor Charles IV reformed it, established it, and reduced it to the Golden Bull. Justus Gebhardus, in his Discourse on the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation (published together with others by Nicolaus Hampelius in the Nucleus of Discourses, or Disputations on Public Law, Giessen, 1681), thesis 49, says: If you ask who was the author of the electoral college, and if you undertake an inquiry into the modern constitution of the seven electors, I could hardly point to anyone other than Charles IV, the author of the Golden Bull, who alone, along with Beuter, first completed the number seven in such a way that there were three ecclesiastical and four secular electors. Antonius Colerus agrees with us in his work on the law of the German Emperor, §§ 47–48: For I do not think it absurd that the electors gradually took up the office; but I would say that the right, acquired by custom and fixed for these families, was most fully confirmed by Charles IV. Dresserus, whom he cites in that place, is of the same mind. Bernhard Bertram, on the Diets of the Roman-German Empire, §29: My view, which I have defended elsewhere, is this: in obscure beginnings, and not unjustly, with the other princes assenting for the sake of the common good after an interval of some years, the electors reclaimed their right within a more sacred and restricted council, following Dressler, Heigius, Paurmeister and others. The reasons by which I am persuaded are weighty; but since I have left them out here, I will set them out more fully in another place. Johannes Nordermannus, on the right of princely power, §§19 and 84: It is more probable that the right of electing the Emperor was transferred by Otto III to all the princes, who were afterwards reduced to the number seven. Johannes Limnaeus, on public law of the Holy Roman Empire, book III, chapter 1, whose statement in On the Republic or State of the Roman-German Empire, vol. II, p. 127, on the institution of the electors, supported by several arguments, is as follows: the electoral college was introduced not so much by any special and express constitution as by custom gradually approved by the consent of the estates, and after some changes intervened, it was at last framed in the Golden Bull by Charles IV and the other nobles of the Empire. Benedict Carpzov, on the Lex Regia of Germany, chapter 10, section 5. I have found these opinions of ours on the origin of the electors in the Empire, so that the Papists or the Pope should no longer be heard when they rashly claim their institution for themselves. Likewise, in the recent making of peace, the princes of the Empire took no care of this at all: they settled the number of electors without consulting the Pope, as seemed fit to them, and although he was indignant and raged vehemently, they thoroughly exploded his vain opinion and arrogance, and by this decisive argument showed how we ought to refute and confound it.

units.la: Octavus, inquit Papa, Electoratus in favorem Caroli Ludovici Comitis Palatini Rheni hereticí institutitur. Itane hereticí ex lensu Papæ: id est, revera religiosissimi, & bene orthodoxi. ΑΣ ΑΛΛΟΙ ΝΕ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΙΣ III Cor. vi. 8. Scilicet hæc in Papis morum est civilitas & modestia, Celsissimum Principem ista insignire & in hujus quidè negotii argumento, nomenclatura, tam solita ferri constanter & gloriosè in modum ab illustrissima domo Palatinâ, ac à Papis in optimos quosque Principes excrari. Scilicet ita etiam docuerant Papani, statim à defectione, Principem Eduardum, Palatinum Comitem, in litteris ad fratrem hunc suum Electorem Serenissimum Carolum Ludovicum scribere a. cIↄ Iↄ cxlv. d.x. Novembris, quando mutate turpiter religionis causam tralatitie exponens, fratrem Electorē hereticis indecenter accensebat Rom. xv. 3. Convitia ceeorum, qui convitiantur tibi, inciderunt in me. Et sic oportet nos sustinere ὑπομονὴν Christi, quem Moses tantas opes æstimabat, ut omnibus Ægypti thesauris longe præponeret. Heb. xi.26. Neque aliter Palatini Electores, qui quam bene cum isto Mosis exemplo à nobis conferantur, ipsi Orbem hactenus exemplo satis suo docuerunt.
units.tr: The eighth electorate, says the Pope, was instituted in favour of Charles Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine, a heretic. Are they heretics, then, in the Pope's sense? That is, in truth most religious and thoroughly orthodox. [ΑΣ ΑΛΛΟΙ ΝΕ ΑΛΛΗΛΟΙΣ] (2 Cor. 6:8, as deceivers and yet true, as printed: III Cor. vi. 8.) Of course this is the civility and moderation of the Papists: to brand a most serene prince in this way; and, as proof of this matter, the name is constantly and gloriously borne by the illustrious house of the Palatinate, while the Papists hurl it against all the best princes. Thus indeed the Papists had taught immediately after the defection: Prince Eduard, Count Palatine, writing to his brother, the most serene Elector Charles Louis, on 10 November 1645, when he had shamefully changed sides and was explaining the cause of religion in the usual way, indecently called his brother Elector a heretic. Romans 15:3: The reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me. And so we must endure the patience of Christ, whom Moses esteemed greater riches than all the treasures of Egypt (Heb. 11:26). Nor have the Palatine electors done otherwise; how well they may be compared with that example of Moses, they themselves have hitherto shown the whole world by their own example.

units.la: Electoratus octavus in favorem Caroli Ludovici) Quorum fuit Electores primò instituere, & tali ordine ac numero scribere, quod Principum Imperii fuisse jam ostensum est, eorundem manet de illis disponere, & vel contrahere numerum vel ampliare, prout vilum necessitates Imperii exigere. Aurea Bulla septem facit Electores, sed ut illa ad unitatem inter Electores tenendam, & detestanda divisioni variisque periculis ex ea sequentibus aditum praeludendum, (quemadmodum in præfatione ejus loquitur Imperator) sic constituit, ita propter eandem similesque causas quin potest as perpetua sit Imperii Proceribus vel octavum addere Electoratum, aliove modo res ordinare, non rogato unquam vel audito Papa, quis ambigat? In Instrumento Pacis nostræ, ubi de octavo constituendo Electoratu, Imperator cum Imperio dicitur in eum consentire, nullius ultra facta mentione. Extincta linea Guilielmiana masculina Bavarica, ad superstites Palatinos redibit Electoralis dignitas, octavo tunc electoratu prorsus extinguendo. Et quidem Palatinus Electoratus, in ordine Electorum Secularium, post Regem Bohemiæ, ex antiquo jure, secundus, non debuit non servari, ut cui familiæ Electoralis dignitas infixa semper hæsit. Otho der erst Pfaltzgraff bey Rhein/ Der Pfaltzgraff Henrichs techterlein/ Mit mannheit ers also erslecht/ Des Reichs Churbleib seinem geslecht.
units.tr: The eighth electorate in favour of Charles Louis. It belongs to those who first established the electors, and in such order and number as has already been shown belongs to the princes of the Empire, that it remains for them to dispose of them, and either to reduce or to enlarge their number, as the needs of the Empire seem to require. The Golden Bull makes seven electors, but, as the Emperor says in its preface, it did so to keep unity among the electors and to forestall the detestable division and the various dangers that follow from it. For the same and similar reasons the princes of the Empire may, and indeed always could, add an eighth electorate or arrange matters otherwise, without ever asking or hearing the Pope. Who can doubt it? In our Treaty of Peace, where the establishment of an eighth electorate is mentioned, it is said that the Emperor, with the Empire, consented to it, with no further mention of anyone. When the Bavarian male line of William is extinct, the electoral dignity will return to the surviving Palatines, the eighth electorate then being wholly abolished. And indeed the Palatine electorate, second after the King of Bohemia in the order of the secular electors by ancient right, ought not to be overlooked, since the electoral dignity has always clung fixedly to that family. Otto, the first Palatine on the Rhine, the daughter of the Palatine Henry: by his manhood he thus obtained it; the electorate of the Empire remained to his line.

units.la: Quos versus Nauclerus, & Freherus Orig. Palatin. pag. 98. adducunt. Nempe Otto Bavariæ Dux, a. clo ccxxvi. alii clxccxv. ducta in uxorem Henrici ultimi Palatini Rheni filia, non Gertruda, sed Agnete (quo conjugio in unum coiere illustrissimæ in Germania familiæ Palatina & Bavarica) cū Palatinatu, etiam Electoriam dignitatem, isti annexam, dotalem obtinuit, inque domum Bavaricam primus intulit. Unde Palatinum nomen Ducali adeo semper præponere consueti Bavariæ Duces, aliique, eo quod Palatinatui Electoria dignitas, quæque eam sequuntur, Vicariatus & Archidapiferia per se annexa sint, ut etiam in Instrumento jam Pacis ubi Maximiliano Bavariæ Duci Electoratus adscribitur, ordo is quoque servetur: maneant penes Dominum Maximilianum, Comitem Palatinum Rheni, Bavariæ Ducem. Cumque haud diu ante tempora Caroli IV. his circa electionem Imperatoris inter Principes suboriretur, inter Ottocarum Bohemiæ Regem Electorem, & Henricum ducem Bavariæ, una cum fratre suo Ludovico Comite Palatino; tum inter Rudolph. & Ludovicum, Fratres, Comites Palatinos, Carolus IV. omissis Ludovici Bavari Imp. filiis, Electoratum in Rudolpho agnovit, ejusque stemmate, propter comitatum Palatinum, cui ille annexus sit. Unde a. MCCCLIV. biennio ante factam auream Bullam, Oppenheimio ad Electores Imperii scripsit, Rudolphi istius filium Rupertum, verum Electorem esse; memoratque ibidem visas sibi fuisse genitoris sui Iohannis, Bohemiæ Regis, litteras, expresse continentes, quod felicis rec. Illustris Rudolphus, olim Comes Palatinus Rheni & Dux Bavariæ &c. ratione dicti Comitatus Imperii esset Elector. Atque a. MCCCLVI. eadem de causa iterum, Norinbergæ scripsit: Rupertum Comitem Palatinum esse in possessione juris eligendi, & Electoratus ac Archidapiferi dignitatem Palatinatui esse annexam indissolubili connexione; ita ut quicunque de Electoris gradu quæstionem moveret, eidem onus probandi incumberet, si jus ad Palatinatum & Archidapiferatum habere: Ita testatur Carolus Cæsar tunc Rex Bohemiæ Sac. Rom. Imp. Archipincerna & Coelector, addens cateros quoque Coelectores idem secum sentire & profiteri. Norinbergæ Anno Domini MCCCLVI. quinta feria post Epiphaniam Domini. Atque hinc illa sunt in Aurea Bulla, pro Elector Palatino, & succedentibus in Electoratum familiæ istius primogenitis, Cap. VII. ut salubris semper unio inter sacri Imperii Principes Electores jugiter vigeat, & eorum corda in syncera concordia conferventur. primum constituit cum Electoribus Ecclesiasticis, hos quatuor seculares, illustres Reges Bohemiae, Comitem Palatinum Rheni, Ducem Saxoniae, & Marchionem Brandenburgensem, virtute Regni, & Principatuum suorum, in electione Regis Romanorum, in Caesarem promovendi, cum ceteris Principibus Electoribus, jus, vocem, & locum habere, & una cum ipsis censeri, & esse veros & legitimos sacri imperii Principes Electores.
units.tr: Naucler and Freher, Origines Palatinae, p. 98, cite these verses. Namely, Otto, Duke of Bavaria, in the year 1226 (others say 1215), married not Gertrude but Agnes, daughter of Henry, the last Palatine of the Rhine (by which marriage the illustrious Palatine and Bavarian houses in Germany came together into one), and obtained as her dowry the Palatinate together with the electoral dignity attached to it, and was the first to bring it into the Bavarian house. Hence the Dukes of Bavaria and others have always been accustomed to put the name Palatine before the ducal title, because the electoral dignity of the Palatinate, and the offices that follow it, the vicariate and the arch-cupbearer's office, are attached to it in such a way that even in the treaty of peace, where the electorate is assigned to Maximilian, Duke of Bavaria, this order is kept: let them remain with Lord Maximilian, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria. And when, not long before the time of Charles IV, disputes arose among the princes about the election of the Emperor, between Ottokar, King of Bohemia, an elector, and Henry, Duke of Bavaria, together with his brother Louis, Count Palatine; and then between Rudolph and Louis, brothers and Counts Palatine, Charles IV, passing over the sons of Louis the Bavarian Emperor, acknowledged the electorate in Rudolph and in his stock, on account of the county Palatine to which it was attached. Hence in 1354, two years before the Golden Bull was made, he wrote to the electors of the Empire at Oppenheim that Rupert, the son of this Rudolph, was the true elector; and he related there that he had seen letters of his father John, King of Bohemia, expressly stating that the felicitous and illustrious Rudolph, formerly Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, etc., was elector by reason of the said county of the Empire. And in 1356, again for the same reason, he wrote at Nuremberg: that Count Rupert is in possession of the right of election, and that the electorate and the dignity of arch-cupbearer are attached to the Palatinate by an indissoluble bond; so that whoever should raise a question about the rank of elector would bear the burden of proving that he had a right to the Palatinate and the arch-cupbearership. So testifies Charles Caesar, then King of Bohemia, Holy Roman Emperor, arch-cupbearer and co-elector, adding that the other co-electors also think and profess the same. Given at Nuremberg in the year of the Lord 1356, on the Thursday after the Epiphany of the Lord. Hence come those provisions in the Golden Bull for the Elector Palatine and for the eldest sons of that family who succeed to the electorate, chapter 7, so that a wholesome unity may always flourish among the electors of the holy Empire, and their hearts may be preserved in sincere concord. It first establishes that with the ecclesiastical electors these four secular electors, the illustrious kings of Bohemia, the Count Palatine of the Rhine, the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg, by virtue of their kingdom and principalities, shall have the right, voice and place in the election of the King of the Romans, to be promoted to Caesar, together with the other princes-electors, and shall be counted together with them, and be true and lawful princes-electors of the holy Empire.

units.la: Inde, quod ad successionem Electorum. Ne inter eorundem Principum secularium Electorum filios super jure, voce, & potestate praefata, futuris temporibus scandalorum & dissensionum possit materia suscitari, & sic bonum commune periculosis dilationibus impediri, futuris, auctore Deo, cupientes periculis salubriter obviare, statuimus, & Imperiali auctoritate praesenti lege perpetuis temporibus valitura decernimus, ut postquam iidem Principes Electores seculares, & eorum quilibet esse desierint, jus, vox, & potestas electionis hujusmodi ad filium suum primogenitum legitimum laicum, illo vero non existente ad ejusdem primogenitum similiter laicum, & sine contradictione cujuspiam devolvatur. Si vero primogenitus hujusmodi absque haeredibus masculinis legitimis laicis, ab hac luce migraret, virtute praesentis Imperialis edicti, jus, vox, & potestas Electionis praedictae, ad seniorem fratrem laicum per veram paternam lineam descendentem, & deinceps ad illius primogenitum laicum devolvatur, & aliis successio in primogenitis & haeredibus Principum eorundem iure, voce, & potestate praemissis, perpetuis temporibus observetur.
units.tr: As to the succession of the Electors: so that no matter for scandal and dissension may arise in future times among the sons of the same secular Electoral Princes concerning the aforesaid right, vote and power, and so that the common good is not hindered by dangerous delays, we, desiring with God's help to meet such dangers beneficially in future, have decreed and by imperial authority establish by this present law, to remain valid in perpetuity, that once these same secular Princes Electors, or any one of them, have ceased to be, the right, vote and power of election of this kind shall pass without contradiction from anyone to their eldest legitimate lay son, and, if he does not exist, to the eldest similarly lay son of the same. But if such an eldest son should depart this life without legitimate lay male heirs, then by virtue of this present imperial edict the aforesaid right, vote and power of election shall pass to the elder lay brother descended in the true paternal line, and thereafter to his eldest lay son; and the succession to the eldest sons and heirs of the same Princes, with the aforesaid right, vote and power, shall be observed in perpetuity.

units.la: Ergo Comiti Palatino, ejusque familiae Promogenitis Principibus Electoratus, vi fundamentalis istius in Aurea Bulla constitutionis debetur, quae[?] favere Palatinatui, & Electoratum ei addicere, non negant quoque ipsi Bavarici, utcumque in causa Electoratus, quem volunt Ducatui Bavariae, non Comitatui Palatino, annexum, adversarii. Ioh. Adelzreiter, Consiliarius Bavaricus, in Refutatione Vindiciarum Causa Palatina. pag. 336. 340. Quæ qualiaque hac in parte scripta, jam ab a.clɔ lɔcxxı prodierunt, inter Consiliarios Palatinos, & Bavaricos, primo inter Marquardum Frecherum, & Christophorum Gewoldum, illum Palatinum, hunc Bavaricum consiliarium. Utriusque argumenta summatim exhibet Ioh. Limnæus, Ienensis, Tom. I. Disput de jure publico Imp. Rom. lib. III. cap. IX. quæ descripta in Rep. Germaniæ part. II. pag. 177. Inde a. clɔ lɔcxxxix. & annis proxime sequentibus, Manifestis, AntiManifestis, Manifestationibus, Anti-Manifestationibus, hinc à Ioh. Ioachimo Rusdorfio, pro Palatinis, item Ioh. Conrado Blarer; ex adverso pro Bavaris, à Nicolao Burgundo, tum Iohanne Adelzreiter, aliisque pugnatum ut sit, orbi satis notum. Sed pugna hæc chartacea nitebatur, sed alia violenta magis armataqui, qua detrusis loco Palatinis, in Electoratum, reclamantibus quamvis Saxone, & Brandenburgico, Electoribus, etiam Lantgravio Hassiæ, & Principe Wolfgango Wilhelmo Duce Neoburgico, & Duce Brunvicensi, iurrogabatur ab Imp. Ferdinando II. Maximilianus Dux Bavariæ. Quam novam investituram utpote vi tutam, scriptis oppugnare, quam evertere, facilius fuit. Certe si, quemadmodum Bavari amabant disputare, sequatur, Electoratum, qui ad Bavariæ Principes spectabat, inde non potuisse avelli; indubitatæ veritatis fuit, quia juxta Aureæ Bullæ διαπτυξιν decisionem, Electoratus ad Domum spectat Palatinam, non Bavaricam, inde non debuisse abstrahi. Atque ultra centena argumenta, sive ex rationibus, jure, exemplis protulerunt Palatini, pro sua domo, ejusque annexo Electoratu, quæ in compendium contraxit, atque exhibuit Conradus Blarer, Electoratus Palatini part. III. pag. 9. 36. etiam ex testimoniis Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Romanistarum, ipsiusque Cardinalis Bellarmini, qui in libro de Translatione Imperii part. III. agens de Electorum Imp. institutione, Palatinam domum, non Bavaricam, pro Electorali habuit. Atque in istius primogenitis fundata Electoratus successio fuit: ut adversus Carolum Ludovicum Palatinum Principem nihil omnino sit, quod objici ab aliquo possit. Adde Bullam Sigismundi Imp. de jure & successione Electorum Palatinorum, convenientem cum Aurea Bulla, apud Melch. Goldastum, Constitut. Imperial. pag. 143. tum Dissertationem, de Successione in Electoratibus ex jure Primogenitura, Arnoldi Engelbrechti, inter Collectanea Discursuum Hampelii. Caeterum quo consilio, & sine Papa urserit, obtinueritque Electoratus Palatini, pridem a. cIↄ Iↄcxxii. d. xxv. Februarii à Friderico, Bohemorum Rege, in Maximilianum Bavarum translationem, nempe tum ut ἰσοκαθμίων inter Electores, oppositis ad tres Clericales Pontificios æquo numero aliis sæcularibus Protestantibus subversum iret, tum ut erutum religionis Reformatæ in Germania asylum Palatinatum, & aliis quaBelgis, qua Gallis, rerum suarum, ubi id tempora exegerunt, magnum fulcimentum, cui quid non, dum fere omnia, debemus? obtentâ etiam authoritatis Papalis hac occasione in Electorale Collegium praetensa potestate, dum hunc ejici curat, ille petitum venit Electoralis dignitatis à Papa confirmationem, ne alia addam, omnibus nimis quam nota, & ipsi satis prodidere Papales; primum in litteris interceptis a. cIↄ Iↄc xxi, Cardinalis Ludovisii, Comitis Ognatensis, Balthasaris Zuniga, aliorumque: tum Guiljelmus Germæus, de Lamormaini lesuita Ferdinando ii à sacris & Confessionibus, in lib. de Ferdinand. ii. Romanorum Imp. virtutibus: Carolus Caraffa, Episcopus Averlanus, duorum Pontificum Gregorii xv. & Vrbani viii. in aula Caesarea Nuncius, lib. Germania sacra restaurata; ex quibus in hanc rem excerpta protulit in Vindiciis Palatinis, cap. xxxv. & seq. Ioachimus à Rusdorf. Michael Lonigus, praefectus Vaticani, Gregorio xv. consilium offerens de persuadendo Maximiliano Bavaro, ut Electoratus obtenti confirmationem peteret (quod & fecit) à Papa; sic illud inchoat: Beatissime Pater, Maximum ad „Romanam Ecclesiam emolumentum accederet, & ingenti „gloriæ decore Sanctitas Vestra felicissimum Pontificatum „ubi à Deo creditum cumularet, si Bojorum Dux, nuper ad Electoratus Imperialis dignitatem evectus, in illam sententiam pelliceretur, ut ab Sedis Apostolicæ auctoritate hunc sibi titulum confirmari expostularet. Hoc enim uno obtento tantum in præsentia Beatitudo Vestra lucrifaceret, quantum ne ducentorum quidem annorum curriculo ab superioribus Pontificibus acquisitum fuit; aut potius, ut verius loquar, rursum illud vindicaret, atque redimeret, quod à Gregorii XI. temporibus ad hæc usque nostra de juribus, quæ in constituendis rebus, & ordinibus Imperii ad Ecclesiam attinebant, ceteri amiserunt. Ipse agnoscit, hoc à ducentis annis ab Imperio vel Electoratu Paparum neminem obtinere potuisse, quod neq; unquam debuisset, adeo faciens contra jura & splendorem Imperii, atq; Illustrissimi Collegii Electoralis. Et in Aphorismis, de Statu Ecclesiæ restaurando, Romano Papalis scilicet, ex decreto & approbatione Collegii Cardinalium, exhibitis P. Gregorio XV. per eundem istum Lonigum, probatur evidenter, hinc dilatandæ Pontificiæ usurpationis causa, inde ad ejiciendos (si fieri posset) Imperio & Electorali Collegio Protestantes omnes, & non unum Palatinum, sed propter eandem causam, Saxonem quoque & Brandenburgicum, qui expresse eum in finem designantur, actitata illa adversus Palatinum fuisse, quæ adscribemus, ut patet tum ex qua sede funesta illa consilia orta fuerint, Papali nimirum, tum quid in eo spectarint, nempe Palatini, & cum eo reliquorum Protestantium extremam internecionem. Aphrismo quinto: Cum Leo III illam potestatem habuerit, propter hæresi ostrimen Orientale imperium ab Occidentali abscindere, & divellere, ac ex Græcorum manibus eripere, & ad Gallos transmittere: quare non Pontifex maximus eandem potestatem habebit, Electoratum à Palatinato, ut principalis hæresiarcha, abripere, & in Bojorum ducem, ut obedientissimum filium Ecclesiæ transferre? Ex eodem falso ac inani principio, translati per Leonem P. Imperii (Imp. Fridericus I. a. MDCLVII.) quicunque nos Imperialem coronam pro beneficio à Domino Papa suscepisse dixerit, divina institutioni & doctrina Petri contrarius est, & mendacii reus erit)Lonigus iterum. Aphorismo vii. Ita Electoralis dignitatis in Bojorum ducem Catholicissimum transmissionem sagacitas & oppositio resistantis haeresiarchae Saxonis non impedire, multo minus impugnare potest, quia juribus & privilegiis imperii, ut haereticus, sanctitatem & antiquitatem fontalis originis imperii non agnoscens, de jure frui non potest: Aphor. viii. Si haec ita, ut revera sunt, tunc Pontifex summus cum sancta Liga omnes vires contra haeresiarcham Saxonem & ab illo dependentes rebelles adhibere tenetur, ut sanctitas sedis Apostolicae, & antiquitas Imperii Romani, in translatione Electoralis dignitatis conservari possit. Aphor ix. Post Leonem alii quoque Pontifices sola sedis auctoritate illud idem imperium Occidentale sape ab una ad aliam transtulerunt nationem: quare non eadem Sedis auctoritate Pontifex maximus, & Electorales dignitates ex manibus haereticorum eripere, & ad Catholicos principes transmittere poterit, ut facies imperii Romani Sancta rursum in haereticis extirpandis firmetur. Aphor. x. Ita Pontifex maximus, Imperator, & Sancta Liga, absque violatione Sedis Apostolicae, qua sancta semper in antiquitate conservanda tueri debet, Saxoni & Brandenburgico non permittere possunt, qui auctoritatem antiquitatis in transferendo Electoratu a Sede Romana divellere, & ad collegium Electorum pertrahere tentant. Aphor. xxvii. Cum translatio Electoralis dignitatis in Bojorum ducem Maximilianum facta, jam a beatissimo Patre confirmata sit: ideo penes Imperatorem, aut Regem Hispaniarum, non amplius stat, Palatinum haeresiarcham, vel haeredes Comitis Palatini, in distonem, de qua parens est dejectus, vel in Electoratum reponere. Nam hac controversia ad beatissimam sedem Apostolicam, non ad Imperatorem, vel Regem Hispaniarum pertinent. Aphor. xxviii. Cum translationem Electoratus Pontifex summus confirmaverit: ideo Reges Angliae, Daniae, Suxo, & Brandenburgicus, restitutionem Palatini in distones & Electoratum inique ab Imperatore postulant. Nam nihil aliud est hoc petere, quam sedem Apostolicam de jure suo Majestatis sue deturbare, & fontalem originem contra antiquitatem & sanctitatem Ecclesiae, & imperii, Imperatori adjudicare. Ex quibus omnibus haec tria sole contra clarius elucent ac sequuntur 1. Propriam & Primam causam eripi Palatino pridie Electoraa€storatus fuisse Papalibus non aliam, quam religionis. II. Idem ab iisdem intentari reliquis Protestantibus Imperii Principibus, Electoribus ipsis, nominatim Ducibus Saxonicis & Brandeburgicis: haberique illis ipsorum Electoratus nullos, quia scilicet non sint à Papa confirmati. Aperte quoqj eundem animum prodidit Thomas Campanella, lib. de Monarchia Hispaniæ, cap. v. ubi inquit: res ipsa postulat, ut Rex Hispan. eo omnes vires suas intendat, quo illud Imperium in potestatem suam redigat? Hoc ut fiat, agendum ipsi est cum Papa ut maledictione devoveat hæreticos, tres Electores protestantes. comminando, ni ad Ecclesiam Romanam redeant, se illos Electorali dignitate, quam ab ipso Papa acceperunt, rursus exuturum; & cum jam asseverent, papam esse Antichristum, convincentur suis verbis se ipsos Antichristianos esse; atque ideo ipsis ultro dignitatem illam esse deponendam, si Catholicam fidem recipere nolint. Quo fine Galli, Itali, & Hispania, conciliante Papa, conjunctim contra illos conspirare debent, (quod sane plurimum adjumenti ad hanc rem adferret) illorumque subjugatorum sectas funditus eradicare, novasque colonias in illorum locum mittere. Aliud eodem libro cap. xxiii. habet, quod quoque concernit Electores, & Principes Protestantes, in Germania: Adhibenda vero etiam summa opera est ut spargantur perpetua discordiæ semina inter Marchionem Brandenburgicum, Landgravium Hassia, Ducem Saxoniæ, Brunsvigæ, Palatinum ad Rhenum, Ducem item VVirtebergensem, & minutas illas respublicas Germaniæ: quod facile fieri potest, si præeminentia quastio ipsis moveatur, quod respublicas semper suspensas tenuit. Quæ omnia sane expergiscere jubet Protestantes, atque intendere assiduis Papapum adversum ipsos molitionibus, & insidiis. Henricus Vendramenus, Controv. Venet. ii. pag. 31: Nisi viderentur Pontifices summam Principum secularium auctoritatem aspirare, non esset cur tantopere omnes Principes sibi timendum esse putarent. iii. Nullos in Imperio, jurium & dignitatum Imperii vindices esse æque probos ac constantes, quam Principes Protestantes. Sed hoc nim. adeo dolet Papæ, se neutiquam auditum fuisse in condendo octavo Imperii Electoratu, & quidem in favorem, uti ait, Comitis Palatini, revera Ducis Bavarici. Nam & hic locum habet, quod scripsit Fridericus III Imp. a. cIↄ cccclxliv. ad P. Eugenium IV. de regnis legitimo hæredi non auferendis, aut in alium transferendis; pro Ladislao Hungariæ Rege, puero, quæ apud Goldastum legitur epistola, Constit. Imperial. Tom. III. pag. 477. Sic jam in fumū abiit consilium istud Cardinalium, & Lonigi, P. Gregorio XV. pridem in caula Bavarica exhibitum: & aliter hæc intelligenda esse, nimirum Imperii, non Paparum esse de Electoratibus disponere, ipso, eoque illustri, facto Imperator, & Principes ostenderunt.
units.tr: Therefore the Count Palatine, and the first-born princes of his family, are owed the electorate by virtue of the fundamental provision in the Golden Bull. Even the Bavarians, who favour the Palatinate in this respect, do not deny this, though in the question of the electorate they, who want it annexed to the Duchy of Bavaria and not to the County Palatine, are opponents. Johann Adelzreiter, Bavarian councillor, in Refutation of the Vindication of the Palatine Cause, pp. 336, 340. The writings on this point that have appeared since the year 1621 were produced between the Palatine councillors and the Bavarian councillors, first between Marquard Freher, the Palatine councillor, and Christoph Gewold, the Bavarian councillor. Johann Limnaeus of Jena gives a summary of both sides' arguments in Tom. I, Disputation on the Public Law of the Holy Roman Empire, book III, chapter IX, which is reproduced in the Report on Germany, part II, p. 177. From the year 1619 and the following years, Manifestos, Anti-Manifestos, Manifestations, Anti-Manifestations, were fought over, on the Palatine side by Johann Joachim Rusdorf and likewise Johann Conrad Blarer, and on the opposing side for the Bavarians by Nicolaus Burgundus, then Johann Adelzreiter and others. The world knows this well enough. But this war of paper rested on paper, and another, more violent and armed war followed, by which the Palatines were thrust from their place. Although the Saxon and Brandenburg electors protested, as did the Landgrave of Hesse, Prince Wolfgang Wilhelm, Duke of Neuburg, and the Duke of Brunswick, Maximilian, Duke of Bavaria, was granted the electorate by Emperor Ferdinand II. It was easier to attack this new investiture in writing, since it was secured by force, than to overturn it. Certainly, if (as the Bavarians liked to argue) the electorate, which belonged to the princes of Bavaria, could not thereby have been torn away, it was an indubitable truth that, according to the decision of the Golden Bull's διαπτυξις, the electorate belongs to the Palatine house and not the Bavarian, and so it ought not to have been taken away. And the Palatines brought forward more than a hundred arguments, drawn from reasons, law and examples, for their house and its annexed electorate. Conrad Blarer gathered these together and set them out in summary in Electorate of the Palatinate, part III, pp. 9, 36. They also drew on the testimony of the Roman Church, of the Romanists, and of Cardinal Bellarmine himself, who in On the Translation of the Empire, part III, discussing the institution of the Electors of the Empire, held the Palatine house, not the Bavarian, to be electoral. And the succession to the electorate was founded on the first-born of that house, so that there is nothing at all that anyone can object against Prince Charles Louis, the Palatine. Add the Bull of Emperor Sigismund on the right and succession of the Palatine Electors, agreeing with the Golden Bull, in Melchior Goldast, Imperial Constitutions, p. 143; and the dissertation On Succession in the Electorates by the Right of Primogeniture by Arnold Engelbrecht, among the Collected Discourses of Hampelius. Moreover, with what purpose, and without the Pope, the Palatine electorate was obtained and transferred to Maximilian of Bavaria, long ago, on 25 February 1622, by Frederick, King of Bohemia, is clear. It was done, first, so that the balance among the electors, which had been secured by the opposition of three Catholic Papist clerical electors to an equal number of secular Protestant electors, would be overturned; and second, so that the Palatinate, the refuge of the Reformed religion in Germany that had been rescued, and a great prop to our affairs (to the Belgians and to the French, and to us, where times demanded it), would be destroyed. Our debt to it is almost total. With the papal power over the Electoral College claimed on this occasion, the Papalists themselves have revealed well enough, and everyone knows too well, that the Palatinate's electoral dignity was sought for confirmation from the Pope, while they took care to eject him. I will add nothing else. Their own writings reveal it: first, in the letters intercepted in 1621 from Cardinal Ludovisi, the Count of Oñate, Baltasar Zúñiga and others; then Wilhelm Germanus, in the book by the Jesuit Lamormaini, confessor to Ferdinand II, On the Virtues of Ferdinand II, Roman Emperor; and Carlo Carafa, Bishop of Avellino, nuncio at the imperial court of two Popes, Gregory XV and Urban VIII, in Sacred Germany Restored. From these writings Johann Joachim Rusdorf brought forward excerpts on this matter in the Palatine Vindications, chapter xxxv and following. Michael Lonigo, prefect of the Vatican, offering Gregory XV a plan for persuading Maximilian of Bavaria to seek papal confirmation of the electorate he had obtained (which he did), begins thus: "Most Blessed Father, the greatest gain would accrue to the Roman Church, and Your Holiness would crown your most fortunate pontificate with the great glory given you by God, if the Duke of Bavaria, lately raised to the dignity of the Imperial Electorate, were persuaded to this view, that he should petition for this title to be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See.
