For by this one thing obtained, Your Beatitude would gain at present as much as was not acquired even in the course of two hundred years by the earlier Popes; or rather, to speak more truly, you would reclaim and redeem that which the others have lost, from the times of Gregory XI down to our own, of the rights which pertained to the Church in settling the affairs and orders of the Empire." He himself acknowledges that for two hundred years no Pope has been able to obtain this from the Empire or the Electorate, which indeed he ought never to have done, acting so much against the laws and the splendour of the Empire and of the most illustrious Electoral College. And in the Aphorisms on the Restoration of the Church's State, presented to Pope Gregory XV by the same Lonigo, by decree and approval of the College of Cardinals, it is clearly proved that, on the one hand, the papal usurpation was to be extended, and on the other, all Protestants were to be expelled (if it could be done) from the Empire and the Electoral College, and not only the Palatine but, for the same reason, the Saxon and the Brandenburger too, who are expressly named to this end; and that those measures taken against the Palatine were directed, as we shall set out, as much from the sinister seat from which those plans arose, namely the Papal, as from the aim they had, namely the Palatine, and with him the extreme destruction of the remaining Protestants. Aphorism 5: Since Leo III had the power, on account of heresy, to cut off the Eastern empire from the Western, to tear it away, to snatch it from the hands of the Greeks and transfer it to the Franks, why should not the supreme Pontiff have the same power to snatch the electorate from the Palatinate, as the chief heresiarch, and transfer it to the Duke of Bavaria as the most obedient son of the Church? From the same false and empty principle: whoever says that we have received the Imperial crown from the Lord Pope as a benefit, the Empire having been transferred by Leo I (Emperor Frederick I, in 1157), is contrary to the divine institution and to the teaching of Peter, and will be guilty of a lie. Lonigo again. Aphorism 7: Thus the wisdom and the opposition of the heresiarch, the Saxon who resists, cannot impede, much less oppose, the transfer of the electoral dignity to the most Catholic Duke of Bavaria; for he, not acknowledging the holiness and antiquity of the original source of the Empire, as a heretic, cannot enjoy the rights and privileges of the Empire by right. Aphorism 8: If these things are as they truly are, then the supreme Pontiff, with the Holy League, is bound to bring all forces against the Saxon heresiarch and the rebels dependent on him, so that the holiness of the Apostolic See and the antiquity of the Roman Empire may be preserved in the transfer of the electoral dignity. Aphorism 9: After Leo, other Popes too, by the authority of the See alone, often transferred that same Western Empire from one nation to another. Why therefore should the supreme Pontiff, by the same authority of the See, not be able to snatch the electoral dignities from the hands of heretics and transfer them to Catholic princes, so that the holy face of the Roman Empire may be firmly restored in the extirpation of heretics? Aphorism 10: Thus the supreme Pontiff, the Emperor and the Holy League, without violating the Apostolic See, which must always defend what is holy in preserving antiquity, cannot permit the Saxon and the Brandenburger, who try to tear the authority of antiquity away from the Roman See in transferring the electorate and draw it into the College of Electors. Aphorism 27: Since the translation of the electoral dignity made to the Bavarian Duke Maximilian has already been confirmed by the most blessed Father, it no longer rests with the Emperor or the King of Spain to restore the Palatine heresiarch, or the heirs of the Count Palatine, to the dignity from which their father has been deposed. For this controversy pertains to the most blessed Apostolic See, not to the Emperor or the King of Spain. Aphorism 28: Since the supreme Pontiff has confirmed the translation of the electorate, the Kings of England, Denmark, Sweden, and the Brandenburger unjustly demand from the Emperor the restoration of the Palatine to the dignity and the electorate. For to ask this is nothing else than to dethrone the Apostolic See from its right of Majesty, and to adjudge the original source to the Emperor against the antiquity and holiness of the Church and the Empire. From all of these, these three things shine out and follow more clearly than the sun: 1. That the proper and first cause for which the Palatine was stripped of the electorate was, for the Papalists, nothing other than religion. II. That the same things are being planned against the other Protestant princes of the Empire, and the electors themselves, namely the Saxon and Brandenburg dukes by name; and that their electorates are regarded by them as null, because, of course, they have not been confirmed by the Pope. Thomas Campanella also openly revealed the same intention, in On the Monarchy of Spain, chapter v, where he says: Does the matter itself not demand that the King of Spain direct all his strength to bring that Empire under his power? To do this, he must deal with the Pope, that he curse the heretics, the three Protestant electors, threatening that, unless they return to the Roman Church, he will strip them of the electoral dignity which they received from the Pope himself; and since they already assert that the Pope is Antichrist, they will be convicted by their own words of being Antichristian themselves; and therefore that dignity should be taken from them of their own accord, if they refuse to accept the Catholic faith. For this purpose, the French, the Italians, and the Spanish, with the Pope's agreement, ought to conspire together against them (which would certainly bring great help to this affair), and root out utterly the sects of those subjugated, and send new colonies into their place. In the same book, chapter xxiii, he has another passage, which also concerns the electors and Protestant princes in Germany: But great effort must be applied so that the perpetual seeds of discord are scattered among the Margrave of Brandenburg, the Landgrave of Hesse, the Duke of Saxony, the Duke of Brunswick, the Palatine on the Rhine, likewise the Duke of Württemberg, and those small republics of Germany; which can easily be done if the question of precedence is raised among them, which has always kept the republics in suspense. All these things surely bid the Protestants to wake up, and to pay attention to the Papists' constant plots and snares against them. Henricus Vendramenus, Controversies of Venice, II, p. 31: Unless the Popes were seen to aspire to the supreme authority over secular princes, there would be no reason for all princes to think they must fear them so greatly. III. There are no defenders of the rights and dignities of the Empire in the Empire more upright and steadfast than the Protestant princes. But this, indeed, grieves the Pope greatly, that he was not heard at all in establishing the eighth electorate of the Empire, and indeed, as he says, in favour of the Count Palatine, though in truth of the Bavarian Duke. For what Frederick III, Emperor, wrote in 1444 to Pope Eugenius IV, about not taking away the kingdoms from their lawful heir or transferring them to another, applies here too; that letter, for Ladislaus, a boy King of Hungary, is read in Goldast, Imperial Constitutions, Tom. III, p. 477. Thus that plan of the Cardinals and of Lonigo, presented to Pope Gregory XV long ago in the Bavarian cause, has already gone up in smoke; and that these matters must be understood otherwise, namely that it is for the Empire, and not for the Popes, to dispose of the electorates, the Emperor and the princes have shown by this very act, and that a distinguished one.

units.la: §. XVI. Et quamvis Venerabilis Frater Episcopus Neritonensis noster, & Sedis prafata ad Tractum Rheni, & inferiores Germaniæ partes Nuncius extraordinarius in executionem mandatorum nostrorum, fuerit palam nostro, & ejusdem Sedis Apostolica nomine protestatus.) Videlicet mente alta repostum manet ípreti Nuntii sui Episcopi Neritonensis authoritas, & protestatio. Maluisset hic alterum Caraffam intromissum fuisse, suasque egisse partes; sed sapientiores Principes fœtum hunc Papalem semovendum ab interioribus consiliis prudenter sciverunt, qui certo certius omnia ipsorū interturbasset consilia, & omnibus viribus paci jugiter intercessisset. Nec aliter fieri potest, primo per prætensam Papæ in Imperialia potestatem, Principibus nunquam persuadendam, verum execrandam omnibus & reprimendam: deinde propter odium adversus Protestantes, ipsorum religionem, causam, & Principes Papale, quibuscum tamen pax firmanda erat. Eliminato proinde Papali nuntio, Principes quod Principum, quodque Imperii fuit, peregerunt, & hoc ad se pertinere, nihil ad Papam, merito censebant.
units.tr: §. XVI. And although our venerable brother, the Bishop of Nerita, our nuncio extraordinary to the Rhine district and the lower parts of Germany, who was sent to carry out our mandates, was openly protested in our name and in the name of the same Apostolic See.) Namely, the authority and protest of the Bishop of Nerita, the Nuncio, remain fixed deep in the minds of the Princes. He would have preferred another Caraffa to have been admitted and to have played his own part. But the wiser Princes knew prudently that this papal offspring must be kept away from the inner councils, since he would have thrown all their plans into confusion and continually stood in the way of peace by every means. Nor could it be otherwise: first, because of the pretended power of the Pope over imperial affairs, which Princes could never be persuaded to accept but which all must loathe and reject; and then because of the hatred against the Protestants, their religion, their cause and their Princes, with whom peace nevertheless had to be made. The papal nuncio therefore being removed, the Princes did what belonged to the Princes and to the Empire, and rightly judged that this concerned themselves and had nothing to do with the Pope.

units.tr: Let him rule his own Church, and let him temper the divine laws,

units.la: Temperet: Imperium nobis fasceque relinquat.

units.la: Vti apud Guntherum, in Liguricis loquitur Imperator Fridericus. Et quid hic Nuncius Papalis? quorsum, quid ipsi cum Imperii Comitiis, ut ceu Davus in Comœdia Principibus assiduo obmurmuret, & placita Numinis Vaticani crepet? nihil lul certe boni spectandum à tali persona, tyrannidis Papalis jurato mancipio, potuisset. Quare quod Pontifici Paulo v. consilium dabat Perronus Cardinalis, ut ad pacem inter Christianos Principes colendam, ad eos mitteret solum Nuncios non partiales, prudenter factum dicerem, si talis quiret homo esse Papæ nuncius, & non implicare mihi videretur, quod dicebat des Nonces non partiaux, & qui ne dependissent que d'elle, pendentes à sola Papali sede: eo etenim quod Papæ sunt debentque esse in solidum devoti, nequeunt non partes sequi, & facere, quas nusquam non Papæ captant. Et quis ferat erectioris indolis Princeps, mucosum Nuncium in plenis Comitiis, nomine Papæ protestari, Paces articulos esse irritos, nullos, iniquos, ac per non habentes potestatem temere contractos, atque pro talibus ab omnibus habendos esse? Pessimus rabula irrita dicet acta & fœdera Principum, iniquam pacem, & pro nulla à quibusvis habendam, ac per non habentes potestatem conditam? quid, non potestatem habet Imperator, non Imperii primores pacis tractare negotia? non Rex Galliæ, non Sueciæ Regina? quibuscum pacis fœdus iactum est. Vel quis, quinam potestatem talia agendi habent, si non illi? an forte Papa, & quibus ille potestatem tribuat? Bestia, nam hoc symbolo Spiritus S. in Sacris Papalem illam stoliditatem describit, & sibi arrogans quæ aliis debentur: imitata potius illū, qui Christo dicebat ad ostensa mundi regna, eorumque gloriam: hæc tibi dabo omnia. De Gregorio vii. dixit Onuphrius Panvinus, in ejus vita, quod suis decretis dimidium Cæsari tolleret. si audiatur in Bulla sua Innocentius, hic ab Imperatore totum tollit, dum nec potestatem ei relinquit faciendi pacem. Itane Papa potestatum supremarum, quibus omnes subditos vult esse Paulus, omnem animam, adeo sine anima sit oportet, se qui hinc eximat, arbiter erit, & ab eo scilicet emendicatam omnes habebunt ac precariam potestatem Principes, Reges, Imperatores? ita ut nec pacis tractare negotia possint, nisi ab illo auctorati? o ingentem arrogantiam, improbitatem, blasphemiam! scilicet hoc premii loco referunt Principes à Papa, prepropter accumulatam huic tam prodige auctoritatem & concessa imprudenter omnis generis dona, jura, potestatem. Neque aliter puniendi melius erant, quam per ipsum illum, in quo exaltando tam perniciose peccarunt. Nullam corporalem jurisdictionem de se habet Papa, omnia vel usurpatione mera, vel iniqua & prepostera Principum liberalitate, qua nec abuti ille debuerat, imo nec accipere quæ dare illi volebant, non item poterant, ipsi autem possidere prohibitum. Iam vero illis omnibus ad id fastigium pervenit, ut omnibus major regibus, leges dare, omnem potestatem a se dependere, & Dei loco haberi, se velit. Horrenda sunt, quæ de potestate Papæ, ex Papisticis & Curialibus Paparum Doctoribus viri docti in catalogum collegerunt, ut ostenderent, quale Numen in Papa colant & colere debeant quotquot ei se submittunt. Ne alios dicam, Ioh. Wolfius Lection. Memorab. Centur. xv. a pag. 990. & deinceps. Nuper Laurentius Banck I. C. Professor Franckeranus, lib. de Tyrannide Papa, per totum, præsertim cap. xi. de Papæ Tyrannide in Rebublicas. Quis recenseat Auctorum plurimorum non dicta aliqua, sed scripta integra, libros & tractatus adversus enormem illam Paparum arrogantiam & usurpationem, præcipue in temporalia & politica? Scriptorum Germanorum, Gallorum, Anglorum, Venetorum: quorum multa, egregio instituto & fructu, collegit, ediditque Melchior Goldastus, lib. Monarchia S. Romani Imperii. Sed Scriptorum, Doctorumque sit illis obloqui: Principum est, sua authoritate ac vi reprimere Papalem istum fastum ac coercere. Id est, dum nunquam eo adducentur Papæ, ut sponte deponant vel remittant suam ambitionem, adimenda illis potestas ea temporalis, per istos, quibus eam abstulerunt: neque prius cum Imperio, vel mundi regnis bene habebit, quam hoc factum fuerit. Sic Petrus de Ferraria, apud Boërium I.C. Decision. lxix. bene & sancte faceret Papa, inquit, si totam temporalem jurisdictionem in manibus Imperat. remitteret, nec aliter unquam Resp. & maxime Italia quiesceret, nec ulterius tale scisma de Papatu, quale fuit prateritis annis, ullo tempore am-plius plius accidet. Et ex hoc Status universsu Clericorum magis reddetur Deo ac populo devotus. Et ipse Papa cum Cardinalibus quietus vivent. &c. Sed ut ipsi Papæ proprio motu hoc agant, ne cogitandum quidem est, at Principes eo minus officio deesse oportet, ut illud hic agant, quod & Papis, & sibi æque foret salutare. Neque enim Papis convenit temporalis iurisdictio, præter Theologos, idem quoque satis ostendentibus Iurisconsultis, præcipue Gallis, qui aliis hic semper cordatiores. Rudolphus Prællæus, de Potestate Pontificali & Imperiali. Sub R. Carolo v. Somnium Viridarii. Molinæus, Hottomanus, Ludovicus Servinus; Iacobus Lefchaflerius; Iohannes Bedæus de la Germandiere; Iulius Pacius, Illustr. Quæst. 1. Maynardus, Quæst. Notab. de droit eferit. li. 1 v. ch. 100. aliisque. Vnde Peronus in legatione pro Henrico iv. ad P. Clementem viii. ne pilum se de potestate Regis temporali concessisse scribit ad Regem, in articulis reconciliationis: mais ils n'ont dependu un seul poil de l'authorité temporelle de Roy. Leodienses, in epistola quam ad P. Paschalem ii scripserunt a. cIↄ cvi i. unde praeter gladium verbi Dei & martirii tertius quem in nos porrigit Roberto armigero suo? &c. Epistola illa, ob elegantiam & dignitatem suam, apud varios legitur. In secundo tomo Concilorum in Chronica Colonensi; apud Goldastum in Constitut. Imper. & inter Apologias pro Henrico iv. pag. 188. dicitur à Sigeberto Abbate Gemblacensi scripta, nomine Ecclesiæ Leodiensis, a. cIↄ cIII. Apud Simonem Scardium, in Syllogę Historico-Politico-Ecclesiastica. Bochellum, Decret Eccles. Gallic. lib. v. Venturam Vincentinum Consil. Venet. cap. ix. Atqui ideo Leodienses fidelitatis suæ adeo commendabat Henricus iv. in epistola, a. cIↄ cvi. qua conqueritur de injuriis sibi à Papa tactis: postea Leodium veni. In quibus locis fideles viros, & in fide regni constantes semper inveni. Adeoq; auferenda Papis temporalis potestas omnis & iurisdictio, ut urbem quoque Romam vendicare iterum Imperio, vel regimini seculari, in eamq; dominationem exercere antiquam Principes oporteat. Quo demum pacto optime & radicitus ista Paparum potestas exscindetur. Quod Fredericus I. P. Adriano, urbis potentiam & possessionem fastuose jactanti ita ingerebat, epist. a.clɔ clv. Penes nos cuncta haec sunt. Ad nos simul omnia haec cum imperio dimanarunt. Non cessit nobis nudum imperium; virtute sua amictum venit, ornamenta sua secum traxit. Penes nos sunt Consules tui, penes nos est Senatus tuus, penes nos est miles tuus. Et anno clɔ clix. ad articulos a Papa sibi per certos ad id Cardinales expositos: Nuntios nostros, inquit, non esse recipiendos in palatiis Episcoporum asserit: Concedo, si forte aliquis Episcoporum habet in suo proprio solo & non nostro palatium. Si autem in nostro solo & allodio sunt palatia Episcoporum, cum profecto omne quod aedificatur solo cedat, nostra sunt & palatia. injuria ergo esset, si quis Nuntios nostros a Regiis palatiis prohiberet. Legatos ab Imperatore ad urbem non esse mittendos affirmat, cum omnis magistratus inibi B. Petri sit cum universis regalibus. Haec res, fateor, magna est & gravis, graviorique & maturiori egens consilio. Nam cum divina ordinatione ego Romanus Imperator & dicar, & sim: speciem tantum Dominantis effingo, & inane utique porto nomen ac sine re, si Urbis Romae de manu nostra potestas fuerit excussa. Ludovicus IV. Bavarus, in Edicto a.clɔ cccxxxviii. adversus Iohannem xxii. inter alia hoc etiam objicit, quod praeter fas atque aequum Italiam a regno Germaniae separare conatus fuerit. Fridericus II. a. clɔ ccxxxvi ad Papam, ipsum Italia jubentem abstinere: Italia hereditas est mea, & hoc notum est toti orbi. Sic sic demum, ubi Italiae quod tenet Papa dominum, & urbis Romae eo auferetur, in ordinem redigi, & Principibus suis splendor & dignitas restitui postlimino poterit, illudque impleri tandem, quod egregio versu jam olim cantatum: Roma dum stitubans variis erroribus alla Corruet, & mundi desinet esse caput.
units.tr: So the Emperor Frederick speaks in Günther's Liguricis. And what does the papal nuncio have to do here? Why, and what has he to do with the Imperial Diet, that like Davus in comedy he should keep muttering at the Princes without cease and rattle off the decrees of the Vatican deity? Certainly nothing good could be expected from such a person, a hired slave of papal tyranny. So what Cardinal Perron advised Pope Paul V, that to cultivate peace among Christian Princes he should send only nuncios des Nonces non partiaux, & qui ne dependissent que d'elle (impartial nuncios who depend on her alone), I would call a prudent thing, if such a man could be a papal nuncio and if this did not seem to me to contradict itself, since they depend solely on the papal see. For since the Popes' men are and must be wholly devoted to the Popes, they cannot help following the factions which the Popes everywhere seek to win. And who could bear a Prince of higher spirit when a snivelling nuncio protests in full Diet, in the Pope's name, that the articles of peace are void, null, unjust, and rashly concluded by men who have no power, and must be held as such by all? Would the worst pettifogger declare that the acts and treaties of Princes are void, an unjust peace, to be held as nothing by anyone, drawn up by men without power? What, has the Emperor no power, nor the chief men of the Empire, to conduct the business of peace? Not the King of France, not the Queen of Sweden, with whom the treaty of peace was struck? Or who, if not they, has the power to do such things? Or perhaps the Pope, and to whom does he grant that power? A beast! For by this symbol the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures describes that papal stupidity, which arrogates to itself what is owed to others, imitating rather him who said to Christ, showing the kingdoms of the world and their glory: All these things will I give you. Onuphrius Panvinus said of Gregory VII, in his life, that by his decrees he took half from Caesar. If Innocent is heard in his Bull, he takes everything from the Emperor, since he does not even leave him the power of making peace. So is the Pope to be the arbiter of the supreme powers, to which he wishes all men to be subject, every soul, so that whoever escapes from him must be without a soul? And will all Princes, Kings and Emperors hold their power begged from him and by his sufferance, so that they cannot even treat of peace unless authorized by him? O immense arrogance, wickedness, blasphemy! Clearly this is the reward the Princes receive from the Pope, for having so recklessly piled up such prodigious authority on him and imprudently granted him every kind of gift, right and power. Nor could they be punished better than by that very thing in whose exaltation they sinned so destructively. The Pope has no corporeal jurisdiction of his own; he has everything either by sheer usurpation or by the unjust and preposterous generosity of Princes, which he ought neither to abuse nor even accept, since what they wished to give him they could not give, and what they possessed was forbidden to them. And now he has come to such a height that he wishes to be above all kings, to give laws, to have all power depend on himself, and to be held in the place of God. Horrible are the things which learned men have gathered into a catalogue, from the Papistical and Curial teachers of the Popes, concerning the power of the Pope, to show what deity those who submit to him worship in the Pope, and ought to worship. To say nothing of others, John Wolf, Lectiones Memorabiles, Century 15, from p. 990 onward. Lately Laurentius Banck, J.C., professor at Franeker, in his book de Tyrannide Papa, throughout, especially cap. xi, on the Pope's tyranny over commonwealths. Who could list the many authors who have written not merely some sayings but whole writings, books and treatises against that enormous arrogance and usurpation of the Popes, especially in temporal and political matters? Of German, French, English and Venetian writers, many of which Melchior Goldast gathered and published, with an excellent plan and profit, in his Monarchia S. Romani Imperii. But it is for writers and teachers to speak against these things; it is for Princes, by their authority and force, to repress and restrain that papal pride. That is to say, since the Popes will never be brought to give up or lay aside their ambition of their own accord, that temporal power must be taken from them by those from whom they took it; nor will the Empire or the kingdoms of the world fare well until this is done. So Peter of Ferrara, cited by Boërius J.C., Decision 69: The Pope would act well and holily, he says, if he gave back all temporal jurisdiction into the hands of the Emperor; in no other way would the commonwealth, and Italy above all, ever be quiet, nor would such a schism over the papacy as occurred in past years ever happen again at any time. And from this the whole estate of the clergy would be made more devoted to God and the people, and the Pope himself with the Cardinals would live in peace, etc. But that the Popes should do this of their own motion must not even be thought; and the Princes must the less fail in their duty to do here what would be equally wholesome for the Popes and for themselves. For temporal jurisdiction does not suit the Popes, as the theologians show, and the jurists also show sufficiently, especially the French, who are always more sensible than the rest here: Rudolph Prälleus, de Potestate Pontificali & Imperiali. Under King Charles V, Somnium Viridarii. Molinaeus, Hotman, Louis Servin; James Lefchaflerius; John Bedaeus de la Germandière; Julius Pacius, Illustr. Quæst. 1; Maynard, Quæst. Notab. de droit eferit. li. 1, vol. v, ch. 100; and others. Hence Perron, in his embassy on behalf of Henry IV to Pope Clement VIII, writes that he had not conceded a hair of the King's temporal power to the King in the articles of reconciliation: mais ils n'ont dependu un seul poil de l'authorité temporelle de Roy (but they have not depended on a single hair of the King's temporal authority). The people of Liège, in the letter they wrote to Pope Paschal II in the year 1106, say: unde praeter gladium verbi Dei & martirii tertius quem in nos porrigit Roberto armigero suo? (whence, beyond the sword of God's word and martyrdom, does he hold out a third, which he gives to his armour-bearer Robert against us?) and so on. That letter, on account of its elegance and dignity, is read in various places: in the second tome of the Councils, in the Cologne Chronicle; in Goldast's Constitut. Imper.; and among the Apologias pro Henrico iv., pag. 188, where it is said to have been written by Sigebert, abbot of Gembloux, in the name of the Church of Liège, in 1103. It is also in Simon Schard, Syllogę Historico-Politico-Ecclesiastica; Bochellus, Decret Eccles. Gallic. lib. v.; Venturas Vincentinus, Consil. Venet. cap. ix. And indeed Henry IV commended the loyalty of the Liège people so highly, in a letter of 1106 in which he complains of the injuries done to him by the Pope: afterwards I came to Liège. In those places I have always found men faithful and steadfast in the faith of the kingdom. And so all temporal power and jurisdiction must be taken from the Popes, so that the Princes must also win back the city of Rome for the Empire or for secular rule, and exercise over it their ancient dominion. In this way, at last, the power of the Popes will be rooted out most thoroughly. Quod Frederick I wrote to Pope Adrian, who boastfully vaunted the power and possession of the city, in a letter of 1155: All these things are in our hands. All these things flowed to us together with the Empire. The Empire did not come to us bare; it came clothed in its own virtue and drew its ornaments with it. Your consuls are in our hands, your senate is in our hands, your soldiers are in our hands. And in 1159, in reply to the articles which the Pope had set before him through certain Cardinals chosen for this purpose: Our envoys, he says, you assert are not to be received in the palaces of the bishops. I concede this, if perhaps some bishop has a palace on his own soil and not on ours. But if the palaces of the bishops are on our soil and estate, since whatever is built goes with the soil, they too are ours. It would be an injury, therefore, if anyone barred our envoys from the royal palaces. You affirm that the Emperor should not send envoys to the city, since every magistracy there belongs to St Peter with all the royal rights. This matter, I confess, is great and grave, and needs a weightier and more mature counsel. For though by divine ordinance I am and am called Roman Emperor, I only display the appearance of a lord, and bear an empty name without the substance, if the power of the city of Rome is shaken from my hand. Louis IV the Bavarian, in his Edict of 1338 against John XXII, objects among other things that contrary to right and justice he has tried to separate Italy from the kingdom of Germany. Frederick II, in 1236, to the Pope, who bade him keep away from Italy: Italy is my inheritance, and this is known to the whole world. So, when what the Pope holds as lord of Italy, and of the city of Rome, is taken from him, then at last he can be brought into order, and splendour and dignity can be restored to his Princes by right of return; and that can at last be fulfilled which was long ago sung in an excellent verse: Rome, while staggering, will fall amid its various errors, and will cease to be the head of the world.

units.la: Omni quidem principatui semper supra modum adversantur Papae, atque uti Iudas loquitur in epistola, χυεἰσπται ἀγαπηταί, maxime tamen adversus Imperium sese opponunt, & hoc sibi subigere imprimis allaborant. Nullus unquam Imperio fidelis Papa: & hic mihi jam quoque perfidus exitit, adeo nullum Papam fidum reperi, dicebat de Leone X. Maximilianus, verum (addebat) velit Deus, ut hic sit ultimus. Et ante eum Conradinus a. cIↄ cclxviii. in querimonia ad Principes Imperii, de injuriis sibi per Romanos Pontifices illatis: Ha Deus, quomodo sic universi Pontifices in nostri juris injuriam juraverunt! Quae eo minus ferenda, quo ab Imperio, vel saeculari Principum jurisdictione male tenet Papa, quidquid temporalis dominii potestatisque habet. Unde Ludovicus Bavarus a. cIↄ cccxxiv. in appellatione adversus P. Iohannem xxii. quam ubique fecit denuntiari: Nos Ludovicus Romanorum Rex, proponimus adversus Ioannem, qui se dicit esse Papam, quod Christi testamentum de pace male exequitur, publicam Christianitatis pacem perturbans: nec reminiscitur a sancto Constantino id, quicquid nunc habet, honoris latitanti Silvestro permissum, male gratus Romano Imperio: unde desumpsit omnem, quo nunc abutitur, splendorem, &c. Item in Apologia, Francofurti scripta a. cIↄ cccxxxviii. Insuper post dictos processus, quasdam literas sub bulla sua dicitur fecisse, & per multum publice transtulisse, in quibus se asserit totam Italiam ab Imperio & Regno Alemannia separasse, insinuans per sua scripta & dicta, quod Papa, tanquam Dominus universalis, non solum in spiritualibus, sed etiam in temporalibus, potest tam de Imperio quam de omnibus regnis & dominiis temporalibus totius mundi ad suum libitum disponere & ordinare. Ad quae omnia duximus respondendum, quod dicti omnes processus, assertiones & literae, & omnia & singula, quae per dictum Iohannem in praedictis, & contra praedicta, gesta seu attentata fuisse dicuntur, fuerunt & sunt nulla, & nullius valoris & momenti, rationibus infra scriptis. Prima ratio est. & quae sequuntur. Consultum ego arbitror compendio imperiis, si Papis auferrent saecularia, & quae in temporali jurisdictione heterogenea & aliena usurpant in quavis mundi ditiones & regna. Quid Episcopo cum sceptro? quid Papis cum Imperio? Adigantur exemplum sequi P. Leonis viii. cujus Bulla legitur restituens Ottoni a. bcccclxiv. temporalia quecunque ab Imperio possiderent Papæ; in quam Scholia scripsit Theodoricus à Niem; & vindicias pro eâ, adversus Baronium, Goldastus, in Rationali Constitut. Imperial. pag. 36. At-que uti olim Gregorius M. se scribebat famulum Imperii, ita Principibus secularibus omnino subjici Papas,& præstare obedientiam, juxta cum aliis, oportet.Significavit hoc olim Innocentio III Balduinus I. Imperator Constantinopolitanus a.cIↄ ccv. Miratur nostra Imperialis Sublimitas, quod nos tua Sanctitas ausa sit in suis literis increpare, cum meminisse debueris, quod non dominus Imperatoris, sed subditus sis, & Imperium Sacerdotio dignitate ac potestate præferendum esse, juxta id quod beatus Petrus Apostolorum Princeps scripsit, præcipiens; Subditi estote omni humanæ creaturæ propter Deum, Sive Regi tanquam præcellenti, sive Ducibus tanquâ ab eo missis, ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum. Verissime Hieronymus Vendramenus, Theologus Venetus dixit, in Disquisit. Controvers. Venet. III. pag. 54. Vtinam adulatores silerent, quippe viri sanctissimi atque doctissimi hæc de re solum loquerentur, nullam dignitatem à summo Pontifice aucupantes, nullum lucrum, nullam prabendam, ob quam clare constaret, S. Pontificem nullam prorsus temporalem potestatem in principum regnis atque imperio haberel Immo si illa res à viris non præoccupatis ipse aut pretio, vel cæcâ erga Papalem sedem præposteraque devotione, examinaretur, nihil certius esset planiusque, quam nihil secul膜 potestatis Papæ concedendum aut relinquendum esse. Erasmus, Præfat. ad Hilarium: Sit hoc vanum, nisi rem ipsa docebam in libellis quorundam, qui jam annis aliquot hinc multi provolarunt, Pontificia majestatis ὑπερμεγεθεῖ esse quedam, qua dum impense tuentur hominis dignitatem, apertum habent contumeliam in Christum. Hoc nisi res evicerit ipsa, sine ego vanus auctor. Vnum imprasens ejus dabo argumentum. Alexander Vellutellus, in Comœdiam Dantis Aligerii, de inferno, purgatorio, & paradiso, rationem dans cur Papæ ista offerat, ait: sopra ognuna de le quali essa tua santa predomina, & ha somma autorita per successione da quel Monarcha, che tutte le impere. Intelligetur facilia hæc satis, ut non necesse sit Latine reddere, & quaelibet sua qua tradita Lingua habent nescio quid energiæ, & splendoris, quem amittunt multum, in alium ubi transfunduntur sermonem. Vel an illud vis ex Cæremoniali Romano, lib. 1. de ente, qui in nocte nativitatis Domini à Papa solenniter consecratur, dein Regi vel Principi alicui do no mittitur? quod ita ibidem exponitur: Figurat denique Pon tificalis hic gladius potestatem summam temporalem à Christo Ponti ficis ejus in terris Vicario collatam, juxta illud: Data est mihi o mnis potestas in cælo, & in terra. Et alibi, Dominabitur à mari usque, usque ad mare, & à flumine, usque ad terminos orbis ter rarum, quam & declarat cappa illa fericea, quam Pontifices ge stare solent in nocte nativitatis Domini.
units.tr: The Popes have always been excessively opposed to every secular authority. As Jude says in his epistle, they are "spots at your love-feasts" [σπιλάδες ἐν ταῖς ἀγάπαις], but they set themselves most strongly against the Empire and labour above all to subject it to themselves. No Pope has ever been faithful to the Empire. Maximilian said this of Leo X: "I have found no faithful Pope; this one has now proved faithless to me too, but (he added) may God grant that he be the last." Earlier, Conradin, in his complaint to the princes of the Empire about the wrongs done to him by the Roman Pontiffs, in the year 1268, said: Alas, God, how all the Pontiffs have conspired to violate my right! These wrongs are all the less tolerable because the Pope holds whatever temporal dominion and power he has from the Empire, or from the secular jurisdiction of princes, and holds it wrongly. Hence Louis of Bavaria, in his appeal against Pope John XXII in the year 1324, which he had proclaimed everywhere: We, Louis, King of the Romans, charge against John, who calls himself Pope, that he carries out Christ's testament of peace badly, disturbing the public peace of Christendom. Nor does he remember that whatever honour he now has was granted by the holy Constantine to Silvester, who was then in hiding, and he is ungrateful to the Roman Empire, from which he has drawn all the splendour which he now abuses, etc. Likewise in the Apology written at Frankfurt in the year 1338: Moreover, after the said proceedings, he is said to have issued certain letters under his seal and to have had them widely published, in which he asserts that he has separated all Italy from the Empire and the kingdom of Germany, declaring by his writings and speeches that the Pope, as universal lord, not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters, can dispose and ordain at his pleasure both the Empire and all the kingdoms and temporal dominions of the whole world. We have thought it necessary to answer all these things by saying that all the said proceedings, assertions and letters, and everything and each thing which is said to have been done or attempted by the said John in the aforesaid matters and against them, were and are null, of no validity or weight, for the reasons written below. The first reason is, etc. I think it would be the best remedy for the Empires if the Popes were stripped of secular affairs, and of those things which they usurp in temporal jurisdiction, which is foreign and alien to them, in every region and kingdom of the world. What has a bishop to do with a sceptre? What have Popes to do with the Empire? Let them be compelled to follow the example of Pope Leo VIII, whose Bull is read restoring to Otto in the year 964 whatever temporal possessions the Popes held from the Empire; Theodoric of Niem wrote notes on it, and Goldast, in the Rational Constitutions of the Empire, p. 36, wrote in its defence against Baronius. And just as Gregory the Great once called himself the servant of the Empire, so it is right that Popes should be entirely subject to secular princes and render them obedience, along with others. Baldwin I, Emperor of Constantinople, made this clear to Innocent III in the year 1205: Our Imperial Majesty marvels that your Holiness has dared to rebuke us in your letters, since you ought to remember that you are not the lord but the subject of the Emperor, and that the Empire is to be preferred to the Priesthood in dignity and power, according to what the blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, wrote, commanding: Be subject to every human creature for God's sake, whether to the King as supreme, or to governors as sent by him, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Hieronymus Vendramenus, a Venetian theologian, said most truly in his Disquisitions on the Controversies of Venice, III, p. 54: Would that flatterers were silent, and that men most holy and learned spoke alone on this matter, grasping for no dignity from the supreme Pontiff, no gain, no prebend, by which it would clearly be established that the holy Pontiff has no temporal power at all over the kingdoms and empire of princes. Indeed, if that question were examined not by men who are prejudiced, whether by bribery or by blind and perverse devotion to the Papal See, nothing would be more certain or plainer than that no secular power should be granted to or left with the Pope. Erasmus, in his preface to Hilary: This would be empty talk, were it not that the thing itself teaches it, in the little books of certain men which for some years now have flown forth in great numbers, that there is something in the excessive majesty of the Pontiff which, while they zealously defend the dignity of a man, plainly contains an insult to Christ. Unless the thing itself proves this, let me be considered a vain author. I will give one of his arguments here. Alexander Vellutello, in his commentary on Dante Alighieri's Comedy, on Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, giving the reason why the Popes offer these things, says: sopra ognuna de le quali essa tua santa predomina, & ha somma autorita per successione da quel Monarcha, che tutte le impere. These words will be understood well enough without any need to render them into Latin; and each language has I know not what energy and splendour of its own, which it loses to a great extent when it is poured into another language. Or do you want that from the Roman Ceremonial, book 1, on the sword, which the Pope solemnly consecrates on the night of the Lord's Nativity and then sends as a gift to a king or some prince? It is explained there as follows: This Pontifical sword signifies the supreme temporal power conferred by Christ on his Vicar on earth, according to that saying: All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. And elsewhere: He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth; which the silken cape that the Pontiffs are accustomed to wear on the night of the Lord's Nativity also declares.

units.la: Ex illa, quam diximus, Papæ prætensa potestate est hoc, quod pacem Germaniæ irritare hac sacrâ Bullâ ausit, quando post præfata multa concludit: ipso jure nulla, irrita, „invalida, iniqua, injusta, damnata, reprobata, inania, viri„busque, effectu vana omnino fuisse, esse, & in perpetuo fo„re, neminemque ad illorum, & cujuslibet eorum, etiamsi „juramento vallata sint, observantiam teneri, neque ex illis „cuiquam aliquod jus, vel actionem, aut titulum coloratum, „vel causam prescribendi, etiam si longissimi, & immemo„rabilis temporis possessio, seu quasi possessio etiam citra ul„lam interpellationem, seu interruptionem subsequatur, ac„quisitum fuisse, nec esse, minusve ullo tempore acquiri, & „competere posse, neque illa ullum statum facere, vel fecisse, „atque perinde, ac si nunquam emanassent, pro non exstan„tibus, & non factis perpetuo haberi debere, tenore earum„dem præsentium, decernimus, vel declaramus, & nihilo„minus ad abundantiorem cautelam, & quatenus opus sit, „articulos præfatos, aliaque præmissa, ut præfertur, præju„dicialia motu, scientia, & deliberatione, & potestatis pleni„tudine penitus damnamus, reprobamus, nullamus, cassa„mus, annullamus, viribusque & effectu vacuamus, & con„trailla, deque eorum nullitate coram Deo protestamur, & quatenus ibidem opus fit, easdem Sedem Apostolicam, Romanamque, & inferiores Ecclesias, ac quaelibet loca pia, & quafcunq; personas Ecclesiasticas, adversus illa, in integrum ac pristinum, etiam in quo ante prædictam & qualcunq; alias assertas seu prætenfas anteriores transactiones, seu pactiones conventiones circa præmissa ubicunque & quomodocunque factas, erant, statum restituimus, repanimus, ac plenarie reintegramus. Hactenus Papa. Diftinctius annotanda sunt, quae in modo quo pacem hic abrogat, & pronunciat nullam, sigillatim observanda. Nam & utitur protestationi de eorum nullitate coram Deo protestamur. Quasi ejus protestatio hic multum audienda vel curanda fit. II. pronunciat pacis articulos irritos, nullos, iniquos. III. Compositos per non habentes potestatem. IV. ab omnibus pacem hanc pro nulla habendam: quasi ejus fit omnibus imperare, quid servare vel minus, pacis præsertim publicæ, debeant. V. non obstantibus juramentis: etiamsi juramento vallata, frangenda in gratiam Papæ, pacisque irritandæ. VI. nullam præscriptionem adversus hoc ejus interdictum currere. VII. se contra decretum pacis, secus ac huic visum, restituere. VIII. Bullam hanc suam valere debere etiamsi magno & substantiali defectu laboret. IX. Imo non obstantibus in contrarium Apostolicis tam generalibus, quam specialibus statutis. X. vel Comitiis & legibus Imperialibus, aut Regalibus. Hæc videlicet audet Papa, in conspectu totius mundi, tantamque Principibus omnibus, Regibus, Imperatoribus impingere ignominiam: & hoc impune? Miror ego Principum ignaviam, sas mihi sit ita eam appellare, quum ferunt uno in homine, sibique subjecto tantam adversus ipsos petulantiam & improbitatem, illum ipsis excutere imperium e manibus, ad se rapere, ipsos sibi subjicere, leges refigere, neminem audire, cunctis imperitare, certe haud ferendum videtur ultra vel ipsis, vel Deo. Verum illud est juxta scitum Bonifacii Subesse Romano Pontifici omnem humanam creaturam declaramus, dicimus, definimus & pronunciamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis. Vel ut P. Sixtus V. suam adversus Regem Navarrae, & Condaum Prin-
units.tr: From the power of the Pope that we have mentioned comes the fact that he has dared, in this sacred Bull, to annul the peace of Germany. After many preliminary statements he concludes: "We decree and declare, by the tenor of these presents, that the said articles and the other matters mentioned above are, by law itself, null, void, invalid, iniquitous, unjust, condemned, rejected, empty, worthless in themselves and in their effect, and that they have been, are, and shall forever remain such. No one is bound to observe them or any of them, even if they have been confirmed by oath. No right, action, or colourable title, nor any ground for prescription, may arise from them for anyone, even if possession or quasi-possession has continued for a very long and immemorial time, even without any interruption or challenge. Nor have they been acquired, nor can they be acquired or belong to anyone at any time. They do not create, and have never created, any status; and they must be held in perpetuity as if they had never been issued, as things that do not exist and were never done. Nevertheless, for greater caution, and insofar as it is necessary, we, by our own motion, knowledge, deliberation, and the fullness of our power, wholly condemn, reject, nullify, quash, and render void in force and effect the aforesaid articles and the other prejudicial matters mentioned above, and we protest before God protestationi de eorum nullitate coram Deo protestamur. And insofar as there is need, we restore and fully reinstate the Apostolic See, the Roman Church and the lower churches, all pious places, and all ecclesiastical persons against those articles, to the entire and former state in which they were before the aforesaid and any other alleged or pretended earlier transactions or agreements concerning these matters, however and wherever made." Thus the Pope. These points should be noted more distinctly, in the manner in which he abrogates the peace and pronounces it null, and each should be observed separately. For he uses the phrase we protest before God the nullity of these things, as if his protestation were to be heard or heeded here. (II) He pronounces the articles of peace void, null, iniquitous. (III) They were agreed by those who did not have the power. (IV) He declares that this peace must be held as null by all, as if it were his place to command all men what they should or should not keep, especially in matters of public peace. (V) He sets aside oaths: even those confirmed by oath must be broken for the Pope's favour and to annul the peace. (VI) He declares that prescription cannot run against this interdict of his. (VII) He restores matters against the decree of peace, otherwise than seems good to him. (VIII) He wants his Bull to stand even if it suffers from a great and substantial defect. (IX) Indeed, he wants it to stand notwithstanding the contrary Apostolic statutes, both general and special. (X) Or the diets and Imperial or royal laws. Does the Pope dare to do these things, in the sight of the whole world, and to inflict such dishonour on all princes, kings, and emperors? And does he do so with impunity? I marvel at the cowardice of princes (may I be allowed to call it so) when they bear that in one man, and one who is subject to them, there is such insolence and wickedness against them, that he should wrest the empire from their hands, seize it for himself, make them his subjects, rewrite the laws, listen to no one, and rule over all. Surely this seems no longer tolerable, either to them or to God. Yet it is according to the decree of Boniface: "We declare, state, define, and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff." Or as Pope Sixtus V began his excommunicating Bull against the King of Navarre and Prince Condé in 1585: From the immense power of the eternal King, authority was handed to blessed Peter and his successors over all the powers of earthly kings and princes.

units.la: I cipem Bullam excommunicatoriam a. cIↄ lᴐIxxxv. exordiebatur : eAb immensa æterni Regis potentia beato Petro, ejusque successoribus tradita auctoritas omnes terrenorum Regum, & Principum superemines potestates. Quale proœmium subinde miratus sui quod Innocentius in hac sua Bullâ non adhibuerit, nisi forte sciverit ista jam pridem Principibus, orbique universo risum concitare, & explodi solita. Potestatem illam Papæ observamus dupliciter se habere, & supra, & contra omnes, quin ideo contra eos, quia omnes supergredi temere affectat. De Paulo iv. Historia Concilii Tridentini (cujus auctor Paulus Sarpius, Servita, Theologus Venetus: translationis in Latinum, nam scripta ab Auctore est Italice, Adamus Neutonus Scotus, de quo Cl. Dauberus I. C. orat. Funebri in Excessum Andreæ Riveti, pag. 15. Hic ille Neutonus est (nam eo Sammaxentinæ Scholæ moderatore, seque Pontificium tum simulante, magnus Rivetus Græcas Litteras addidicerat) versionis latinæ Historiæ Concilii Tridentini auctor, qui in Scotiam reversus Principis Scotiæ, filii primogeniti Regis Henrici Ephorus, tandem Salisburiensis Ecclesiæ Decanus obiit. De illo libro vere Grotius, in epist. ad Io. Cordesium (est inter ejus ad Gallos epistolas cxxii) Maximum omnes quibus vera sapientia cordi est lucrum fecerunt, reperto libro viri incomparabilis Pauli Servita, præsertim de argumento tam nobili &c) illa dico Historia lib. v. de P. Paulo iv. hæc refert: Quoties cum Oratoribus colloquebatur, in eorum aures hujusmodi sermones crebro intonabat, se Regibus cunctis esse superiorem; nolle se arctam cum quovis eorum familiaritatem; sibi concessam Regnorum immutandorum potestatem; se eorum, qui Reges Imperatoresque e solio suo deturbat, esse successorem. Sape illud memorabat, se authoritatis sua clarum documentum in ipso Pontificatus introitu dedisse, erecta in regnum Hibernia. nec erubuit in Consistorio, in mensa, atque in publico multis audientibus dictitare, se nullum Principem sibi comparem, aut socium velle agnoscere: sed æquum esse, ut suo pedi (humum eo tum percutiebat) omnes subjiciantur, quandoquidem ita visum ei, qui Ecclesiam hanc ædificaverit, & se in hoc sastigio collocaverit. Neque continebat se, quin interdum adderet,malle se centies mori, ac facibus quatuor mundi plagis subditis, incendium rerum omnium ruina restinguere, quam vile quidpiam suoque loco indignum committere. En quales Papas in sinu suo foveant, quotquot illis fidem addixere Principes, & Reges? debentque (sic Caeremoniale loquitur) coram eo genuflectere, ejusque oculari manus pedesque Omnes mortales, & praesertim Christi fideles, cujuscunque sint dignitatis & praeminentia, cum primum in conspectum Pontificis advenient, distantibus spatiis ter debent ante illum genuflectere, & in honorem Salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi, cujus vices in terris gerit, ejus pedes osculari. Imperator, Reges, maximi principes, principum seu Potentatuum Oratores, prima vice & ad osculum manus, & orit recipiuntur, alii ad pedes tantum. Ita Sacrarum Caeremoniarum scriptor, Christophorus Marcellus, Corcyrensis Archiepiscopus, lib. III. cap. III. Hinc, quod idem Auctor Historiae Concilii Tridentini narrat lib. V. P. Pius IV. a Legato Caesaris Scipione Comite Arcoense, non satis habuit reverentiam omnem cultumque accepisse, ni & obedientiam professus fuisset. Ad haec non possum quin exclamem cum Abbate Trithemensi, in Chronico, ad expositam historiam Bonifacii VIII. ostendentis utrumque gladium, ecce duo gladii hic: o Domine Iesu, ecce quo typhus processit ejus, qui servus tuus audit! Bene monebat, si moneri vel ab Imperatoribus vellent Papae, Carolus V. P. Clementem VII. in Rescripto a. MDXXVI. Videat quaso S. V. quib. fundamentis moveatur: consideret an haec pastorali congruant officio: an hic sit gladius per V. Sanct. evaginandus exercendusque, quem Christus in vaginam potius recondendum censuit, & qui etiam in hostes fidei ab ipso Christiani gregis pastore regulariter exerceri prohibetur. Nos in praesenti Papae adversus Germaniam, ejusque pacem facto tria haec praecipue spectamus, 1. quid agat: nempe pacem abrogat Germaniae II. adversus quos: nominatim impetit Imperatorem, & Gallia Regem, ac Reginam Sueciae: id est, summa Christiani orbis capita. III. quo pacto? ut pacem quamvis juramento firmatum, vel quocunque modo alio fortissimo stabilitam servari tamen nolit. Adversus pacem ar-
units.tr: Prince's Bull ... I wonder at this preamble, since Innocent did not use it in this Bull of his, unless perhaps he knew that such words had long since made princes and the whole world laugh and had become a thing to be scorned. We observe that this power of the Pope stands in a twofold relation: above all, and against all, not therefore against them because he rashly aims to surpass them all. Concerning Paul IV, the History of the Council of Trent (whose author was Paolo Sarpi, a Servite, a Venetian theologian; it was written by him in Italian, and translated into Latin by Adam Newton, a Scot, of whom the learned Dauber speaks in his funeral oration on the death of Andreas Rivetus, p. 15) says: This is that Newton (for under the master of the Saumur school, when he was pretending to be a Papist, the great Rivet had learned Greek letters) the author of the Latin version of the History of the Council of Trent, who, returning to Scotland, became tutor of the Prince of Scotland, the eldest son of King Henry, and at last died as Dean of the Church of Salisbury. Grotius truly said of that book (in his letter to John Cordesius, which is among his letters to the French, number 122): All who hold true wisdom dear have gained greatly by finding the book of the incomparable man Paul the Servite, especially on so noble a subject, &c. I mean that History, book 5, concerning Pope Paul IV. It reports this: Whenever he conversed with ambassadors, he often thundered such words into their ears: that he was superior to all kings; that he did not wish to be on close terms with any of them; that the power of changing kingdoms had been granted to him; that he was the successor of him who casts down kings and emperors from their thrones. He often recalled that he had given a clear proof of his authority at the very beginning of his pontificate, when he raised the kingdom of Ireland; and he did not blush to repeat, in the Consistory, at table, and in public, before many listeners, that he would acknowledge no prince as his equal or companion, but that it was fitting that all should be subjected to his foot (he was then striking the ground with it), since it had seemed good to him who built this Church and placed him on this summit. Nor could he restrain himself from sometimes adding that he would rather die a hundred times, and, with the four quarters of the world made subject, extinguish the fire of all things by the ruin of the world, than commit anything vile or unworthy of his position. Behold what kind of Popes they cherish in their bosom, all those princes and kings who have given themselves over to them! And they must (so the Ceremonial speaks) kneel before him and kiss his hands and feet. All mortals, and especially the faithful of Christ, whatever their dignity and eminence, when they first come into the presence of the Pope, must kneel three times before him at a distance, and in honour of our Saviour Jesus Christ, whose vicar he is on earth, kiss his feet. The Emperor, kings, great princes, and the ambassadors of princes or potentates are received first with a kiss of the hand, and then with an embrace; others only at the feet. So writes the author of the Sacred Ceremonies, Christopher Marcellus, Archbishop of Corfu, book 3, chapter 3. Hence, as the same author of the History of the Council of Trent relates in book 5, Pope Pius IV, when he received reverence and every homage from the Emperor's legate, Count Scipio of Arco, did not think it enough unless he had also professed obedience. To these things I cannot help but exclaim with the Abbot of Trittenheim, in his Chronicle, on the account of Boniface VIII showing the two swords: Behold, here are two swords. O Lord Jesus, see how far the pride of him has gone, who calls himself your servant! Charles V rightly warned, if the Popes would be warned even by emperors, when he wrote to Pope Clement VII in a rescript of 1526: Let Your Holiness consider, I pray, on what foundations he is moved; let him consider whether these things agree with the pastoral office, whether this is the sword that Your Holiness is to unsheath and wield, which Christ thought should rather be returned to its sheath, and which is ordinarily forbidden even to the shepherd of the Christian flock to wield against the enemies of the faith. In the present action of the Pope against Germany and its peace, we chiefly observe these three things: (1) what he does, namely, he abrogates the peace of Germany; (II) against whom, namely, he expressly attacks the Emperor, the King of France, and the Queen of Sweden, that is, the highest heads of the Christian world; (III) in what manner: he is unwilling that the peace be kept, even though it has been confirmed by oath or established in any other most firm way. Against the peace he arms himself, the enemy of peace, disrupting and disturbing the peace now everywhere established, to use the words of Charles V to Clement VII, though he knows well that his own people commonly sing of it even in the Masses and pray to God: Graciously give us peace…

units.la: K k armat se pacis in terris inimicus, pacem jam ubique contrectam disfrumpens atque perturbans, ut verbis utar Caroli v. ad Clementem vii. quantumvis etiam in Missis decantari illud vulgo à suis, & precari ad Deum sciat: Da propitius pacem in diebus nostris. Et pacem Germaniæ oppugnat, scilicet ut sic incurrat in Constitutionem de pace publica, ejusque reus ut damnari poena possit, quæ illâ continetur. Imperator Sigismundus, ab habito Constantiensi Concilio, in Reformatione Secularari, cap. xxi. graviter edixit: Ihr Fürsten/ihr Herrn/ wie vegleicher in seinem Stat sey / ich ermahn euch bey deß Reichs Huͤden/ deßgleichen alle Stet / niemant außgenummen/ bey der heiligen Christenlichen Ermanung / daß ihr verhütent alle Kreiß zu wenden / Friede zu haben. Wer die Ermanung oberst sicht/ der sol kein getrewer Christ geheyssen seyn / noch sol sein Stamm kein Freiheyt noch leben von dem Reych nymmer gewynnen. Er sol stehen under den Christen als ein Heyden vnd falscher Christ. Quamvis extra Imperium Germanicum Papa sit, quatenus tamen hoc per Rescripta sua arroganter turbat, coercendus, & qua parte potest, etiam ab omnibus, quos tangit, multandus jure venit. Tumultuetur ille; at ne impune: velnon liceat illi, saltem non possit, pro voto turbare omnia, accendere bella iterum, ac miscere superis ima. Hic quidem ejus genius, hoc studium, sed in quo videre debent Principes, & tanto diligentius cavere ne ipsis ipsorumq; ditionibus noceat & sit exitio. Non quidem potest aliter Papalis sedes, quam lites serere & contentiones; sed hic ut primus fortitudinis gradus illam contemnere, ita proximus ab eo est, illam in ordinem redigere & cancellis suis coercere. Imperatorem in sua Bullâ Papa primo adoritur, tum & Galliæ Regem. Utinam ille priscos prædecessorum animos aliquando lumat, eorumque virtus redeat in Nepotum præcordia, ut doceantur ab ipsis Papæ, non amplius in res Imperii involare, & Reges inter se Principesque committere, vel de illarum disceptare suo pro arbitrio juribus ut palam de illis scribant, eos non habuisse potestatem pangendæ pacis, quibus illam acceptum fert orbis Christianus universus. Papa nempe Suprematum potestatum arbiter erit. Sed vetustiora sunt nomina Henricorum, Fredericorū, Conradinorum, Sigismundorum, Carolorum, quam ut recordetur hodie Papa quid Imperatores in se possint, quid egerint aliquando à Papis provocati, quoique terrores & angustias ipsis sæpe immiserint: recentiori exemplo docendi sunt non impune Imperium vexari, aut ejus prostitui majestatem, vel in istud licere Papis, quod lubet. Ex Maximiliano Philone, Trevirense, de Friderico III. ad ejus Reformationem Ecclesiasticam refert Goldastus, in Rationali Constitut. pag. 115. quod ejus hoc votum fuerit: ach daß Gott einem Kaiser solche Kraffte und sicgabe / daß er den Bapst jur gleichheit und billichkeit bringen mochte / atque hoc exoptandum aliquando, ut imperatore instituatur; neque minus dolendum, Imperatores ita ignorare vel vim suam, vel negligere dignitatem ut quod tam facile possunt, adeoque debent, non citius exequantur, & se sibi vindicent.
units.tr: He arms himself as the enemy of peace on earth, "breaking and disturbing the peace now everywhere established," to use the words of Charles V to Clement VII, however much he knows that the people sing that in the Masses and pray to God, "Graciously grant peace in our days." He also attacks the peace of Germany, so that he falls under the Constitution concerning public peace and becomes liable to the penalty contained in it. The Emperor Sigismund, after the Council of Constance, in the Reformation of the Secular Estate, chapter 21, sternly decreed: "You princes, you lords, whoever holds a position in his state, I admonish you for the protection of the Empire, and likewise all cities, no one excepted, by the holy Christian admonition, that you prevent all circles from turning, so that there may be peace. Whoever disregards this admonition shall not be called a faithful Christian, nor shall his family ever again gain freedom or life from the Empire. He shall stand among Christians as a heathen and a false Christian." Although the Pope is outside the German Empire, insofar as he disturbs it arrogantly by his rescripts, he rightly deserves to be restrained and, wherever possible, punished by all whom he touches. Let him make his uproar; but not with impunity. If it is not permitted to him, he at least may not be able to disturb everything at will, to kindle wars again and to mix up the heights with the depths. This is indeed his character and his zeal, but princes ought to see in it, and take all the more careful heed, lest it harm them and their dominions and bring them to ruin. The papal see cannot act otherwise than to sow quarrels and contentions. But just as the first step of courage is to despise it, so the next is to bring it into order and restrain it within its own bounds. The Pope first attacks the Emperor in his Bull, and then the King of France. Would that the Emperor might at some time rouse the old spirit of his predecessors, and that their courage might return to the hearts of their descendants, so that they might be taught by those same Popes no longer to intrude into the affairs of the Empire, to set kings and princes against one another, or to decide their rights at his own discretion, so that they might openly write that those to whom the whole Christian world attributes the making of peace had no power to make it. For the Pope, of course, will be the arbiter of the supreme powers. But the names of the Henries, Fredericks, Conrads, Sigismunds and Charles are older than that today's Pope should remember what Emperors could do against him, what they once achieved when provoked by Popes, and what terrors and distresses they often inflicted on them. By a recent example they must be taught that the Empire is not vexed with impunity, nor its majesty prostituted, nor that Popes may do whatever pleases them. Goldast, in the Rational Constitutions, page 115, reports from Maximilian Philo of Trier, concerning Frederick III and his Ecclesiastical Reformation, that his wish was this: "Ah, that God would give an Emperor such strength and victory that he might bring the Pope to equality and fairness." This is something to be wished for at some time, that it might be carried out by an Emperor. Nor is it less to be lamented that Emperors are so ignorant of their own power, or so neglectful of their dignity, that they do not more quickly carry out, and claim for themselves, what they can so easily do, and indeed ought to do.

units.la: Certe Galliæ Reges hic minus defuerunt officio suo quam alii multi, in repellendo Papæ fastu, & arrogantia, quem siquis adhuc apud eos dixerit in temporalibus supra Regem esse, vel in prejudicium libertatum & exemptionum Ecclesiarum istarum (qua de re multi egregiiq; tractatus à Gallorum Doctissimis conscripti sunt) audiendum vel interrogandum, digne luit, & libros pro Papæ illa potestate scriptos igne, Auctores supplicio persequuntur. Thuanus lib. xxviii. a. cIↄ Iↄ lxi. de disputatione Ioh. Tanquerelli, in qua Pontificii inter alia adscripserat, eum tanquam solum Christi vicarium & Ecclesiæ Monarcham potestate spirituali & seculari omnes fideles subjectos continere, principesque sui præceptis rebelles regno ac dignitatibus exuere posse, refert, Tanquerellum, vel, quia aberat, cujus nomine Petrum Gustum damnatum fuisse, ut publice in Sorbona, præsentibus L Theologis, nudo capite errorem à Bonifacio VIII. invectum, & post ejus mortem passim damnatum ignominiosa confessione recantaret. Ita & errare Papas in rebus fidei etiam ex cathedra definiendis Galli agnoscunt, & nequidquam illos dubitant in personis suorum Clientum παπομανίαν παθεδικαιοσύνην, Viginti quatuor annis post exemplum illud Tranquerelli, decretum idem renovatum a. cIↄlↄ xcv. ob similes theses ad disputationem propositas a Florente Iacobo, sub praesidio Thomae Blanzii, Parisiensis Theologi; nam in carcerem conjecti ambo, inde in magnam Sorbonae aulam adducti, praesentibus ex aula & Schola quam plurimis, publica palinodia poenitentiam testati fuere, & a Deo, Rege, judicibus precati veniam. Thesibus disruptis, Doctoribus imperatum ne talia unquam docerent, & hoc ut certius observaretur, decretum in Acta Academica relatum, ea lege, ut quotannis primo post novi anni exordium Theologorum conventu recitaretur, & repeteretur, quo in recenti apud illos semper esset memoria. Egregiam ad haec praesidis Iohannis Forgeti exhibet orationem Thuanus, historiae lib. cxiv. in principio. Quando a. cI)I)Ixxxvi. Parisiis Tomus operum Bellarmini primus, quo continetur Disputatio de summo Pontifice, ex editione Ingolstadiensi, recuderetur, Procurator Regius impressa quae reperit folia abstulit, atque editionem libri, propter illam de authoritate Pontificis disputationem, inhibuit.
units.tr: Certainly the Kings of France have been less wanting in their duty here than many others in repelling the Pope's haughtiness and arrogance. If anyone should still say among them that the Pope is above the King in temporal matters, or should speak in prejudice of the liberties and exemptions of their churches (on which matter many excellent treatises have been written by the most learned Frenchmen), he pays the penalty: he is not to be heard or even questioned, and the books written in favour of that papal power are burned, and their authors prosecuted with punishment. Thuanus, book 28, year 1561, reports on the disputation of John Tanquerel, in which the Papists had asserted, among other things, that the Pope, "as the sole vicar of Christ and monarch of the Church, may hold all the faithful subject to him in both spiritual and secular power, and may strip of kingdom and dignities those princes who rebel against his precepts." Tanquerel, or, since he was absent, Peter Gust in whose name he had been condemned, was made to retract publicly, bareheaded, in the Sorbonne, in the presence of fifty theologians, with a shameful confession, the "error introduced by Boniface VIII and condemned everywhere after his death." Thus the French acknowledge that the Popes also err in matters of faith, even in those defined ex cathedra, and in vain do they doubt that those men are in the grip of [papomania] and [pathodikaiosyne] in the persons of their clients. Twenty-four years after that example of Tanquerel, the same decree was renewed in 1595, on account of similar theses put forward for disputation by Florent Jacob, under the presidency of Thomas Blanzy, a Parisian theologian. For both were thrown into prison, then brought into the great hall of the Sorbonne, and in the presence of very many from the hall and the school they gave public evidence of repentance by a public recantation, and asked pardon from God, the King and the judges. With the theses torn up, the teachers were ordered never again to teach such things; and, so that this might be more certainly observed, the decree was entered in the academic records, on the condition that every year, at the first gathering of the theologians after the beginning of the new year, it should be read out and repeated, so that it might always remain fresh in their memory. Thuanus gives an excellent speech of the president John Forget at the beginning of his history, book 114. When in 1586 the first volume of Bellarmine's works, which contains the disputation On the Supreme Pontiff, was reprinted at Paris from the Ingolstadt edition, the royal prosecutor removed the pages he found printed, and prohibited the edition of the book on account of that disputation about the authority of the Pope.

units.la: Ejusdem Bellarmini tractatus de potestate summi Pontificis, in rebus temporalibus, adversus Guiljelmum Barclayum condemnatus Arresto Parlamenti Parisiensis fuit, eo quo primum prodiit, anno, cI)Ixcx.d.xxvi. Novemb. (quo eodem anno d. x. Iunii Mariana librum quoque damnarant) urgentibus negotium Regiis Cognitoribus, interque illos primo Ludovico Servino I. C. cujus cordata & erudita hac super re extat ad Parlamentum Commonefactio. Inter Excerpta ex illo Bellarmini libro, quibus summam ejus, facilioris judicii ergo, comprehendebant, haec etiam erant, Cap. xi. Potest ac debet Summus Pontifex Regibus imperare, ut non abutantur potestate Regia ad Ecclesiam evertendam, ad haereses, & schismata fovenda, &c. Et si non obtemperent, cum admoniti fuerint, potest eos de Ecclesia per censuram excommunicationis ejicere, & populos a juramento fidelitatis absolvere, denique etiam eos exuere, & Regia potestate privare. Ex cap. iii. Ipsos vero Apostolos fuisse in potestate temporali Principum Ethnicorum, scripsi olim cum Alberto Pighio, & aliis nonnullis: sed postea recognoscens, & expendens diligentius libros meos, meos, censui & Apostolos de facto subjectos fuisse Principibus illis, non de jure, ut recognitione mea posui. Istiusq; commatis plura erant, quæ ad evertendum potestatem supremarum a Deo constitutarum & ordinatarum pertinere, subditos acuere ad rebellionem, & principum ingenio fabricare, ad machinandum in eorum capita distonesque, ad turbandam denique tranquillitatem & quietem publicam meditare, Parisiensis curia haud immerito judicavit. Scio quidem, mox sententiæ huic, ad querelas Nuntii Papalis, intercessisse Regem, sed non hoc quod res dubia esset, verum quia Cardinalis Auctor libri erat, urgebant negotium ad Papale Consistorium deferendum; quod facilius propter Regis Ludovici XIII minoritatem, sub regimine Mariæ Medicææ, indultum. Mansit tamen inde, ut pro diverso hominum de Bellarmini illo libro & disputatione judicio, aliter quam Bellarminus, & Iesuitæ vulgo sentientes appellarentur Catholici regales, catholiques royaux; ex adverso alii, hereticques d'estat, hæretici status. Atque a. clo Ioc xi. in contentione Sorbonæ cum Iesuitis, ubi audita elegans illa Petri Martillerii, nomine Rectoris atque Universitatis, oratio contra Iesuitas, à nullis non historicis ad annum istum memorata, reductio Iesuitarum in Galliam, & in Scholas concessa, verum ita ut subscriberent ante omnia hisce veritatibus. I. quod Concilium supra Papam. II. quod Papa nullam temporalem supra Reges habeat potestatem, & quod non posset illos per excommunicationem privare regnis suis & Statibus. III. quod Ecclesiastici in Consessione audientes insidias vel conjurationem contra Regem vel Statum suum, vel cujusque criminis Læsæ Majestatis, tenentur illa revelare Magistratui. IV. quodque Ecclesiastici sunt subjecti Principi seculari, vel Magistratui Politico. Ita solertius Galli semper vigilarunt pro authoritate regni, adversus usurpationes Paparum, & doctrinas eò facientes. Et Reges quid dicam, illorumque Pragmaticas contra iniquum Paparum dominatum, & tyrannidem? vel Gallicarum Ecclesiarum, pro suis libertatibus decreta & constitutiones? nam ut in Regno illo omnes & singuli Ordines varia adversus Paparum injurias generoso animo sæpe dissignarunt, ita in has illa classes omnia distribuo, ut sint vel Regum Pragmaticæ & sanctiones, seu rescripta; vel statuta & Acta Parlamentorum, supremarum in regno Curiarum; vel decreta Ecclesiarum, pro suis libertatibus; vel ejusdem argumenti scripta & Tractatus Doctorum: quæ omnia quam varia, quamque egregia singula sint, nil opus dicere; nec memorare ex Regum catalogo Philippos, Carolos, Ludovicos; vel inter Scriptores, Molineos, Hottomannos, Servinos, Prellæos, Achillinos, Almainos, ne recentiores addam, vel qui inter prohibitos à Collegio Cardinalium libros a. cIↄ lↄ cxl. collocari meruit: Traitté des Droits & libertez de l'Eglise Gallicane, par M. Pierre Pithou: ut præterea Tilletum, Bochellum, alios de juribus Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ. Hæc indicasse, & revocasse in memoriam, apud talium facile oblivios, Papas videlicet Papalesque, impræsentiarum suffecerit. Vnum quin exhibeam continere me non possum, quia rarius, & exemplo potest esse Regibus, terorri Papis, quod à Goldasto, ex libello quodam de Actis Gallicanæ Legationis depromptum legitur inter Constitutiones ejus Imperiales Tom. III. Caroli VIII Regis edictum a.cIↄ cccxcv. d. xII. Iul. per Legatos suos Romæ publicatum, contra P. Alexandrum VI. in controversia de regno Neapolitano: Sæpe Oratoribus, sæpius literis, te apud, Alexandre Sexte, sollicitavit Rex noster, quod annueres auxilioque esses ut Regnum suum Neapolitanum, quo injuste cum spoliarunt Reges Arragonum, eoque in hunc usque diem contra jus falsque & honestum potiuntur, consequentur. Credebat te tam licitis suis desideriis obtemperaturum, & id agere, ne Christiani Principes bello implicarentur. Sed cum plane videat se omnia surdis auribus cecinisse, ferro decrevit curare vulnera, quæ non sentiunt beneficia medicinæ: Nosque iterum ad te misit præcipiens, te admoneremus ut Serenitatis suæ voluntati non incautius reluctareris, Quod si non possemus persuasionibus apud te efficere, ut tibi & tuis denunciaremus bellum, quod Regem nostrum ,,non minori animo, quam nos denuntiamus, gesturum ,,confidas. Nec tibi persuade, eam gentem, quæ florentes ,,Romanorum res sæpe periclitavit & subvertit, urbem hanc ,,diruit, populi orbis terrarum domini invictum exercitum ,,fudit, devicit Lucium Papirium, Torquatum, illustres ,,Fabios, cæterosque præstantissimos belli duces, pusillanimes ,,Sacerdotes, & qui molliciei & delitiis insueti bella timent, ,,reverituram. aliaque quæ sequuntur. In fine dicunt: Bello itaque te accinge, quoniam pacem perferre non potuisti. Neque prius pacem reddent regnis & orbi Principes, quam Papam perpetuum dissidiorum bellorumque omnium fomitem & cloacam suis ditionibus primo prohibuerint, tum urbe & mundo exegerint, juxta oraculum illud Lodovici xii Galliarum Regis: Perdam Babylonem. Ferendumne Regibus est, ut minari audeat P. Iulius ii. Henrico ii. quod si ei Rex Parmam auferat, se Galliam ipsi erepturum?
