units.tr: Bellarmine's own treatise on the power of the supreme Pontiff in temporal matters, written against William Barclay, was condemned by an arrest of the Parlement of Paris in the same year it first appeared, 1606, on 26 November. (In that same year, on 10 June, they had also condemned Mariana's book.) The royal prosecutors pressed the case, and first among them Louis Servin, a learned jurist, whose wise and learned Commonefactio on the matter is still extant, addressed to the Parlement. Among the excerpts from Bellarmine's book, which were made to give a summary of it for the sake of easier judgement, were these: chap. xi: The supreme Pontiff can and must command kings not to abuse their royal power to overthrow the Church, or to foster heresies and schisms, etc. And if they do not obey when they have been admonished, he can expel them from the Church by the censure of excommunication, absolve peoples from their oath of fidelity, and finally also strip them of their office and deprive them of royal power. From chap. iii: I once wrote, with Albert Pighius and some others, that the Apostles themselves were under the temporal power of the heathen princes; but afterwards, on re-examining and weighing my books more carefully, I judged that the Apostles were subject to those princes in fact, not by right, as I have stated in my retractation. There were many more passages of this sort, which tended to overthrow the power of the supreme authorities ordained and established by God, to stir subjects to rebellion, to devise plots against the princes' persons and dignity, and finally to contrive the disturbance of public peace and quiet; and the Parisian court judged, not undeservedly, that these were to be condemned. I know indeed that soon after this sentence the king intervened at the complaints of the papal nuncio, not because the matter was doubtful, but because the cardinal was the author of the book; they pressed for the case to be referred to the papal Consistory. This was more easily obtained because of the minority of King Louis XIII, under the rule of Maria de' Medici. Nevertheless from this it remained that, according to the differing judgements of men about that book of Bellarmine and the dispute, those who thought otherwise than Bellarmine and the Jesuits were commonly called Catholiques royaux, royal Catholics; and on the other side others were called hereticques d'estat, heretics of state. And in 1611, in the dispute of the Sorbonne with the Jesuits, where that elegant speech of Pierre Martillier against the Jesuits, given in the name of the Rector and University, was heard, a speech mentioned by almost all historians at that year, the Jesuits were readmitted into France and into the schools, but only on condition that they first subscribed to these truths: I. that a Council is above the Pope; II. that the Pope has no temporal power over kings, and cannot deprive them of their kingdoms and states by excommunication; III. that ecclesiastics hearing confessions who learn of plots or conspiracy against the king or his state, or of any crime of treason, are bound to reveal these to the magistrate; IV. that ecclesiastics are subject to the secular prince or the political magistrate. Thus the French have always watched more shrewdly for the authority of the kingdom against the usurpations of the Popes and the doctrines that tend that way. And why should I speak of the kings, and their pragmatic sanctions against the unjust domination and tyranny of the Popes? Or of the decrees and constitutions of the Gallican Churches for their liberties? For as in that kingdom all and each of the orders have often with a generous spirit made known their various objections to the wrongs of the Popes, so I distribute all these into these classes: they are either the pragmatic sanctions and edicts of the kings, or rescripts; or the statutes and acts of the Parlements, the supreme courts in the kingdom; or the decrees of the Churches for their liberties; or the writings and treatises of the Doctors on the same subject. How various and how excellent each of these is, there is no need to say; nor to mention from the catalogue of kings Philip, Charles, Louis; or among the writers Molinaeus, Hotman, Servin, Prellaeus, Achillini, Almain, not to add more recent ones, or the book which deserved to be placed among the books forbidden by the College of Cardinals in 1640: Traitté des Droits & libertez de l'Eglise Gallicane, par M. Pierre Pithou; as well as Tillet, Bochellus, and others on the rights of the Gallican Church. It will suffice for the present to have pointed these things out and recalled them to memory, for the Papists and the partisans of the Pope, who easily forget such matters. I cannot refrain from setting out one thing, because it is rarer, and can serve as an example to kings and a terror to Popes: it is read, taken by Goldast from a certain little book on the proceedings of the French embassy, among the Imperial Constitutions, vol. III: the edict of King Charles VIII, dated 12 July 1495, published at Rome by his legates against Pope Alexander VI in the dispute over the kingdom of Naples: "Our King has often urged you, Alexander VI, by envoys and still more often by letters, that you would agree and give help so that he might gain and hold his kingdom of Naples, which the kings of Aragon unjustly and against right, truth and honour have seized, and hold to this day. He believed that you would comply with his so lawful desires and would act so that Christian princes are not entangled in war. But since he plainly sees that he has sung to deaf ears in everything, he has decided to treat with iron those wounds which do not feel the benefits of medicine. And he has sent us again to you, commanding us to admonish you not to resist the will of his Serenity too rashly. And if we cannot bring it about by persuasion that we declare war on you and yours, you may trust that the King will wage it with no less spirit than we declare it. Nor persuade yourself that that nation, which has often endangered and overthrown the flourishing affairs of the Romans, destroyed this city, routed the invincible army of the masters of the people of the world, and defeated Lucius Papirius, Torquatus, the illustrious Fabii, and the other most eminent leaders in war, will shrink back from a fight, like timid priests who are used to softness and pleasures and fear wars," and what follows. At the end they say: So gird yourself for war, since you could not bear peace. Nor will the princes return peace to the kingdoms and the world before they have first forbidden the Pope, the perpetual kindler of all discords and wars and his sewer, in their own dominions, and then driven him out of the city and the world, according to that oracle of Louis XII, King of the French: I will destroy Babylon. Must kings endure that Pope Julius II dared to threaten Henry II, that if the King took Parma from him he would snatch France from him; or if the King tried to take away his obedience in France, he would forbid him all commerce with the Christian world? These things are related in the History of the Council of Trent, book iv. Can the Pope take away kingdoms? The kingdom of France? Over which he has no right, not even according to the constitution of Boniface VIII, Unam sanctam, in which it is nevertheless so shamelessly asserted that the sword is under the sword, and temporal authority is subject to spiritual power: for to him, it had been decided, the double sword belonged. "We are taught by the evangelical words that in his power and authority there are two swords, the spiritual and the temporal. For when the Apostles said, 'Behold, here are two swords,' that is, in the Church, when the apostles were speaking, the Lord did not answer that it was too many, but enough." Certainly he who denies that the temporal sword is in the power of Peter pays little heed to the word of the Lord who said, 'Put your sword back into its sheath.' Both are in the power of the Church, the spiritual sword and the material. But the latter is to be wielded for the Church, the former by the Church. The one by the hand of the priest, the other by the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the nod and sufferance of the priest. And at the end: "Furthermore we declare that it is necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff," dici-

Epistol. P. v. Sed precipue tangunt Gallorum foedera cū-Exteris-Patrocin. Genev. Unde Auctor lib. Gesta Imperiorum per Francos, p. 8. adeo excandescit, & se coprehendere posse negat, quomodo cū Christianissimi appellatione conveniat Geneva protectio & Patrocinium suscept um ja ab a. millesimo quingentesimo septuagesimo nono, & semper continuatum ad hac usque tempora. Quod monstrum, quod portentum, qua Chimera? Qua conventio lucis ad tenebras? qua communicatio Christi cum Belial; quid arca Dei cum Idolo Dagon, quid Sioni cum Babilone? quid, sanctitati cum impietate, quid Christo cum Beelzebub, quid Christianissimo cum Geneva? Tum Foedus Gallorum Belgicum, de quo Idem pag. 10. Putaban fingi vix quidquam posse Christianissimi nomine indignius, nec quidquam Christianismo existialius, quam Geneva tutelam & patrocinium, uti supra ostensum est: veruntamen postea considerati Foedus Hollandicum, quod jam pridem Gallia studiosissime excoluit, tanto illud perniciosius esse religioni visum est, quanto plures in Statibus illis Hollandicis inesse Genevas cernit (enitque incredibili suo malo Ecclesia. De foedere Gallo-Sucvico, pag. 16. Ab Aquilione pandetur omne malum. Revivisenut in uno Gothorum & Wandalorum Regè (quem nunc Suecia vocant) Alarici & Genserici, qui rursus Imperium & Ecclesiam Dei miserrime diripiunt, deformant, lacerant; non illi quidem à Ruffino & Eudoxia exciti, qui ambo postea hujus evocationis poenas ultori Numini justissimas dederunt; sed (quis credat?) à Gallia Christianissima animati facto foedere cum mortalium furiosissimo, consilio, pecunia, armis adjuti: Quae omnia quid de nostrae religionis Principibus Statibusq;, & foederibus iisdem pactis, Romanenses statuant, quamque nil praeter bella spirent, & nostrorum omnium excidium, quamque pessimus politiis consiliarius Papa sit, ostendunt. Illis, quę adeo exagitant alii in Gallis praecipue de foederibus eorum, cum Hollandis, Germanis, Suevis copiose respondit Auctor Vindiciarum Gallicarum, adversus Alexandrum Patricium, Armacanum, a. cap. xix. & deinceps,qui huic negotio, ut nihil nos ultra respondere necessum habeamus, satisfaciet. Quin & publico sæpe judicio Gallia contumelias istas repressit, condemnavit. In Francisco Surgerio Monacho, qui ubi publice Parisiis, a. cIↄ Iↄxcv. pro concione in Elisabetham Angliæ Reginam debacchatus esset, & pro hæreticis traduxisset omnes, qui cum eo fœdus inirent, ad palinodiam actus, & habendarum concionum potestas ei ablata fuit: injunctumque Concionatoribus, ut à contumeliis spargendis in fœderatos Regi Principes & Status, sub gravi pœnâ, abstinerent. Thuanus, lib.cxiv. Grotius in epistolis, ad Benj. Aurerium, a.cIↄ Iↄcxxvi memorat idem ab Ecclesiasticis Galliæ hoc tempore decretum fuisse: Gallia est quod gratulemur, cujus Episcopi nuper emendarunt id quod olim in Rhotomagi conventu peccatum fuerat, aperte definita Regis supremâ potestate, nulli hominum, ne Ecclesia quidem obnoxia; & damnatis armis quæ in Reges, quamvis persecutores, moventur; & probatis fœderibus, quæ cum iis ineuntur, quos mos facuLi Hereticos vocat. Sed in Pace jam Germaniæ, præterquám de Hæreticis quod dicunt, Electores præcipuos, & Status, & Suecię Regnum tangit, quos opprobrio isti vindicando objicimus; non cum solis Hæreticis inita est, sed plurimam quidam partem cum Romanę fidei sectatoribus, seu Germanis, seu Gallis, & tamen universam pacem uno loco habet Papa, pronunciatque irritam. Vbi nec attendit satis inter quos pacem abroget, nec qualem, quanta firmitate & quot Supremorum in terris Nominum fide, quodque supra illa solum est, solenni per Dei Nu men juramento constabilitam. Verum quid juramenti religio cohibeat Papam, qui ad exemplum iniqui istius in Euangelio judicis, neque Deum veretur, neque homines? Multa ejus facinora in Bulla hactenus notavimus, quæ tamen omnia supergreditur hoc, quod pacem frangit etiam juramento, confirmatione Apostolica, vel quavis firmitate alia roboratam. Hoc enim paragrapho simul & humana quævis, & Apostolica, & divina contemnit atque proculcat. Quo censu authoritates habeat ἐπισκόποις sape nunc vidimus, etiam quo loco Apostolica, quæ sic appellat: quasi quę sibi apertè adversantur Apostolica dici possint; vel Papalia isthoc nomine (quod hic faciunt) insignire, non sit directe contra Apostolos. Audiendus potius, quamvis etiam Pontificius, Ventura Vincentinus, Consil. super Controvers. Venet. cap. ix. Non necesse est semper esse verum quod Papa asserit, quia videmus quod circa eandem rem contrarias opiniones diversi Pontifices habuerunt, & tamen non possint contraria vel contradictoria simul esse vera. Haud semel vero in hac Nostra Bulla Innocentius Apostolicas constitutiones iuxe adversas facit, eoque & rejicit. Sed & in Bulla Coenæ Dominicæ, art. xvi. Seculares quoscumque Magistratus excommunicant & anathematizant, qui se quoquo modo interponunt (audite Galli, Venetii, vos enim præ aliis hoc (pçêat) in causis capitalibus, seu criminalibus cōtra personas ecclesiasticas, illas banniendo, capiendo, seu sententias contra illas proferendo, vel exequendo, etiam prætextu quorumcumque privilegiorum à sede Apostolica ex quibusvis causis, ac sub quibuscunque tenoribus, & formis, in genere & specie concessorum quibuscunque Regibus, Ducibus, Principibus, Rebuspublicis, Monarchiis, Civitatibus, & aliis quibuscunque potentatibus quocunque nomine censeantur, quæ nolumus illis in aliquo suffragari: illa omnia ex nunc in irritum revocando. Tam facile & consuetum Papis est, tum se opponere potestatibus Magistratuum quorumcunque, eoque ob ea, quæ ipsorum ex divino humanoque jure sunt, excommunicare; tum etiam Apostolicis (quę dicunt) derogare. Insuper juramenti religionem non vilipendit solum, sed rescindit, & iuxe potestatis existimat, fidem ejus posse facere irritam. Aliud est, dicere juramenti vim non tenere, quando causæ injustitia illud pronunciat nullum; aliud, ex authoritate superiori, quemadmodum alias sibi obstantes Constitutiones, ita, non per illam causæ explicationem, sed simpliciter juramento, vel quavis firmitate roborata (ut ita in juramento firmitatem agnoscas, quod alioqui per causæ defectum non firmum, nullum. lumque est) rescindere & annullare. Nempe Papa est supremus in terris Dominus, Deusque, qui dispenset super Euangelia, Apostolos, religionem, atque etiam juramenta: & qui illis omnibus apertissimum se persæpe præbet adversarium. Innocentius III. lib. II. Decret. tit. xxiv. c. sicut Nostris. Juramentum contra Ecclesiæ utilitatem præstitum non tenet. adeo ut proprium Pontificum dixerit esse Guiccardinus, Histor: Ital. lib. viii. non curare promissa. Et jam olim jacta- tum fit illud Hildeberti Cenomanensis episcopi distichon, in Romam: Vrbs selix, vel si dominis urbs illa careret, Vel Do- minis esset tarpe carere fide. Ecclesiæ utilitatem quum interpretari & extendere pro arbitrio possint Papæ, juramenta omnia ipsis tantum ludus sunt & jocus. Quod jam pridem universus observavit orbis, Papas juramentis ludere, ceu pueri astragalis solent. Carolus V. in Rescripto ad P. Clementem VII. a. cIɔIↄ xxvi. Et sunt qui affirmant, ut ex quibus„dam literis percepimus: quod V.S. ipso etiam Gallorum re„ge non petente, eidem juramentmm relaxaverit, quod no„bis præstiterat pro sœdere nobiscum prius inito, quod ta„men credere nolumus: quandoquidem res talis omnino „à pastore Christi vicario aliena esse debeat, ne ipsius jurif„jurandi sine causa spreta religio ad deteriora innocentium „præberet. Certe illa Pastorem Christi decerent quidem minime, sed quod se vix dicit credere, humanitas magis Imperatoris fuit, quâ fides. Dabo ergo testem ejus in Papis pervicacię ac perjurii alium, & Cardinalem Ossatum, ab Henrico IV Galliarum Rege, Romam ad Clementem VIII ablegatum, ut una cum Perrono Regis perficeret reconciliationem cum Papa: quo perafto negotio, variis literis testatur, quam assidue sollicitaret Regem Papa, ut fœdus quod ei erat cum Angliæ Regina, quamvis solenni (pro istorum fœderum more) juramento confirmatum disrumperet: inter alia lib. III, epist. lxxxvii hac de re verba facit observatione & censurâ dignifsima: Le Pape me dit, que le serment avoit esté fait à un heretique & que sa Majesté avoit fait un autre serment à Dieu, & à luy Pape; & puis adjoufta ce qu'il m'avoit dit autrefois & en l'audience precedente, que les Roys & autres Princes fouverains fe permettoient toutes chofes que tournoyent à leur profit, & que la chofe en estoit venuë si avant, qu'on ne leur imputoit point, & ne leur en scavoit on point de mauvais gre: & allegua un dire de Francefco Maria Duc d'Vrbin, qui souloit dire, que si un simple Gentil-homme ou un Seigneur non souverain manquit de sa parole, il en feroit deshonoré, & blasmé d'un chacun, mais les Princes souverains, pour raison d'estat, pouvoient sans autre grand blasme faire des traictez & s'en departir, prendre des alliances & les laisser, mentir, trahir, & toutes telles autres choses.
units.tr: Thence he has reproached the peace, however, that was confirmed between the King and the princes and subjects of the Religion, more intimately and likewise in written letters; all of which are extant in book 4 of the Epistles of P. V. But they especially touch the treaties of the French with Geneva, the Exteris-Patrocin. Genev. Hence the author of Gesta Imperiorum per Francos, p. 8, becomes so inflamed, and says he cannot grasp how the protection and patronage of Geneva, undertaken in the year 1579 and continued ever since to the present time, agrees with the title of Most Christian. What monster, what portent, what chimera is this? What agreement of light with darkness? What communion of Christ with Belial? What has the ark of God to do with the idol Dagon, Sion with Babylon? What has holiness to do with impiety, Christ with Beelzebub, the Most Christian King with Geneva? Then the French alliance with the Belgians, of which the same author says on p. 10: One would think hardly anything could be more unworthy of the name of Most Christian, or more hostile to Christianity, than the protection and patronage of Geneva, as has been shown above. Yet when they later considered the Dutch alliance, which France has for some time cultivated most zealously, it seemed to religion so much the more pernicious, as they see more Genevas among those Dutch States, and the Church is sorely troubled to its incredible hurt. On the Franco-Swedish alliance, p. 16: All evil will be unleashed from the North. In one king of the Goths and Vandals (whom they now call Sweden) the Alarics and Genserics have come back to life, who again most wretchedly plunder, deform and tear apart the Empire and the Church of God; not indeed roused by Rufinus and Eudoxia, who both afterwards paid most justly the penalty of that summoning of the avenging divinity; but (who would believe it?) spurred on by Most Christian France, aided by counsel, money and arms, by an alliance with the most frenzied of mortals. All these things show what the Romanists think of the princes and states of our religion, and of the alliances made with them on the same terms, and how they breathe nothing but war and the destruction of us all, and how the most wicked Pope is a counsellor of policy. To those objections which others, especially in France, urge so vehemently against their alliances with the Dutch, Germans and Swiss, the author of the Vindiciae Gallicae, against Alexander Patricius of Armagh, has answered at length in chapter 19 and following, who will satisfy this matter, so that we need not reply further. Indeed France has often suppressed and condemned these slanders by public judgment. When the Franciscan monk Francis Surgerius, after he had raged publicly in a sermon at Paris in the year 1595 against Queen Elizabeth of England, and had called all who entered alliance with her heretics, was forced to recant, and his power to preach was taken from him; and it was enjoined on preachers that they should abstain, under severe penalty, from spreading slanders against the princes and states allied with the King. Thuanus, book 114. Grotius, in his letters to Benjamin Aurerius, year 1626, records that the same decree was issued at this time by the French ecclesiastics: It is a matter for us to rejoice in France, whose bishops have lately corrected what was once a sin at the council of Rouen, plainly defining the supreme power of the King as subject to no man, not even to the Church; and condemning arms that are raised against kings, however persecuting; and approving the alliances that are made with those whom custom calls heretics. But in the present peace of Germany, apart from what they say about heretics, it touches the chief Electors and States and the kingdom of Sweden, whom we set against that reproach in vindication; it was not concluded with heretics alone, but for the most part with adherents of the Roman faith, whether Germans or French, and yet the Pope in one place annuls the whole peace and pronounces it void. Here he has not sufficiently considered between whom he is annulling the peace, nor of what kind, nor with how great a firmness, and under the faith of how many supreme names on earth, and established besides all this by a solemn oath in the name of God. But what restraint of oath can hold the Pope, who, after the example of that unjust judge in the Gospel, fears neither God nor men? We have so far noted many of his crimes in this Bull, yet all of them are surpassed by this, that he breaks the peace even with an oath, strengthened by apostolic confirmation or any other firmness. For in this paragraph he at once despises and tramples underfoot every human, apostolic and divine authority. What authority he gives to the [ἐπισκόποις, episcopis] we have often seen now, even where he calls them apostolic; as if things that openly oppose the apostles could be called apostolic; or as if the Papal decrees (which they do here) under that name were not directly against the apostles. Rather let us hear Ventura of Vicenza, though himself a Papist, in his Consilia super controversiis Venetis, chapter 9: It is not necessary that what the Pope asserts should always be true, because we see that different Popes have held contrary opinions about the same matter, and yet contrary or contradictory things cannot both be true. Indeed more than once in this our Bull, Innocent makes apostolic constitutions contrary to one another, and so both rejects and abolishes them. But also in the Bull In Coena Domini, article 16, he excommunicates and anathematizes all secular magistrates who interpose themselves in any way (hear this, French and Venetians, for you above others): those who in capital or criminal cases against ecclesiastical persons, by banishing, seizing or pronouncing or executing sentences against them, even under pretext of any privileges whatever granted by the Apostolic See, for whatever causes and under whatever terms and forms, in general or in particular, to whatever kings, dukes, princes, commonwealths, monarchies, cities or other powers whatsoever, under whatever name they are called, which we do not wish to support in any respect: all these we now revoke as void. So easy and so customary is it for the Popes both to set themselves against the powers of whatever magistrates, and so to excommunicate them for those things which belong to them by divine and human law; and also to derogate from what they call apostolic. Moreover he not only despises the sanctity of an oath, but annuls it, and thinks it within his power to make its faith void. It is one thing to say that an oath has no force when the injustice of the cause declares it null; it is another, by superior authority, as he annuls other constitutions opposed to him, to rescind and annul an oath, not by any explanation of the cause, but simply because it is confirmed by an oath or any other firmness (so that you may acknowledge a firmness in the oath, which otherwise, through a defect in the cause, would be unfirm and null). Indeed the Pope is the supreme Lord and God on earth, who dispenses above the Gospel, the apostles, religion, and even oaths; and who very often shows himself the most manifest adversary of all of them. Innocent III, Decretals book 2, title 24, chapter Sicut nostris: An oath taken against the advantage of the Church does not bind. So much so that Guicciardini, History of Italy, book 8, said it is peculiar to the Popes not to care about promises. And long ago that couplet of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, about Rome was bandied about: A happy city, or if that city lacked masters, it would be a shame for masters to lack faith. Since the Popes can interpret and extend the advantage of the Church at their pleasure, all oaths are mere sport and jest to them. The whole world has long observed this, that the Popes play with oaths as boys play with knucklebones. Charles V, in his rescript to Pope Clement VII, year 1529: And there are those who affirm, as we have learned from certain letters, that Your Holiness has released him from an oath, even without the request of the King of France himself, which he had sworn to us for the earlier alliance made with us; which we are unwilling to believe, since such a matter ought altogether to be far from the vicar of Christ the shepherd, lest the religion of the oath, scorned without cause, should give the innocent an example of worse things. Certainly those things hardly become the Shepherd of Christ, but what he scarcely says he believes was more the humanity of the Emperor than his faith. I shall therefore produce another witness to the Pope's obstinacy and perjury: Cardinal Ossat, sent by Henry IV, King of France, to Clement VIII at Rome, to bring about with Perron the reconciliation of the King with the Pope. When that business was finished, he testifies in various letters how persistently the Pope urged the King to break the alliance he had with the Queen of England, though confirmed by a solemn oath (as is the custom of such alliances). Among other things, in book 3, letter 87, he speaks on this matter with observations and censure most worthy of note: The Pope said to me that the oath had been made to a heretic, and that His Majesty had made another oath to God and to him, the Pope; and then he added what he had told me before and at the previous audience, that kings and other sovereign princes allow themselves all things that turn to their profit, and that the matter had gone so far that they are not charged with it, nor is ill will borne them for it; and he alleged a saying of Francesco Maria, Duke of Urbino, who used to say that if a simple gentleman or a non-sovereign lord broke his word, he would be dishonoured and blamed by everyone, but sovereign princes, for reasons of state, could without great blame make treaties and depart from them, take alliances and abandon them, lie, betray, and all such other things.

units.la: Quis non merito cohorrescat ad diabolica hujusmodi apud Papam axiomata & dogmata? siquidem docet hic quid facere liceat; & scribit hæc de Papa non nostræ partis aliquis, sed Ossatus,ad Regis,Consiliarium de Villeroy. Vtar hic simplici argumento: interrogo Papanos omnes, ipsosque adeo Cardinales, an quando Papa docet mentiri, fallere, prodere, & quidem de jure licita esse, peccet? an non vel tum, turpiter graviterque erret, quin in communem hominum societatem? vel quis illum spiritus ducat, qualemve sequatur, quando infanda ejusmodi exempla, quale hic Vrbini Ducis, qui dicebat probrosum quidem in vulgari homine aut Nobili esse si verbis fallat, non ita in Principe, proponit? illene infallibilis, aut judex & arbiter religionis nobis erit? Scribit sibi quidem multa in promtu fuisse, quæ respondisset, Ossatus, je n'avois que trop à repliquer à tout cela, sed non consultum visum diu illis insistere. Interim tamen hoc in fine epistolæ suum de illo judicium nobis imprimis, quibus multum refert Papas intime nosse, tum etiam quibuscumque prudentibus, nā & sagacis valde animi Ossatus ille fuit, utile audire: La haine qu'il porte, loquitur de Papa, aux heretiques le transporte si avant, qu'il se laisse echapper de la bouche, bien que sous le nom d'autruy, des maximes pernicieuses, & indignes de tout homme de bien; & par le mesme haine s'est laissé persuader par les Espangols tout ce qu'ils ont voulu. Deinde, & sa sainctete é trouve bonnes toutes façons de separer sa majeste d'avec ses alliez, pour ce qu'ils ne sont Catholiques, & ne recognoissent le saincte siege, encores que lesdites facons fussent infames & dommageables à la Majesté, & à son Royaume. Quis nobis Papas melius exponat, describatque hoc ipso, tam intimæ apud Papam admissionis, Paparum fratre? sed & quis non hinc omnes istius ordinis vel sedis despuat, hominum & humanæ societatis probra ac pestes? Principes monere, sollicitare ad frangenda fœdera; & obiectis pessimis exemplis extra lineas honestatis evagari, nedum religionis? Adde Oslati epist.v. lib.1. ubi de eodem argumento, dissolvendo videlicet Regis fœdere cum Reginâ Angliæ:quodquc ille valde improbat. nc dicam, quod lib.11. epist.77. aperte conqueritur, fraudem in Bullâ absolutionis Regiæ cômissam,in Regis, regnique grave præjudicium, & contra fidem multa illi inserta fuisse, aliter ac in articulis cum utrimque signatum fuerat. Intelligo jam, quomodo in Papabilem cadant ejusmodi conditiones,quales in Cardinale Tosco prædicat Perronus, quando eum alii conabantur Papam eligere, in locum Leonis XI. Homme, qui'navoit point mené une vie forte exemplaire, promt à la colere, & accoustumé à dire des paroles peu honnestes, & à d'autres habitudes mal-seantes, non seulement à un chef de l'Eglise, mais aussi à quelque personne que ce soit. ne vetera repetam, inter quæ notum de Papis plura hujusmodi emicare. Et tamen tales erunt capita Ecclesiæ, & fundamenta fidei, & judices religionis! avertat Deus, ne unquam talibus charam illam animarum nostrarum ψυχῶν committamus. In tribus manifesta est Paparum perfidia. 1. quod irritant juramenta quævis, ubi ipsis, & statui ipsorum videntur minus convenire. II. fœdera cum hæreticis (uti vocant) inita, ut quæ per hoc censent ipsis præjudicare. III. dum à fidelitatis juramento subditos erga suos Principes, & Magistratus absolvunt. Neque solum illos caulam hæresis hic attendere, argumento est vel præsens Bulla, quæ pacem abrogat, juratam etiam, non cum Sueco solum, sed & cum Gallo. Eant nunc, qui super sententia Ecclesiæ Romanę Paparumque disputant de fide hæreticis servanda; ubi nec Romanensibus Pontificiis illam servari hac in Bulla vult Papa, nedum Nostris. Atque ex illis quivis judicet de responsione Martini Becani, Iesuitæ, ad Calvinistarum (ut solet loqui) Aphorism. v. pro invalidis & plane nullis habere debent Imperatorum, Regum, Principum, aliorumque Ordinum constitutiones, pacta conventa, capitulationes, fraternitates, concessiones, quibus alia religio, quam moderna Romano-Catholica indulgetur, etiamsi juramenta intervenerint. Vt ad hanc propositionem dicat: totum aphorismus merum mendacium est. Ego unumquemque lectorem constituo judicem, ut videat, annon ex Bulla nostra, tum iis quæ hic ad eam dicimus, consequatur, totam illam Becani responsionem vel inficiationem, meram esse tergiversationem, & ut ejus verbo utar, mendacium? de hæreticis servanda fide, nil necesse ex alto contentionem hanc revocare, ab Actis Constantiensis Concilii, aut ex variis Doctorum Papisticorum testimoniis ostendere, ita eos docere, vid. non servandam fidem hæreticis esse nullo, nullo, nullo modo fidem hæreticis servandam esse, etiamsi juramento firmata sit, clamat Episcopus Pacensis, Simancha, addens ad poenam & odium hæreticorum hoc pertinere; unde occurro exceptioni, quâ ad eum facit Becanus & qui Clarissimus quidem Iurisconsultus, ex quo Rolwcydus suam formam exceptionem, quod è Iurisperitorum sit legione; sed quoque Episcopus fuit, & Institutionem scripsit Catholicam. Omnium maxime se prodit ad testimonium illud Simanchæ Robertus Sweertius, Disiert. de fide haret. serv. sect. ix. qui illa intelligenda dicit, non de Republica, aut Principe aliquo fidem dante, sed de privato homine, ita ut servatus sit: ad hæreticorum privatorum & particularium personarum pœnam & odium pertinet, quod fides illis à privatis quoque Catholicis data servanda non sit. Lego enim Iureconsultos aliquos (vide illos citatos apud Vdalricum Zazium apologia ad Ioannem Eckium) affirmare fidem hæretico à privato Catholico datam servandam non esse, idque ex eo capite, quod velint hostili publico fidem à privato datam, nullam ac irritam esse &c. Vnde infert: neque poterit, ex sententia quorundam Iurisperitorum, privatus homo militans in castris Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, injussu ducis sui Pontificis privato haretico fidem dare, cum unquam licitum videatur cum adversa parte communicare vel pacisci. Sic illi bene an male, non disputo. Sunt enim Iureconsulti omnes quibus Simancha annumerandus. Sed nec jam adeo quaerimus, quid verum, & utrum bene an male doceatur, ac de facto, num, & quid doceatur. Id est, inter Pontificios doceri, juramenta & foedera cum haereticis inita, ideo quod videntur haeretici, rescindi posse: jam (uti videmus) inter privatos etiam: omnemque horum fidem pendere ex arbitrio & beneplacito Pontificis. Nam, ubi Plancius dixisset: die jodes, nonne in confesso est apud vos, Principi haretico aut excommunicato fidem nullam deberi, ubi Pontifex jusserit? Gratian. cauf. 15. qu. 9. & Decret. tit. 7. cap. 5. & ibi glossa. respondet Sweertius aperte, & immediate: In confesso est: nec inventus est hactenus magni nominis Theologus, qui non in hanc terit sententiam. & Clarus lib. v. sent. sententiam illam frequentiori Doctorum calculo receptam dicit; & Tiberius Decianus, omnium consensu quoque ait illam obtinere, de fide haereticis non servanda: quorum & plurium hanc in rem testimonia collegit (ne Iacobum Cappellum dicam, adversus Rosweydum, in praefatiuncula, vel, a quo cum Iesuita Antverpiano, primum hujus certaminis initium fuit, a. MDCXVII Danielem Plancium, qui Elenchi pag. 7. adduxerat in istam sententiam Episcopum Simancham, & quos hic testes allegat, Marium Salomonium, & Menochium. Denique Thomam 22. qu. 70. art. 1.) diligentissimus Theologus, Iohannes Gerhardi, Confess. Cathol. lib. 1. part. 11. cap. XIX. quem Scriptorem, ob copiam quam nobis in Papisticis controversiis, multifaria sua lectione praebet ex variis Auctoribus, in omnibus consulendum semper dico, videndumque ut post ipsum alia quis adferat. Thuanus lib. LXIII narrat, ada. MDCLXXXVII passim & publice pro concione Doctores Pontificios clamitasse, Magistratum ad fidem haereticis servandam non teneri, juxta decretum Constantiensis Concilii. Eodemque effugio sponsalia inita inter Caesaris Caroli V. filium, & Electoris Saxoniae filium Iohannem Fridericum rupta fuisse, legato Caesaris Haumart mani aperte dicente : hæreticis fidem servandam non esse, referunt Sleidanus, & Scultetus, ad A.cIↄ Iↄ xxvii. Aliter quidem nunc disputant, vel disputare videri volunt Iesuitæ, & incrustatores Papismi, Becanus, Molanus, Sweertius, Rosweydus, ęgregue ferunt ipsis thesim illam opponi; sed uti illud gratum nobis, quod hoc à Nostris correpti dedidicerunt, saltem ne ita simpliciter thesim illam tueantur, quam adeo nolumus invitis obtrudere, (invitis nobis ac reluctantibus inquit Rob. Sweertius, pag. 15.) ut consensum nobiscum illis ex animo gratulemur, si consensus animorum verus sit, ita ab aliis communiter illam arreptam defensamque sententiam fuisse jam indicavimus: denique & magnâ prudentia Nostris opus esse in iis, quæ cum Papistis agitant & tractant, ne quando juramento nos fallant, vel illa opinionum varietas & inconstantia satis docet. Et quidquid sit communiter de Pontificiis, qui thesim illam forte improbent, pauci ex illis erunt, non certe illi qui super hac opinione multum disputant, quin ubi Papa edixerit, fidem hæreticis non esse servandam, vel omnes eam facile sint violaturi, neque negaturi penes Papam potestatem esse ut disponendi de juramento, ita speciatim hoc quod apud hæreticos interpositum, negligere hac etiam de causa licere. Vt ita sive thesim illam ajant, vel negent, æque incerti adhuc hæreamus super fœderibus iisdem initis, quamdiu & solvi à Papis illa posse, vel ex acceptâ hæresis causa, statuunt. Etquis non videt hanc in Bullâ servatam methodum ab Innocentio ? rumpit pacis fœdera, utcumque juramentis & quavis firmitate stabilita, & inter causas primas vidimus fuisse ei alterius partis hæresim, & quæ hæreticis per pacem videbantur accedere, ob quæ sc. pacem pronunciet irritam & nullam. Neq; ad illud quod ex Offato, de Papa; & de Papisticis Doctoribus, ex Thuano adduximus, respondari potest simplici negatione, quasi inaudita in Ecclesia Romana esset opinio, de frangenda hæreticis fide, neque dicta neque scripta unquam, inquit Rosweydus, pag. 2. Dissertat. de fide hæreticis servanda, contra Plancium.
units.tr: Who would not rightly shudder at such diabolical axioms and dogmas of the Pope? For this man teaches what it is lawful to do, and no one on our side writes this about the Pope, but Ossat, to the King's counsellor de Villeroy. I will argue simply here: I ask all the Papists, and the Cardinals themselves, whether the Pope sins when he teaches that it is lawful by right to lie, deceive and betray. Does he not then err shamefully and gravely, so as to be a danger to human society? Or what spirit leads him, and what kind of spirit does he follow, when he sets forth such abominable examples, like this one of the Duke of Urbino, who said that it was shameful for a common man or a nobleman to deceive with words, but not so for a prince? Will this man be infallible for us, or the judge and arbiter of religion? Ossat writes that he had indeed many things ready to answer, I had only too much to reply to all that, but that he judged it not advisable to dwell on them for long. Meanwhile, however, it is useful to hear his judgment of the Pope at the end of the letter, chiefly for us, to whom it matters greatly to know the Popes intimately, and also for all prudent men, for Ossat was a man of very keen mind: The hatred he bears, he speaks of the Pope, towards the heretics carries him so far that he lets slip from his mouth, though under another's name, pernicious maxims unworthy of any good man; and through the same hatred he has allowed himself to be persuaded by the Spaniards of whatever they wished. Then: and his Holiness finds good all ways of separating his Majesty from his allies, because they are not Catholics and do not acknowledge the holy see, even though those ways were infamous and harmful to his Majesty and to his kingdom. Who could expose and describe the Popes better than this, by the very fact of such intimate admission to the Pope's confidence, than the Pope's own brother? But who would not spit on all the men of this order or see, the scourges and plagues of mankind and of human society? To urge princes, to press them to break covenants, and, having put forward the worst examples, to wander beyond the bounds of honesty, let alone of religion? Add Ossat's letter 5, book 1, where on the same subject, namely the dissolving of the King's covenant with the Queen of England, he strongly disapproves. I say nothing of what he openly complains of in book 11, letter 77, that fraud was committed in the bull of the King's absolution, to the grave prejudice of the King and kingdom, and that many things were inserted in it against faith, otherwise than had been signed on both sides in the articles. I now understand how such qualities fall to a man who might become Pope, such as Perron ascribes to the Cardinal of Tuscany, when others tried to elect him Pope, in place of Leo XI: a man who had not led a strictly exemplary life, quick to anger, and accustomed to speak unseemly words and to other ill-fitting habits, not only for a head of the Church but for any person whatever. I will not repeat older instances, among which many such things about Popes are well known to stand out. And yet such will be the heads of the Church, and the foundations of faith, and the judges of religion! God forbid that we should ever entrust that dear life of our souls [ψυχῶν] to such men. The Popes' perfidy is evident in three things: 1. that they annul any oaths whatever, wherever they seem less suited to themselves and their state; II. covenants made with heretics (as they call them), since they think these prejudice them; III. when they absolve subjects from the oath of fidelity to their princes and magistrates. That they do not consider only the cause of heresy here is shown by the present bull, which annuls the peace, sworn to not only with the Swede but also with the Frenchman. Let those now go and dispute about the opinion of the Roman Church and the Popes on keeping faith with heretics, since the Pope in this bull does not wish that faith to be kept even by the Roman Pontifical men, let alone by us. And from those things anyone may judge the answer of Martin Becanus, the Jesuit, to the Calvinists' (as he likes to call them) fifth aphorism: the constitutions of emperors, kings, princes and other orders, agreed pacts, capitulations, fraternities, and grants by which a religion other than the present Roman Catholic one is permitted, must be held as invalid and altogether null, even if oaths have intervened. In reply to this proposition he says: the whole aphorism is pure lie. I appoint each reader as judge, to see whether it does not follow from our bull, and from what we say here about it, that all that answer or denial of Becanus is mere evasion and, to use his own word, a lie. As for keeping faith with heretics, there is no need to draw this contention from the Acts of the Council of Constance, or to show from various testimonies of Papist teachers that they teach this, namely that faith is not to be kept with heretics, in no way, in no way, in no way, that faith is to be kept with heretics even if it has been confirmed by oath. The Bishop of Pacensis, Simancha, cries out, adding that this pertains to the punishment and hatred of heretics. Here I meet the objection to which Becanus, and the most distinguished jurist, Rolwcydus, from whom he took his form of objection, appeals, namely that he is one of the legion of jurists; yet he was also a bishop and wrote a Catholic Institution. Robert Sweertius most of all betrays himself in regard to Simancha's testimony, in his dissertation on keeping faith with heretics, section 9, who says that those words must be understood not of a commonwealth or of some prince giving faith, but of a private man, so that it is kept: it pertains to the punishment and hatred of heretics, private and particular persons, that faith given to them even by private Catholics need not be kept. For I read that some jurists (see those cited by Udalricus Zasius in his apology to John Eck) affirm that faith given to a heretic by a private Catholic is not to be kept, and this on the ground that faith given by a private person to a public enemy is null and void, and so on. From this they infer: nor, according to the opinion of certain jurists, can a private man, serving in the camp of the Catholic Church, without the order of his leader the Pontiff, give faith to a private heretic, since it never seems lawful to communicate or make terms with the opposing party. Whether they say this well or badly I do not dispute. For all the jurists are such that Simancha may be counted among them. But nor now do we ask what is true, or whether it is taught well or badly, but what in fact is taught and whether it is taught at all. That is, it is taught among the Papists that oaths and covenants entered into with heretics may be rescinded for the reason that they seem heretical; and now (as we see) among private persons too; and all their faith depends on the will and pleasure of the Pontiff. For when Plancius had said: come now, is it not admitted among you that no faith is owed to a heretical or excommunicated prince, when the Pontiff has ordered it? Gratian, cause 15, question 9, and Decretals, title 7, chapter 5, and the gloss there, Sweertius answers plainly and directly: It is admitted: nor has any theologian of great name been found until now who has not gone into this opinion; and Clarus, book 5 of the Sentences, says that this opinion is received by the more frequent count of the doctors; and Tiberius Decianus also says that it holds by the consensus of all, on the matter of not keeping faith with heretics. Of these and many more testimonies on this point he gathered a collection (not to mention James Cappellus, against Rosweyd, in the little preface, or from whom the first beginning of this contest came with the Antwerp Jesuit in 1617, who had cited Daniel Plancius, in his Elenchus, page 7, Bishop Simancha in that opinion, and the witnesses he here cites, Marius Salomonius and Menochius). Finally, the most diligent theologian John Gerhard, Confessio Catholica, book 1, part 2, chapter 19, whom I always say must be consulted in all matters, because of the abundance he offers us in Papist controversies, from his many-sided reading of various authors, and whose position must be looked at so that someone else may bring forward something after him. Thuanus, book 63, relates that in 1587 Popish teachers openly and publicly cried out from the pulpit that the magistrate is not bound to keep faith with heretics, according to the decree of the Council of Constance. And by the same evasion, the betrothal entered into between the son of Emperor Charles V and John Frederick, son of the Elector of Saxony, was broken, the Emperor's envoy Haumart openly declaring that faith is not to be kept with heretics; Sleidanus and Scultetus report this under the year 1527. Now the Jesuits and the defenders of Papism, Becanus, Molanus, Sweertius, Rosweyd, argue differently, or wish to seem to argue differently; and they bring forward that thesis against us, which is pleasing to us, since those who are rebuked by our side have unlearned it; at least they do not defend that thesis so simply, which we are unwilling to force upon the unwilling, (unwilling and reluctant on our part, says Rob. Sweertius, page 15), so that we may heartily rejoice in their agreement with us, if the agreement of minds is true. But as we have already shown, that opinion has been commonly seized upon and defended by others. And finally, great prudence is needed by us in those matters which we handle and discuss with Papists, lest at some time they deceive us with an oath; that variety and inconstancy of opinions teaches enough. And whatever is commonly held about the Papists, if some of them perhaps disapprove that thesis, they will be few, and certainly not those who dispute much about this opinion, but rather, when the Pope has decreed that faith is not to be kept with heretics, they will all easily break it, nor will they deny that the Pope has power to dispose of an oath, and so, specifically, that it is lawful to neglect even an oath made with heretics on this ground. So whether they affirm or deny that thesis, we remain equally uncertain about the covenants themselves, as long as they decide that those covenants can be dissolved by the Popes, either on account of an alleged heresy. And who does not see that Innocent has observed this method in the bull? He breaks the covenants of peace, however firmly established by oaths and by any security, and among the first causes we have seen was the heresy of the other party, and that things which seemed to accrue to the heretics through the peace, on account of which he pronounces the peace void and null. Nor can what we have adduced from Ossat about the Pope, and from Thuanus about Papist teachers, be answered by a simple denial, as if the opinion of breaking faith with heretics were unheard of in the Roman Church, neither said nor written at any time, says Rosweyd, page 2, of his dissertation on keeping faith with heretics, against Plancius.
