units.la: Et primus ille Iesuita, qui cum Plancio telam hanc exorsus fuit: haereticis servandam fidem unamini consensu & voce docet Ecclesia Catholica. Iesuita Becanus constanter Catholici docent, servandam esse. Nam quaestio quum hic duplex sit, altera juris, an fides haereticis servanda sit? quam videri volunt hodie nobilcum affirmare Pontificii, & multis confirmare; facti altera, circa sententiam Ecclesiae Romanae, annon hic sint, & fuerint, qui secus doceant? hoc adeo liquidum; ex dictis, factisque, ut praeterquam ex aliis, ex illorum etiam disputationibus, qui ignominiam illam ab Ecclesia sua abluere satagunt, & maculam emendare, confirmare in proclivi sit. Becanus, Opusc. Theolog. Tom. II. responsurus ad objectum canonem Gregorii IX. qui est Decretal. lib. v. tit. VII de Haereticis. c. ult. Absolutos se noverint a debito fidelitatis domini & totius obsequii, quicunque lapsis manifeste in haeresim aliquo pacto quacumque firmitate vallato tenebantur adstricti. ita hoc solvit, inter Quaestiones Miscell. post lib. de fide haereticis servanda, pag. 120. Quomodo ergo Gregorius docit, Haereticis non deberi fidelitatem, & obedientiam a subditis? Dicam. Gregorius novam poenam constituit in haereticos sui temporis, quae nec ex natura rei, nec jure divino constituta, & determinata erat. Hae autem poena fuit legitime constituta pro illo tempore. Resp. I. bene dicit, disputavitque multis Becanus, quod nec ex natura rei, nec jure divino sequatur, ut haereticis non servetur fides: ergo certe Papa contrarium constituens, id decernit, quod est praeter naturam rei, & jus divinum. Imo & contra: nam quum jus divinum jubeat, fidem omnibus servare, haereticis non minus quam catholicis, uti inquit ipse, aliter qui jubet, divinae legi repugnare convincitur. Per ipsa Becani verba, cap. VII pag. 35. „Ratio sumitur ex dictis. Nam virtutes illae, ex quibus oritur „obligatio servandae fidei in promissis, equae nos obligant, si„ ve apud Catholicos, sive apud haereticos versemur. Nulquam „enim licet mentiri; nusquam jus alterius violare; nusquam „injustitiam committere; nusquam perjurum esse. Et sane; „si semel concedas, haec ideo licite fieri, quia haeretico men„tiris, hæretici jus violas, hæretico injuriam facis, hæretico „perjurus es; quid ni consequenter dicas, licere tibi hæreti„cum occidere, furto res ejus auferre, odio eum prosequi? „quæ omnia absurda sunt, & divinæ legi repugnantia. Hæc „ratio confirmari potest ex iis, quæ supra dixi, in hunc mo„dum. Quæ intrinsecè & ex natura sua sunt mala & illicita, „nunquam bene & licitè fieri possunt, quocunque prætextu „fiant: atqui mendacium, violatio juris alterius, injustitia, & „perjurium, intrinsecè & ex natura sunt mala & illicita: Ergo „nunquam bene & licite fieri possunt, quocunque prætextu „fiant. Ergo sive apud hæreticos sis mendax, perfidus, inju„stus, & perjurus; æquè reus es & æquali scelere obstringeris.
units.tr: And the first Jesuit who began this web with Plancius: "The Catholic Church teaches with one united consent and voice that faith is to be kept with heretics." The Jesuit Becanus teaches that Catholics constantly hold that it must be kept. For the question is twofold: one of right, whether faith is to be kept with heretics, which the Papists today wish to affirm with us and confirm with many arguments; and one of fact, concerning the opinion of the Roman Church, whether there are not, and have not been, some who teach otherwise. This is so clear from words and deeds that, besides other sources, it is easily confirmed from the disputations of those who strive to wash that disgrace from their Church and to remove the stain. Becanus, in Opusc. Theolog. Tom. II, responding to the objected canon of Gregory IX, which is Decretal. book v, title VII, On Heretics, last chapter: "Let them know that they are absolved from the debt of fidelity and of all obedience to a lord, whoever had been bound to those who have manifestly fallen into heresy, by any pact however firmly secured." He solves it thus, among the Miscellaneous Questions after the book on the faith to be kept with heretics, p. 120: "How then does Gregory teach that heretics are not owed fidelity and obedience from their subjects? I will say. Gregory established a new penalty against the heretics of his time, which was neither constituted nor determined by the nature of the thing or by divine law. This penalty, however, was legitimately established for that time." Response I: Becanus rightly says, and argues at length, that it does not follow from the nature of the thing or from divine law that faith is not to be kept with heretics. Certainly, then, the Pope, in decreeing the contrary, decrees what is beyond the nature of the thing and beyond divine law. Indeed, on the contrary: since divine law commands that faith be kept with all, "no less with heretics than with Catholics," as he himself says, whoever commands otherwise is shown to be opposed to the divine law. In Becanus's own words, chap. VII, p. 35: "The reasoning is drawn from what has been said. For those virtues from which arises the obligation to keep faith in promises bind us equally, whether we live among Catholics or among heretics. For it is never lawful to lie, never to violate another's right, never to commit injustice, never to be perjured. And indeed, if you once concede that these things are done lawfully because you lie to a heretic, violate a heretic's right, do him wrong, or are perjured toward a heretic, why not consistently say that it is lawful for you to kill a heretic, steal his goods, or pursue him with hatred? All of which are absurd and repugnant to divine law. This reasoning can be confirmed from what I said above, in this way: whatever is intrinsically and by its nature evil and unlawful can never be done well and lawfully, under whatever pretext it is done. But lying, violation of another's right, injustice, and perjury are intrinsically and by nature evil and unlawful. Therefore they can never be done well and lawfully, under whatever pretext they are done. Therefore, whether you lie, are faithless, unjust, and perjured among heretics, you are equally guilty and bound by an equal crime."

units.la: „Secundo confirmatur ex Scripturis in hunc modū &c. Ergo absurdum habetur, & divinæ Legi repugnans, & intrinsecè & ex natura sua malum & illicitum, quodq; nunquam bene & licite fieri potest, quocunq; prætextu fiat, ut fidem hæretico negemus: quare nec à Papa, nec sive pro tempore tale aliquid, legitime constitutum dicere alibi Auctor potest. II. Patet, quod quomodocunq; contrarium legi divinæ & justitiæ sciant Papani esse, ut fides frangatur hæreticis, & disputent hoc non licere, tamen ad Papam recurrendo, huic facile potestatem concedunt & frangendi fidem, & ut frangatur ab aliis, edicendi.
units.tr: "Secondly, it is confirmed from the Scriptures in this manner, etc. Therefore it must be held absurd, repugnant to divine law, and intrinsically and by its nature evil and unlawful, and something that can never be done well and lawfully under whatever pretext, that we should deny faith to a heretic. Wherefore the author cannot elsewhere say that any such thing was legitimately constituted by the Pope or by any temporal authority. II. It is plain that, however much the Papists know that breaking faith with heretics is contrary to divine law and justice, and however much they dispute that it is not lawful, yet by appealing to the Pope they readily grant him the power both to break faith and to order that it be broken by others."

units.la: Quod quousque tenent, nobis perinde est, sive disputent fidem hæreticis datam violari posse, simpliciter; sive ex arbitrio Papæ, qui novimus quam annexa Papali authoritati sint illorum fides, & anima, & omnia; vel dum, non à solo Papa, sed Clero, & Concilio etiam fidem data solvi posse disputant.
units.tr: As long as they hold this, it makes no difference to us whether they argue that faith given to heretics may simply be violated, or that it may be violated at the discretion of the Pope, whom we know to be the one to whose authority their faith, their souls, and everything else are closely bound; or whether they argue that given faith can be dissolved not by the Pope alone but also by the clergy and even by a Council.

units.la: Vti Iesuita Antverpianus, qui super hac quæstione primum certamen cum Plancio Ministro Ecclesiæ, & Scholæ Rectore Delfis, iniit, ad objectum decretum Concilii Constantiensis, respondit: Cæsar obsignavit, Christianus orbis resignavit. Vides, signatam fidem Huffo à Cæsare, solutam & resignatam agnoisci, & non ita aliud egisse Imperatore, & Synodum, ut non super ide quod Imperator consignarat, disposuerit Synodus, & huic aliter viso, soluta fuerit fides Huflo ab Imperatore solenniter data. III. Quod ait Iesuita, in poenam sic constitui, maxime temerarium: nam non potest id in poenam constitui, in quo committitur manifestum peccatum, mendacium & perjurium. Aliud est, ut in poena ponatur, ne quis de cetero huic aut illi fidem det: at ut bene datam & servandam licite, non praestet, & hoc, ceu quaevis alia, poenae nomen induat, absonum merito videtur. Quod si dicas, solvi fidem in re injustā hoc ut poenae loco statuatur, vel ab alio superiore edicatur, non necesse, neque exspectandum est, quum res ipsa fidem ibi nullam agnoscat, & juramentum non tenet, non ex poena aliqua, ab alio hic statuta, sed ex culpa, quae juramento adhaeret: ut hinc solutio objectionis tum petenda fit, non inde. Istud de servanda haereticis fide, vel neganda, tripliciter accipitur, vel ut inter privatos, de re quavis; vel inter Principes, de Foederibus; vel inter Subditos & Magistratus, de fidelitate, & obedientia. Postremum hoc variis locis & temporibus a Papis tentatum fuisse, neque ita pridem in Anglia, & Gallia, cuivis notum. Verum uti in Gallia Extravagantiis illis Paparum, a Politicis, & Doctis quibusque acriter reclamatum; ita in Anglia quoque multi ex Pontificiis non audienda ea Papae Brevia, quae juramento fidelitatis Regi exhibendo derogarent, censuerunt, interque illos praecipuus Georgius Blacvellus, cujus haec a. cI⁠ↄ lxcvii. d. III Iulii, professio: quod & Iacobum Regem agnosceret legitimum, & statueret insuper, neque posse Romanum Pontificem vel a se, vel ullius authoritatis vi ab Ecclesia aut Sede Romana acquisitae, vel alia quavis ratione etiam cum aliis conjuncta, Regem deponere, aut de ipsius vel dominiis disponere, vel extraneo cuivis Principi ipsum, aut ipsius territoria invadendi aut infestandi potestatem facere; vel ex suis subditis quemlibet a fide atque obedientia Majestati suae debita exauthorare; vel illorum cuipiam facultatem permittere arma in eum gerendi, tumultus ciendi, aut Majestatis suae personae, statui, regimini, vel subditis suis, intra dicionis suae ambitum, vim aut noxam inferendi. Item ex a,,nimo juro, quod non obstante qualibet declaratione, five ,,sententia Excommunicationis aut Privationis facta vel con,,cessa, aut facienda vel concedenda per Papam aut ejus suc,,cessores, vel cujusvis authoritatis vi ab ipso aut ab ejus Sede ,,derivatæ, vel derivari prætensæ contra prædictum Regem, ,,illiusve hæredes, aut successores, vel quavis dictorum sub,,ditorum à sua obedientia exauthoratione, ego tamen fidem ,,& fyncerum obsequium Majestati suæ ac ejus hæredibus & ,,successoribus præstabo. Porro etiam juro me ex animo ab,,jurare execrabilem hanc doctrinam & assertionem: Princi,,pes à Papa excommunicatos, vel jure Regali exutos, licite ,,posse à subditis suis vel quocunque alio, Regno vel etiam ,,vita privari. Quinetiam credo & certa conscientia teneo, ,,neque Papam, neque quemvis alium posse me ab hoc jura,,mento, vel ulla ejus particula absolvere. Qualem etiam fidelitatis professionem antea Elisabethæ Reginæ a. cIↄ Iↄ c I I. multi ex secularibus Sacerdotibus ; in quos primus Guiljelmus Bishop, dederunt. Atque pro juramento fidelitatis, à Papistis etiam Regi deferendo, multi ex Pontificiis moderatioribus (ne Regem, vel Regiarum, nostrarumque partium Scriptores dicam) steterunt: Wilhelmus Warmington, Anglice scripsit, à Moderate defence of the oath of allegiance, & (quod nequaquam prætereundum duxi) pag. 127. probat à Sixto v. habitam in Consistorio Romæ a.cIↄ Iↄ lxxxix d. xI Septembris illam orationem de Henrici III. morte, gratulatoriam, quæ extat in Anti-Sixto, & quam Bellarminus, aliique Papales negant veram esse, quæ incipit: Animo meo sæpe, ac serio revolvens, mentisque actem intendens in ea, quæ nuper Dei voluntate acciderunt, videor mihi verè posse illud Prophetæ Abacuch usurpare: Quia opus factum est in diebus vestris, quod nemo credet, cum narrabitur. Mortuus est Rex Francorum per manus Monachi. Nam ad istud potest recte applicari: licet de alia re, nempe de incarnatione Domini, quæ omnia mira, ac mirabilia superat, Propheta proprie locutus sit. *Et deinde: Atque nos, dolentes sane, aliquoties prædiximus fore, ut quemadmodum erat sanitum & exemptionis, qua juramento alios facile solvunt Papæ, & reverentia Optimatibus debita. Sed uti jam diu pro perfidiæ sede celebrari Roma cæpit, ita Germanis propria hactenus laus mansit sinceritatis ac constantiæ, adeo ut si toto orbe exularet rerum promissarum fides, apud Imperatorem tamé consistere oportere, bene dixerit Carolus V. Principi eum interroganti, eccur Lutherum Wormatia sic sivisset abire, & non potius homini hæretico fefellisset? fidem illa præclara vox, inquit Becanus; & merito, & digna Catholico Imperatore! Pejor Campanella, is lib. de Monarchi: Hispaniæ cap. xxvi 1. de illo Imperatoris erga Lutherum facto, & fide verba faciens, inquit: recte quidem Luthero fidem servavit in ipsis Comitiis, at post in domitione illum eundem opprimere debuisset. Ipseque Scioppius, monstrum hominis, & quod de Tiberio olim, lutum sanguine maceratum, in præfat. ad Classicum Sacrum, non omisit dicere, Sacris enim conventis stare Catholicorum hominum, maxime Germanorum est officium. Et hæc nostra doctrina est, fidem sacrosanctam ubique esse oportere, neque alicui fallendam, non quamlibet damnum tibi inde oriatur. Psalm. xv. 4. præsertim inter Principes hoc debere esse ἀμεμπτοι, Heb. vi. 17. 18. Theologi Belgæ, in epistola ad Iohannem Nassovium, Gubernatorem Geldriæ scripta, præcedenti sæculo, circa annum octuagesimum, quæ inter Epistolas Illustrium Belgarum est, Centur. II. pag. 844. adeo hanc ἀτιμίαν detestantur ac condemnant etiam quâ quis non stet promissis datis Pontificiis, de toleranda illorum religione, (videlicet quando pacta ejus præcesserunt, quæ non ipsi fregerint, vel quo temerarint modo) ut ei caulam affigunt regnorum & Imperiorum multorum perditorum: Et sane videmus plerumque Regum ac populorum vol potentissimorum interitus hanc esse causam, quod vel principes impotentes dominandi libidine, vel populi lasciviente protervia, hæc fæderum & sponsionum publicarum sapta non verentur transfilire. Nota toti Christianismo, & nunqua non dolenda strages ad Varnam illa, qua Vladislao Hungariæ Rege,
units.tr: Thus the Antwerp Jesuit, who first took up battle on this question with Plancius, minister of the Church and rector of the school at Delft, answered the objection concerning the decree of the Council of Constance: The Emperor sealed it; the Christian world unsealed it. You see that the faith pledged to Huss by the Emperor is acknowledged as undone and cancelled, and that the Emperor and the Synod did not act so differently that the Synod did not dispose of the matter on which the Emperor had set his seal, and that, once this was judged otherwise, the faith solemnly given to Huss by the Emperor was dissolved. III. What the Jesuit says, that this was imposed as a punishment, is most rash. For nothing can be imposed as a punishment when a manifest sin, lying and perjury, is committed in it. It is one thing to be laid down as a penalty that no one should in future give faith to this or that person; but that a faith rightly given should not be kept lawfully, and that this should take on the name of punishment like anything else, seems rightly absurd. But if you say that faith is dissolved in an unjust matter, and that this is set down as a penalty or decreed by some other superior, there is no need or call to wait for this, since the thing itself acknowledges no faith there and does not keep the oath; it is not from some penalty imposed here by another, but from the fault that clings to the oath. So the answer to the objection must be sought from this, not from that. This matter of keeping or refusing faith to heretics is taken in three ways: between private persons, about any matter whatever; between princes, concerning covenants; and between subjects and magistrates, concerning fidelity and obedience. That this last has been attempted by the Popes at various places and times, and not so long ago in England and France, is known to everyone. But just as in France those Extravagants of the Popes were fiercely protested against by the Politicians and by all the learned, so in England too many of the Papists judged that those Papal Briefs, which would detract from the oath of fidelity to be given to the King, were not to be heeded; and among them the chief was George Blackwell, whose profession, dated 3 July 1607, was this: that he acknowledged James as the lawful King, and further declared that the Roman Pontiff could not, either by his own power or by the force of any authority acquired from the Church or the Roman See, or by any other reason even conjoined with others, depose the King, or dispose of his lordships, or give to any foreign prince the power of invading or harassing him or his territories; nor could he release any of his subjects from faith and obedience owed to His Majesty, or grant to any of them the right to bear arms against him, to stir up tumults, or to inflict violence or harm on His Majesty's person, government, or subjects within the bounds of his dominion. Likewise I swear from my heart that, notwithstanding any declaration or sentence of excommunication or deprivation made or granted, or to be made or granted, by the Pope or his successors, or by any authority derived or supposedly derived from him or from his See, against the aforesaid King or his heirs or successors, or against any release of the said subjects from their obedience, I will nonetheless pay faith and sincere obedience to His Majesty and his heirs and successors. Further, I swear from my heart that I abjure this execrable doctrine and assertion: that princes excommunicated by the Pope or stripped of their royal right may lawfully be deprived of their realm, or even of their life, by their subjects or by anyone else. Moreover I believe, and hold with a certain conscience, that neither the Pope nor anyone else can absolve me from this oath, or from any part of it. Many of the secular priests, against whom the first was William Bishop, likewise made such a profession of fidelity earlier, in the year 1602, to Queen Elizabeth. And in support of the oath of fidelity to be rendered to the King even by Papists, many of the more moderate Papists (I say nothing of the writers of the King's and of our party) have stood firm: William Warmington, who wrote in English, A Moderate Defence of the Oath of Allegiance, and (which I thought must by no means be passed over) at page 127 he proves that Sixtus V delivered in consistory at Rome, on 11 September 1589, that oration on the death of Henry III, a congratulatory one, which is found in the Anti-Sixtus, and which Bellarmine and other Papalists deny to be genuine; it begins: Turning over in my mind often and seriously, and directing the attention of my thoughts to those things which lately came to pass by the will of God, I seem to myself truly able to use the words of the Prophet Habakkuk: "For a work is done in your days which no one will believe when it is told." The King of the French has died by the hand of a monk. For this can rightly be applied to it, although the Prophet spoke properly of another matter, namely the incarnation of the Lord, which surpasses all wonderful and marvellous things. *And then: "And we, truly grieved, have several times foretold that there would be, as there was, sanctioned and exempt, a means by which others easily release themselves from an oath, namely the Pope, and the reverence due to the nobles. But just as Rome has now long begun to be celebrated as the seat of perfidy, so the Germans have hitherto kept their own praise of sincerity and constancy, so that if the faith of promises were to be banished from the whole world, it ought nevertheless to remain with the Emperor," Charles V spoke well when, asked by a prince why he had let Luther go from Worms in this way and had not rather deceived that heretic man?" An excellent saying, says Becanus, and rightly so, and worthy of a Catholic Emperor! Worse is Campanella, who in his book on the Monarchy of Spain, chapter 26, speaking of that act of the Emperor towards Luther and of faith, says: Indeed he kept faith with Luther at the very Diet, but afterwards in the subjugation he ought to have crushed him. And Scioppius himself, a monster of a man, who once, as was said of Tiberius, was mud steeped in blood, did not omit to say in the preface to the Sacred Classic: For it is the duty of Catholic men, and especially of the Germans, to abide by sacred agreements. And this is our doctrine: that sacred faith must everywhere be kept, and must not be broken to anyone, however much loss may arise from it to you. Psalm 15:4; especially that among princes this should be blameless [ἀμεμπτοι], Heb. 6:17, 18. The Belgian theologians, in a letter written to John of Nassau, governor of Gelderland, in the previous century, around the year 1580, which is among the Letters of the Illustrious Belgians, Centur. II, p. 844, so detest and condemn this dishonour [ἀτιμίαν], even where someone does not abide by promises given to the Papists about tolerating their religion (namely when their pacts came first, and they themselves did not break them, or broke them in some reckless way), that they assign to it as cause the ruin of many kingdoms and empires: And indeed we see that for the most part the destruction of kings and peoples, whether very powerful, has this cause: that either princes, impotent through lust for domination, or peoples, wantonly insolent, do not hesitate to leap over these sacred covenants and public pledges. Known to all Christendom, and a slaughter never to be lamented enough, is that at Varna, where Ladislaus, King of Hungary,

units.la: gc. ge, suasu Iuliani Cardinalis (Bonfinium vide, Rerum Vngarie. Decad. iii.lib. vi.pag. 459) fœdus cum Amurate Turcarum Rege frangente, & in acie cū luis misere cæso,res Christiana Turcis in prædam cessit, & hi tot locorum ditionumque domini, oppressis quaquaversum delectisque Christianis, evaserunt, tantoque exemplo docuerunt, quod in epitaphio Vladislai inde celebratum:
units.tr: at the persuasion of Cardinal Julian (see Bonfinius, Rerum Ungaricarum, Decad. III, book 6, p. 459), broke the treaty with Murad, King of the Turks, and, having been wretchedly cut down in the battle with his troops, the Christian army was given up as prey to the Turks; and these, having overwhelmed and cut down the Christians on every side, became masters of so many places and lands, and by so great an example taught what is celebrated in the epitaph of Ladislaus made thereafter:

units.la: Discite mortales non temerare fidem.
units.tr: Learn, mortals, not to violate faith rashly.

units.la: Me nisi Pontifices jussissent rumpere fœdus,
units.tr: Had the Pontiffs not ordered me to break the treaty,

units.la: Non ferret Scythicum Pannonis ora jugum.
units.tr: The Pannonian would not have borne the Scythian yoke.

units.la: Adeo verum semper est illud Aristotelis ad Alexandrum M. monitum: perfidiæ fœdos ac sunestos nunquam non esse exitus. Quo magis videndum cuilibet homini, ut fidem temere nec det, nec frangat. Sacra res fides est, & magna juramenti religio. In Iure sæpe religio pro juramento ponitur, & ceu synonyma occurrunt juramentum & religio: adeo quid religionis homo sit vel habeat, in juramento ostendit. Præcipue in fœderibus, juramento vallatis sollicite videndum, ut fides inviolabilis existat. Iezech. xvii.15.18. Machiavelli vox est: fidem accipi & dari, ut pacta conventa deinde ex commodo rumpi ac solvi possint. lib. de Principe cap. xviii. Quid Machiavellum dico? Papas nominare debueram, Alexandros, Iulios, quorum ille, nominis scilicet ejus sextus, dicere solebat: fidem omnibus dandam, nulli servandam esse. Hic Iulius ii. se cum Gallis Germanisque, quos barbaros appellabat, pacisci quidem, sed fallendi causa. Innocentium nostrum iis annumero, qui Principes, Reges, Imperatores, quodque hic speciatim respicio, Germanos docet, monet pacemsfrangere, & fœdus, & juramentum, nempe cum hæreticis non solum, sed & in istorum aliqualem favorem, ut ipsi videtur, composita: certe nec minus ē re Romanensium. Sed si hoc urgere pergat, & in stare apud confœderatos hac pace Principes, efficere non dicam; sciat in se primum illorum iram exonerandam, & dignas sua perfidia perfidisq; monitionibus & molitionibus egregie ipsum daturum pœnas, atq;hoc pacto, dum aliter noluit, doctu-ros eum Principes, quid sit juxta vetus illud & solemne Prætoris edictum, pacta servabo. Inter Regulas juris sui respiciat lxxiii. Factum legitime retractari non debet, licet casus postea eveniat, à quo non potuit inchoari.
units.tr: So true is that warning of Aristotle to Alexander the Great, that the ends of treachery are always foul and baleful. All the more should every man see to it that he neither gives faith rashly nor breaks it. Faith is a sacred thing, and great is the sanctity of an oath. In law, religion is often put in place of oath, and oath and religion appear as synonyms: so much does a man show of what religion he is or has, in his oath. Especially in covenants, fortified by oath, one must take care that faith remains inviolable. Ezek. 17:15, 18. It is a saying of Machiavelli that faith is accepted and given so that agreed pacts may then be broken and dissolved when it suits. Book on the Prince, ch. 18. But why do I speak of Machiavelli? I should have named Popes: Alexanders, Julius, of whom the sixth of that name used to say that faith is to be given to all and kept by none. Here Julius II did make peace with the French and Germans, whom he called barbarians, but for the sake of deceiving them. I count our Innocent among those who teach princes, kings and emperors, and, what I have especially in view here, the Germans, to break peace, covenant and oath: a peace composed not only with heretics but also, as it seems to him, in some favour toward them. Certainly it is no less to the advantage of the Romanists. But if he persists in urging this, and in not allowing the princes bound together by this peace to abide by it, I will not say he will succeed. Let him know that the anger of those princes will first be discharged upon himself, and that he will pay the penalties his perfidy deserves, together with his perfidious admonitions and schemes. In this way, since he was unwilling otherwise, the princes will teach him what the old and solemn edict of the praetor means: "I will keep agreements." Among the rules of his law let him consider number 73: "What has been done lawfully ought not to be retracted, although a case arises later from which it could not have begun."

units.la: §. xviii. Denique ad formam Papalis Bullæ, quam suo motu, ex potestatis plenitudine fecisse significat (motus proprius dicitur illis, quando aliquid expeditur, non ad instantiam alterius, gl. in c. si motu proprio de præb. & dignit. in vi.) denique sic concludit: Volumus autem, ut earundem præsentium transsumpti, etiam impressis, manu Notarii publici subscriptis, & Sigillo persona in dignitate ecclesiastica constituta munitis, eadem prorsus fides ubique locorum & gentium in judiciis, & extra illud adhibeatur, quæ ipsis præsentibus adhiberetur, si forent exhibita, vel ostensa. Datum Romæ apud Sanctam Mariam majorem sub annulo Piscatoris die 26. Novembr. & solenniter ibidem publicatum 3. Jan. Anno M.DC.LI. Pontificatus Nostri octavo.) Quæ hic occurrunt sunt communium formularum, in Curia Romana observatarum. Bulla coenæ Dominicæ in fine §.24. Volentes earundem præsentium transumtis, etiam impressis, Not. publici manu subscriptis, & sigillo Judicis ordinaris Rom. Curiæ, vel alterius persona in dignitate ecclesiastica constituta munitis, eandem prorsus fidem in judicio, & extra illud ubique locorum adhibendam fore, quæ ipsis præsentibus adhiberetur, si essent exhibita, vel ostensa. Datum Romæ.
units.tr: §18. Finally, as to the form of the papal Bull, which he states he issued of his own motion, from the fullness of power (a motu proprio is said of those matters which are dispatched not at the instance of another, gloss on c. si motu proprio, de praebendis et dignitatibus, in Sexto), he concludes thus: "We wish moreover that copies of these present letters, even printed, signed by the hand of a public notary and fortified with the seal of a person constituted in ecclesiastical dignity, be given entirely the same faith everywhere, in all places and peoples, in judgments and outside them, as would be given to these present letters if they were exhibited or shown. Given at Rome, at St Mary Major, under the Fisherman's ring, on 26 November, and solemnly published there on 3 January in the year 1651, the eighth of Our pontificate." What occurs here is the common formula observed in the Roman Curia. The Bull of the Lord's Supper, at the end of §24: "Wishing that copies of these present letters, even printed, signed by the hand of a public notary and fortified with the seal of the ordinary judge of the Roman Curia or of another person constituted in ecclesiastical dignity, the same faith be given everywhere in judgment and outside it, as would be given to these present letters if they were exhibited or shown. Given at Rome."

units.la: O Roma, à Româ quantum mutata vetusta est:
units.tr: O Rome, how much changed from ancient Rome!

units.la: Nunc caput est scelerum, qua caput orbis erat.
units.tr: Now it is the head of crimes, which once was the head of the world.

units.la: Quod inter Poëmata variorum, ante ætatem nostram conscripta, & edita ab Illyrico a.cl0 lvi. de corrupto Ecclesiæ statu legitur pag.417. Ad quæ glossæ instar quid ni addam, quod dicit Thomas à Iesu Carmelita Monachus de Conversione Gentium, lib.iii.pag.112. Quinto, ne omnes, qui ad Seminarium Romanum pertinent, in ipsa urbe Româ nutriantur, ob varias causas: vident enim & audiunt aliqua scandala, tam in Ecclesiastica, quam civili vita, quæ omnino ipsis decet esse ignota.
units.tr: This is read among the poems of various authors written before our age and published by Illyricus in 1556, on the corrupt state of the Church, p. 417. To these verses, by way of gloss, why not add what Thomas à Jesu, the Carmelite monk, says in his book On the Conversion of the Gentiles, book 3, p. 112: "Fifthly, that those who belong to the Roman Seminary should not be brought up in the city of Rome itself, for various reasons: for they see and hear some scandals, both in ecclesiastical and civil life, which they ought altogether to be ignorant of."

units.la: Sub annulo Piscatoris) Petri nimirum. Imo talem vel annulum Petrus olim habuit, aut usurpavit potestatem; vel hodie Papa Piscatorem refert. Iuste. Die 26 Novemb. & publicatum d. 3. Januar. clo Io cl I.) Publicatio illa solet fieri ad valvas Ecclesiæ S. Iohannis Lateranensis, & Basilicæ S. Petri, item Cancellariæ Apostolicæ, & in acie Campi Flori. Mirarer magis, quod tam sero, & triennio fere post pacem factam a xlvIII. hæc Papæ Bulla prodeat, nisi scirem quam tarde sæpe negotia istius Curiæ procedant, de quo conquestus Ossatus in litteris ad Regem, lib. I. ep. IV. scripsit: en cette cour ils font fort formalistes, & longs en toutes choses. Quare in mandatis hoc expresse habuit Perronus, il a charge expresse de s'en revenir, s'il apperçoit que l'on veuille tirer les choses à longue. Ad quæ nihil aliud dico, quam quod est in regulis juris Bonifacii: mora sua cuilibet est nociva.
units.tr: "Under the Fisherman's ring": that is, Peter's. Indeed, Peter once had such a ring, or else he used such power; or else today the Pope is referring to the fisherman. Rightly so. "Given 26 November and published 3 January," 1651. That publication is usually made at the doors of the church of St John Lateran and the basilica of St Peter, likewise at the Apostolic Chancery and in the Campo de' Fiori. I would be more surprised that this Bull of the Pope appears so late, almost three years after the peace of 1648 was made, did I not know how slowly the business of that Curia often proceeds. Ossat complained of this in his letters to the King, book I, letter IV, writing: "In this court they are very formalistic and long-winded in everything." Hence Perron had this expressly in his instructions: "He has express charge to return home if he perceives that they wish to draw matters out at length." To which I say nothing else than what is in the rules of law of Boniface: "Delay is harmful to everyone."

units.la: §. XIX. Atque ita hactenus vidimus, quid egerit Papa, vel quid dixerit potius: bulla quippe est, quam audivimus; sed quâ ille plus quam meras bullas captat. Imperatorem, Reges Principes hac unâ committere studet, & quam concordiam inierunt, bono Reip. Christianæ, iterum diffringere. Vniri Christianorum est; Paparum, disjungere ac dissipare. Sed bene est quod in id adductæ pridem sunt Papales Bullæ pretium, ut & apud suos parum, apud alios nihili æstimentur. quippe nec aliter meritæ. Animos distrahere, pacem rumpere, lites injicere, bella inchoare ut facile, ita hoc Germaniæ, & mundi statu à Papis jam tentari, impium prorsus est: & quod olim Sorbona dixit, in appellatione, pro Concilio Basileensi, adversus Leonem x. Si quod injustum est, faciendum esse præceperit, patienter sustinere debet; si non fiat quod ei prava suggestione fuerit suggestum. Videlicet male tui sæculi Pontifices descripserit Clemanges, in epist. ad Ioh. Gersonem, quæ est epistolarum ejus xxxI. Non enim salutem ovium sed sanguinem sitiunt, non doctrinam sed ruinam, non pastum sed fastum, non ducatum sed erratum, non sanare vitia sed auferre spolia; non foetus fovere sed lac mulgere, Lanamque removere. Agrippa, lib. de vanitate scientiar. cap. lxi. Ipse Romanus Pontifex jam omnibus gravissimas & intolerabilis est, cujus pompam & fastum nullus unquam tyrannorum aquavit. Vere dixit, intolerabilis, neque quidpiam unquam minus mirari desino, quam tam patienter & ignave ferri unius Papæ arrogantiam & potestatem à Regibus, & Imperatoribus, quæ toti Christianismo adeo semper est infesta. Iusta est Octavii Menini I. C. Foro Iulieṇsis, Cenetensisque præfecti Oratio, de immensa Curia Romana potentia moderanda, ad imperii Principes, quæ incipit: Quousque tandem vestra summi Principes, humanitate incredibilique patientia Sacris institutis ordo, rerum divinarum administratione non contentus ad novam sibi potentiam comparandam, ad vestram evertendam abutetur? digna quæ hic conferatur. Excommunicare Reges & Principes jam dedoctus videtur, ubi vidit ab aliquo tempore Censuras suas ceu bruta fulmina à prudentibus & cordatis exsibilari. Et ne ultra tale quid tentet, moneo, quamvis quidem illa sedis Romanæ methodus sit, ad recuperanda bona sua à monitionibus pergere ad excommunicationem, inde ad arma. Baronius, Annal. Tom. ix. ad a. 715. num. iii. de Pontifice Gregorio ii. castrum Cumanum per Neapolitanos recuperante: Sed observa ordinem quo processit, nimirum ut primum, paternis monitionibus tem ageret; deinde, ut contemptores Ecclesiasticis censuris exterreret; demum vero, ut in eos hac omnia contemnentes ageret armis, eisque castrum expugnandum curaret. Sic Deus rem tantum aggredi voluit Pontificem & doctrina & sanctitate insignem, ejusque exemplo sanciri disciplinam, qua successores eruditi, ablata bona Ecclesiastica ab iniquis possessoribus vindicarent, etiam si opus sit armis, si catera remedia contemnantur. quibus tamen ut abstineat noster Innocentius, ego ei Auctor sum. Zuinglii verba hic usurpem, quæ ille in epistola ad Myconium, a. cIↄIxx. suadebo ut Pontificem admoneat, ne excommunicationem ferat, quod putem hoc maxime ere ejus futurum, nam si feratur, augurer, Germanos cum excommunicatione Pontificem quoque contemptuos. Hoc tum temporis Zuinglius, hodie quo magis accisa Pontificis authoritas, eo magis id verendum, vel potius optandum esset. Durandus, S.Palatii Magister tract. pro celebrando Concilio part. I. Rubric. 8. Proverbium vulgare, qui totum vult, totum perdit, unde timendum est, ne Ecclesia Romana, qua universa vendicat, universa perdat. Satis superque causarum est Germanis, vel ex praesente sola Bulla ipsum, qui ejus pacem, abrogare, ejusque nomen referre inter infames atque perduelles. Me si audiant, hoc primo fecerint: quomodo olim in Comitiis Brixiensibus, a.cIↄ lxxxvii. Kal. Iulii, Papam Gregorium vii. qui inter concordes seminavit discordiam, inter pacificos lites, inter fratres scandala, inter conjuges divortia, & quidquid quiete inter pie viventes stare videbatur, concussit, judicabant idcirco, sic loquuntur, canonice deponendum & expellendum: & nisi ab ipsa sede his auditis descenderit, in perpetuum condemnandum. Atque omnino oportEret quidem Germaniae Principes adversus hanc Papae Bullam ejusque interdictum decernere, quod Ludovicus iv. Bavarus a.cIↄ cccxxxviii. viii. Id. Augusti, adversus P. Iohannem xxii. ejus processum excommunicationis & sententias fuisse nullas, & nullos, & nullius valoris & momenti & nullatenus observandas, ac universis & singulis sub nostro Imperio degentibus, cujuscunque status, dignitatis, ac conditionis existant, discrete praecipimus & mandamus, quatenus nulla persona singularis, aut communitas vel universitas, dictas excommunicationis & interdicti sententias praesumat observare, vel facere ac sustinere quomodolibet observari. Quicunque autem contra hoc nostrum mandatum praesumpserit facere, vel venire, cum omnibus feudis, quae ab Imperio tenet, ac omnibus jurisdictionibus, gratiis, & privilegiis, libertatibus & immunitatibus, a nobis vel praedecessoribus nostris ei concessis, ex nunc privamus. Et prosecto quid ni respondeant Bullae Papali, Edicto alio illi, quorum interest suam Majestatem a petulantia & contemtu Papae vindicari, & pacis foedus servari sanctum atque inviolabile? Carolus v. vetera ut praeteream, a.cIↄ lxxxvi. prolixum & vere Imperatorium Rescriptum oppoluit Criminationibus P.
units.tr: §19. And so far we have seen what the Pope has done, or rather what he has said, for it is a bull that we have heard; yet by it he seeks more than mere bulls. He strives by this one act to commit the Emperor, kings and princes, and to shatter again the concord they have entered into, to the harm of the Christian commonwealth. It belongs to Christians to unite; it belongs to Popes to separate and scatter. But it is good that Papal bulls have long since been brought to such a price that among their own people they are of little worth and among others are valued at nothing, since they have deserved nothing else. To distract minds, break peace, stir up quarrels and start wars is as easy as it is impious for Popes to attempt in the present state of Germany and of the world. What the Sorbonne once said, in its appeal on behalf of the Council of Basel against Leo X, is apt: "If he commands that something unjust be done, he must patiently endure it; if what has been suggested to him by a wicked suggestion is not done." Clearly Clémangis, in his letter to John Gerson, which is letter 31 of his letters, described the Popes of his own age badly: "For they thirst not for the salvation of sheep but for their blood, not for teaching but for ruin, not for pasture but for pride, not for leading but for straying, not to heal vices but to carry off plunder, not to cherish the young but to milk the milk and strip off the wool." Agrippa, in On the Vanity of the Sciences, ch. 61: "The Roman Pontiff himself is now most grievous and intolerable to all; no tyrant ever equalled his pomp and pride." Rightly did he say "intolerable," and nothing do I cease to wonder at more than that the arrogance and power of one Pope should be borne so patiently and idly by kings and emperors, when it has always been so hostile to the whole of Christendom. Worth comparing here is the oration of Ottavio Menini, jurisconsult, prefect of Forlì and Cesena, On Moderating the Immense Power of the Roman Curia, addressed to the princes of the Empire, which begins: "How long at last, most high princes, will you, with your humanity and incredible patience, suffer the Pope, not content with the administration of divine things under sacred institutions, to abuse them to acquire for himself new power and to overthrow yours?" He seems already to have unlearned excommunicating kings and princes, since for some time he has seen his censures hissed off like brute thunderbolts by the prudent and sensible. And lest he attempt anything more of the kind, I advise him that, although it is indeed the method of the Roman See to recover its goods by proceeding from admonitions to excommunication and then to arms, Baronius, Annals, vol. 9, at the year 715, no. 3, on Pope Gregory II recovering the castle of Cuma from the Neapolitans, writes: "But observe the order in which he proceeded: first he acted with paternal admonitions; then he frightened the contemners with ecclesiastical censures; finally he acted with arms against those who scorned all these things, and had the castle stormed. Thus God willed that a Pontiff distinguished for learning and holiness should undertake the matter, and by his example that a discipline should be sanctioned by which learned successors might vindicate church goods taken away by unjust possessors, even by arms if the other remedies are scorned." Whether our Innocent will refrain from these measures, I am his adviser. I will borrow here the words of Zwingli, who wrote in a letter to Myconius in 1520: "I would advise that the Pope be admonished not to pronounce excommunication, since I think this would be especially to his disadvantage; for if it is pronounced, I predict the Germans will hold the Pope in contempt along with the excommunication." Zwingli said this at that time; today, the more the authority of the Pontiff has been diminished, the more this ought to be feared, or rather wished for. Durandus, Master of the Sacred Palace, in his tract on the celebration of a council, part I, rubric 8: "The common proverb: he who wants everything loses everything; whence it is to be feared that the Roman Church, which claims everything, may lose everything." There are more than enough reasons for the Germans, from this present Bull alone, to abrogate his peace and to count him among the infamous and enemies of the state. If they listen to me, they will do this first, as once at the Diet of Brixen, on the Kalends of July 1080, when they judged that Pope Gregory VII, "who sowed discord among the harmonious, strife among the peaceable, scandals among brothers, divorces among spouses, and shook whatever seemed to stand quietly among the piously living, should be canonically deposed and expelled; and unless he came down from that see after these charges had been heard, he should be condemned forever." And indeed the princes of Germany ought surely to decree against this Papal bull and its interdict, as Louis IV of Bavaria did in 1338, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, against Pope John XXII: that his process of excommunication and his sentences were null, void, of no validity or weight, and in no way to be observed; and we sharply command and order all and each living under our empire, of whatever rank, dignity or condition, that no single person, community or corporation presume to observe the said sentences of excommunication and interdict, or to do or allow them to be observed in any way. Whoever presumes to act or proceed against this our command, we deprive from now on of all fiefs he holds from the Empire, and of all jurisdictions, favours and privileges, liberties and immunities granted to him by us or our predecessors. And indeed why should other edicts not answer the Papal Bull, for those whose interest it is that their Majesty be vindicated from the insolence and contempt of the Pope, and that the covenant of peace be kept holy and inviolable? Charles V, to pass over older examples, in 1586 [as printed] set forth against the accusations of Pope Clement VII, and against his letters both to the Cardinals and to the princes of the Empire, a lengthy and truly imperial rescript, in which he vindicated his own name and imperial majesty.

units.la: ClcClementis VII. aliisque tum ad Cardinales, tum Imperii Principes epistolis nominis sui famam, & majestatem Imperatoriam vindicavit. Quomodo etiam anno seq. propria manu ad eundem Papam scripsit: quod si is se gereret bonum patrem, ipse quoque se ei probaret humillimum filium. est inter Epistolas Principum Hieron. Ruscelli. ut & haec Albani Ducis a. clo lo lvi. quando Romam obsideret, ad P. Paulum IV. Hactenus Imperator, & Rex Philippus dissimularunt dolores & injurias à Sanctitate tua perpessas. De initio Pontificatus tui, eorum subditos opprimere, persequi, & bonis suis spoliare tentasti, exinde alios principes tecum incitasti, quo dictarum Majestat. regna ac dominia occuparent. Satis indicio, ut tibi pax in bonum universi Christianissimi conclusa, displiceat; utque tibi non sufficiat consanguineos tuos, honestis mediis, distasse, quos dicta Majest. sponte de suorum bonis tibi largiuntur, &c. Conclusio haec est: Deum illum rogo, ut tot annis conservet, quot pro bono Christianismi erunt necessarii. non dicit annos multos; sed quot bono publico forent necessarii. Maximilianus II. a. clo lo lxxiii. acri edicto castigavit libellum Consiliarii sui Aulici Georgii Ederi, turbulentum, adversus pacem religionis, & in Protestantes imprimis injuriosum. Prohibet quidem Pacis nuperae Edictum, ne quis ei se opponat, vel in ejus praejudicium agat quippiam, seu Ecclesiastici ordinis sit, seu politici; & Imperator a. clo lo cl. d. xxvi I Iunii severius iterum attentata omnia & Disputationes contraventiones adversus Pacis conclusionem proscripsit. Iam quid contra Papae Bullam hanc aperta fronte in ista incurrente decreturus sit, & an eam placidis oculis sit contuiturus, passuruque tum pacem, tum majestatem suam prostitui, videbimus. Gallia praeteritorum modo, in Papales ejusmodi Bullas constitutorum, & Veterum exempla renovet oportet, quando vel a. clo cccc i. d. xxvi Iulii, duos Papae Bullistas ex arce Lupara, per Lictores, in publicum produci, & mitris chartaceis redimiri, tum plaustro stercorario per urbis compita trahi; & eodem mense paucis ante diebus, libellum Papalem coram ejus tabellariis, ex Curiae Parisiensis senatusconsulto, lacerari conspexit: vel Paparum Bullis Pragmaticas oppoluit Ludovicus ix. Philippus Pulcher, Carolus v. & vi. Vt recentius aliquod, & quod huc non male quadrat, dem exemplum: quum in Galliam allatæ essent Bullæ monitoriales Gregorii xiv. adversus R. Henricum iv. quibus mandabantur subditi,& regni Primores Henricum deserere excommunicatum,& cavere ne eum reciperent Regem,primo Curia Parlamenti Turonensis Bullas illas,& Auctorem, & Nuncium, qui illas ferebat,a.cIↄ Iↄ xcı.d.v. Augusti sic excepit: Curia constituit litterarum Complicaturam inscribi: Lecta, publicata, & in tabulas relata, audito, & hoc requirente Procuratore generali Regis. Et ratione habita reliquarum ab ipso illatarum conclusionum, declaravit & declarat Bullas Monitoriales, datas Romæ, primo die Martii 1590. nullas, abusivas, seditiosas, damnandas, impietatum & impostturarum plenas, sanctæ decretis, juribus, immunitatibus & libertatibus Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ contrarias. Constituit exempla sigillata Marcellini Landriani sigillo, à Sestiliano Lampineto subsignata, per supremum justitiæ exsecutorem lacerari, & uri, igne ad eam rem pro foribus Palatii accenso. Inhibuit & vetuit, sub crimine & pœna Læsæ Majestatis, ne quis Prælatus, Parochus, Vicarius, aut alius Ecclesiasticus ea publicet: neve quis, cuiuscunque status, qualitatis, conditionis sit, in pareat, eave habeat, aut retineat. Declaravit & declarat Gregorium, qui se Papam dicit XIIII. ejus nominis, hostem pacis & concordiæ Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Apostolicæ Romanæ, Regis Regnique, adhærentem Hispanicæ conjurationi; rebellium fautorem; reum crudelissimi omnium & inhumanissimi & maxime detestandi parricidii, commissi in personam Henrici III. Regis, felicissimæ memoriæ, Christianissimi, & in primis Catholici. Inhibuit & vetuit, inhibet & vetat sub pœna simili, Ne quis nummularius ex mensa sua Romam aureum au argenteam pecuniam ad bullas, provisiones, dispensationes aut alias expeditiones quascunque impetrandas referibat. Si quæ impetrata sint, judices vetat earum habere rationem. Constituit ut Marcellinus Landrianus, qui se prefati Gregorii Nuntium dicit, bullarum gerulus, apprehendatur, & captivus in carceres Palatii adducatur, ut istic causa ejus agatur & peragatur. Si vero capi & apprehendi non poteft, trinundino citetur, in loco tuto accessus, Suessonum urbi proximo. Iubet omnes urbium Praefectos, Capitaneos arcium & locorum munitorum, qua in Regis fide sunt, supradicto decreto subsidium & auxilium dare. Neque aliter Curia Catalaunensis, in eodem negotio d xxix. Augusti, ejusdem anni. clɔ Iɔ xcı. Curia ad provocationem a dicto Generalis Procuratore factam judicium reddens, & de absente secundum praesentem judicans, statuit ac pronunciat, quicquid contra defunctum Henricum III. felicissimae memoriae Regem, & hunc, qui Regni gubernacula nunc tenet, ejusque clientes, & ditioni atque imperio subjectos cives constitutum, tentatum, assumaque fuerit, id perperam, vane & falso constitutum, tentatum & actum: ideoque ab actore publico & Regio recte appellatum fuisse. Supradictas omnes Bullas, acta, excommunicationes, & fulminationes, ut brutas & irritas, odiosas & invisas, seditionis faces, impoflurarum plenas, atque adversus sacra decreta, Canonicas constitutiones, approbataque Concilia, nec non Gallicana Ecclesiae jura & privilegia conexta confregit, revocavit, antiquavit & confringit ctiamnum, revocat & antiquat. Sanxit, & sancit, ut, si quis ejusmodi Bullarum & actuum virtute excommunicati fuerint, hac poena solvantur: istaque Bulla & omnes inde profectae actiones, in publica hujusce urbis platea per supremam jurisdictionis ministrum, carnificem, concrementur. Edicit ut praedictus Landrianus, Nuntius vulgo habitus, qui clandestina via in hoc Regnum, nulla a Rege impetrata venia, irrepsit, manu in ipsum injecta comprehendatur; & in Regiam Catalauni oppidi custodiam tradatur, quo in eum ex legibus extra ordinem statuatur. Qui si nulla comprehendi ratione poterit, in trinundinum dies illi confuto more dicatur: ei vero, qui virum illum in Curia potestatem tradiderunt, decem aureorum milia persolvantur. &c. Declaravit ac declarat Cardinales, qui Romae agunt, itemque Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, aliosque Ecclesiasticos, qui Bullas ipsas & excommunicationes suscepserunt & consignarunt, quisque immanissimum, per quam abominandum, & detestabilissimum in Christianissimum & Catholicum in primis vita defunctam Regem perfidiosissime admissum parricidium comprobarunt, Sacerdotiorum, quibus in hoc Regno potiuntur, possessione exturbatos esse. Hæc describere nequidquam piguit, tum ob argumenti dignitatem & præstantiam; tum ob exemplum, quod hodie & Gallis, & aliis, æqualiter à Papæ Bulla nupera læsis, præbere possunt. Vin' & Venetorum exemplum? quando illos anno hujus seculi sexto, d. xvii. Aprilis excommunicarat P. Paulus v. haud multo post, die nimirum vi. May, ejusdem anni, Reipublicæ nomine dux Venetiarum Leonardus Donatus iniustam Bullam, Edicto alio ad Patriarchas, Episcopos &c. dominii Veneti scripsit, inter alia dicens: Præ"dictum Breve non modo ut injustum, indebitumque, verum etiam uti nullum, nulliusque roboris aut momenti Nobis habendum esse non dubitamus; Atque ita invalidum, irritum & fulminatum illegitime, & de facto, nulloque juris ordine servato, ut ea remedia adhibenda non duxerimus, quibus Majores nostri, & alii supremi Principes usi sunt cum Pontificibus, qui potestatis, à Deo sibi inædificationem traditæ, limites ac modos egressi fuerunt.&c. Quod secuti Iohannes Marsilius Neapolitanus, & Theol. Doctor apud Venetos; Paulus Venetus, ordinis Servorum; Fulgentius Manfredus, ordinis Observantium, adversus citationes & excommunicationes Romanas mox eodem anno, nimirum cIↄ Iↄ cvi singuli suas accuratas, doctas, cordatas responsiones dederunt, contra Cardinales Romanos, fidei scilicet generales Inquisitores. Vtq; similiter in hac causa irritæ per Papam, & abrogatæ pacis, quod plurimos & summos Christianismi Principes tangit læditque, dignum illis, dignum Papa Edictum aliquod adversarium condatur, pro asserenda pace, & Principum Christianorum inter se fœderibus, ego quidem auctor sum; nisi existiment omnes, haud tanti Papam faciendum esse, ut ejus garritum curare ultra debeant, & ejus Bullas insuper habendo sic optime evanescere: ut quibus applicare quoque debeas quod de Paparum legibus Doctores Papistici vulgo docent, Becanus, Theol. Scholasticæ part. II. Tract. IIII. cap. v. qu. VIII. Neque leges Pon-tific.
units.tr: Clement VII, and also to the cardinals and the princes of the Empire, in letters under his own name, defended his reputation and the Imperial majesty. In the following year he also wrote to the same Pope in his own hand, saying that if the Pope conducted himself as a good father, he himself would also prove to be a most humble son. Among the letters of princes collected by Hieronymus Ruscelli is also this one from the Duke of Alba, dated 1556, when he was besieging Rome, addressed to Pope Paul IV: Hitherto the Emperor and King Philip have concealed the grief and injuries they have suffered at Your Holiness's hands. From the beginning of your pontificate you have tried to oppress and persecute their subjects and to despoil them of their goods, and afterwards you have stirred up other princes against you, so that they might seize the kingdoms and dominions of the said Majesties. It is sufficient evidence that the peace concluded for the good of all Christendom displeases you, and that it is not enough for you that your kinsmen have been set apart by honest means, whom the said Majesties freely enrich with the goods of their own subjects, etc. The conclusion of the letter is this: I pray God to preserve him for as many years as shall be necessary for the good of Christendom. He does not say "many years", but as many as the public good shall require. In 1573 Maximilian II, by a sharp edict, rebuked the turbulent pamphlet of his court counsellor Georg Eder, which was aimed against the religious peace and was especially injurious to the Protestants. Indeed, the recent Edict of Peace forbids anyone to oppose it or to do anything to its prejudice, whether he belongs to the ecclesiastical or to the civil order. And on 26 June 1550 the Emperor again, more severely, proscribed all attempts, contraventions and disputations against the conclusion of the peace. What he will now decree against this Bull of the Pope, which rushes into these matters with open brow, and whether he will look upon it with calm eyes and allow both the peace and his own majesty to be exposed to contempt, we shall see. France ought to renew the examples of past times, when such Papal Bulls were issued. In 1401, on 26 July, the two Papal Bullists were brought out in public from the citadel of Lupara by the lictors, crowned with paper mitres, and then dragged through the streets of the city on a dung cart. And a few days earlier in the same month, the Papal libel was seen torn up in the presence of its couriers, by decree of the Parliament of Paris. Or again, Louis IX, Philip the Fair, and Charles V and VI set the Pragmatic Sanction against the Papal Bulls. To give some more recent example, which fits the present case not badly: when the monitory Bulls of Gregory XIV against King Henry IV had been brought into France, by which subjects and the chief men of the kingdom were ordered to desert Henry, who was excommunicated, and to take care not to receive him as King, the Parliament of Tours first, on 5 August 1591, dealt with those Bulls, their author, and the nuncio who carried them, in this way: The Court has decided that the letters shall be inscribed in the register of the cases to be pursued. Having been read, published and entered in the records, and upon hearing the King's Attorney General make this request, and having taken into account the other conclusions he has brought forward, it has declared and does declare the Monitory Bulls, given at Rome on 1 March 1590, null, abusive, seditious, deserving condemnation, full of impieties and impostures, and contrary to the sacred decrees, rights, immunities and liberties of the Gallican Church. It has decreed that the sealed copies bearing the seal of Marcellinus Landrianus, subscribed by Sestilianus Lampinetus, be torn up and burned by the chief executioner of justice, with a fire lit for that purpose before the doors of the Palace. It has forbidden and prohibited, under the charge and penalty of treason, that any prelate, parish priest, vicar, or other ecclesiastic publish them, and that anyone, of whatever rank, quality or condition, obey, keep or retain them. It has declared and does declare that Gregory, who calls himself the fourteenth Pope of that name, is an enemy of the peace and concord of the Catholic, Apostolic and Roman Church, of the King and the kingdom; that he adheres to the Spanish conspiracy, is a favourer of rebels, and is guilty of the most cruel and inhuman of all, and most detestable, parricide, committed against the person of King Henry III, of most happy memory, most Christian and above all Catholic. It has forbidden and does forbid, under a similar penalty, that any money-changer send from his bank to Rome gold or silver money to obtain Bulls, provisions, dispensations or any other expeditions whatsoever. If any have been obtained, it forbids the judges to take any account of them. It has ordered that Marcellinus Landrianus, who calls himself the nuncio of the said Gregory, the bearer of the Bulls, be seized and led as a prisoner into the prisons of the Palace, so that his case may be heard and concluded there. But if he cannot be taken and arrested, he shall be summoned on three market days, at a safe place of access, in the town of Soissons, near at hand. It orders all the governors of towns and the captains of citadels and fortified places that are in the King's allegiance to give aid and assistance to the above decree. In the same matter the Parliament of Châlons, on 29 August of the same year 1591, likewise did not act otherwise: rendering judgment upon the challenge made by the said Attorney General, and judging the absent man as if present, it has decided and pronounced that whatever has been decreed, attempted or undertaken against the late King Henry III, of most happy memory, and against the present holder of the reins of government, and against the citizens subject to his rule and empire and his clients, has been decreed, attempted and done wrongly, vainly and falsely; and therefore that it was rightly appealed against by the public and royal agent. It has broken, revoked, abolished and still breaks, revokes and abolishes all the aforesaid Bulls, acts, excommunications and fulminations, as void and null, hateful and odious, torches of sedition, full of impostures, and joined with the sacred decrees, canonical constitutions and approved Councils, as well as with the rights and privileges of the Gallican Church. It has decreed and does decree that if any have been excommunicated by virtue of such Bulls and acts, they shall be absolved by this penalty; and that this Bull and all actions proceeding from it shall be burned in the public square of this city by the chief minister of justice, the executioner. It orders that the aforesaid Landrianus, commonly regarded as a nuncio, who crept into this kingdom by a secret route without obtaining pardon from the King, be seized by the hand laid upon him, and be handed over to the royal custody of the town of Châlons, where a sentence shall be passed upon him according to the laws, outside the ordinary course. But if he cannot be taken in any way, he shall be summoned on three market days in the customary manner; and to those who handed that man over to the power of the Court, ten thousand gold crowns shall be paid, etc. The Parliament has declared and does declare that the Cardinals who reside at Rome, as well as the archbishops, bishops and other ecclesiastics who received and signed the Bulls and excommunications, have, by approving that most monstrous, most abominable and most detestable parricide, perfidiously committed against the Christian and above all Catholic King who has died, forfeited the possession of the ecclesiastical benefices they hold in this kingdom. I have not been ashamed to set out these things at length, both because of the dignity and excellence of the subject, and because of the example that they can today offer to France and to others who have been equally injured by the recent Papal Bull. Or do you want the example of the Venetians too? In the sixth year of this century, on 17 April, Pope Paul V excommunicated them; and not long afterwards, namely on 6 May of the same year, Leonardo Donato, Doge of Venice, in the name of the Republic, wrote by another edict to the patriarchs, bishops, etc. of the Venetian dominion, saying among other things: We do not doubt that the aforesaid Brief must be regarded by us not only as unjust and undue, but also as void, and of no force or weight; and so invalid, ineffective and fulminated illegitimately, and in fact, without any order of law being observed, that we have not thought fit to apply those remedies which our ancestors and other supreme princes used against Pontiffs who have passed the limits and bounds of the power given to them by God for building up. etc. Following them, Giovanni Marsili of Naples, Doctor of Theology among the Venetians; Paolo Sarpi of Venice, of the Servite order; and Fulgenzio Manfredi, of the Observant order, each gave, in the same year, namely 1606, their careful, learned and judicious replies against the Roman citations and excommunications, against the Roman cardinals who were, of course, the general inquisitors of the faith. And I, for my part, am of the opinion that in this matter, where a Papal act has been made void and peace annulled, which touches and injures very many of the greatest princes of Christendom, a counter-edict worthy of them and worthy of the Pope should be drawn up, to assert the peace and the covenants of the Christian princes among themselves; unless everyone thinks that the Pope is not to be regarded so highly that they ought to attend to his babbling any further, and that by disregarding his Bulls they will vanish most easily of all. To these one may apply also what the Papist doctors commonly teach about the laws of the Popes: Becanus, Scholastic Theology, part II, tract IV, chapter 5, question 8. "Nor do the laws of the Pontiff bind unless they are accepted by the subjects." Or also what Bellarmine says about the Popes themselves, in On the Roman Pontiff, book II, chapter 29: "Just as it is lawful to resist a Pontiff who attacks the body, so it is lawful to resist one who attacks souls or disturbs the commonwealth, and much more if…"

units.la: Vin' ... tificia obligant: nisi acceptentur à subditis. vel etiam quod de ipsis Papis Bellarminus lib. 11. de Rom. Pontif. cap. xxix. Sicut licet resistere Pontifici invadenti corpus, ita licet resistere invadenti animas, vel turbanti Remp. & multo magis si Ecclesiam destruere niteretur, licet, inquam, ei resistere, non faciendo quod jubet, & impediendo, ne exequatur voluntatem. Nec Suecia Regina, quae quantum inter sui sexus Regina, ita inter has ipsa eminet, haud ita (opinor) abire inultam sinet contumeliam, à Papa Nomini suo iniustam, quando negat sibi pacificendi potestatem, & ob haeresis criminationem indignâ clamat, cui pacis serventur & conditiones & commoda: imo quos magnus Parens sanguine suo peperit triumphos, & ipsa prudentia sua pacem, quin pro dignitate etiam tuitura sit nullus dubito, adversus eum, cujus authoritatem & saltum merito eversumante voluit Gustavus I. Rex, quam regnaret. Praeterquam quod ad vilipendium Regine hoc quoq; interpretor, in Bulla quod ejus nulla mentio, tantummodo Suecorum in genere, quum & Imperatoris, & Galliae Regis, atque Electoris Palatini exserta legantur nomina, ejusque ut praecipuae quoque partis nomen haud taceri oportuisset; nisi docendus à Suecis Papa sit Regium quod apud Suecos nomen est, & hoc si quod aliud Papis formidandum. Sed dicam plane quid hoc sit, quod Regem aut Reginam Sueciae, vel regnum non appellet Papa, quia nimirum pro illegitimo habent Papae, quod isti in Suecia regnant. Quod doceo ex libro, qui inscribitur: Provinciale omnium Ecclesiarum, quod ex Cancellaria Apostolica excerptum, & citatum Azorio, Instit. moral. part. ii. lib. xi. cap. v. ubi haec: Rex Suetiae. Suetia septentrionalis provincia est, cujus regnum jure pertinet ad Sigismundum catholicum regem, nunc in Polonia regnantem, Quae quomodo Succi à judicio Papali vindicaturi sint, equidem illis relinquo. Ecce habent illustre argumentum, inquo se jam pacis aeque, ac pridem belli arbitros ostendere possunt, & unum, qui superest, Papam pro merito exagitare, & constringere, ut belli olim causam, ita nunc & assiduo hostem pacis unicum & maximum. Haec illis, &
units.tr: Do the laws of the Popes bind? Only if they are accepted by their subjects. The same holds for what Bellarmine says of the Popes themselves, Book 11 of On the Roman Pontiff, chapter 29: Just as it is lawful to resist a Pontiff who attacks the body, so it is lawful to resist one who attacks souls or disturbs the commonwealth, and much more if he tries to destroy the Church. It is lawful, I say, to resist him by not doing what he orders and by preventing him from carrying out his will. Nor, I think, will the Queen of Sweden, who stands out among the queens of her sex as much as she does among them, allow the insult to her name to go unavenged. The Pope has wrongly denied her the power to make peace and, with an unworthy accusation of heresy, has cried out against her, though the terms and advantages of peace should be kept for her. I have no doubt that she will defend peace by her own prudence, and with dignity too, against the man whose authority and jurisdiction King Gustavus I rightly wished to overthrow before he reigned, that authority which the great Father won by his blood and his triumphs. I also read this as a slight to the Queen: in the Bull her name is never mentioned, only the Swedes in general, although the names of the Emperor, the King of France and the Elector Palatine are set out plainly. Her name, as that of the chief party, should not have been passed over in silence, unless the Pope needs to be taught by the Swedes what the royal title is among them, and this, if anything, is what Popes should fear. But I will say plainly why the Pope does not call the King or Queen of Sweden, or the kingdom, by those names. It is because he regards as illegitimate the rule of those who reign in Sweden. I show this from the book entitled Provinciale omnium Ecclesiarum, excerpted from the Apostolic Chancery and cited by Azor, Instit. moral. part. ii. lib. xi. cap. v., where the text reads: King of Sweden. Sweden is a northern province, whose kingdom rightly belongs to Sigismund, the Catholic king, now reigning in Poland. How the Swedes will vindicate themselves against this papal judgment I leave to them. Behold, they have an illustrious cause by which they can show themselves the arbiters of peace as they were once arbiters of war, and can call to account and constrain the one Pope who remains, as he deserves. As he was once the cause of war, so now he is the sole and greatest constant enemy of peace.

units.la: Principibus Christianis restat gloria, compescere hominem, qui Christianorum damnis inhiat semper & exitio. Succi autem imprimis hoc Papæ debent, videlicet pro censu, quem super omnes illos se habere, tributario scilicet Romanæ sedi isto quoque regno, Pontifices & Pontificum adulatores scribunt. Imo rependant Papæ, & cum egregio fœnore, quod census ei debent, quodq; meretur; quod erit, pro Bullâ Bella, ut dum, pacem non sert in aliis neque ulla gaudeat apud le Beatus qui prehendet, & dissipabit parvulos tuos ad petram. Psalm. cxxxvii.9. Et Apoc.xviii.6. Reddite ei sicut & ipsa reddidit vobis, & duplicate ei duplum secundum opera ejus. Hoc Suecus agat, hoc Gallus, hoc Imperator denique, & sic demum paci sua constabit firmitas, orbi Christiano, & ipsis libertas sua, & gloria, & salus.
units.tr: The glory remains for the Christian princes to restrain the man who constantly gapes for the ruin and destruction of Christians. The Swedes above all owe this to the Pope, for the tribute which the Pontiffs and their flatterers write that they hold over all those kingdoms, this one included, as tributary to the Roman see. Indeed let the Popes repay what they owe as tribute, and with excellent interest, and what they deserve: which, in return for the Bull, will be wars. So, while he does not endure peace in others and rejoices in no peace among them, Happy shall he be that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones. Psalm 137:9. And Apoc. xviii.6: Render unto her even as she rendered unto you, and double unto her the double according to her works. Let the Swede do this, let the Frenchman do this, let the Emperor finally do this, and so at last the firmness of their peace will stand for the Christian world, and their freedom, glory and safety for themselves.

units.la: ADDENDA.
units.tr: ADDENDA.
