In the same place, Michael Schiferer, On the Origin and Power of the Modern Electors, § 49 and following. The anonymous author, On the Translation of the Empire, chapter 6, in Goldast's Imperial Politics, vol. 9. Carpzov, on the German Lex Regia, chapter 2, sections 6 and 7.

units.la: Pag. 41. hoc quidem numero, non vero recte signata: lin.pen. Scioppius, in Consil. Reg. pag. 44. 45. multus est in titulo Catholici, Regi suo appropriando, & praeferendo alteri, qui Regum Galliae est, Christianissimi: cui praeter Theodosium Berenicum, in Tuba Pacis, pag. 47. contra Scioppii Classicum sacrum; opponendae Vindiciae Gallicae, adversus Alexandrum Patricium §. vi. pag. 61. & deinceps, atque p. 126. quibus primum Clodovcum a Remigio Rhemensi episcopo, illo titulo Christianissimi insignitum; ut & alios Galliae Reges ab alio titulo Catholico, asserit. Et utrumque titulum Francis Regibus a Pontificia sede tributum, scribit etiam Renatus Choppinus, lib. ii. de sacra polit. tit. 3. p. 287. Distinguo inter titulorum illorum adscriptionem, quando aliquibus htc vel ille tribuitur; & appropriationem, ubi alicui proprius quasi factus discrimen & distinctionem inducit. A primo tempore, quo vel Galliae Rex Christianissimus audiit, vel Hispanus Catholicus, fume in Recaredo, uti illud in Clodoveo, distinctione hos titulos scisse nulli facile persuaseris: sed nec Pontificibus Romanis id tribuero, quod titulorum haec,
units.tr: Page 41. This number is correctly given here, though not properly marked, in the last line. Scioppius, in his Royal Counsel, pages 44–45, labours at length to appropriate the title of Catholic to his own king and to prefer him to another, who belongs to the kings of France, the Most Christian. Against him should be set Theodore Berenicus, in The Trumpet of Peace, page 47, against Scioppius's Sacred Trumpet Call; and The Gallic Vindications, against Alexander Patricius, § 6, page 61 and following, and p. 126, where he asserts that Clovis was first decorated with the title Most Christian by Remigius, bishop of Reims, and that other kings of France received the other title, Catholic. Renatus Choppinus, book 2, On Sacred Polity, title 3, p. 287, also writes that both titles were granted to the Frankish kings by the Apostolic See. I distinguish between the ascription of those titles, when this or that one is given to some person, and their appropriation, when a title becomes, as it were, peculiar to someone and introduces a difference and distinction. From the earliest time, when the King of France was first heard as Most Christian, or the Spanish king as Catholic (assume it in Reccared, as it was in Clovis), you could hardly persuade anyone that these titles were divided by distinction. But nor do I credit the Roman pontiffs with the fact that the present approval or distinction of these titles comes from them. I think it came about rather through use and long custom, and through the kings themselves, or through their judgement and zeal, than through the popes, whom we know to have attributed to themselves, from ancient ambition, the founding and authority of almost all things whatsoever. Finally I add that in the book, Provincial Title of All Churches, excerpted from the Apostolic Chancery, which Azorius mentions, the King of France is placed first at the beginning of the first chapter, then the King of León and Castile.

units.la: que quæ nunc obtinet approbatio vel distinctio ab illis veniat; sed usu & longa consuetudine, & per ipsos magis Reges, vel per eorum arbitrium & studium illud accidisse reor, quam per Papas, quos ex antiqua ambitione sibi scimus attribuere perperam rerum quarumcunque fere institutionem, & auctoritatem.
units.tr: Translate: the approval or distinction of these titles that now prevails comes from those sources; but I think it happened through use and long custom, and through the kings themselves rather than through the popes, whom we know from ancient ambition to have wrongly claimed for themselves the establishment and authority of almost all things whatsoever.

units.la: Pag.42. post lin. 27. In Concilio Tridentino vehementer illa inter Gallos, & Hispanos, de præcedentia agitabatur contentio: non solum illis primum à Legato Imperatoris locum petentibus, sed & nolentibus, ut Orator Hispani Regis alio quo singulari ab illis loco sederet, sed ordine post eos: aliter se protestari, non adversum Legatos, aut Philippum Regem, aut Concilium, aut Ecclesiam Romanam; sed adversus ipsum Papam Pium IV. non pro legitimo illum habentes Papa, & provocare se ad Concilium aliud liberum, in Gallia cogendum. Ubi illud facetum accidit, quod quando adversus Gallici Oratoris expostulationem diceretur, cum scommate: Gallus cantat. hic concinnè protinus respondit: Utinam isto gallicinio Petrus ad resipiscentiam & fletum excitaretur! Illaque causa postmodum Gallis fuit præter alias, quo minus Concilium Tridentinum in regno & Ecclesiis Gallicanis, vel ejus publicatio admissa fuerit. Sed præterquam quod iterum illa disputatio inter utriusque Regni Legatos erupit a. MDXCVIII in conventu Vervinensi, prima istius occasio data fuit Venetiis a. MDLVII. postquam Carolus V. se abdicarat regnis suis, & Imperio, eaque sic diviserat, ut non idem esset Hispaniæ Rex & Imperator; atq; tum apud Venetos Legatus Vargas, qui suerat Caroli antea, jam Philippi Regis, tacite conabatur quasi eandem, quam prius, personam ageret, Legato Gallico se præferre: quo hic ferendum non duxit, quia non Imperatori nunc, ut antea, sed Hispaniæ Regi cedere videretur: atque uti injustum ille judicabat, ita pro se sententiam Senatus super ea re anno sequente MDLVIII. obtinuit. Atque utcumque Imperatori quidem locum cedere Gallus haud recuculet, attamen non domui ideo Austriacæ, quia dignitas Imperialis electiva, hoc se facere, vel ei hoc deberi existimat: & an Regi Romanorum, disputatum etiam in Concilio Tridentino ab Antonio Quetta fuisse, & ab aliis examinari, supra diximus. Certe ad portam Ottomannicam, à tempore Henrici IV Galliarum Regis, sibi etiam supra Legatum Imp. Rudolphi datam præcedentiam scripsit in Historiâ Legationis suæ Dominus de Breves. Disputat Azorius, Lorcitanus, Iesuita Institut. Moral. Tom. II. lib. XI. cap. v. de Regum præcedentia, & postquam ex Chassanæo argumenta attulisset pro Rege Francorum, concludit: si ordo ex antiquitate temporis existit, ac pendet, non est dubium, quin Rex Francorum sit omnium primus. Quem Scioppio objicio, qui Consil. Regio pag. 43. contrarium temerè asserit, & Reges Hispaniæ multo prius Christianos fuisse, quam Franciæ Reges, dicit. Postremo addo, quod in libro, tit. Provinciale omnium Ecclesiarum, ex Cancellaria Apostolica excerpto, cujus Azorius meminit, in initio capitis primo loco ponitur Rex Francorum, inde Rex Legionis, & Castellæ.
units.tr: Page 42, after line 27. At the Council of Trent there was a vehement dispute between the French and the Spanish over precedence. The French first demanded the place of the Emperor's legate, and the Spanish, unwilling to yield, asked that the envoy of the Spanish king sit not in some separate place but after them in order. Each party protested that its quarrel was not with the legates, nor with King Philip, nor with the Council, nor with the Roman Church, but with Pope Pius IV himself, whom they did not regard as a lawful pope, and they appealed to another free council to be held in France. There a witty thing happened. When the French envoy's complaint was answered with a sneer, "The Gaul crows!", he promptly replied neatly: "Would that by this crowing Peter might be roused to repentance and tears!" That matter afterwards gave the French, among other reasons, cause not to admit the Council of Trent in the kingdom and French churches, or its publication. But apart from the fact that this dispute broke out again between the legates of the two kingdoms in 1598 at the Vervins meeting, its first occasion was given at Venice in 1557, after Charles V had abdicated his kingdoms and the Empire and divided them so that the King of Spain was no longer the Emperor. Then at Venice the legate Vargas, who had formerly been Charles's, now the envoy of King Philip, tacitly tried to play the same role as before and to place himself above the French legate. The Frenchman did not think this should be endured, since precedence would now seem to yield not to the Emperor, as before, but to the King of Spain. As he judged it unjust, so in the following year, 1558, the Senate decided the matter in his favour. And however much the Frenchman does not hesitate to yield place to the Emperor, he does not for that reason yield it to the house of Austria, since he thinks the imperial dignity is elective and that this is not owed to it. We have said above that whether it is owed to the King of the Romans was also debated at the Council of Trent by Antonio Quetta and examined by others. Certainly, from the time of Henry IV, King of France, the Lord de Brèves wrote in the history of his embassy that precedence was granted to him at the Ottoman Porte even above the legate of Emperor Rudolph. Azorius, the Lusitanian Jesuit, in his Moral Institutes, vol. II, book XI, chapter 5, discusses the precedence of kings, and after bringing arguments from Chassanée for the King of the Franks, concludes: "If order arises from and depends on antiquity of time, there is no doubt that the King of the Franks is first of all." I object this to Scioppius, who in his Royal Counsel, page 43, rashly asserts the contrary and says that the kings of Spain were Christians much earlier than the kings of France. Finally I add that in the book Provincial Title of All Churches, excerpted from the Apostolic Chancery, of which Azorius speaks, the King of France is placed first at the beginning of the first chapter, then the King of León and Castile.

units.tr: Page 57, line 8. See the Tax of the Bishops of France, which is extant in volume XIV of the Treatises on Law.

units.la: Pag. 61. lin. 20. Quæ de Wiclephi, & Hussi sententia à me adducta, non huc solum spectant, quod ab Ecclesiasticis abutentibus auferendas docent opes, sed vel imprimis quod nolint ideo ablatas, promiscuè quo quis velit impendi; verum in usus Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Page 61, line 20. What I have adduced from the opinions of Wycliffe and Hus does not bear only on this, that they teach that wealth must be taken away from abusive churchmen; above all it bears on the fact that they do not want the wealth, once taken away, to be spent indiscriminately on whatever anyone pleases, but for the uses of the Church.

units.la: Pag. 59. lin. 10. Certe sub Papatu, bona etiam donata Ecclesiæ fuisse purè, id est, non ad Papalem superstitionem, sed Ecclesiæ ad Christi ædificationem, & usum, vel pauperibus &c. &c. nemo negare potest, qui vel Ecclesiæ statum, vel diplomata, & Doctorum hac super re testimonia, quæ nos suo loco adserimus, inspexerit. Neque necesse est, ut nos ostendamus, data illa fuisse Ecclesiæ à Papali fermento defæcatæ, quando nondum secessionem à Papatu, vel non ita generalem fecerat Christi Ecclesia, quam tamen etiam sub Papatu fuisse nemo Orthodoxus negat. Sufficit, non ita ab omnibus Papatum agnitum, acceptum, professumque suisse, vel non æque, quin puro animo etiam donaria sua Christo, Ecclesiæ, pauperibus (utut alii impurius, id est, magis superstitioso animo & fine) illa attulerint. Cæterum Papalem Ecclesiam, ut talem (sub qua alios probos latuisse diffiteri non possumus), sive ut Calvinus loquitur, totam illam Romanensis Ecclesiæ congeriem, ex imposturis, & furtis &c. conflatam esse, quis est qui nesciat? at vero ideo non præter illam fuisse quoque & alios melioris notæ homines, vel non data etiam sub Papatu bona, quæ verè Ecclesiastica jure dixeris, non Calvinus unquam negavit, qui quantum etiam pro bonis illis Ecclesiis, cui data in usus Ecclesiasticos, vindicandis clamaverit, ipsum suo loco testantem audimus. Hoc primum quaeritur, inquit Idem ad Bullam P. Pauli III. in quem usum destinata sint Ecclesia bona. Sic & Ecclesiæ bona hic agnoscit, & de usu laborat solum, ut in eum impendantur, in quem data olim fuerint, usum videlicet Ecclesiæ. Neque aliter nos volumus, verbo ut omnia comprehendam, quam ut diplomata Ecclesiasticarum donationum introspiciantur, atque ex illis de hac tota re definiatur, quibus solis stare paratus sum, aut cadere. Atque ne mirum tibi videatur (alloquor Auctorem Scripti nuperi, Dissertat. de Bonis vulgo Ecclesiast.) sub Papatu fuisse adeo etiam liberos à Papatu nonnullos, in consignandis suis bonis Ecclesiæ Christi, vel pauperibus; exemplum dabo quod magis adhuc mirum tibi videatur, in maxima Papatus dominatione, quum Monachales certatim erigerentur ordines, etiam tum in Diplomatis nunquam haud ullam fieri Missæ tamen mentionem, quam vis de canticis & lectionibus Ecclesiasticis quædam præciperent. Tumultuaberis tu, quando dicitur, donaria quædam sub Papatu fuisse simpliciter Ecclesiastica, ubi hæc audis de tabulis erectorum Monasteriorum, ordinumque Monachalium, & velis à nobis credi vix factam olim donationem ; quæ non Missatica superstitione laboraret? & tamen id quod dico, apud Helvetios sic se deprehendisse auctor est Zuinglius, cujus verba, ne in me temere incurras, hic tibi subjicio. Sic ille Operum Tom. 1. in Exegesi Eucharistici negotii, ad M. Lutherum, pag. 333. Instrumenta habet Collegium nostrum Tigurinum annos nata plus septingentos, in quibus nulla missa fit mentio. Ordinis Benedictini ac Bernhardini monachi passim inter Helveticos sic sunt instituti, ut corporis domini aut missæ nulla fiat mentio in Diplomatis eorum: etiamsi quidam intra trecentos annos instituti sunt. Atque hæc omnia similiaque si perpetuo rejicitis, vera tamen sunt, & potiora vestris omnibus. Deinde iterum, in Sermone primo Bernæ habito, pag. 533. Accedunt his infinita alia conjectura & signa, quæ nostris in religionibus palam idem illud docere possunt. Tale enim quiddam est, quod omnia instrumenta vel fundatoria collegiorum aut monasteriorum tabula vetustiores, quæ vel ante trecentos duntaxat annos descripta sunt, nullam omnino Missarum mentionem faciunt, etiamsi de canticis & lectionibus ecclesiasticis quædam illis continentur.
units.tr: Page 59, line 10. Certainly under the Papacy goods given to the Church were given purely, that is, not for papal superstition but for the building up of the Church in Christ and for its use, or for the poor, and so on. No one can deny this who has examined the state of the Church, the charters, and the testimonies of the doctors on this matter, which we shall set forth in their proper place. Nor is it necessary for us to show that those gifts were made to a Church already purged of the papal leaven, since the Church of Christ had not yet made its secession from the Papacy, or not so general a one, though no orthodox person denies that it was under the Papacy. It is enough that the Papacy was not acknowledged, accepted and professed by all in the same way or to the same degree, so that people could not with a pure heart bring their gifts to Christ, to the Church, and to the poor (however others brought them more impurely, that is, with a more superstitious mind and purpose). Moreover, who does not know that the papal Church as such (under which we cannot deny that other good people lay hidden), or, as Calvin puts it, that whole heap of the Roman Church, was put together from impostures, thefts and so on? But that there were also other men of better repute outside it, and that goods given even under the Papacy, which you could rightly call truly ecclesiastical by law, Calvin never denied. As far as he cried out for the vindication of those goods given to churches for ecclesiastical uses, we hear him bearing witness to this in his own place. "This is the first question," says the same man, against the bull of Pope Paul III, "to what use the goods of the Church were destined." So here he acknowledges the goods of the Church, and labours only over their use, that they be spent on the use for which they were once given, namely the use of the Church. Nor, to sum it up in a word, do we wish anything else than that the charters of ecclesiastical donations be examined, and that the whole matter be decided from them; to these alone I am ready to stand or fall. And lest it seem strange to you (I address the author of the recent writing, Dissertation on Goods Commonly Called Ecclesiastical) that under the Papacy some people were quite free of the Papacy in assigning their goods to Christ's Church or to the poor, I will give an example that will seem even stranger to you. In the greatest dominance of the Papacy, when monastic orders were being set up eagerly, the charters never make any mention of the Mass, although they prescribe certain things about canticles and ecclesiastical readings. You will be astonished when it is said that certain donations under the Papacy were simply ecclesiastical, when you hear this about the deeds of monasteries and monastic orders that were founded, and would have us believe that a donation was scarcely ever made which was not burdened by Mass superstition? Yet what I say, Zwingli reports that he found to be so among the Swiss. Lest you rashly attack me, I set down his words here for you. Thus he, in vol. I of his works, in his Exegesis of the Eucharistic Affair, addressed to M. Luther, p. 333: "Our Zurich college has documents more than seven hundred years old, in which there is no mention of the Mass. The monks of the Benedictine and Bernardine orders, scattered among the Swiss, were founded in such a way that no mention of the Lord's body or of the Mass is made in their charters, even though some of them were founded within three hundred years. If you reject all these and similar things always, they are nonetheless true and weightier than all your arguments." Then again, in the first sermon preached at Berne, p. 533: "Countless other conjectures and signs add to these, which can plainly show the same thing in our religion. For it is a fact that all the founding documents of colleges or monasteries, the older tablets, which were written even only three hundred years ago, make no mention of Masses at all, even though they contain certain things about canticles and ecclesiastical readings."

units.la: Pag. 209. lin. 27. Iohannes Nordermannus, de Iure Principatus ad Conclus. 90. Res enim Ecclesiarum, Christi „sunt patrimonium c. cum ex eo, de Eleet. 6. Et quæ ad pias „causas sunt collatæ, non debent alio transferri, l. si quis, C. de „Episc. & Cler. l. illud l. sancimus. ut inter divinum. C. de S. Eccles. „arg. Matt. h. 26. 11. c. mos est, c. aurum, 12. q. 2. c. præsulum, 16. „q. 3. Latt. c. 7. de offic. Dei. Summum est peccatum, si ea quæ „semel Deo sunt consecrata, in usu transferantur profanum: „erant Ecclesiæ seminaria, jam vero ad illicitos usus, & ejus „bona à Monachis malè utentibus transferuntur ad malè fe„riatos milites, qui lusu, luxuria, libidine, & omnis generis „voluptatibus illa consumunt. Piissimi nostri majores illa ad bo,,bonum usum voluerunt concessa, non vero luxuriam & abusum. Eratque finis illorum gloria Dei, & proximi dilectio, quę non in abusu, sed vero consistunt usu. Cessante itgitur fine (qui omnium actionum est terminus, & ad perfectionem rei requitur) & dispositionis causa, cessabit quoque & dispositio, l. 1. & 2. C. de donat. quae fuc. mod. l. ult. C. de revocand. donat. c. verum, in fi. extr. de condit. appof. & ibi. gloff. Molin. art. 83. de Trid. Concil. Recte igitur fit & ad fundatorum intentionem propius accedit, si ad alias pias causas, puta redemptionem captivorum, dotes filiarum pauperum, sustentationem egenorum, reparationes Ecclesiarum, & similia conferantur. Sic fortissimus Germaniae Heros, Philippus, Hassiae Landgravius, fugatis otiosis ac libidini deditis Monachis, eorum ditissima Monasteria mutavit in viduarum, orphanorum variis modis afflictorum, mente captorum & furiosorum utriusque sexus receptacula, in quibus non solum aluntur & curantur, sed ad omnem etiam pietatem instituuntur. Reliqua vero in Scholas, & Ecclesiae prioris ministros contulit. Sic Darius non solum abstulit cibum Baalitis, cum animadverteret abusum & dolum eorum: sed etiam altaria & delubra destruxit, & perfidos necidedit. c. 14. Daniel. Rejicimus igitur decretum Tridentini Concilii, quod potestatem concedit Clericis partem redituum Xenedochiorum capere, & quoque de decimis Laicorum. Molin. artic. 43. & 82. de Trid. Concil. Est in Nucleo Discursuum, seu Disputationum juris publici Hampelii. Similiter Petrus Syringius, Differt. de Pace religionis §. 38. ibidem pag. 118. Justus Mejerus, I. C. Argentinensis, in Iuris publici Quaestione: sintne Protestantes jure Caesareo haeretici, & ultimo supplicio afficiendi? contra Classicum Scioppii, ita loquitur.
units.tr: Page 209, line 27. John Nordermann, On the Right of Principality, Conclusion 90. For the property of the Churches is "the patrimony of Christ" (c. cum ex eo, de Electione 6). And what has been conferred for pious causes ought not to be transferred elsewhere (l. si quis, C. de Episcopis et Clericis; l. illud; l. sancimus; ut inter divinum, C. de Sacrosanctis Ecclesiis; argument from Matt. 26. 11; c. mos est; c. aurum, 12 q. 2; c. praesulum, 16 q. 3; Lat. c. 7, de officio Dei). It is the greatest sin when things once consecrated to God are turned to profane use. They were the seminaries of the Church, but now they are put to unlawful uses, and its goods are transferred by misusing monks to ill-behaved soldiers, who squander them on gambling, luxury, lust and every kind of pleasure. Our most pious forefathers wished these things to be granted for good use, not for luxury and abuse. Their end was the glory of God and love of neighbour, which consist not in abuse but in true use. Therefore, when the end ceases (which is the limit of all actions and is required for the perfection of a thing), and with it the cause of the disposition, the disposition too will cease (l. 1. & 2. C. de donat. quae sub modo; l. ult. C. de revocand. donat.; c. verum, in fi. extr. de condit. appos. and the gloss there; Molin. art. 83. de Trid. Concil.). It is therefore right, and comes closer to the founders' intention, if the goods are conferred on other pious causes, such as the redemption of captives, dowries for poor daughters, the support of the needy, the repair of churches, and similar things. Thus the most valiant hero of Germany, Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, having put to flight the idle monks given over to lust, changed their very rich monasteries into refuges for widows, for orphans afflicted in various ways, and for the mentally captive and insane of both sexes, where they are not only fed and cared for but also taught all piety. The rest he gave to schools and to the ministers of the earlier Church. So Darius not only took away food from the Baalites when he saw their abuse and deceit, but also destroyed their altars and shrines and put the faithless men to death (c. 14. Daniel.). We therefore reject the decree of the Council of Trent, which grants clergy the power to take a part of the revenues of hospitals, and likewise of the tithes of laymen (Molin. artic. 43. & 82. de Trid. Concil.). It is in the Nucleus of Discourses, or Disputations on Public Law, of Hampelius. Similarly Peter Syringius, Dissertation on the Peace of Religion §. 38., and at p. 118 of the same. Justus Meierus, jurist of Strasbourg, in his question of public law, whether Protestants are heretics under Imperial law and to be punished with the ultimate penalty, speaks against the Classicum of Scioppius thus:

units.la: ,,Pag. 77. Quid, quod & hęc ultro sese ipsis offerant, quamvis a nemine subjiciantur: quod ea quae Praesules & Clerici per Imperium possident regna, territoria, latifundia, si quidem honori Numinis divini cultuique religioso primitus sint olim consecrata: jam ului suo verεque pietati sint reducenda, vel si ex superstitione & errore superiorum se,,seculorum sint Papisticæ impietatis vanitati dedicata vin,,dicanda & liberanda, & expurganda, sint ab omni impie,,tate Papistica, veroque Christianorum cultui,& orbis Chri,,stiani necessitatibus adserenda. & quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: "Page 77. Moreover, these things offer themselves of their own accord, though no one puts them forward: that the lordships, territories and great estates which the prelates and clergy hold within the Empire, if they were originally consecrated to the honour of the divine Majesty and to religious worship, should now be brought back to their proper and true piety; or, if they have been dedicated by superstition and error of past ages to the vanity of Papistical impiety, should be claimed, freed, and purged, and cleansed of all Papistical impiety, and reserved for the true worship of the Christians and for the needs of the Christian world. And what follows."

units.la: Pag.166. lin.19. Duplicem fere adhibuerunt in suis Testamentis piis, quo ea observarentur, adversus profanatores comminationem, iræ divinæ primum, & pœnarum infernalium;tum corporalem,& tantæ ac abstulissent,vel majoris mul&æ persolutionem Fisco. In Donatione Cancronis Comitis, in pago Rhenensi a.MCCCLXXIV. Si quis vero (quod futurum esse minime credimus) si nos ipsi aut ullus de hæredibus nostris,seu qualibet ulla extranea opposita persona contra hanc donationem à nobis factam venire tentaverit, aut eam infringere vel immutare voluerit, cavcat ne iram Dei omnipotentis acquirat, & insuper inferat una cum socio fisco auri libras XII, argenti V. multam sustineat,& quod repetit evindicare non valeat, sed præsens donatio ista omni tempore firma & inviolabilis permaneat, stipulatione, subnixa. Alias, sin minus bene testamenta illorum pia servarentur, instituebant hæredes suos ad bona reposcenda. In Donatione Antridi ComitisPalatini,a.CIↃCCCLXII. Quod si factum fuerit,hæredes mei illud inde abstrahere licentiam habeant, atque inter se dispertiri. Apud Marquardum Frehcrum, in Originibus Palatinis,in Utrique partis appendice;ubi varia ejusmodi monumenta.
units.tr: Page 166, line 19. In their pious testaments they used almost a twofold means to secure that these were observed against profaners: first a threat of the wrath of God and of infernal punishments; then a bodily penalty, namely the payment of a fine to the treasury, of as much as they had taken away, or of a greater sum. In the donation of Count Cancro, in the Rhine district, in 1374: But if anyone (which we do not believe will happen) should attempt, whether we ourselves or any of our heirs or any outside person, to come against this donation made by us, or to break or alter it, let him take care lest he incur the wrath of Almighty God, and moreover let him pay, together with the joint treasury, twelve pounds of gold and five of silver as a fine, and let him not be able to recover what he seeks to claim; but let this present donation remain firm and inviolable at all times, supported by a stipulation. Otherwise, if their pious testaments were not well kept, they appointed their heirs to reclaim the goods. In the donation of Count Palatine Antridus, in 1362: But if this should be done, let my heirs have the right to take it away from there and to divide it among themselves. In Marquard Freher, Origines Palatinae, in the appendix to the Utrique partis, where there are various monuments of this kind.

units.la: Pag.196.lin.25. Agnoscit hoc ipse Cardinalis Bentivoglius, in Relatione delle Provincie Vnite di Fiandra lib. III.cap. III. ubi hæc ejus verba diligenter noto, & quia intelle&u facilia, suo sermone; loquitur de Papistis inHollandia: Ma i Cattolici viveno d'esercitio tutto rubbato in materia di religione, e restano molmolto abbatuti similmente, nelle altre cose, e non tanto per effer Catto-lici, quanto par effer tenuti ò ben disposti, o non così male affetti verso gli Spangnoli, come sono gli heretici da quelle parti.
units.tr: Page 196, line 25. Cardinal Bentivoglio himself acknowledges this, in his Relatione delle Provincie Unite di Fiandra, book III, chapter III. I note his words here carefully, since they are easy to understand in his own language. He speaks of the Papists in Holland: But the Catholics live in an exercise entirely beaten down in matters of religion, and they are likewise very much cast down in other things, and not so much for being Catholics as for being thought well disposed, or not so ill-affected towards the Spaniards, as the heretics in those parts are.

units.la: Ejusdem Scioppii liber, Ecclesiasticus, authoritati Serenissimi Domini Iacobi magnæ Britanniæ Regis oppositus, ubi non hunc solum Regem, sed & alios indigne & improbe tractat, Regem quoque Galliæ Henricum IV. cui adaptat cap. III. illud Psalmistæ: ecce homo qui non posuit Deum adiutorem suum, Parisiis a. MDCXI. condemnatus publice & combustus fuit.
units.tr: The same Scioppius's book, Ecclesiasticus, set against the authority of the Most Serene Lord James, King of Great Britain, in which he treats not only this king but others unworthily and wickedly, and also King Henry IV of France, to whom in chapter III he applies the words of the Psalmist, "Behold the man who did not make God his helper". It was condemned and publicly burned at Paris in 1611.
